cards.title: KRW formula-size conjecture with constant loss
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(\alpha>0\) such that for every pair of positive integers \(n,m\) and every pair of nonconstant total Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), \(g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\),
\[\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(g\circ f)\ge\alpha \operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(g)\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)?\]
Here \((g\circ f)(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})=g(f(x^{(1)}),\ldots,f(x^{(m)}))\) on \(m\) disjoint \(n\)-bit blocks, and \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size. The constant is chosen before all dimensions and functions.

This card retains the constant-factor formula-size version displayed as Conjecture 5.13 in the source book. It is stronger than versions permitting a growing multiplicative loss. The original KRW paper formulates a depth-composition question; the card does not identify that question, weakened quantitative versions, and the displayed constant-loss formula statement as equivalent.
cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(r\), a total Boolean function is \(h:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\). Nonconstant means that it takes both values, not that it depends on every input. Use [De Morgan formula leaf size](definitions.html#formula-size), denoted \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(h)\). Formulas are trees of binary AND/OR and unary NOT, with no shared internal values, and must agree with \(h\) on every input. This is a positive finite minimum for a nonconstant function. There is no randomness, promise, threshold gate or unbounded fan-in.

The composed function has exactly \(mn\) designated coordinates \(x^{(j)}_i\), with \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Block coordinates are distinct and unconstrained. The same inner function \(f\) is applied to every block, and its outputs, in block order, become the inputs of \(g\). The composition symbol here means this block operation, not ordinary composition of two maps with the same domain. Both functions and their composition may be specified by arbitrary finite truth tables, and no uniformity, polynomial-time evaluability, or monotonicity is assumed.

Since both functions are nonconstant, every Boolean vector supplied to \(g\) can be realized by some collection of blocks, and the composition is nonconstant. The usual substitution bound gives \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(g\circ f)\le \operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(g)\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\). The question is whether the ratio to that upper bound is bounded away from zero uniformly over all functions and dimensions. Equivalently, is the infimum of these positive ratios strictly positive? This infimum need not be attained. Restricting \(0<\alpha\le1\) is equivalent.

The negation says that for every positive \(\alpha\), some pair and dimensions have ratio smaller than \(\alpha\). Thus a single saving relative to exact multiplication, or even failure of one proposed constant, is insufficient to refute the claim. Allowing constant functions with the convention \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(h)=0\) would add only trivial inequalities; their exclusion makes the ratio formulation well-defined. Minimum depth, which counts gates along a longest path, is a different measure from the number of leaves.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the constant-loss formula-size statement. A positive answer must establish one strictly positive factor for every permitted pair and dimensions. A negative answer must establish ratios arbitrarily close to zero, not merely a finite violation of equality or an unbounded additive saving in formula depth. Bounds for almost all functions, for special inner functions, for monotone formulas, or for a stronger communication search task do not alone prove the all-function claim. A composition inequality with a loss depending on either dimension, even polylogarithmically, is a weaker result unless upgraded to the fixed constant required here.
cards.why: A formula for a composition can substitute an inner computation wherever an outer input is used, multiplying the leaf counts. A universal matching lower bound would show that alternative Boolean factorizations cannot save more than a constant factor on arbitrary block compositions. This is a strong structural statement about formulas, closely connected to the source’s superpolynomial formula lower-bound question.

cards.context:
The book displays an absolute multiplicative constant in Conjecture 5.13. Its accompanying footnote also permits investigation of weaker losses and typical-function variants. The title and acceptance criterion identify which of those possibilities this record actually asks for.

The 1995 paper’s Open Question 4.1 asks about depth under composition and records examples with a growing additive loss in that measure. Those depth examples are not, by themselves, counterexamples to a constant-factor statement about minimum formula leaf count. The original paper and the later size formulation must be distinguished.

The 2023 paper explicitly distinguishes the original depth conjecture from the formula-size variant. Its Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 8.2 prove composition bounds involving a separate inner-function complexity measure and dimension-dependent losses. Those theorems give important restricted comparisons without supplying the universal constant asserted in this card.

The 2025 STACS result concerns strong composition of communication relations: in addition to finding a differing input bit, the answer must lie in a block where the two inner-function outputs differ. That added requirement makes a different search task. The paper explicitly says its lower bounds do not directly translate into ordinary formula-depth lower bounds, and they also do not establish the present size inequality.

cards.title: Majority outside constant-depth modular circuits
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{MAJ}\notin\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)? Precisely, for every fixed modulus \(m\geq2\), depth bound \(d\geq1\), constants \(C\geq1\), \(k\geq1\), and \(N\geq1\), is there an input length \(n\geq N\) for which no depth-at-most-\(d\) circuit over AND, OR, NOT and \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\), with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates, computes \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}\) exactly?
cards.definitions: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}(x)=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\geq\lceil n/2\rceil\). An ACC circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with one output, unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and constants. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\) gate outputs one precisely when the sum of its Boolean inputs is divisible by \(m\). Depth is the maximum number of noninput gates on an input-output path, including NOT gates. Size is the number of noninput gates; counting wires instead gives the same polynomial-size class. The modulus, depth and polynomial-size constants are fixed for the whole family and cannot depend on \(n\). Circuits may be chosen separately for every length, without any construction algorithm, uniformity or bound on fan-out. The class \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) is the union of these polynomial-size, constant-depth families over all fixed moduli. Allowing a fixed finite collection of moduli is equivalent, by using their common multiple with a constant-size gate substitution. All assignments must be computed correctly; no probability of error is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal lower-bound statement, or refute it by proving the existence of fixed \(m,d,C,k\) and circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\) computing majority for every input length. Refuting one fixed size exponent is insufficient for a positive answer. Results for a prime modulus, a restricted wiring symmetry, uniform circuits alone or a different hard function do not meet the complete criterion.
cards.why: Majority is a basic threshold operation. Showing that constant-depth modular circuits cannot compute it would separate ordinary threshold counting from the full fixed-modulus ACC⁰ model on a simple explicit function.

cards.title: Berman–Hartmanis conjecture
cards.formal: For every pair of NP-complete languages \(A,B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), is there a bijection \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that both \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) are computable in deterministic polynomial time and \(x\in A\iff f(x)\in B\) for every binary string \(x\)?
cards.definitions: Take [NP](definitions.html#p-np) and completeness under [deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions](definitions.html#reductions). Membership in \(A\) and \(B\) is defined on all binary strings. The forward and inverse algorithms can depend on the pair \(A,B\). Each runs in polynomial time in its own input length, and the bijection may change lengths. The assertion is unconditional.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pair of polynomial-time many-one NP-complete languages is polynomial-time isomorphic, or prove that some pair has no bijection with both directions computable in polynomial time. The statement is unconditional: \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is not an added hypothesis.
cards.why: A fundamental test of what NP-completeness means beyond mutual reducibility: does it impose one efficiently reversible structure on all complete decision problems? It links padding, cryptographic inversion, uniformity and the limitations of relativizing methods.

cards.context:
NP-completeness normally identifies problems by their ability to simulate one another. A reduction may map many distinct instances to the same target instance, leave most target strings unused, and erase information that would be needed to reconstruct its input. The isomorphism conjecture asks for a much more rigid relationship: an efficiently reversible relabelling of the entire instance space. Its claim includes every artificially constructed NP-complete language, not only the familiar examples used in applications.

The distinction is visible in the quantifiers. Choosing one clever reduction from SAT to another problem and discovering that it is many-to-one says nothing decisive about whether some other reduction could be a bijection. Conversely, an abstract bijection between two infinite sets is not enough: it might take exponential time to compute or invert. The conjecture requires both computations to be efficient, while allowing a polynomial change in the lengths of instances.

Padding supplies the strongest classical evidence. A paddable language has an efficient injective way to append arbitrary recoverable auxiliary information without changing the answer. For satisfiability, fresh variables and a suitably delimited formula encoding can carry extra bits while preserving whether the original formula has a satisfying assignment. Berman and Hartmanis used padding to show that the standard NP-complete examples known at the time are polynomial-time isomorphic. The unresolved step is proving that arbitrary complete languages possess enough recoverable structure.

The conjecture implies \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), but its negation does not automatically imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). To see the first point, suppose \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Then the nontrivial languages {0} and \(0\{0,1\}\)* would both be NP-complete: decide the source problem and output a fixed yes string or no string. Yet a bijection preserving membership cannot map a one-element yes-set onto an infinite yes-set. This elementary obstruction also explains why the unconditional conjecture must be distinguished from its version conditional on \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

The connection with one-way functions depends on more than difficulty inverting a particular reduction. An NP-complete language can have many reductions from SAT, and invertibility of one map does not determine whether a different efficient isomorphism exists. The Hartmanis problem column distinguishes one-way functions, scrambling functions and easy-cylinder hypotheses; these additional structural conditions are not interchangeable.

Oracle results go in both directions. Kurtz, Mahaney and Royer construct random-oracle counterexamples using scrambling functions. Fenner, Fortnow and Kurtz construct a different oracle setting in which the conjecture holds. These are results about relativized computation, where the algorithms can query a supplied set. They do not settle the ordinary conjecture, but they show that an argument valid uniformly across all such oracle settings cannot choose its truth value.

Restricting the completeness reductions can produce affirmative theorems. Agrawal, Allender and Rudich prove an isomorphism theorem for sets complete under nonuniform \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) reductions, with nonuniform depth-three \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) circuits computing the isomorphisms and their inverses. Here \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) means polynomial-size Boolean circuits of constant depth with unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and negations. Both the restricted completeness hypothesis and the availability of nonuniform circuits matter; dropping them would be a stronger statement.

Agrawal and Watanabe further relate structural assumptions about one-way functions to nonuniform isomorphisms. Under their stated hypotheses they obtain P/poly isomorphisms, permitting polynomial advice that depends on input length. This does not provide the uniform polynomial-time algorithms demanded here. The broad question remains whether NP-completeness itself forces reversible structure, or whether some complete languages have an intrinsically different organization of their yes and no instances.

Nareddy and Mishra’s 2025 preprint studies recovery of Boolean truth tables after random corruptions. It states the Berman–Hartmanis conjecture explicitly and derives, conditionally on it, recovery guarantees for every NP-complete language after partitioning instances by the length of their image under an isomorphism. This is an application of the conjecture as a hypothesis, not a proof of it.

cards.title: Directed reachability in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space
cards.formal:
Is there one deterministic algorithm that decides directed reachability using polynomial time and polylogarithmic working space simultaneously?

Precisely, does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing decider \(M\) and fixed positive integers \(a,k,c\) such that, for every encoded instance \((G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), it correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), while
\[\operatorname{time}_M(G,s,t)\le c(N+2)^a\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{space}_M(G,s,t)\le c\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil^k?\]
Both bounds must hold for the same computation on every input. This is the question whether directed reachability belongs to the class SC.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(v\ge1\), the directed graph \(G=([v],E)\) has \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and \(E\subseteq[v]\times[v]\). Loops are allowed, and repeated edges have no separate meaning. The graph may have cycles, arbitrary in- and out-degree and arbitrarily many paths. No planarity, acyclicity, uniqueness, few-path or connectivity promise is imposed. The marked vertices satisfy \(s,t\in[v]\).

Reachability means that for some integer \(\ell\ge0\) there are vertices \(u_0,\ldots,u_\ell\) with \(u_0=s\), \(u_\ell=t\) and \((u_i,u_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i<\ell\). The zero-edge path makes every vertex reachable from itself. Whenever reachability holds, a path with at most \(v-1\) edges also exists. The required output is one membership bit; a path itself need not be output.

Use the explicit binary encoding \(1^v0\), followed by the \(v^2\) adjacency-matrix bits in row-major order, followed by fixed-width binary encodings of \(s,t\). Each vertex field has \(b_v=\lceil\log_2(v+1)\rceil\) bits and must represent an integer between \(1\) and \(v\). The total length is
\[N=v+1+v^2+2b_v.\]
There are no trailing fields. Any binary string failing this format is rejected. The machine must also meet the same time and space bounds on malformed inputs, measured by their actual length. This representation is polynomially related to the vertex count; it is not a succinct circuit description of an exponentially large graph.

The machine has one two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of ordinary work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, initially blank. Each step changes the finite control, reads or writes a bounded number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Time is the total number of steps until its accept/reject halt, in the worst case. Space is the maximum number of work-tape cells ever visited during the run, multiplied by a fixed number of bits sufficient to encode a tape symbol. In particular all counters, indices, remembered input bits and temporary data count toward space. Input storage and the finite control do not count. The single decision bit is the halting state, so no uncharged output tape can be used as working memory.

No random bits, nondeterministic choices, quantum register, oracle, advice, writable input or extra catalytic memory are available. The same finite program and constants work for all graph orders and all valid and malformed inputs. An algorithm may depend on the fixed encoding, but cannot be chosen separately for each graph. The input is read sequentially by its head rather than supplied as a unit-cost adjacency oracle; scanning it is charged to time.

For an ordinary language of binary strings, SC means decidability by a single uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound and a fixed-power logarithmic space bound as above. It differs from merely supplying one polynomial-time algorithm and another polylogarithmic-space algorithm. The exponent \(k\) is allowed to be any fixed positive integer; the target does not specifically demand logarithmic or squared-logarithmic space.

Equivalently, the question is \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{SC}\). Here NL consists of languages decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine with logarithmic charged work space and a fixed polynomial clock on every branch, accepting an input exactly when at least one branch accepts. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions, and those reductions preserve membership in SC. In particular, \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\) would imply an affirmative answer, but this card asks only for the weaker simultaneous bounds and does not assert the converse.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the simultaneous-bound existence statement. An affirmative answer must give one exact deterministic decider for all directed graphs and prove its polynomial time and fixed-power logarithmic space bounds with constants independent of the instance. A negative answer must prove that no such decider exists: for every correct uniform decider and every proposed constants, some input violates at least one bound. Separate algorithms meeting separate bounds, a restriction to a special graph family, or a simulation with randomness, advice or catalytic memory is insufficient.
cards.why: Directed reachability captures nondeterministic logarithmic space and is a basic model of exploring a large state graph. The question asks whether exploration can be both computationally efficient and extremely economical in reusable memory. Its resolution would clarify the relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic space while separating a genuine simultaneous resource bound from two individually achievable guarantees.

cards.context:

cards.title: Ruling out quasilinear-time SAT without a space restriction
cards.formal:
Is Boolean-formula satisfiability outside deterministic quasilinear time, with no independent bound on the algorithm’s working memory? In the uniform random-access model below, the exact target is
\[\mathrm{SAT}\notin\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left[N\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k\right],\]
where \(N\) is the full bit length of the explicitly written formula and \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. Thus every fixed polynomial-logarithmic factor must be excluded. The formulation uses this meaning of the source’s “near-linear time”; the stronger exclusion of all \(N^{1+o(1)}\)-time algorithms is not required.
cards.definitions:
Use [SAT](definitions.html#sat) on fully written formula trees with Boolean constants. Each variable occurrence carries a binary identifier in \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), and identifiers may be unused. The formula uses a self-delimiting prefix encoding with gate tokens and delimited identifiers. Every token and occurrence counts toward \(N\). Reject malformed strings.

Fix a uniform deterministic word-RAM with logarithmic-size words. A machine is one finite program independent of \(N\), together with a fixed integer \(b\ge1\) giving word length \(w_N=b\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). It has a fixed number of word registers and an initially zero writable memory array addressed by \(w_N\)-bit integers. The input is separately read-only, packed into words with zero padding in its final word, and its bit length is available. One step is a register copy, Boolean bitwise operation, addition or subtraction modulo \(2^{w_N}\), comparison, conditional branch, shift by a register-specified count, or indexed read/write of one word. Shifts by at least \(w_N\) return zero. Registers and memory words contain exactly \(w_N\) bits; no unbounded-integer operation has unit cost. The program has no advice, oracle, nondeterminism or random bits. It halts with a single accept/reject answer on every input. Standard additional arithmetic operations on logarithmic words can be implemented with polynomial-logarithmic overhead and do not change the union of time bounds in this question.

There is no logarithmic, sublinear or other independent workspace requirement. The algorithm may use any addressable working memory it can access during its allowed running time. Initial memory is zero, not an input-dependent precomputed table; reading and writing memory are charged. The word-size/address convention is the ordinary polynomial-address-space convention of this RAM model, not a small-space promise. In particular, maintaining an input-sized array is allowed. The purpose of random access is to charge actual computation rather than the distance a sequential input head must travel.

For a fixed \(k\), membership in the displayed time class means that some one machine and constant \(D\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) correctly decide every input \(x\) within
\[D(N+2)\left\lceil\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil^k\]
steps, including parsing and rejection of malformed inputs. Here \(k,D,b\) and the finite program are independent of the particular input and its length. The target’s positive statement excludes every such choice. Its negative statement requires just one correct algorithm and one fixed exponent \(k\); it does not require a linear-time algorithm.

The chosen bound is \(N\,\mathrm{polylog}(N)\), the union over all fixed logarithmic powers. It is smaller than the broader \(N^{1+o(1)}\) family: for example, \(N2^{\sqrt{\log_2 N}}\) is in the latter family but exceeds \(N(\log N)^k\) for every fixed \(k\). Excluding every \(N\,\mathrm{polylog}(N)\) algorithm does not require proving a fixed exponent lower bound \(N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The clarification retains the absence of a memory restriction and records which of these meanings is being benchmarked.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed time-only nonmembership statement for the stated uniform machine and input model. A positive answer must exclude all fixed \(k,D,b\) and all correct total programs, with no extra workspace restriction. Equivalently, for every correct total program, every \(k\), and every \(D\), some input exceeds its proposed quasilinear bound. A negative answer must provide one program and fixed constants and prove correctness and that time bound on all inputs. A lower bound only for logarithmic-memory algorithms, a restricted SAT-solver family, a particular input distribution, or a sequential-access model does not establish this RAM target. A conditional lower bound under P ≠ NP or an exponential-time hypothesis is not an unconditional solution. Exact asymptotic quantifiers apply; no finite timing experiment or numerical error tolerance settles the question.
cards.why: An unconditional time-only lower bound for SAT in a general random-access model would cross a fundamental barrier in complexity theory. Even this comparatively weak exclusion remains separate from the substantial lower bounds known when memory is restricted.

cards.context:
P versus NP asks whether SAT admits any polynomial-time algorithm. This card asks for a much smaller first exclusion: algorithms only a fixed logarithmic factor slower than reading the input. Such an exclusion would still be consistent with a quadratic or higher-degree polynomial-time SAT algorithm.

Checking a supplied assignment is easy relative to the size of an explicit formula, but this does not show that deciding whether an assignment exists must take longer. The target requires an unconditional separation between existence testing and this very fast deterministic computation, over all possible programs.

Known time-space bounds exclude algorithms that are simultaneously fast and use little writable memory. Williams’s theorem reaches a polynomial time exponent below 2 cos(π/7) when workspace is subpolynomial. Here memory is unrestricted, so that qualification cannot be dropped.

The 2016 column also describes an either/or theorem: SAT cannot have both a quasilinear-time algorithm and a logarithmic-space algorithm, even if these are different algorithms. An either/or conclusion does not identify the time alternative as the true one. It therefore leaves this time-only target unresolved.

Hirahara, Lu and Ren’s 2023 Remark 47 explicitly separates simultaneous time-space bounds from separate-algorithm alternatives. Their discussion still allows the unresolved possibility of quasilinear-time SAT together with polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth parallel circuits. That discussion supplies no quasilinear SAT algorithm and no time-only lower bound.

The source uses “near-linear” informally. The selected meaning excludes every fixed logarithmic power, including arbitrarily large fixed ones. This gives a definite success condition without demanding the stronger exclusion of every subpolynomial overhead or a particular positive power improvement. The selection was made.

cards.title: PH versus PSPACE
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PH}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? Equivalently, does TQBF belong to \(\Sigma_k^{\mathrm{P}}\) for some fixed \(k\ge0\)?
cards.definitions: Use the [polynomial hierarchy and TQBF](definitions.html#polynomial-hierarchy) and [PSPACE](definitions.html#space). The input formula uses AND, OR and NOT. Its prefix binds each variable once and its entire binary encoding, including variable names, is available on a read-only tape. The number of input quantifier blocks can grow, while the proposed hierarchy level \(k\) is fixed for every input.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq \mathrm{PH}\); the reverse inclusion is already known. cards.context:
Polynomial space lets a computation reuse a bounded amount of memory for a potentially very long time. The polynomial hierarchy instead organizes efficiently checked conditions by a fixed number of alternating existential and universal choices. For example, an existential block asks for a witness, a following universal block checks every challenge to it, and another existential block can give a response depending on that challenge. The question asks whether any polynomial-space computation can be expressed with a fixed number of such blocks.

The formula \(\forall x\exists y (x=y)\) is true: after the value of x is fixed, y can take the same value. The formula \(\exists y\forall x (x=y)\) is false because one bit cannot equal both possible values of x. Thus replacing a sequence of dependent choices by one initial guess changes the problem. A formula with arbitrarily many alternating choices describes a potentially long strategy, even though testing its final Boolean condition is straightforward.

A quantified formula can be evaluated by recursively trying the two values of each variable and combining the answers according to its quantifier. The procedure reuses memory after finishing each branch; it need not store the exponentially large game tree. TQBF is PSPACE-complete. The standard alternation theorem also identifies polynomial-time alternating computation, with no fixed bound on its number of alternations, with PSPACE. Neither characterization shows that an arbitrary number of rounds compresses to a constant.

The definition of PH initially lets different languages use different fixed numbers of blocks. Nevertheless, equality with PSPACE would imply one common finite level containing all of PSPACE: TQBF would belong to some \(\Sigma ^{p}_{k}\) and every PSPACE language reduces to it. Therefore \(\mathrm{PH}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) would collapse the hierarchy. Conversely, proving that the hierarchy has infinitely many distinct levels would separate it from PSPACE. A separation \(\mathrm{PH}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\) alone does not establish that every hierarchy level is distinct; this is why the card differs from the non-collapse question.

Grüne, Johannes, Orlin and Wulf’s February 2026 results make many multilevel optimization problems complete for individual hierarchy levels or for PSPACE. Completeness locates the problems within the classes; it does not prove the classes different. Egidy’s 2026 oracle construction illustrates another distinction: relative to that oracle, PH collapses while remaining strictly below PSPACE. This is a statement in a model with an additional oracle, rather than a resolution for ordinary machines. Historical preprints claim equality or non-collapse, but the sources checked here do not establish either as a settled theorem. The review did not independently audit those claimed proofs.

cards.title: Containment of PPAD in PLS
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PPAD}\subseteq\mathrm{PLS}\) under uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions? Here PPAD represents directed endpoint search and PLS represents potential-based local search, with precise definitions below. Equivalently, do there exist uniform deterministic polynomial-time computable maps \(F,G\) that transform every End-of-Line input \(I\) into a Localopt instance \(F(I)\), and transform every accepted Localopt answer \(w\) for that instance into an accepted End-of-Line answer \(G(I,w)\)? This asks only the displayed direction of containment.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean circuit is given by an explicit topologically ordered list of gates over fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, and constants 0 and 1, with listed input nodes and ordered output nodes. Counts, gate types, wire indices and delimiters use an unambiguous binary encoding. All lists are part of the input, rather than a program generating them; the numbers of input and output bits therefore contribute to the encoding length. The notation \(\{0,1\}^n\) denotes length-\(n\) bit strings, and \(0^n\) is the all-zero string.

Polynomial time means one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a bound \(a(N+1)^d\), for fixed integers \(a,d\ge1\), on inputs of complete bit length \(N\). All bit operations and output bits count. Machines receive and may inspect full circuit gate lists; they have no advice, oracle or randomness unless randomness is explicitly allowed below. A malformed circuit encoding is efficiently recognizable. For a search task with such an input, INVALID is its only accepted answer, and INVALID is forbidden on valid inputs. Tags and bit strings in all answers have a fixed unambiguous binary encoding.

A total NP search problem is a relation \(R(x,y)\) on bit strings with a valid answer on every input \(x\), a fixed polynomial bound on the length of every accepted answer \(y\), and a deterministic polynomial-time test of \(R(x,y)\). TFNP denotes the class of these relations. A deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reduction from \(R\) to \(Q\) consists of maps \(F,G\) such that, for every \(x\) and every valid \(Q\)-answer \(z\) on \(F(x)\), the output \(G(x,z)\) is a valid \(R\)-answer on \(x\). Both maps are uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithms, with time measured in their full input bit lengths. Here FP means total search relations admitting a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that selects a valid answer, without requiring a unique answer.

An End-of-Line input consists of circuits \(S,P:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n\), for \(n\ge1\). The input is valid when \(P(0^n)=0^n\) and \(S(0^n)\ne0^n\), conditions checked by circuit evaluation. An answer is any \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\) with
\[P(S(v))\ne v\quad\text{or}\quad\bigl(v\ne0^n\ \text{and}\ S(P(v))\ne v\bigr).\]
Thus zero is accepted only for the first condition, not merely for being the designated start. Failed input conditions, like malformed encodings, have only the answer INVALID. No global inverse promise is imposed. The graph intuition uses an edge \(u\to v\) when \(u\ne v\), \(S(u)=v\) and \(P(v)=u\); the displayed answer relation is authoritative. Answers need not lie in the component of zero. The directed endpoint principle guarantees an answer. PPAD, short for Polynomial Parity Argument, Directed, is the subclass of TFNP reducible to this End-of-Line task by the many-one search reductions just defined.

A Localopt input consists of circuits \(T:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}^m\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}^r\), where \(m,r\ge1\). Read the output of \(V\) as an unsigned binary integer with the first output bit most significant. A valid answer is any \(w\in\{0,1\}^m\) satisfying
\[V(T(w))\ge V(w).\]
The circuit \(T\) proposes a next state and \(V\) assigns its cost; a solution is a state where that proposal does not improve the cost. A global minimum of \(V\) is always an accepted answer. There is no specified starting state or reachability restriction. Malformed encodings have only INVALID as an answer. Allowing distinct state and cost widths is polynomially equivalent by padding to the equal-width formulation in the cited source. PLS, short for Polynomial Local Search, is the subclass of TFNP reducible to Localopt by the specified many-one search reductions.

The required maps \(F,G\) are fixed for all circuit sizes. The output of \(F\) must be a well-formed Localopt instance even on a malformed End-of-Line encoding; such inputs can be sent to a fixed trivial instance, and \(G\) must then return INVALID. For every other input, correctness must hold for every accepted Localopt witness, not only for one chosen minimum or one reachable state. The time and output length of \(F\) are polynomial in \(|I|\); the time and output length of \(G\) are polynomial in \(|I|+|w|\). Consequently all output circuit sizes and the parameters \(m,r\) are polynomially bounded by \(|I|\). Neither map uses an oracle for solving either search task. This is one many-one reduction, not an adaptive sequence of calls. Since End-of-Line and Localopt are the defining complete tasks, existence of these maps is equivalent to the stated class containment.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the specified maps F and G exist, including their polynomial bounds and correctness for every target answer, or prove that no such pair exists in the ordinary uniform model. A single hard-looking example, an oracle separation, a query lower bound or a conditional cryptographic claim is insufficient. A positive proof need not provide an efficient algorithm for solving Localopt. Establishing only the reverse containment does not answer this card.
cards.why: Determine whether every directed parity search problem can be expressed as potential-based local search through an ordinary polynomial-time reduction. This resolves a central relationship between two major total-search classes, and would identify PPAD with their known intersection CLS if affirmative.

cards.context:
Directed endpoint search guarantees another endpoint from a known start. Local search instead guarantees a state where a proposed move does not decrease an integer cost. PPAD and PLS collect the total search relations reducible to these two mechanisms; Definitions specifies the exact tasks and reduction.

Papadimitriou explicitly asks whether PPAD is contained in PLS. This is not the reverse containment and is not a demand for a polynomial-time algorithm that solves Localopt. A positive answer would show that local search can represent every directed parity task with a correct translation of every solution.

CLS denotes Continuous Local Search, a class built around continuous potential-based search. Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender and Savani prove that CLS is exactly the intersection of PPAD and PLS. Their theorem makes this card equivalent to CLS = PPAD. CLS versus FP, where FP means efficient solution algorithms, remains a different question.

The literature discusses PPAD and PLS as conjecturally incomparable and gives oracle evidence. An oracle separation restricts access to a hidden function and does not by itself rule out a reduction that inspects explicit circuits. The target allows such circuit inspection and requires an ordinary-model conclusion.

A polynomial-time solver for End-of-Line would imply the requested containment by letting the output translator solve the original input directly. Thus a negative answer here would also separate PPAD from FP. It would not, by itself, settle the reverse containment of PLS in PPAD.

cards.title: P versus NP intersect coNP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates for both membership and nonmembership, but no uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm?
cards.definitions: For a binary string \(x\), write \(n=|x|\). Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\) means that there are one polynomial \(q\) and two deterministic polynomial-time Boolean verifiers \(V_1,V_0\) such that, for every \(x\), \[x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_1(x,y)=1,\qquad x\notin L\iff\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_0(x,z)=1.\] In particular, no input has accepted certificates of both types and every input has an accepted certificate of one type. Verifier time is polynomial in the combined bit length. Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). The proposed language must defeat every such machine and polynomial bound. Algorithms have no advice, oracle or random bits. This is a total language-class comparison, not a promise problem or a requirement to output certificates. Witness lengths and machines are uniform over all input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a language in \((\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP})\setminus\mathrm{P}\), including both verifiers and an unconditional uniform lower bound, or prove that every language satisfying the two verifier conditions belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\). An unproved hardness assumption, a promise-problem separation or hardness of finding witnesses alone does not decide this statement.
cards.why: This asks whether computational difficulty can persist even when every yes answer and every no answer has a short efficiently checkable proof. It isolates a basic boundary between verification and decision that is finer than the usual one-sided NP condition.

cards.context:
A deterministic polynomial-time decision supplies trivial short certificates for either answer, so P is contained in NP ∩ coNP. The conjecture asks whether this containment is strict: efficiently checking either kind of answer need not give a method for deciding which kind exists.

Wigderson states this as Conjecture 3.9. The surrounding discussion uses problems such as linear programming and primality to illustrate that two-sided verification alone is not evidence of a separation; those problems have deterministic polynomial-time algorithms.

A strict separation would imply P ≠ NP, but the P versus NP question alone does not specify whether the intersection is larger than P. Search problems associated with finding certificates introduce another task and are not the language-class comparison asked here.

cards.title: Existence of TFNP-complete problems
cards.formal:
Does the class of total polynomially bounded search problems with polynomial-time verifiable answers contain a complete problem under deterministic polynomial-time many-one search reductions?

Writing this class as \(\mathrm{TFNP}\) and the reduction as \(\le_m^p\), the target is
\[\exists Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \forall R\in\mathrm{TFNP},\qquad R\le_m^p Q.\]
The same fixed relation \(Q\) must work for every \(R\). For each \(R\), a reduction computes one \(Q\)-instance from the input and converts every valid answer to that instance into a valid \(R\)-answer. The question is unrelativized and concerns the whole class, including problems whose totality follows from different mathematical principles.
cards.definitions:
Use [TFNP](definitions.html#counting) on all finite binary strings, including the empty input. The relation is decidable by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier, every input has an answer, and every valid answer obeys the relation's fixed polynomial length bound.

Use the [many-one search reduction](definitions.html#reductions) \(R\le_m^p Q\) with maps \(F,G\). Encode the pair for \(G\) as \(1^{|x|}0xz\). Both maps are total uniform bit algorithms and may return a fixed output on malformed tuple encodings. The decoder receives the original \(x\) and must work for every \(z\) satisfying \(Q(F(x),z)\).

A complete \(Q\) is chosen before \(R\). The maps and their polynomial bounds can depend on the pair. The negation is \(\forall Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\ \exists R\in\mathrm{TFNP}: R\not\le_m^p Q\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement. An affirmative answer must specify one relation \(Q\), prove its polynomial balance, deterministic polynomial-time verifiability and totality on all binary inputs, and establish the stated reductions from every \(R\in\mathrm{TFNP}\). A negative answer must prove that every candidate \(Q\in\mathrm{TFNP}\) fails to receive such a reduction from some relation in the class. No effective enumeration of all TFNP problems is additionally required. A subclass-completeness result, a separation relative to an oracle or a conditional consequence alone is insufficient.
cards.why: A complete problem would give one universal task against which the difficulty of every efficiently verifiable total search problem could be compared. Its nonexistence would establish a structural limitation on extending the completeness framework from decision problems to all total search. This is a central question connecting complexity classes defined by semantic conditions, mathematical existence principles and the strength of formal proof systems.

cards.context:
The source states nonexistence of a many-one complete TFNP problem among the central conjectures connecting computational complexity and proof systems. This card asks the equivalent yes-or-no existence question, so the commonly stated conjecture predicts a negative answer.

Polynomial verifiability and a polynomial answer bound can be given by machine descriptions, but totality asserts a condition over all inputs. This semantic requirement prevents simply treating every polynomial-time verifier as a total search problem. Pudlák relates the general completeness question to the ability of fixed arithmetical theories to capture total search, and proves a universal-problem result for suitable classes whose totality is provable in a fixed theory.

Many important subclasses have complete problems tied to particular existence principles. The December 2025 manuscript studies further oracle hierarchies and collapses within TFNP; these subclass results do not supply a complete problem for the entire class.

The MFCS 2024 oracle permits a TFNP-complete problem while SAT has no polynomial-time optimal proof system. This separates two conjectures in that relativized setting; it neither constructs an ordinary TFNP-complete problem nor rules one out. Worst-case completeness alone also does not specify an average-case cryptographic hardness guarantee.

The MFCS 2024 oracle permits a TFNP-complete problem while SAT has no polynomial-time optimal proof system. This separates two conjectures in that relativized setting; it neither constructs an ordinary TFNP-complete problem nor rules one out. Worst-case completeness alone also does not specify an average-case cryptographic hardness guarantee.

cards.title: NL versus UL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist one nondeterministic Turing machine \(M\) and constants \(C,D,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, on every explicitly encoded directed-reachability input \(x=(G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), every computation branch halts within \(D(N+2)^k\) steps and visits at most \(C\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) work-tape cells, and
\[\#\{\text{accepting computation branches of }M(x)\}=
\begin{cases}1,&t\text{ is reachable from }s\text{ in }G,\\0,&\text{otherwise}?\end{cases}\]
The constants and machine are independent of the input. Unreachable and malformed inputs must have no accepting branch.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Use a self-delimiting explicit binary list of all vertices and all directed edges, together with \(s,t\in[n]\). In particular, isolated vertices are represented and \(N\ge n\); a binary vertex count is not a succinct description of an exponentially large graph. Edges are ordered pairs of vertices. Self-loops are allowed, and repeated edge entries may be interpreted as the same edge. A directed path from \(s\) to \(t\) follows the listed edge directions, and the length-zero path is allowed when \(s=t\). No planarity, acyclicity, bounded-degree or unique-path promise is present. Invalid list structure or out-of-range vertices make the encoding malformed. Validity is deterministically checkable in logarithmic space, by rescanning the input if needed. Explicit adjacency lists, edge lists and adjacency matrices are interchangeable here through deterministic logarithmic-space reductions of polynomial output length.

The machine has a finite description with a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed number of initially blank read/write work tapes over finite alphabets. Heads use ordinary Turing-machine moves. The space bound counts all distinct work-tape cells visited on a branch, including blank cells crossed, counters and every temporary record. Input cells and finite control do not count. The output is acceptance or rejection. No advice, randomness, oracle, writable input, catalytic tape or other uncharged storage is available. Every branch, including a rejecting branch, obeys the same polynomial clock and logarithmic-space bounds.

A computation branch is a complete sequence of transition choices from the initial configuration to halting. Two sequences that merge into the same configuration still count as distinct branches. The condition counts successful computations, not distinct accepting configurations, output values, graph paths or certificates after identifying equivalent strings. Rejecting branches need not be unique. The machine is not required to output the graph path or to behave deterministically.

For languages of binary strings, \(\mathrm{NL}\) is acceptance by nondeterministic machines under these time and space bounds, allowing any positive number of accepting branches on a yes input and none on a no input. The subclass \(\mathrm{UL}\) requires at most one accepting branch on every input, hence exactly one on a yes input. A polynomial all-branch clock is the usual equivalent convention for logarithmic-space acceptance. The class equality quantifies separately over languages and machines: every language in NL must have some UL machine. It does not additionally require an effective compiler mapping descriptions of arbitrary NL machines to UL machines.

Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions. Such reductions preserve the answer and can be composed with a UL machine by deterministically recomputing required output bits; this does not add accepting branches. Its membership in UL therefore implies \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\); the reverse inclusion follows from the definitions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\) for the specified uniform model. An affirmative reachability construction must supply one machine and fixed constants and establish its exact accepting-branch count, correctness on all inputs, and every-branch time and space bounds. A negative answer must prove that some NL language is outside UL, equivalently exclude every proposed reachability machine with these guarantees; the class/reachability equivalence must be justified if used. The graph itself may have arbitrarily many paths, so a promise of a unique graph path cannot replace the required algorithmic unambiguity. A larger-space simulation, nonuniform advice, catalytic memory, an oracle, an unproved hardness assumption or a lower bound only for a restricted isolation procedure does not settle the exact question. No approximate branch count or resource estimate is accepted.
cards.why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.

references.locator: Theorems 1.1 and 1.3, using the Reinhardt–Allender simulation.

cards.context:
A nondeterministic computation may have many successful branches. Unambiguity permits extensive guessing and arbitrarily many rejecting branches, but requires only one successful branch on each yes input. The restriction is on computations of the algorithm, not on the number of paths that happen to exist in the input graph.

The inclusions \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\) explain the stakes. An equality \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{UL}\) would not by itself remove nondeterminism. A separation would also imply \(\mathrm{L}\ne\mathrm{NL}\). Requiring every reachable machine configuration to have a unique path from the start is a stronger condition, called reach unambiguity, and is not imposed here.

Reinhardt and Allender’s theorem connects unambiguous reachability with min-isolation: positive integer edge weights are min-isolating when every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. With polynomially bounded weights that are available in deterministic logarithmic space, this condition supports logarithmic-space unambiguous reachability. Existence of suitable weights alone does not guarantee that a uniform small-space machine can obtain them.

Their nonuniform result is \(\mathrm{NL}/\mathrm{poly}=\mathrm{UL}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here an advice string of polynomial length may depend on the input length and be shared by all inputs of that length, with no efficient procedure required to generate it. Ordinary UL has no such advice.

Van Melkebeek and Prakriya prove that every NL language has an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation using \(O((\log N)^{3/2})\) workspace. This is an unconditional simulation for all inputs, but the extra square-root-of-logarithm factor is unbounded and prevents this theorem from establishing membership in UL.

The 2025 hardness-based result concerns the scaled-up inclusion \(\mathrm{NSPACE}[n]\subseteq\mathrm{USPACE}[O(n)]\): these classes use linear nondeterministic and unambiguous workspace. Its hypothesis is a circuit lower bound with specified uniformity and unambiguous-space oracle access. The 2026 survey’s Theorems 3.12 and 3.13 distinguish an older conditional logspace equality from the refined conditional linear-space theorem. Neither is an unconditional resolution.

The February 2026 catalytic result permits \(O((\log N)^2)\) additional writable bits initially containing arbitrary data, whose contents must be restored, as well as a UL oracle. It keeps ordinary workspace logarithmic and time polynomial. Both the extra restorable tape and the oracle are absent from the machine model in this card.

Hoza’s July 2026 theorem concerns a single weight function chosen without inspecting which edges are present. If it must min-isolate every layered graph of width \(w\ge2\) and length \(\ell\ge2\), the maximum weight must be at least \(2^{\Omega(\log w\log\ell)}\). Layered means there are \(\ell+1\) successive layers of \(w\) vertices each, with edges only to the next layer. This excludes polynomially bounded universal weights in the general regime, but does not exclude graph-dependent weights or arbitrary unambiguous algorithms.

The August 2026 MFCS paper gives unambiguous and co-unambiguous logarithmic-space algorithms for recognizing simple path graphs and for their reachability problem. Such a graph has at most one simple path from the specified start to each vertex; directed cycles are still permitted. Recognition is part of the result, but the graph restriction remains essential.

cards.title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(a,b,d,q\), real constants \(c>0\) and \(K>0\), and one uniform deterministic oracle Turing machine \(V\) satisfying the following conditions? For every encoded 3-CNF formula \(F\) of bit length \(N\), set
\[
 r_N=\left\lceil a\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil,\qquad
 M_N=(N+2)^b,\qquad \Sigma_N=\{0,1,\ldots,M_N-1\}.
\]
Given \(F\), a uniformly random string \(R\in\{0,1\}^{r_N}\), and oracle access to a fixed proof \(\pi\in\Sigma_N^{M_N}\), the verifier makes at most \(q\) symbol queries, halts in at most \(K(N+2)^d\) bit operations, and accepts or rejects. It must have perfect completeness and inverse-polynomial soundness:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 F\text{ satisfiable}&\ \Longrightarrow\ 
   \exists\pi\ \forall R:\ V^\pi(F,R)=1,\\
 F\text{ unsatisfiable}&\ \Longrightarrow\ 
   \forall\pi:\ \Pr_R[V^\pi(F,R)=1]\le (N+2)^{-c}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All constants and the verifier are independent of \(F\) and \(N\).
cards.definitions:
A Boolean literal is a variable or its negation. A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals. Satisfiability means that some assignment of Boolean values to all variables appearing in the formula makes every clause true. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false; repeated literals and repeated clauses are allowed.

Fix the following explicit encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(z\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) be its binary expansion, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\), and encode it by \(1^t0\operatorname{bin}(z)\), where \(t\) is the expansion length. Encode a formula by its clause count, then for each clause its length in \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), then its literals. A literal is one sign bit followed by the code of its positive integer variable index. There is no additional declared variable count and no trailing data. The parameter \(N\) is the length of this entire binary representation, including indices and delimiters. Invalid encodings may simply be rejected and are not part of the completeness and soundness requirements.

The proof has \(M_N\) addressable locations, each containing one symbol from \(\Sigma_N\). A query specifies one index in \(\{1,\ldots,M_N\}\) and returns that symbol encoded in \(\lceil\log_2 M_N\rceil\) bits. The same index always gives the same answer. A query reads one whole symbol, not one arbitrary subset of the proof or an unbounded-length answer. Repeated requests count again toward the query limit. The verifier has no other access to the proof; it may not scan the proof without paying queries. Forming addresses and reading or processing the returned bits count toward its bit running time.

The proof is chosen before \(R\) and is fixed throughout the verification. On a satisfiable formula, the same witnessing proof must be accepted for every random string. On an unsatisfiable formula the error bound holds for every possible proof, including proofs produced with unlimited computation and proofs unrelated to any satisfying assignment. No proof may depend on the subsequently sampled verifier randomness. The verifier may choose later query addresses using earlier answers, as allowed by the existing card; it is otherwise deterministic once the input, random string and oracle are fixed. A standard nonadaptive verifier satisfying these guarantees would in particular meet the target, but nonadaptivity is not an additional requirement here.

Using exactly the displayed proof length, alphabet and random-tape length is a padding convention. Shorter proofs and smaller alphabets can be embedded in these bounds and unused random bits can be ignored. Positive integer exponents absorb constant polynomial factors and logarithmic ceiling effects. The common exponent \(b\) bounds both proof length and alphabet size; it need not be optimal. There is no required relation between \(a,b,c\) beyond positivity. The query bound \(q\) is a fixed integer, while each queried symbol contains \(O(\log(N+2))\) bits. Thus the target permits more than a constant number of proof bits, but not a growing number of queried symbols.

The verifier is a single finite classical program, with no advice, cryptographic assumption, trusted setup, interaction or quantum operations. All of its computation, including parsing, computing the displayed parameters, reading randomness, generating query addresses and computing the decision, must satisfy the polynomial bit-time bound for every valid formula, proof and random string. The construction of a witnessing proof need not be efficient; the assertion is its existence. There is no separate honest prover participating during verification.

Only some fixed positive exponent \(c\) is requested. The question does not demand an optimal exponent, a two-query verifier, an alphabet of constant size, or proof length linear in the formula size. The near-linear-size constant-error PCP problem is a different parameter target.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the constants and uniform verifier, including the two proof/randomness quantifier orders, the resource bounds on every execution, perfect completeness and the stated information-theoretic soundness; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation.

A positive result must achieve polynomial length, polynomial alphabet, logarithmic randomness, constant symbol-query complexity and inverse-polynomial error simultaneously. A constant-error construction, an error exponent tending to zero, a superconstant query bound, or a superpolynomial-size proof is insufficient without an additional proved transformation establishing every required bound. A negative answer must exclude every choice of the fixed constants and every permitted verifier, including adaptive verifiers. Conditional implications under unproved assumptions do not unconditionally decide the target.
cards.why: Achieving very small verification error while reading only a constant number of logarithmic-size proof symbols would strengthen the quantitative reach of PCP theory and its hardness-of-approximation consequences.

cards.title: \(\exists\mathbb{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Is \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{NP}\) in the ordinary bit-cost Turing model? Equivalently, is truth of every finitely encoded existential sentence over the ordered real field certifiable by a polynomial-length binary string checked in deterministic polynomial time?

For the language ETR defined below, the concrete target is the existence of one deterministic Turing verifier \(V\) and polynomial bounds \(p,q\) such that, for every binary string \(u\),
\[u\in\mathrm{ETR}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|u|)}:\ V(u,w)=1,\]
with \(V\) halting within \(q(|u|)\) steps on every permitted pair. The question is unconditional and has no oracle or advice.
cards.definitions:
ETR is a language of finite binary strings describing sentences
\[\exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R:\ \Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_m).\]
Here \(m\ge0\), the entire list of quantified variables is written explicitly, and \(\Phi\) is an explicitly listed finite Boolean formula, using \(\land,\lor,\neg\) and parentheses, whose atomic predicates are \(p=0\) or \(p>0\). Boolean constants true and false are permitted. Each polynomial is a finite monomial list
\[p(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{j=1}^{s}c_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}x_i^{e_{ij}},\qquad c_j\in\mathbb Z,\quad e_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.\]
Every coefficient is a signed binary integer and every exponent is a nonnegative binary integer. Each monomial has its coefficient and its full exponent vector, explicitly delimited. Zero coefficients and repeated monomials are allowed with their usual algebraic meaning. The empty sum is zero and the empty product is one. The convention \(x^0=1\) applies also at \(x=0\). No degree bound is imposed.

Use a fixed finite-alphabet, explicitly delimited encoding of the variable declarations, formula tree, monomial lists, signs and binary integers, then a fixed binary encoding of its symbols. Variable names are indices from 1 through \(m\); no implicit generation of an exponentially long formula is allowed. Let \(L=|u|\) be the entire encoding length, counting every bit of every coefficient and exponent as well as all syntactic structure. Ill-formed strings, invalid indices and unmatched lengths are rejected. With no quantified variables, the sentence has its ordinary closed-form truth value. Inequalities such as \(p\le0\) and comparisons between two polynomials can be expressed with the stated atoms and connectives.

A well-formed string is in ETR precisely when there exists an exact real tuple satisfying its sentence. There is no numerical tolerance or robustness promise. The reals occur as mathematical values of the quantified variables, not as infinite objects supplied to a Turing machine. Binary exponents and coefficients are counted by their bit lengths. This explicit sparse-polynomial representation is polynomially interreducible with the standard arithmetic-term definition of ETR; it does not encode an exponentially long formula by a separate succinct circuit description.

For languages \(A,B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), a polynomial-time many-one reduction is one total function \(f\) computed by a deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in \(|u|\), such that \(u\in A\) if and only if \(f(u)\in B\). Define \(\exists\mathbb R\) as all languages with such a reduction to ETR. A language is \(\exists\mathbb R\)-complete when it lies in that class and every language of the class reduces to it in this sense.

Use [NP](definitions.html#p-np), with ordinary binary witnesses and a uniform bit-cost verifier. The program and polynomial bounds are fixed independently of the instance and its length. A verifier must reject every allowed witness on a no-instance and accept at least one on every yes-instance. Every finite-alphabet tape transition costs one; arithmetic on large integers and manipulation of algebraic descriptions are charged their actual bit cost. There is no randomness, oracle, nonuniform advice or exact-real primitive. A witness may encode any finite mathematical certificate with an efficiently checkable interpretation: it need not list a satisfying coordinate tuple or use rational coordinates.

The known inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\exists\mathbb R\), and closure of NP under these reductions, make class equality equivalent to \(\mathrm{ETR}\in\mathrm{NP}\). Its negation is \(\mathrm{ETR}\notin\mathrm{NP}\). The other known upper bound uses PSPACE, the class decidable by deterministic Turing machines using polynomially many work-tape cells.

For comparison, a constant-free BSS verifier stores exact reals and performs field operations and order tests at unit cost, using only the fixed constants 0 and 1. Restricting its input to bits while allowing polynomially many real witness coordinates gives \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}^{0})=\exists\mathbb R\). In the full BSS class comparison, inputs and finitely many fixed machine constants may also be arbitrary reals. That is a different target. The present question asks whether ordinary binary certificates with a bit-cost verifier suffice.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{ETR}\in\mathrm{NP}\) or of \(\mathrm{ETR}\notin\mathrm{NP}\) for the encoding and model above, equivalently proving or refuting \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer must supply a uniform binary-certificate verification scheme and prove completeness, soundness, a polynomial certificate-length bound and a polynomial bit-time bound for all instances. A negative answer must exclude every such scheme. Showing only that some solutions are irrational, that a chosen coordinate representation needs many bits, or that a particular geometric problem is NP-hard does not exclude other certificate encodings. An oracle separation or a theorem conditional on unequal classes does not settle this unrelativized comparison. The decision target is exact, without numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: The answer would decide whether a broad class of geometric and algebraic existence problems has ordinary efficiently checkable finite certificates. It tests the boundary between discrete verification and exact continuous witnesses, with consequences across every problem complete for the existential theory of the reals.

cards.context:
Geometric realizations and continuous constraints naturally supply real-valued witnesses. For example, \(\exists x\in\mathbb R:\ x^2=2\) is true and has no rational solution, while \(\exists x\in\mathbb R:\ x^2+1=0\) is false. The first example nevertheless has an elementary finite certificate; irrationality alone is no obstruction to membership in NP.

The established containments are \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\exists\mathbb R\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\). The lower inclusion comes from expressing Boolean constraints over the reals, and the upper inclusion is a theorem about ordinary polynomial space. Neither containment is known to be strict in the May 2026 source.

The class unifies many geometric recognition and realization problems, including stretchability of pseudoline arrangements and variants of the art-gallery problem. Equality with NP would give ordinary polynomially checkable certificates for every complete problem; separation would establish a limitation shared by all such complete problems.

The 2025 structural paper proves opposite oracle behaviors in its specified real-machine oracle model. Its oracle is a subset of \(\mathbb R^{*}\), and the real verifier may ask about arbitrary real tuples, whereas a Turing machine can only construct finite discrete queries. In particular, an exact integer-membership oracle creates a separation in that enlarged model. These results do not determine the unrelativized classes, and should not be read as a separation using identical finite-string query capabilities.

The same paper proves a conditional analogue of Ladner’s theorem: if \(\exists\mathbb R\ne\mathrm{NP}\), then some problem belongs to \(\exists\mathbb R\setminus\mathrm{NP}\) without being \(\exists\mathbb R\)-complete. The hypothesis is the unresolved comparison, rather than a consequence of the theorem.

The March 2026 tutorial restates the machine characterization using finite binary inputs, real witnesses and restricted constants. Its real verifier checks exact arithmetic at unit cost, so the characterization does not provide a polynomial-time bit-cost NP verifier.

A May 2026 preprint reports a probabilistically checkable proof theorem with real-valued proof entries and a verifier using exact real operations. It also reports obstacles to short coordinate descriptions even for some approximate solutions. Those are different guarantees from a polynomial-length binary certificate checked in polynomial bit time; the preprint explicitly leaves the NP comparison unresolved.

cards.title: Polynomial formulas versus linear circuits
cards.formal:
Does there exist a family of total Boolean functions \(f_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for integers \(n\ge1\), such that
\[\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)=O(n)\qquad\text{but}\qquad \operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\notin n^{O(1)}?\]
Here \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}\) is minimum bounded-fan-in De Morgan circuit gate count and \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf count. Both are nonuniform and require exact correctness on every input. Precisely, the question asks for one family and a finite constant \(C>0\) satisfying \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\le Cn\) for all \(n\ge1\), while
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall n_0\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge n_0:\quad \operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)>n^k.\]
For each fixed exponent \(k\), the violation may occur along its own unbounded sequence of lengths.
cards.definitions:
Use the shared [Boolean circuit](definitions.html#boolean-circuits) and [formula leaf-size](definitions.html#formula-size) conventions. For the same total single-output function \(f_n\), \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\) counts the minimum number of binary AND/OR and unary NOT gates; inputs, constants and wires are free. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. The quantity \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\) counts the minimum number of variable-leaf occurrences in a formula tree; constants are free, so constant functions have size zero and a literal has size one. Exact correctness is required on every input, and neither quantity imposes a uniform generator.

The sequence of functions, and the optimal circuits and formulas at different lengths, need not have an efficiently computable description. In particular this card does not impose an extra polynomial-time evaluator or uniform circuit-generation algorithm on the family. The source's conjecture is stated using its nonuniform size measures. A family with such extra uniformity would also qualify if it has the required sizes.

The same constant \(C\) bounds circuit size at every length. Allowing finitely many exceptions would be equivalent, since increasing \(C\) absorbs them. The formula condition is equivalent to saying that there do not exist constants \(D>0\), integer \(k\ge1\) and onset \(n_0\) with \(\operatorname{FS}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\le Dn^k\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). Thus arbitrarily large violating lengths may depend on the polynomial exponent; the family itself may not. The target asserts no particular exponential or quasipolynomial lower-bound rate.

The two minima compare computations of the same single-output function. Linear circuit size does not bound circuit depth by a logarithm. A size separation using unbounded-fan-in threshold gates, only monotone formulas, or a growing number of outputs is a different statement.

The existence claim is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\subsetneq\mathrm{P/poly}\) for nonuniform Boolean circuit families. Here \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) means \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f_n)\le a(n+1)^b\) for some fixed positive integers \(a,b\), and \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) means a family of binary De Morgan circuits of depth at most \(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for one constant \(d\); such circuits can be taken polynomial in size. No uniform generation is required in either class. Polynomial-size formulas and logarithmic-depth circuits are equivalent by formula balancing and expansion of a bounded-depth circuit into a tree.

The restriction to linear circuit size does not change this family-existence question. A separating polynomial-size family can be regarded, at lengths \(N_n=a(n+1)^b\), as a function of \(N_n\) variables that ignores the extra variables; at other lengths set the function to a constant. The circuit bound becomes linear, whereas a polynomial formula bound in \(N_n\) would give a polynomial formula bound in \(n\). This is a comparison of nonuniform families and retains the arbitrarily-large-length quantifiers. Conversely, a linear-size family is already in \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). Thus an answer to the equality question has the opposite Boolean polarity from the separation question in this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed family-existence claim. A positive answer must specify or mathematically establish the existence of one family satisfying both the single linear circuit bound and failure of every polynomial formula bound. A nonconstructive family can qualify; no efficient generator is part of the target. A negative answer must show that every family with a uniform linear circuit-size constant has some polynomial formula-size bound, whose exponent and coefficient may depend on that family. Proving only one fixed polynomial separation, even with a large exponent, or refuting one candidate family does not settle the question.
cards.why: Circuits can reuse intermediate values and formulas must duplicate the computation when it is needed again. This question asks whether reuse can turn a task requiring superpolynomial tree size into a circuit of only linear size. It isolates a fundamental limitation of formulas while allowing the circuit computation to have unrestricted depth.

cards.context:
Theorem 5.10 records families with linear-size circuits and nearly cubic formula lower bounds. Conjecture 5.11 asks for a qualitative increase beyond every fixed polynomial, not a further fixed-power improvement.

The 2023 paper proves nearly cubic De Morgan formula bounds for a family already computable by polynomial-size constant-depth unbounded-fan-in formulas. This strengthens the class of target functions for a known lower-bound scale; its Theorem 1.1 does not state the superpolynomial separation requested here.

The source connects its conjecture to questions about formula size under block composition. The related KRW card records a particular formula-size composition statement. This connection is contextual; the present target is stated directly in terms of the two computational size measures.

The STACS 2025 paper continues to describe super-logarithmic formula-depth lower bounds as a major open challenge. Its result is for a strengthened communication relation, and the authors explicitly distinguish it from a formula lower bound for ordinary composition.

Open Problem 8.3 in the Rao–Yehudayoff draft asks whether every polynomial-size circuit family has logarithmic-depth circuits. Formula balancing and polynomial padding give precisely the equivalence recorded in the definitions. The former active card TCS-6712 is consolidated here, preserving its source question rather than retaining two benchmark entries for opposite polarities of the same proposition.

Amarilli’s companion question asks more broadly whether the known nearly cubic circuit/formula gap can be improved. That broader quantitative question motivated the earlier consolidation, but a fixed-power improvement alone would not meet this card’s superpolynomial target.
