cards.title: Is ARRIVAL solvable in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Does the deterministic decision problem \(\mathrm{ARRIVAL}\) defined below belong to \(\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, is there one deterministic Turing algorithm and constants \(K,c>0\) that, on every valid explicitly encoded switch graph of bit length \(N\), decides whether its token reaches destination \(d_1\) before \(d_0\) within \(K(N+1)^c\) bit steps? The two-destination termination condition and initial switch settings are part of the definition.
cards.definitions:
An instance is \(I=(n,o,s_0,s_1)\), where \(n\ge1\), the ordinary vertices are \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(o\in V\) is the origin, and \(d_0,d_1\notin V\) are two distinct destination symbols. Each successor table is a function \(s_b:V\to V\cup\{d_0,d_1\}\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Thus every ordinary vertex has two labelled outgoing arcs, its even arc to \(s_0(v)\) and its odd arc to \(s_1(v)\). These successors may coincide, and self-loops are allowed. The destinations have no outgoing arcs. There are no other edges, weights or choices.

Require that from every ordinary vertex there is a directed path in this switch graph to at least one of the two destinations. A path may use either labelled arc at each vertex for the purpose of checking this condition. It need not follow the token dynamics. This condition is checkable by ordinary reverse graph reachability and guarantees that the actual token process eventually reaches a destination. It does not require that both destinations be reachable from every vertex.

Initially the token is at \(x_0=o\), and every switch bit is zero: \(b_0(v)=0\). If the current position \(x_t\) is a destination, the process stops. Otherwise, writing \(v=x_t\), set
\[x_{t+1}=s_{b_t(v)}(v),\qquad b_{t+1}(v)=1-b_t(v),\]
and leave all other bits unchanged. The successor is selected using the old bit before the bit is flipped. Consequently successive departures from a vertex alternate even, odd, even, odd, starting with even. There is a single token and no player, randomness or external control. The instance is YES if the first reached destination is \(d_1\), and NO if it is \(d_0\).

Encode \(n,o\) and the two length-\(n\) successor tables explicitly using binary integers, with distinguished codes for the two destinations. The input length is \(\Theta(n\log(n+2))\) under this representation, up to fixed delimiters. A graph given by a succinct circuit, a binary multiplicity of initially placed tokens, or an exponentially long switch sequence is not part of this input model. The initial all-zero setting requires no additional table; any fixed initial setting could instead be represented by exchanging the corresponding two successor names.

For an ordinary language rather than a promise problem, reject malformed encodings and well-formed tables failing the reachability condition. Their validity can be checked in polynomial time, so this convention does not alter polynomial-time solvability on the valid instances. Membership in [P](definitions.html#p-np) uses the shared uniform bit-cost convention. The program need only output the answer bit. It is not required to list, or simulate, the token's full trajectory.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that this language is in \(\mathrm{P}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that it is not. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic decision algorithm, prove correctness on every valid graph and polynomial worst-case bit complexity, and handle invalid encodings according to the stated convention. A negative answer must exclude all such polynomial-time decision algorithms; an exponential example for direct token simulation or for one particular algorithm is insufficient. Polynomial time only for a restricted graph class, subexponential time, a randomized algorithm without a deterministic conversion, and succinctly encoded variants do not answer the exact question. No numerical tolerance applies to the Boolean answer or the complexity bound.
cards.why: ARRIVAL isolates the complexity of a finite deterministic process with one bit of memory at each switch. Its outcome has short verifiable evidence on both sides, but a general efficient decision algorithm would need to go beyond following the potentially exponential trajectory.

The local rule is elementary, but a vertex remembers which of its two arcs should be used next. With n vertices there are 2ⁿ possible switch configurations in addition to the token position. Long deterministic runs therefore do not contradict the small size of the graph. Ordinary reachability ignores these switch settings and does not decide which sink the token actually reaches.

The source gives short verifiable certificates for both answers using switching flows: counts of traversals that obey conservation and alternation. This places the decision problem in NP ∩ coNP. Certificates can establish the outcome without listing an exponentially long trajectory, but their existence does not itself provide a polynomial-time way to find them.

The 2021 algorithm runs in \(2^{O(\sqrt n\log n)}\) time and becomes polynomial when deleting a fixed number of vertices makes the graph acyclic. The former is a general improvement over direct simulation; the latter keeps a structural restriction. Neither is the all-instance polynomial bound asked for here.

The 2025 work gives a bound \(2^{O(k\log^2 n)}\) for treewidth \(k\), which is quasipolynomial, not polynomial, even when \(k\) is fixed. It also relates ARRIVAL to approximate fixed points of contractions in the ℓ₁ metric. The paper explicitly distinguishes polynomially many function evaluations from a polynomial total running time.

The 2026 paper proves polynomial time for binary ladders: simple switch graphs with exactly two vertices at each occupied distance level from the two sinks. Such graphs can frustrate earlier algorithms, so solving them is meaningful progress. The restriction concerns the shortest-distance layers of the graph and is not satisfied by general instances.

A polynomial-time algorithm would settle a basic deterministic process whose YES and NO answers already have efficiently checked evidence. A lower bound excluding all such algorithms would be a major complexity separation; the difficulty of simulating the process is only one part of that question.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), stable ternary compaction \(S_n:\{0,1,2\}^n\to\{0,1,2\}^n\) is computable by a Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates? The function deletes all symbols \(2\), retains all symbols \(0,1\) in their original relative order, and appends the deleted number of \(2\)s on the right. Circuits use the binary alphabet encoding and bounded-fan-in basis specified below, with no depth or uniformity restriction.
cards.definitions: Encode symbols \(0,1,2\) by \(00,01,10\), respectively, using a fixed ordered pair of bits for each input position. A circuit for length \(n\) is a finite acyclic directed Boolean circuit with \(2n\) ordered input bits and \(2n\) ordered output bits. Its non-input gates are binary AND, binary OR, unary NOT and optional constant-0 or constant-1 gates. Each such gate, including a constant gate, contributes one to size. Fan-out is unrestricted. Wires and output designations have no separate cost, and the same gate or input can feed multiple gates and outputs. The circuit is deterministic. It must be correct on every concatenation of valid input encodings; behavior on any input containing a pair \(11\) is unrestricted. For \(a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\{0,1,2\}^n\), let \(i_1<\cdots<i_m\) be exactly the indices where \(a_i\ne2\). The required output encodes \(a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_m}\) followed by \(n-m\) copies of \(2\). This definition includes \(m=0\) and \(m=n\). In particular, it preserves the relative order of a \(0\) and a \(1\); it does not sort them against each other. All output positions must be produced by one circuit and their gates are counted jointly. Let \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM+c}}(S_n)\) be the minimum circuit size for the binary-encoded promise function. Here \(\mathrm{DM+c}\) names the local convention above: constant gates count, unlike the free-constant \(\mathrm{DM}\) convention in the shared glossary. The quantifiers are \(\exists C\ge1\;\forall n\ge1\;\exists\mathcal C_n\), with \(|\mathcal C_n|\le Cn\) and exact correctness on all valid inputs. The circuit may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and no algorithm constructing \(\mathcal C_n\) is required. The circuit may compute on the individual encoding bits; it is not restricted to comparing or routing indivisible records.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM+c}}(S_n)\le Cn\) for some universal \(C\) and all \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation \(\forall C\ge1\;\exists n\ge1,\ \operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM+c}}(S_n)>Cn\). The negative statement rules out every nonuniform family in the defined unrestricted Boolean model; a lower bound for comparators or indivisible-record routing does not suffice. A conditional result under an additional conjecture settles only that conditional version. A positive answer must retain the original order of the \(0\)s and \(1\)s, with an exact linear size bound rather than a bound multiplied by an unbounded iterated-logarithm factor.
cards.why: This is an elementary deterministic rearrangement whose output preserves an arbitrary binary subsequence. Its sequential simplicity contrasts with the difficulty of arranging all output bits in a fixed circuit. Resolving linear circuit size would sharpen the boundary between data movement with input-dependent access and unrestricted bounded-fan-in Boolean computation.

cards.context:
Regan’s July 2007 problem defines precisely the order-preserving movement of all dummy symbols to the right. The present two-bit encoding and complete Boolean basis make its nonuniform linear-size target explicit.

Ordinary ternary sorting discards the order between retained zeros and ones. Stable compaction must preserve that binary sequence, so a circuit that only counts occurrences of the three symbols computes a different function.

Asharov, Lin and Shi obtain improved Boolean circuits for compaction and sorting short keys, but their construction deliberately does not preserve stability. Their discussion distinguishes unrestricted Boolean computation from the indivisible-payload model used in some stable-compaction lower bounds.

Lin and Shi’s SODA 2022 work improves the depth of short-key sorting circuits while retaining near-linear size bounds with iterated-logarithm factors in the relevant short-key regime. Its Introduction explicitly states that the sorting is not stable. This result therefore does not provide a linear-size circuit for the stable ternary function.

The checked literature also discusses conditional lower bounds based on the Li–Li network-coding conjecture. Such conditional bounds and lower bounds for restricted data-movement models are not unconditional impossibility results for this card.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
cards.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

cards.context:
Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’\(s O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

cards.title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.

cards.context:
The input is small compared with the output. For \(X=(0,3)\) and \(Y=(1,4)\), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are \(n^{2}\) output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for \(n^{2}\) unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix \(M_{ij}=x_{i}+y_{j}\) increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as \(M_{ij}+M_{kl}=M_{il}+M_{kj}\). The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all \(n^{2}\) sums takes \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) time. Writing the required output already takes \(\Omega (n^{2})\) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of \(X+Y\). The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

For bounded-integer inputs on a word RAM, a linear-time algorithm for sorting arbitrary word-sized integers would also sort the explicitly generated pairwise sums in quadratic time, allowing a constant-factor increase in word length for the sums. The present target instead allows arbitrary exact real inputs, without floor or bit extraction. An integer-sorting result therefore does not automatically answer this real-RAM question.

cards.title: Size-bounded approximate multicommodity-flow sparsifiers
cards.formal: Does there exist a function \(f:\{2,3,\ldots\}\times(0,1)\to\mathbb N\) such that every finite undirected capacitated graph \(G\) with a labelled set \(T\) of \(k\) terminals admits a finite undirected capacitated graph \(H\), containing the same labelled terminals and at most \(f(k,\varepsilon)\) vertices, for which \[\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\le\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\] holds simultaneously for every nonnegative terminal demand vector \(d\)? Here \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and new nonterminal vertices and arbitrary capacities in \(H\) are permitted.
cards.definitions:
A capacitated graph has finitely many vertices, undirected edges and strictly positive finite real capacities \(c_e\). Zero-capacity edges may be deleted and parallel edges combined by summing capacities. The terminals are distinct designated vertices. A demand vector assigns a nonnegative real number \(d_{st}\) to each unordered pair of distinct terminals \(\{s,t\}\).

For each terminal pair, assign nonnegative flow amounts to the finitely many simple paths joining the pair, so that their sum is \(d_{st}\). Commodities may split across paths. The load on an edge is the sum of the assigned amounts over all paths using it, regardless of direction or commodity. The congestion of a routing is \(\max_e \operatorname{load}(e)/c_e\). Define \(\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\) as the infimum over all such routings; set it to infinity if some positive demand cannot be routed. Zero demand has congestion zero, including in an edgeless graph. Inequalities involving infinity use the extended nonnegative reals. Integral, unsplittable and directed flow models are not intended.

Equivalently, let \(P_G\) be the set of demand vectors routable with loads at most the capacities. The requirement is \(P_G\subseteq P_H\subseteq(1+\varepsilon)P_G\), where scalar multiplication multiplies every demand coordinate. This fixes the one-sided normalization of quality. A single \(H\) must work for all demands; choosing a different graph after seeing \(d\) is not allowed.

Size means the number of vertices, including terminals. For simple graphs it also bounds the number of edges quadratically, but no bound on the bit complexity of real capacities is required. The bound is uniform over original graph size, topology and capacity magnitudes. This is an existence question: no efficient construction algorithm or computability requirement on \(f\) is added. The graph \(H\) may be entirely new and need not be a minor, quotient, contraction or subgraph of \(G\). Exact preservation corresponds to zero error and is outside the stated positive-error domain.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must provide fixed \(k\) and fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) for which no finite vertex bound works for all input graphs. Exact-sparsifier lower bounds alone, or lower bounds restricted to contraction-based sparsifiers, do not refute this statement. A positive answer must produce a graph realizing the simultaneous routing inequalities; a non-graph encoding of feasible demands does not suffice.
cards.why: This tests whether terminal flow behavior admits an arbitrarily accurate finite summary independent of the original network.

cards.title: Hypergraph cut sparsifiers with \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) hyperedges
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H\) on \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) admit a nonnegatively weighted hypergraph \(H'\) on the same vertices with \(|E'|\le Cn/\varepsilon^2\) and \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\le\operatorname{cut}_{H'}(S)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cut}_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\)?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.
cards.why: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.

cards.context:
A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.

The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

cards.title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm that lists all attainable subset sums up to a given threshold in time near-linear in the explicit input size plus the number of distinct output values?

More precisely, for integers \(n,t\ge1\) and an input list \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{1,\ldots,t\}^{n}\), put
\[
S(X,t)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I}x_i:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\right\}
\cap\{0,\ldots,t\},\qquad q(X,t)=|S(X,t)|.
\]
Does there exist one finite program \(A\), a fixed integer \(d\ge1\), a constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(b\ge0\), chosen independently of every input, such that on the word RAM defined below, with
\[
w=d\left\lceil\log_2(n+t+2)\right\rceil,
\]
both of the following hold for every valid \(n,t,X\)?
\[
\forall r\quad T_{A,d}(X,t;r)
\le C\bigl(n+q(X,t)\bigr)\bigl(\log_2(n+t+2)\bigr)^b,
\]
\[
\Pr_r\!\left[\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\right]\ge \frac23.
\]
Here success means that the complete output lists every element of \(S(X,t)\) exactly once and no other value. The time bound applies to every random execution, including unsuccessful executions. The algorithm is not given \(q(X,t)\) or any subset-sum information as additional input.

This card retains the previously selected bounded-error, worst-case word-RAM formulation of the source's near-linear output-sensitive question. Its explicit instruction set and requirement on every random execution are editorial model conventions; the source's expected-time or high-probability bounds are reported separately below.
cards.definitions:
The input is a list of \(n\) positive integers and an integer threshold \(t\), with \(1\le x_i\le t\). Repeated values represent distinct available items, and each index may be selected at most once. Thus the input is an explicitly listed multiset, not a binary encoding of item multiplicities. The empty subset contributes zero. The set \(S(X,t)\) contains distinct integer sums, not a count of subsets. The required output is a finite sequence of \(q(X,t)\) integers in arbitrary order, containing each element of \(S(X,t)\) once. There is no requirement to output witnessing subsets. The threshold is inclusive.

For each fixed choice of \(d\), a word holds an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The input occupies a read-only word array containing \(n,t,x_1,\ldots,x_n\) at addresses \(0,1,\ldots,n+1\), one integer per cell; these values fit in a word. Reading that array at a larger address returns zero. The machine starts at its designated first instruction, with register zero containing \(w\) and all other registers zero. Its separate writable memory consists of word-addressed cells with addresses in the same range, initially zero. Initially zero memory is a machine convention, not an instruction that scans the entire address space. Every initialization performed by the program, and every subsequent memory access, is charged. A computation has a fixed finite control and a fixed finite number of word registers; additional storage uses the charged memory instructions.

Each of the following is a unit-cost instruction on a fixed number of words: copying; reading one addressed input word; loading or storing one addressed writable word; comparing unsigned words and conditional branching; bitwise Boolean operations; logical left or right shifts; addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\); integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; generating one independent uniform random word; and appending one word to the output. A shift by an amount at least \(w\) returns zero. Arithmetic on larger integers must be implemented using these instructions and is charged accordingly. The program may use fixed integer constants encoded in its finite description, interpreted modulo \(2^w\) when placed in a word. It has no advice, input-dependent tables, or additional oracle instructions. Tables constructed during a run are allowed and all their construction costs count. A halt instruction ends the output sequence and costs one step; an invalid operation, such as division by zero, halts with failure. Output words already appended cannot be withdrawn.

One finite program and one constant \(d\) must serve all \(n,t,X\); neither the program nor its constants may vary with the input parameters. This is the uniformity requirement. All input reads, preprocessing, random-word generation, internal computation and output writes count toward running time. The memory bound comes only from word addressing; no further space restriction is imposed.

For a fixed input and \(d\), let \(r=(r_1,r_2,\ldots)\) be an infinite sequence of independent uniform words from \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), consumed in order by random-word instructions. This product distribution defines \(\Pr_r\). A deterministic program is permitted as a special case that ignores \(r\). Let \(T_{A,d}(X,t;r)\) be the number of executed instructions, or \(+\infty\) for a nonhalting run. The event \(\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\) means that the run halts normally and its output sequence has exactly the required distinct values. Failure includes a missing sum, an extra value, a duplicate, an invalid operation or nontermination. The probability guarantee concerns this single event for the entire output, rather than a separate probability for each attainable value. The condition on time includes even random sequences having probability zero as individual infinite sequences.

The logarithm is base two, and \(b\) is any fixed nonnegative integer. Allowing an arbitrary fixed real exponent \(b\ge0\) would give the same existence question, since rounding that exponent up only enlarges this bound. The notation \(\widetilde O\) used in the context suppresses fixed powers of logarithms in the specified parameters; the displayed bound itself is the exact target. In particular, dependence polynomial in the numerical threshold \(t\), or in \(q(X,t)\) beyond its first power, is not hidden in the target's logarithmic factor.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal existence assertion or its full logical negation, using exactly the input, machine, randomness, output and cost conventions above.

A positive answer must specify one finite program \(A\) and constants \(d\ge1\), \(C>0\), and \(b\ge0\), with \(d,b\) integers, and prove for every valid input both the running-time bound on every random execution and probability at least \(2/3\) of the complete correct output. The constants may depend on the program but not on \(n,t,X\). An expected-time estimate or a bound that holds only with high probability does not by itself prove the required bound on every execution.

A negative answer must prove the following full negation. For every finite program \(A\) in the defined model, every integer \(d\ge1\), every constant \(C>0\), and every integer \(b\ge0\), there exist integers \(n,t\ge1\) and a list \(X\in\{1,\ldots,t\}^{n}\) such that
\[
\left[
\exists r\quad
T_{A,d}(X,t;r)>
C\bigl(n+q(X,t)\bigr)\bigl(\log_2(n+t+2)\bigr)^b
\right]
\quad\lor\quad
\left[
\Pr_r\!\left[\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\right]<\frac23
\right].
\]
The defeating input may depend on \(A,d,C,b\), so no single fixed instance must defeat all algorithms. A lower bound only for a restricted class of algorithms does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound proves only its conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also established. The target is an exact existence question about an asymptotic resource bound; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not replace either required proof.
cards.why: The question tests whether a basic dynamic-programming problem can be solved at essentially the cost of reading its input and writing its distinct answers. A positive resolution would avoid paying for a large unused numerical range even when the input contains repeated items. A negative resolution would establish an additional computational cost beyond input and output size for a fundamental exact problem. This is a general algorithmic endpoint, not a request to count solutions or to improve one implementation.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.
cards.why: All-pairs distances are a basic graph primitive. A fixed improvement over the cubic exponent would also change the complexity of several equivalent path, matrix and weighted-triangle problems. Their reductions make the exact weight and machine assumptions essential to interpreting claimed improvements.

cards.context:
If the edges from u to v, u to z and z to v have weights 8, 5 and −2, and there are no other edges, then the shortest u-to-v distance is 3. Negative edges are compatible with a finite exact answer. By contrast, a negative cycle reachable on a u-to-v walk would make its weights unbounded below; the input promise excludes that case. An unreachable ordered pair is reported separately from every finite distance.

The corresponding min-plus matrix operation is \((X\star Y)_{ij}=\min_k(X_{ik}+Y_{kj})\). This uses minimum and addition, whereas ordinary matrix multiplication uses addition and multiplication. Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish subcubic equivalences among APSP, min-plus products, negative edge-weighted triangles and related tasks. Their integer-range theorem carries weight-length factors; Section 4.3 separately gives a randomized strongly polynomial reduction whose overhead depends on the matrix dimension instead. These equivalences preserve existence of some positive saving, not necessarily its exact exponent.

Williams gives a randomized real-RAM bound \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), and a deterministic subpolynomial improvement with a different exponent in the denominator. These are substantial savings over cubic time. Nevertheless, for each fixed \(c>0\), the expression \(n^3/2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{3-c/\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) has an exponent tending to three. That bound alone does not establish \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) for any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). The algorithms permit ordinary computation on finite words as well as comparisons and additions of weights.

Abboud and coauthors study graphs with at most \(d\) distinct weights on the outgoing edges of each vertex. Their Theorem 1.4 gives a fixed exponent saving when \(d\le n^{3-\omega-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(\omega\) is the ordinary matrix-multiplication exponent. This theorem is stated in their bounded-integer word-RAM setting. Theorem 1.2 for one outgoing weight per vertex also has an explicitly stated real-weight extension in Section 4.4. Neither statement covers unrestricted arbitrary real edge weights with up to \(n\) different outgoing weights per vertex.

Akmal and Fischer’s ICALP 2026 Theorem 1 solves zero-sum node-weighted triangle detection in \(O(\mathrm{MM}(n))\) time. Here a triangle’s value is the sum of three vertex weights, and \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\) denotes an admissible running-time bound for ordinary matrix multiplication, with the paper’s monotonicity convention. This is different from independently weighting every edge. The introduction explicitly retains the unresolved fixed-exponent improvement for minimum edge-weighted triangles. The paper uses \(\mathrm{MM}(n)\), rather than asserting that the infimum exponent \(\omega\) must be attained.

Polak and Schmidt’s July 2026 preprint gives an exact APSP algorithm with supplied prediction certificates and running time \(O(n^{2.83}+\eta n)\) for its chosen parameters. The error measure \(\eta\) counts vertex pairs whose induced distance estimates are incorrect or fail the paper’s verification condition. It can be as large as \(n^2\), so this guarantee can still be cubic. Obtaining a sufficiently accurate certificate at no charged cost is an additional input assumption, not a uniform worst-case solution of this card.

Sheffield, Vassilevska Williams and Xi’s August 2026 preprint proves limits on reductions that treat a triangle relation as a black box and must work for every such relation. Its Definition 1 makes this uniformity across relations essential. These limits concern the strength of a particular reduction model, not a lower bound excluding every algorithm for the fixed shortest-path problem.

cards.title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal:
Does exact symmetric weighted travelling salesman admit a classical algorithm with a fixed exponential base below two, allowing bounded-error randomization and polynomial dependence on the input bit length?

Precisely, do there exist a real constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\), positive integers \(K,c,B\) with \(B\ge2\), and one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(\mathcal A\) such that, for every \(n\ge3\) and every complete undirected graph on vertices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with nonnegative integer edge weights encoded as below, both of the following hold?
\[\Pr[\mathcal A\text{ outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle}]\ge\frac23,\]
\[\text{number of charged operations on every random execution}\ \le\ K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+N)^c.\]
Here \(N\) is the total bit length of the explicit input, and the machine model is fixed below using \(B\). All constants and the algorithm precede the quantifiers over the graph, its weights and its encoding length. A deterministic algorithm qualifies as a special case.
cards.definitions:
Instance and encoding. There is one weight \(a_{ij}=a_{ji}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for each unordered pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), and no loops. Weights are exact integers of arbitrary finite bit length. Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary representation of a nonnegative integer \(t\), without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\). Define the self-delimiting code
\[U(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t).\]
The input is \(U(n)\) followed by \(U(a_{ij})\) in lexicographic order of \((i,j)\), for all \(1\le i<j\le n\). Its length in bits is \(N\). No matrix entry is supplied implicitly by an oracle or by a succinct circuit.

Objective and output. A tour is any permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), interpreted cyclically. Set \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\). Its cost and the optimum are
\[\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_{\pi(i),\pi(i+1)},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(a)=\min_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{cost}_a(\pi),\]
where \(S_n\) is the finite set of all such permutations. The graph is complete, so a tour always exists and the minimum is attained. The output is the explicit list of its \(n\) vertex labels, each in \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Any minimum-cost tour is accepted, including any rotation or reversal of one; no uniqueness is required. An invalid list, an explicit failure output, or a suboptimal tour counts as failure. Returning only the optimum value, a bound or an approximate tour is not the required output.

Machine and charges. Use a word RAM whose word length on this input is
\[w=B\left\lceil n+\log_2(N+2)\right\rceil\text{ bits}.\]
The algorithm has one finite program independent of \(n,N\) and all weights. A word is an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); a memory address is one word. The input bits are packed in order into consecutive read-only words, padding the last word with zeros and exposing the true input length. Working memory is initially zero and contains no advice or precomputed tables. Reading or writing one addressed word, copying a word, comparing two words, branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and a left or right shift by a word-specified amount each cost one operation. A shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\) and cost one operation; integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one operation. Division by zero is not permitted. A fresh independent fair random bit costs one operation. Outputting a word, including the final partial word, costs one operation.

Integers longer than one word must be represented and processed using multiple charged operations; there is no unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers or exact real numbers. Reading and decoding the input, constructing tables, generating random bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing the entire tour are included in the clock. Addressing exponential-size subset tables is allowed by the linear-in-\(n\) word length. There is no separate polynomial-space restriction, and no quantum memory, quantum query, advice string or ideal oracle. The fixed polynomial overhead permitted in \(n+N\) accommodates the bit cost of operations on these finite-width words; this does not assert that sequential simulation of arbitrary random memory access has only polynomial overhead.

Probability and uniformity. For each fixed input the probability is over the machine’s independent fair coin stream. The same success guarantee holds on every input, not just on average over a distribution of weights. The running-time bound holds for every possible coin stream, including unsuccessful executions, so it is a worst-case clock rather than an expected-time bound. The constants \(\varepsilon,K,c,B\) cannot depend on the weights, their range or any property of the instance.

Scope. There is no triangle inequality, Euclidean geometry, bounded-weight, small-doubling or other structural promise. Polynomial dependence on \(N\) is allowed; polynomial dependence on the numerical maximum or sum of the weights is not automatically allowed. The fixed saving \(\varepsilon>0\) cannot tend to zero with \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation. A positive proof must specify one uniform classical algorithm and fixed constants, prove the worst-case clock including input and output costs, and prove per-instance success probability at least \(2/3\) for an exactly optimal tour. A negative proof must exclude every such algorithm and every permitted choice of constants in the stated randomized word-RAM model. A conditional lower bound settles only that conditional assertion. A restriction on one dynamic-programming framework, a local-search rule or a polynomial-space algorithm does not exclude all allowed algorithms. Faster Hamiltonicity detection, pseudo-polynomial dependence on weight magnitudes, a restricted weight class, approximate optimization or a quantum algorithm does not meet the full positive target.
cards.why: Exact weighted TSP is a basic test of whether optimization over all orders of a set fundamentally requires base-two exponential time. A fixed reduction of that base would save an exponential factor for every sufficiently large instance, even when costs have arbitrary binary representations. Understanding this boundary would distinguish the difficulty of selecting an optimal tour from the already faster task of merely detecting a tour.

cards.context:
In a complete graph the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle is automatic. The difficulty is selecting the cheapest one among the possible orders. Two tours with almost identical edges can have very different costs, and there is no restriction tying those costs to a geometric distance. The card therefore concerns exact optimization rather than finding any spanning cycle.

The Bellman and Held–Karp algorithms from 1962 give the familiar \(O(2^n n^2)\) arithmetic-operation bound. Stoian’s 2024 result improves this to deterministic time \(2^n n^2/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) in its stated model. This is a real improvement to the long-standing bound, but its exponent is still \(n-o(n)\). It does not give a fixed constant \(\varepsilon>0\) in \((2-\varepsilon)^n\). Arbitrary-length costs still require the bit-length accounting stated in this card.

Björklund gives a Monte Carlo \(O^*(1.657^n)\) algorithm for undirected Hamiltonicity. The weighted extension in Theorem 3 has running time \(O^*(W1.657^n)\), where \(W\) is the sum of the positive integer edge weights. A value \(2^b\) needs only \(b+1\) binary digits, so a factor polynomial in \(W\) can be exponential in the number of input bits used for weights. That extension does not establish the arbitrary-binary-weight target.

The input-bit distinction is not a demand for strongly polynomial arithmetic complexity. A polynomial factor in the total binary encoding length is expressly allowed. What is excluded is hiding dependence on enormous numerical weights inside that factor. Likewise, randomized success must hold on each fixed instance, and every execution must obey the clock. A favorable average over sampled instances is a different guarantee.

The STACS 2026 small-doubling result goes beyond numerically small weights. If \(A\) is the set of distinct input weights and \(A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}\), its promise is \(|A+A|\le C|A|\) for a fixed constant \(C\). Under that additional structure, the stated TSP time matches the unweighted exponential scale, with factors depending on \(C\). Arbitrary weight sets need not have a bounded doubling constant; allowing \(C\) to grow with the input does not give this card’s fixed uniform bound.

Time and memory are separate resources. Dallant and Kozma’s April 2026 paper improves interior time-space tradeoffs: it studies running time \(T^{n+o(n)}\) and space \(S^{n+o(n)}\) for \(2<T<4\), obtaining a product \(ST<3.572\) at one point. An improvement in the product does not assert \(T<2\). The paper explicitly retains the base-two running-time question as open.

The July 2026 follow-up improves the achievable time-space product to roughly \(3.1819\) in the relevant set-system framework. Its lower bound of more than \(3.1818\) is a limitation of that framework, whose parameters describe families of subsets and their chains. It is not a lower bound against arbitrary randomized TSP algorithms. The introduction still identifies \(O^*(2^n)\) as the best known unrestricted classical time scale.

Quantum algorithms form a different comparison. Dallant’s July 2026 theorem assumes quantum computation and quantum random-access memory. The saving from quantum search cannot be treated as an implementation on a classical RAM with independent random bits. The selected target permits classical randomization but supplies no quantum operations.

The ESA paper published on 25 August 2026 similarly reports a time base of 1.859 with a QRAM space base of 1.315. The inspected official abstract makes the quantum resource explicit. Those sub-two numbers therefore do not constitute a classical solution to this card; the full theorem was not independently audited in this review.

The SODA 2026 paper on \(k\)-opt proves that prescribed local-improvement processes can take exponentially many iterations even with an optimal choice of improving move. Its conclusion concerns those processes, including particular three- and four-edge neighborhoods. The card allows all uniform algorithms, and asks for a global optimum, so that lower bound is not the logical negation of the target.

The question also imposes no polynomial-space requirement. An exponential-space algorithm with a fixed time base below two would qualify. Limits on a specific time-space curve, a subset recurrence or a local search rule do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem. The reviewed sources distinguish this open algorithmic question from a conjectured hardness assumption for another problem.

cards.title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
cards.formal:
Do there exist universal constants \(C,B\ge1\), an integer \(b\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(\mathcal A\) with the following property? For every integer pair \(N\ge2\), \(2\le s\le N\), given the pair in binary, \(\mathcal A\) outputs an explicitly listed rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times N}\), with an integer row count \(m\ge1\), in at most \(BN^b\) Turing-machine steps, such that
\[m\le C s\ln(eN/s)\]
and
\[\forall x\in\mathbb R^N\text{ with }|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\le s,\qquad \frac23\|x\|_2^2\le\|Ax\|_2^2\le\frac43\|x\|_2^2?\]
The complete binary output must also have length at most \(BN^b\). The constants and the algorithm are common to every pair \((N,s)\).
cards.definitions:
For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\), set \(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}:x_j\ne0\}\) and \(\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^N x_j^2\). A vector is \(s\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(s\), including the zero vector and all smaller supports. Matrix multiplication has its usual exact real meaning, \((Ax)_i=\sum_{j=1}^N A_{ij}x_j\), with rational entries viewed as reals. The displayed inequalities are the restricted isometry property of order \(s\) with distortion \(\delta=1/3\), for squared Euclidean norms. They must hold simultaneously for every support and every real choice of coefficients; no input distribution, typical-signal exception or probability of correctness is permitted. Columns need not be individually normalized to exactly one, provided the inequalities hold. The matrix is real, not complex.

Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(e=\exp(1)\), so \(\ln(eN/s)=1+\ln(N/s)\), which equals \(1\) when \(s=N\). The real-valued row upper bound is an inequality on the integer chosen by the algorithm; no additional rounding convention is needed. Constants \(C,B,b\) cannot depend on dimension, sparsity, a signal or a support. The case \(s=1\), excluded from the main domain, has the trivial single-row all-ones construction; at \(s=N\), the identity matrix satisfies the geometric requirement. No compression promise such as \(m<N\) is imposed in the dense regime.

Use one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite alphabet, no advice, randomness or oracle, and ordinary bit-level computation. Time is polynomial in the ambient dimension \(N\), not necessarily in the length of its binary input. In particular, the full matrix must be written; a succinct circuit for entries, an existential matrix description, or a real-number computation with unit-cost exact arithmetic is not the stated output model. All computation and output steps count toward the bound.

For a concrete self-delimiting binary encoding, let \(u(t)=1^k0\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) for \(t\ge0\), where \(k\) is the length of the binary expansion of \(t+1\) without leading zeroes. The input is \(u(N)u(s)\) with no extra bits. The output is \(u(m)\) followed in row-major order by the \(mN\) rational entries. Encode \(p/q\) by one sign bit, \(u(|p|)\) and \(u(q)\), where \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\ge1\), \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\), and zero has numerator zero, denominator one and sign bit zero. The sign bit is zero for nonnegative numerators and one for negative numerators. No trailing bits are allowed. This represents every output entry exactly and counts its denominator and numerator lengths. Requiring reduced fractions is an encoding convention, since integer gcd computation is polynomial time. Invalid binary inputs can be rejected without changing the valid-input target; no asymptotic bound is required on malformed encodings.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a uniform deterministic construction exists, or an unconditional proof that it does not in the stated model. A positive answer supplies the finite algorithm and fixed constants and proves termination within the bit-time and output-length bounds, the row inequality and exact RIP for all permitted inputs and all real sparse vectors. The Lean proof must justify any rounding of other representations to the rational output actually printed. A negative answer must rule out every polynomial-time algorithm and choice of universal constants, not just one matrix family or verification method. A conditional lower bound alone is not an unconditional negative answer. Random existence, shorter random seeds, successful numerical recovery, statistical restricted isometry, a different norm, or an asymptotically larger row count does not suffice. This asks whether an algorithm meets the specified exact distortion guarantee; the numerical-target tolerance of 1/100 does not enlarge that guarantee.
cards.why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.
