references.locator: Kanpur 2006; first RIP construction question. Full source checked in the saved Sublinear.info compilation; the separate Fourier-multiplication questions are not adopted.

cards.context:
Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The condition has an equivalent spectral formulation. For a set \(S\) of column indices, let \(A_S\) denote those columns. Every eigenvalue of the real symmetric Gram matrix \(A_S^{\mathsf T}A_S\) must lie in \([2/3,4/3]\) whenever \(1\le|S|\le s\). Thus the target controls every linear combination within every small column set, not only column lengths or pairwise inner products.

Restricted isometry of order \(2t\) implies that different \(t\)-sparse signals have different measurements, since their difference has at most \(2t\) nonzero entries. At distortion \(1/3<\sqrt2-1\), the recovery theorem recorded by Bandeira and coauthors also gives robust reconstruction through \(\ell_1\) minimization. The reconstruction problem and its additional sparsity parameter are consequences, not extra outputs required of this construction task.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

The standard existence benchmark is compatible with rational entries. Normalized Bernoulli matrices with a square number of rows \(m=t^2\) have entries \(\pm1/t\), and rounding a positive row target up to a square changes its size by at most a constant factor. Thus the rational representation requirement does not itself obstruct optimal-order existence. The remaining demand is one deterministic algorithm with the proved time bound.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova give explicit matrices beyond the square-root bottleneck. Their Theorem 1 specifies a restricted relation between row count and column count, with sparsity slightly above the square root of the row count. This is a positive construction theorem in that regime, but does not give the required optimal row order uniformly over all ambient dimensions and sparsities.

Rao’s construction attains the optimal row order using \(O(s\log(N/s)\log s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime stated in the paper, with distortion fixed. Its guarantee remains probabilistic and still uses a seed whose length depends on sparsity and dimension. Reduced randomness is distinct from a deterministic rule whose single output is proved to satisfy RIP on every allowed input.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The parameter range matters. For \(s\) comparable to \(N\), the identity matrix is compatible with the requested row order. The problem also includes all intermediate sparse regimes and arbitrary integer dimensions, whereas many algebraic constructions only give particular dimension sequences or sparsity ranges. Statistical guarantees for typical signals and restricted isometries in \(\ell_1\) are different targets.

The August 2026 preprint by Moonchaisook, Kumam and Sriwongsa gives further deterministic incidence matrices from finite orthogonal spaces. Its guarantee uses \(\delta_s\le(s-1)\mu\), where \(\mu\) is the normalized column coherence, and evaluates particular geometric parameter families. It does not claim the uniform \(O(s\ln(eN/s))\)-row construction required here. Numerical recovery comparisons in that paper are separate from the all-vector RIP theorem.

An older milestone, posed by Strauss at Kanpur 2006 and formerly indexed as TCS-0987, asks for a deterministic polynomial-time construction of a matrix with \(N\) columns and at most \(C s(\log_2(N+2))^a\) rows for fixed constants \(C,a\), preserving every \(s\)-sparse Euclidean norm within a factor of two after normalization. A precise rational-output specialization asks \(\|x\|_2\le\|Mx\|_2\le2\|x\|_2\) for every such vector. This card's optimal-row target implies that milestone: for its matrix \(A\), the rational scaling \(M=(3/2)A\) gives \((3/2)\|x\|_2^2\le\|Mx\|_2^2\le3\|x\|_2^2\), and \(\ln(eN/s)\le1+\ln N\). The weaker milestone does not conversely establish the optimal row count. The source also asks about certification and fast multiplication of Fourier submatrices; those separate questions are not additional requirements of the present construction target.

context_blocks.text: Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The condition has an equivalent spectral formulation. For a set \(S\) of column indices, let \(A_S\) denote those columns. Every eigenvalue of the real symmetric Gram matrix \(A_S^{\mathsf T}A_S\) must lie in \([2/3,4/3]\) whenever \(1\le|S|\le s\). Thus the target controls every linear combination within every small column set, not only column lengths or pairwise inner products.

Restricted isometry of order \(2t\) implies that different \(t\)-sparse signals have different measurements, since their difference has at most \(2t\) nonzero entries. At distortion \(1/3<\sqrt2-1\), the recovery theorem recorded by Bandeira and coauthors also gives robust reconstruction through \(\ell_1\) minimization. The reconstruction problem and its additional sparsity parameter are consequences, not extra outputs required of this construction task.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

The standard existence benchmark is compatible with rational entries. Normalized Bernoulli matrices with a square number of rows \(m=t^2\) have entries \(\pm1/t\), and rounding a positive row target up to a square changes its size by at most a constant factor. Thus the rational representation requirement does not itself obstruct optimal-order existence. The remaining demand is one deterministic algorithm with the proved time bound.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova give explicit matrices beyond the square-root bottleneck. Their Theorem 1 specifies a restricted relation between row count and column count, with sparsity slightly above the square root of the row count. This is a positive construction theorem in that regime, but does not give the required optimal row order uniformly over all ambient dimensions and sparsities.

Rao’s construction attains the optimal row order using \(O(s\log(N/s)\log s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime stated in the paper, with distortion fixed. Its guarantee remains probabilistic and still uses a seed whose length depends on sparsity and dimension. Reduced randomness is distinct from a deterministic rule whose single output is proved to satisfy RIP on every allowed input.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The parameter range matters. For \(s\) comparable to \(N\), the identity matrix is compatible with the requested row order. The problem also includes all intermediate sparse regimes and arbitrary integer dimensions, whereas many algebraic constructions only give particular dimension sequences or sparsity ranges. Statistical guarantees for typical signals and restricted isometries in \(\ell_1\) are different targets.

The August 2026 preprint by Moonchaisook, Kumam and Sriwongsa gives further deterministic incidence matrices from finite orthogonal spaces. Its guarantee uses \(\delta_s\le(s-1)\mu\), where \(\mu\) is the normalized column coherence, and evaluates particular geometric parameter families. It does not claim the uniform \(O(s\ln(eN/s))\)-row construction required here. Numerical recovery comparisons in that paper are separate from the all-vector RIP theorem.

An older milestone, posed by Strauss at Kanpur 2006 and formerly indexed as TCS-0987, asks for a deterministic polynomial-time construction of a matrix with \(N\) columns and at most \(C s(\log_2(N+2))^a\) rows for fixed constants \(C,a\), preserving every \(s\)-sparse Euclidean norm within a factor of two after normalization. A precise rational-output specialization asks \(\|x\|_2\le\|Mx\|_2\le2\|x\|_2\) for every such vector. This card's optimal-row target implies that milestone: for its matrix \(A\), the rational scaling \(M=(3/2)A\) gives \((3/2)\|x\|_2^2\le\|Mx\|_2^2\le3\|x\|_2^2\), and \(\ln(eN/s)\le1+\ln N\). The weaker milestone does not conversely establish the optimal row count. The source also asks about certification and fast multiplication of Fourier submatrices; those separate questions are not additional requirements of the present construction target.

cards.title: Subset Sum below the meet-in-the-middle exponent
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(c\ge1\) and a uniform classical bounded-error randomized algorithm deciding whether a subset of \(n\) positive integers sums to a nonnegative integer target in \(O(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}N^{c})\) worst-case time, where \(N\) is the total binary input length?
cards.definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(N\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(N+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,N\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}N^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.
cards.why: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.

cards.context:
Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. Exponential memory is allowed and addressable in the specified RAM; a polynomial-space restriction would ask a different question.

cards.title: Small Implicit Graph Conjecture
cards.formal: Does every hereditary small graph class \(\mathcal C\) admit an adjacency labeling scheme using at most \(K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits per vertex on every \(n\)-vertex graph in \(\mathcal C\), for some constant \(K\) depending only on \(\mathcal C\)?
cards.definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under isomorphism; it is hereditary when every induced subgraph of every member also belongs to it. Write \(\mathcal C_n\) for its members with labeled vertex set \([n]\). Small means that there is a constant \(c\geq1\) with \(|\mathcal C_n|\leq n!c^n\) for every \(n\geq1\). A labeling scheme consists of an encoder and a decoder, fixed for the class and all input lengths. The encoder, given an adjacency-matrix encoding of \(G\in\mathcal C_n\), assigns one finite binary label to each vertex. The decoder receives only two labels and returns whether the corresponding distinct vertices are adjacent; it receives no graph description, class-membership oracle, additional table or external value of \(n\). Any size information needed by the decoder must be encoded within the labels. Both are deterministic algorithms, with no imposed time bound; encoding must halt on every graph in the class and decoding must halt on every pair of finite labels. Outside-class encoder behavior is unrestricted. All answers for pairs of vertices of an input member must be exact and simultaneous. Label length is the sole resource being bounded. No polynomial-time recognition of the class is assumed. Monotone, which is a stronger condition, means closed under deletion of both vertices and edges; this question assumes only hereditary closure.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of a labeling scheme and a class-dependent logarithmic length constant for every hereditary small class, or exhibit such a class and prove that no scheme satisfying these conditions exists. No efficient encoding or decoding time is required beyond the source’s algorithmic definition. A result for monotone or weakly sparse classes alone does not settle the universal claim.
cards.why: A short global description of every graph does not by itself make adjacency locally decodable from two short vertex descriptions. The conjecture asks whether a precise growth restriction and induced-subgraph closure suffice to bridge this gap.

cards.title: Four-additive spanners with four-thirds-power size
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every connected simple undirected unweighted graph \(G\) on \(n\ge2\) vertices has a spanning subgraph \(H\) with \[|E(H)|\le Cn^{4/3}\qquad\text{and}\qquad d_H(u,v)\le d_G(u,v)+4\quad\text{for all }u,v\in V(G)?\] Distances count edges. New edges, weights and vertices are not permitted, and no construction-time bound is imposed.
cards.definitions: Each original edge has length one. \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path, with \(d_{G}(u,u)=0\). A spanning subgraph H has the same vertex set and a subset of G’s edges, with unchanged unit lengths. If u,v are disconnected in H put \(d_{H}(u,v)=\infty\), so the requirement forces H to be connected. The lower inequality \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) follows from being a subgraph. The cost is number of retained edges; neither construction time nor weights, shortcuts, missing vertices, terminal subsets or faults are part of the model. New weighted edges would be an emulator and are not allowed. Restricting to connected inputs only removes disconnected bookkeeping; applying a universal bound componentwise recovers its usual all-graph form.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one constant \(C\) suffices for every graph and all vertex pairs. A refutation must give, for every proposed \(C\), a graph for which every spanning subgraph with at most \(Cn^{4/3}\) edges violates the additive bound on some pair.
cards.why: The +4 additive-spanner regime is the classical remaining constant-error sparsity-exponent gap, making it a central distance-compression problem rather than a peripheral parameter choice.

cards.title: Additive-error exponent of linear-size spanners
cards.formal: For every fixed real edge-budget coefficient \(c\ge1\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)=\inf\{a\ge0:A_c(n)+1=O_c(n^a)\text{ as }n\to\infty\}.\] Here \(A_c(n)\), defined below, is the largest, over simple undirected unweighted \(n\)-vertex graphs, minimum additive all-pairs distance error of a spanning subgraph with at most \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) edges and the same connected components. The edge budget is genuinely linear; no hidden logarithmic factor in the budget is allowed.
cards.definitions: For every \(n\geq1\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on \([n]\). Every edge has length one. A spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) has the same vertices, retains only original edges, and must have the same connected components as \(G\). There are no Steiner vertices, shortcut edges or changed edge lengths. Let \[\Delta(G,H)=\max_{u,v:\,d_G(u,v)<\infty}\bigl(d_H(u,v)-d_G(u,v)\bigr),\qquad A_c(n)=\max_{G\in\mathcal G_n}\min_{\substack{H\subseteq G,\ |E(H)|\leq\lfloor cn\rfloor\\ H\text{ preserves components}}}\Delta(G,H).\] Distances count edges. Pairs with \(u=v\) are included, so the maximum is defined and nonnegative even in an edgeless graph. A spanning forest is feasible for \(c\geq1\); thus the quantity is finite. This measures optimal structural approximation, not the running time for finding a spanner; no algorithmic cost bound is imposed. The explicit coefficient \(c\) makes the source’s unspecified linear-size constant a parameter of the target. Define the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ A_c(n)+1\le Cn^a\}.\] For each fixed real \(c\ge1\), the constants may depend on \(c\) and \(a\), but not on the graph or \(n\). Adding one removes zero-value conventions without changing any positive power of growth. A spanning forest has finite distances at most \(n-1\) within its components, so \(0\le x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)\le1\). The infimum need not be attained; no ordinary logarithmic-growth limit is assumed. In particular, exponent zero permits polylogarithmic or other subpolynomial error and does not promise bounded error.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all real \(c\ge1\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(c)-x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(c)\le x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)\le U(c)\) and \(U(c)-L(c)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). Use the same edge budget \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) on both sides.
cards.why: The linear edge regime compresses a graph to a constant number of retained edges per vertex. Determining its unavoidable distance loss would quantify a fundamental limit on how accurately arbitrary graph metrics can survive such strong sparsification.

cards.title: Explicit binary codes with efficient list decoding up to capacity
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\delta,R\) satisfying
\[
 0<\delta<\frac12,\qquad 0<R<1-H_2(\delta),
 \qquad H_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t),
\]
there are uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and list-decoding algorithms for binary codes
\[
 E_m:\{0,1\}^{m}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{N(m)}
 \quad(m\ge1),\qquad \frac{m}{N(m)}\ge R,
\]
such that every \(E_m\) is injective and the decoder, on every received word \(y\in\{0,1\}^{N(m)}\), outputs exactly
\[
 \{x\in\{0,1\}^{m}:d_H(E_m(x),y)\le\lfloor\delta N(m)\rfloor\}?
\]
The binary alphabet is fixed even as the gap to capacity tends to zero. The algorithms may depend on the two fixed constants but must handle all message lengths.
cards.definitions:
A binary word is a finite sequence of zeros and ones. Hamming distance \(d_H(u,v)\) counts the coordinates at which equal-length words differ. A code here is an injective encoding of every \(m\)-bit message into a word of a common length \(N(m)\ge m\); it need not be linear or systematic. Its rate is the number of message bits divided by the number of encoded bits.

For each fixed admissible pair \((\delta,R)\), the claimed construction consists of finite deterministic classical multitape Turing programs for an encoder and decoder, constants \(K>0\) and integer \(b\ge1\), and an integer length function \(N(m)\). On an input message \(x\) of length \(m\), the encoder outputs \(E_m(x)\) in at most \(K(m+1)^b\) steps; the output length depends only on \(m\). Thus the length and code construction are effective. On input \((1^m,y)\), where \(y\) has length \(N(m)\), the decoder halts in at most \(K(N(m)+1)^b\) steps. It explicitly lists all qualifying messages, once each, and no others; an empty list is allowed. All reading, code construction, arithmetic, auxiliary computation and output are charged. There is no nonuniform advice, free block-length-dependent code table, external oracle or uncharged preprocessing.

The polynomial output-time bound also bounds the list size polynomially in the block length. No constant list-size bound is imposed. Requiring an exact list is equivalent to allowing additional candidates that can be removed within polynomial time using the encoder and a distance check, provided every qualifying message is included.

The decoder must work for every received word, so the errors may be adversarial. The task is global list decoding, not unique decoding, local decoding, erasure correction or reliable communication only under a random-noise distribution. The code must be binary; a larger alphabet whose size grows as the capacity gap shrinks is insufficient.

The constants, programs and polynomial exponent may depend arbitrarily on the fixed pair \((\delta,R)\). No polynomial dependence on the inverse capacity gap and no single algorithm taking these constants as variable input is requested. Rational constants give a precise countable formulation without changing the strict-slack capacity target: any real pair strictly inside the region is dominated by rational parameters with a slightly larger permitted error fraction and a slightly larger rate. A family is supplied for every message length; it need not attain every possible block length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply the uniform algorithms, encoding injectivity, rate bound, exhaustive decoding correctness and polynomial running-time bounds for every fixed admissible parameter pair. A negative answer must refute this quantified existence assertion; an unproved hardness assumption establishes only a conditional obstruction.

A randomized code construction, inefficient exhaustive decoding, capacity over a variable alphabet, success only on randomly corrupted words, or a construction for only one rate/radius pair does not meet the target. The goal approaches the binary capacity from below; it does not ask to exceed that information-theoretic limit. No numerical tolerance is applied to this existence question.
cards.why: Explicit binary codes with efficient adversarial list decoding throughout the capacity region would close a central gap between information-theoretic existence and deterministic usable constructions. Fixing the smallest alphabet prevents larger-symbol constructions from bypassing the main difficulty.

cards.title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for Steiner Tree
cards.formal:
Determine the real constant \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\), the infimum of achievable expected-cost approximation ratios for undirected weighted Steiner Tree under worst-case polynomial running time. For the valid instances \(\mathcal I\) and the uniform randomized, always-feasible algorithms \(\mathcal A\) defined below, put
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}=
\left\{r\in\mathbb R:
r\ge1\ \land\
\exists A\in\mathcal A\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\
\mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I;\omega))\right]
\le r\,\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=\inf\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}.
\]
Supply an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial time bound may depend on \(r\), but must work for every valid instance. The expectation concerns output cost, not running time. No complexity assumption is part of the definition. The requested error is additive in this dimensionless approximation ratio.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A valid instance \(I=(n,E,R,w)\) consists of a connected simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), a set of terminals \(R\subseteq[n]\) with \(2\le |R|\le n\), and nonnegative rational weights \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices; each pair occurs at most once. Connected means every two vertices are joined by a finite path. The whole graph, terminal list and all weights are explicitly given. There is no restriction on the topology, number of terminals, weight magnitudes, or ratio between positive weights.

A feasible solution is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) such that the graph on vertex set
\[
W=R\cup\bigcup_{\{u,v\}\in F}\{u,v\}
\]
with edge set \(F\) is connected and has no cycle. Thus the output is one tree containing all terminals; its other vertices may be any subset of the available nonterminals. Its cost and the optimum are
\[
\operatorname{cost}_I(F)=\sum_{e\in F}w(e),
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=
\min\{\operatorname{cost}_I(F):F\text{ is a feasible solution of }I\}.
\]
Every valid instance has a feasible solution, so the minimum is over a nonempty finite set and is attained. Output edges must be original input edges. Neither new Steiner points outside \([n]\), a separate cost for selected vertices, a set of pairwise connection demands, nor directed edges are part of this problem.

The following encoding fixes the full bit cost. Write each weight uniquely as \(p_e/q_e\), where \(p_e\ge0\), \(q_e\ge1\), and the integers are relatively prime, so a zero weight is encoded as \(0/1\). Order edges lexicographically by their endpoints \(u<v\), obtaining \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), and order terminal labels increasingly, obtaining \(r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Form one list of integers consisting of \(n\), the explicit vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), \(m\), the four entries \(u,v,p_{e_j},q_{e_j}\) for each edge \(e_j=\{u,v\}\) in order, then \(h,r_1,\ldots,r_h\). Encode each integer in ordinary binary without leading zeros, with \(0\) represented by one zero. Put a separator \(\#\) between consecutive integers and no trailing separator. Finally encode the three symbols by \(0\mapsto00\), \(1\mapsto01\), \(\#\mapsto10\). The length of the resulting binary string is \(L(I)\). A valid output is the list consisting of \(|F|\) followed by the strictly increasing indices of the selected edges in \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), using the same integer, separator and binary-symbol encoding. All numerator, denominator, endpoint and output bits count; arithmetic on rational numbers is not a unit-cost operation.

An algorithm is a single probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only input tape, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, and a sequential output tape. The input is delimited by end markers. Each transition reads the scanned symbols, can write one symbol per writable tape, and moves each head by at most one cell; it counts as one step. A transition may additionally read at most one fresh independent fair random bit. The program and tape count do not depend on the input length. There is no advice, oracle, real-arithmetic instruction or uncharged preprocessing. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the random bits.

The set \(\mathcal A\) contains exactly the machines \(A\) for which there exist integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, on every binary input \(z\) and every random sequence \(\omega\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\), the machine halts within \(C(|z|+1)^k\) steps, and on every valid instance and every such sequence its output encodes a feasible solution. Invalid inputs may receive any output within that same bound. The constants \(C,k\) may depend on \(A\), but not on the instance or the random bits. This is a bound on every execution, not merely an expected-time bound.

The random sequence \(\omega\) has the product distribution of independent fair bits; there is no probability distribution on inputs. Since at most \(C(L(I)+1)^k\) bits can be read, the expected cost is the finite average over all bit strings of that length, each with equal probability, disregarding unused bits. Infeasibility has no permitted error probability. The multiplicative bound must hold on every valid instance, with no additive cost term or exception for small inputs. Instances with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\) are included: their expected output cost must be zero. As every finite random execution has positive probability and costs are nonnegative, this requires zero output cost on every execution of such an instance.

Known polynomial-time approximations make \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{ST}}\) nonempty; it is bounded below by \(1\), so its infimum is a finite real number. An algorithm attaining exactly \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) need not exist. In particular, \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}=1\) would mean that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some eligible algorithm achieves ratio at most \(1+\varepsilon\), without requiring an exact algorithm or one program that takes \(\varepsilon\) as an additional input.

For the conditional results in the context, use [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np) and [RP](definitions.html#randomization) as defined in the shared glossary. No equality or separation among these classes is assumed in \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\).
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer supplies an unambiguous real value \(a\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
\left|a-\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\right|\le\frac1{100}
\]
for precisely the instance class and machine model above. A certified interval \([\ell,u]\) with
\[
\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u,\qquad u-\ell\le\frac1{50}
\]
qualifies through \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). The value need not be an integer, rational number or decimal expansion; exact determination is welcome but is not required. Merely renaming the defining infimum does not specify an answer.

The proof must respect the infimum's endpoint convention. To establish an upper bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le u\), achievable ratios approaching \(u\) from above suffice; an algorithm achieving \(u\) itself is not required. Equivalently, one may prove that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an eligible algorithm whose expected cost on every instance is at most \((u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\). A lower bound \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) must exclude every eligible algorithm from achieving each ratio \(r\) with \(1\le r<\ell\). For every such \(r\) and algorithm, this requires some valid instance with expected cost strictly greater than \(r\operatorname{OPT}\).

A hardness bound under an unproved complexity assumption proves only the corresponding conditional statement. It does not by itself certify the unconditional constant requested here. A gap for a particular linear-programming relaxation, the worst case of one selected algorithm, a guarantee only for a restricted graph family, or computations on finitely many input sizes do not determine this infimum over all eligible algorithms and all valid instances.
cards.why: Steiner Tree is a basic network-design problem and a recurring subproblem in more general connectivity objectives. Determining its efficient approximation threshold would establish how closely polynomial-time algorithms can approach optimal connection cost in unrestricted weighted graphs. The target compares all algorithms, making it broader than the accuracy of one method or the strength of one relaxation.

cards.context:
The source model is an undirected weighted graph with a terminal subset; passing to shortest-path distances preserves the approximation problem. This card retains the canonical graph input with nonnegative rational weights, explicit binary encoding, worst-case polynomial time and expected feasible-output cost. These machine and encoding conventions make the inherited numerical target precise.

Byrka, Grandoni, Rothvoß and Sanità obtain a polynomial-time \((\ln 4+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), and their full account derandomizes the algorithm. Consequently the infimum satisfies the unconditional bounds \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\le\ln 4\), without an assertion that the upper endpoint is attained.

Traub and Zenklusen obtain the same limiting guarantee by a combinatorial algorithm, first presented in their 2021 preprint and SODA 2022 paper and incorporated into their 2025 journal article. Their model discussion explicitly explains the compatibility of positive and nonnegative edge weights.

Chlebík and Chlebíková prove NP-hardness of achieving factors below \(96/95\). For the always-feasible randomized expected-cost model of this card, their gap reduction excludes those factors assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\); that randomized-model consequence is an editorial inference, not an unconditional lower bound.

The 2024 result bounding the bidirected cut relaxation's integrality gap by \(1.9988\) settles a different question about a specified relaxation.

A July 2026 primary paper still reports \(\ln 4+\varepsilon\) as the best known general Steiner Tree approximation guarantee. The checked bounds do not determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{ST}}\) within absolute error \(1/100\).

cards.title: Strongly polynomial planar minimum-cost flow
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm for minimum-cost flow in a planar directed graph whose worst-case number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is \(o(n^{2}\log(n+2))\), where \(n\) is the number of vertices? The algorithm must return an exact minimum-cost feasible flow, or correctly report infeasibility, for all rational capacities, costs and vertex supplies.
cards.definitions: The input is a finite directed graph with vertex set \([n]\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. The underlying undirected graph is planar, and a combinatorial planar embedding is supplied. Thus the number of arcs is \(O(n)\). Each arc \(a\) has a finite rational capacity \(u_a\geq0\) and rational cost \(c_a\), and each vertex \(v\) has rational supply \(b_v\), with \(\sum_v b_v=0\). All numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary; no magnitude bound is imposed. A feasible flow assigns rational \(f_a\) with \(0\leq f_a\leq u_a\) and \(\sum_{a\text{ out of }v} f_a-\sum_{a\text{ into }v}f_a=b_v\) at each vertex. Its cost is \(\sum_a c_a f_a\). Strong polynomiality means a bound polynomial in \(n\) on exact rational arithmetic operations, comparisons and index/memory operations, independent of all numeric bit lengths, together with a polynomial bound in total input bit length on every intermediate number’s encoding length. Arithmetic uses addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values. The algorithm has finite uniform code and no advice, randomness or oracle. The little-o improvement means that there is a function \(T(n)\) bounding its operation count on every such \(n\)-vertex input with \(T(n)/(n^{2}\log(n+2))\to0\). The source’s instruction to beat the stated bound is interpreted as an asymptotic little-o improvement, not merely a smaller leading constant. The simple planar-network convention prevents arbitrarily many parallel arcs from hiding an unbounded input size in \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the exact flow guarantee, little-o operation bound and polynomial intermediate bit lengths, or prove that no such deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm exists. A speedup for bounded numerical data, an approximation algorithm, or a lower leading constant at the same asymptotic order does not answer the stated question.
cards.why: This asks how much planarity can accelerate exact flow optimization when numerical magnitudes cannot enter the operation count. It separates combinatorial graph structure from progress that relies on bounded capacities and costs.

cards.title: Complexity of general vertex-connectivity augmentation
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a simple undirected graph \(G\) and a target \(1\leq\lambda<|V(G)|\), computes the minimum number of new edges needed to make \(G\) \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected, when every missing edge is available at unit cost?
cards.definitions: The graph is finite, undirected and simple, with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\geq2\), and an explicit binary adjacency matrix. The integer \(\lambda\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) is part of the input, encoded in binary, and need not be fixed. The available links are exactly \(\binom{V(G)}{2}\setminus E(G)\). An augmentation is any subset \(F\) of these links; its cost is \(|F|\), and no new vertices are permitted. The graph \(G+F\) is \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected if deleting any set of fewer than \(\lambda\) vertices leaves a connected graph. The condition \(\lambda<n\) excludes ambiguous conventions on graphs with too few vertices. The optimum is finite because adding every missing edge produces a complete graph. The algorithm must output the exact minimum integer; equivalently it may decide, for a binary budget \(k\geq0\), whether some augmentation has \(|F|\leq k\). The two tasks are polynomial-time equivalent using the finite \(\binom n2\) budget range. Running time is worst-case bit time bounded by one fixed polynomial in the whole input length, with no exponent or multiplicative nonpolynomial dependence on \(\lambda\). The input graph may have arbitrary initial connectivity; there is no promise that the target increases connectivity by only one.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time exact algorithm for all target values, or prove that no such algorithm exists. An algorithm polynomial only for fixed target connectivity, a parameterized algorithm exponential in the target or budget, an approximation, or a one-increment result does not meet the guarantee. A proof of NP-hardness alone establishes the implication from a polynomial-time augmentation algorithm to \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Using this implication for an unconditional negative answer also requires a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
cards.why: The question asks whether optimal resilience to vertex failures can be added efficiently when all new links have the same cost and are freely available. These simple input conditions isolate the difficulty of vertex connectivity itself from costly or forbidden links.

cards.title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
cards.formal: Do there exist one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and a constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(A\) outputs \[\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j)\in[n]^2:i<j\ \text{and}\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\] exactly, using at most \(Cn\) machine instructions in the worst case? The word length and allowed instructions are specified below. The constant and the program must be independent of \(n\) and \(\pi\).
cards.definitions: The input contains \(n\) and the array \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\), promised to contain each integer from one through \(n\) exactly once. The output is the single integer inversion count, between zero and \(n(n-1)/2\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Choose \(d\ge3\), so the count fits in a word. All constants are independent of the permutation and \(n\). No randomness is allowed. The values are already ranks, so no conversion from arbitrary ordered keys is required. The array has one entry per word; no compressed representation, streaming restriction or comparison-only restriction is imposed. The algorithm may use auxiliary random-access memory, but allocating, initializing and accessing that memory consumes the counted steps. The output is one word containing the exact nonnegative integer. Neither a list of all inverted pairs nor individual per-position counts are required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence assertion or its negation. A positive answer must specify one fixed program and prove its exact count and linear worst-case running time for every legal permutation in the specified model. A negative answer must exclude all such programs and all fixed constants. A relative-error estimate, an algorithm that is linear only on nearly sorted inputs, an expected-time randomized algorithm, or an improvement still superlinear in the worst case does not meet this target. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication.
cards.why: Exact inversion counting compresses a permutation’s pairwise disorder into one integer and is a fundamental offline aggregation task. Its complexity remains separated from the cost of sorting already rank-bounded integers. The 2025 hardness connections show that a linear-time solution would also change the algorithmic frontier for packed-string processing.

In that Dictionary Matching problem, the input consists of a packed binary text occupying a linear number of logarithmic-size words and a linear number of patterns, each of logarithmic bit length; the output says whether any pattern occurs. cards.title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for every integer \(m\ge 1\), every family \(S\subseteq 2^{[m]}\), every weight vector \(w\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) and every \(0<\varepsilon <1\), there is a reweighting \(\tilde\{w\}\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) with at most \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) nonzero coordinates and satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\le \sum _{i\in A}\tilde\{w\}_{i}\le (1+\varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\) simultaneously for every \(A\in S\)?
cards.definitions: Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots ,m\}\), and S is any finite collection of subsets, including possibly the empty collection. The support of w̃ is \(\{i:\tilde\{w\}_{i}>0\}\); coordinates outside it are dropped, while retained coordinates may receive arbitrary nonnegative real weights. No normalization such as \(\sum w_{i}=1\) is imposed. Following the source’s witness definition, a chain of length \(\ell\) consists of distinct coordinates \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{\ell}\) and distinct sets \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{\ell}\in S\) with \(a_{i}\in A_{i}\) for every i and \(a_{j}\notin A_{i}\) whenever \(i<j\). \(CL(S)\) is the maximum possible \(\ell\), allowing \(\ell =0\). Equivalently, take the union-closure \(U(S)=\{\bigcup T:T\subseteq S\}\), including the empty union; \(CL(S)\) is the largest number of strict inclusions in an ascending chain starting from \(\varnothing\) in \(U(S)\). Thus \(CL(S)=0\) when S is empty or contains only \(\varnothing\). It is not merely the largest chain in the original family. A \((1\pm \varepsilon )\) sparsifier is a reweighting satisfying the simultaneous inequalities in the statement. Sets of original weight zero must retain weight exactly zero. All data and weights are quantified mathematically; the question places no running-time, oracle-access, randomness or bit-complexity requirement on finding w̃. The same C must work independently of m, S, w and \(\varepsilon\). The source allows \(\varepsilon >0\); values \(\varepsilon \ge 1\) admit the zero reweighting, so restricting the nontrivial question to \(0<\varepsilon <1\) preserves it.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence bound with one absolute constant C, or refute it by showing that for every C there are a family, weights and an accuracy parameter for which every multiplicative sparsifier needs more than \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) coordinates. Bounds with an additional unbounded logarithmic factor do not meet the conjecture; an efficient construction is not required.
cards.why: Would give a sharp structural bound for simultaneous multiplicative compression of arbitrary weighted set families. It asks whether chain length and squared inverse accuracy fully account for the necessary support, without logarithmic losses.

references.title: Multiplicative Error Set System Sparsification: A Simpler Proof via Chain Length Contraction
references.authors: Brakensiek, Joshua; Guruswami, Venkatesan; Putterman, Aaron
references.locator: ICALP 2026, article 44. Introduction and Theorem 2, Section 2.1’s sparsifier and chain definitions (especially Definition 6), and Conjecture 23 on p. 44:13 read. The conjecture asks for an existential support bound, not an efficient construction.

cards.context:
A coordinate can represent an edge, a constraint or a position of a codeword. A sparsifier removes coordinates and compensates by reweighting those it keeps. The same reweighting must preserve every specified set’s weight, including small-weight sets, which makes multiplicative error stronger than a global additive-error allowance.

If S contains only the whole nonempty universe, its chain length is one. Placing the entire total weight on any one coordinate preserves that sole set weight exactly. A large universe alone therefore does not force a large sparsifier.

If S consists of all m singleton sets, the original sets are pairwise incomparable. Their unions nevertheless form a chain of m strict inclusions, so \(CL(S)=m\). With unit original weights and \(\varepsilon <1\), every singleton must retain positive weight; all m coordinates are necessary. This explains why the conjecture uses chain length in the union-closure.

The paper gives support \(O(CL(S)\cdot \log ^{2}(CL(S)/\varepsilon )\cdot (\log  \log (CL(S)/\varepsilon ))^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2})\), with the usual constant-size adjustments to logarithms near one. This already removes dependence on the universe size from the overhead. Conjecture 23 asks whether all remaining logarithmic factors can be removed.

The source notes that its main existence bound is not efficiently implementable in full generality. The conjecture itself only asks whether a small reweighting exists. Proving such a bound for every set family would already sharpen broad cut, code and constraint sparsification principles.

cards.title: Complexity of planar 3-edge-colorability
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple planar graph \(G\), decides whether its edges can be properly colored with three colors?
cards.definitions: The input graph is undirected, without loops or parallel edges, and encoded by an adjacency matrix on the labeled vertex set \([n]\). The planarity promise means it admits a crossing-free embedding in the plane; no embedding is required as input. A proper three-edge-coloring is a function \(\chi:E(G)\to\{1,2,3\}\) assigning different colors to any two distinct edges with a common endpoint. Graphs may be disconnected, have bridges or isolated vertices, and need not be regular. A vertex of degree greater than three forces rejection, but no other special degree pattern or augmentation promise is imposed. Running time is worst-case bit time \(C(n+1)^k\) for fixed constants on a deterministic Turing machine, with no advice, randomness or oracle. The answer must be exact on every planar input. A total-language version may reject nonplanar encodings, since planarity can itself be tested in polynomial time. This card asks for decision, not for a prescribed structural characterization of all colorable graphs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for all planar inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. NP-hardness together with a Lean theorem conditional on P ≠ NP establishes conditional intractability and must be labeled as such; it is not by itself an unconditional refutation. Solving only cubic graphs or graphs admitting a particular augmentation is insufficient.
cards.why: This is a basic unresolved coloring decision problem on planar graphs with very small maximum degree. A resolution would clarify exactly how far the algorithmic consequences of the Four-Color Theorem extend beyond regular planar graphs.

cards.title: Polynomial-time minimum-total-length disjoint paths for fixed k
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an undirected unweighted graph G and k prescribed terminal pairs \((s_{i},t_{i})\), outputs pairwise vertex-disjoint paths \(P_{i}\) from \(s_{i}\) to \(t_{i}\) minimizing \(\sum _{i}|E(P_{i})|\), or correctly reports that no such collection exists? Randomized algorithms with success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input are admitted in this reading, consistently with the randomized \(k=2\) baseline cited by the source. Polynomial degree and constants may depend on k; an FPT bound with exponent independent of k is not requested.
cards.definitions: G is a finite simple connected undirected graph with n numbered vertices and unit length on every edge, encoded by an adjacency matrix and the terminal labels. Take the 2k terminals to be distinct; repeated endpoints across different pairs make vertex-disjointness infeasible, and a pair with \(s_{i}=t_{i}\) uses the zero-edge path at that vertex and can be handled separately. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. Vertex-disjointness includes endpoints and means \(V(P_{i})\cap V(P_{j})=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Pairings are fixed: connecting a source to a different pair’s target is not acceptable. Define OPT as the minimum sum of edge counts over all feasible collections and set OPT=∞ when there is none. The output consists of the k vertex sequences of an optimal collection, or an infeasibility answer. For each fixed k the algorithm is a probabilistic Turing machine, with one finite program handling all n and all inputs for that k, running in at most \(C_{k}(n+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps on every random-bit sequence. Constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\) are independent of n. With probability at least \(2/3\) over its independent fair bits, the full output must be correct, including exact optimality. A deterministic algorithm is included as the zero-error case. The formulation asks for polynomial time for each fixed k and does not demand a uniform procedure generating these programs as k varies. The source compares this target with k-DSP, which requires every \(P_{i}\) separately to have length \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s_{i},t_{i})\). Such a collection, when it exists, has the smallest possible total length; minimum-total-length routing must also handle inputs where disjoint routes exist but no collection of individually shortest routes exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish or refute polynomial-time solvability, with the stated bounded-error allowance, for every fixed \(k\ge 3\). A positive answer must output an exactly optimal collection or detect infeasibility on all inputs. A negative answer must exclude every allowed bounded-error polynomial-time algorithm for at least one fixed \(k\ge3\). Any additional hypothesis used to prove this exclusion must itself be established. Hardness only when k grows with n, an FPT lower bound, approximation, or an algorithm restricted to individually shortest paths does not decide this question.
cards.why: Would determine whether exact length optimization preserves the polynomial-time solvability of undirected disjoint routing with a fixed number of prescribed terminal pairs.

cards.title: A dichotomy for edge deletion with finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs
cards.formal: For every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is the following decision problem either in \(\mathrm{P}\) or \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integer \(k\geq0\), decide whether there is \(S\subseteq E\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) has no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of \(\mathcal F\).
cards.definitions: A simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges. For \(U\subseteq V\), its induced subgraph contains every edge of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). Graph isomorphism is an adjacency-preserving bijection of vertex sets. The class of \(\mathcal F\)-free graphs consists of all finite graphs with none of the forbidden induced subgraphs; it is hereditary, meaning closed under taking induced subgraphs. Deleting \(S\) retains all vertices and exactly the edges in \(E\setminus S\). Edges cannot be added, vertices cannot be removed, and every deleted edge costs one. The empty graph and the empty forbidden family are permitted. The input graph uses its adjacency matrix on numbered vertices; \(k\) is binary. The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before the input varies and is not part of the input to this decision problem. For each fixed family, its finite graph list may be built into the program, and polynomial exponents and constants may depend on it. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}\) if a deterministic Turing machine decides it in polynomial input length. It is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if polynomial-size certificates can be checked in polynomial time. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(K\) to \(L\) is one deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) on finite binary strings such that \(x\in K\) iff \(f(x)\in L\). NP-completeness means membership in NP and such a reduction from every NP language. Each problem here is in NP because a deletion set can be checked and all induced copies of the finitely many fixed forbidden graphs can be enumerated in polynomial time. The dichotomy is inclusive; it assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) nor its negation.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite family \(\mathcal F\) satisfies the stated P-or-NP-complete alternative. Alternatively specify one finite family and prove in Lean that its decision problem is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated reductions. A theorem for a single forbidden graph or a fixed selection of graph classes is insufficient. No separate effective procedure for classifying the family \(\mathcal F\) is imposed by this proposition.
cards.why: Edge deletion is a basic graph-repair operation whose tractability changes with the desired hereditary property. A dichotomy for every finite forbidden list would explain this variation across many graph classes and locate a general boundary between efficient repair and NP-completeness.

cards.context:
The survey describes the absence of a general polynomial-time versus NP-hard classification for hereditary edge deletion. Editorial specialization: this card selects the finite-forbidden-induced-subgraph domain, giving the graph properties a finite description and ensuring that every resulting decision problem is in NP. The source’s broader direction also encompasses hereditary classes without such a finite forbidden list.

There are immediate tractable families. If the only forbidden graph is a single edge, all input edges must be removed. If the forbidden graphs are the three-vertex path and the triangle, every remaining component must be an isolated vertex or an isolated edge: maximizing the retained edges is maximum matching, which is polynomial-time solvable.

Deleting an edge can create a forbidden induced subgraph. For example, removing one edge from a triangle creates an induced three-vertex path. Consequently, eliminating all forbidden copies initially visible in the input need not produce a valid final graph.

The survey contrasts edge deletion with the classical broad hardness theorem for vertex removal into nontrivial hereditary properties. That contrast motivates a structural classification for edge operations; it does not transfer the vertex-removal theorem to the problem defined here.

The 2023 journal version still states the absence of a general edge-removal dichotomy. Its detailed tables also concern parameterized algorithms and kernelization. A bound depending arbitrarily on the deletion budget, or the existence of a polynomial kernel, addresses a different question from ordinary polynomial time in the entire input.

Completing the dichotomy would rule out NP-intermediate behavior inside this finite-description family, even if such behavior exists elsewhere in NP. Proving just that some cases are hard is weaker: every finite forbidden family must fall into one of the stated alternatives.

cards.title: Černý conjecture
cards.formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with \(n\ge1\) states have a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\)? The statement quantifies over all finite nonempty alphabets. A reset word sends every possible initial state to the same state, under the transition model below.
cards.definitions: An automaton is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta)\), where \(|Q|=n\ge1\), \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty alphabet and \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\) is total. Extend it to words by \(\delta(q,\epsilon)=q\) and \(\delta(q,wa)=\delta(\delta(q,w),a)\). A word \(w\) is a reset word if \(|\{\delta(q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\); its length is its number of letters. Synchronizing means that at least one reset word exists. Its final state is not prescribed. Initial and accepting states play no role, and the empty word handles \(n=1\). There is no strong-connectivity, fixed-alphabet or other structural promise. Partial or nondeterministic automata, and synchronization of only a prescribed subset of states, are different models. No time bound for constructing the word is imposed. In the context, \(T(n)\) denotes the maximum shortest-reset-word length over all such synchronizing automata with \(n\) states; duplicate letter transformations can be removed, so this maximum exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that every synchronizing \(n\)-state automaton has a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\), or exhibit a synchronizing automaton and prove that every word up to that length fails to reset it.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

references.locator: Version 1, 22 July 2026; abstract and §1; restricted-class preprint claim, not a general resolution

cards.context:
The selected binary question is the Černý conjecture. Its \((n-1)^2\) upper bound would match the classical worst-case family. A counterexample to the universal bound also answers this card; it need not determine the entire extremal function.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(L(D)=L(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma^{*}\), and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

cards.context:
All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq L\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(L=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.

cards.title: Generalized star-height problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\) and a regular language \(L\subseteq \Sigma^{*}\) such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma^{*}\) is the set of all finite words over \(\Sigma\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\). A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from \(\varnothing , \varepsilon\), and the letters \(a\in \Sigma\) using binary union \(E\cup F\), concatenation EF, complement \(E^{c}\), and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, \(\{\varepsilon\}, \{a\}\), language union, all concatenations uv with \(u\in L(E)\) and \(v\in L(F), \Sigma^{*}\setminus L(E)\), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of \(L(E)\), including power zero \(\{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(h(\varnothing )=h(\varepsilon )=h(a)=0, h(E\cup F)=h(\mathrm{EF})=\max \{h(E),h(F)\}, h(E^{c})=h(E)\), and \(h(E*)=h(E)+1\). Define \(h_{g}(L)=\min \{h(E):L(E)=L\}\), which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether \(h_{g}(L)>1\) for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation \((E^{c}\cup F^{c})^{c}\) and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
cards.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

cards.context:
Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over \(\Sigma =\{a,b\}\), the language of all words has the ordinary expression \((a\cup b)\)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply \(\varnothing ^{c}\) and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is \((\Sigma^{*}ab\Sigma^{*})^{c}\); replacing each displayed \(\Sigma^{*}\) by \(\varnothing ^{c}\) makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet \(\{a\}\), the even-length language \((aa)\)* has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes \(x^{N}=x^{N+1}\) for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.

The ordinary, or restricted, star-height problem disallows complement. In that setting, arbitrarily high heights exist and the minimum height is computable. These facts cannot be transferred to generalized height by reusing an ordinary expression or an automaton cycle measure: allowing complement introduces additional descriptions that the old lower-bound argument may not exclude. Pin’s problem page explicitly distinguishes these two versions and separately lists the existence of height two and the algorithmic computation of height.

Pin, Straubing and Thérien prove height at most one for several algebraic classes, including languages recognized by finite nilpotent groups of class at most two, and eliminate a proposed height-two example. They also show that every regular language is the inverse image of an ordinary height-one language under a suitable word morphism. That representation does not bound generalized height without an additional closure statement: inverse morphisms preserve regularity, but their preservation of generalized height one is part of the unresolved issue.

Bourne and Ruškuc extend the height-one territory using factor-counting arguments. Their results cover specified counting cases and languages recognized by Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. A factor here is a contiguous occurrence of a word, which differs from counting scattered subsequences. The theorem handles a substantial recognizing-semigroup class, while leaving the existence of a language above height one unresolved.

Daviaud and Paperman study languages generated from sets u* with a single word u, under Boolean or lattice operations and, in some cases, quotients. They give effective equational characterizations of those particular classes. These are deliberately restricted families inside the broader problem: a full height-one expression may take the star of an arbitrary star-free language and combine the resulting languages by concatenation and Boolean operations. Their paper describes its result as a step toward that larger structural challenge.

Cotumaccio’s 2025 account of connections between compressed indexing and automata again identifies generalized star height as an open structural question. It does not supply a new separation or universal flattening theorem. The relevance extends beyond a formal-expression puzzle: a solution would clarify how finite-state iteration, modular behaviour and Boolean operations interact, while allowing descriptions to grow arbitrarily large.
