cards.title: Decidability of equivalence for unambiguous context-free grammars
cards.formal: Is it decidable, given two finite context-free grammars \(G_1,G_2\) over the same finite terminal alphabet and promised that both are unambiguous, whether \(L(G_1)=L(G_2)\)?
cards.definitions: A context-free grammar \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\) has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of productions \(A\to u\), with \(A\in V\) and \(u\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed. A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\) whose nonterminal nodes expand by productions; its terminal leaves read from left to right form the generated word, possibly empty. The language \(L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^*\) consists of words with such a tree. Unambiguous means at most one parse tree for each word, not at most one order of expanding a fixed tree. Both grammars, alphabet lists and full production strings are explicit finite inputs with binary symbol identifiers and delimiters; duplicate written productions are identified. The decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that terminates on every syntactically valid pair and is correct whenever both grammars satisfy the promise. On pairs violating the promise it may return either answer. Invalid syntax may be rejected. It receives no proof of unambiguity and need not decide that promise. There is no running-time bound, determinism promise for the grammars or restriction to regular or unary languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such a decision machine exists, or a Lean proof that the promised equivalence problem is undecidable. A result for deterministic pushdown presentations, comparison with only a finite automaton, or a semidecision procedure for inequivalence does not settle the complete two-grammar question.
cards.why: This basic equivalence problem tests the algorithmic power of unique parsing beyond deterministic context-free language descriptions.

cards.title: First-order definability of regular tree languages
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a finite bottom-up automaton A for finite unranked ordered labeled trees, always halts and decides whether some first-order sentence \(\varphi\) using label predicates, strict descendant and sibling order satisfies A accepts t if and only if \(t\models \varphi\) for every finite input tree t?
cards.definitions: A tree is a finite nonempty set T of finite words over positive integers, containing the empty word \(\varepsilon\), closed under prefixes, and such that \(ui\in T\) implies \(uj\in T\) for \(1\le j\le i\). Its root is \(\varepsilon\); the children of u are \(u1,\ldots ,uk\) in that order. Each node has exactly one label from a nonempty finite alphabet \(\Sigma\). There is no fixed bound on k. \(Desc(x,y)\) means x is a proper prefix of y, so y is a strict descendant of x. \(Sib(x,y)\) means \(x=ui\) and \(y=uj\) for the same parent u with \(i<j\); it orders siblings, not all incomparable nodes. Equality and the unary predicates \(P_{a}(x)\), one per label \(a\in \Sigma\), complete the logical vocabulary. First-order sentences are finite formulas formed from these atomic predicates by Boolean connectives and quantification over individual nodes only, with any finite number of variables and alternations. No quantification over sets, counting quantifier or extra transitive-closure operator is allowed. The parent relation is definable from Desc. The lexicographic order used in the primary paper is equivalent to Desc plus Sib: x precedes y if \(Desc(x,y)\), or some sibling s of t precedes it with s equal to or an ancestor of x and t equal to or an ancestor of y. Conversely Sib is definable from parent and lexicographic order. To fix a finite input presentation, a bottom-up automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a binary operation ⊕ and identity 0 making \((Q,\oplus ,0) a\) monoid, a table \(\delta _{a}:Q\to Q\) for each \(a\in \Sigma\), and an accepting subset \(F\subseteq Q\). A node labeled a with ordered child states \(q_{1},\ldots ,q_{k}\) receives state \(\delta _{a}(q_{1}\oplus \cdots \oplus q_{k})\); the empty sum is 0. The tree is accepted when its root state lies in F. These finite tables, alphabet and state indices are explicitly encoded in binary; this is an algebraic bottom-up presentation of regular unranked tree languages. The algorithm must work for every valid finite presentation, without a complexity bound beyond termination. The sentence \(\varphi\) may depend on A, but must be a single sentence for all finite trees and all their sizes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove decidability by an algorithm that terminates correctly on every valid automaton description, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Recognizing trees with a fixed supplied automaton, deciding whether one supplied sentence agrees with an automaton, or testing definability in a fixed quantifier fragment does not decide existence of an arbitrary first-order definition.
cards.why: The tree analogue of effective first-order definability for regular word languages.

cards.context:
An automaton combines finitely many states from the children and passes one state to their parent. A first-order sentence instead describes relationships between named nodes. For instance, “every a-labeled node has a b-labeled descendant” is the sentence \(\forall x\,\bigl(P_a(x)\Rightarrow\exists y\,(\operatorname{Desc}(x,y)\land P_b(y))\bigr)\). The question asks whether the entire language recognized by a given automaton has some description of this logical kind.

A two-state bottom-up computation can track whether the total number of nodes is even or odd: combine child parities and then count the parent. First-order logic with order cannot express arbitrary parity even on trees that are single paths. Thus finite-state recognition is strictly more expressive. The task is to tell, from an automaton’s finite description, on which side of that expressiveness boundary its language lies.

A descendant relation permits a sentence to refer directly to nodes arbitrarily far below another node. A child relation concerns just one edge. Decidability results for the child-only vocabulary therefore do not settle this card. Order among siblings is also part of the input structure: permuting subtrees can change the truth of a formula. The chosen vocabulary matches the ordered ancestor-plus-lexicographic setting of the source rather than an unordered or purely local variant.

Bojańczyk and Segoufin decide definability in \(\Delta _{2}\), the languages having both an existential-then-universal and a universal-then-existential definition. They do not decide arbitrary first-order definability. Blumensath’s 2024 finite-tree work supplies decidable necessary and sufficient conditions separately, but no one condition that is both. A necessary condition can fail to reject every nondefinable language, while a sufficient condition can fail to accept every definable language. The remaining gap is a complete test.

The 2025 automata characterization studies first-order logic over unordered infinite trees. The August 2026 result decides a common fragment of particular branching-time and linear-time temporal logics. Their domains or logical restrictions differ from the full finite ordered-tree question. They do not supply the all-input terminating test requested here. A solution would turn an expressiveness boundary into a mechanically checkable property of finite-state tree specifications.

cards.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to \(DD_{k}(A)\), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
cards.definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, \(\varepsilon\) the empty word, and \(A+=A*\setminus \{\varepsilon\}\). Set \(DD_{0}(A)=\{\varnothing ,\{\varepsilon\},A+,A*\}\). For a class C of languages over \(A, Pol(C)\) consists of all finite unions of marked products \(L_{0}a_{1}L_{1}\cdots a_{r} L_{r}\), where \(r\ge 0\), each \(a_{i}\in A\), and every \(L_{i}\in C; r=0\) gives \(L_{0}\). Let \(Bool(C)\) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define \(DD_{k+1}(A)\)=Bool(\(Pol(DD_{k}(A))\)). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is \(L(M)\). The question quantifies \(\forall k\exists a\) total Turing algorithm \(A_{k}\forall M\), with \(A_{k}(M)\)=yes exactly when \(L(M)\in DD_{k}(A)\). Each \(A_{k}\) must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that membership in \(DD_{k}\) is decidable for every fixed integer \(k\ge 0\), with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.
cards.why: Determine whether bounded logical alternation can be recognized effectively throughout a fundamental hierarchy of regular languages.

cards.context:
Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and \(b, A*aA*bA\)* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by \(\{\varepsilon\}\) requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

MeSCaL implements established membership tests, including computations for level two and intermediate levels, while its 2025 account explicitly retains the general hierarchy problem. Such tools make existing decision theorems usable without implying that every level is decidable.

Lambert’s July 2026 paper develops effective methods that turn automata into logical descriptions for dot-depth one and specified extensions. Its target classes are fixed; it does not claim a procedure for every level of this hierarchy.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.

cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
cards.definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and \(m(q)\) output-tree parameters, and an initial state \(q_{0}\) with \(m(q_{0})=0\). For each state q and input symbol \(\sigma\) of arity k there is at most one rule \(q(\sigma (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}),y_{1},\ldots ,y_{m})\to r\). The finite right-hand side follows the grammar \(r ::= y_{j} | \delta (r_{1},\ldots ,r_{l}) | q' (x_{i},r_{1},\ldots ,r_{m(q' )})\), with \(\delta\) an output symbol of arity l and \(1\le i\le k\). Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input \(\sigma (t_{1},\ldots ,t_{k})\), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call \(q'\) on the indicated child \(t_{i}\) with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.
cards.why: Locate the decidability boundary for equivalence of terminating recursive tree programs with copying and nested output parameters.

cards.context:
A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by \(b(y,y)\) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

context_blocks.text: A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by \(b(y,y)\) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. cards.title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, on every pair \((G,H)\) of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether \[\operatorname{Tree}(G)=\operatorname{Tree}(H)?\] Both schemes may have arbitrary finite type order, with their orders supplied by their finite descriptions. Equality is exact equality of the possibly infinite ordered value trees, including the nullary divergence symbol \(\bot\). No safety or productivity promise is imposed.
cards.definitions:
A ranked alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite set of terminal symbols with ranks \(r(a)\in\mathbb N\). Simple types are finite expressions generated by a base type \(o\) and the arrow constructor \(\tau\to\sigma\), associating to the right. A terminal of rank \(r\) has the type with \(r\) arguments of type \(o\) and result \(o\); rank zero means type \(o\). A scheme has a finite set of typed nonterminals, one distinguished start nonterminal \(S:o\), and exactly one rule \[F x_1\cdots x_k\longrightarrow t\] for each nonterminal \(F:\tau_1\to\cdots\to\tau_k\to o\). Here the distinct variables \(x_i:\tau_i\) are the only variables allowed in \(t\), and \(t:o\) is a finite well-typed applicative term over terminals, nonterminals and these variables. Terms are symbols or applications \(uv\), with \(u:\alpha\to\beta\) and \(v:\alpha\) giving \(uv:\beta\); application associates to the left. Rules may be mutually recursive and may duplicate or discard parameters. There are no data tests, constructor equations, pattern matching or nondeterministic alternatives. No syntactic restriction called safety is required.

Starting at the closed ground term \(S\), expose the head constructor by repeatedly replacing a fully applied head nonterminal \(F u_1\cdots u_k\) by \(t[u_1/x_1,\ldots,u_k/x_k]\). When a terminal head \(a u_1\cdots u_{r(a)}\) is exposed, output a node labeled \(a\) with the ordered child trees obtained in the same way from the ground terms \(u_i\). If the head unfolding never exposes a terminal, output a single \(\bot\) node with no children. In particular, unfolding does not require finishing a constructor's arguments before exposing that constructor. This defines \(\operatorname{Tree}(G)\) over \(\Sigma\cup\{\bot\}\). A node address is a finite sequence of positive integers specifying successive child positions, starting with the empty address at the root. A terminal of rank \(r\) has precisely children numbered \(1,\ldots,r\), and \(\bot\) has none. Equality means the same set of addresses and the same label at every address. The number of unfolding steps and the names of internal nonterminals are not observable.

Type order is defined by \(\operatorname{ord}(o)=0\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(\tau\to\sigma)=\max\{\operatorname{ord}(\tau)+1,\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\}\). A scheme's order is the maximum order of its nonterminals; the two input orders need not agree. An input explicitly lists the finite alphabet and ranks, type syntax trees, nonterminal symbols, start symbols and rule syntax trees, with binary indices and delimiters. Well-typedness and the syntactic conditions are effectively checked; invalid descriptions are rejected. The sought machine must work uniformly over all valid encodings, alphabets, finite orders and rule sizes. It returns an exact Boolean answer, without approximation, random error, an oracle, or any additional time or space requirement beyond termination.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of decidability or undecidability of the input language defined above. A positive answer must supply one effective algorithm and prove its termination and correctness on every valid pair, including equal infinite trees and divergent schemes, uniformly in the finite input orders. A negative answer must prove that no total computable decider exists; undecidability for one fixed order already suffices for this unrestricted problem. A positive algorithm only for a restricted order or safety class, model checking of one tree, or a theorem conditional on another unresolved decision problem is not a full positive answer. No finite-depth approximation to tree equality is accepted.
cards.why: This is a central comparison problem for finite programs with higher-order recursion. Their complete output can be an infinite tree, and strong logical properties of each individual tree are already decidable. Deciding equality would establish an effective method for identifying identical observable recursive behavior across different finite descriptions; undecidability would locate a fundamental boundary beyond single-program verification.

cards.context:
A finite recursive program can describe an infinite object without listing its nodes. The rule \(S\to a S\), for unary a, describes an endless chain of a labels. The two-rule system \(S\to a T\) and \(T\to a S\) describes exactly the same chain even though its internal call structure differs. This card asks whether such equality of the entire observable unfolding can always be decided when functions may also be passed as arguments.

The output is an uninterpreted constructor tree. A binary constructor named plus is merely a label with two ordered children; the model does not add the arithmetic equation \(plus(0,x)=x\). Likewise, it does not include a program context allowed to inspect generated values. This narrow semantics matters because equivalence questions for richer programming languages can be undecidable for reasons absent from recursion schemes.

Divergence is also observable in a precise way. The rule \(S\to S\) generates ⊥, while \(S\to a S\) generates an infinite productive chain. A scheme \(S\to b S c\), with binary b and nullary c, can expose infinitely many labels despite never completing its left subtree. Head unfolding therefore differs from an evaluation convention that insists on fully evaluating every argument before producing a constructor.

At order zero, generated trees have finite-state descriptions and equality is decidable. At order one, equivalence is interreducible with deterministic pushdown-language equivalence, whose decidability follows from Sénizergues’s theorem. The higher-order setting permits functions as parameters of recursive definitions. Jochems’s §5 explicitly distinguishes this unresolved general problem from the established order-one result.

Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre prove that recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata describe the same classes of trees, with effective translations at each order. A collapsible pushdown automaton has a nested stack structure with links allowing restoration of earlier stack contents. The paper transfers value-tree equality to language equivalence for deterministic machines of this kind, but its final discussion explicitly leaves that comparison problem open. Equivalence of two representation models does not itself decide equality of two represented objects.

Powerful properties of a single tree are nevertheless decidable. Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre provide effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for monadic second-order logic and the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. Reflection can enrich node labels with the truth of a chosen logical property. Having this machinery does not automatically turn two unrelated infinite descriptions into one object in the same decidable class on which all corresponding nodes can be compared.

Jochems’s 2021 result is a conditional decidability theorem: a specified semidecidability property of coinductive higher-order constrained Horn clauses would imply decidability of scheme equivalence. These clauses describe relations using higher-order logical rules with a greatest-model interpretation. The required semidecidability remains an assumption in Theorem 4.1, so the paper does not provide a completed equality algorithm.

The same paper proves that allowing explicit divergence leaves does not change the decidability question: its transformation to divergence-free trees preserves and reflects equality. The present formulation retains divergence because it is part of the semantics of an arbitrary input scheme, with no productivity promise. A productive infinite tree and a computation that never exposes a constructor remain distinct outputs.

The April 2026 polyregular result proves undecidability for equality of functions at higher-order types in a calculus with list operations and extensional semantics over function arguments. The paper’s language has no recursion and its programs terminate. Its comparison problem is different from equality of closed, possibly infinite constructor trees generated by the recursion rules in this card; no reduction between the two problems is assumed.

The July 2026 probabilistic-verification result decides almost-sure termination for a type-restricted class of probabilistic recursion schemes. That is a question about a termination probability in a restricted model. It does not settle equality of deterministic value trees at arbitrary finite orders.

cards.title: Linear-time minimization of deterministic finite automata
cards.formal: For every fixed alphabet size \(a\ge2\), is deterministic minimization of complete finite automata over \([a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}\) possible in \(O(n)\) worst-case time on the word-RAM defined below? More explicitly, the target is \[\forall a\ge2\ \exists M_a,C_a,n_a\ \forall n\ge n_a\ \forall A\text{ with }n\text{ states},\quad M_a(A)\text{ outputs a smallest equivalent complete DFA in at most }C_a n\text{ steps}.\] Here \(M_a\) is a single finite program independent of \(n\); \(C_a\) and \(n_a\) may depend on \(a\), and \(n_a\ge a\) may be assumed. The task is exact language-preserving minimization, with no prescribed canonical naming of output states.
cards.definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), an input DFA is \(A=([n],[a],\delta,s,F)\), where \(\delta:[n]\times[a]\to[n]\) is total, \(s\in[n]\), and \(F\subseteq[n]\). Its explicit input consists of \(n\), \(s\), the \(an\) transition targets, and \(n\) accepting-state bits, one target or bit per input word. Extend \(\delta\) to finite words by \(\delta^*(q,\varepsilon)=q\) and \(\delta^*(q,ub)=\delta(\delta^*(q,u),b)\). The recognized language is \(\{u:\delta^*(s,u)\in F\}\). The output is an explicit complete DFA \(B=([k],[a],\delta',s',F')\), \(1\le k\le n\), recognizing exactly that language, with \(k\) minimal among all complete DFAs over the same alphabet. Unreachable input states may be discarded; no equivalence partition for them is required. Both input and output transitions are explicitly represented.

Use one sequential deterministic word-RAM with word length \(w=\lceil2\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), addressed word memory and finitely many registers. Reading or writing one addressed word, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), Boolean bit operations, shifts by an amount less than \(w\), comparisons and conditional branches each cost one step. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, oracle instruction or externally supplied lookup table is available. The finite program may depend on the fixed alphabet size but not on the input size. All algorithmic preprocessing, auxiliary-table construction, initialization and output writing are charged to the running time; memory beyond the input has a fixed blank initial value. The asymptotic target is considered for \(n\ge n_a\ge a\), so the explicit \(an\)-word transition table fits the chosen word address space. Finitely many smaller sizes for each fixed alphabet are finite exceptions to the asymptotic claim. This spells out the input-addressing convention without changing the saved logarithmic word formula. The cost is in word operations, not bit operations: the input uses \(\Theta(n)\) words for fixed \(a\). There is no randomization, expected-time qualification, distribution on inputs, language approximation or promise on the transition graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation, including correctness, minimality, explicit output and the stated RAM cost. A positive proof must cover every fixed \(a\ge2\) by a uniform-in-\(n\) finite program and fixed constants. A negative proof must establish that for some fixed \(a\ge2\), every correct program in this full RAM model fails an \(O(n)\) worst-case bound: no constants \(C,n_0\) work for all sufficiently large inputs. A lower bound restricted to partition refinement, a comparison model or one particular minimization algorithm does not prove this negation. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional version.
cards.why: DFA minimization is a basic preprocessing step for recognizers, regular-language operations and finite-state verification. Its classical algorithm is almost linear, and the logarithmic factor has resisted removal for general transition graphs. Resolving the target would distinguish an inherent cost of the problem from the cost of the partition-refinement paradigm.

cards.context:
Two reachable states are equivalent exactly when every continuation word is either accepted from both or rejected from both. A smallest recognizer retains one representative of each such behavior. The task asks for the resulting explicit automaton, not merely a test of whether the input is already minimal.

Hopcroft’s algorithm minimizes a complete DFA in \(O(an\log n)\) time. For a fixed alphabet this is \(O(n\log n)\), while the input and a largest possible minimal output each occupy only linearly many words. The target is therefore removal of one logarithmic factor in worst-case sequential time.

Partition refinement begins with blocks distinguished by acceptance and repeatedly separates states whose transitions lead to different blocks. The 2023 lower-bound paper formalizes costs of such refinements and proves a logarithmic-factor obstruction even on deterministic systems with two actions. Its theorem quantifies over that method class, not over all multiplication-capable word-RAM programs.

Unary automata have a functional-graph structure that admits linear-time methods outside ordinary partition refinement. The saved target deliberately starts at alphabet size two, where two successor functions can interact. The successful unary case cannot be substituted for the multi-letter statement.

There are also linear-time results for special transition graphs, such as those whose nontrivial strongly connected components are cycles. These are meaningful positive cases but do not impose the arbitrary transition-graph guarantee requested here.

The source concerns symbolic automata, where transitions can carry predicates describing large or infinite alphabets. This card uses only its ordinary finite-alphabet minimization baseline. The precise word operations, input layout and uniformity convention are editorial choices already present in the saved target; they are not attributed as a conjecture made verbatim by the source authors.

cards.title: Decidability of the nondeterministic tree-automaton index problem
cards.formal: Is it decidable, given a nondeterministic parity automaton A on infinite full binary trees and a nonempty integer priority interval J={i,…,j}, whether some nondeterministic parity tree automaton over the same alphabet, using only priorities in J, recognizes exactly the same language as A?
cards.definitions:
An input tree is a function from finite binary strings to a supplied finite nonempty alphabet Sigma. An automaton has a finite state set Q, an initial state q0, a transition relation Delta contained in Q×Sigma×Q×Q, and a map assigning a nonnegative integer priority to each state. A run labels every tree node by a state, starts with q0, and at each node obeys one transition specifying the left and right child states. A run accepts if, on every infinite branch, the largest priority appearing infinitely often is even. A tree is accepted if at least one accepting run exists. Missing transitions simply preclude a run.

All tables and priorities are explicit finite input data; i and j are binary integers with 0≤i≤j. The sought automaton may have any finite number of states and need not use every priority in J. Equivalence quantifies over all infinite Sigma-labelled binary trees. The decision algorithm is a total Turing machine with no complexity bound. The max-even convention is fixed for both automata; shifting or reversing priorities must preserve this convention and the target interval.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked decision procedure for all such inputs, or prove undecidability. A characterization with an undecided boundedness condition is insufficient. Results restricted to deterministic, alternating or word automata do not answer the nondeterministic tree problem.
cards.why: The index problem measures how much acceptance complexity is inherently needed to describe a tree language.

cards.title: Separating words problem
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that any two distinct binary words of length \(n\ge1\) can be distinguished by a deterministic finite automaton with at most \(C\log_2(n+1)\) states? Distinguishing means accepting exactly one of the two words, with unrestricted behavior on all other words. The automaton may depend on the pair, and its complete one-pass transition model is defined below.
cards.definitions:
The parameter \(n\) is a positive integer and both words have exactly \(n\) symbols. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of a finite nonempty set \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a total transition function \(\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\to Q\), and an accepting set \(F\subseteq Q\). It reads its word once from left to right, starting at \(q_0\), applies \(\delta\) for each symbol and accepts exactly when its final state lies in \(F\). There are no epsilon transitions, auxiliary storage or external position counters. All states, including any rejecting sink, count toward size. The automaton may depend on the pair of words, and either orientation of acceptance is allowed. Its behavior on other words is unrestricted. The minimum is finite, since a DFA can recognize a singleton word, and the maximum is over a finite nonempty set of pairs. No efficiency requirement is imposed on finding the automaton.

Precisely, write
\[
s(n)=\max_{\substack{u,v\in\{0,1\}^n\\u\ne v}}
\min\bigl\{|Q|:\text{a DFA with state set }Q\text{ accepts exactly one of }u,v\bigr\}.
\]
The maximum and minimum use the model above. A complete DFA recognizing one fixed length-\(n\) word has at most \(n+2\) states, so \(1\le s(n)\le n+2\).

The assertion \(s(n)=O(\log n)\) is expressed for all positive lengths using \(\log_2(n+1)\). One universal constant must cover every length and every pair of distinct words; no efficiency bound is imposed on constructing the separating automaton.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one constant \(C\) works for every pair of distinct equal-length binary words. To refute the bound, show that for every \(C>0\) some pair requires more than \(C\log_2(n+1)\) states.
cards.why: Determining the polynomial exponent would quantify the worst-case finite-state memory needed to distinguish two long binary words, while separating polynomial growth from finer logarithmic factors.

cards.title: Primitive words and context-freeness
cards.formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) with \(|\Sigma|\ge2\), is the language \[\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)=\{w\in\Sigma^+ : \text{there are no }u\in\Sigma^+,\ k\ge2\text{ with }w=u^k\}\] not context-free?
cards.definitions: An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. A word is a finite sequence of symbols; \(\Sigma^*\) includes the empty word and \(\Sigma^+\) excludes it. The power \(u^k\) is the concatenation of \(k\) copies of \(u\), where \(k\) is an integer. All one-letter words are primitive. A context-free grammar consists of a finite set \(V\) of nonterminals disjoint from \(\Sigma\), a start symbol \(S\in V\), and a finite set of rules \(A\to x\) with \(A\in V\) and \(x\in(V\cup\Sigma)^*\). Its language is the set of all terminal words derivable from \(S\) by finitely many applications of rules. Empty productions, unit productions and ambiguity are allowed. The assertion is that no such grammar has language exactly \(\operatorname{Prim}(\Sigma)\), for every allowed alphabet. It concerns all word lengths, with no algorithmic size or running-time parameter. Nonprimitive words are excluded even when their repeated root is itself nonprimitive.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that the primitive-word language is non-context-free for every finite alphabet of size at least two, or a Lean counterexample consisting of an allowed alphabet and a context-free grammar generating exactly its primitive words. Excluding only unambiguous grammars, deterministic grammars or grammars of bounded size is insufficient.
cards.why: The primitive-word language is a basic boundary case linking periodicity of words with the expressive power of context-free grammars.

cards.title: Complement closure of conjunctive languages
cards.formal: For every finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every conjunctive grammar G over it, does there exist a conjunctive grammar H over the same terminal alphabet with \[L(H)=\Sigma^*\setminus L(G)\,?\]
cards.definitions: A conjunctive grammar has a finite terminal alphabet \(\Sigma\), a disjoint finite set N of nonterminals, a start symbol S, and finitely many rules \(A\to\alpha_1\mathbin{\&}\cdots\mathbin{\&}\alpha_k\), with \(k\ge1\) and \(\alpha_i\in(\Sigma\cup N)^*\). Interpret a terminal as its singleton language, a word of symbols as concatenation of their languages, a conjunction as intersection, and alternative rules for A as union. The language tuple is the least fixed point of these monotone equations, equivalently the union of their iterations starting with empty nonterminal languages. An empty right-hand-side word denotes \(\{\varepsilon\}\); a nonterminal with no rules denotes the empty language. No negation appears in the grammar. The complement is relative to all finite words over the declared alphabet, including the empty word. H may use arbitrarily many new nonterminals and rules. The target is closure of the language class: no computable transformation, grammar-size bound, linearity or unambiguity requirement is added. Boolean grammars may use negation and have different semantic issues; their complement properties do not provide a conjunctive grammar automatically. Linear conjunctive grammars restrict each conjunct to at most one nonterminal and are not the full class in this question.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the closure statement in Lean, with an equivalent conjunctive grammar for every input language, or give a conjunctive grammar and prove that its complement has no conjunctive grammar whatsoever. Showing that a complement is not context-free, not linear, or not unambiguous does not prove non-closure of the full conjunctive class.
cards.why: This asks whether grammar conjunction and recursion can express negation without an explicit negation operation.

cards.title: Dense periodic behavior in surjective one-dimensional cellular automata
cards.formal: For every finite nonempty alphabet A, radius r≥0 and local rule \(f:A^{2r+1}\to A\), let \(F:A^{\mathbb Z}\to A^{\mathbb Z}\) be defined by \(F(x)_i=f(x_{i-r},\ldots,x_{i+r})\). If F is surjective, must its temporally periodic configurations be dense in \(A^{\mathbb Z}\)?
cards.definitions:
A configuration is a two-sided infinite sequence of letters. Give A the discrete topology and A^Z the product topology: specifying finitely many coordinates gives a basic open cylinder. Surjectivity means every configuration y has a preimage x with F(x)=y. Temporal periodicity means F^p(x)=x for some positive integer p, which may depend on x. Density means that every finite word u over A occurs, at coordinates 0 through |u|−1, in some temporally periodic x. This cylinder condition is equivalent to topological density.

The target does not require x to be periodic under spatial translation. Joint spatial and temporal periodicity is a stronger stated property and must not replace the requested condition without a proved implication. Eventual temporal periodicity also differs from periodicity from time zero. The full shift includes every A-valued sequence; no forbidden-word subshift, special algebraic alphabet or reversibility promise is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that every surjective local rule satisfies the cylinder condition, or give an explicit finite local rule, prove it is surjective, and exhibit a finite cylinder containing no temporally periodic configuration. Failure of spatial periodicity or of a particular period alone is insufficient.
cards.why: The conjecture connects reversible coverage of configurations with recurrence in a basic discrete computation model.

cards.title: Exponential complementation lower bounds for unambiguous automata
cards.formal: Can complementing a binary unambiguous finite automaton require exponentially many states even if the complement may be represented ambiguously? For \[C(n)=\max_A\min\{|Q_B|:L(B)=\{0,1\}^{*}\setminus L(A)\},\] where \(A\) ranges over binary unambiguous automata with between one and \(n\) states and \(B\) over binary nondeterministic automata, does \[\exists c>0\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N,\qquad C(n)\ge2^{cn}\] hold?
cards.definitions:
Both kinds of automaton are finite tuples \((Q,\{0,1\},\Delta,I,F)\), where \(Q\) is the state set, \(I,F\subseteq Q\) are the initial and final state sets, and \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\}\times Q\) is a transition relation. Multiple initial states, missing transitions, unreachable states and empty initial or final sets are allowed. There are no epsilon transitions or duplicate parallel transitions.

An accepting run on a word \(a_1\cdots a_m\) is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_0\in I\), \(q_m\in F\), and \((q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)\in\Delta\) for every \(1\leq i\leq m\). A word belongs to the language if it has an accepting run. For the empty word the accepting runs are the states in \(I\cap F\). The input automaton is unambiguous when each word has at most one accepting run; there is no restriction on the number of rejecting runs.

Only the number of states is charged, not transitions, the alphabet description or computation used to construct the automaton. Up to state renaming there are finitely many eligible inputs. Determinization and complementation give an output with at most \(2^{n}\) states, so the minimum and maximum defining \(C(n)\) exist.

The function \(C(n)\) is the worst-case minimum complement size defined in the statement. The lower bound asks for arbitrarily large input-size bounds, not for a hard example at every size. The constant \(c\) is universal; the automaton may depend on the size bound. No construction-time bound is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one positive \(c\) gives \(C(n)\ge 2^{cn}\) for arbitrarily large state budgets \(n\), even when the complement automaton may be ambiguous. A refutation shows that for every \(c>0\), eventually \(C(n)<2^{cn}\).
cards.why: Unambiguity limits the number of positive certificates without directly describing negative certificates. The optimal cost of complementing this representation measures how much succinctness is lost under logical negation and tests the reach of communication-based lower bounds for finite-state models.

cards.title: A \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) dichotomy for visibly pushdown languages
cards.formal: For every visibly pushdown language \(L\) of well-matched finite words, is \(L\in\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) or is \(L\) complete for \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) under constant-depth truth-table reductions? The circuit families and reductions are nonuniform, as defined below; the alternatives are inclusive.
cards.definitions: The alphabet is a fixed finite disjoint union \(\Sigma=\Sigma_{\mathrm{call}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{ret}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{int}}\). A word is well-matched when every prefix has at least as many calls as returns and the whole word has equally many. A deterministic visibly pushdown automaton has finite control states, a finite stack alphabet with a bottom marker, an initial state and designated final states. It reads one letter per step, starting with just the bottom marker. A call pushes one non-bottom symbol, a return pops one symbol, and an internal letter leaves the stack unchanged; the finite transition table may inspect the state, letter and stack top. Acceptance requires a final control state and a stack containing just the bottom marker. Words that are not well-matched are rejected. Missing transitions reject. A language recognized by such an automaton is a visibly pushdown language (VPL); the automaton is fixed, while word length grows. Letters use a fixed-length injective binary code, and invalid codes are rejected. A nonuniform circuit family has one Boolean circuit for each input length, with no requirement that a machine generate the circuits. In \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\), circuits have polynomial size and constant depth and may use NOT and unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and majority gates. A majority gate returns one precisely when more than half its inputs are one. In \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\), circuits have polynomial size, depth \(O(\log(n+2))\), and AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two, together with NOT gates. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on the fixed language. The reduction \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) consists of nonuniform constant-depth polynomial-size Boolean circuits with AND, OR and NOT gates and polynomial-length oracle gates for membership in \(L\). No directed path goes from an oracle output to an oracle input. The circuit decides \(K\), and its size includes the oracle-query wires. Completeness means \(L\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) and \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) for every \(K\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated alternative for every VPL. Alternatively specify a VPL and prove in Lean both that it is outside \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) and that it is not \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)-hard under the stated reductions. The target does not additionally require an algorithm assigning automata to the alternatives. A classification using a different reduction or uniformity convention must establish that it implies this proposition.
cards.why: This asks whether visible stack structure admits a complete boundary between constant-depth threshold computation and general logarithmic-depth circuits. Such a theorem would explain parallel complexity across an infinite language family, beyond deciding individual automata or proving one circuit lower bound.

references.title: The \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\)-Complexity of Visibly Pushdown Languages
references.locator: Sections 1, 2 and 2.1 for VPLs, circuits and truth-table reductions; Section 6, PDF page 16, for the dichotomy.

cards.context:
The input itself prescribes when the machine uses its stack. Nested calls can therefore carry information that finite-state machines cannot store, while the matching structure remains visible before the control computation is performed. Well-matched words can nest arbitrarily deeply; the question does not impose a depth bound.

Every VPL is in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The unresolved issue is whether any VPL occupies an intermediate position: requiring more than constant-depth threshold computation while failing to represent every logarithmic-depth bounded-fan-in computation. The known upper bound makes hardness and completeness equivalent here.

The 2024 paper classifies many VPLs relative to \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\), the constant-depth class without majority gates, and isolates a family whose \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) membership remains unresolved. That three-way outcome does not decide the present \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) question.

A lower bound against \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) is insufficient: majority and modular counting can require gates absent from \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) but still lie in \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). Conversely, knowing that a language has a logarithmic-depth circuit is only an upper bound, not a completeness proof.

The source separately asks whether membership in the threshold-circuit class can be decided from an automaton. This card selects the stated dichotomy proposition itself, preserving that distinction. It also retains the source’s constant-depth truth-table reductions, which allow several parallel oracle queries, rather than silently strengthening completeness to a single-query many-one reduction.

The two classes are not assumed to be different. If they coincide, the first alternative holds for every VPL. A negative answer would in particular separate them, so a conjectural class separation cannot be used as an unstated premise.

cards.title: Equivalence of discounted-sum automata
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that always halts and decides, given a rational \(\lambda\) with \(0<\lambda<1\) and two total nondeterministic discounted-sum automata \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) over the same finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), whether \[\forall w\in\Sigma^\omega,\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\mathcal B(w)?\] Both automata have rational transition weights and use the same discounted-sum value function \(\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}\). Their word values are the suprema of their run values. The input factor is arbitrary rational, with no reciprocal-integer restriction.
cards.definitions: Such an automaton is \(\mathcal A=(Q,q_0,\Sigma,E,\gamma)\), where \(Q\) is a finite nonempty state set, \(q_0\in Q\), \(E\) is a finite set of transitions with source, target and label in \(Q,Q,\Sigma\), and \(\gamma:E\to\mathbb Q\) gives their weights. Parallel transitions, including differently weighted transitions with the same endpoints and label, are allowed. Totality means that every pair \((q,a)\in Q\times\Sigma\) has at least one outgoing transition. There are no empty-label transitions, final-state tests, fairness requirements or restrictions on which infinite runs count. For an infinite word \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run \(\rho=e_0e_1\cdots\) starts at \(q_0\), consecutive transitions have matching endpoints, and \(e_i\) has label \(a_i\). Set \[\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i\gamma(e_i),\qquad \mathcal A(w)=\sup_{\rho\text{ a run of }\mathcal A\text{ on }w}\operatorname{DSum}_{\lambda}(\rho).\] If \(W=\max_{e\in E}|\gamma(e)|\), every series converges absolutely and has absolute value at most \(W/(1-\lambda)\); totality ensures a nonempty run set, so the supremum is a finite real number. Nondeterministic choices are optimized separately for each complete word. No single online strategy is required to select them. All finite sets and transition tables are explicit, and rational weights and the common multiplier \(\lambda\) are encoded as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. The deciding machine takes these finite descriptions, not an infinite word as an oracle input. It must answer correctly on every well-formed pair and every allowed factor, without a resource bound. Equality is exact equality of real-valued functions on all infinite words; this yes-or-no decidability question has no approximation tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one total computable algorithm decides the stated equality for every encoded input, or prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A positive result must handle arbitrary rational \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), unrestricted finite nondeterminism, signed rational weights and all infinite words under supremum semantics. A result for deterministic or functional automata, reciprocal-integer factors, finite words, or comparison up to a positive tolerance does not settle the full target. A negative result obtained by permitting different discount factors on different transitions does not settle this single-factor problem.
cards.why: Exact equivalence is a basic correctness test for quantitative specifications: it asks whether replacing one finite-state description by another preserves the value of every possible infinite behavior. Discounting makes each value convergent but leaves a difficult interaction between exact arithmetic and nondeterministic choices. Resolving equivalence for the basic rational single-factor model would establish a central algorithmic boundary for quantitative automata.

cards.context:
A transition weight represents a local reward or cost. Multiplication by successive powers of the discount factor gives later weights less influence. The automaton chooses the best run separately on each input word, producing a quantitative language rather than a set of accepted words. Equivalence compares those whole functions.

The source considers total automata, rational weights and supremum semantics on infinite words. Its shared value-function convention is made explicit by supplying one multiplier for both automata. Some papers instead divide the weight at position \(i\) by \(\beta^i\), with \(\beta>1\), and take infima; their discount corresponds to \(\lambda=1/\beta\), and negating all weights interchanges the two extremum conventions.

Convergence does not turn exact function equality into a test of finitely many sampled behaviors or fixed-precision values. The 2023 paper can decide whether one discounted-sum automaton defines a constant function while explicitly leaving arbitrary equivalence open. Constancy is a special case and does not give the required pairwise comparison procedure.

Later results depend sharply on the model. Reciprocal-integer multipliers belong to a decidable family, and more general real-valued Pisot-base results extend that family outside the rational domain. Conversely, undecidability with transition-dependent discount factors concerns a richer interface. Neither result settles all rational multipliers shared throughout a pair of nondeterministic automata.

progress.text: The CONCUR paper defines the supremum semantics in §2 and explicitly leaves discounted-sum equivalence open in §3. Its Theorem 3.3 proves PSPACE-completeness of deciding whether a discounted-sum automaton defines a constant function.

cards.title: Deciding pattern avoidance over a prescribed alphabet
cards.formal: Is the following set decidable: pairs (p,k), where p is a nonempty finite word of variables and k≥2, such that there exists an infinite word \(w\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^{\mathbb N}\) containing no nonerasing substitution instance of p as a contiguous factor?
cards.definitions:
The input pattern is an explicitly written finite sequence of variable identifiers; only equality of identifiers matters. The integer k is encoded in binary. A nonerasing substitution maps every variable occurring in p to a nonempty finite word over the k-letter alphabet and extends to p by concatenation. Repeated occurrences of a variable receive the same word; different variables may receive the same word. A forbidden occurrence is an interval of consecutive positions in w whose word equals h(p) for some such substitution h. The infinite word is one-sided, indexed by the nonnegative integers, with no computability, morphic-generation or eventual-periodicity requirement. It may use fewer than k symbols.

Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite pair and answers yes exactly when such an infinite avoiding word exists. No running-time bound is imposed. The question fixes the available alphabet size as part of the instance; testing whether some unspecified finite alphabet permits avoidance is a different decision problem. Partial words with holes and abelian pattern occurrences are also outside this target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked total decision procedure with equivalence to the stated infinite-word existence property, or a complete undecidability reduction whose outputs are valid pairs of the specified kind. A procedure that decides only avoidability over some finite alphabet, or verifies one proposed infinite construction, is insufficient.
cards.why: This distinguishes decidability with a prescribed alphabet from the easier unrestricted-alphabet existence question.

cards.title: Nondeterminism versus determinism with two two-way heads
cards.formal: Is there a finite alphabet Sigma and a language L⊆Sigma* recognized by a nondeterministic two-way two-head finite automaton but by no deterministic two-way two-head finite automaton, under the nonsensing model below?
cards.definitions:
The input tape is read-only and contains a left endmarker, the finite input, and a right endmarker. A machine has finitely many states and two labelled heads. Initially both heads scan the first input symbol, or the right endmarker for empty input. A transition depends only on the current state and the ordered pair of scanned symbols; it chooses a new state and, for each head, a movement in {−1,0,1}. Heads cannot move outside the endmarkers. There is no extra predicate testing whether the heads occupy the same position: seeing identical symbols does not reveal coincidence.

A run accepts if it is finite and halts in an accepting state with no enabled transition. A word is accepted by a nondeterministic machine when at least one run accepts. Other runs may reject or continue forever. A deterministic machine has at most one transition per state and scanned-symbol pair; it need not halt on words outside its language. The finite control may be arbitrarily large but is fixed independently of input length. Neither machine has a work tape, counter, stack, advice or extra head. The question compares language classes, not state-size blowups for simulating a specific machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked language separation, including a nondeterministic recognizer and a proof excluding every deterministic two-head recognizer, or prove equality of these two language classes in Lean. A simulation using more heads or a separation only for one-way input is insufficient.
cards.why: This isolates the power of nondeterminism at a fixed number of heads, rather than the state cost of simulation.

cards.title: Recognizing good-for-games and good-for-MDP automata
cards.formal: Determine the exact worst-case computational complexity of each of the following two recognition languages: \[\mathrm{GFG}_{\mathrm{par}}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-games parity automaton}\},\qquad \mathrm{GFM}_{\mathrm B}=\{\langle\mathcal A\rangle:\mathcal A\text{ is a good-for-MDP Büchi automaton}\}.\] The input is an explicit finite nondeterministic automaton, and the number of parity priorities is unbounded and part of the first input. The requested classification is for each language separately, with matching complexity-class upper and hardness bounds under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The source's two recognition tasks are retained; no particular class membership conjecture is substituted for either classification.
cards.definitions:
An automaton has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), an initial state \(q_0\), and a complete transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\). Completeness means that every state and letter admit a transition; a rejecting sink handles missing transitions. A run on \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\) follows transitions \((q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\) from \(q_0\). A parity automaton has a map \(p:\Delta\to\mathbb N\) and accepts a run when the largest priority appearing infinitely often is even. A Büchi automaton has a marked set \(F\subseteq\Delta\) and accepts a run when transitions in \(F\) occur infinitely often. Its language \(L(\mathcal A)\) contains the words with some accepting run. A good-for-games (GFG) automaton admits a single deterministic rule that selects each next transition using only the finite input prefix read so far, so that its induced run accepts every \(w\in L(\mathcal A)\). The rule may remember the entire past; it cannot inspect future letters. One rule must work on all words.

A finite Markov decision process (MDP) over \(\Sigma\) has finite state and action sets \(S,U\), an initial state \(s_0\), a nonempty set \(U(s)\) of enabled actions at each state, a label \(\ell(s,u)\in\Sigma\), and a distribution \(P(s,u,\cdot)\) on \(S\) for each enabled pair. Distribution entries are real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one. A policy maps the observed finite history of states and actions to a distribution on the enabled actions. It generates a path by choosing \(u_i\), emitting \(\ell(s_i,u_i)\), and sampling \(s_{i+1}\) using \(P\); products of these conditional probabilities give the path measure. Define \[V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)=\sup_\pi\Pr_M^\pi[\ell(s_0,u_0)\ell(s_1,u_1)\cdots\in L(\mathcal A)].\] In the product with \(\mathcal A\), a policy observes the joint state \((s_i,q_i)\), chooses an enabled pair consisting of \(u_i\) and a transition \((q_i,\ell(s_i,u_i),q_{i+1})\), then samples \(s_{i+1}\) from \(P(s_i,u_i,\cdot)\). Thus the automaton choice precedes that next random state and sees no future. Let \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)\) be the supremum, over all such history-dependent randomized product policies, of the probability that the selected automaton run satisfies its Büchi condition. The automaton is good-for-MDP (GFM) if \(V_{\mathrm{syn}}(M,\mathcal A)=V_{\mathrm{sem}}(M,\mathcal A)\) for every finite MDP over its alphabet and every initial MDP state. The product policy may depend on the MDP. This is exact equality of probabilities, without approximation or a probability-one promise.

Only the automaton is input to recognition; MDPs, policies and GFG rules are quantified objects. States, letters and transitions are explicitly enumerated; indices and priorities use binary integers with delimiters. Input size \(n\) is the total bit length, and invalid descriptions are rejected. The alphabet size, graph size and number of priorities are not fixed parameters. Computational bounds use uniform Turing machines and worst-case resource use over inputs of length at most \(n\), with exact acceptance and no randomized error. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(X\) to \(Y\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) with \(x\in X\iff f(x)\in Y\). A language is \(\mathcal C\)-complete if it belongs to \(\mathcal C\) and every language in \(\mathcal C\) reduces to it in this sense. Use the shared definitions of [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np), [PSPACE](definitions.html#space) and [EXP, also called EXPTIME](definitions.html#exponential-time).
cards.answer_criterion: Give Lean-checked matching complexity classifications for both recognition languages with the specified explicit input encoding and reduction convention. Numerical approximation of the MDP values is not the acceptance criterion.
cards.why: These recognition problems measure the cost of checking whether a compact nondeterministic specification supports composition with an adversarial system or with a probabilistic controller. Their semantic definitions quantify over infinitely many behaviors, although their inputs are finite graphs. Matching classifications would explain the computational price of certifying these useful restrictions on nondeterminism and the difference between their game and probabilistic settings.

cards.context:
Existence of an accepting run is a hindsight property: a nondeterministic automaton can have a successful branch for each word without any single online method selecting those branches. GFG demands such a uniform method. The input automaton is not promised to have the property; recognizing whether it does is the task.

GFM asks a different compositional question. An MDP describes both choices controlled by a policy and transitions sampled from fixed distributions. Its semantic objective only asks that the generated word have some accepting run. Its product objective also requires choosing that run as the word is produced. The second probability cannot exceed the first, and GFM requires equality for every finite MDP.

The policy in the product may be designed for the particular MDP, observing its current state and its past behavior. GFG instead requires one prefix-based resolution valid for every input word. This distinction makes GFM more permissive; it does not turn the two recognition languages into the same problem.

The 2-token theorem settles a major structural characterization of GFG parity automata and yields polynomial-time recognition at each fixed priority count. It does not yield one polynomial-time bound uniform in the number of priorities. The unrestricted input family remains NP-hard and in PSPACE in the checked 2026 survey.

GFM Büchi recognition is already decidable, with a PSPACE hardness lower bound and an EXPTIME algorithm. Consequently the missing result is a matching complexity classification, not an existence proof for some terminating algorithm. The source proves that a qualitative version based on probability-one preservation agrees with its quantitative GFM property, but the card states the original full-probability definition.

The interpretation of “exact complexity” here is the complexity-class classification used by the source when presenting these gaps. Both problems and the unrestricted priority parameter are preserved. Recognition does not ask for a smallest equivalent automaton, and recent minimization or state-reduction results do not automatically classify it.

cards.title: Isomorphism of tree-automatic ordinals without addition
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm which, given two injective finite-tree-automatic presentations promised to describe well-orders using only their domain and strict order relations, decides whether those well-orders are isomorphic?
cards.definitions:
A code is a finite rooted ordered binary tree with labels in a finite alphabet. Every node has either zero or two children. A finite bottom-up tree automaton assigns a state to a leaf from its label, and to an internal node from its label and its children’s states; acceptance means the root receives a designated accepting state in some run. A presentation consists of an automaton for a language D of codes and an automaton for the relation < on D. To recognize a pair, read their convolution: use the union of their tree domains and pad a missing component by a new blank symbol.

Codes are the elements themselves, so distinct accepted trees represent distinct elements; no quotient or equality automaton is supplied. The promise is that < is a strict linear order on D and every nonempty subset of D has a least element. Empty D is allowed and denotes ordinal zero. The promise is semantic, not a finite proof or ordinal notation attached to the input. Isomorphism means existence of a bijection between the domains preserving and reflecting <. Only domain and order automata are supplied: there is no presentation of ordinal addition.

A decision procedure must halt and be correct on every pair satisfying the promise. It may behave arbitrarily on inputs violating it. No complexity bound is requested, and the task does not include deciding whether an arbitrary presentation is well-founded.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked promise-decision algorithm with termination and correctness on all well-order presentations, or a complete undecidability proof whose reduction always produces valid well-order presentations. A procedure requiring an additional automaton for ordinal addition does not meet the input specification.
cards.why: The problem tests whether ordinal structure can be compared algorithmically without an additional automatic addition operation.

cards.title: Deterministic separability of nondeterministic timed languages
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given two nondeterministic timed automata \(A,B\) with epsilon transitions over the same finite alphabet, always halts and decides whether there exists a deterministic timed automaton \(S\) such that \(L(A)\subseteq L(S)\) and \(L(S)\cap L(B)=\varnothing\)? Languages contain finite timed words. The separator may use any finite number of clocks and any finite integer constants: no resource bound is supplied or fixed in advance.
cards.definitions:
A finite timed word over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) is \((a_1,t_1)\cdots(a_n,t_n)\), where \(n\geq0\), \(a_i\in\Sigma\), and \(0\leq t_1\leq\cdots\leq t_n\) are real timestamps. Equal timestamps and the empty word are allowed.

A timed automaton has finite sets of locations \(Q\), clocks \(X\), initial locations \(I\subseteq Q\), final locations \(F\subseteq Q\), and transitions \((p,a,\phi,Y,q)\). Here \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\), \(Y\subseteq X\), and \(\phi\) is a Boolean combination of true, false, \(x\mathrel{\sim} z\), and \(x-y\mathrel{\sim} z\), with clocks \(x,y\), integer \(z\), and \(\sim\in\{=,<,\leq,>,\geq\}\). There are no location invariants. All sets, transitions and guard formulas are explicitly encoded, with signed binary integer constants.

A run starts at time 0 in an initial location with all clocks zero. Time may advance by any nonnegative real amount, adding that amount to every clock. A transition can then fire when its guard is true; it changes the location and resets precisely the clocks in \(Y\) to zero. Its label and absolute firing time form an event. A finite run is accepting when its final location belongs to \(F\). The language \(L(A)\) consists of the timed words obtained from accepting runs by deleting all epsilon-labeled events and preserving the timestamps of all other events. Arbitrarily many but finitely many epsilon steps, including before the first and after the last visible event, are allowed.

A deterministic separator has exactly one initial location, no epsilon transitions, and at most one enabled transition for each location, input letter and clock valuation. Incomplete transition relations are permitted and a missing transition rejects. Equivalently one can merge overlapping guards when their target location and reset set coincide. The number of locations, number of clocks and magnitudes of constants can all depend on the input pair.

The decision algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions and must halt on every valid pair; no complexity bound or disjointness promise is imposed. A pair with intersecting languages necessarily has answer no. Malformed descriptions can be rejected.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of decidability for this input model and unrestricted finite separators, or a Lean-checked proof of its undecidability. Decidability for each fixed clock bound does not supply a decision algorithm for the unrestricted problem; the algorithm must also terminate on negative instances.
cards.why: Deterministic timed descriptions support complement and monitoring operations that arbitrary nondeterministic descriptions do not. Settling unrestricted separability would identify whether the existence of such a classifier can be decided without an advance bound on the memory of time represented by clocks.
