cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.formal:
For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is first-order model checking fixed-parameter tractable with a computable parameter dependence?

Precisely, does every such \(\mathcal C\) admit a single deterministic algorithm \(A_{\mathcal C}\), a total computable function \(f_{\mathcal C}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and a constant integer \(d_{\mathcal C}\ge0\) such that, for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every first-order graph sentence \(\varphi\), the algorithm outputs whether \(G\models\varphi\) within
\[f_{\mathcal C}(|\varphi|)\,(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{\mathcal C}}\]
steps? The algorithm receives only the graph and the sentence, in the encodings below, and must halt on every input. The exponent may depend on the class but not on the sentence. The effective structural hypothesis is the computable powerset-obstruction bound defined below.
cards.definitions:
Graph class and promise. A finite simple undirected graph has a finite vertex set and a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation \(E\); the empty graph is permitted. A class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under graph isomorphism. It is hereditary if \(G[S]\in\mathcal C\) for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every \(S\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[S]\) retains exactly the edges with both endpoints in \(S\). The class is fixed before the algorithm is chosen, not given as part of an instance. No decision procedure for membership in the class is assumed. Correctness and the displayed time bound are required only when the input graph belongs to the class. On other inputs the algorithm may return either answer, but must halt.

First-order syntax and truth. The graph signature has equality and a binary adjacency symbol, with variables \(x_i\) indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\). Formulas are built from atoms \(x_i=x_j\), \(E(x_i,x_j)\), negation, binary conjunction, and existential quantification \(\exists x_i\); other connectives and universal quantification are abbreviations expanded into this syntax. A sentence has no free variables. Atoms are interpreted using actual equality and graph adjacency; Boolean operations have their usual truth tables, and quantifiers range over all vertices. On the empty graph an existential statement is false and a universal statement is true. The query language has no unary predicates, vertex order, arithmetic, function symbols or set quantification. Write \(G\models\varphi\) for truth of the sentence.

Encoding and computation. For a nonnegative integer \(i\), let \(\ell\) be the binary length of \(i+1\), and encode it as \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), where the last part has exactly \(\ell\) bits. Encode \(G\) with labeled vertex set \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) as \(U(n)\) followed by its upper-triangular adjacency bits, in lexicographic order of pairs \(i<j\). All these bits are supplied explicitly. Formulas use prefix syntax: tags 000, 001, 010, 011, 100 respectively stand for equality, adjacency, negation, conjunction and existential quantification. An atom tag is followed by \(U(i)U(j)\), negation by one encoded subformula, conjunction by two in order, and the existential tag by \(U(i)\) and one subformula. The parameter \(|\varphi|\) is this binary length, including variable indices. A valid input concatenates the graph code and one sentence code; invalid inputs may be rejected. An algorithm is a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite tape alphabet and no oracle, advice or randomness; time counts its transitions. Polynomial simulation overhead between the usual explicit graph representations and finite-word computational models can be absorbed in the class-dependent exponent and parameter function.

Unary expansions for the structural condition. For this purpose only, allow additional unary symbols \(P_j\), \(j\in\mathbb N\), with atom \(P_j(x_i)\) encoded by tag 101 followed by \(U(j)U(i)\). Each formula uses finitely many such symbols. They are interpreted independently as arbitrary vertex subsets; they may overlap. Their names and variable indices are included in formula length. There are no additional parameters or constant symbols.

Transduction. Let \(\theta(x_0,x_1)\) be any formula in this expanded syntax whose only possible free variables are \(x_0,x_1\). Given \(G\), choose arbitrary interpretations of all unary symbols used in \(\theta\). On the same vertex set, form an undirected graph by putting an edge between distinct \(u,v\) exactly when \(\theta(u,v)\lor\theta(v,u)\) holds in that expansion of \(G\). Finally keep any subset of vertices and take the induced graph on it. Denote by \(T_\theta(G)\) the set of all graphs obtainable in this way, up to isomorphism. Colors are discarded in the output. There is no copying of vertices or tuple-valued output domain in this definition.

Monadic dependence and its effective version. A class is monadically dependent when no single formula \(\theta\) produces every finite simple graph among the outputs \(T_\theta(G)\) as \(G\) ranges over the class. To state the quantitative promise, for an integer \(s\ge1\) let \(P_s\) be the bipartite powerset graph with disjoint vertex sets \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_s\}\) and \(\{b_S:S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}\}\), and edges exactly \(a_i b_S\) with \(i\in S\). It has \(s+2^s\) vertices and no edges within either part.

The class \(\mathcal C\) is effectively monadically dependent if there is a total computable function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that
\[\forall\theta\ \forall G\in\mathcal C:\quad P_{b(|\theta|)}\notin T_\theta(G).\]
Absence means that no choice of unary predicates and retained vertex subset yields a graph isomorphic to that powerset graph. The bound is uniform over all formulas of the given length, all graphs in the class, and all their colorings. It is the effective dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24, which in particular implies monadic dependence. The finite program computing \(b\) may depend on \(\mathcal C\).

Uniformity of the requested algorithm. For each class, one finite program \(A_{\mathcal C}\) must handle all input sentence lengths. It may depend on the class and its effective dependence witness, but receives neither a class-membership certificate nor a graph decomposition on an instance. The quantifiers are class-wise existence of the algorithm, computable function and exponent; no single procedure that accepts arbitrary descriptions of classes and constructs their algorithms is required. There is no prescribed growth rate for \(f_{\mathcal C}\), beyond total computability.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish, for every class satisfying the hereditary and effective-dependence promises, one total deterministic algorithm and one computable parameter bound with a sentence-independent polynomial exponent, for the specified graph-and-sentence input model.

A negative answer must establish a particular hereditary effectively monadically dependent class for which no such algorithm, computable parameter function and fixed exponent work. In particular, every candidate total deterministic algorithm and bound must fail on some graph in that class and some sentence, either in correctness or in running time. An obstruction applying only to one proposed algorithm, an ineffective class, or a restricted decomposition method is insufficient. A conditional hardness result alone does not refute this unconditional target unless its additional assumption is also proved. Structural existence theorems, a different algorithm for each sentence length, randomized algorithms, or algorithms supplied with extra decompositions do not by themselves meet the criterion.
cards.why: First-order formulas express a broad family of graph queries, but direct evaluation lets the graph-size exponent grow with the query. The proposed structural condition aims to explain when that dependence can be confined to a computable function of the query alone, even on dense graph classes. Settling this tractability direction would complement the established hardness of hereditary classes that can logically encode arbitrary graphs.

cards.context:
First-order model checking asks whether a finite graph satisfies an input sentence. Clique, independent-set and dominating-set queries of a specified size are basic examples. Trying all assignments of vertices to variables gives polynomial time for each fixed sentence, but its exponent depends on the sentence. Fixed-parameter tractability requires one exponent for all sentences on the chosen class.

For example, a sentence can assert the existence of a fixed number of vertices such that every other vertex is adjacent to at least one of them. Increasing that number increases the sentence length and the direct enumeration cost. The target permits an arbitrarily large computable cost depending on sentence length, while keeping a fixed polynomial dependence on the graph size. It is a uniform guarantee across the whole query language.

The hereditary condition is closure under deleting vertices, keeping all remaining edges. It allows sparse and dense classes alike. Complete graphs illustrate why edge density is not itself the barrier: a dense class may still have tightly controlled logical behavior. The conjectured boundary uses what a fixed formula can encode after arbitrary unary marking, rather than an edge-count bound.

A transduction changes the edge relation according to a formula, after vertices have been marked by finitely many unary predicates, and may discard vertices. The formula is fixed while graph size grows. Monadic independence means that one such fixed scheme can yield every finite graph. Dependence excludes this unrestricted encoding, while allowing richer structure than monadic stability.

Computability is a genuine qualification in the saved target. A class can have a finite obstruction bound at each formula length without any computable function dominating those bounds. The dissertation illustrates this distinction with graph classes indexed by Busy Beaver growth. That example shows why a proof with arbitrary class-dependent constants cannot automatically be advertised as a computable FPT bound; it is not itself an unconditional counterexample to the present effective conjecture.

The structural witness and the query algorithm play different roles. The function b bounds powerset graphs obtainable by all short colored formulas; it does not recognize which graphs belong to the class. The requested algorithm receives a promised member of the class and an uncolored sentence. Neither a membership test nor a decomposition oracle is included in the input.

Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that model checking is \(\mathrm{AW}[*]\)-hard on every hereditary monadically independent class. Their stronger interpretation theorem produces uncolored instances efficiently, so this is not merely a hardness statement with extra vertex colors supplied. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{AW}[*]\), the independent side cannot have FPT model checking. That conditional intractability does not prove the positive dependent side.

Monadic stability is the stronger condition excluding arbitrarily large half-graphs under transductions: a half-graph of order \(s\) has two disjoint parts \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\), with edge \(a_i b_j\) exactly when \(i\le j\). The stable-class model-checking theorem gives a major positive case. The dissertation makes its parameter function computable under effective stability bounds; ordinary stability alone should not silently be substituted for that effective hypothesis.

Merge-width measures graph construction sequences that merge vertex groups and resolve pairs as edges or nonedges. At radius r, the width bounds how many current groups a vertex can reach using at most r resolved pairs. The existing bounded-merge-width model-checking theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied. Existence of a useful sequence alone does not meet the card’s input model.

The July 2026 paper proves almost linear neighborhood complexity for every monadically dependent class. Writing \(N_G(v)\) for the neighbors of \(v\), for every \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}\) such that for all \(G\in\mathcal C\) and all nonempty \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the number of distinct sets \(N_G(v)\cap S\) is at most \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}|S|^{1+\eta}\). The nonempty-set qualification avoids the zero-size edge case.

The same paper constructs radius-one merge-width sequences in \(O(n^5)\) time, with width \(n^{o(1)}\) on every monadically dependent class. Here \(n^{o(1)}\) means that for every fixed positive exponent the width is eventually at most a constant times that power of \(n\), with constants depending on the class. This is meaningful algorithmic progress, but gives neither a constant width bound nor corresponding control at all larger radii.

Dreier and Kuske’s February 2026 work speeds up low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, with a faster model-checking application for monadically stable classes. Its ordering and cover subroutines use randomness. A faster theorem on that already understood subclass does not establish the deterministic guarantee for every effectively monadically dependent class.

The July 2026 paper explicitly retains the general tractability direction as open. A positive answer here would establish the effective algorithmic direction of the proposed classification. A negative answer would require an effective hereditary class that defeats every single uniform algorithm with computable parameter dependence, not merely a class whose currently known decomposition bounds are ineffective.

source_formulation.text: Preserves importance 96 and the already selected effective, class-wise deterministic FPT formulation for plain graph sentences. The computable powerset-obstruction convention is explicitly grounded in Mählmann Definition12.24; the general survey deliberately suppresses such computability qualifications. This review fixes concrete finite encodings and time semantics without imposing an exponent uniform over all classes, a class-recognition algorithm, a supplied decomposition or colored per-instance query input. Different reasonable syntax encodings transfer computable structural bounds effectively.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The July 2026 primary paper explicitly keeps the full dependent-class tractability direction open. Its almost linear neighborhood complexity and polynomial-time radius-one construction do not give the stated deterministic, decomposition-free algorithm with computable parameter dependence. The effective hypothesis is the dissertation’s precise powerset-obstruction convention, retained from the saved target. No general resolution was found in bounded later searches; the review checked theorem statements and computational scope rather than independently verifying every long proof.

progress.text: First-order model checking is established for monadically stable classes; effective parameter bounds are treated explicitly in the dissertation.
The flip-breakability paper proves the hardness direction on every hereditary monadically independent class.
The dissertation distinguishes computable obstruction and runtime bounds in Definition 12.24 and Theorem 12.25.
Merge-width yields a general model-checking theorem with a supplied witnessing construction sequence.
Randomized faster ordering and cover algorithms improve the monadically stable model-checking application.

Almost linear neighborhood complexity and polynomial-time radius-one merge-width constructions are proved for all monadically dependent classes; the full tractability conjecture remains explicitly open.

sentences: First-order model checking evaluates a vertex-quantified logical sentence on an explicitly given finite graph.

The question asks for a uniform deterministic algorithm on each hereditary effectively monadically dependent class, with computable parameter dependence and a sentence-independent graph-size exponent.
Effective monadic dependence bounds the powerset graphs obtainable through short formulas with arbitrary unary vertex markings.
The algorithm receives no graph decomposition or class-membership certificate, and must work for all sentences on its fixed class.
Hereditary independent classes have a hardness theorem and effectively stable classes have algorithms, while the July 2026 radius-one results leave the full positive direction open.

cards.title: Asser’s problem
cards.formal:
Is the class of finite first-order spectra closed under complement within the positive integers?

For every finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) and every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) over \(\tau\), does there exist a finite relational vocabulary \(\sigma\) and a first-order sentence \(\psi\) over \(\sigma\) such that
\[\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\quad \bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\sigma\text{-structure satisfying }\psi\bigr)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \neg\bigl(\exists\text{ an }n\text{-element }\tau\text{-structure satisfying }\varphi\bigr)?\]
The vocabulary and sentence \((\sigma,\psi)\) may depend on \((\tau,\varphi)\), but must work simultaneously for every positive size \(n\). They need not use the original vocabulary. No effective procedure for obtaining \(\psi\), or bound on its length, is required.
cards.definitions:
Vocabulary and syntax. A finite relational vocabulary is a finite, possibly empty list \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) of distinct relation symbols with specified positive integer arities \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). There are no function or constant symbols. Equality is a logical symbol and is always available. Variables are drawn from a countable supply. Formulas are finite expressions built from equality atoms \(x=y\), relation atoms \(R_i(x_1,\ldots,x_{a_i})\), negation, conjunction, and first-order existential quantification; other Boolean connectives and universal quantification have their usual equivalent definitions. Variables in an atom may repeat. A sentence has no free variables. Neither the number of symbols, their arities, the number of variables nor quantifier depth has a fixed global bound.

Structures and semantics. A structure over \(\tau\) consists of a nonempty finite domain \(A\) and, for each symbol \(R_i\), an arbitrary interpretation \(R_i^A\subseteq A^{a_i}\). Equality is actual equality of elements. A relation atom holds under a variable assignment exactly when the assigned tuple belongs to its interpreted relation; equality, Boolean operations and existential quantification are evaluated in the usual way, with quantified variables ranging over elements of \(A\). Write \(\mathcal A\models\varphi\) when a sentence is true in this structure. There is no built-in order, arithmetic, graph condition or fixed interpretation of a relation. A sentence may itself require such properties.

Spectrum. Define
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)=\{n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:\exists\mathcal A,\ |A|=n\text{ and }\mathcal A\models\varphi\}.\]
The existence quantifier ranges over all interpretations of all symbols at that size. One may fix the domain to \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), since relabeling does not affect truth. The target is
\[\operatorname{Spec}(\psi)=\mathbb Z_{>0}\setminus\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi).\]
Only cardinalities are retained; the spectrum does not count how many models or isomorphism types exist at a size. Empty and infinite structures are outside this definition, and the complement does not include zero.

Scope. The restriction to relational vocabularies preserves the ordinary class of first-order spectra: finite-arity functions and constants can instead be represented by relations, together with first-order conditions enforcing their graph or unique-value interpretation on the same domain. No second-order quantifiers over relations or arbitrary external numerical predicates are added to the representing sentence. The target is an existence statement about finite formulas and their entire sets of model sizes. It imposes no computational model, sentence-construction resource bound or model-search algorithm requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal complement-closure statement or its full logical negation. A positive proof must establish a single representing first-order sentence for the whole positive-integer complement of each input spectrum; the new vocabulary is unrestricted except for finiteness and the stated relational syntax. A negative proof must establish a first-order spectrum whose complement is not the spectrum of any first-order sentence over any permitted finite vocabulary. Equivalently, for that input sentence, every candidate representing sentence must fail at some positive size, which may depend on the candidate. Checking finitely many sizes, ruling out a fixed vocabulary or variable bound, or showing that literal sentence negation fails is insufficient. The theorem must be unconditional unless it also proves every additional assumption used.
cards.why: A first-order sentence can describe rich finite structures, while its spectrum keeps only the possible domain sizes. Asser’s question asks whether the sizes excluded by one such description can always be the sizes admitted by another. Its equivalence with closure of nondeterministic exponential time under complement makes this a fundamental meeting point of finite model theory and computational complexity.

cards.context:
Scholz asked in 1952 how to characterize the sets of finite sizes admitted by first-order sentences. Asser’s 1955 complement question asks for a particular closure property of that class. Characterizing the class in another language does not by itself settle its closure under complement; the historical survey treats these as distinct questions.

The quantifier over structures is essential. For example, over a unary predicate \(P\), the sentence \((\exists x\,P(x))\land(\exists y\,\neg P(y))\) has a model exactly at sizes at least two. Its logical negation has a model at every positive size, since \(P\) can be empty. The complement of the original spectrum is just \(\{1\}\). Thus truth of a negated sentence in some structure is different from absence of every model of the original sentence at that size.

A spectrum forgets which structures realize a size. It can be empty, finite, cofinite or infinite with large gaps. The survey records closure under finite unions and intersections, with relation vocabularies allowed to vary. Complement is the missing general Boolean closure operation. Requiring a representative in the original vocabulary would impose an additional condition not present in Asser’s question.

The computational characterization uses binary representations of sizes. If \(m\) is the number of bits in \(n\), the class \(\mathrm{NE}\) consists of languages accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine in time \(O(2^{cm})\) for some fixed constant \(c\). Jones and Selman, and independently Fagin, identify first-order spectra with the sets whose canonical binary representations belong to this class. Here a canonical positive representation begins with a one and has no leading zeros.

Consequently, general spectrum complement closure is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{coNE}\), where the latter class contains complements of languages in \(\mathrm{NE}\). The input-size convention matters: unary encoding has length \(n\), whereas binary encoding has length proportional to \(\log n\). The relevant complexity class is single-exponential nondeterministic time in that binary length, not polynomial time in an explicitly supplied structure.

A negative answer would also imply \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), and therefore \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), as noted in the two-variable paper. The converse is not asserted. This is a precise one-way connection to those complexity questions, not an identification of Asser’s problem with P versus NP.

For two-variable logic with counting, denoted \(C^2\), Kopczyński and Tan prove a complete answer: its spectra are exactly the semilinear sets and are closed under complement even within \(C^2\). This logic reuses only two variable names, with quantifiers asserting that at least a fixed number of elements satisfy a formula. In one dimension, semilinear sets are ultimately periodic: beyond a finite threshold, membership depends only on the residue modulo some positive period.

The variable-hierarchy paper shows that allowing more variables genuinely increases spectrum expressibility along an infinite hierarchy. Nevertheless, its complement problem reduces to input sentences with only three variables and binary relations. These are different claims: a reduction of the complement question does not say that every spectrum itself has a three-variable description. The complement representative in that reduction may use arbitrarily many variables.

The 2018 paper sharpens the reduction further to input sentences using three variables and one symmetric binary relation, all of whose models are undirected bipartite graphs. Its encoding changes model sizes by a fixed affine transformation. The resulting equivalence still asks whether each restricted input spectrum’s complement is some first-order spectrum; it does not require a three-variable bipartite representative for that complement.

The 2024 paper extends the two-variable spectrum analysis to ultimately periodic counting conditions. Its Theorem 9.1 effectively describes finite model sizes by a formula of Presburger arithmetic, the first-order arithmetic of addition and order. That is substantive progress for an expressive restricted logic. It does not remove the two-variable restriction or settle complement closure for arbitrary first-order sentences.

Finite satisfiability asks whether a sentence has any finite model at all; Asser’s problem asks about the entire set of its possible finite sizes. The known undecidability of the former does not refute the latter’s non-effective existence claim. Likewise, a positive answer here would not, by itself, provide a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.

context_blocks.text: Scholz asked in 1952 how to characterize the sets of finite sizes admitted by first-order sentences. Asser’s 1955 complement question asks for a particular closure property of that class. Characterizing the class in another language does not by itself settle its closure under complement; the historical survey treats these as distinct questions.

The quantifier over structures is essential. For example, over a unary predicate \(P\), the sentence \((\exists x\,P(x))\land(\exists y\,\neg P(y))\) has a model exactly at sizes at least two. Its logical negation has a model at every positive size, since \(P\) can be empty. The complement of the original spectrum is just \(\{1\}\). Thus truth of a negated sentence in some structure is different from absence of every model of the original sentence at that size.

A spectrum forgets which structures realize a size. It can be empty, finite, cofinite or infinite with large gaps. The survey records closure under finite unions and intersections, with relation vocabularies allowed to vary. Complement is the missing general Boolean closure operation. Requiring a representative in the original vocabulary would impose an additional condition not present in Asser’s question.

The computational characterization uses binary representations of sizes. If \(m\) is the number of bits in \(n\), the class \(\mathrm{NE}\) consists of languages accepted by a nondeterministic Turing machine in time \(O(2^{cm})\) for some fixed constant \(c\). Jones and Selman, and independently Fagin, identify first-order spectra with the sets whose canonical binary representations belong to this class. Here a canonical positive representation begins with a one and has no leading zeros.

Consequently, general spectrum complement closure is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NE}=\mathrm{coNE}\), where the latter class contains complements of languages in \(\mathrm{NE}\). The input-size convention matters: unary encoding has length \(n\), whereas binary encoding has length proportional to \(\log n\). The relevant complexity class is single-exponential nondeterministic time in that binary length, not polynomial time in an explicitly supplied structure.

cards.title: NP membership of word-equation satisfiability
cards.formal:
Let \(\mathrm{WE}\) be the language of encodings of satisfiable word equations \(u=v\) over finite free monoids, as defined below. Is
\[
\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}?
\]
Explicitly, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(V\), a constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(V\) halts on every pair of bit strings \((e,w)\) within \(C(|e|+|w|+1)^k\) steps and, for every valid equation encoding \(e\) of length \(N\),
\[
e\in\mathrm{WE}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ 
\bigl(|w|\le C(N+1)^k\ \text{and}\ V(e,w)=1\bigr)?
\]
The verifier rejects invalid equation encodings. The same machine and constants work for all alphabets, equations and variable sets.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(a\ge1\), the constant alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{a_1,\ldots,a_a\}\). Its free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) is the set of finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as the operation. Concatenation is associative and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity; distinct letters do not commute by assumption.

The variable set is \(\mathcal X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_r\}\), disjoint from \(\Sigma\), where \(r\ge0\). An equation is a pair \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Both sides are explicitly written token sequences. A solution assigns one word \(\sigma(X_i)\in\Sigma^*\) to each variable, fixes every constant letter, and extends by concatenation. The equation is satisfiable exactly when \(\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)\) for some assignment. All occurrences of a variable receive the same word. Empty words, repeated variables, variables on both sides, and equations with empty sides are allowed. There are no length constraints, regular-language restrictions, inverse symbols or inequalities.

One precise binary encoding is as follows. Write \(1^a0\,1^r0\,1^{\ell_u}0\,1^{\ell_v}0\), where \(\ell_u=|u|\) and \(\ell_v=|v|\) count tokens. Follow this header by all tokens of \(u\) and then all tokens of \(v\). Each token is encoded in \(b=\lceil\log_2(a+r+1)\rceil\) bits: code \(i\) for \(a_i\) and code \(a+j\) for \(X_j\). Codes outside \(1,\ldots,a+r\) are invalid. There must be exactly \(\ell_u+\ell_v\) token blocks and no trailing data. Thus
\[
N=a+r+\ell_u+\ell_v+4+b(\ell_u+\ell_v).
\]
This explicit encoding fixes bit complexity without allowing compressed input equations.

Use [NP](definitions.html#p-np), with precisely the soundness and completeness quantified above. A certificate is any finite binary string. It need not contain the substituted words explicitly, and no particular compressed representation is prescribed. A satisfiable input must have some short accepting certificate; an unsatisfiable input must have none.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer must specify the verifier and prove the polynomial time and certificate bounds together with soundness and completeness for every input. A negative answer must prove that no such verifier exists; failure of one certificate format or long explicit solutions is insufficient. This binary target has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Results only for boundedly many variables, bounded occurrences, or added constraints do not decide the full statement.
cards.why: Word equations are a basic model of string constraints and associative unification. Their decidability is established, but the gap between NP-hardness and polynomial-space algorithms leaves the complexity of short verifiable evidence unresolved. NP membership would place the unrestricted satisfiability problem at the familiar NP-complete boundary.

cards.context:
A variable stands for an entire finite word, not for one letter. For example, an equation can require two occurrences of the same unknown word to match material appearing at different positions on the other side. Concatenation couples the lengths and contents of all substitutions.

Makanin established decidability, and later work reduced the space needed to decide satisfiability. The 1998 RTA question predates the polynomial-space improvement, so its much larger upper bound is historical provenance rather than the current frontier.

Jeż’s 2017 theorem places satisfiability in nondeterministic linear space measured in input bits. This implies membership in PSPACE, the class decidable using polynomial working space. A space bound alone need not limit the number of computation steps to a polynomial, so it does not supply NP membership.

An explicit substitution may be much longer than the input equation. The NP question is therefore about succinct evidence that can be checked quickly, not about requiring a short fully expanded solution. Existing work on compressed solutions explains this distinction, but the card does not mandate any particular evidence format.

Saarela’s 2026 theorem simplifies parametric descriptions for constant-free equations on three variables. Its introduction still lists NP membership for general word equations as open. A result about the structure of that restricted solution set does not settle the unrestricted decision problem.

The June 2026 preprint claims stronger hardness for formulas that combine word equations with length constraints. Those extra arithmetic constraints change the input language. The claim therefore does not establish a lower bound excluding NP for plain equations, and its full proof was not independently audited in this review.

The earlier two TCS500 benchmark records used different historical names for overlapping complexity questions. This card is now the single active NP-membership target. The duplicate’s source and provenance remain available, while the broader request for an exact complexity classification is no longer the benchmark question.

cards.title: Decidability of multiplicative-exponential linear logic and branching VASS reachability
cards.formal: Is provability decidable in propositional multiplicative-exponential linear logic (MELL)? Given a finite sequent \(\Gamma\), the algorithm must halt and decide whether \(\vdash\Gamma\) has a derivation in the calculus below. Equivalently, is exact reachability decidable for branching vector addition systems with states (branching VASS)? Given a finite system of input dimension \(d\) and a target \(q(x)\), decide whether a finite derivation tree has root \(q(x)\).
cards.definitions:
MELL. Use finite formula trees. Leaves are atoms \(p_i\), their dual literals \(p_i^\perp\) for \(i\ge 0\), or units \(1,\bot\). The constructors are tensor \(A\otimes B\), par (⅋), written \(A\mathbin{\mathrm{par}}B\), and the modalities \(!A,?A\), with arbitrary nesting. A sequent is a finite multiset of formulas. A comma denotes multiset union. The one-sided cut-free calculus has two axioms, \(\vdash p_i,p_i^\perp\) and \(\vdash 1\). From \(\vdash\Gamma,A\) and \(\vdash\Delta,B\), tensor derives \(\vdash\Gamma,\Delta,A\otimes B\). From \(\vdash\Gamma,A,B\), par derives \(\vdash\Gamma,A\mathbin{\mathrm{par}}B\). From \(\vdash\Gamma\), the unit rule derives \(\vdash\Gamma,\bot\). Dereliction takes \(\vdash\Gamma,A\) to \(\vdash\Gamma,?A\). Weakening takes \(\vdash\Gamma\) to \(\vdash\Gamma,?A\). Contraction takes \(\vdash\Gamma,?A,?A\) to \(\vdash\Gamma,?A\). Promotion takes \(\vdash ?\Gamma,A\) to \(\vdash ?\Gamma,!A\), where every formula in \(?\Gamma\) has outermost symbol \(?\). Contexts may be empty. A derivation is a finite tree built from these rules. Input sequents list the formula trees explicitly with binary atom indices.

Branching VASS. The input specifies a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), a dimension \(d\ge 1\), and finitely many rules \((S,a,q)\) with \(S\subseteq Q\), \(a\in\mathbb Z^d\), and \(q\in Q\). A configuration \(q(x)\) has \(x\in\mathbb N^d\), with zero allowed. To apply a rule, supply a child \(s(x_s)\) for each \(s\in S\). The parent is \(q(a+\sum_{s\in S}x_s)\), provided every output coordinate is nonnegative. An empty \(S\) gives a leaf \(q(a)\) under the same condition. A target is reachable if it occurs at the root of a finite tree of rule applications. Rules may be reused. The system, child-state sets and target are explicit, and all coordinates are in binary.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a decision procedure for either formulation and prove that it halts and answers correctly on every valid input, or prove undecidability. The established reductions carry either answer to the other formulation. The reachability target is exact and the dimension is part of the input.
cards.why: A proof in MELL tracks which assumptions are consumed, copied or discarded. A branching counter system tracks the same resources as vectors in a computation tree. Their equivalence turns a foundational proof-search question into a reachability problem for an infinite-state system.

cards.context:
Linear logic treats assumptions as resources whose occurrences matter. An ordinary assumption cannot automatically be copied or discarded. For example, the resource-reading of \(p\to p\otimes p\) asks for two copies from one and is unavailable in general; marking the input !p permits reuse. MELL keeps multiplicative composition together with these reuse modalities.

The rules make each proposed finite proof checkable. That does not by itself make provability decidable: searching through larger proofs will eventually find a proof when one exists, but need not terminate when none exists. The question asks for a single procedure that also gives a terminating negative answer.

The restrictions on contraction and promotion are part of the problem. Allowing unrestricted contraction gives a different logic, and adding additive connectives or several interacting subexponential modalities changes the decidability boundary. A published 2015 decidability argument was challenged in Straßburger’s 2019 paper, which identifies gaps and separates MELL from its decidable relevant variant.

A branching rule adds the resource vectors of its children. For example, leaves in two distinct states carrying two and three tokens can feed a rule whose output carries five. Exact reachability asks whether a specified state and vector can be derived in this way.

In 2004, de Groote, Guillaume and Salvati showed how to translate a MELL proof-search instance into a branching reachability instance and how to translate back. Decidability of either problem therefore implies decidability of the other.

Bizière, Leroux and Sutre show that every unreachable vector can be separated from the reachable set by a semilinear inductive invariant. Enumerating derivations and candidate invariants in parallel gives a terminating decision procedure. Their July 2026 preprint also draws the consequence for MELL.

cards.title: Decidability of Presburger arithmetic with primes
cards.formal: Is the full first-order theory of the fixed structure \[\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}=(\mathbb Z;0,1,+,-,<,\mathrm{Pr})\] decidable, where \(\mathrm{Pr}(n)\) means that \(n\ge2\) is a positive prime? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every finite encoded sentence \(\varphi\) of this language and returns YES exactly when \(\mathcal Z_{\mathrm{Pr}}\models\varphi\)? The question is unconditional and permits arbitrary finite first-order quantifier alternation.
cards.definitions: All variables range over the standard integers \(\mathbb Z\). The symbols \(0,1,+,-,<\) denote their usual constants, addition, unary negation and strict order. The predicate \(\mathrm{Pr}\) is false for negative integers, zero and one; for \(n\ge2\), it is true exactly when the only positive divisors of \(n\) are \(1\) and \(n\). This defines the intended predicate in the mathematical metatheory; multiplication and variable divisibility are not additional symbols of the input language. Terms are variables, integer numerals, sums and negatives. Atoms are term equality, strict inequality and \(\mathrm{Pr}(t)\); formulas use the ordinary Boolean connectives and individual-variable \(\exists,\forall\). A sentence has no free variables. Arbitrary signed integer numerals and multiplication by a specified integer coefficient are harmless abbreviations for expressions in this language, not products of two variables. Inputs are explicit finite syntax trees with variable identifiers and numerals encoded in binary. Malformed encodings may be rejected. The machine is uniform over all formula lengths, variable counts and alternation depths, with no prescribed resource bound, randomness or oracle. It must give exact truth in this one intended structure, rather than satisfiability over arbitrary structures or provability from an unspecified axiom set. There is no numerical tolerance. Removing the definable unary-negation symbol does not change decidability: its graph is \(x+y=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that such a total computable truth classifier exists, or that none exists. A positive proof must formalize finite syntax, satisfaction in the standard integer structure, the algorithm, termination on every sentence and correctness in both truth directions. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this exact full theory. A result conditional on an unproved number-theoretic hypothesis must discharge that hypothesis to meet the unconditional criterion. Deciding a quantifier-restricted fragment or testing the primality of a supplied integer does not cover the target. No Lean formalization is supplied by this editorial review.
cards.why: Addition and order alone admit a complete decision procedure, while the prime predicate brings the distribution of primes into quantified arithmetic without directly adding multiplication. This is a classical boundary question linking effective first-order reasoning, definability and deep number theory. The standard ordered structure can express prime-pattern assertions, so a truth decider would have consequences far beyond individual primality tests.

cards.context:
Presburger arithmetic allows arbitrary first-order quantification but restricts its numerical operations to addition, order and fixed integer coefficients. Adding one decidable predicate can still change decidability of the full theory: the issue is the interaction with unbounded quantifiers, not the cost of evaluating that predicate at a known integer.

The source works over integers and writes an order-based twin-prime sentence. Accordingly, this card includes order and takes primes to be positive. For example, the twin-prime assertion is \(\forall x\,\exists y\,(x\le y\land\mathrm{Pr}(y)\land\mathrm{Pr}(y+2))\).

The source also invokes Goldbach’s conjecture. Its even-input restriction must be explicit: one correct sentence is \(\forall n\,(n\ge2\Rightarrow\exists p\,\exists q\,(\mathrm{Pr}(p)\land\mathrm{Pr}(q)\land p+q=n+n))\). The printed illustrative sentence on p. 29 omits that restriction; the open decision question itself does not depend on this typo.

Bateman, Jockusch and Woods prove, assuming the linear case of Schinzel’s hypothesis, that multiplication is definable in the natural-number structure with addition and primes, yielding undecidability. The nonnegative integers are definable in the ordered integer structure, so this conditional obstruction applies to the present target too. The hypothesis is essential to the stated theorem.

Dickson’s prime-tuples conjecture is the assertion that finitely many integer affine forms with positive leading coefficients take simultaneous prime values infinitely often whenever no prime divides their product for every integer argument. The card does not assume this conjecture.

Kaplan and Shelah prove conditional decidability for the unordered additive integer structure whose predicate includes both primes and their negatives. Their introduction explicitly retains the number-theoretic assumption on the ordered undecidability result, although the abstract abbreviates that qualification. The absence of order and the symmetric prime convention are substantive differences.

The 2024 survey explicitly retains the present decision question. The September 2026 bounded primary-source search found no matching unconditional resolution; this is dated evidence and a search limit, not a proof that the question remains open.

cards.title: Scott-continuous lambda models with theory \(\lambda \beta\)
cards.formal: Do there exist a pointed directed-complete partial order \(D\) and Scott-continuous maps \(F:D\to[D\to D]\) and \(L:[D\to D]\to D\) with \(F\circ L=\mathrm{id}_{[D\to D]}\), such that two finite untyped lambda terms have equal interpretations in every environment exactly when they are beta-convertible?
cards.definitions:
Terms are built from countably many variables using application \(MN\) and abstraction \(\lambda x.M\), up to renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility \(=_\beta\) is the least congruence containing \((\lambda x.M)N=_\beta M[N/x]\), using capture-avoiding substitution.

A directed subset is nonempty and each pair of its elements has an upper bound in the subset. The partial order \(D\) has a least element and suprema of all directed subsets. A Scott-continuous function is monotone and preserves directed suprema. The function space \([D\to D]\) contains all such functions ordered pointwise.

An environment \(\rho\) assigns an element of \(D\) to each variable. Write \(I_\rho(M)\) for the interpretation of a term. Define
\[I_\rho(x)=\rho(x),\qquad I_\rho(MN)=F(I_\rho(M))(I_\rho(N)),\qquad I_\rho(\lambda x.M)=L\bigl(d\mapsto I_{\rho[x:=d]}(M)\bigr).\]
The target is \((\forall\rho,\ I_\rho(M)=I_\rho(N))\iff M=_\beta N\) for every \(M,N\). The domain may have arbitrary cardinality and need not be algebraic or effectively presented. Only \(F\circ L\) must be the identity. These are set-based models with the full Scott-continuous function space.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that a pointed dcpo and continuous retraction F,L satisfying the stated exact-theory condition exist, or prove that none exist. A negative answer must cover all such dcpos, without assuming an effective presentation, algebraicity or extensionality.
cards.why: A foundational completeness question for denotational semantics: does the mathematical structure used to describe approximation and recursion inevitably identify programs beyond beta-conversion, or can it preserve every distinction made by that computation rule?

references.title: Lambda Galore
references.authors: Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini; Besik Dundua; Furio Honsell
references.locator: FoSSaCS 2026, 262–284, published 15 April 2026; Definition 10 and Section 6, sensible models not extending Böhm-tree theory.

cards.context:
The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation \(F\circ L=\mathrm{id}\) ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates \(\lambda x\).f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing \(L\circ F=\mathrm{id}\) would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly \(\lambda \beta\) or \(\lambda \beta \eta\). They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. The 2025 filter-model paper studies when unsolvables receive nontrivial interpretations and which type-theoretic conditions govern that behavior.

Lambda Galore, published in 2026, constructs sensible filter models representing all continuous functions whose theories do not contain the full Böhm-tree theory. It separates two semantic properties and resolves a different question about models. Sensibility still identifies unsolvables, so these constructions do not realize exactly \(\lambda \beta\). Continuous representability alone does not make their equational theory the one requested here.

cards.title: Barendregt–Geuvers–Klop conjecture
cards.formal: For every pure type system \((S,A,R)\) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
cards.definitions:
A pure type system has sorts \(S\), axioms \(A\subseteq S^2\) and product rules \(R\subseteq S^3\). The finite terms are variables, sorts, applications \(tu\), abstractions \(\lambda x:B.t\), and products \(\Pi x:B.C\), up to renaming bound variables. Variables come from a countably infinite set. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. The typing judgment is the least relation satisfying the following rules, with \(s,s_1,s_2,s_3\) ranging over sorts and each fresh declaration using a new variable.

For \((s_1,s_2)\in A\), derive \(\varnothing\vdash s_1:s_2\). From \(\Gamma\vdash B:s\), derive \(\Gamma,x:B\vdash x:B\) for fresh \(x\). Weaken \(\Gamma\vdash t:B\) to \(\Gamma,x:C\vdash t:B\) if \(\Gamma\vdash C:s\) and \(x\) is fresh.

From \(\Gamma\vdash B:s_1\), \(\Gamma,x:B\vdash C:s_2\) and \((s_1,s_2,s_3)\in R\), derive \(\Gamma\vdash(\Pi x:B.C):s_3\). From \(\Gamma,x:B\vdash t:C\) and \(\Gamma\vdash(\Pi x:B.C):s\), derive \(\Gamma\vdash(\lambda x:B.t):(\Pi x:B.C)\). From \(\Gamma\vdash t:(\Pi x:B.C)\) and \(\Gamma\vdash u:B\), derive \(\Gamma\vdash tu:C[u/x]\). Finally, from \(\Gamma\vdash t:B\), \(\Gamma\vdash C:s\) and \(B=_\beta C\), derive \(\Gamma\vdash t:C\).

One beta step contracts \((\lambda x:B.t)u\) to \(t[u/x]\) at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. Substitution avoids capture, and \(=_\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of these steps. A term is typable if it has a type in some finite context. Weak normalization means each typable term has a finite reduction to a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means every reduction from every typable term is finite. Both notions include open terms. The system may be infinite, undecidable or nonfunctional.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.
cards.why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.

references.title: Normalization in Lambda-Calculus and Type Theory
references.locator: PhD dissertation submitted April 1997; hosted revised edition with April 1998 preface; Chapter 3, generalized non-dependent PTS results and technical hypotheses.

cards.context:
A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let \(\Omega\)=(\(\lambda z\).zz)(\(\lambda z\).zz). The term (\(\lambda x\).y)\(\Omega\) reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce \(\Omega\) forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.

cards.title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every finite modal formula \(\varphi\) and decides whether there exists a substitution \(\sigma\) for its propositional variables such that \(\sigma (\varphi )\) is valid on every Kripke frame?
cards.definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables \(p_{i} (i\in \mathbb{N} ), \perp\), negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in \(\varphi\), may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation \(R\subseteq \mathrm{W}\times \mathrm{W}\), finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and \(w\models\)□\(\psi\) iff \(v\models \psi\) for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a total decision procedure correct for every finite formula in the stated language, or prove that no such Turing machine exists. The unbounded substitution and arbitrary-frame semantics must remain those of parameter-free, single-modality K.

cards.context:
A modal formula talks about truth at a world and at worlds accessible from it. Unification asks whether its variables can be replaced by formulas so that the result becomes valid on every frame. This is a global requirement on one syntactic replacement, shared across all worlds and models. Choosing a satisfying assignment in one model is a different and weaker task.

For example, □p is unifiable: replacing p by ⊤ makes it valid. In contrast, ◇p is satisfiable in a model with an accessible world where p holds, but has no unifier in K. At a world with no successors, ◇\(\psi\) is false for every replacement \(\psi\). Such dead ends are allowed by K’s unrestricted frame semantics. These examples distinguish satisfiability from the existence of a valid substitution instance.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula \(p\to\)□p, unifiers exist, including \(p\mapsto \top\), but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.

cards.title: Decidability of termination for one-rule string rewriting
cards.formal: Is global termination of a one-rule string rewriting system decidable? The input is a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two explicitly written words \(\ell,r\in\Sigma^{*}\). Define \(u\to v\) when \(u=x\ell y\) and \(v=xry\) for some \(x,y\in\Sigma^{*}\). Decide whether there exists no infinite sequence \(w_0\to w_1\to w_2\to\cdots\) of finite words. The quantifier includes every starting word and every choice of replacement position.
cards.definitions:
The alphabet is a finite nonempty set listed by distinct binary symbol indices. Both sides of the rule are explicit finite sequences of these symbols, including possibly the empty word \(\varepsilon\). No variables, compressed word descriptions, contexts supplied as inputs, or additional rewrite rules occur.

One rewrite step chooses one contiguous occurrence of \(\ell\) and replaces it with \(r\), preserving the prefix \(x\) and suffix \(y\). If \(\ell=\varepsilon\), any boundary in a word, including its ends, is an occurrence. A rule application counts as a step even when the resulting word is identical to the original word. Thus \(\ell=r\) admits a constant infinite reduction sequence from \(\ell\).

Global termination means that for every \(w_0\in\Sigma^{*}\) there is no function \(w:\mathbb{N}\to\Sigma^{*}\) with first value \(w_0\) and \(w_i\to w_{i+1}\) for all \(i\geq0\). There is no fixed leftmost or rightmost evaluation strategy. Requiring only that each word has some terminating sequence would be a different property.

Decidability asks for a single deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid finite description and outputs yes exactly for globally terminating systems. No running-time bound is imposed. Malformed descriptions can be rejected. The rule itself varies across instances; neither its length nor the alphabet size is a fixed constant.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a total decision algorithm for all one-rule systems in this model, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. Deciding termination from one supplied start word, analyzing one strategy, or handling a restricted family of rules alone is insufficient.
cards.why: A single literal replacement is among the simplest possible descriptions of an unbounded computation. Settling its global termination problem would locate a sharp limit on automatic reasoning about repeated symbolic transformations, without relying on a large instruction set or richer term syntax.

cards.title: Commutativity of the full probabilistic powerdomain monad
cards.formal: Editorial subprobability variant: for all dcpos X,Y, all continuous subprobability valuations mu on X and nu on Y, and every Scott-continuous \(f:X\times Y\to[0,\infty]\), must \[\int_X\!\left(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d\nu(y)\right)d\mu(x)=\int_Y\!\left(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\right)d\nu(y)\,?\] This is commutativity of the full continuous-subprobability valuation monad.
cards.definitions:
A dcpo is a partially ordered set in which each nonempty directed subset has a supremum. A directed set is one in which every finite subset has an upper bound within the set. A Scott-open subset is upward closed and, whenever a directed supremum belongs to it, contains an element of that directed set. A map is Scott-continuous when it is monotone and preserves directed suprema. X×Y has the componentwise dcpo order and its Scott topology; do not substitute a potentially different topological product of Scott spaces. The target [0,infinity] has its usual order and Scott topology.

A continuous subprobability valuation mu assigns a number in [0,1] to each Scott-open U, with mu(empty)=0, mu(X)≤1, monotonicity, modularity mu(U)+mu(V)=mu(U union V)+mu(U intersection V), and preservation of suprema of directed families of open sets. For a nonnegative Scott-continuous h define its integral by the layer-cake formula integral_0^infinity mu({x:h(x)>t}) dt, allowing infinity. Iterated integrals in the statement use this definition.

The monad orders valuations pointwise; its unit sends x to the Dirac valuation U↦1 if x∈U, zero otherwise. For a Scott-continuous kernel K:X→V(Y), extension maps mu to U↦integral_X K(x)(U)dmu(x). These definitions specify the same independence-interchange question through the displayed Fubini identity. All continuous valuations of total mass at most one are allowed, not just finite combinations of Dirac valuations or their directed-supremum closure, called minimal valuations. Choosing total mass at most one is an explicit specialization; the card does not claim equivalence with every unbounded-mass convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed identity for the entire stated domain, or explicit dcpos, continuous subprobability valuations and a Scott-continuous integrand with different iterated integrals. A nonminimal valuation alone is not a counterexample, and commutativity proved only for minimal valuations does not settle the full class.
cards.why: Commutativity determines whether a central denotational model supports unrestricted exchange of probabilistic effects.

cards.title: Univalence, impredicativity and propositional resizing
cards.formal: Does there exist a nondegenerate model of ordinary dependent type theory, with the type formers and computation rules specified below, containing a univalent impredicative universe \(U\) of data types into which every homotopy proposition can be resized?
cards.definitions: A model is a set-based category with families: it has contexts and substitutions forming a category with an empty terminal context, types over each context, terms of each type, and context extension \(\Gamma.A\) classifying a substitution into \(\Gamma\) together with a term of its reindexed type \(A\). Reindexing of types and terms obeys identity and composition strictly. Type-forming operations, constructors and eliminators commute strictly with reindexing. Require dependent products \(\prod_{x:A}B(x)\), dependent sums \(\sum_{x:A}B(x)\), intensional identity types \(\operatorname{Id}_A(a,b)\), empty and unit types, binary coproducts, and natural numbers. Products have abstraction and application with the usual judgmental beta and eta equations; sums have pairing, projections and dependent elimination with their usual computation equations. Identity types have reflexivity and the unrestricted dependent eliminator \(J\), whose reflexivity computation equation holds judgmentally. Empty, unit, coproduct and natural-number types have their usual dependent eliminators and judgmental constructor equations. Also require function extensionality: the canonical map from an identity of dependent functions to their pointwise identities is an equivalence. Judgmental equations are equalities of the interpreted operations, rather than merely inhabited identity types. Nondegenerate means that the interpreted empty type has no closed term. A Tarski universe is an ambient type \(U\) with a decoding family \(\operatorname{El}:U\to\mathrm{Type}\). It has codes for empty, unit, binary coproduct and natural-number types and is closed under dependent sums and identity types of decoded small types. It is impredicative when, for every ambient type \(A\) and family \(b:A\to U\), the dependent product \(\prod_{x:A}\operatorname{El}(b(x))\) has a code in \(U\). These coding operations and their decoding identifications must be specified and stable under substitution; decoded closure may hold up to specified isomorphism. The domain \(A\) need not itself have a code in \(U\). There is no requirement that \(U\) code itself. Write \(\operatorname{isProp}(P)=\prod_{x,y:P}\operatorname{Id}_P(x,y)\). A type is contractible if it has a point identified with every point; a map is an equivalence if every fiber \(\sum_x\operatorname{Id}(f(x),y)\) is contractible. Univalence means that, for all \(a,b:U\), the canonical transport map \(\operatorname{Id}_U(a,b)\to\operatorname{Equiv}(\operatorname{El}(a),\operatorname{El}(b))\) is an equivalence. Propositional resizing means that for every ambient type \(P\), in every context with a term of \(\operatorname{isProp}(P)\), there is a small proposition code \(p:U\) and an equivalence \(P\simeq\operatorname{El}(p)\), uniformly under substitution. These are internal structures of the model; external equivalence of isolated fibers is insufficient. No particular assembly, cubical or path-category presentation, no Church’s thesis and no higher inductive types are required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a model exists, specifying its semantic structures and verifying all rules, closure, univalence, resizing and nondegeneracy; or prove in Lean that no such model exists. A merely postulated model, a model with only propositional universes, or a model validating only weaker identity or dependent-product computation rules does not satisfy this formulation. A failure of resizing in one candidate model is not a universal nonexistence proof.
cards.why: Determine compatibility of univalence, impredicative data-type universes and propositional resizing under ordinary dependent computation rules, clarifying a substantive boundary in foundations for proof assistants.

cards.context:
A universe is a type whose elements name other types. Ordinary predicative universes generally move to a larger level when one quantifies over a larger domain. Impredicativity instead keeps a product small whenever its values are small, even if the domain is large. Here the universe includes natural numbers and other data types; it is not only a collection of propositions.

Univalence says that equivalent small types are identified in the universe, with the appropriate higher identity structure. Resizing asks a different question: whether every ambient proposition already has a small representative. A proposition is a type whose any two inhabitants are identified, which does not require it to have an inhabitant.

Uemura constructs a cubical assembly model with a univalent impredicative universe and proves that resizing into that universe fails. His concluding question asks for compatibility of the three principles in another model, rather than for a proof of resizing in the displayed countermodel.

This card spells out the ordinary-type-theory reading of that question. The data-type codes and nondegeneracy prevent a vacuous or proposition-only interpretation; strict substitution and the stated computation rules specify the coherence demanded of a model. It does not add a requirement for a particular semantic construction.

Van den Berg gives related positive path-category constructions, including an impredicative univalent universe of sets with resizing. Uemura explicitly distinguishes their weaker identity and dependent-product structure from a model of ordinary homotopy type theory. Those positive results therefore need their semantic qualification when compared with this target.

Speight’s later groupoidal realizability work constructs an impredicative universe of 1-types, but the model does not validate function extensionality in general. Its concluding questions still distinguish univalent universes and resizing. The presence of an impredicative universe alone does not supply the full structure requested here.

A resolution would clarify whether a universe supporting ordinary data, equivalence-based identity and quantification over larger domains can coexist with small representatives for all propositions. This affects the foundations of dependent reasoning and proof-assistant universe systems, rather than the runtime of a program.

cards.title: Decidability and completeness of concurrent Kleene algebra with parallel iteration
cards.formal: Settle both parts of the source question for the full concurrent Kleene-algebra signature, including unbounded finite parallel iteration. For finite expressions \(e,f\), write \(e\preceq f\) when \(\downarrow\llbracket e\rrbracket\subseteq\downarrow\llbracket f\rrbracket\), using the pomset refinement semantics below. (1) Is there a total computable procedure deciding \(e\preceq f\) on every pair of such expressions? (2) Are the stated Kleene-algebra axioms for both products, together with weak interchange, complete for this semantics: \[\forall e,f,\quad e\preceq f\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{CKA}\vdash e+f=f?\] The already settled fragment without parallel iteration is recorded in the context. The two remaining questions are separate: neither an algorithm alone nor an axiomatic completeness theorem alone is a complete answer to this paired target.
cards.definitions:
An input supplies a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) and two finite syntax trees generated by \[e ::= 0\mid1\mid a\ (a\in\Sigma)\mid e+e\mid e\cdot e\mid e\parallel e\mid e^*\mid e^\dagger.\] The alphabet and syntax trees have explicit finite encodings, with labels represented by binary indices; no succinctly shared circuits, numerical iteration counts or bound on nesting is imposed. A pomset is a finite partially ordered set of events labelled in \(\Sigma\), considered up to label-preserving order isomorphism. The empty pomset interprets \(1\), the singleton labelled \(a\) interprets \(a\), and \(0\) denotes the empty language. A sequential product \(P\cdot Q\) uses disjoint copies and places every event of \(P\) before every event of \(Q\); a parallel product \(P\parallel Q\) uses disjoint copies with no additional cross-order. Lift products to sets by taking every pair, and interpret \(+\) as union. The language of \(e^*\) is the union of all finite sequential products of members of \(\llbracket e\rrbracket\); \(e^\dagger\) is the analogous union of finite parallel products. Both include the empty product. These are finite executions of unbounded size, not infinite executions. A pomset \(P\) refines \(Q\), written \(P\sqsubseteq Q\), if there is a bijection from the events of \(Q\) to those of \(P\) preserving labels and every order comparison in \(Q\); \(P\) may add further comparisons. Put \(\downarrow L=\{P:\exists Q\in L,\ P\sqsubseteq Q\}\), ranging over all finite pomsets. Thus \(e\preceq f\) equivalently says every pomset of \(\llbracket e\rrbracket\) refines some pomset of \(\llbracket f\rrbracket\). For example, \(a\cdot b\preceq a\parallel b\).

The proof system \(\mathsf{CKA}\) uses ordinary finite equational reasoning (reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, substitution and congruence) and the following axiom and inference schemas on arbitrary full-signature terms. Write \(x\le y\) as an abbreviation for \(x+y=y\). Addition is associative, commutative and idempotent, with identity \(0\). For each pair \((\circ,\star)\in\{(\cdot,*),(\parallel,\dagger)\}\), the product is associative, has identity \(1\), has absorbing element \(0\), distributes over addition on both sides, and satisfies \[1+x\circ x^\star=x^\star=1+x^\star\circ x.\] Its induction rules are \[x\circ y\le y\ \Longrightarrow\ x^\star\circ y\le y,\qquad y\circ x\le y\ \Longrightarrow\ y\circ x^\star\le y.\] Parallel product additionally commutes. Finally impose weak interchange \[(x\parallel z)\cdot(y\parallel w)\le(x\cdot y)\parallel(z\cdot w).\] Premises of induction rules must themselves be derived; no extra assumptions about the input letters are available. Soundness holds for the downward-closed pomset semantics. The decision question requires exact deterministic halting answers, with no error allowance, oracle or complexity bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide complete Lean-checked resolutions of both parts, with a separate conclusion for each. Decidability requires a total computable classifier for the displayed semantic preorder and a correctness proof; undecidability requires a proof that no such classifier exists. Completeness requires derivability of every valid refinement inequality from exactly the stated finite-proof schemas. Incompleteness requires a valid inequality and a proof of its nonderivability, for example through a fully verified algebraic countermodel to derivability. A proof for terms omitting \(\dagger\), or for plain language equality before refinement closure, is partial. A theorem about validity in all continuous models does not by itself prove completeness of the specified finitary axioms.
cards.why: The two questions ask whether unrestricted finite spawning of concurrent computations remains algorithmically comparable, and whether every valid refinement can be justified by a fixed algebraic calculus. Parallel iteration crosses the bounded-width boundary where existing decision and completeness results apply. Resolving the full signature would clarify the expressive and proof-theoretic cost of unbounded concurrency.

cards.context:
A pomset records which events must precede which other events. Refinement adds ordering constraints while preserving all events and labels. It can turn parallel behavior into more sequential behavior; it cannot delete an event or arbitrarily rename its action.

The operation \(e^\dagger\) permits any finite number of copies of \(e\) to run in parallel. Even the expression \(a^\dagger\) has executions with arbitrarily many mutually unordered events. Expressions without this operation have a width bound depending on their syntax, even when sequential star permits executions of unbounded length.

The source’s introductory paragraph recalls both the general question and its bounded-width fragment. Its own Theorem 26 then proves that refinement of series-rational expressions, without parallel star, is EXPSPACE-complete. The imported excerpt stopped before that result, so it was misleading to leave the whole historical paragraph marked unreviewed and open.

Laurence and Struth establish completeness and decidability for equality of full bi-Kleene pomset languages, before adding refinement closure. Their bounded-width refinement theorem and the ESOP 2018 result establish completeness in the smaller signature. None of these theorems removes the parallel-iteration qualification in the active question.

The ESOP 2018 paper explicitly omits parallel star. Its conclusion shows why its syntactic closure method cannot simply be reused: refinement closure of a parallel iteration can contain series-parallel pomsets with arbitrarily deep alternation of sequential and parallel composition, beyond any single plain series-parallel rational expression.
