cards.title: Superpolynomial semidefinite extension complexity of perfect matching
cards.formal:
Is the semidefinite extension complexity of the perfect-matching polytopes of complete graphs unbounded by every polynomial in the number of vertices? Precisely, is
\[
\forall B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\exists n\in\mathbb N\quad
\bigl(n\ge2\ \land\ 2\mid n\ \land\
\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SDP}}(P_n)>Bn^b\bigr)
\]
true, for the exact real semidefinite lifts defined below?

This is a statement about the existence of representations, with arbitrary real coefficients and no symmetry or efficient-construction requirement. The quantifiers ask whether no single polynomial bounds the entire family; they do not require a specified exponential rate or a lower bound holding at every sufficiently large even size. Integer constants express the same assertion as the inherited formulation with every pair of positive real constants \(C,c\).
cards.definitions:
For each even integer \(n\ge2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let
\[
E_n=\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in[n],\ i<j\},
\]
and let \(K_n=([n],E_n)\) be the finite simple undirected complete graph. A perfect matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E_n\) in which every vertex belongs to exactly one edge. Its incidence vector \(\chi^M\in\mathbb R^{E_n}\) has coordinate one on edges in \(M\) and zero on all other edges. Define
\[
P_n=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }K_n\}.
\]
The convex hull of a finite set consists of all weighted sums of its elements with nonnegative real weights summing to one. Thus \(P_n\) includes exactly those convex combinations, with one coordinate for each of the \(\binom n2\) edges.

For a positive integer \(r\), let
\[
\mathbb S^r=\{Y\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}:Y^{\mathsf T}=Y\},
\qquad
\mathbb S^r_+=\{Y\in\mathbb S^r:\forall z\in\mathbb R^r,\ z^{\mathsf T}Yz\ge0\}.
\]
An affine subspace of \(\mathbb S^r\) is a translate of a real linear subspace. An affine map into \(\mathbb R^{E_n}\) has the form \(\pi(Y)=A(Y)+a\), with \(A\) real linear and \(a\in\mathbb R^{E_n}\). A size-\(r\) semidefinite lift of \(P_n\) is a pair \((L,\pi)\), where \(L\subseteq\mathbb S^r\) is an affine subspace and \(\pi:\mathbb S^r\to\mathbb R^{E_n}\) is affine, satisfying the exact equality
\[
P_n=\pi(L\cap\mathbb S^r_+).
\]
The quantity \(\operatorname{xc}_{\mathrm{SDP}}(P_n)\) is the least positive integer \(r\) admitting such a pair. Every finite polytope has a finite such representation, so this minimum exists. Restricting sizes to positive integers also fixes the convention for the singleton \(P_2\).

Size means the order of this single positive semidefinite matrix, not the number of scalar entries or inequalities. If several positive semidefinite blocks are used, their block-diagonal combination counts their total order. Coefficients of \(L\) and \(\pi\) may be arbitrary real numbers. No bit-length bound, computability condition, uniform algorithm producing the representations, or efficient numerical procedure is imposed. The lifted feasible set need not be bounded or strictly feasible. No invariance under permutations of graph vertices or matrix coordinates is required. The condition \(Y^{\mathsf T}=Y\) is ordinary matrix symmetry and does not impose such an invariance requirement. Approximate outer representations do not meet the exact equality.

The inherited card uses affine projection maps. The cited survey defines lifts using linear projection maps; these conventions differ by at most one in matrix order and hence give the same polynomial-boundedness question. The original thesis asks about the polytope of all matchings, including nonperfect ones. Its family has polynomial-size exact semidefinite lifts if and only if the complete-graph perfect-matching family does, so the retained target is a polynomially equivalent formulation of the source question, not a claim that those polytopes are identical.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its full logical negation, for exactly the objects and size convention above.

A positive answer must prove that for every \(B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) there is an even \(n\ge2\) for which no exact semidefinite lift has matrix order at most \(Bn^b\). This includes all real affine slices and affine projection maps, without imposing symmetry, uniformity, strict feasibility or coefficient restrictions.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists B,b\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\forall n\ge2\text{ with }2\mid n\quad
\exists r\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists L\subseteq\mathbb S^r\ \exists\pi:\mathbb S^r\to\mathbb R^{E_n}\quad
\bigl(r\le Bn^b\ \land\ L\text{ is affine}\ \land\pi\text{ is affine}\
\land\ P_n=\pi(L\cap\mathbb S^r_+)\bigr).
\]
The polynomial is common to all sizes, while the representations may depend arbitrarily on \(n\); an efficient construction algorithm is not additionally required.

A lower bound for linear lifts, coordinate-symmetric semidefinite formulations, a fixed relaxation hierarchy, or a restricted coefficient field is insufficient by itself. An approximation result or an efficient matching algorithm is not an exact semidefinite representation. Conditional results must also establish any extra hypothesis needed for the unconditional target. This is an asymptotic representation-existence proposition, so no additive numerical tolerance replaces its quantified bounds.
cards.why: Perfect matching is a canonical problem with efficient optimization algorithms and strong combinatorial structure. Deciding whether it nevertheless lacks polynomial-size exact semidefinite representations would clarify the limits of a major convex-optimization model beyond the established limits of linear programming. A polynomial-size family would instead demonstrate a substantial representational advantage over linear lifts for this central tractable polytope.

cards.title: Nearly quadratic oracle complexity for convex-body volume
cards.formal: Is there a randomized classical membership-oracle algorithm such that, for every fixed \(a\ge1\), every \(n\ge2\), and every convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) with \(B_2^n\subseteq K\subseteq n^a B_2^n\), it returns \(V\) satisfying \[\Pr[|V-\operatorname{vol}_n(K)|\le\operatorname{vol}_n(K)/10]\ge2/3\] using at most \(C_a n^2(\log(2+n))^{c_a}\) membership queries in expectation? The polynomial-radius promise and origin are supplied; no isotropic position or uniform-sampling oracle is given.
cards.definitions:
A convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior, and \(B_2^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\le1\}\). Volume means n-dimensional Lebesgue measure. More generally, supplied concentric radii \(r,R\) and center \(z\), with \(R/r\le n^a\), can be rescaled to this normalization; volume scales by \(r^n\). The exponent \(a\) is fixed independently of dimension, and the constants may depend on it.

The only access to the unknown body is the exact bit indicating whether a queried real point belongs to \(K\), including its boundary. Queries can be adaptive and randomized. The information model permits measurable choices of exact real points and arbitrary measurable computation between queries, all of which are uncharged. Every membership answer costs one query. No separation, optimization, boundary, quantum-superposition or conditional-sampling oracle is available. Randomness belongs to the algorithm; the body itself is adversarially fixed.

The algorithm must terminate almost surely. Both its expected query bound and success guarantee hold for each eligible body. An expected bound is the selected interpretation of oracle complexity, rather than a bound on every random tape. Preprocessing, rounding and production of auxiliary samples must pay for all membership queries they use. In particular, one cannot assume an isotropic transformation has already been found for free.

The relative accuracy \(1/10\) and probability \(2/3\) are fixed constants in the computational task. The TCS500 benchmark's absolute \(1/100\) rule for numerical answers does not replace this algorithmic success condition. The target bounds information from the oracle, not total arithmetic operations or the bit length needed to represent continuously distributed query points.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm with the stated uniform relative-accuracy and expected-query guarantees, or its negation in the classical query model. A bound assuming free isotropic rounding, a quantum algorithm, or an estimate for a constant-dimensional high-precision regime does not suffice. A matching-order lower bound alone does not prove the requested upper bound.
cards.why: This targets the dimension dependence of a fundamental randomized integration problem.

cards.title: CLS versus FP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm solve the following Either-Solution problem: given an End-of-Line instance and an independent Localopt instance, return a valid solution of at least one of them?
cards.definitions:
Every circuit is an explicitly encoded acyclic Boolean circuit with fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}, \mathrm{NOT}\), constants, listed wires and ordered input/output nodes. An End-of-Line instance consists of \(S,P:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,1\}^{n}, n\ge 1\), satisfying \(P(0^{n})=0^{n}\) and \(S(0^{n})
e 0^{n}\). An accepted output is a bit string \(v\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with \(P(S(v))
e v\), or with both \(v
e 0^{n}\) and \(S(P(v))
e v\). In particular \(v=0^{n}\) is permitted only for the first condition. A Localopt instance consists of \(T:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{r}\), with \(m,r\ge 1\). Treat V’s output as an unsigned binary integer; an accepted local-search output is w with \(V(T(w))\ge V(w)\). The joint instance contains both independent sets of circuits; n,m,r may differ. A solution is a tag selecting one instance and a string meeting that instance’s condition. On malformed encodings or failure of the two easily checkable End-of-Line conditions, output INVALID; on a valid joint instance INVALID is forbidden. The algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial in the combined encoded length, including all circuit input/output nodes. It receives no advice, randomness or oracle. Total NP search problems are polynomially bounded input-output relations with polynomial-time verifiable outputs and at least one output for each input. A reduction maps an input to an instance and transforms every valid answer back to a valid original answer, using deterministic polynomial time for both maps. cards.title: Polynomial-time linear convergence for geodesically convex optimization
cards.formal: In the geometric arithmetic model below, is there a deterministic first-order algorithm and absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) that minimize every Lipschitz geodesically convex function on a strongly geodesically convex ball in a complete Riemannian manifold, using at most \(C(d+\zeta)^a\lceil\log(2/\varepsilon)\rceil\) objective-oracle queries and at most \(C(d+\zeta)^b\) additional operations between consecutive queries? Here \(d\) is the manifold dimension, \(\zeta=r\sqrt K/\tanh(r\sqrt K)\), with value one at \(K=0\), and the required additive objective error is \(\varepsilon Lr\). The same polynomial overhead bound applies before the first query and after the last.
cards.definitions: The input consists of a complete connected smooth \(d\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), \(d\geq1\), a reference point \(x_0\), a radius \(r>0\), a Lipschitz bound \(L>0\), a sectional-curvature bound \(K\geq0\), and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\). All sectional curvatures lie in \([-K,K]\). The distance \(\operatorname{dist}\) is the infimum of lengths of connecting curves in the given Riemannian metric. The closed ball \(D=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x_0,x)\leq r\}\) is promised strongly geodesically convex: every two points of \(D\) have a unique minimizing geodesic in \(\mathcal M\), and its whole segment lies in \(D\). If \(\gamma\) is such a segment parametrized on \([0,1]\) at constant speed, the unknown function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(f(\gamma(t))\leq(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+tf(\gamma(1))\), and \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\). A function query at \(x\in D\) returns \(f(x)\) exactly and any tangent vector \(g\in T_x\mathcal M\) satisfying \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rangle_x\) for every \(y\in D\); correctness is required for every valid sequence of returned subgradients. Here \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) is the initial velocity at time zero of the unit-time minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). Only functions and subgradient oracles meeting these conditions are inputs. The output must be a point \(\widehat x\in D\) with \(f(\widehat x)-\min_D f\leq\varepsilon Lr\). Completeness makes the closed bounded ball compact, so this minimum exists. The algorithm has no access to a formula for \(f\). For computational access to geometry, points and tangent vectors are exact typed objects supplied by a geometric oracle; the input includes an orthonormal basis of \(T_{x_0}\mathcal M\). The available geometric operations are: distance between points; inner product of two vectors in one tangent space; linear combination of such vectors; \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)\), the time-one point of the geodesic with initial velocity \(v\); \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) for \(x,y\in D\); and parallel transport of a tangent vector along the explicitly specified geodesic \(t\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_x(tv)\), \(0\leq t\leq1\). Each such operation is charged \((d+1)^3\) units, irrespective of point or vector magnitude. Object storage and access cost one unit; objects cannot be inspected except by these operations. Exact real scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root on nonnegative arguments, exponential, logarithm on positive arguments, comparisons and integer indexing operations each cost one unit. There is no floor or extraction of bits from a real register. All computation, including geometric operations, is charged apart from the separately counted function queries. One uniform finite program must work for every admissible manifold, basis, oracle and parameter tuple. There is no randomization, integral oracle, convex-hull oracle or free optimization subroutine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the required uniform objective accuracy, logarithmic query dependence on inverse accuracy, and polynomial overhead independent of inverse accuracy, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated access model. A query bound with an uncomputable geometric step, a theorem only for a particular manifold, or an additional logarithmic factor in the query count does not meet the target. A negative result must allow the full list of geometric primitives provided here.
cards.why: Euclidean cutting-plane methods show that high accuracy need not require a polynomial number of inverse-accuracy steps. Extending that efficiency to geodesic convexity would provide a general computational foundation for optimization on curved spaces, including matrix geometries used in scaling and statistical models.

This retains the manifold, curvature, ball and objective quantifiers of the source’s Open Question 1. The source leaves the computational representation of a general manifold implicit. The listed exact geometric primitives and their costs are an explicit editorial choice making its arithmetic-overhead requirement testable. A result in this model is not automatically a polynomial bit-complexity result for an arbitrary encoded metric.

The parameter \(\zeta\) is comparable within universal constants to \(1+r\sqrt K\). It allows dependence on the curvature scale and radius. The source explains that curvature dependence cannot generally be removed, even though logarithmic dependence on inverse accuracy remains the requested target.

The source distinguishes methods with good query complexity but expensive geometric work from subgradient methods with cheap steps but slower precision dependence. Thus proving either resource guarantee separately does not settle the joint question.

For constant-curvature spaces the source gives an ellipsoid-like method with \(O(\zeta d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and polynomial per-query work. This is a substantial partial result, but its extra logarithm and restricted geometry are both relevant to the full statement.

Positive definite matrices with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric are an important nonconstant-curvature example discussed by the source. Boumal’s textbook gives explicit distance, exponential and logarithmic maps for that geometry. These differ from the log-Euclidean metric, under which a coordinate logarithm makes convexity Euclidean.

Criscitiello and Kim’s 2025 work develops algorithms for horospherical convexity, a stronger geometric notion with additional structure. It does not by itself supply the required method for every geodesically convex objective in this question.

cards.title: Optimal approximation for nonmonotone submodular maximization over a matroid
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal expected approximation ratio for maximizing a nonnegative, not necessarily monotone submodular set function subject to one matroid independence constraint, in the polynomial-time oracle model specified below.

For an instance \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\), write
\[
\operatorname{OPT}(J)=\max\{f(S):S\in\mathcal I\}.
\]
Let \(\mathscr A\) be the class of uniform randomized oracle algorithms defined below: each always outputs an independent set and has a polynomial bound on its total number of elementary operations, on every valid instance and every random tape. Define
\[
\mathcal R=\left\{\alpha\in[0,1]:
 \exists A\in\mathscr A\ \forall J\
 \mathbb E_{\omega}\!\left[f\!\left(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega)\right)\right]
 \ge \alpha\,\operatorname{OPT}(J)\right\},
\qquad
\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}=\sup\mathcal R.
\]
The universal quantifier ranges over every finite ground-set size, every nonnegative submodular function on that ground set, and every matroid on it. The approximation constant and algorithm are chosen before the instance. The target is the real number \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\); it is not assumed that an algorithm attains the supremum. Supply a real answer \(a\) with a Lean-checked proof that
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}.
\]
cards.definitions:
For \(n\in\mathbb N_{0}\), the ground set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\), and \(2^{[n]}\) denotes its power set. The objective is a function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) satisfying
\[
f(S)+f(T)\ge f(S\cup T)+f(S\cap T)
\quad\text{for all }S,T\subseteq[n].
\]
This is submodularity. Monotonicity would additionally require \(f(S)\le f(T)\) whenever \(S\subseteq T\); no such requirement is imposed. Nonnegativity applies to every subset, including infeasible ones. No normalization \(f(\varnothing)=0\) is required.

A matroid independence family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) satisfies three axioms: \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\); every subset of an element of \(\mathcal I\) belongs to \(\mathcal I\); and if \(S,T\in\mathcal I\) with \(|S|<|T|\), then some \(t\in T\setminus S\) satisfies \(S\cup\{t\}\in\mathcal I\). An output is any set in \(\mathcal I\), and need not be maximal. The rank, defined as \(\max_{S\in\mathcal I}|S|\), is unrestricted. A cardinality constraint is the special case \(\mathcal I=\{S:|S|\le k\}\).

The input explicitly supplies the integer \(n\) in binary, with zero represented by the single bit zero. Sets supplied to or returned by an oracle are represented by their \(n\)-bit incidence vectors. Two exact oracles are available: a value oracle returns the real number \(f(S)\), and an independence oracle returns the bit indicating whether \(S\in\mathcal I\). The oracles remain fixed throughout a run. Neither the full table of \(f\) nor a list of all independent sets is supplied, and there is no oracle for a continuous extension, its derivatives, or an optimum.

Fix the following exact-real oracle computation convention. An algorithm is one finite program with finite control, finitely many ordinary bit tapes and finitely many tapes of exact real cells. It may contain finitely many rational constants, each specified by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator. Initially work tapes are blank or zero. Elementary instructions are ordinary bit-tape read/write and one-cell head moves; one-cell real-tape head moves; copying or loading a real cell; addition, subtraction, multiplication or division of a fixed finite number of currently addressed real cells; exact comparison of two such cells; obtaining one independent fair random bit; or one of the two oracle calls. Each instruction costs one operation. Division must have a nonzero divisor on every valid run. The query incidence vector must already have been written on the query tape; reading and writing its bits are charged by the bit-tape instructions. An oracle answer is deposited in a designated real cell or bit cell in one operation. Outputting the final incidence vector is also charged. Real cells have no instruction for inspecting a binary expansion or converting an arbitrary real directly into an integer.

This is a unit-cost exact-arithmetic oracle model: the size parameter is \(n\), and real answers are not charged by a bit length. All computation between queries is counted. Programs have no advice depending on \(n\) or the instance, no arbitrary real constants, and no other oracles. This explicit convention completes the source's polynomial-time/value-oracle formulation; it does not assert equivalence to a bit-complexity model for rational objectives.

Formally, \(A\in\mathscr A\) means that there are integers \(C\ge1\) and \(q\ge0\), fixed for that program, such that for every valid \(J=(n,f,\mathcal I)\) and every random tape \(\omega\), the program makes only valid operations and queries, halts within \(C(n+1)^q\) elementary operations, and outputs an \(n\)-bit vector encoding a member of \(\mathcal I\). Thus both its number of oracle queries and its other work are polynomially bounded. No feasibility error is allowed. The expectation in the guarantee concerns objective value, not feasibility or running time.

The random tape consists of independent fair bits, so each specified prefix of length \(r\) has probability \(2^{-r}\). For a program with the above clock, at most \(C(n+1)^q\) bits are read; its expected value is consequently a finite average over that many fair bits, with unused bits ignored. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(J)=0\), the multiplicative guarantee is automatically satisfied; no quotient by zero is used. Always returning the empty set guarantees factor zero, so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and its supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[
|a-\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}|\le \frac{1}{100}
\]
for exactly the instance class and algorithm class above. Merely restating the supremum that defines \(\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\) is not a determination.

A certified interval is sufficient: give \(l,u\in[0,1]\), prove
\[
l\le\rho_{\mathrm{mat}}\le u,\qquad u-l\le\frac{1}{50},
\]
and use \(a=(l+u)/2\). To make explicit what both sides mean, the lower bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists A\in\mathscr A\
\forall J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
\ge(l-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
The upper bound can be certified by proving
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \forall A\in\mathscr A\
\exists J\
\mathbb E_{\omega}[f(A^{f,\mathcal I}(n;\omega))]
<(u+\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(J).
\]
Membership in \(\mathscr A\) includes the full program, uniform polynomial clock and unconditional feasibility requirements from the definitions. In the lower statement the program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(J\); the upper statement ranges over every such program and all possible polynomial degrees. This permits approaching a supremum without attaining it.

Exact determination is welcome but is not mandatory. A guarantee for a subclass of matroids or objectives, for deterministic algorithms alone, or for polynomially many queries with unrestricted computation does not by itself determine this target. Nor does an upper bound assuming an unproved complexity separation constitute the unconditional upper certificate above.
cards.why: This is a central approximation question for a general combinatorial optimization model, rather than a guarantee for one application or a running-time refinement. Matroids include cardinality, partition and linear-independence constraints, and submodularity encompasses many cut, coverage and information objectives. Determining the optimal guarantee would identify the inherent cost of combining diminishing returns, potentially harmful additions and independence constraints. Unlike several neighboring monotone or unconstrained models, the known algorithmic and information-theoretic bounds still leave a substantial gap.

cards.title: Superlinear randomized query lower bounds for submodular minimization
cards.formal: Let \(R(n)\) be the minimum worst-case number of value-oracle queries needed by a randomized algorithm to find an exact minimizer of every real-valued submodular function on \(n\) elements, with success probability at least \(2/3\). Is \(R(n)=\omega(n)\), meaning \(R(n)/n\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
cards.definitions: The ground set is \([n]\), and a function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular if \(F(A)+F(B)\geq F(A\cup B)+F(A\cap B)\) for all subsets \(A,B\). No monotonicity, nonnegativity, symmetry or normalization is promised. A query specifies any subset \(S\) and receives its exact real value \(F(S)\). The algorithm may adapt later queries to all previous values and its own random choices. Its final answer is a subset \(S_*\) satisfying \(F(S_*)\leq F(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq[n]\); any minimizer is acceptable, including the empty or full set. For every fixed valid oracle \(F\), the probability of a correct output is at least \(2/3\). In the definition of \(R(n)\), a cost bound \(q\) requires at most \(q\) oracle calls on every input and every outcome of the random choices, not just in expectation. Arbitrary finite local computation and exact operations on the oracle answers are free. The algorithm has no direct access to a formula, table or circuit for \(F\). We use classical randomized query complexity: for each dimension, random coins select a deterministic adaptive query procedure, independently of \(F\); the maps and distributions must define measurable success events. An algorithm may depend on \(n\), so lower bounds also apply to nonuniform choices. The value magnitudes and their bit encodings do not enter the query cost. Exhaustively querying all \(2^n\) subsets shows that \(R(n)\) is finite. A superlinear lower bound means that for each real constant \(C>0\), all sufficiently large \(n\) satisfy \(R(n)>Cn\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked superlinear lower bound in the specified randomized bounded-query model. Alternatively prove the negation of that growth statement: a fixed constant C and infinitely many dimensions admit correct algorithms using at most Cn queries. An O(n)-query algorithm for all dimensions would suffice for a negative answer but is stronger than the logical negation. A deterministic lower bound, a lower bound on parallel rounds, or hardness only for finding a nonempty proper minimizer does not establish the target.
cards.why: Submodular minimization is a central tractable optimization problem, yet its information requirements remain far from its best general algorithms. A superlinear randomized lower bound would establish that even unlimited computation and adaptive random querying cannot reduce exact minimization to a linear amount of oracle information.

cards.context:
The source proves an Ω(n log n) deterministic query lower bound and explicitly asks for a superlinear randomized one. The selected target is any unbounded multiplicative improvement over n, rather than a demand for the same n log n expression.

In the deterministic construction, an adversary can exploit the algorithm’s fixed queries to delay discovery of a hidden set. The paper explains why random subsets can defeat the local obstruction used for that logarithmic factor. Transferring the deterministic proof without a new randomized argument is therefore insufficient.

The paper also proves a nearly linear lower bound on the number of adaptive parallel rounds when each round permits polynomially many queries. This measures how often answers must be used to choose the next batch. It does not imply a superlinear lower bound on the total number of sequentially adaptive queries.

Earlier lower bounds include a linear bound for general minimization and stronger statements for nontrivial minimizers of certain function classes. The requirement to exclude the empty and full sets changes the optimization problem; this card allows both and asks for the usual unconstrained minimum.

Exact oracle values can reveal more than comparisons between candidate subsets. A lower bound in this model must survive that extra information and cannot assume a bounded numeric range unless it constructs hard functions within that range. Conversely, bit complexity of evaluating an oracle is outside the target.

Strongly polynomial query upper bounds do not depend on the range of function values. The source compares algorithms with different amounts of local computation, including exponential local time; the lower-bound target here deliberately imposes no polynomial-time restriction.

cards.title: Input-sparsity relative spectral low-rank approximation
cards.formal: Is there a randomized algorithm and absolute constants \(C,b>0\) that, for every real \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), integer \(1\leq k<n\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\), returns \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) with orthonormal columns such that \[\|A-ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\|_2\leq(1+\varepsilon)\min_{\operatorname{rank}(B)\leq k}\|A-B\|_2\] with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C\operatorname{nnz}(A)+Cn(k/\varepsilon)^b\) operations?
cards.definitions: The matrix is given as a list of its nonzero entries, each with its row index, column index and real value; unspecified entries are zero and index pairs do not repeat. The integer \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) is the length of this list. The spectral norm is \(\|D\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Dx\|_2\). For singular values \(\sigma_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n(A)\geq0\), the optimum on the right is \(\sigma_{k+1}(A)\). Orthonormality means \(Z^{\mathsf T}Z=I_k\), so \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}\) is an orthogonal projection of rank \(k\). The output is the explicit matrix \(Z\); forming the generally dense product \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\) is not required. All real input matrices are included, with no gap, conditioning, spectral-decay, positivity or distributional promise. If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq k\), the required residual is exactly zero on a successful run. The selected arithmetic model is a uniform real RAM with unit-cost addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root of a nonnegative value, real comparison, and indexed memory access. Registers store exact reals or integer indices; integer indexing arithmetic is charged, and no real-to-integer floor or bit extraction is a free primitive. Independent fair random bits and independent standard normal real samples are available at unit cost. This explicitly adopts the ideal arithmetic and sampling convention used in randomized numerical linear algebra; bit complexity is not the target. The operation bound includes reading the input, all preprocessing, random sampling and writing the output, and must hold on every random run. Only correctness may fail with probability at most one third, separately for each fixed input. A single algorithm and the same constants work for all parameters; \(n\geq2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of its probability guarantee and stated arithmetic running time, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The coefficient of the nonzero-entry term must be an absolute constant: multiplying that term by k, inverse accuracy or logarithms of n misses the target. Frobenius-norm error, additive spectral error, extra output rank, or a bound conditional on a singular-value gap does not establish the displayed claim.
cards.why: Relative spectral approximation protects every direction of a compressed linear operator, making it useful where a small average error is insufficient. Resolving the question would determine whether this stronger guarantee can share the basic input-reading cost of fast Frobenius approximation, without rank or accuracy multiplying the sparse-data term.

cards.context:
Woodruff’s Open Question 1 asks whether the input-sparsity bound for relative Frobenius approximation can also give the relative spectral projection guarantee in Equation (65). The card makes the arithmetic model, success probability and output representation explicit; it retains the square-matrix target.

The Frobenius norm sums squared errors over all entries, whereas the spectral norm controls the largest error in a unit direction. A relative Frobenius guarantee therefore need not provide a relative spectral guarantee when many small singular values contribute to the total tail energy.

The survey presents a spectral approximation based on repeated matrix products, but its dependence on repeated passes and the target rank does not have the requested additive input-sparsity form. Its Frobenius result already achieves that form.

Bakshi, Bhattacharyya, Kannan, Woodruff and Zhou’s 2021 latent-simplex algorithm obtains input-sparsity time under a spectral-mass assumption. Their paper connects removal of that assumption to a breakthrough for spectral low-rank approximation, rather than claiming to solve the unrestricted matrix problem.

A bound of the form input size plus a polynomial in rank and accuracy times n matters especially when a large sparse matrix can be read once but cannot cheaply be multiplied by many vectors. The additive second term also accommodates the n-by-k output. No explicit n-by-n projection is requested.

cards.title: Gap-entropy conjecture
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\) such that, for every Gaussian best-arm instance \(I\) defined below and every \(0<\delta<1/10\), \[cH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)\leq L(I,\delta)\leq CH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)?\] Here \(L\) is the order-oblivious instance-wise optimum over globally correct sampling algorithms, not the performance of one algorithm required to attain the bound on every instance.
cards.definitions: An instance has \(n\geq2\) independent arms with distributions \(\mathcal N(\mu_i,1)\), unknown means \(\mu_i\in[0,1]\), and a unique largest mean \(\mu_*\) at index \(*\). Each pull of arm \(i\) reveals a fresh independent sample from its distribution. An adaptive sampling algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\delta\), chooses pulls using earlier samples and independent internal randomness, and eventually outputs an arm index. It is \(\delta\)-correct if on every valid instance it stops almost surely and outputs its unique best arm with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Local computation is unrestricted; the resource is total number of pulls, and expectations include sampling noise and algorithmic randomness. Algorithms are measurable so that these probabilities and expectations are defined. Let \(T_A(I)\in[0,\infty]\) be the expected number of pulls. If \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of arm labels and \(\pi I\) is the corresponding relabeled instance, define \(L(I,\delta)=\inf_A (1/n!)\sum_{\pi\in S_n}T_A(\pi I)\), where the infimum ranges over algorithms correct on every instance of the same Gaussian model. The infimum is taken separately for each \(I,\delta\): an algorithm selected for favorable performance at I must nevertheless remain correct on all other instances. It need not attain the infimum. For each suboptimal arm, set \(\Delta_i=\mu_*-\mu_i\in(0,1]\), and \(H(I)=\sum_{i\ne *}\Delta_i^{-2}\). For integers \(r\geq0\), set \(G_r=\{i\ne *:2^{-(r+1)}<\Delta_i\leq2^{-r}\}\), \(H_r=\sum_{i\in G_r}\Delta_i^{-2}\), and \(p_r=H_r/H(I)\). The gap entropy is \(\operatorname{Ent}(I)=\sum_{r:p_r>0}p_r\log(1/p_r)\), with natural logarithms. Only finitely many groups are nonempty. The constants in the conjecture are independent of n, all means, the number of gap scales and δ.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of both uniform constant-factor bounds, or prove that no such universal pair of constants exists. A result only as δ tends to zero with the instance fixed, only for dyadic gaps or monotone algorithms, or an algorithm with an extra closest-gap term does not by itself prove the displayed claim about L. The recent claimed proof must meet the same mathematical and Lean-checking requirement.
cards.why: The conjecture predicts the full instance-sensitive cost of identifying the best alternative, including the cost of learning which gap scales matter. Its entropy term would explain why instances with the same total inverse-square gap can have different exploration costs at fixed confidence.

references.authors: P. M. Aronow; Nathan Kallus; Patrick Lopatto
references.locator: Version 1, 9 September 2026: definitions (1.1)–(1.2), Theorems 1.1–1.2, Corollary 1.3 and Appendix A conventions.

cards.context:
This card selects Chen and Li’s Conjecture 3.5, which gives an explicit formula for the instance-wise optimum. Their separate Conjecture 3.2 asks for one algorithm attaining that optimum up to an additive two-arm adaptation term. The two statements are related but are not interchangeable.

Averaging over relabelings prevents an algorithm from gaining an artificial advantage because the best arm was placed at a preferred index. Taking an infimum over globally correct algorithms still permits a different favored sampling schedule for each target instance; it does not allow an algorithm to simply output a known best label without verifying correctness elsewhere.

Gap entropy weights a scale by its share of the inverse-square sampling burden, not by its fraction of arms. It vanishes when all gaps fall in one group and can grow when many scales carry comparable burden. The specified dyadic endpoint convention includes gaps equal to one; changing boundary conventions affects the full proposed complexity by at most constant factors.

Chen, Li and Qiao’s 2017 progress gives a nearly matching algorithmic bound and a lower bound for dyadic-gap instances under a monotonicity condition on algorithms. These restrictions and extra factors are relevant because the conjecture quantifies over all Gaussian instances and all correct algorithms.

A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 by Aronow, Kallus and Lopatto states the displayed two-sided result as Theorem 1.1. It also states a separate uniform-algorithm theorem with the closest-gap adaptation term. The present review matched their definitions and theorem statements, but has not independently certified the complete proof.

Asymptotic confidence-optimal algorithms study δ tending to zero for a fixed instance, when log(1/δ) eventually dominates its fixed entropy. Such a limit does not determine the uniform cost when gap scales and confidence vary together. This is why the nonasymptotic quantifiers matter.

cards.title: Constant-factor entrywise \(\ell_1\) rank-\(k\) approximation with variable \(k\)
cards.formal: Do a uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm \(A\) and an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) exist such that, for every rational matrix \(M\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and input integer \(0\le k\le\min(m,n)\), \(A\) returns rational factors \(U\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times k}\), \(V\in\mathbb{Q}^{k\times n}\) satisfying \[\|M-UV\|_1\le C\operatorname{OPT}_k(M),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_k(M)=\min_{\substack{B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k}}\|M-B\|_1,\] with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input?
cards.definitions: \(m,n\ge 1\); dimensions, k and each signed rational numerator and positive denominator are explicitly encoded in binary. The input length N counts the whole dense matrix description. \(\|W\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|W_{ij}|\) is the entrywise norm; rank is matrix rank over \(\mathbb{R}\). The optimum is over all real \(m\times n\) matrices of rank at most k and is attained, since a minimizing sequence can be confined to a bounded closed sublevel set. The output consists of binary rational entries of U and V; for \(k=0\) their product denotes the zero matrix. There is a single polynomial P such that A halts within \(P(N)\) Turing-machine steps on every input and every random tape, including the time to write its factors. Therefore the factors have polynomial total encoded length; no unit-cost exact real arithmetic or implicit algebraic-number oracle is available. The approximation factor C and polynomial exponent are independent of m,n,k and entry magnitudes. The probability is over independent fair algorithm coins for each fixed input. Only the displayed multiplicative error is allowed. In particular, when \(\operatorname{rank}(M)\le k\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{k}(M)=0\), success requires exact equality \(UV=M\). When the optimum is positive the output need not be an exact real minimizer: the task asks for rational factors meeting the constant-factor inequality. This is the explicit rational bit-model completion of the imported approximation question, not a claim that optimal real factors are rational or efficiently computable.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such an algorithm and absolute factor exist with the stated uniform bit bounds, or a Lean proof of their nonexistence. A factor depending on the rank, a polynomial exponent depending on the rank, output rank above the requested rank, or uncharged exact-real computation does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: Determine whether robust low-rank compression remains computationally tractable with unrestricted target rank.

cards.title: Log-squared query complexity of fixed-dimensional Tarski fixed points
cards.formal: For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(k\ge1\), let \(Q(n,k)\) be the minimum worst-case number of deterministic adaptive value queries needed to find a fixed point of an unknown monotone function \(f:[n]^k\to[n]^k\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Is \[\forall k\ge1\ \exists C_k>0\ \forall n\ge2:\quad Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2?\] A query at \(x\in[n]^k\) reveals the entire vector \(f(x)\) at cost one. Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. The constant \(C_k\) may depend on \(k\) but not on \(n\) or \(f\); no polynomial bound on its dependence on \(k\) is required.
cards.definitions: The grid \([n]^k\) consists of all integer vectors with \(k\) coordinates in \([n]\). Its order is coordinatewise: \(x\le y\) means \(x_i\le y_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). The oracle promise is that \(x\le y\) implies \(f(x)\le f(y)\). A fixed point is a vector \(x\) with exact equality \(f(x)=x\); any fixed point is an acceptable output, with no least or greatest requirement. For given \(n,k\), a deterministic oracle decision tree is finite. Each internal node names a query vector and has branches indexed by possible returned vectors; the next query depends only on \(n,k\) and the preceding transcript. Each leaf outputs a vector that is a fixed point for every promised oracle consistent with that leaf. Paths inconsistent with every promised oracle impose no correctness requirement. The tree’s cost is the maximum number of internal nodes on the path followed by any promised oracle. \(Q(n,k)\) is the minimum such cost over all correct trees, with a separate tree allowed for each pair \(n,k\). Thus no uniform or efficient construction of the optimal trees is built into the target. The only access to the unknown function is through the counted queries; no table, circuit, auxiliary advice about \(f\), randomness or quantum query is provided. Reading or manipulating a returned vector and other finite internal computation do not add query cost. Monotonicity on this finite complete lattice guarantees existence of a fixed point. Every logarithm in the bound has base two.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed bound or its negation. A positive answer must establish correct decision trees with the stated worst-case query bound for every fixed dimension and every side length. A negative answer must show that there exists one fixed \(k\) such that, for every \(M>0\), some \(n\ge2\) satisfies \(Q(n,k)>M(1+\log_2 n)^2\). A logarithmic exponent that increases with \(k\), or a lower bound whose contradiction requires \(k\) to increase with \(n\), does not settle the assertion. The target places no bound on internal computation time; a query-efficient result need not yield a polynomial-time algorithm for succinctly encoded functions.
cards.why: Fixed points of monotone maps underpin equilibrium existence and program semantics. The oracle problem isolates how much information about a function is needed to find one. A dimension-independent logarithmic exponent would reveal a strong structural limit on that information requirement, even with dimension-dependent constants and unrestricted internal computation.

cards.context:
Etessami’s 2022 seminar question asks for improved bounds for finding any Tarski fixed point, distinguishing black-box queries from a succinct circuit input. This card retains the previously selected concrete question of a squared logarithm for every fixed dimension. It does not claim that such a query bound alone supplies a time-efficient solution of the broader circuit problem.

Chen, Li and Yannakakis prove an \(O(\log_2^2 n)\) query upper bound in dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Together with previous bounds this gives \(\Theta(\log_2^2 n)\) in dimensions two, three and four. Their general upper bound is \(O((\log_2 n)^{\lceil(k-1)/3\rceil+1})\), with constants permitted to depend on \(k\).

Brânzei, Phillips and Recker prove a lower bound \(\Omega(k(\log_2 n)^2/\log_2 k)\) for \(n,k\ge2\), even for randomized algorithms measured by expected queries with success probability at least \(9/10\). It also applies to the deterministic worst-case model, but for each fixed \(k\) its extra dimension factor is only a constant.

The conclusion of the March 2026 paper explicitly leaves a generic squared-logarithm bound with dimension-dependent multiplier as a possibility. It also states that its new query algorithm is not time-efficient, which is compatible with this card’s unrestricted internal-computation model.

A September 2026 preprint of Li, Ma, Yang and Zhao gives an \(\Omega(k\log_2 n)\) lower bound for quantum queries. This newer result does not contradict the squared-logarithm target at any fixed dimension. Only its primary abstract and model summary were used in this bounded later-work check.

cards.title: First-order convergence to local minimax optima
cards.formal:
Consider sequential minimax optimization \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^p}\max_{y\in\mathbb R^q} f(x,y)\), with \(p,q\ge1\), \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^{p+q},\mathbb R)\), and a supplied constant \(L>0\) satisfying
\[\|\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(w)\|_2\le L\|z-w\|_2\qquad\text{for all }z,w\in\mathbb R^{p+q}.\]
Does there exist one uniform deterministic first-order oracle method, in the model below, that produces iterates \(z_k=(x_k,y_k)\) from every initial point and has both of these properties for every such \(p,q,f,L\)?

First, for Lebesgue-almost every initial point \(z_0\), whenever the complete sequence \((z_k)_{k\ge0}\) converges to a finite point \(z^*\), that point is a local minimax point in the neighborhood definition below. Second, every strict local minimax point has an open neighborhood of initial points from which the method converges to that point. The second requirement excludes a method that satisfies the first merely by never converging.
cards.definitions:
The order of play is fixed: \(x\) is the minimization variable and \(y\) is the maximization variable. All norms are Euclidean. A point \(z^*=(x^*,y^*)\) is a local minimax point if there exist \(\delta_0>0\) and a function \(h:(0,\delta_0]\to[0,\infty)\), with \(\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}h(\delta)=0\), such that for every \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\) and all \(x,y\) with \(\|x-x^*\|_2\le\delta\) and \(\|y-y^*\|_2\le\delta\),
\[f(x^*,y)\le f(x^*,y^*)\le
 \max_{\|y'-y^*\|_2\le h(\delta)} f(x,y').\]
The closed maximization ball is nonempty and compact, so the maximum exists. The radius function may depend on \(f,z^*\). There is no additional bound on \(h(\delta)/\delta\), no restriction to a Hessian range, and no assumption of concavity in \(y\). In particular, local minimax does not mean a simultaneous local Nash equilibrium or a global minimax solution.

A stationary point satisfies \(\nabla f(z^*)=0\). Define its Hessian blocks
\[A=\nabla^2_{xx}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p},\quad
 B=\nabla^2_{yy}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{q\times q},\quad
 C=\nabla^2_{xy}f(z^*)\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}.\]
A strict local minimax point here means a stationary point satisfying
\[B\prec0,\qquad A-CB^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}\succ0.\]
For a symmetric matrix, positive definiteness means that its quadratic form is positive on every nonzero vector; negative definiteness is defined with a negative sign. These sufficient conditions imply the neighborhood definition above. They define the points at which attraction is required, not a promise on every stationary point or every local minimax point of the input. Degenerate and non-strict points remain subject to the first, limit-selection requirement.

A first-order oracle queried at \(z\in\mathbb R^{p+q}\) returns the exact pair \((f(z),\nabla f(z))\). The function is available only through this oracle, not through its formula, a Hessian oracle, a maximization oracle or a best-response oracle. A method is one fixed finite real-arithmetic program supplied with \(p,q,L,z_0\), initialized with empty history and fixed rational constants. It uses scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero numbers, exact comparisons, branching, copying, and integer loop/address operations. Real registers cannot be inspected digit by digit. Oracle calls may be adaptive, at points computed from the supplied data and earlier replies. Finite differences or other numerical quantities computed from finitely many permitted replies are allowed; direct derivative queries above first order are not.

The program may retain finite history and use iteration-dependent or adaptively chosen parameters. On every permitted input and after every finite iteration count it must finish the finite work needed to produce the next iterate, using finitely many elementary operations, stored values and oracle calls. No infinite inner loop, exact limit operation, uncharged auxiliary oracle, function-dependent advice or external randomization is allowed. Auxiliary storage is finite at each finite stage but need not have a fixed bound over the infinite run. This is an asymptotic convergence question: no polynomial iteration bound, oracle-complexity rate or bit-complexity bound is requested. The real oracle and exact arithmetic are part of the model, not claims about finite-precision implementation.

For precision, let \(z_k^{f,L}(u)\) be the sequence produced from initial point \(u\), with dimensions understood and \(z_0^{f,L}(u)=u\). The first guarantee means that, for each \(p,q,f,L\), there exists a set \(E_{f,L}\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}\) of Lebesgue outer measure zero such that
\[\forall u\notin E_{f,L}\ \forall z^*,\quad
 \lim_{k\to\infty}z_k^{f,L}(u)=z^*
 \ \Longrightarrow\ z^*\text{ is a local minimax point of }f.\]
The one exceptional set must cover all possible bad limits, not a separate uncountable union of exceptions for individual points. Equivalently, the same implication must hold almost surely for every initialization distribution with a density with respect to Lebesgue measure. The algorithm itself is deterministic.

The second guarantee means that for every strict local minimax point \(z^*\), there exists \(r>0\), depending on \(f,L,z^*\), such that
\[\forall u\in\mathbb R^{p+q},\quad
 \|u-z^*\|_2<r\ \Longrightarrow\ \lim_{k\to\infty}z_k^{f,L}(u)=z^*.\]
Every start uses the same program initialization; no target point or attracting radius is supplied to it. The requirements permit divergent or nonconvergent runs outside these local basins. They concern limits of the full sequence, not every subsequential accumulation point, and do not require global convergence or attraction to every non-strict local minimax point.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of a method meeting both guarantees, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must specify one finite oracle program, establish that it produces every next iterate after finite work, prove the common measure-zero exception statement for every permitted objective and every valid supplied \(L\), and prove local attraction at every point satisfying the strict Hessian conditions.

A negative proof must exclude every method in this specified oracle model from satisfying the conjunction. Counterexamples only to gradient descent-ascent, extragradient or another named update do not exclude every method. A method that never converges, convergence only to stationary points or second-order necessary-condition points, local linear stability without the stated limit guarantees, or a theorem assuming additional curvature or neighborhood-radius restrictions does not meet this target. No finite iteration rate is demanded, and the benchmark's numerical tolerance does not replace exact convergence or exact local minimaxity.
cards.why: Sequential adversarial optimization needs the minimization and maximization roles to be respected at the limiting solution. Reaching a stationary point alone can select the wrong kind of equilibrium. A first-order selection theorem that remains valid with degeneracy would clarify what gradient information can guarantee beyond the curvature-restricted cases already analyzed.

cards.context:
Both \(f(x,y)=x^2-y^2\) and \(g(x,y)=-x^2+y^2\) have zero gradient at the origin. For the prescribed minimization in \(x\) and maximization in \(y\), the first has a strict local minimax point there, while the second fails even the required local maximization in \(y\). Thus stationarity does not identify the intended local solution.

The local minimax definition allows the maximizing player’s response neighborhood to shrink at a different rate from the minimizing player’s neighborhood. It describes the sequential order of play. Requiring the minimizing player to keep the maximizer’s action fixed instead gives the stronger local Nash notion; reversing the players gives a different local optimization question.

The original convergence literature distinguishes sufficient strict curvature conditions from necessary second-order conditions. With degeneracy, satisfying the latter need not certify a local minimax point. A guarantee stated only for strict linearly unstable points also does not automatically exclude convergence to every other undesirable stationary point.

The ICLR 2024 two-timescale extragradient paper extends analysis beyond an invertible maximizing-player Hessian. Its theorems still retain conditions on the restricted Schur complement, the full saddle-gradient Jacobian or spectral thresholds. Its stable points are characterized using necessary second-order conditions in the relevant regimes; this is not the unrestricted true-minimax limit guarantee selected here.

The ICML 2024 double-step alternating extragradient work improves local stability for further non-strict cases and studies increasing timescale separation. Its local results retain nondegeneracy conditions on specified Hessian-derived matrices; the increasing-timescale stability theorem additionally assumes a third derivative. The paper’s separate global-convergence result assumes star-convex–star-concave structure. Those hypotheses are absent from this card’s objective class.

Follow-the-Ridge gives a related local fixed-point theorem using second-order information and an invertible maximizing-player Hessian. Its distinction between strict linear stability and weak spectral stability also matters. This is a useful comparison with the first-order question, but its Hessian-assisted theorem is not a solution for every objective in the model here.

Lu and Wang’s August 2026 constrained minimax paper proves complexity bounds for approximate stationary points under a local Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz condition on a lifted inner problem. That condition restricts the relation between objective residuals and generalized gradients. The assumptions and approximate-stationarity target differ from exact local-minimax limit selection for arbitrary smooth objectives.

The probability qualifier concerns the initial point. It allows, for example, an exceptional initialization exactly at an undesirable stationary point when such starts form a null set. The local-attraction condition supplies a positive guarantee near strict solutions. No convergence assertion is being made for every trajectory of a nonconvex–nonconcave game.

source_formulation.text: Editorial choice of a concrete benchmark variant, as authorized for source questions that leave the target unspecified. The COLT 2023 contribution poses a broad first-order convergence question and discusses both local stability and alternative notions of local optimality; it does not specify one complete oracle model or every convergence quantifier. This card keeps its original Jin–Netrapalli–Jordan neighborhood definition, includes degenerate objectives, and fixes deterministic exact first-order oracle access. This is stronger than a statement only about linearly stable fixed points and is not asserted to be a verbatim or proved-equivalent formulation of the source title. Global convergence, attraction to all non-strict points, fixed-step restrictions, and a different restricted-minimax definition are not part of this selected variant.

Bounded searches did not establish a validated solution of both guarantees here. A further OpenReview submission advertises calmness-based selection in indexed passages, but its full current text and status were inaccessible in this pass and have not been verified. cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.

cards.context:
Isotropy fixes scale in every linear direction. For a unit vector \(\theta\), the function \(f(x)=\sum_i\theta_i x_i\) has variance one and gradient energy one, so every admissible universal constant is at least one. The conjecture asks whether nonlinear observables can have an arbitrarily greater variance relative to their average squared local change. Log-concavity is much weaker than independence of coordinates or a uniformly curved smooth potential.

The geometric formulation compares the boundary size of a set with the probability mass it separates. For a Borel set \(S\), let \(S_\varepsilon=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\varepsilon\}\), where distance is the infimum of \(\|x-y\|_2\) over \(y\in S\), and define \(\mu^+(S)=\liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(\mu(S_\varepsilon)-\mu(S))/\varepsilon\). The Cheeger expansion constant is \(h_\mu=\inf_{0<\mu(S)<1}\mu^+(S)/\min\{\mu(S),1-\mu(S)\}\). KLS asserts a positive universal lower bound on this expansion after isotropic normalization. A small value describes a separator with little boundary relative to the masses on its sides.

Notation changes across sources: Lee and Vempala’s survey uses its isoperimetric symbol for expansion itself, while Klartag and Letwin use \(\psi_\mu=1/h_\mu\), the reciprocal. With the latter convention, \(\psi_\mu^2\) and \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)\) differ by at most universal factors for log-concave measures, as recalled in Klartag’s equation (1.4). Thus an upper bound \(O((\log n)^{1/4})\) on the reciprocal expansion means an upper bound \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) on the Poincaré constant, rather than the same exponent.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks: poor expansion can slow movement between substantial parts of a convex body. The Lee–Vempala survey explains how sampling supports volume estimation, integration and optimization. These algorithmic consequences also depend on access to the input body or density, initialization and the chosen walk; the analytic inequality alone is not a complete computational-cost statement.

Klartag and Lehec’s 2022 Theorem 1.1 gives a polylogarithmic upper bound on reciprocal expansion, with exponent five in that paper. This broke the earlier subpolynomial dimension dependence. It is a historical bound, not a dimension-free resolution.

Klartag’s 2023 Theorem 1.2 improves reciprocal expansion to \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)=O(\log n)\). These logarithmic estimates are stated for \(n\ge2\); no formula involving \(\log1=0\) is asserted for the one-dimensional case.

Klartag and Lehec’s thin-shell paper, first posted in 2025 and revised in February 2026, proves \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le a n\) and consequently \(\mathbb E(\|X\|_2-\sqrt n)^2\le a\) for a universal \(a\) and isotropic log-concave \(X\). These results control particular radial observables. Their relation to the now resolved slicing problem does not turn them into the full inequality for every locally Lipschitz function.

Chen and Klartag’s July 2026 preprint states the sharp radial bound \(\operatorname{Var}(\|X\|_2^2)\le8n\), with equality for independent centered exponential coordinates. The statement of Theorem 1.1 was inspected, but its complete new proof was not independently verified here. This optimizes the thin-shell constant, not the universal Poincaré constant over all test functions.

Letwin’s preprint of 27 July 2026 states \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\le2\mathbb E\|\nabla(X^{\mathsf T}MX)\|_2^2\) for every real symmetric matrix \(M\), where \(X\) is isotropic and log-concave. It derives \(\psi_n=O((\log n)^{1/4})\) for \(n\ge2\), where \(\psi_n=\sup_\mu\psi_\mu\) over the measures in dimension \(n\). Its general-function consequence is \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu)=O(\sqrt{\log n})\), which still grows. The paper’s new proof was not independently verified in this review.

Zhang’s sampling preprint, revised on 5 September 2026, still explicitly calls KLS open. It claims an improved mixing theorem for hit-and-run, the walk that chooses a random line through its current point and then a uniform point on the chord inside the body. The result requires a warm initial distribution, whose density is bounded by a finite multiple of the uniform target density, and retains dependence on the KLS constant. Resolving that mixing-time question is therefore distinct from proving a universal Poincaré bound.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite simple graph \(H\), there exists a real constant \(C_H\ge1\) such that, for every nonempty finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with no \(H\) minor and every edge-length function \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), there exist an integer \(m\ge1\) and a map \(f:V\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
d_{G,w}(u,v)\le
\sum_{j=1}^{m}|f(u)_j-f(v)_j|
\le C_H\,d_{G,w}(u,v)
\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in V?
\]
The constant may depend only on \(H\). The dimension and map may depend on the whole weighted graph, with no bound on dimension or on the time needed to construct them.
cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, called edges. Connected means every pair of vertices is joined by a path. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges, followed by removal of loops and duplicate edges, can produce a graph isomorphic to \(H\). Exclusion concerns the underlying unweighted graph.

The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths. The shortest-path distance \(d_{G,w}(u,v)\) is the minimum length of a path from \(u\) to \(v\), and \(d_{G,w}(u,u)=0\). Positivity and finiteness make this a finite metric. A one-vertex graph is allowed and satisfies the target trivially.

The target space is finite-dimensional \(\ell_1^m\): the vector space \(\mathbb R^m\) with distance \(\|a-b\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^m|a_j-b_j|\). The first inequality fixes a noncontracting normalization, and the second allows expansion by at most \(C_H\). Allowing an arbitrary common scaling factor instead gives the same distortion notion.

All edge lengths are arbitrary positive real numbers. Neither graph size nor the ratio of the largest to the smallest edge length may affect \(C_H\). There is no requirement that the graph or its lengths be efficiently encoded, since this is a mathematical existence question. All pairs must satisfy the inequalities simultaneously for the same map.

The source also allows zero edge lengths and hence zero distances between different vertices. That convention is equivalent for this conjecture: contract each component of zero-length edges, retain the shortest parallel edge when necessary, and map the original vertices through this quotient. The quotient is still a minor of the original graph. The positive-length statement above avoids treating distinct points at distance zero as a metric space.

No Euclidean target, restriction to selected terminals, average-distance guarantee, or transformation of the distances by a power is part of this statement. Here a terminal, when used in the context, simply means a selected vertex whose distances must be preserved.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain a finite constant for every fixed excluded minor, uniformly over all weighted graphs in that class and all vertex pairs. It need not determine the best constant or construct the embeddings efficiently. A negative answer must give one fixed graph \(H\) such that for every real \(C\ge1\), some finite connected positively weighted \(H\)-minor-free graph admits no map into any finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) space satisfying both inequalities with factor \(C\). Failure at one fixed distortion value is insufficient if a larger uniform value remains possible. This binary existence claim has no additive numerical tolerance.

cards.context:
The conjecture links a qualitative restriction on graph structure to quantitative preservation of every distance. Removing one fixed graph from the set of permitted minors is predicted to prevent any distortion that grows with graph size, despite arbitrary edge lengths.

Finite \(\ell_1\) metrics are exactly nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric has value one on pairs separated by a vertex subset and zero on other pairs. This connects distance representation to weighted separation of vertices and hence to graph partitioning.

In the equivalent routing formulation, capacities are attached to graph edges and demands to arbitrary vertex pairs. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every demand, allowing a demand to split among paths. The flow-cut gap compares the best achievable fraction to the upper bound imposed by the sparsest cut. The conjecture predicts a constant gap on every fixed-minor-free family.

Demands in this correspondence may join any pairs; they need not themselves form a planar or minor-free graph. The multiflow/multicut optimization studied in recent work has a different objective and gap, so its constant bounds do not resolve the conjecture.

The planar case is already unresolved in the checked 2026 account: the upper bound grows as the square root of the logarithm of the number of vertices, while no superconstant lower bound is known there. Trees and several other restricted families do have constant bounds.

Lee and Sidiropoulos establish a constant bound on every minor-closed family excluding a fixed tree. Their stronger random-tree result applies to bounded pathwidth, a restriction stronger than bounded treewidth.

A constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on fixed-treewidth graphs is known using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. The authors explicitly distinguish its stronger relaxation from the ordinary concurrent-flow relaxation, whose gap is the relevant one here.

For planar graphs with a selected terminal set covered by \(\gamma\) faces of a drawing, Filtser obtains distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log(\gamma+1)})\). The added one handles the single-face boundary case in asymptotic notation. The number of covering faces is unbounded in the general conjecture.

Mori’s February 2026 preprint states that the worst distortion over edge lengths of \(K_{2,n}\) is \((3k-2)/(2k-1)\), where \(k=\lceil n/2\rceil\) and \(n\ge1\). Here \(K_{2,n}\) has two independent parts of sizes two and \(n\), with all edges between them. These values tend to \(3/2\), so this is progress within a bounded-distortion family.

cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(M\), a real constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every valid explicit knot-diagram encoding \(D\) of bit length \(N\), the machine halts within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps and outputs
\[
M(D)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{the knot represented by }D\text{ is ambient isotopic to the unknot}?
\]
It must output zero for every nontrivial knot. The same machine and constants must work for all diagrams, without auxiliary certificates or advice.
cards.definitions:
The \(3\)-sphere is \(S^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\sum_{i=1}^4x_i^2=1\}\), equivalently the one-point compactification of \(\mathbb R^3\). A tame knot is an embedded circle in \(S^3\) that can be carried by an ambient isotopy to a finite polygonal embedded circle in \(\mathbb R^3\). Wild embeddings are excluded.

An ambient isotopy is a continuous map \(H:S^3\times[0,1]\to S^3\) such that each \(H_t=H(\,\cdot\,,t)\) is a homeomorphism and \(H_0\) is the identity. Two knots have the same type if some such \(H_1\) takes one onto the other. The unknot is the type of a round planar circle. Knots are not given an orientation.

A knot diagram is a plane drawing of one immersed circle with finitely many transverse double crossings and a choice of overpassing strand at every crossing. The drawing determines a tame knot by separating the two strands locally in the third coordinate. Its input representation is combinatorial, so real coordinates are unnecessary.

For a diagram with \(n\ge1\) crossings, encode a connected graph with \(n\) vertices and four half-edges at each vertex. A half-edge is one end of an edge; an explicitly listed pairing of the \(4n\) half-edges forms the edges. Loops and parallel edges are allowed. At every vertex list the four incident half-edges in cyclic order, and mark which of the two opposite pairs is overpassing. The other pair is underpassing. Also designate one face as the outer face.

The cyclic orders must define a cellular embedding in the sphere: replace each vertex by an oriented disc, join paired half-edges by bands respecting the orders, and cap each resulting boundary circle by a disc. The resulting surface must be a sphere. Equivalently for this connected rotation system, its face cycles must give Euler characteristic \(n-2n+f=2\), where \(f\) is their count. The outer face gives a plane drawing.

Following edges and continuing through the opposite half-edge at each crossing must trace a single unoriented closed component. Thus the representation describes a knot, not a multi-component link. A separate fixed code represents the crossing-free circle. All indices, pairings, cyclic lists and crossing bits are written explicitly in binary with fixed delimiters. They can be checked combinatorially in polynomial time; malformed encodings may be rejected.

The parameter \(N\) is the length of the supplied finite encoding. A standard indexing uses \(O(n\log(n+1))\) bits, with the crossing-free code handled separately. It is neither the smallest possible crossing number of the knot nor the length of a compressed program describing a larger diagram.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic Turing-machine program with finitely many tapes. A step reads and writes a bounded number of tape symbols; arbitrary-length integer operations are not unit-cost operations. It receives no spanning disc, invariant, simplification sequence, random bits, oracle or length-dependent advice. The required output is one bit, not an isotopy or diagram simplification.
