cards.context:
A complicated knot diagram can represent a circle that has merely been drawn in an awkward way. The task is to distinguish such projections from actual knots, using a finite description of crossings and planar incidence. No physical model of rope or numerical geometry is involved.

Both positive and negative instances have short efficiently checkable certificates. The NP theorem certifies unknottedness, and the coNP theorem certifies knottedness. These are existence statements about verifiable evidence; they do not show how to find the evidence in deterministic polynomial time.

Thus the problem belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\). Here NP consists of decision problems with polynomial-size witnesses verifiable in polynomial time, and coNP contains their complements. NP-hardness of this particular problem under polynomial-time reductions would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\); a proof that it is outside P would in particular separate P from NP.

Lackenby proves that an unknot diagram with \(n\) crossings admits a simplification using at most \((236n)^{11}\) Reidemeister moves. These are local changes of diagrams that preserve knot type. The theorem bounds a successful sequence’s length, while an algorithm must determine appropriate moves without an uncontrolled search.

The March 2021 Oxford announcement states a recognition algorithm with running time \(n^{O(\log n)}\). The checked SoCG 2025 article still describes that result as announced. Such a quasipolynomial bound allows a growing exponent and therefore does not give the fixed exponent requested here.

The SoCG 2025 factorisation work distinguishes practical performance from worst-case guarantees. It reports that Regina’s recognition algorithm behaves polynomially in experiments despite an exponential worst-case bound. Testing many diagrams cannot establish a bound for every possible input.

Lackenby’s July 2026 hierarchy algorithm gives another recognition method. Section 9 bounds iteration counts by \(L(g+1)^L\), where \(L\) is a hierarchy-length bound and \(g\) bounds surface pattern complexity. These parameters are not bounded there as functions of the original diagram size, and some operation costs also remain unspecified. The displayed iteration estimate is not a polynomial-time theorem for this card.

Musick’s September 2026 preprint claims a positive solution. A bridge presentation separates the knot into trivial arcs in two balls. The preprint claims to find a locally minimal bridge presentation in polynomial time using compressed data, then invokes the fact that a locally minimal presentation of the unknot has one bridge.

The claim’s key dependencies include completeness of the permitted simplifications for local bridge minimality and polynomial manipulation of arc multiplicities. This review read those arguments but did not independently certify them. The scientific status remains uncertain pending validation; no counterexample to the claim is asserted.

cards.title: Planar k-set growth exponent
cards.formal: Determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le Cn(k+1)^a\}.\] Here \(K_2(n,k)\) is the largest number of distinct \(k\)-point subsets strictly separable by a line in an \(n\)-point planar set with no three collinear points. Its full definition is below. The bound must be uniform in both integer parameters. Logarithmic factors and exact extremal counts are not requested.
cards.definitions:
For a finite set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
\mathcal S_k(P)=\bigl\{S\subseteq P:\ |S|=k,\ 
\exists(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\ 
\exists t\in\mathbb R:\ 
a x+b y<t\ \forall(x,y)\in S,\ 
a x+b y>t\ \forall(x,y)\in P\setminus S\bigr\}.
\]
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), define
\[
K_2(n,k)=
\max_{\substack{P\subseteq\mathbb R^2,\ |P|=n\\
                 \text{no three points of }P\text{ are collinear}}}
|\mathcal S_k(P)|.
\]


The plane \(\mathbb R^2\) has arbitrary real coordinates. A point set contains distinct points. General position here means exactly that no three points lie on one affine line; there is no grid, precision, distribution or convex-position restriction.

The affine line \(a x+b y=t\) has nonzero normal vector \((a,b)\). The strict inequalities in the definition place all points of \(S\) on one side and all other points on the opposite side. In particular the separating line contains no input point. A member of \(\mathcal S_k(P)\) is a k-set. Each subset is counted once, regardless of how many lines separate it.

The maximum is well-defined: every count is an integer between zero and \(\binom nk\), and there are general-position point sets of each permitted size. Thus the set of attained counts is a nonempty finite set of integers even though coordinates range over infinitely many possibilities.

Complementing subsets gives the same count for \(k\) and \(n-k\). Sizes zero and \(n\) each give one subset, so the stated domain captures the nontrivial range. The target is a combinatorial extremal function, not the time complexity of listing k-sets.

In the context, a directed j-edge joins two input points and has exactly \(j\) other points strictly to its left. For even \(n\), an undirected halving edge has \((n-2)/2\) other points on each side of its supporting line. The line through this edge is not a strict separator, since it passes through two points. The requested exponent is \[x_{\mathrm{kset}}=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall 1\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\ K_2(n,k)\le C n(k+1)^a\}.\] The integer parameter domain is the same as above. The coefficient \(C\) may depend on \(a\), but not on either parameter or the point configuration. The cited upper bound ensures \(0\le x_{\mathrm{kset}}\le1/3\). The infimum need not be attained. Thus a value zero permits subpolynomial dependence on \(k\) and does not assert a linear bound \(O(n)\). This records the exponent of the dependence on subset size after factoring out the linear dependence on the number of points; it does not assert a two-sided power-law asymptotic.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply \(a\) and prove \(|a-x_{\mathrm{kset}}|\le1/100\) in Lean. For each feasible exponent, one coefficient \(C\) must work for every legal pair \((n,k)\). To exclude an exponent, show that every proposed \(C>0\) fails at some such pair. The infimum need not be attained. A [certified enclosing interval](definitions.html#numerical-answers) of width at most \(1/50\) also suffices via its midpoint.
cards.why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. Its persistent gap tests the strength of crossing-number methods and geometric constructions, with consequences for output-sensitive and parametric algorithms.

cards.context:
A linear cut realizes only a restricted collection of subsets of a point set. Fixing the subset size measures this restriction more precisely than counting all possible cuts together. The planar problem already exhibits the persistent gap in the broader higher-dimensional question.

For \(k=1\), the separable points are precisely the vertices of the convex hull, the smallest convex set containing \(P\). Their maximum number is \(n\). The unresolved part concerns how the count grows when the selected subset size grows too.

Point-line duality relates these counts to levels in arrangements of lines. A level follows the positions with a prescribed number of arrangement lines below them. Such complexity bounds occur in geometric selection and parametric optimization, where the preferred solution changes with a parameter.

Dey’s general upper bound is \(O(nk^{1/3})\) on the domain of this card. Tóth’s constructions give \(n\exp(\Omega(\sqrt{\log k}))\) k-sets. Thus the existing upper and lower estimates do not differ by only a universal constant when \(k\) increases.

In the plane, k-sets correspond to directed \((k-1)\)-edges. For even \(n\), subsets of size \(n/2\) therefore correspond to the two orientations of undirected halving edges. Consequently \(K_2(n,n/2)\) is twice the maximum number of halving edges. The index \((n-2)/2\) counts points on one side of a halving edge, not the size of a halving subset.

Nivasch’s construction gives \(\Omega\!\left(n\exp(\sqrt{\ln4}\sqrt{\ln n})/\sqrt{\ln n}\right)\) halving edges for every even \(n\), with an asymptotically larger exponent constant than earlier constructions. Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This lower-bound expression grows faster than \(n(\log n)^A\) for every fixed \(A\), but slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). These comparisons concern the displayed construction, not a proved upper bound on the unknown optimum.

The 2024 halving-line paper improves lower-order and finite-size terms while retaining the leading four-thirds upper power in the balanced case. Such lower-order changes do not themselves determine the uniform exponent selected here.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? There exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that for every integer \(d\ge1\) and every nonempty, full-dimensional, pointed convex polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), writing \(n\) for its number of facets,
\[
\operatorname{diam}G(P)\le C(n+d)^k?
\]
The same \(C\) and \(k\) must work for all dimensions, all facet counts and all real coefficients defining \(P\). Both bounded and unbounded polyhedra are included.
cards.definitions:
A polyhedron is a set \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\) is a real matrix with finitely many rows, \(b\) is a real vector of matching length and inequalities are coordinatewise. Its affine hull is the smallest affine subspace containing it. Full-dimensional means this affine hull is \(\mathbb R^d\); a polyhedron in a larger ambient space is considered in its own affine hull.

Pointed means that there are no \(x\in P\) and nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) for which \(x+tv\in P\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\). A nonempty pointed polyhedron has at least one vertex. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope.

A nonempty proper face is a set \(P\cap\{x:a\cdot x=\beta\}\), where \(a\ne0\), the dot denotes the usual real inner product and \(a\cdot x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in P\). Face dimension means the dimension of its affine hull. A facet is a face of dimension \(d-1\); \(n\) counts the distinct geometric facets, not duplicate or redundant rows of a chosen inequality description. A vertex is a face consisting of one point.

The undirected graph \(G(P)\) has the vertices of \(P\) as its graph vertices. Two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when the segment joining them is a one-dimensional face. Such a segment is a bounded edge. An unbounded one-dimensional face contributes no new graph vertex and no edge to infinity.

A graph path is a finite sequence of vertices with successive terms adjacent, and its length is its number of edges. Distance is the minimum path length between a pair of vertices, and diameter is the largest such distance. These polyhedral graphs are finite, nonempty and connected; a graph with one vertex has diameter zero. Distances count edges of unit cost, not their Euclidean lengths.

The coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers, and no simplicity, general-position or nondegeneracy hypothesis is imposed. The constants cannot depend on coordinate values or an encoding length. Paths may use edges in either direction; no objective function, monotonicity condition or algorithm for finding a path is specified. Polynomiality requires one exponent independent of dimension.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply universal \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) and cover every permitted polyhedron and vertex pair. A negative proof must show that for every real \(C>0\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), some permitted \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron with \(n\) facets has a pair of vertices at graph distance greater than \(C(n+d)^k\). Refuting one fixed linear expression, requiring a long path under one pivot rule, or bounding a different notion of distance is insufficient. This binary existence question has no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.

cards.context:
A linear program optimizes a linear function over a polyhedron. Moving between adjacent vertices is the geometric operation behind simplex pivots. The conjecture asks whether every pair of feasible vertices is joined by a short sequence of these moves, before any navigation rule or objective is chosen.

The facet count measures the number of essential inequalities. It can be much smaller than the number of vertices: the cube \([0,1]^d\) has \(2d\) facets and \(2^d\) vertices, but diameter only \(d\). Merely bounding distance by the number of vertices therefore does not give the desired polynomial.

A bound such as \(n^d\) allows the exponent to increase with the dimension. The conjecture demands one fixed exponent, and allows neither the multiplicative constant nor that exponent to depend on the particular polyhedron.

Santos’s 43-dimensional polytope with 86 facets has diameter greater than 43, refuting the original Hirsch bound \(n-d\) for bounded polytopes. This leaves open all sufficiently large polynomial bounds. The bounded counterexample does not itself show superpolynomial growth.

Todd proves the general bound \((n-d)^{\log_2 d}\), with the single-vertex boundary cases treated separately. The earlier Kalai–Kleitman bound was \(n^{2+\log_2 d}\). These estimates are quasipolynomial when both parameters vary.

Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has exponent \(\log_2 d-\log_2\log d+O(1)\) for large \(d\). The exponent still grows without bound, so this improvement does not establish the conjecture.

The length of the best available path is different from the length of a path selected by a particular pivot rule. A positive answer would give geometric existence, without supplying a fast procedure for choosing the next edge or guaranteeing objective improvement.

Wulf proves that computing diameter is \(\Pi_2^p\)-hard even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, the convex hulls of incidence vectors of perfect matchings in bipartite graphs. This is a hardness classification at the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. It concerns finding the value, and is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on that value.

Natura’s February 2026 preprint states a circuit-diameter bound \(O(r^2\log r)\) for standard-form polyhedra \(\{x\in\mathbb R^N:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has full row rank \(r\ge2\). A circuit direction is a nonzero kernel vector whose set of nonzero coordinates contains no smaller support of another nonzero kernel vector. A circuit step moves maximally in a feasible circuit direction and may pass through a higher-dimensional face. Such a walk need not follow graph edges.

A monotone path increases a chosen linear objective. A coherent monotone path is more restricted: it traces optimizers as a second linear objective varies along a line in objective space. Black and Xue’s July 2026 preprint gives polytopes for which every coherent monotone path for the chosen orientation is long. Their restriction is absent from ordinary graph distance.

More precisely, their Theorem 1.1 gives, for each \(q\ge3\), a polytope of dimension \(q+1\) with \((2q+1)(q+1)+1\) facets and an objective for which every coherent monotone path has length at least \(2^{q-1}-1\). The paper continues to list the unrestricted polynomial Hirsch question as open.

Santos’s 43-dimensional polytope with 86 facets has diameter greater than 43, refuting the original Hirsch bound \(n-d\) for bounded polytopes. This leaves open all sufficiently large polynomial bounds. The bounded counterexample does not itself show superpolynomial growth.

Todd proves the general bound \((n-d)^{\log_2 d}\), with the single-vertex boundary cases treated separately. The earlier Kalai–Kleitman bound was \(n^{2+\log_2 d}\). These estimates are quasipolynomial when both parameters vary.
Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has exponent \(\log_2 d-\log_2\log d+O(1)\) for large \(d\). The exponent still grows without bound, so this improvement does not establish the conjecture.

The length of the best available path is different from the length of a path selected by a particular pivot rule. A positive answer would give geometric existence, without supplying a fast procedure for choosing the next edge or guaranteeing objective improvement.

Wulf proves that computing diameter is \(\Pi_2^p\)-hard even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, the convex hulls of incidence vectors of perfect matchings in bipartite graphs. This is a hardness classification at the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. It concerns finding the value, and is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on that value.

Natura’s February 2026 preprint states a circuit-diameter bound \(O(r^2\log r)\) for standard-form polyhedra \(\{x\in\mathbb R^N:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has full row rank \(r\ge2\). A circuit direction is a nonzero kernel vector whose set of nonzero coordinates contains no smaller support of another nonzero kernel vector. A circuit step moves maximally in a feasible circuit direction and may pass through a higher-dimensional face. Such a walk need not follow graph edges.

A monotone path increases a chosen linear objective. A coherent monotone path is more restricted: it traces optimizers as a second linear objective varies along a line in objective space. Black and Xue’s July 2026 preprint gives polytopes for which every coherent monotone path for the chosen orientation is long. Their restriction is absent from ordinary graph distance.

More precisely, their Theorem 1.1 gives, for each \(q\ge3\), a polytope of dimension \(q+1\) with \((2q+1)(q+1)+1\) facets and an objective for which every coherent monotone path has length at least \(2^{q-1}-1\). The paper continues to list the unrestricted polynomial Hirsch question as open.

cards.title: Logarithmic \(\ell_1\) distortion lower bound for planar Earth Mover Distance
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that \[D(n)\ge c\log_2 n\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0?\] Here \(D(n)\), defined below, is the least bi-Lipschitz distortion into \(\ell_1\) of the space of all probability measures on \(\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}^2\), equipped with Earth Mover Distance using Euclidean ground distances.
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), a probability measure is a vector \(\mu:X_n	o[0,1]\) with \(\sum_x\mu(x)=1\); all real weights are allowed. For two such vectors put \[W_n(\mu,
u)=\min_\pi\sum_{x,y\in X_n}\|x-y\|_2\pi(x,y),\] where \(\pi(x,y)\geq0\), \(\sum_y\pi(x,y)=\mu(x)\) for each \(x\), and \(\sum_x\pi(x,y)=
u(y)\) for each \(y\). The minimum exists because the set of transport plans is a nonempty compact polytope. Thus unit total mass is transported, with cost equal to distance rather than squared distance. The space \(\ell_1\) consists of real sequences \(z=(z_i)_{i\geq1}\) with \(\sum_i|z_i|<\infty\), and norm \(\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|\). Define \(D(n)\) to be the infimum of all \(D\geq1\) for which a single map \(F\) from the whole probability simplex on \(X_n\) into \(\ell_1\) satisfies \(W_n(\mu,
u)\leq\|F(\mu)-F(
u)\|_1\leq D W_n(\mu,
u)\) for every pair \(\mu,
u\). Allow arbitrary nonlinear maps; the lower inequality normalizes scale and ensures injectivity. No restriction to distributions of bounded support size, uniform weights or a fixed denominator is imposed. No linearity, sketch length, algorithmic runtime or finite output dimension is required. Finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) maps remain admissible by padding with zeros. The infimum need not be attained; matching constant-factor bounds do not require an optimum-achieving map. If no finite-distortion map exists, the infimum is infinity, although the cited upper bound rules this out for each finite grid.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof that \(D(n)\ge c\log_2 n\) at every sufficiently large grid size for one \(c>0\). The matching logarithmic lower bound is recorded below among the dated results.
cards.why: The result identifies the optimal loss when representing planar transport by coordinatewise absolute differences. It closes a longstanding metric-embedding gap relevant to image comparison and nearest-neighbor methods, and shows that the logarithmic loss of classical representations is inherent. The completed result belongs in the historical archive rather than the active open benchmark.

cards.context:
Naor and Schechtman establish the historical gap between an \(\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})\) lower bound and an \(O(\log n)\) upper bound. The binary target selects the logarithmic lower endpoint that was open at the benchmark cutoff; constant distortion was already ruled out earlier.

Gartland and Ostrovskii’s STOC 2026 paper closes that gap: Theorem 1.1 gives \(\Theta(\log n)\) distortion for the transportation-cost space of the planar grid. Their reduction to linear maps identifies its distortion with that of the Earth Mover space of probability measures.

The 2026 grid theorem uses the shortest-path grid metric, which is the planar Manhattan metric. On the same vertices, Euclidean distance is between \(1/\sqrt2\) times that metric and that metric. The corresponding transport distances satisfy the same comparison, so the logarithmic order transfers to the Euclidean ground metric here.

The lower bound is proved even for embeddings into the larger Lebesgue space \(L_1\), so it also applies to \(\ell_1\). The historical upper-bound constructions can be realized with finitely many \(\ell_1\) coordinates for each finite grid. The target-space notation therefore does not leave an asymptotic gap in this card.

A separate 2026 paper by Gartland, Ostrovskii, Rabani and Young extends the sharp dependence to higher-dimensional grids with dimension-uniform constants. Its planar case explicitly relies on the Gartland–Ostrovskii theorem. It is supporting later context, not the sole basis for identifying a planar resolution.

Grid side length and the number of grid vertices differ by a square, which changes a logarithm only by a constant factor. The number of support points of an individual distribution is a different parameter and is not substituted for grid size. Sketching independently represented point sets is likewise a separate computational question.

cards.title: Lang–Plaut problem
cards.formal: For every integer \(K\geq2\), do there exist a finite integer \(N(K)\geq1\) and a finite real constant \(D(K)\geq1\) such that every \(K\)-doubling subset \(X\) of real Hilbert space admits a map \(F:X\to\mathbb R^{N(K)}\) satisfying \[\|x-y\|_2\leq\|F(x)-F(y)\|_2\leq D(K)\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in X)?\]
cards.definitions: It suffices to use the real Hilbert space \(\ell_2=\{(x_i)_{i\geq1}:\sum_i x_i^2<\infty\}\), with norm \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\). A doubling subset of any Hilbert space is separable and isometrically identifies with a subset of this space. Give \(X\subseteq\ell_2\) the restricted Hilbert distance. It is \(K\)-doubling if, for every \(x\in X\) and \(r>0\), the closed ball \(B_X(x,r)=\{y\in X:\|x-y\|_2\leq r\}\) is covered by at most \(K\) closed balls \(B_X(z,r/2)\) with centers \(z\in X\). No boundedness, closedness, compactness or finiteness of \(X\) is assumed. Empty sets and singletons cause no difficulty. The codomain has its ordinary Euclidean norm. The displayed lower inequality makes the map injective and fixes its arbitrary scale; without that normalization, distortion is the product of the Lipschitz constants of a map and its inverse on its image. The functions \(N,D\) must be chosen before \(X\), and may depend only on \(K\), not on the number of points, diameter, aspect ratio or ambient Hilbert dimension. The embedding may be nonlinear and may be chosen separately for each \(X\). There is no algorithm, continuity beyond the displayed bounds, or prescribed polynomial dependence on \(K\) required. Distances themselves must be preserved within these factors; replacing them by a power smaller than one changes the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal statement in Lean, or give a complete Lean-checked refutation with a fixed doubling bound for which no uniform pair of finite dimension and distortion bounds works. Equivalently, the qualitative Lang–Plaut formulation can be settled by proving that every doubling Hilbert subset has some finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding, or by exhibiting one that has none; the source proves the equivalence with the quantitative formulation. A restriction to linear maps, snowflaked distances, or bounds growing with the number of points does not resolve the question.
cards.why: The problem asks whether intrinsic local metric dimension completely controls Euclidean dimensional reduction once Hilbert embeddability is available. Its resolution would clarify a central obstruction to finite-dimensional metric representation and the limits of geometry-based compression independent of dataset size.

cards.context:
Naor and Neiman state the Lang–Plaut question in Section 1.1 and justify its quantitative form in Section 4. This card uses that form so the dependence of dimension and distortion is explicit. The original question is attributed there to Lang and Plaut’s Question 2.4.

Every subset of a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space is doubling, with a bound controlled by dimension, and is already a subset of Hilbert space. A positive answer would make these two necessary conditions sufficient for finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embeddability.

Naor and Neiman prove that for an arbitrary doubling metric \((X,d)\), every snowflake \((X,d^{1-\eta})\), \(0<\eta<1/2\), embeds into a Euclidean space whose dimension depends only on the doubling constant. The distortion still depends on \(\eta\). Letting \(\eta\) tend to zero therefore does not supply the uniformly controlled embedding asked for here.

Lafforgue and Naor construct, for every \(p>2\), a doubling subset of \(L_p\) that has no bi-Lipschitz embedding into any finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Their theorem explicitly leaves the Hilbert case \(p=2\) open, so replacing Hilbert space by a general Banach space changes the answer.

Usual finite-set dimension reduction allows dimension to grow with the logarithm of the number of points. Here arbitrarily large or infinite sets with the same doubling bound must share a finite target dimension and distortion bound. This is a geometric existence question rather than a request for a faster implementation of a known projection.

cards.title: Weak \(\varepsilon\)-net size exponent
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge2\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:f_d(\varepsilon)=O_d(\varepsilon^{-a})\text{ as }\varepsilon\downarrow0\}.\] The function \(f_d(\varepsilon)\), defined below, is the worst-case minimum cardinality of a weak \(\varepsilon\)-net hitting all convex sets that contain at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a finite point set in \(\mathbb R^d\). Net points may lie outside the input set. The requested answer concerns the exponent, with no requirement to determine logarithmic factors.
cards.definitions: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) be real. A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net is a finite set \(N\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(N\cap C\ne\varnothing\) for every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(|P\cap C|\geq\varepsilon|P|\). A set is convex if it contains the segment joining any two of its points. All convex ranges, including unbounded and lower-dimensional ones, are allowed; no restriction to halfspaces, simplices or a given finite family is made. Equivalently it is enough to hit \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) for every \(Q\subseteq P\) with \(|Q|\geq\lceil\varepsilon|P|\rceil\), so using only closed convex ranges gives the same condition. Net points can lie anywhere in \(\mathbb R^d\) and need not belong to \(P\). Put \(w(P,\varepsilon)=\min\{|N|:N\text{ is a weak }\varepsilon\text{-net for }P\}\) and \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\subset\mathbb R^d,\,0<|P|<\infty}w(P,\varepsilon)\). The minimum exists since \(N=P\) is feasible. The supremum ranges over every size and configuration with the same fixed dimension and accuracy; a bound depending on \(|P|\) is not a bound on \(f_d\). The weak-net theorem ensures \(f_d(\varepsilon)<\infty\). There is no general-position, rational-coordinate, uniform-measure-on-space, algorithmic or randomized guarantee in the target: the only measure is the uniform counting measure on the given finite set. The problem measures extremal cardinality, not construction time. For each fixed integer \(d\ge2\), define \[x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists\varepsilon_0\in(0,1/2]\ \forall\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_0],\ f_d(\varepsilon)\le C\varepsilon^{-a}\}.\] Constants may depend on \(d\) and \(a\), but not on the accuracy or point set. The classical polynomial upper bound and inverse-accuracy lower bound give \(1\le x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)\le d\), so every requested value is a finite real number. The infimum need not be attained; a polylogarithmic factor in \(1/\varepsilon\) does not change the exponent. Different fixed dimensions may use different constants, with no uniform bound on their growth requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all integers \(d\ge2\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(d)-x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(d)\le x_{\mathrm{net}}(d)\le U(d)\) and \(U(d)-L(d)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). The weak-net asymptotics take \(\varepsilon\) to zero at each fixed dimension.
cards.why: Weak nets quantify how many representatives can preserve every large convex part of an arbitrary finite configuration. Sharp bounds would settle a basic gap in discrete geometry and clarify the geometric cost underlying transversal, selection and approximation results.

The source asks for the true asymptotic behavior of weak-net size in every fixed dimension. the benchmark convention selects its polynomial exponent in inverse accuracy, rather than matching the entire function within constant factors.

A strong net is required to choose its points from the input. Allowing auxiliary points is essential for arbitrary convex ranges: arguments for bounded-complexity range families do not automatically supply weak nets for all convex sets.

Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch prove the general lower bound \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\Omega_d(\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d-1}(1/\varepsilon))\). In particular, already in the plane a universal bound proportional to \(1/\varepsilon\) is impossible.

Rubin improves the planar upper bound to \(O_\gamma(\varepsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\). The constant can depend on \(\gamma\); this theorem is not the assertion of an \(O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})\) bound with a uniform constant.

Rubin’s higher-dimensional work, including its December 2023 revision, improves the previously known upper bounds in all fixed dimensions at least three. Those bounds still do not match the lower bound above. Their dependence on dimension does not turn the problem into a joint large-dimension asymptotic question.

The same net must hit all heavy convex ranges simultaneously. Choosing a different auxiliary point after seeing each range would be a different and trivial requirement. This simultaneous coverage is what makes the extremal bound relevant to geometric transversals and sampling.

cards.title: Decidability of PL four-sphere recognition
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(M\) with the following property? For every finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\), encoded by its facets as below and promised to be a nonempty closed combinatorial \(4\)-manifold, \(M\) halts and outputs a bit satisfying
\[
M(\operatorname{enc}(K))=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
K\cong_{\mathrm{PL}}\partial\Delta^5.
\]
Here \(\partial\Delta^5\) is the standard PL \(4\)-sphere. Output zero is required on every promised input that is not PL homeomorphic to it. There is no running-time or space bound, and connectedness is not part of the promise.
cards.definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex \(K\) is a finite family of finite subsets of a finite vertex set \(V\), containing the empty set and closed under taking subsets. Its members are faces; inclusion-maximal faces are facets. The dimension of a nonempty face \(\sigma\) is \(|\sigma|-1\). Pure dimension four means that all facets have exactly five vertices.

Vertex labels are distinct nonnegative integers. The input lists each facet once, sorting labels increasingly within facets and sorting the facet lists lexicographically. Each label is written in binary with no leading zero except for the label zero itself. A fixed separator between labels and a second separator between facets make this a finite string over a fixed alphabet. The full complex is the family of all subsets of the listed facets, and its vertex set is their union. Renaming vertices does not affect the correct answer.

The geometric realization \(|K|\) is the subset of \(\mathbb R^V\) consisting of vectors \((t_v)_{v\in V}\) with \(t_v\ge0\), \(\sum_vt_v=1\), and \(\{v:t_v>0\}\in K\). Each face is realized as the convex hull of its coordinate unit vectors. A finite simplicial subdivision is a finite triangulation of this realization by simplices contained in old simplices, whose union on each old simplex equals that simplex.

Two finite complexes are piecewise-linearly homeomorphic, written \(K\cong_{\mathrm{PL}}L\), when they admit finite subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic. A simplicial isomorphism is a bijection on vertices taking faces to faces in both directions. Equivalently, their realizations have a homeomorphism that is affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions.

The simplex \(\Delta^q\) is the complex of all subsets of a set of \(q+1\) vertices. Its boundary \(\partial\Delta^q\) consists of all proper subsets of that vertex set. The standard PL \(j\)-sphere is \(\partial\Delta^{j+1}\), up to PL homeomorphism.

The link of a vertex \(v\) is
\[
\operatorname{lk}_K(v)=
\{\sigma\in K:v\notin\sigma,\ \sigma\cup\{v\}\in K\}.
\]
In this card, a nonempty closed combinatorial \(4\)-manifold means a finite pure four-dimensional complex for which every vertex link is PL homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^4\). Multiple connected components are allowed. No orientation, simple-connectivity, homology-sphere or prior topological-sphere promise is imposed.

A deterministic Turing machine has a finite transition rule, finite tape alphabet and finitely many tapes; it starts with the encoded complex on its input tape. Halting with output one means acceptance, and halting with output zero means rejection. Termination and correctness are required on all and only promised inputs; behavior on malformed strings or complexes outside the promise is unrestricted. The same finite machine must work for complexes of every size.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of the stated machine or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish termination and the exact PL classification on every promised input, without additional unproved hypotheses. A negative answer must establish that every deterministic Turing machine has a promised input on which it either fails to halt with a bit or gives the wrong bit. A lower bound ruling out only polynomial time, a procedure that can return “unknown,” or a classifier proved correct only on a finite census does not settle this target. This is a binary decidability statement with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: Locate the remaining decidability boundary for recognizing spheres in the piecewise-linear category.

cards.context:
Finite input does not guarantee algorithmic decidability of a global geometric property. The question concerns existence of any always-terminating decision procedure, even one whose resource use is far beyond practical computation.

The PL sphere-recognition problem is decidable through dimension three and undecidable in dimensions at least five. The four-dimensional case is the exceptional gap in the checked account. This card fixes that dimension and promises a manifold rather than asking for manifold recognition itself.

The promise is local: links of vertices have the standard three-sphere type. The output concerns the entire four-dimensional space. Local manifold structure alone does not force the global space to be a sphere.

The topology category matters. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, whereas PL equivalence adds finite piecewise-affine structure. The standard PL sphere cannot be replaced silently by a merely topological sphere.

Pachner’s theorem characterizes PL equivalence of closed triangulated manifolds by finite sequences of bistellar moves, local replacements that preserve PL type. Such finite certificates are useful for individual positive instances. Existence of a certificate does not ensure a recognition procedure terminates on negative instances.

The 2022 computational study explicitly allows an inconclusive outcome. Its successful classifications establish properties of those tested triangulations, without proving that every permitted input will eventually be classified.

The 2026 census work examines closed orientable four-manifolds with at most six four-dimensional simplices. Among triangulations topologically equivalent to the four-sphere, it leaves at most four potentially distinct PL types and conjectures that all are standard. These are unresolved classifications, not a proof that four distinct structures exist.

That census uses generalised triangulations, permitting identifications among faces of a simplex. The card instead uses abstract simplicial complexes with the explicit vertex-set encoding. Neither the finite census limit nor its orientability restriction is added to the benchmark promise.

An algorithm here must reject disconnected promised manifolds as well as connected non-spheres. It must also answer correctly for any PL structures that actually exist, without assuming a conjectural classification of four-manifolds.

cards.title: \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) lower bound for binary edit distance in \(\ell_1\)
cards.formal:
For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\) be the infimum distortion of embeddings of all length-\(n\) binary strings, with unit-cost edit distance, into finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\). Distortion measures the worst multiplicative change in any distance after a common rescaling; its precise all-pairs definition is below.

Do there exist an absolute real constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that
\[
D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\ge 2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}
\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0?
\]
This is the assertion that binary edit distance requires \(\ell_1\) distortion at least \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\).
cards.definitions:
Let \(X_n=\{0,1\}^n\), the set of all \(2^n\) binary strings of length \(n\). The distance \(\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform \(x\) into \(y\), each at cost one. Inserted and substituted characters are binary, and intermediate strings may have any finite length. For \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), the \(\ell_1\) norm is \(\|v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^m|v_i|\).

Define the optimal distortion by
\[
D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)=\inf\bigl\{D\in[1,\infty):\ \exists m\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\ \exists f:X_n\to\mathbb R^m,\ \exists a>0,\ \forall x,y\in X_n,\ a\,\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\le\|f(x)-f(y)\|_1\le D a\,\mathrm{ED}(x,y)\bigr\}.
\]
The dimension \(m\) is any finite positive integer, coordinates are arbitrary real numbers, and the map need not have an efficient or computable description. There is no bound on dimension or construction/evaluation time, and no requirement for a uniform algorithm across different \(n\). The same map \(f\) and positive scale \(a\) must satisfy both inequalities simultaneously for all pairs in \(X_n\); \(f,m,a\) may depend on \(n\). The infimum ranges over all such choices and need not be attained. Every finite metric space has a finite-distortion embedding into some finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\), so \(1\le D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)<\infty\).

All logarithms in the target are to base two. The constants \(c\) and \(n_0\) in the proposed lower bound must be independent of \(n\), the dimension and the embedding. The assertion concerns every sufficiently large string length, not just an infinite subsequence. Its exponent contains \(\sqrt{\log_2 n}\), with no additional \(\log\log n\) factor.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) for which the lower bound holds for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), against all unrestricted finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) embeddings in the definition. A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall c>0\;\forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\;\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge N}:\quad
D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)<2^{c\sqrt{\log_2 n}}.
\]
A single exceptional length does not refute the asymptotic assertion. This is an exact yes/no target; neither a matching upper bound nor optimization of the constant \(c\) is required. A lower bound restricted to a chosen dimension or family of maps does not establish the claim for unrestricted embeddings.
cards.why: Such a lower bound would show that representing binary edit distance by sums of coordinate differences necessarily incurs distortion larger than every fixed power of the logarithm of string length. It would substantially strengthen the logarithmic obstruction and clarify how far the geometry of sequence editing is from that of l1.

cards.context:
The formulation uses this specific \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\) lower-bound question on 6 November 2026. It replaces the previous request to determine the entire optimal-distortion function up to constant factors. The threshold is an editorial target, not a conjecture attributed verbatim to the cited papers.

Ostrovsky and Rabani prove \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)\le 2^{O(\sqrt{(\log n)(\log\log n)})}\). This is a subpolynomial upper bound whose displayed growth exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Their geometric theorem places no algorithmic constraint on the embedding. Here and in the asymptotic bounds, logarithms may be taken to base two and the displayed formulas concern sufficiently large \(n\).

Krauthgamer and Rabani prove \(D_{\mathrm{ED}}(n)=\Omega(\log n)\). Together with the upper bound, this leaves a gap between logarithmic and subpolynomial distortion. Both of these papers explicitly include unit-cost substitutions, matching this card's distance.

The earlier Khot–Naor lower bound is \((\log n)^{1/2-o(1)}\), rather than logarithmic. That paper permits only insertions and deletions. If \(\mathrm{ED}_{\mathrm{indel}}\) denotes this convention, then \(\mathrm{ED}\le\mathrm{ED}_{\mathrm{indel}}\le2\mathrm{ED}\), so the two optimal distortion functions agree within a factor of two; they need not agree pointwise.

Near-linear-time constant-factor approximation of the distance between two supplied strings concerns a different mathematical guarantee. It does not give a single map of the entire binary-string metric into ordinary \(\ell_1\) with constant distortion.

The FOCS 2025 work develops average embeddings into similarity measures and obtains polylogarithmic approximation for edit-distance nearest-neighbor search. The primary abstract states this different target; it does not claim the all-pairs ordinary-l1 embedding required here.

cards.title: Near-linear-time exact Euclidean minimum spanning trees
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge3\), is there one deterministic algorithm \(A_d\), a constant \(C_d>0\), and an integer \(a_d\ge1\) that compute an exact Euclidean minimum spanning tree of any \(n\ge2\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^d\) in at most \[C_d n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^{a_d}\] worst-case steps in the real-arithmetic model below? The input is an array of coordinates \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\). The output is a list of \(n-1\) index pairs forming a connected acyclic graph \(T\) minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in T}\|p_i-p_j\|_2\). The program and constants may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates.
cards.definitions: The Euclidean distance is \(\|p-q\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d(p_j-q_j)^2)^{1/2}\). Coordinates are arbitrary exact reals; there is no general-position, bounded-spread or unique-optimum promise. Any minimum tree is a correct output. The complete graph and its edge weights are implicit, so reading every possible edge is not a required part of the input. For each fixed \(d\), the algorithm is one finite deterministic program for all \(n\) and all coordinates, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, nonnegative square root, comparison, copy, indexed read or write costs one step. Addresses and counters are integers of \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits after \(t\) steps, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged per word operation. There is no floor or bit extraction from real registers, advice depending on the input size, or geometric oracle. All input access and output steps count. Worst-case time is the supremum over all valid size-\(n\) inputs. Constants and programs may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates; no simultaneous polynomial dependence on variable dimension is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: For each fixed \(d\ge3\), prove in Lean that a deterministic algorithm returns an exact minimum spanning tree within the stated worst-case real-arithmetic bound. A refutation must exclude every such algorithm and exponent for at least one fixed dimension.
cards.why: The problem asks how effectively fixed-dimensional geometry can accelerate one of the most basic graph optimization tasks. Sharp complexity bounds would clarify the algorithmic cost of exact geometric connectivity and its relation to proximity searching.

cards.context:
The original entry asks whether exact Euclidean MST computation can approach the sorting-scale \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound. This card selects an \(n\operatorname{polylog}n\) deterministic worst-case upper bound in each fixed dimension. This is an explicit interpretation of “close,” without requiring the optimal logarithmic exponent.

An MST has only a linear number of edges. Nevertheless, applying a graph algorithm after explicitly creating the complete graph already processes quadratically many candidate edges. The unresolved issue is the cost of identifying the optimum from the much smaller coordinate description.

Agarwal, Edelsbrunner, Schwarzkopf and Welzl relate Euclidean MST computation to bichromatic closest pairs: given red and blue points, find a shortest pair with opposite colors. Their 1991 results include subquadratic expected-time algorithms in fixed dimensions. Those randomized guarantees are not silently assigned to the deterministic model used here.

The plane admits a sorting-scale exact MST algorithm, whereas higher fixed dimensions are the subject of the source question. Large-dimensional distance problems, approximate spanning trees and dynamic maintenance ask for different guarantees.

Cabello, Chan and Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations and related MST tasks with predictions in 2026. Their stated setting is planar and includes additional prediction data, so it does not resolve this arbitrary-input higher-dimensional complexity question.

Exactness here refers to the combinatorial tree. In particular, edge ordering can use squared distances because squaring preserves the order of individual nonnegative lengths. This does not require replacing the objective by an approximation or outputting the total length as a decimal number.

cards.title: Dürer’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every bounded three-dimensional convex polytope \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with nonempty interior, is there a connected edge unfolding whose distinct face interiors do not overlap in the plane?
cards.definitions: A convex polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of real points. Its faces here are its maximal two-dimensional facets, and adjacent facets share an entire polytope edge. Choose a spanning tree of the facet adjacency graph. Make separate copies of all facets and glue only the pairs of matching edges selected by that tree, retaining the edge identifications inherited from \(P\). An edge unfolding is a map of this glued polygonal surface to \(\mathbb R^2\) whose restriction to each copied facet is a Euclidean isometry and whose restrictions agree on glued edges. Require images of the relative interiors of distinct facets to be disjoint. Contacts between boundary points are permitted; cuts may run only along original polytope edges. The glued surface and its image are connected. This is a geometric existence statement with arbitrary real coordinates, not an algorithmic runtime claim.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every convex polytope in the stated domain has a spanning tree of facet adjacencies and compatible planar facet isometries with pairwise disjoint relative interiors, or prove a counterexample in Lean: one such polytope for which every permitted gluing tree and planar realization fails. No algorithmic runtime or stricter boundary-injectivity claim is required.
cards.why: This long-standing question asks whether every convex three-dimensional shape has an edge-based planar net, a basic unresolved principle in geometric folding and representation.

cards.context:
A net lays out the actual faces of a solid in one plane without stretching them. A cube provides familiar examples: its six squares can remain connected along selected edges and spread out without their interiors covering one another. The conjecture asks for such a choice for every convex polytope, regardless of the number, shape or arrangement of its facets.

The connected gluing pattern matters independently of overlap. Keeping a tree of facet adjacencies attaches every face to one planar assembly. It does not guarantee that faces far apart in that tree avoid one another after flattening. The existence question concerns a suitable choice of the whole pattern, not whether every possible net succeeds.

Only original polytope edges are available for cuts. Triangulating a facet and then allowing cuts on the new diagonals, slicing through face interiors, or returning disconnected pieces changes the task. Nonconvex examples without suitable unfoldings likewise do not refute a statement restricted to convex input.

This card retains its explicitly chosen nonoverlap convention: relative interiors of distinct facets must be disjoint, while boundary contacts are allowed. A requirement that the entire unfolded boundary be a simple Jordan curve is an additional condition; no equivalence to that stricter condition is assumed. The distinction is explicit in the unfolding literature.

O’Rourke’s March 2026 preprint still identifies even the general prismatoid case as unresolved. A prismatoid is a convex polytope whose vertices lie in two parallel planes. Its nested special cases concern a restricted geometric arrangement, leaving arbitrary convex polytopes outside their guarantee.

The July 2026 overlap construction finds convex polyhedra with particular edge unfoldings of arbitrarily large overlap thickness. Showing that one choice of cuts overlaps is different from showing that every choice overlaps. The latter universal failure would be needed for a counterexample to the existence question.

cards.title: Near-linear-time exact planar Euclidean matching
cards.formal: Is there one uniform deterministic algorithm and universal constants \(C>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) that compute a minimum-length perfect matching of any \(2n\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^2\), for every \(n\ge1\), in at most \[Cn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\] worst-case steps in the exact real-arithmetic model below? The output is a list of \(n\) unordered index pairs, each index occurring once, minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in M}\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}\). The input consists only of the coordinates, with no bipartition or geometric promise.
cards.definitions: The coordinates are arbitrary real numbers supplied in an indexed array. No general-position, bounded-spread, coordinate-precision or unique-optimum promise is made; any minimizing matching is acceptable. An algorithm is one finite deterministic program, valid for every input size, with rational program constants, no advice and no oracle. It has exact real registers and an indexed memory. A real arithmetic operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, a nonnegative square root, a comparison, a register copy, or an indexed read or write costs one step. Integer addresses and loop counters use ordinary arithmetic and comparisons on \(O(\log(n+t+2))\)-bit words after \(t\) steps, with a program-dependent constant in this word bound; there is no floor, bit extraction from reals, or operation that solves an entire optimization problem. Input access, memory operations and output are charged. Running time is the supremum of the number of steps over all valid inputs of the given size. All programs must halt and be correct on every valid input. This fixes the conventional geometric arithmetic interpretation of the source; it is not a bit-complexity question about sums of square roots. The main problem is unrestricted perfect matching: no red/blue partition is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one deterministic algorithm computes a minimum-length perfect matching within the stated worst-case time for all planar point sets, or that every proposed algorithm and bound fail on an admissible input.
cards.why: Exact Euclidean matching is a basic geometric optimization primitive. Its unresolved complexity tests how far geometric structure can reduce the cost of optimization over an implicit complete graph, beyond the easier approximation guarantees.

The Open Problems Project asks for the optimal complexity of exact planar Euclidean matching. This card selects the concrete near-linear deterministic upper-bound target, retaining unrestricted matching rather than the separately mentioned bipartite variant.

A matching contains only a linear number of edges, but the coordinate input describes quadratically many possible pairs. Its objective is the sum of their Euclidean lengths; replacing lengths by squared lengths can change the minimizing matching.

Varadarajan proves an \(O(n^{3/2}\log^5 n)\) exact algorithm. The separator subroutine in the author manuscript has a deterministic implementation, so this is an upper bound for the deterministic target rather than merely an expected randomized bound.

Hougardy and Tammemaa’s April 2026 journal article still identifies Varadarajan’s bound as the fastest known exact algorithm. Their new results improve fast approximation guarantees and do not compute the exact optimum.

The same article recalls an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for deterministic geometric approximation algorithms with approximation ratio depending only on input size. Thus the exact task has a substantial known gap even before finer logarithmic factors are considered.

The arithmetic convention matters because the objective involves square roots and comparisons between sums of lengths. Counting each such arithmetic step is different from bounding the number of bit operations needed to certify every comparison for rationally encoded points. The requested output here is an optimal pairing, not a decimal expansion of its total length.

cards.title: Decidability of contractibility for finite two-dimensional complexes
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm that, on every finite nonempty simplicial complex \(K\) of dimension at most two, halts and decides whether \(K\) is simple-homotopy equivalent to a point? Equivalently, can contractibility of all such \(K\) be decided?
cards.definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.
cards.why: This is a basic boundary of algorithmic topology: whether a finite two-dimensional description admits any reliable procedure for recognizing a space with no nontrivial homotopy. It separates unrestricted computability from practical simplification and from resource-bounded versions of topological reduction.

The source explicitly asks about deciding whether a two-dimensional complex admits a simple-homotopy equivalence to a point. Its separate parameterized problems bound expansions or ask to reach a graph; those are different computational tasks.

The source relates this decidability question to recognizing the trivial group from balanced finite presentations, which have the same number of defining relators and generators. The 2023/2024 random simple-homotopy paper gives practical simplification methods and successful examples while explicitly retaining the open low-dimensional decidability question. A heuristic that finds reductions on many contractible inputs does not provide a halting, correct procedure for every input.

cards.title: Constant-distortion Steiner point removal
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every finite connected undirected graph \(G\) with nonnegative real edge lengths and every terminal set \(K\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|K|\geq2\), there is a reweighted terminal-preserving minor \(H\) with vertex set exactly \(K\) satisfying \[d_G(s,t)\leq d_H(s,t)\leq C\,d_G(s,t)\qquad(s,t\in K)?\]
cards.definitions: The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_G\) is the minimum path length between its endpoints. Zero-length edges are allowed, so distinct terminals can have distance zero; the displayed inequalities then require their distance in \(H\) to be zero too. To specify precisely the terminal-preserving minor condition, choose pairwise disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets \(B_t\subseteq V(G)\), one for each \(t\in K\), with \(B_t\cap K=\{t\}\). The graph \(H\) is a simple graph on the labeled set \(K\); an edge \(st\) of \(H\) is permitted only if some edge of \(G\) joins \(B_s\) to \(B_t\). Not all such permitted edges have to be kept, and vertices outside the branch sets may be deleted. Thus vertices can be deleted, edges deleted or contracted, and parallel edges or loops removed, but no two terminals are identified and no surviving vertex is a nonterminal. Each edge of \(H\) may receive an arbitrary new nonnegative real length, independent of the original length of an edge witnessing its adjacency. This is a topological minor relation with allowed reweighting, not a requirement that contraction preserve inherited edge lengths. Define \(d_H\) by shortest paths and as infinity for disconnected pairs; the guarantee forces finite terminal distances. Both inequalities must hold simultaneously for all pairs in one chosen minor. The same \(C\) must work independently of the numbers of vertices, edges and terminals, graph topology, edge-length magnitudes and aspect ratio. The target is existential and imposes no construction-time, input-encoding or randomness requirement on a proof of existence.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of such a universal constant and the required rooted minor for every input in Lean, or prove its negation: for every finite \(C\), some graph and terminal set admit no minor meeting all the inequalities. A family with unbounded necessary distortion is a valid negative answer; a single fixed lower bound on the constant is not. Expected distortion for each pair, additional surviving Steiner vertices, or a guarantee only in a restricted graph class does not settle the statement.
cards.why: Steiner point removal asks how much of a network’s geometry and topology can survive when only designated terminals remain. A universal constant would establish a strong form of graph compression; an unbounded lower bound would show that the topology of general graphs forces a growing loss even when edge lengths may be redesigned.

references.title: Shortcut Partitions in Minor-Free Graphs: Steiner Point Removal, Distance Oracles, Tree Covers, and More
references.authors: Hsien-Chih Chang; Jonathan Conroy; Hung Le; Lazar Milenković; Shay Solomon; Cuong Than
references.locator: Section 1.1, Question 1.3 and Theorem 1.4; arXiv:2308.00555.

references.locator: SODA 2018, pages 1361–1373; general-graph guarantee and terminal parameter.

cards.context:
The source describes Steiner point removal for general graphs before solving the version excluding a fixed graph minor. This card retains the general-graph question from the inherited record. The word minor includes terminal identities and permitted edge reweighting, which are made explicit in the branch-set definition.

Filtser obtains distortion \(O(\log k)\) for arbitrary graphs with \(k\) terminals. This bounds the loss in terms of the size of the surviving vertex set, but does not provide a constant independent of that size.

For trees, the source recounts an upper bound of eight and examples with necessary distortion approaching eight. Thus even on trees exact preservation is not generally possible, and a universal positive answer must allow nontrivial distortion.

Chang, Conroy, Le, Milenković, Solomon and Than prove constant distortion for every class excluding a fixed complete graph minor. More specifically, for \(K_r\)-minor-free graphs their Theorem 1.4 gives \(2^{O(r\log r)}\) distortion. This settles the planar case and much more, but the constant depends on the excluded minor and is not uniform over all graphs.

If the minor condition is dropped, the complete graph on the terminals with original shortest-path distances as edge lengths preserves every terminal distance exactly. The scientific constraint is preserving a graph-minor representation while removing every other vertex. Distances alone would give a much easier problem.

Choosing a distribution over minors with a small expected stretch for each pair need not produce a single minor that has small stretch on every pair. Likewise, allowing a few extra vertices changes the compression target. Neither relaxation is silently included here.

cards.title: Polynomial-time recognition of the 3-sphere
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether a finite simplicial triangulation of a closed connected piecewise-linear \(3\)-manifold is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the standard \(3\)-sphere?

Precisely, let \(\mathcal P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) be the promised encodings below, and let \(S(x)\) assert that the encoded complex is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{4}\). Does there exist one uniform deterministic Turing machine \(M\), an integer \(C\ge1\), and an integer \(d\ge0\) such that
\[
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists b\in\{0,1\}\
\left[
H_{M}\bigl(x,C(|x|+1)^{d},b\bigr)
\ \land\
\bigl(x\in\mathcal P\ \Rightarrow\ (b=1\Longleftrightarrow S(x))\bigr)
\right]?
\]
Here \(H_{M}(x,t,b)\) means that \(M\) halts within \(t\) transitions with output bit \(b\). The running-time bound holds on every binary string, including malformed encodings and inputs outside the manifold promise; correctness is required on \(\mathcal P\). The machine and both polynomial constants are fixed before the input is chosen.
cards.definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex on \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is a collection \(K\) of subsets of \([m]\), closed under taking subsets and containing every singleton. Its elements are simplices; a simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). A tetrahedron is a simplex with four vertices.

An input complex is given by integers \(m\ge4\) and \(N\ge1\), and \(N\) distinct tetrahedra
\(\tau_{j}=\{v_{j1},v_{j2},v_{j3},v_{j4}\}\), where
\[
1\le v_{j1}<v_{j2}<v_{j3}<v_{j4}\le m.
\]
The quadruples are listed in strictly increasing lexicographic order, and every vertex in \([m]\) occurs. Define
\[
K_{x}=\{\sigma\subseteq[m]:\ \sigma\subseteq\tau_{j}
\text{ for some }j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\}.
\]
All lower-dimensional faces are implicit. Thus the listed tetrahedra are exactly the maximal simplices. There are no coordinates, edge lengths or geometric drawings in the input.

Fix a binary encoding as follows. For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(b(r)\) be the ordinary binary representation of \(r+1\), with no leading zero, and let \(\ell=|b(r)|\). Encode \(r\) by \(1^{\ell}0b(r)\). The input string is the concatenation of the codes of \(m,N\), followed by the codes of \(v_{11},v_{12},v_{13},v_{14},v_{21},\ldots,v_{N4}\) in that order, with no trailing bits. A syntactically valid string parses uniquely and obeys the preceding inequalities, ordering and vertex-coverage conditions. Set \(L=|x|\), the total number of input bits. Since every vertex occurs, \(m\le4N\); these explicit encodings have length \(O(N\log(N+2))\).

The geometric realization is the polyhedron
\[
|K|=\left\{(a_{1},\ldots,a_{m})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{m}:
\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}=1,\ 
\{i:a_{i}>0\}\in K\right\}.
\]
Each abstract simplex is realized as the convex hull of its coordinate unit vectors. A finite geometric simplicial complex is a finite collection of convex hulls of affinely independent finite point sets, containing all their faces, with the intersection of any two simplices empty or a common face. A subdivision of a realization \(|K|\) is such a geometric complex with underlying set \(|K|\), each of whose simplices is contained in an original simplex, and for which every original simplex is the union of simplices of the subdivision. New vertices may be arbitrary real points; they are not additional input data.

Two finite complexes are PL-homeomorphic if they have finite subdivisions whose abstract simplicial complexes are isomorphic. An isomorphism is a bijection of their vertices carrying simplices to simplices in both directions; its affine extension on each simplex supplies the piecewise-linear homeomorphism. There is no required bound on the size of these subdivisions in the definition of the topological property. For \(r\ge1\), \(\Delta^{r}\) is the full simplex on \(r+1\) vertices and \(\partial\Delta^{r}\) consists of all its proper faces. The standard PL \(3\)-sphere is \(|\partial\Delta^{4}|\); the standard PL \(2\)-sphere is \(|\partial\Delta^{3}|\).

For a vertex \(v\) define its link by
\[
\operatorname{lk}_{K}(v)=
\{\sigma\in K:v\notin\sigma,\ \sigma\cup\{v\}\in K\}.
\]
A link has as its vertex set the union of its simplices; when realizing it, use those vertices as the coordinate indices. The same definitions apply to any finite vertex set by replacing \([m]\) with that set. The promise set \(\mathcal P\) consists of syntactically valid strings such that the graph with vertex set \([m]\) and edges the two-element simplices of \(K_{x}\) is connected, and every vertex link is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{3}\). This is the simplicial formulation of a closed connected PL \(3\)-manifold: finite realization gives compactness, and the spherical-link condition gives the local manifold condition without boundary. No orientation, homology calculation, fundamental-group presentation or certificate of the promise is supplied. Nonorientable manifolds are permitted by the promise. For every binary string \(x\), define \(S(x)\) to be false if \(x\) is not syntactically valid, and otherwise to mean that \(K_{x}\) is PL-homeomorphic to \(\partial\Delta^{4}\).

The machine model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes. Its tape alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. Tape cells have nonnegative integer indices and every head initially scans cell zero. The input tape initially holds exactly \(x\) followed by blanks. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; a left move at cell zero stays there. The two halting states output zero and one, respectively. Each transition costs one unit, so all parsing and arithmetic are charged at the bit level. The number of tapes, state set and transition table are independent of \(L\). There is no advice, randomness, oracle or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers.

An answer of one is required for every promised triangulation of the standard PL sphere, and an answer of zero for every other promised manifold. For all other binary strings either bit is permitted, but the same uniform polynomial time bound is mandatory. Neither efficient performance on sampled inputs nor an algorithm restricted to a proper subclass of the promised manifolds meets this definition.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition, including one machine, its uniform polynomial clock on all binary strings and both correctness directions on \(\mathcal P\), or a complete Lean proof of its full logical negation.

Explicitly, the negative answer must prove
\[
\forall M\ \forall C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall d\in\mathbb N_{0}\
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^{*}
\]
such that, writing \(t=C(|x|+1)^{d}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\bigl(\neg H_{M}(x,t,0)\land\neg H_{M}(x,t,1)\bigr)\\
&\quad\lor\
\left[
x\in\mathcal P\ \land\
\left(
\bigl(H_{M}(x,t,1)\land\neg S(x)\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(H_{M}(x,t,0)\land S(x)\bigr)
\right)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every candidate machine and polynomial clock must fail either the total time bound or correctness on a promised input. The witness input may depend on the candidate and clock. A lower bound for one algorithm, a conditional complexity implication, NP or coNP membership, or a proof of decidability alone does not decide this unconditional target.
cards.why: Recognizing the simplest closed three-dimensional manifold is a basic test of whether global topological structure can be determined efficiently from local combinatorial data. A polynomial-time algorithm would also give polynomial-time unknot recognition for diagram input, while separating decidability and short certificates from efficient decision in a central example of computational topology.

cards.title: Linear-size universal point sets for planar graphs
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some set \(U_n\subset\mathbb R^2\) of at most \(Cn\) distinct points supports a crossing-free straight-line drawing of every simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices?
cards.definitions: The point set \(U_n\) is chosen as a function of \(n\) before the graph is supplied. For each finite simple undirected planar graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), there must be an injective map \(\phi:V(G)\to U_n\). Every edge is drawn as the closed line segment between its endpoint images. Two edge segments may intersect only at the image of a shared endpoint, and the relative interior of an edge may contain no vertex image. Unused points in \(U_n\) are allowed. The injection may depend on \(G\); the same prescribed correspondence of labels to points is not required. The graph need not have a prescribed planar embedding. Coordinates are arbitrary reals, and no grid-size, computability or runtime constraint is imposed. A planar graph means one admitting a plane embedding by arcs with these same incidence and nonintersection requirements.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that a constant \(C>0\) and sets \(U_n\) with the stated universal drawing property exist for every \(n\), or prove the logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some \(n\) has the property that every point set of size at most \(Cn\) fails to support at least one simple planar graph on \(n\) vertices. The point set precedes the graph in the quantifiers, and each successful drawing may choose its own vertex assignment.
cards.why: This asks whether a linear geometric host can represent all planar combinatorial structures of a given size, rather than dedicating a separate layout to each graph.

cards.context:
A universal point set is chosen before the graph is known. Once a graph arrives, its vertices may be assigned to any suitable distinct points of that same set. The question is whether a constant number of available points per graph vertex always suffices for every planar graph of that size.

Location matters even for four vertices. The complete graph on four vertices is planar, but putting all four vertices on the corners of a convex quadrilateral forces its two diagonals to cross. A planar straight-line drawing can instead place one vertex inside the triangle formed by the other three. Thus a large collection of points in convex position is not by itself universal for planar graphs.

Classical straight-line grid-drawing theorems give a universal \(O(n)\)-by-\(O(n)\) grid and therefore \(O(n^2)\) available points. Lower bounds exceeding \(n\) show that using exactly one point per vertex is too restrictive in general, but a constant-factor lower bound does not refute the existence of some larger universal linear constant.

The 2023 work gives linear-size sets for restricted classes of planar graphs. A host set for a class with additional structural constraints need not support all planar graphs. This is why the quantified graph family, as well as the number of points, is part of the target.

A preprint posted on 10 September 2026 claims universal sets of size \(n^{1+o(1)}\) for unrestricted planar graphs. This improves the stated general upper frontier if its proof is correct, but it does not assert \(Cn\) for a fixed constant. For example, \(n\log n\) also has the form \(n^{1+o(1)}\) while its ratio to \(n\) is unbounded. The preprint’s claim is recorded without an independent proof audit.

The input graph has no prescribed embedding or fixed correspondence between vertex labels and host points. Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers. Allowing a bend in each edge, prescribing the vertex-to-point assignment, or requiring a small integer grid would change the existence question.
