cards.title: Flip graph connectivity in three dimensions
cards.formal:
For every finite point set \(P\subset\mathbb R^3\) with \(|P|\ge4\) and no four points coplanar, is the graph of all geometric tetrahedralizations of \(P\) connected under \(2\leftrightarrow3\) bistellar flips?

A tetrahedralization must use exactly the vertices \(P\), consist of straight, nondegenerate tetrahedra meeting along common faces, and cover \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). A legal flip replaces two tetrahedra filling a convex triangular bipyramid by the three tetrahedra with the same five vertices and the same union, or performs the reverse replacement. Every intermediate tetrahedralization must retain all points of \(P\) as vertices.

Equivalently, for every such \(P\) and every pair \(T,T'\) of its tetrahedralizations, must there exist a finite sequence \(T=T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m=T'\) in which each consecutive pair differs by one legal flip?
cards.definitions:
The set \(P\) is finite and consists of distinct points with arbitrary real coordinates in ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space. General position here means that every four distinct points are affinely independent, equivalently that no four lie in a common plane. Together with \(|P|\ge4\), this ensures a three-dimensional convex hull and nonzero volume for every tetrahedron with four vertices in \(P\). Points may lie in the interior of \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\); they are not assumed to be in convex position. No additional condition on cospherical points is imposed.

For a finite set of points \(A\), its convex hull \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is the set of all convex combinations of points of \(A\), with \(\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing\). A geometric tetrahedron with vertex set \(A\subset P\), \(|A|=4\), is the closed set \(\operatorname{conv}(A)\). Its faces are the convex hulls of subsets of its vertices, including vertices, edges, triangles, the tetrahedron itself and the empty face.

A tetrahedralization is a collection \(T\) of four-element subsets of \(P\) satisfying all of the following conditions. Every point of \(P\) belongs to some member of \(T\). The union of the corresponding closed tetrahedra is \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\). For every \(A,B\in T\),
\[\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\operatorname{conv}(B)=\operatorname{conv}(A\cap B).\]
Thus different tetrahedra have disjoint interiors and any intersection is their common face; overlaps, crossing faces and hanging vertices inside another tetrahedron are excluded. All faces of the tetrahedra are understood to belong to the resulting simplicial complex. This is a full geometric triangulation, not merely an abstract complex homeomorphic to a ball. No extra vertices, curved faces or gaps in the convex hull are allowed.

The local replacement can be specified by five distinct points \(a,b,c,d,e\in P\). They must all be vertices of their convex hull, and that hull must be the convex triangular bipyramid formed by the two tetrahedra \(\{a,b,c,d\}\) and \(\{a,b,c,e\}\) sharing triangle \(abc\). In particular, \(d\) and \(e\) are on opposite sides of the plane of \(a,b,c\). Write
\[U_2=\bigl\{\{a,b,c,d\},\{a,b,c,e\}\bigr\},\qquad U_3=\bigl\{\{a,b,d,e\},\{b,c,d,e\},\{c,a,d,e\}\bigr\}.\]
These are the two tetrahedralizations of this bipyramid: \(U_2\) uses the interior triangle \(abc\), while \(U_3\) uses the interior edge \(de\). A \(2\)-to-\(3\) flip is allowed when \(U_2\subseteq T\) and
\[T'=(T\setminus U_2)\cup U_3\]
is a tetrahedralization of the same \(P\), with the replaced tetrahedra and the new tetrahedra having exactly the same geometric union. A \(3\)-to-\(2\) flip is the inverse operation under the same conditions. Requiring both configurations to be valid tetrahedralizations makes the local move compatible with all tetrahedra outside the replaced region.

The flip graph \(\mathcal F(P)\) is the finite undirected graph whose vertices are these tetrahedralizations and whose edges join pairs related by one such flip. Reversing a legal move is legal. Connectivity means that every pair of graph vertices can be joined by a finite path. The path may have length zero when the two tetrahedralizations coincide. No polynomial bound, sharp diameter, monotonicity condition or prescribed target triangulation is part of the proposition.

Only \(2\)-to-\(3\) and \(3\)-to-\(2\) moves are permitted. A \(1\)-to-\(4\) move inserts an interior vertex into a tetrahedron, and a \(4\)-to-\(1\) move removes a vertex; neither is allowed, even if the point is restored later. Points cannot be moved or perturbed along a path. Allowing such operations changes the graph under study.

The quantifier order is \(\forall P\;\forall T,T'\;\exists m\ge0\;\exists(T_i)_{i=0}^m\). All tetrahedralizations and all intermediate coordinates refer to the same fixed geometric point set. A negative answer consists of a set meeting the general-position hypothesis and two valid tetrahedralizations in different components, with a proof that no finite legal path joins them. Merely showing that one particular greedy rule gets stuck, or displaying an abstract nonrealizable tetrahedral complex, is insufficient.

Regular tetrahedralizations are a special class mentioned in the known results. A tetrahedralization \(T\) is regular if there is a height assignment \(w:P\to\mathbb R\) such that, for each \(A\in T\), an affine function \(\ell_A:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R\) equals \(w\) on the four points of \(A\) and is strictly below \(w\) at every point of \(P\setminus A\). These are the tetrahedralizations obtained by projecting the simplicial lower hull of the lifted points. The target includes nonregular tetrahedralizations as well. It is an exact geometric existence question; there is no coordinate encoding, running-time or approximation tolerance to optimize.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of connectivity for every finite point set in the stated general position. A positive proof must establish a finite legal \(2\leftrightarrow3\) path between every pair of full geometric tetrahedralizations, with all intermediate complexes using the same point coordinates and vertex set. No efficient path-finding algorithm or polynomial path length is required. A negative proof must establish the general position and geometric validity of a counterexample and prove that two tetrahedralizations lie in different components of its full flip graph. A result only for regular triangulations, higher-dimensional point sets, abstract complexes, or paths that remove or add vertices does not settle the target. Numerical experiments and approximate coordinate pictures alone are insufficient.
cards.why: This is a basic reachability question for three-dimensional meshes: can local bistellar moves explore every tetrahedralization without changing the underlying points? A resolution would identify a fundamental difference, or an essential commonality, between planar triangulation algorithms and their three-dimensional counterparts.

references.title: Connectivity of Triangulation Flip Graphs in the Plane
references.locator: Discrete & Computational Geometry 68, 1227–1284; full published text, abstract and §1 introduction distinguish full/partial triangulations and explicitly retain the open connectivity questions in dimensions three and four. Full text: https://research-explorer.ista.ac.at/download/12129/12345

cards.context:
A tetrahedral mesh can be changed locally while leaving its boundary and vertex coordinates fixed. Connectivity asks whether these basic local changes can in principle reach every mesh of the same point set, or whether the space of meshes splits into inaccessible regions.

For planar point sets, diagonal flips connect all triangulations. This is an important structural basis for local triangulation algorithms. The analogous conclusion in three dimensions does not follow just from the existence of tetrahedralizations or from the planar argument.

For regular triangulations with a fixed vertex set, Pournin and Liebling prove connectivity by paths that preserve faces common to the two endpoints. TOPP explicitly notes that in the three-dimensional general-position setting this uses the required two-to-three and three-to-two moves. The unrestricted question is whether nonregular tetrahedralizations can also be connected within the full graph.

There are disconnected triangulation spaces in higher dimensions, and TOPP records nonrealizable abstract tetrahedral complexes with no allowed flips. These show why dimensional and geometric-realizability hypotheses matter, but neither gives a counterexample for the three-dimensional point sets in this question.

Wagner and Welzl’s 2022 paper proves stronger connectivity results in the plane and explicitly says in its introduction that connectivity remains open in dimensions three and four. It also carefully distinguishes full triangulations, which retain all points, from partial triangulations that may omit interior points.

A positive answer would establish reachability by the permitted local moves, rather than a running-time guarantee for a mesh optimization heuristic. Even a connected graph can have long routes, and connectivity does not ensure that an objective improves on every move.

context_blocks.text: A tetrahedral mesh can be changed locally while leaving its boundary and vertex coordinates fixed. Connectivity asks whether these basic local changes can in principle reach every mesh of the same point set, or whether the space of meshes splits into inaccessible regions.

For planar point sets, diagonal flips connect all triangulations. This is an important structural basis for local triangulation algorithms. The analogous conclusion in three dimensions does not follow just from the existence of tetrahedralizations or from the planar argument.

For regular triangulations with a fixed vertex set, Pournin and Liebling prove connectivity by paths that preserve faces common to the two endpoints. TOPP explicitly notes that in the three-dimensional general-position setting this uses the required two-to-three and three-to-two moves. The unrestricted question is whether nonregular tetrahedralizations can also be connected within the full graph.

There are disconnected triangulation spaces in higher dimensions, and TOPP records nonrealizable abstract tetrahedral complexes with no allowed flips. These show why dimensional and geometric-realizability hypotheses matter, but neither gives a counterexample for the three-dimensional point sets in this question.

Wagner and Welzl’s 2022 paper proves stronger connectivity results in the plane and explicitly says in its introduction that connectivity remains open in dimensions three and four. It also carefully distinguishes full triangulations, which retain all points, from partial triangulations that may omit interior points.

A positive answer would establish reachability by the permitted local moves, rather than a running-time guarantee for a mesh optimization heuristic. Even a connected graph can have long routes, and connectivity does not ensure that an objective improves on every move.

cards.title: Optimal input-sparsity subspace embeddings
cards.formal: Is the optimal-dimension sparse oblivious subspace-embedding conjecture true? Precisely, does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that for every pair of integers \(n\ge d\ge1\) and every \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\), there are an integer \(m\) and a probability distribution \(\mathcal D\) over real \(m\times n\) matrices with \[1\le m\le\left\lceil C\,\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}\right\rceil,\qquad s=\left\lceil C\,\frac{\log(d/\delta)}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil,\] such that every matrix in the support has at most \(s\) nonzero entries per column and, for every \(d\)-dimensional linear subspace \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\Pr_{\Pi\sim\mathcal D}\bigl[\ \forall x\in W:\ (1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\le\|\Pi x\|_2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\ \bigr]\ge1-\delta?\] The row and column-sparsity bounds must hold simultaneously, with no additional growing factors.
cards.definitions: The ambient dimension is \(n\), the subspace dimension is \(d\), and the reduced dimension is \(m\). All logarithms are natural logarithms; changing the base changes only the universal constant. For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2)^{1/2}\). A linear subspace \(W\) is closed under real linear combinations and has a basis of exactly \(d\) linearly independent vectors. Its embedding is the linear map \(x\mapsto\Pi x\). The distribution is a Borel probability measure on the finite-dimensional real matrix space and is supported on matrices satisfying the per-column sparsity bound. Different matrix entries need not be independent; neither a particular sparsity pattern nor a particular distribution of nonzero values is prescribed. The same \(\mathcal D\), chosen from \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\) alone, must satisfy the probability guarantee for every fixed \(W\). It cannot depend on a basis or other information about \(W\). The order of quantifiers is \(\forall(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists(m,\mathcal D)\ \forall W\); this does not require one sampled matrix to succeed simultaneously for all subspaces. Inside the success event, however, the inequalities must hold simultaneously for every vector of the chosen subspace, rather than separately with fresh randomness for each vector. The failure probability is \(\delta\) for the entire subspace. The statement is distributional existence, with one universal dimension/sparsity constant, and does not require a finite-bit sampling algorithm or bit-complexity bound for arbitrary real entries. This is the explicit dimension-and-sparsity conjecture underlying the source’s input-sparsity application-time discussion. The accuracy and confidence regime \(0<\varepsilon,\delta\le1/3\) is fixed explicitly; neither parameter is assumed to be inverse polynomial in \(d\). There is no restriction relating \(n\) to the desired row bound, and \(m\) is permitted to exceed \(n\) when the parameter bound does. For an \(n\times d\) input matrix \(A\), \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) denotes the number of its nonzero entries. Column sparsity controls the number of scalar contributions needed to form \(\Pi A\); this motivates the running-time terminology but is not an extra end-to-end bit-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must give the simultaneous row and column-sparsity bounds for all stated parameter values and a distribution independent of the target subspace. Constants may not depend on \(n,d,\varepsilon,\delta\). Bounds with extra logarithmic or sub-polylogarithmic factors, only inverse-polynomial failure probabilities, or only inverse-polynomial accuracy do not establish this exact target. A construction chosen after examining the subspace, a guarantee for a finite list of vectors, or a failure example for a single proposed distribution does not settle the general conjecture.
cards.why: Subspace embeddings compress a matrix’s column space while preserving the lengths of all its linear combinations. Small output dimension reduces later computation, and sparse embedding columns reduce the arithmetic needed to apply the map to sparse data. The conjecture asks whether these two advantages can be attained together at the stated dependence on accuracy and failure probability.

cards.title: Klee’s measure running-time exponent
cards.formal: For each fixed integer \(d\ge3\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the optimal deterministic running-time exponent \[x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\text{some uniform exact algorithm has worst-case time }O_d(n^a)\}.\] The task is to compute the exact \(d\)-dimensional volume of the union of \(n\) explicitly given axis-aligned boxes in the real-RAM model below. Programs and constants may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on the coordinates or input size. Logarithmic factors in running time are not part of the numerical answer.
cards.definitions: An input is a list of \(n\ge 0\) closed boxes \(B_i=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_{ij},b_{ij}]\), specified by their 2dn finite real endpoints, with \(a_{ij}\le b_{ij}\). Overlaps, coincident endpoints, duplicate boxes and zero side lengths are allowed. The output is the exact Lebesgue measure of \(\bigcup_i B_i\), returned as a real number; the empty union has volume zero. For clarity, the real-RAM convention here is deterministic computation with exact real registers, unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, comparisons and branching. Random access is through integer addresses. Control and address registers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, with any fixed constant factor depending on the algorithm and d; standard arithmetic, comparison, Boolean and shift operations on these words cost one unit. Integers can be converted to real registers, but real values can affect integer control only through comparisons: no floor, bit extraction or arbitrary real-to-integer conversion is available. A program is finite and independent of n and the coordinates; any hard-coded real constants must be algebraic and finitely specified. Input reads, output writes, preprocessing, memory operations and control steps count. Worst-case time is the maximum over all endpoint lists of size n, regardless of coordinate magnitude. No randomness, approximation tolerance, oracle or precomputed advice depending on n is supplied. For a correct uniform deterministic program \(A\) in fixed dimension \(d\), let \(t_{A,d}(n)\) be its worst-case time on \(n\) boxes. Define \[x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists A\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ t_{A,d}(n)\le Cn^a\}.\] A different uniform program may be selected for each fixed dimension and each exponent bound, but not for each input length. Elementary input access and the cited algorithm give \(1\le x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)\le d/2\). The infimum need not be attained; in particular a value does not prescribe matching logarithmic factors. A lower bound must concern every permitted exact program, without an unproved complexity assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all integers \(d\ge3\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(d)-x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(d)\le x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)\le U(d)\) and \(U(d)-L(d)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). Use the specified exact real-RAM model at each fixed dimension. Lower bounds must cover all permitted uniform exact algorithms for that dimension.

references.title: Near-Optimal Dynamic Data Structures for Maximum Depth and Klee’s Measure of Boxes
references.authors: Sujoy Bhore; Subhash Suri; Jie Xue; Xiongxin Yang; Jiumu Zhu
references.locator: ICALP 2026, article 34. Full abstract and Introduction including Theorems 1–2 read, plus §7. Maintains exact volume dynamically with amortized update guarantees; recalls the O(n^(d/2)) static bound and states conditional, rather than unconditional, optimality claims.

cards.context:
Two boxes may cover the same region, so adding their individual volumes overcounts their intersection. In three dimensions, \([0,2]^{3}\) and \([1,3]\times [0,2]^{2}\) each have volume 8, but their union has volume 12. The task requests this single total volume; it does not request a full description of the union boundary. In higher dimensions a box is simply a product of intervals.

Chan’s 2013 algorithm computes exact union volume in \(O(n^{d/2})\) time for every fixed \(d\ge3\). This gives the finite upper bound \(x_{\mathrm{Klee}}(d)\le d/2\). Connections with clique problems provide conditional evidence, not an unconditional lower bound for all algorithms.

The real-RAM question counts an arithmetic operation on a coordinate as one step even when the coordinate would require many bits to encode. Chan also obtains logarithmic improvements for integer coordinates in a word-RAM setting. Those improvements do not automatically transfer to unrestricted real inputs, and the source explicitly discusses this distinction. The detailed primitive and worst-case conventions above make the inherited real-RAM target explicit.

The SoCG 2025 work speeds up approximation of union volume and proves a lower bound for algorithms restricted to certain object queries. A small relative error is permitted there. The ICALP 2026 work maintains exact volume under insertions and deletions and measures amortized update time. Both are significant results, but neither determines the unconditional optimal time of a single exact static computation in this card’s model.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic exact Euclidean bipartite matching
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform algorithm and absolute constants \(\delta,C>0\) that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every pair of labelled planar point lists \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)\), \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\), returns a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\) minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^n\|r_i-b_{\pi(i)}\|_2\), using at most \(Cn^{2-\delta}\) operations in the real-arithmetic model below, with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input? Deterministic algorithms qualify. Coordinates are arbitrary real numbers and there is no separation, spread or grid promise.
cards.definitions:
The input consists of the two explicit lists of coordinate pairs in \(\mathbb R^2\); coincident points remain distinct labelled objects. A feasible matching pairs each red label with exactly one blue label and conversely. Its edge length is \(\|(x,y)-(u,v)\|_2=\sqrt{(x-u)^2+(y-v)^2}\). The output is the list of matched labels, and any minimizer is acceptable when several matchings tie. Squared Euclidean lengths define a different objective.

The editorial computational convention is a uniform real RAM with exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, comparison and nonnegative square root, each costing one operation. Reading or writing one register, branching, and drawing a fair random bit also cost one. Integer registers are used for addressing and ordinary control; no operation extracts an arbitrarily long binary expansion of a real in one step. Input reals are accessed as atomic coordinates, so this is an arithmetic-operation question rather than a finite-bit encoding theorem. The program is finite and independent of the input size.

The stated operation bound is worst-case over inputs and random choices; success probability refers only to the algorithm's coins on each fixed input. A successful output must attain the exact minimum, not merely an approximation to its cost. This bounded-error convention explicitly resolves the imported draft's unspecified randomization convention. The exponent improvement and constant must be independent of all coordinates, including the ratio between largest and smallest nonzero distances. An estimate containing an uncontrolled coordinate-dependent factor does not meet the bound. No preprocessing of a supplied table of all red-blue distances is free: the given input has only \(4n\) real coordinates.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the displayed operation and success guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation in this specified model. A positive answer includes exact optimality on the successful event and one fixed exponent improvement for every input. A negative answer must exclude every such algorithm and every positive fixed improvement, rather than exhibit a bad case for a particular method. Approximate matching, a guarantee only for random point sets, or a grid-dependent time bound does not establish the proposition.
cards.why: The question tests whether exact geometric bipartite optimization can break the quadratic barrier.

cards.title: Polygon visibility graph recognition
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and a cyclic order \(C=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of its vertices, decides whether some simple polygon with these labelled vertices in boundary order \(C\) has visibility graph exactly \(G\)? Here \(n\geq3\), the graph is given by its complete adjacency matrix and the cyclic order by an explicit list. Both visible and nonvisible pairs must be realized, and the polygon has no holes or additional vertices.
cards.definitions: A realization assigns distinct points \(p_i\in\mathbb R^2\) to the labels. The union of the segments \([p_{v_i},p_{v_{i+1}}]\), with indices cyclic modulo \(n\), must be a simple closed polygonal curve: consecutive segments meet only at their common endpoint and nonconsecutive segments are disjoint. Let \(P\) be this curve together with its bounded complementary component. Vertices \(i\ne j\) are visible exactly when the entire closed segment \([p_i,p_j]\) is contained in \(P\). Visibility along the boundary is allowed, including through other labelled collinear vertices; redundant collinear boundary vertices are permitted as long as the curve remains simple. This closed-region convention is explicit and no general-position promise is imposed. The graph must contain every edge of the specified boundary cycle, otherwise the answer is no. Malformed matrices, a nonsymmetric matrix, loops, a nonpermutation order or \(n<3\) are rejected. The input is a binary encoding of the full matrix and list, of length \(N\); one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine must decide correctly in at most \(K(N+1)^a\) steps for fixed \(K,a\). Real coordinates are existential mathematical witnesses, with no rationality, grid-size or bit-length restriction. The requested algorithm returns a Boolean answer and need not produce coordinates.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of realizable graph/order pairs belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\), or that it does not, for the exact polygon and visibility conventions above. A positive answer must establish correctness and a polynomial worst-case bit-time bound for one uniform decision algorithm on every encoding. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm; an NP-hardness or \(\exists\mathbb R\)-hardness result alone does not prove nonmembership in \(\mathrm{P}\) without the corresponding separation. A necessary graph condition, recognition of a special polygon class, or recognition with extra geometric data is insufficient.
cards.why: The problem is a central inverse question about geometric visibility: whether pairwise sight-line information and a boundary order can be tested for realizability efficiently. It connects graph recognition with geometric representation complexity.

cards.context:
The source problem supplies the boundary order as well as the graph. This removes the need to search for a Hamiltonian boundary cycle, but leaves the geometric realizability question. The statement above fixes simple closed polygons and closed-segment visibility explicitly.

Constructing the visibility graph of an already drawn polygon and recognizing a graph that could arise from some polygon are different tasks. Recognition has to account simultaneously for every edge and every absent edge without being given any coordinates.

The 2024 compendium by Schaefer, Cardinal and Miltzow explicitly retains polygon visibility recognition as open even when the boundary order is supplied. It defines visibility by containment of the complete joining segment in the polygon.

The same compendium distinguishes several related recognition problems with \(\exists\mathbb R\) hardness or completeness results, including polygons with holes and simultaneous interior/exterior visibility. Those results impose different objects or additional data and do not settle this simple-polygon problem. Here \(\exists\mathbb R\) denotes problems reducible in polynomial time to the existence of real solutions of finite systems of polynomial equalities and inequalities.

Lin and Skiena study coordinate requirements for realizing visibility graphs. The fact that a realization is a finite list of real points does not by itself make it a polynomial-length certificate in the Turing model.

A polynomial algorithm would identify when a purely combinatorial collection of sight lines can come from one polygonal environment. The fixed boundary order is part of the scientific question; discarding it or requiring a convex polygon would change the class being recognized.

cards.title: Near-quadratic Voronoi complexity of lines in three dimensions
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that every regular Euclidean Voronoi diagram of \(n\ge2\) distinct affine lines in \(\mathbb R^3\), under the exact stratum convention below, has total complexity at most \(C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}\)?
cards.definitions: A line is the set \(\ell_i=\{p_i+tv_i:t\in\mathbb R\}\), where \(p_i,v_i\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(v_i\ne0\). Distances are ordinary Euclidean point-to-line distances. For every nonempty \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(V_I\) to be the set of points whose set of nearest lines is exactly \(\{\ell_i:i\in I\}\). Regular means that \(V_I\) is empty for \(|I|>4\), and for \(1\le|I|\le4\) each nonempty \(V_I\) is a smooth embedded manifold of dimension \(4-|I|\). The cells counted are the connected components of every nonempty \(V_I\), including unbounded components and zero-dimensional components. Let \(b_0(V_I)\) be the number of such components, with \(b_0(\varnothing)=0\); total complexity is \(\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq[n]}b_0(V_I)\). These semialgebraic sets have finitely many connected components. The statement is an extremal mathematical bound; no bit encoding or construction algorithm for real coordinates is required. The constants depend only on \(\varepsilon\), not on the lines or their coordinates.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated bound for every \(\varepsilon>0\) on all diagrams in the defined regular class, or prove its logical negation in Lean: some \(\varepsilon_0>0\) has unbounded total complexity divided by \(n^{2+\varepsilon_0}\) over that class. The count must include connected components in all four dimensions, including unbounded ones. A bound only for four sites, one ruled-surface family, vertices alone, or a different metric does not establish the full statement.
cards.why: This is a central unresolved complexity gap for a fundamental three-dimensional proximity structure, closely connected to lower-envelope and arrangement bounds.

cards.context:
At each point of space, the nearest-line set describes which sites compete to be closest. Regions with one nearest line, interfaces with two, curves with three, and isolated points with four form the strata counted here. A stratum can have several connected components, and unbounded components count as well. Counting just the input lines would omit this geometric arrangement.

The question concerns Euclidean distance to complete affine lines in three dimensions. The source records a quadratic lower bound and an upper bound of \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), leaving a full exponent gap. A nearest-point diagram, a planar diagram, or a polyhedral distance function is a different object.

The conjectured guarantee is \(n^{2+\varepsilon}\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), with a constant allowed to depend on that exponent slack. It does not require a single \(Cn^2\) bound. Conversely, a bound with one fixed exponent strictly above two does not meet the universal quantifier over \(\varepsilon\).

The source also distinguishes the full diagram from a fixed-distance level set, describable through a union of cylinders. Complexity controlled at one distance does not automatically count all strata of the nearest-site partition throughout space.

The March 2026 four-line classification describes a base case with zero through eight Voronoi vertices under general-position assumptions. The result clarifies local configurations, but fixes the number of sites and supplies no asymptotic bound for arbitrary input size.

The August 2026 regulus preprint claims quadratic total complexity when all lines lie in one ruling of a smooth doubly ruled quadric: one of the two line families covering that surface. Its hypotheses strongly restrict the line configuration. It explicitly retains the broader quadratic-to-cubic gap for arbitrary Euclidean line sites. The present card spells out its own regular-stratum convention rather than leaving “general position” undefined.

cards.title: Fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss transforms for sparse vectors
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute constants \(C_1,C_2>0\), an integer \(q\ge0\), and uniform sampling and application algorithms with the following property? For every integer \(d\ge1\) and every \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), the sampling algorithm produces an input-independent representation of a random linear map \(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\), where
\[
1\le k\le\min\{d,\lceil C_1\varepsilon^{-2}\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil\}.
\]
For every fixed \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), its distribution satisfies
\[
\Pr_A\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\le\|Ax\|_2
                 \le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2\bigr]\ge1-\delta.
\]
Given a sampled representation and the list of the \(s\) nonzero coordinates of any \(x\), the application algorithm must return all coordinates of \(Ax\) in at most
\[
C_2(s+k)\bigl(\log_2(d+2)\bigr)^q
\]
operations in the arithmetic model below, for every sampled representation and input. The same constants and algorithms must work for all parameters. The matrix distribution is independent of \(x\), including its support.
cards.definitions:
The Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d x_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(s=\|x\|_0=|\{i:x_i\ne0\}|\) is input sparsity. The input is an arbitrary-order list of distinct indices in \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and their nonzero real values, together with \(d\). Coordinates absent from the list are zero. Reading this list and writing the dense length-\(k\) output count toward application time. The zero vector is included, with \(s=0\).

A sampled object represents one genuine linear map on all of \(\mathbb R^d\), not a map chosen after seeing the support or magnitudes of the input. The application algorithm must evaluate that map exactly in real arithmetic. The approximation concerns preservation of length, not numerical evaluation of the matrix product. The probability statement is for each vector fixed independently of the sampled map; it does not claim that one dimension-reducing map preserves every vector simultaneously. No promise bounds the ratio of the largest coordinate to the norm.

Use an arithmetic RAM: a real value occupies one cell, and addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and comparison each cost one operation. Memory access and operations on integer indices of logarithmic size in the allocated storage also cost one. There is no floor operation on arbitrary real values, arbitrary real-to-integer decoding, or oracle for matrix-vector multiplication. The programs are finite and uniform, with rational built-in constants; \(\varepsilon,\delta\) are real parameter inputs. This is an arithmetic-operation question, not a bound on the bit complexity of arbitrarily precise real coordinates.

The distribution and its representation may be prepared before the input vector is provided. To fix the construction convention, the sampler uses independent fair bits, has expected time and storage bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(d+\varepsilon^{-1}+\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil\), and terminates with probability one. It outputs a finite read-only representation used by the application algorithm. Setup work is independent of the input vector and is not included in per-vector application time; any subsequent work on the vector, including an input-dependent transformation or preprocessing, is included. Application time is a worst-case bound, not an amortized bound over a favorable collection of vectors. All sampler outcomes with positive probability must define an evaluable map. No logarithmic bound on the number of random bits is requested.

The output dimension \(k\) is selected from the parameters and is fixed before drawing the map. The ceiling handles integer dimensions, and the cap at \(d\) allows the identity when the usual dimension bound would exceed the ambient dimension. The phrase optimal dimension refers to the order of the displayed upper bound, not its best leading constant. The exponent \(q\) and time constant are independent of error and failure probability. In particular, an extra factor depending on \(\varepsilon^{-1}\) or \(\log(1/\delta)\) cannot be hidden in the input-sparsity term unless it is absorbed by the displayed bound.

The source has a separate question about generating the map with \(O(\log(d/\delta))\) random bits. The formulation omits that additional objective. The setup convention above makes the retained application question precise without reinstating the short-seed target.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the uniform existence assertion, including the distribution, dimension bound, pointwise probability guarantee and worst-case sparse-input application bound in the stated model. An affirmative answer must cover every parameter choice and arbitrary real input vector; a result only for constant distortion, constant failure probability, dense inputs, or special coordinate distributions is insufficient. A negative answer is the full negation and must cover every allowed construction and application algorithm, rather than one chosen sparse-matrix family. A proof about the omitted seed-length objective does not answer this card. The benchmark's numerical-value tolerance does not weaken the prescribed asymptotic guarantees.
cards.why: An affirmative answer would make optimal Euclidean dimension reduction almost as cheap as reading a sparse vector and writing its sketch. This would strengthen a general primitive used in similarity search, randomized linear algebra and high-dimensional geometry. A general obstruction would identify a computational cost that dimension bounds alone do not reveal.

cards.context:
Dimension reduction can shorten later computations on high-dimensional data while approximately preserving distances. For sparse data, even scanning every ambient coordinate may waste most of the work. This question seeks a transformation whose application cost follows the amount of input actually present and the amount of output produced.

Sparse Johnson–Lindenstrauss matrices reduce multiplication work by limiting nonzeros per column. Their standard application bound still multiplies input sparsity by a factor of order \(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\). The existence of such matrices therefore does not establish the requested additive dependence on input sparsity and output dimension.

Fast structured transforms use a different route to rapid multiplication. The inspected 2023 improvement retains an ambient-dimension term, which can dominate when the input is sparse. Lower bounds on column sparsity alone do not rule out a different structured map with a faster evaluation algorithm.

Later sparse-embedding work refines parameter regimes, while the 2026 concentration result targets sharper confidence constants. These developments concern the same geometric primitive, but neither inspected statement supplies the full application-time bound selected here.

cards.title: Exact planar Euclidean maximum TSP
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic algorithm that finds an exactly longest Euclidean tour through any finite set of rational points in the plane in time polynomial in the full binary input length?

For an explicitly listed set \(P=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of distinct points in \(\mathbb Q^2\), with \(n\ge3\), define the length of a cyclic ordering \(\pi\) by
\[\ell_P(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sqrt{(x_{\pi(i)}-x_{\pi(i+1)})^2+(y_{\pi(i)}-y_{\pi(i+1)})^2},\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\]
Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(a\ge0\) such that, on every valid input of bit length \(B\), the machine returns a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying
\[\ell_P(\pi)=\max_{\sigma\in S_n}\ell_P(\sigma)\]
within \(C(B+1)^a\) bit operations?
cards.definitions:
The input is a finite list of coordinates \(p_i=(x_i,y_i)\). Each coordinate is a signed binary integer numerator divided by a positive binary integer denominator. Use a fixed self-delimiting encoding of these integers and the list. The bit length \(B\) counts all numerators, denominators and delimiters, as well as the number of points. The coordinates may have arbitrarily many bits. There is no bound on their magnitude, denominators, aspect ratio or minimum separation beyond what the finite input specifies. Equivalent ordinary binary encodings change polynomial time only by polynomial factors.

The points are pairwise distinct. Collinear triples, an entirely collinear set and other degeneracies are allowed. No general-position or convex-position promise is imposed. The algorithm must work for all \(n\ge3\). A machine may reject malformed encodings, repeated points or lists shorter than three; this validation must also take polynomial time. These validity conventions do not permit rejecting any valid instance because its coordinates are numerically difficult.

The symbol \(S_n\) denotes the set of all permutations of the point indices. A tour visits every input point exactly once in that order and then returns to its starting point. Its edges are the straight segments between consecutive points, and its total length is the sum of their ordinary Euclidean lengths. Every pair of points is an available connection. There is no separate graph of allowed edges, and there are no obstacles.

The word “planar” restricts the locations of the points to two-dimensional Euclidean space. It imposes no noncrossing requirement on the tour. Segments may intersect, overlap on collinear inputs or pass through other points; the visits in the tour are specified by its permutation. Cyclic rotations and reversals represent the same undirected cycle, but the output may be any representing permutation. If several tours attain the maximum, any one is acceptable.

The output is the explicit list of \(n\) indices in a maximizing order. It need not include the optimum length, an approximation to that length, a square-root expression or a certificate independently checking optimality. Its size is polynomial in \(B\). Exactness refers to maximizing the real-valued sum in the statement, even though the output itself is a finite combinatorial object.

Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite alphabet and finite program. The constants \(C,a\) are fixed for the entire algorithm, independent of the input length, coordinates and arrangement. All arithmetic, storage, comparisons and output operations are charged by their bit cost. An operation involving arbitrarily large integers or algebraic numbers is not a unit-time primitive. The machine has no exact-real arithmetic oracle and no oracle comparing sums of square roots. Randomized algorithms, advice depending on input length and machines whose polynomial exponent depends on the input do not satisfy this definition.

Each squared edge length is rational, but its square root can be irrational. Distinct tours can also have equal total lengths. A proposed algorithm must justify any precision or exact arithmetic it uses within its polynomial bit bound. A polynomial bound on the number of real-arithmetic operations alone does not provide that justification. Conversely, returning an optimal permutation is not defined to include solving every separate comparison problem for arbitrary sums of square roots.

The objective is the sum of all edge lengths. It differs from minimum-length TSP, from finding a longest spanning path without the closing edge, and from maximum scatter TSP, which maximizes the shortest edge in the tour. Replacing Euclidean distance by squared Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance or a polygonal norm also changes the optimization problem.

A polynomial-time approximation scheme supplies, for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a tour of length at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(P)\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(P)=\max_{\sigma\in S_n}\ell_P(\sigma)\). Its polynomial exponent or constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This does not give exact optimization by simply choosing an unspecified tiny error: the separation between unequal tour lengths and the resulting computation cost would both need proof.

The original source asks broadly for the complexity of finding a maximum tour and mentions a conjecture of NP-hardness. This card selects, the specific existence question for a polynomial bit-time exact-tour algorithm on rational planar inputs. NP-hardness means that a polynomial-time reduction would make this optimization task at least as hard as every problem in NP, with the reduction and output access specified. Such a theorem can establish a conditional obstruction under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\); NP-hardness alone does not prove the unconditional nonexistence quantified here.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the uniform deterministic algorithm in the statement, including correctness on every valid input, handling of exact ties and a polynomial bound in the full bit length. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A negative answer must quantify over every deterministic machine and every fixed polynomial bound. An approximation scheme, a real-arithmetic algorithm without a bit-cost analysis, a result only for a restricted point configuration or a three-dimensional hardness theorem does not settle this target. A planar NP-hardness reduction is substantial progress but gives an unconditional negative answer only together with a proved premise sufficient to rule out the algorithm. There is no additive or multiplicative tolerance: the returned permutation must attain the exact maximum.
cards.why: This is a sharply focused boundary in geometric optimization: nearby versions are tractable under polygonal norms or hard in higher Euclidean dimension, while accurate approximation is available. Settling exact planar optimization would clarify how the geometry of a distance function and the arithmetic of exact lengths affect efficient computation.

cards.context:
Maximizing a tour rewards long connections while requiring all selected edges to form one cycle. Geometry can make some versions unusually structured, but that structure depends on the distance function. This problem asks whether ordinary straight-line distance in two dimensions still permits an exact efficient optimization algorithm.

A longest tour is allowed to cross itself. Restricting the output to a simple polygon would discard valid candidates and could change the optimum. The 2025 work on noncrossing longest structures constructs particular point sets and studies their extremal geometry; it does not give a general optimization algorithm.

Polynomial-time approximation schemes were established for fixed-dimensional normed spaces, including Euclidean distance. They provide arbitrarily good fixed relative accuracy. The exact question retains the need to distinguish tours whose lengths may be extremely close.

Barvinok and coauthors prove polynomial-time exact solvability for fixed polyhedral norms and Euclidean NP-hardness in dimensions at least three. Their rational-input discussion accounts for bit costs in the polyhedral case. Neither result transfers directly to the Euclidean plane.

The arithmetic issue is separate from the number of candidate permutations. Even checking whether a specified tour exceeds a rational length threshold involves a sum of square roots. The present output is a permutation, so the card makes no unsupported equivalence between finding that permutation and every possible square-root comparison problem.

The comparison matters beyond this one tour objective: it isolates how changing only a norm or a dimension can alter the known complexity of an optimization problem. A positive answer would expose algorithmic structure special to the plane; a negative answer would delimit that structure despite the availability of close approximations.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal. This preserves the card’s previously selected linear-size, counted-side-information formulation.
cards.definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must provide a single universal constant and, for each class, a valid compressor and reconstructor with the counted size bound holding on every realizable sample. A negative answer must show that for every integer \(C\ge1\), some class of positive finite VC dimension admits no such scheme of size at most \(Cd\). A lower bound against only proper, stable, efficient, or otherwise restricted reconstruction does not refute this unrestricted target. Neither does failure of a particular embedding construction. Free side information or free ordering of retained points is outside the model. The requirement is exact consistency and linear size with a universal constant; it asks for no additive numerical approximation.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

cards.context:
The compressed object lets a fixed decoder reproduce every label in the original training sample. It need not identify the unknown target on points that were never observed. The same decoder must work at every sample size, so a bound depending only on the class’s VC dimension would be independent of how much training data was supplied.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A domain point may require arbitrarily many bits to describe, but sample compression charges one unit for retaining its labeled record. Conversely, an unbounded uncharged message would evade the intended resource bound. Both the retained kernel and the side information are therefore limited explicitly, and the kernel has no free ordering.

Moran and Yehudayoff prove that every binary class of VC dimension \(d\) has a scheme of total size \(2^{O(d)}\). Their sharper theorem also depends on dual VC dimension, which exchanges the roles of domain points and hypotheses by regarding a point as its vector of labels across the class. That dual dimension can grow exponentially in \(d\), leaving the general linear-versus-exponential gap. The checked result is from the corrected v2 and subsequent journal publication.

Chase and coauthors show that some finite classes require an exponential increase in dimension to be contained in an extremal class, a structured type of class with known tight compression. This limits a previously studied embedding-based route to compression. It does not prove that the original class itself requires an exponential-size scheme.

The April 2026 graph-ball paper explicitly retains the general linear conjecture. It gives proper compression of size \(O(t\log(t+1))\) for graph-ball classes whose underlying graph has treewidth at most \(t\), and an analogous cliquewidth result. The predictors are themselves balls, but the resource parameter is graph width and the family is restricted. These structured results are not a universal linear-VC theorem.

The 2025 reduction paper transfers some binary compression bounds to multiclass, regression and robust-learning settings. The sharper transfers need additional reconstruction or stability properties. The ordinary linear conjecture appears in its introduction; its later robust-compression open problem is a different target.

A March 2026 preprint first claimed a sample-compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result. The current checked version, dated 3 August 2026, is withdrawn and identifies an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. Its stale search-result title and earlier abstract are not evidence that the conjecture has been resolved.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that exactly recovers every hidden parity vector from independent uniform examples with independent label noise of rate \(\eta\)? More explicitly, is the following assertion true? \[\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/2)\ \exists A_\eta,\ C_\eta,k_\eta\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall s\in\{0,1\}^n:\quad \Pr[A_\eta^{\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}}(1^n)=s]\ge\frac23,\] where every execution takes at most \(C_\eta(n+1)^{k_\eta}\) bit-computation steps, including all example requests and output writing, and \(\operatorname{EX}_{n,s,\eta}\) returns a fresh pair \[ (a,b),\qquad a\sim U_n,\quad e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta),\quad b=\langle a,s\rangle\oplus e.\] All vectors, errors and machine coins are independent except for the displayed dependence of each label on its input and the same fixed secret. This retains the existing every-fixed-rate, every-secret search-LPN target.
cards.definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) is the vector space \(\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The parity \(\langle a,s\rangle=(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i s_i)\bmod2\) is the XOR of exactly those input coordinates where \(s_i=1\); \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution giving each input vector probability \(2^{-n}\), and \(e\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta)\) means \(\Pr[e=1]=\eta\). The secret is arbitrary, fixed before the samples and coins are drawn, and unchanged throughout one execution. Each call returns an independent sample under that fixed secret, including a fresh error bit. The learner may decide when to request more samples based on its previous observations, but cannot choose \(a\), observe the error bit, obtain a clean label, or query a coherent quantum example.

\(A_\eta\) is one classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine using fair independent coins and the specified example oracle. It receives the dimension in unary. The fixed rational rate may be built into the machine; there is no promise that one common algorithm or common exponent works uniformly over rates approaching one half with \(n\). The machine, positive integer constant \(C_\eta\), and positive integer exponent \(k_\eta\) are chosen before \(n\) and \(s\). They may depend on \(\eta\), but have no length-dependent advice. All reading, storing, revisiting examples, computation and output bits are charged; the oracle’s internal sample generation is not charged, and one request costs at least one step. The worst-case bound holds for all possible example and coin histories, not just in expectation. Thus time, samples and stored bits are polynomially bounded, while unrestricted repeated access to stored data is allowed. No single-pass or small-memory constraint is imposed.

The output is exactly one \(n\)-bit vector \(\widehat s\); malformed output is failure. Success means \(\widehat s=s\), not merely low noisy-label error or an unspecified prediction advantage. The probability is over the entire training sample stream and learner randomness for each fixed secret, with no distributional promise on \(s\). Neither \(s\) nor the sample inputs are promised sparse. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The target is the existence of a polynomial-time search procedure, rather than the quantitative size of the best subexponential exponent or a numerical approximation requiring a precision convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or its complete logical negation. A positive result must supply a machine and polynomial resource bound separately for every fixed rational noise rate, and prove exact recovery with the stated probability for every dimension and secret. A negative result must exhibit at least one fixed rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\) for which every candidate machine and polynomial bound fail on some dimension and secret, either in the resource guarantee or in recovery probability. Hardness only for a rate depending on \(n\), a restricted statistical-query or small-memory learner, sparse inputs, quantum examples, or under an unproved computational assumption is not the unconditional negation. Recovering a hypothesis with some advantage is sufficient only together with a proved conversion meeting the exact-secret criterion and the same polynomial-resource requirements.
cards.why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.

cards.context:
Without noise, random parity examples yield a consistent system of binary linear equations. Independent label errors remove that exact algebraic consistency while leaving the hidden rule exceptionally simple. The problem is a standard boundary between efficient noiseless learning and learning with random classification noise.

For every fixed noise rate below one half, \(O_\eta(n)\) examples suffice information-theoretically for exact recovery with constant confidence, although an unrestricted decoder may use exponential computation. The true secret agrees with a fresh noisy label with probability \(1-\eta\); every different parity agrees with probability \(1/2\) under uniform inputs. This statistical separation explains why a polynomial sample bound alone does not settle the computational question.

Collecting sample vectors as matrix rows gives \(b=As+e\) over \(\mathbb F_2\): the columns of the uniform matrix generate a random binary linear code, and the label string is a noisy codeword. Worst-case decoding hardness for arbitrary codes is not itself a hardness proof for this randomly generated sample distribution. The code, noise and sample-count quantifiers matter.

Blum–Kalai–Wasserman give a \(2^{O_\eta(n/\log n)}\)-time algorithm with a comparable subexponential number of examples at fixed noise. They also establish a separation between example-based noise-tolerant learning and statistical-query learning for a restricted parity class. A statistical-query lower bound therefore cannot be treated as a lower bound for every machine that observes individual examples.

Lyubashevsky gives time \(2^{O_{\eta,\gamma}(n/\log\log n)}\) using \(n^{1+\gamma}\) examples for every fixed \(\gamma>0\) in the constant-noise regime. This answers the older subexponential-time polynomial-sample question, but its time remains superpolynomial. Its sample regime must not be silently combined with the faster many-sample BKW exponent.

Garg–Kothari–Liu–Raz prove that noisy-parity learning in their streaming memory model needs either \(\Omega(n^2/(1/2-\eta))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples. Their source uses \(\varepsilon=1/2-\eta\) for the noise bias. At fixed \(\eta\), quadratic memory is permitted by this card, so this unconditional storage lower bound does not exclude the target learner.

Aggarwal–Gupta–Li’s May 2026 paper amplifies success on a small fraction of LPN instances into success on almost all instances with changed dimension and noise parameters. It concerns transformations between hardness and success regimes; it neither constructs a polynomial-time algorithm for every fixed noise rate nor proves that none exists. The parameter changes prevent its abstract from being read as fixed-instance amplification without qualifications.

The September 2026 revision by Aggarwal and coauthors gives conditional low-noise LPN hardness from simultaneous worst-case assumptions about decoding a code from random noise and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 4.1 retain this joint alternative; it is not an unconditional worst-case-hardness theorem for the stated constant-rate search problem.

The publisher abstract of a 15 September 2026 optical-computing paper reports a 512-variable experiment with at most two variables per constraint and numerical comparisons. Those structured sparse constraints and finite physical experiments do not supply the arbitrary-dimension uniform classical polynomial-time guarantee requested here. Only its publisher abstract was accessible during this check.

cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings retain the original PAC target without an input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.
cards.why: DNF learning is a central question about whether compact Boolean rules can be inferred efficiently from observations. Polynomial sample complexity is available, but achieving polynomial computation for arbitrary input distributions remains the difficulty. A positive answer would also cover important target classes such as decision trees and juntas through their DNF representations.

cards.context:
A DNF accepts a point when at least one conjunction of feature conditions holds. Learning predicts these labels from observations without receiving the rules. The unknown distribution can concentrate its probability on any subset of the Boolean cube, so uniform-input arguments do not automatically extend to this task.

The obstacle is computational rather than a shortage of samples: the finite DNF class admits sample complexity \(O((ns+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon)\). This statistical guarantee does not give a polynomial-time learner. The 2025 survey explicitly separates sample complexity from the cost of producing an evaluable hypothesis.

For each fixed term bound \(s\), a runtime \(n^{O(s)}\) is polynomial in \(n\), but the required single polynomial in both \(n\) and \(s\) is stronger. Servedio’s Theorem 8 records the general upper bound \(2^{\widetilde O(n^{1/3}\log s)}\), with accuracy and confidence dependence suppressed as specified in that survey; the tilde hides polylogarithmic factors. This remains superpolynomial for polynomially many terms.

Improper learning allows hypotheses outside the DNF class. A lower bound for outputting a small DNF can therefore leave this question open. Daniely–Shalev-Shwartz give an improper-learning hardness result under their random-K-SAT refutation assumption, including polynomially growing term bounds. That assumption is not an established unconditional lower bound.

Daniely–Vardi’s Theorem 3 rules out efficient learning of DNFs with a superconstant number of terms under their Assumption 1 on local pseudorandom generators. Their learning definition permits efficiently evaluable hypotheses outside the target class. The local-generator hypothesis is a specific average-case assumption, not merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) or an unconditional theorem.

The 2025 faster exact learner of Alman and coauthors has access to membership and equivalence queries. A membership query obtains the target value at a chosen point; an equivalence query can provide a counterexample to a proposed hypothesis. Those access guarantees differ from an independent random-example stream, even when the question still concerns small DNFs.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering result obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning in the PQ distribution-shift framework under a uniform training distribution. Its predictor may use a selector to abstain, and training labels and unlabeled test data have distinct roles. Those distribution, runtime and output guarantees do not supply the polynomial-time distribution-free predictor required here.

The January 2026 relative-error DNF result is a property tester: it distinguishes membership in the class from the specified notion of distance using function-query access. Testing whether an unknown function is a DNF is a different output task from learning an accurate predictive circuit from random examples.

Every \(k\)-junta, a Boolean function depending on at most \(k\) coordinates, has a DNF representation with at most \(2^k\) terms. Consequently, a learner meeting this target would give a learner polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\) for juntas, including under the uniform distribution. This implication does not assert that learning juntas alone suffices for general DNF learning.

cards.title: Efficient learning of well-separated Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Is there an end-to-end polynomial-time, polynomial-sample algorithm for learning the parameters of well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures at the source’s square-root-logarithmic separation scale? More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized learner \(A\) and universal constants \(C_{\rm sep},B,a\ge1\) such that the following holds for every integer \(k\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(s\ge k\), \(R\ge1\), \(t\ge3\)? For every mixture \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_i N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2 I_d),\qquad \pi_i\ge1/s,\quad \frac{\max_i\sigma_i}{\min_i\sigma_i}\le R,\] whose means satisfy \[\|\mu_i-\mu_j\|_2\ge C_{\rm sep}\max\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\sqrt{\log(sR)}\quad(i\ne j),\] the learner, given only \(d,k,s,R,t\) and independent unlabeled samples from \(P\), returns \(k\) estimated component parameters with probability at least \(2/3\) for which some permutation \(\tau\) of \([k]\) satisfies, for every \(i\), \[\frac{|\widehat\pi_{\tau(i)}-\pi_i|}{\pi_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{\|\widehat\mu_{\tau(i)}-\mu_i\|_2}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{|\widehat\sigma_{\tau(i)}-\sigma_i|}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1{t\sqrt d}.\] Require at most \(B(d+k+s+R+t)^a\) samples and total arithmetic operations, including output. The learner receives no initial estimates of the means, weights or variances. It need not attain the source’s sharper near-linear sample bound; the selected question asks for polynomial sample complexity and polynomial time simultaneously.
cards.definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.
cards.why: Identifiable clusters need not be easy to locate. This problem asks whether the separation that makes parameter recovery statistically feasible also permits an efficient global algorithm. It is a basic test of the computational cost of fitting latent-variable models when the number of components grows.
