cards.context:
Expectation maximization alternates between estimating component membership probabilities and updating parameters. The source proves strong local refinement guarantees and an information-theoretically sample-efficient initialization. The latter can be computationally expensive, which is why its final initialization discussion still asks for an end-to-end polynomial algorithm.

The source permits unknown unequal spherical variances and unequal weights. Its Theorem 9 measures mean error in units of each component’s standard deviation and asks for a smaller relative scale error as dimension grows. The completed statement preserves those parameter guarantees, rather than replacing them with a total-variation approximation or clustering-only task.

Li–Liu obtain polynomial-time learning for identity-covariance mixtures when separation is \(\Omega(\log^{1/2+c}k)\) for any fixed \(c>0\). Their parameter-estimation guarantee is a major improvement over earlier polynomial separation requirements. The theorem does not set \(c=0\), and its common known covariance differs from the full unequal-scale formulation.

Qiao and coauthors give a Fourier-based algorithm with stronger separation guarantees in the low-dimensional regime \(d=O(\log k/\log\log k)\). Their general runtime is polynomial in \(k\) multiplied by a function of dimension, separation and accuracy. This does not provide one polynomial bound over the full high-dimensional parameter range.

The 2026 sparse-Fourier method efficiently learns mixtures whose component characteristic functions decay sufficiently slowly. The main theorem explicitly excludes Gaussians. Its combined treatment of slow- and fast-decaying components retains separate separation and runtime dependencies for the latter, so it does not establish the present Gaussian threshold.

COLT 2026 gives substantial improvements for nonspherical centered mixtures and mixtures with identical unknown covariance. The centered result retains a nonpolynomial function of inverse minimum weight, and the equal-covariance result retains a weight-dependent exponent. Neither theorem supplies the fully polynomial growing-component guarantee specified here.

The 2026 sparse-Fourier method efficiently learns mixtures whose component characteristic functions decay sufficiently slowly. The main theorem explicitly excludes Gaussians. Its combined treatment of slow- and fast-decaying components retains separate separation and runtime dependencies for the latter, so it does not establish the present Gaussian threshold.

COLT 2026 gives substantial improvements for nonspherical centered mixtures and mixtures with identical unknown covariance. The centered result retains a nonpolynomial function of inverse minimum weight, and the equal-covariance result retains a weight-dependent exponent. Neither theorem supplies the fully polynomial growing-component guarantee specified here.

cards.title: One-way functions from hardness of learning P/poly
cards.formal: Does worst-case computational hardness of distribution-free PAC learning of polynomial-size Boolean circuits from random labeled examples imply the existence of one-way functions? Precisely, let \(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) be the size-parameterized uniform learning assertion below, and let \(\mathsf{OWF}\) mean the existence of an ordinary uniformly computable one-way function secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter. The target is \[\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathsf{OWF}.\] Equivalently, would the nonexistence of all such one-way functions guarantee an efficient learner for every target circuit and every example distribution? Hardness here is the failure of efficient learning in the worst case over targets and distributions; no efficiently samplable distribution of hard target descriptions, depth promise on those descriptions, or hardness reduction from SAT is assumed.
cards.definitions:
Fix ordinary acyclic one-output Boolean circuits with two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants, together with a standard effective binary encoding. For integers \(n\ge1\), \(s\ge n+1\), let \(\mathcal C(n,s)\) be all functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by such a circuit with at most \(s\) input nodes and gates in total. Polynomial-size circuit families, with no uniform construction requirement across lengths, form \(\mathrm{P/poly}\). The public bound \(s\) exposes the source’s usual polynomial-in-target-size learning convention; the hidden target description is not an input to the learner.

\(\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\) means that there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(A\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for all \(n,s\) as above, all integers \(a,b\ge3\), all \(f\in\mathcal C(n,s)\), and all probability distributions \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), the following holds. Given \(1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim D\), the machine runs for at most \(p(n+s+a+b)\) steps on every execution and outputs a deterministic ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) with \[\Pr_{A,\,\text{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le1/a\right]\ge1-1/b.\] The outer randomness consists of the training draws and independent fair machine coins; the inner draw is fresh. Example requests, reading their bits, all computation and output bits count toward the bound. The hypothesis may have size larger than \(s\), but its description and evaluation remain polynomially bounded by the learning time. It needs no further samples or access to \(f\) when evaluated. It is not required to reconstruct the target circuit, identify a unique representation, or be a member of the size-\(s\) class. This avoids imposing proper learning at the prescribed size. The learner has no membership queries, equivalence queries, nonuniform advice or code for sampling \(D\). The example source supplies independent draws even for distributions with no short sampling program. Labels are noiseless values of one fixed target. Arbitrarily large inverse-error and inverse-failure parameters \(a,b\) express ordinary PAC accuracy/confidence. Worst-case hardness is the logical negation of this uniform guarantee, not a lower bound against one particular learner or one restricted type of output.

\(\mathsf{OWF}\) means that there exist a polynomial-time computable length function \(\ell\) and one deterministic polynomial-time machine \(F\) giving maps \(F_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)}\), such that for every uniform randomized polynomial-time machine \(I\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), there is \(N_{I,k}\) for which, for all \(n\ge N_{I,k}\), \[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}\big[I(1^n,F_n(x))\in\{0,1\}^n\ \land\ F_n(I(1^n,F_n(x)))=F_n(x)\big]\le n^{-k}.\] In this display the inverter is run once and its returned string is reused in both tests. \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on \(n\)-bit strings, independent of inverter coins. Equivalently the event says that the one returned string is any length-\(n\) preimage of \(F_n(x)\), not necessarily \(x\) itself. Invalid output is failure. Evaluation of the family is uniform in \(n\), with no secret key, trapdoor or advice; \(1^n\) tells the inverter the input length. Its running time is polynomial in \(n\). The probability bound is negligible: it is eventually below every inverse power. This is the ordinary all-sufficiently-large-lengths strong one-way notion, not only security on infinitely many lengths. These uniformity and length conventions are made explicit because later learning characterizations use several different variants. No efficient transformation with a specified runtime overhead between witnesses is additionally requested; the target is the existential implication itself.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation \(\neg\mathsf{Learn}_{\mathrm{circ}}\land\neg\mathsf{OWF}\). A positive result must derive a single uniform one-way family with negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths from the stated unrestricted worst-case learning failure. It may equivalently prove a distribution-free learner from nonexistence of such families, but the learner must handle every target and distribution, not merely a samplable average or a special low-description-complexity promise. A result giving only an auxiliary-input primitive or infinitely-often security is a different conclusion unless its upgrade to the stated notion is proved. An oracle-relative separation or a limitation on a specified reduction method alone does not refute the ordinary implication. This is an existence question with exact logical quantifiers, not a numerical approximation problem.
cards.why: One-way functions provide the basic computational ingredient for much of classical private-key cryptography. The question asks whether failure of a general-purpose circuit learner is already enough to supply that ingredient, without assuming that hard target functions can be efficiently generated at random.

cards.context:
The forward evaluation of a hidden target circuit is easy when its description is known. Learning is different: from observed input-output examples the learner must build a predictor that works on future draws. The challenge is computational, since a polynomial-size description and enough noiseless examples already give a finite statistical learning problem.

One-way functions are known to yield pseudorandom functions and thereby hard circuit-learning tasks. The reverse direction in this card starts with only failure of a worst-case learner. The source contrasts that question with classical equivalences based on average-case learning hardness, where an efficient process chooses the hidden target from a distribution.

The source proves a worst-case/average-case robustness theorem for learning the stronger concept classes EXP/poly and PSPACE/poly. The corresponding decision-complexity consequences concern those stronger classes. They do not establish that every worst-case obstruction for ordinary polynomial-size circuits contains cryptographic average-case hardness.

FOCS 2023 Hirahara–Nanashima extends learning under nonexistence of one-way functions to richer agnostic and distribution-learning models. Its average-case guarantees sample the hidden advice or target distribution. Its worst-case guarantees have runtime exponential in the computational depth of the hidden description, where depth compares a time-bounded shortest description with an unbounded shortest description. That depth need not be logarithmic for arbitrary target descriptions.

ITCS 2025 Liu–Mazor–Pass Theorem 6 gives a worst-case characterization using black-box PAC learning under an explicit computational-shallowness promise on the joint sampler and predictor description. It also uses failure of infinitely-often polynomial-time learning for ordinary one-way functions. The theorem is stronger than an average-case-only analogy, but its promise and length quantifiers do not supply the unrestricted antecedent of this card.

STOC 2026 Hirahara–Nanashima studies approximation of the minimum program description needed for agnostic learning. Its Theorem 1.5 connects average-case hardness of the GapLearn decision problem to infinitely-often one-way functions, with an approximation factor governed by advice complexity of sampling. A minimum-description decision problem, average-case input choice and infinitely-often security are each distinct from this card’s exact implication.

The 2021 full source expressly retains the question. The 2025 journal version’s metadata and abstract were checked, but its subscription full text was not available. The checked 2023–2026 theorems clarify important partial connections without a matching resolution; the card therefore records uncertain current status rather than treating a bounded literature search as proof of openness.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that every Boolean \(k\)-junta on \(n\) variables can be learned from independent uniform noiseless examples in time polynomial in \(n,2^k\) and inverse error? Explicitly, for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(0\le k\le n\), \(t\ge3\), and every \(k\)-junta \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), the learner receives \(1^n,1^k,1^t\) and an independent-example oracle \(\operatorname{EX}_f\). Every execution takes at most \(B(n+2^k+t)^C\) steps and outputs an ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) for which \[\Pr_{A,\,\operatorname{EX}_f}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23.\] The exponent \(C\), constant \(B\) and machine are independent of \(n,k,t,f\). This preserves the existing full \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) target; it is not merely a separate polynomial-time statement for every fixed \(k\).
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A \(k\)-junta is a Boolean function for which there exist an unknown subset \(S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq[n]\), \(r\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean table \(g:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\quad\text{for all }x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Neither \(S\) nor \(g\) is given to the learner. No monotonicity, sparsity of the truth table or lower bound on variable influence is assumed. For \(k=0\), the class consists of the two constant functions, using the unique empty input to \(g\). The public \(k\) is only an upper bound on the number of relevant coordinates; it need not be the minimal support size.

\(U_n\) gives each binary vector probability \(2^{-n}\). Each call to \(\operatorname{EX}_f\) supplies a new pair \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim U_n\), independent of all previous draws and the learner’s fair random coins. The unknown target is fixed before the data are drawn. The learner can request further independent examples adaptively, but cannot choose their inputs, obtain membership-query labels, or request coupled or neighboring examples. Labels are exact noiseless bits. The outer probability measures confidence over the complete learning execution; the inner probability is zero-one prediction error on a fresh independent input. Reciprocals of positive integers suffice to represent arbitrary desired positive error tolerances up to polynomial rounding overhead. The fixed confidence is \(2/3\).

The output is a finite acyclic ordinary Boolean circuit on the \(n\) input bits, using two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants with a fixed effective binary encoding. It may depend on all coordinates and need not itself be a \(k\)-junta; this is improper learning. It is evaluated without the training oracle and with no stored target-dependent state other than its output description. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, receiving the displayed public integers in unary. All example reading, computation, stored-data access, fair random bits and output writing count in the worst-case bit-time bound, which also bounds the number of example requests and output length. The example generator’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Circuit evaluation is polynomial in the written circuit size under this encoding. Repeated access to stored examples and any polynomial amount of memory within the time bound are allowed. The requirement is predictive approximation; it does not require identifying the exact relevant set, giving a minimum representation or recovering every truth-table entry.

Polynomial dependence on \(2^k\) permits an exponential dependence on the number of relevant variables, since an arbitrary \(k\)-bit table already has \(2^k\) entries. It excludes a degree of \(n\) that grows with \(k\). For every fixed \(c>0\), the displayed guarantee would in particular be polynomial in \(n,t\) for all \(k\le c\log_2 n\); an algorithm that only handles each constant \(k\) with its own exponent need not satisfy it. The accuracy target is the explicitly bounded rational error \(1/t\); the problem asks for exact existence of the learner and universal exponent rather than a numerical optimal value.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof that such \(A,B,C\) exist, or prove the complete negation: for every proposed uniform machine and universal constants, some allowed \(n,k,t,f\) violates the worst-case resource bound, finite hypothesis condition or the stated PAC probability. A positive answer must handle all Boolean junta tables and all support sizes up to \(n\) with one exponent independent of \(k\). A learner using membership queries, correlated random-walk examples, a randomly perturbed marginal distribution, or only monotone targets does not meet the specified interface. A statistical-query, limited-memory or specified-neural-training lower bound does not exclude every allowed machine. Conditional cryptographic hardness must retain its unproved premise and is not the unconditional negation. Neither exact support recovery nor a prescribed proper output is an additional obligation.
cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

cards.context:
A junta uses only a few of the available input features, but its dependence on those features can be completely arbitrary. The problem asks for an efficient predictor from passive observations. It separates the small information content of the hidden rule from the computational cost of locating useful features among many irrelevant ones.

The finite class contains at most \((k+1)n^k2^{2^k}\) functions. At constant confidence, realizable finite-class learning therefore needs only \(O((2^k+k\log(n+1)+\log(k+1)+1)/\varepsilon)\) examples information-theoretically. This fits the desired polynomial resource scale; the unresolved requirement is efficient computation with those examples.

Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio give exact learning in \(n^{(\omega/(\omega+1))k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,\log(1/\delta))\) time, where \(\omega\) is a valid matrix-multiplication exponent. Using the exponent available in their paper gives roughly \(n^{0.704k}\) times polynomial factors. Their model uses independent uniform examples, so this is progress in the required access model.

Valiant’s Corollary 7 improves noiseless junta learning to a bound below \(n^{0.60k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k)\) for the matrix-multiplication exponent and constants used there. Servedio’s November 2025 survey still reports the roughly \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. The exponent of the ambient dimension continues to grow with support size, so this is not the universal polynomial in the formal statement.

Individual-coordinate correlation can vanish even for a relevant coordinate, as in the parity of three selected bits. That illustrates a limitation of certain correlation statistics, not an unconditional lower bound against all example-based learners: noiseless parity itself has an efficient algebraic learner. Statistical-query restrictions must remain distinct from unrestricted observation of the actual samples.

Membership-query algorithms and monotone-junta learners have stronger positive guarantees under their respective conditions. Membership queries let the learner choose which inputs are labeled, while monotonicity restricts the possible truth tables. Neither condition is assumed here.

Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper concerns distributions whose probability mass function depends on a small coordinate set and relates that density-learning task to sparse noisy parity. Its introduction separately describes the persistent difficulty of noiseless Boolean function learning under uniform examples. The distribution-learning equivalence is not a resolution of this card’s prediction problem.

The inherited OpenReview pointer has now been identified as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields, NeurIPS 2025. Its introduction explicitly retains the difficult uniform-example question. Its positive Theorem 1.3 assumes a smoothed Markov random field, a known bounded-degree dependency graph and the stated bounded-width parameters, with success probability also taken over the random external-field perturbation. Even though the unperturbed uniform distribution is a Markov random field, a guarantee over positive random smoothing does not imply a guarantee at that exact unperturbed distribution.

Cornacchia–Mikulincer–Mossel’s May 2026 Theorem 2 studies labeled samples along a lazy random walk on the hypercube. It gives nearly linear ambient-dimension sample dependence for each fixed support size, with the stated target-dependent constants. Consecutive examples are correlated even if each has a uniform marginal. An independent-example source does not provide that temporal information, so the theorem concerns a different learning interface.

A \(k\)-junta has a decision-tree or DNF representation of size at most \(2^k\) under the usual leaf/term convention, with polynomial overhead if literal occurrences are counted. Efficient uniform-example learning for those larger representation classes would therefore imply the requested bound. This explains the junta problem’s role as a basic obstacle within computational learning theory.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, inherited through the consolidation of TCS-0023, asks for polynomial-time uniform learning beyond constant support size, or hardness under a natural complexity assumption. The retained card asks for the specific stronger bound \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) for every \(k\). A positive answer handles \(k=O(\log n)\); success only in a slower-growing regime or a conditional negative answer is not the same assertion. This historical source remains a related milestone, and the earlier consolidation and reserved identifier are preserved as provenance.

The exponent of the ambient dimension continues to grow with support size, so this is not the universal polynomial in the formal statement.

Individual-coordinate correlation can vanish even for a relevant coordinate, as in the parity of three selected bits. That illustrates a limitation of certain correlation statistics, not an unconditional lower bound against all example-based learners: noiseless parity itself has an efficient algebraic learner. Statistical-query restrictions must remain distinct from unrestricted observation of the actual samples.

Membership-query algorithms and monotone-junta learners have stronger positive guarantees under their respective conditions. Membership queries let the learner choose which inputs are labeled, while monotonicity restricts the possible truth tables. Neither condition is assumed here.

Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper concerns distributions whose probability mass function depends on a small coordinate set and relates that density-learning task to sparse noisy parity. Its introduction separately describes the persistent difficulty of noiseless Boolean function learning under uniform examples. The distribution-learning equivalence is not a resolution of this card’s prediction problem.

The inherited OpenReview pointer has now been identified as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields, NeurIPS 2025. Its introduction explicitly retains the difficult uniform-example question. Its positive Theorem 1.3 assumes a smoothed Markov random field, a known bounded-degree dependency graph and the stated bounded-width parameters, with success probability also taken over the random external-field perturbation. Even though the unperturbed uniform distribution is a Markov random field, a guarantee over positive random smoothing does not imply a guarantee at that exact unperturbed distribution.

Cornacchia–Mikulincer–Mossel’s May 2026 Theorem 2 studies labeled samples along a lazy random walk on the hypercube. It gives nearly linear ambient-dimension sample dependence for each fixed support size, with the stated target-dependent constants. Consecutive examples are correlated even if each has a uniform marginal. An independent-example source does not provide that temporal information, so the theorem concerns a different learning interface.

A \(k\)-junta has a decision-tree or DNF representation of size at most \(2^k\) under the usual leaf/term convention, with polynomial overhead if literal occurrences are counted. Efficient uniform-example learning for those larger representation classes would therefore imply the requested bound. This explains the junta problem’s role as a basic obstacle within computational learning theory.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, inherited through the consolidation of TCS-0023, asks for polynomial-time uniform learning beyond constant support size, or hardness under a natural complexity assumption. The retained card asks for the specific stronger bound \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) for every \(k\). A positive answer handles \(k=O(\log n)\); success only in a slower-growing regime or a conditional negative answer is not the same assertion. This historical source remains a related milestone, and the earlier consolidation and reserved identifier are preserved as provenance.

cards.title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that, for every \(n,s\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) represented by a decision tree with at most \(s\) nodes, \(A\), given \(1^n,1^s,1^t\) and independent uniform examples labeled by \(f\), runs on every execution for at most \(B(n+s+t)^C\) steps and outputs a Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{A,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23?\] The hypothesis may be an arbitrary efficiently evaluable circuit. The target remains the previously selected polynomial-time sample-only uniform-PAC question; reciprocal-integer error \(\varepsilon=1/t\) makes the accuracy encoding explicit.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by a coordinate index in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and has two children, with outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), evaluation follows the edge specified by the queried bit at each internal node until it reaches a leaf, whose bit is the output. Coordinates may occur repeatedly and there is no depth, monotonicity, balance, or randomness promise on the hidden tree. Size counts all nodes, as in the existing card. A full branching binary tree with \(\ell\) leaves has \(2\ell-1\) nodes, so the leaf-count convention used by the backdoor-defense source changes this polynomial-size question only by a constant factor. The size bound and input dimension are public; the target tree, its structure and its node labels are not supplied.

\(U_n\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Each example request yields a fresh independent \((x,f(x))\), \(x\sim U_n\), under one fixed target. Labels are exact and noiseless. Requests may be scheduled adaptively, but the learner cannot choose the input to be labeled or require correlations between successive inputs. In particular, there is no membership oracle, equivalence oracle or free access to the tree representation. The learner uses independent fair random bits and no length-dependent advice. Its guarantee is required for every target tree, rather than for a random tree or a randomly perturbed input distribution. The outer probability is confidence over the training draws and internal coins; the inner error probability concerns a fresh independent uniform input.

An output hypothesis is a finite acyclic circuit on the same \(n\) bits, using two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates in a fixed effective binary encoding. It need not be a tree or have size at most \(s\). The output is evaluated without further samples, the hidden target or any unreported target-dependent state. This is improper predictive learning, not exact tree identification or minimum-size reconstruction. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with unary public parameters; every bit operation, request, example read, stored-data access, random bit and output bit is counted. One fixed worst-case bound applies across all parameters and sample histories; the same bound also limits sample count and output length. Circuit evaluation takes polynomial time in the written circuit size. The example source’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Unlimited computation on polynomially many examples does not meet the requirement.

The error parameter ranges over \(1/t\), \(t\ge3\). For any desired real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), choosing \(t=\max\{3,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\) yields error at most \(\varepsilon\) with only polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Thus this encoding retains the ordinary arbitrary-accuracy learning target without treating an arbitrarily long rational spelling as a constant-cost input. Fixed confidence \(2/3\) is retained. The universal polynomial has no degree depending on \(s\), tree depth, the particular target or the accuracy parameter. The problem is a yes/no existence statement; there is no unspecified numerical optimization precision.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the stated uniform learner and universal polynomial bound exist, or prove their logical negation: every proposed machine and constants fail for some allowed dimension, size, accuracy and target, in either the worst-case resource guarantee or the PAC success condition. A positive answer must use only independent uniform labeled examples and cover every target tree. Proper-learning hardness, minimum-consistent-tree hardness, or a lower bound for one greedy heuristic does not rule out the allowed arbitrary circuit output. A result under an unproved computational assumption proves only the corresponding conditional negation. Membership-query learning, random-tree learning, smoothed-distribution learning and correlated-example algorithms have different access or target promises and are not accepted as a resolution of the displayed statement.

cards.context:
Decision trees describe classification through simple successive tests of individual input bits. A small tree may nevertheless hide complicated interactions among the variables. The question asks whether uniform random observations suffice for efficient prediction, even when the learner is free to return a representation different from a tree.

At a fixed node bound, the number of tree descriptions is at most exponential in a polynomial in the size and logarithm of the input dimension. Consequently the realizable information-theoretic sample requirement is polynomial in size, dimension and inverse error. The desired theorem concerns computation as well as data, rather than mere statistical identifiability.

A tree with at most \(s\) nodes has at most \(s\) leaves and can be expressed as a DNF with at most \(s\) terms. Known uniform-example DNF learners therefore provide quasipolynomial algorithms in the polynomial-size regime, as summarized by Servedio’s Theorem 13. That is a useful general upper bound, but a dimension exponent growing logarithmically with size or inverse error is not the requested one fixed polynomial.

Kalai–Teng’s Theorem 1 learns every target tree efficiently for most product distributions obtained by randomly perturbing their coordinate means by a fixed positive amount. Its probability is over both the perturbation and the training examples. The exact vector of uniform means is a particular unperturbed point, so success for almost all perturbed means does not imply the guarantee at that point. The theorem is explicitly improper and outputs a polynomial threshold function.

The ITCS 2025 source again states that efficient uniform-PAC learning of polynomial-size trees is unknown in the sample-only model. Its positive backdoor-defense theorem gives the defender the represented tree, which allows direct examination and evaluation. That observation model differs from receiving only labeled examples of a hidden tree. A fast detector with the representation supplied is not a PAC learner for this card.

Membership queries make uniform decision-tree learning easier because they provide labels at chosen inputs. Proper-learning problems impose a different restriction by requiring a tree output. This target has the passive observation interface and permits arbitrary Boolean circuit output; hardness for a restricted output class cannot be transferred just by matching the words “decision tree learning.”

The checked May 2026 paper on product spaces explicitly allows label queries at arbitrary inputs in §3. Its main size bound also depends on the optimal tree’s maximum and average depths and can be quasipolynomial even for logarithmic-depth trees. These are useful guarantees for the studied greedy procedure, but neither the interface nor the bound supplies the full polynomial sample-only learner.

Every \(k\)-junta has a decision tree with at most \(2^{k+1}-1\) nodes. Thus the desired learner would give time polynomial in \(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon\) for arbitrary juntas from uniform examples. The 2025 survey describes that junta problem as a continuing obstacle. This is a consequence of the tree-learning target, not an added promise that the tree must depend on few variables.

cards.title: Polynomial-time density learning of Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that properly learns every mixture of at most \(k\) nondegenerate Gaussian distributions on \(\mathbb R^d\), to any fixed total-variation accuracy, in time polynomial jointly in \(k\) and \(d\)? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) in the arithmetic model below such that, for every integer \(t\ge3\), there are integers \(C_t,a_t\ge1\) for which the following holds for all integers \(k,d\ge1\) and all \(P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\)? Given \(k,d,t\) and independent samples from \(P\), the algorithm uses at most \(C_t(k+d)^{a_t}\) operations and outputs a description of \(\widehat P\in\mathcal G_{k,d}\) satisfying \[\Pr[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,\widehat P)\le1/t]\ge2/3.\] The time bound holds on every execution and includes sampling and writing the output. Its constants are uniform over all mixture parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(t\) is required: this card asks the source's joint polynomial dependence on the number of components and dimension at each fixed accuracy.
cards.definitions: For a positive integer \(d\), a nondegenerate Gaussian distribution \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\) has mean \(\mu\in\mathbb R^d\) and a symmetric positive-definite matrix \(\Sigma\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\). Positive definite means \(v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0\) for every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\). Its density at \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) is \[(2\pi)^{-d/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right).\] The class \(\mathcal G_{k,d}\) consists of all distributions \(P=\sum_{i=1}^k w_iN(\mu_i,\Sigma_i)\), where \(w_i\ge0\), \(\sum_iw_i=1\), and each component satisfies the preceding conditions. Zero weights allow fewer than \(k\) components; repeated components are allowed. Means, covariance eigenvalues and component separation have no upper or lower promises beyond positive definiteness, and positive weights have no prescribed minimum. If \(p,q\) are the densities of \(P,Q\), their total variation distance is \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}|p(x)-q(x)|\,dx,\] where integration is with respect to Lebesgue measure. The learner has no access to the hidden component label or parameters. Each sampling request returns a fresh independent vector drawn from \(P\). The output consists of \(k\) weights, \(k\) means and \(k\) positive-definite covariance matrices, describing a valid member of the same class on every execution. This requirement is called proper learning. No correspondence between true and output components is required. The success probability is over all sampled vectors and the algorithm's independent fair random bits. Computational convention: \(A\) is one finite program, with rational constants and no nonuniform advice, using exact real registers together with a Turing work tape. Allowed real operations are copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, square root of a nonnegative value, and order or equality comparisons; each costs one operation. Reading or writing a real register costs one operation; a sample vector costs \(d\) operations. Each fair random bit and each ordinary tape step costs one operation. Integer inputs use binary encoding. Undefined arithmetic operations are forbidden. Each output scalar must be written and charged. No integration, optimization, density-evaluation or arbitrary-function oracle is available. The density formula defines the mathematical distribution, not an extra primitive of the program. This explicit arithmetic convention measures computation on real observations; it does not claim polynomial bit complexity for an unspecified finite-precision encoding.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation in the stated model. An affirmative proof must establish validity of the proper output, total execution bound and uniform total-variation guarantee for every allowed mixture and every accuracy parameter. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms in the specified arithmetic model, rather than only statistical-query algorithms or one proposed method. A conditional hardness theorem must be identified with its additional hypothesis and does not by itself settle this unconditional yes/no target. Learning with a fixed number of components, recovering component parameters under separation assumptions, or returning only an arbitrary sampler does not establish the requested statement. The reciprocal-accuracy parameter belongs to the learning guarantee; it is not a single numerical answer to be approximated at the benchmark's default tolerance.
cards.why: Gaussian mixtures are a basic example where enough observations can be available but extracting a useful distribution from them may remain computationally difficult. Joint dependence on dimension and component count distinguishes scalable learning from methods efficient only for a small fixed mixture. Resolving this target would clarify that statistical–computational gap in the absence of separation or conditioning assumptions.

cards.context:
A mixture combines several Gaussian populations without telling the learner which population generated an observation. Density learning asks for a distribution that predicts the whole population well. Two different lists of components can describe the same, or nearly the same, distribution; therefore success does not require reconstructing the original list.

The source defines proper PAC learning and unbounded positive-definite Gaussian components. Its highlighted computational question appears in a paper about private learning, but explicitly remains a question even when privacy is removed. The present target has no privacy requirement.

Section 9.3 recalls near-optimal nonprivate sample complexity \(\widetilde\Theta(kd^2/\alpha^2)\) at accuracy \(\alpha\), with logarithmic factors suppressed. A statistical existence bound does not make the search for a suitable mixture polynomial-time. The private construction also uses a nonconstructive cover, a separate obstacle discussed on page 6.

The statement fixes proper output, exact arithmetic primitives and the order of quantifiers explicitly. The source says polynomial in the two structural parameters and does not specify a bit model in its open-question sentence. Allowing the exponent to depend on fixed accuracy avoids silently strengthening that sentence to a fully polynomial accuracy guarantee.

Statistical-query lower bounds restrict algorithms that obtain information through approximate expectations of bounded test functions. They explain an obstruction for a broad family of learning methods, but alone do not exclude every algorithm with direct sample access.

There is also conditional evidence beyond statistical queries. Gupte–Vafa–Vaikuntanathan derive hardness of Gaussian-mixture density estimation from Learning with Errors assumptions. Those assumptions concern the difficulty of recovering or distinguishing hidden linear structure from noisy modular observations. The reductions and computational assumptions belong to their stated model; the card does not promote them to an unconditional theorem for its exact-real machine.

The score-matching theorem assumes a bounded conditioning/size parameter \(\tau\) and minimum positive weight at least inverse-polynomial in \(k\). It uses \(d^{\operatorname{poly}(k\tau/\alpha)}\) samples, runs in time polynomial in that sample count, and returns a sampler. The dimension exponent grows with the number of components, so this guarantee does not supply the joint polynomial bound sought here.

The 2025 parallel-pancake work studies shared-covariance structure and gives statistical-query limitations even with uniform weights, alongside a quasipolynomial testing guarantee. Its restrictions and model remain explicit.

The August 2026 manuscript concerns unit covariances, bounded means and a fixed component count. Its claimed sharp polynomial-time risk bound for that family does not settle arbitrary covariances or joint polynomial dependence. The card records the claim and its scope without asserting independent verification of the manuscript.

cards.title: NP-hardness of improper learning of \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\)
cards.formal: Is there an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(b\ge a\), there are an integer \(r\ge1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction \(R_b\) which decides SAT with success probability at least \(2/3\) using the following agnostic circuit-learning oracle? A query is a Boolean sampling circuit producing a distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\times\{0,1\}\). Every oracle reply must be a circuit \(h\) of size at most \((m+1)^{b}\) satisfying \[L_D(h)\le\min_{g\in\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}((m+1)^{a})}L_D(g)+(m+1)^{-r}.\] The reduction must succeed for every sequence of valid replies. The exponent \(r\), reduction and its running-time polynomial may depend on \(b\), but not on the SAT instance. No cryptographic or unproved complexity assumption is part of the target. This selects the source's agnostic, efficiently samplable-distribution reduction formulation.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean circuit is an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph with named input wires, constant zero and one wires, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and named output wires. Its size is its number of noninput gates, including constant gates. Gate types and predecessor indices are encoded in binary in topological order; all input and output counts are explicit. Write \(\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}(s)\) for the binary functions on \(m\) input bits computed by one-output circuits with at most \(s\) gates. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) if its restriction to each input length is computed by a circuit family with polynomial size; those circuits need not be generated uniformly.

A sampling-circuit query has some number \(q\ge0\) of random input bits and \(m+1\) output bits, with \(m\ge1\). Uniform independent bits in \(\{0,1\}^{q}\) induce the joint distribution \(D\); the first \(m\) outputs are the example and the last is its label. Labels may be noisy and need not be realizable by a small circuit. The risk is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). The oracle returns the full description of a predictor satisfying the displayed excess-risk guarantee. An answer always exists because the smaller comparator family is finite, contains constant functions, and is included in the allowed output family. The oracle itself has no computational restriction. It may select different valid circuits based on the query history; the reduction must work for all such selections, not only for a favorable learning rule.

The reduction is a randomized multitape Turing machine using independent fair bits. For each fixed \(b\), one polynomial in the SAT input bit length bounds its running time on every random tape and response history, counting construction of all sampling circuits and reading all reply descriptions; oracle computation is uncharged. Queries may be adaptive and may have different \(m,q\). In particular, the entire sampling circuit and every reply must have polynomial encoding length in the reduction's input length. The reduction may inspect hypothesis descriptions and evaluate them; it has no additional oracle or advice. SAT uses an explicit syntax-tree encoding of AND, OR and NOT formulas, with malformed encodings rejected. Probability of a correct SAT answer is over the reduction's coins, for each fixed input and each valid response policy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such an exponent \(a\) and reductions exist, or a proof of the negation. A positive answer must cover every polynomial output-size exponent \(b\ge a\), allowing the stated dependence of the reduction on \(b\). Hardness only when the predictor is restricted to the target size, or only under an additional cryptographic assumption, does not suffice. A negative answer must rule out the displayed family of reductions, not merely one restricted reduction technique.
cards.why: This asks whether learning general small circuits remains hard when the learner is free to use a different and polynomially larger representation. Establishing such hardness from SAT would connect worst-case NP difficulty with a central general learning task, while the known links to witness encryption expose consequences beyond learning itself.

cards.context:
An improper learner may return a larger circuit than any circuit in the comparator class. Showing hardness only for size-preserving output can therefore leave an efficient improper learner possible. The quantification over every fixed polynomial output-size bound makes this distinction explicit.

The source defines learning reductions by giving the oracle a sampling circuit for a distribution and receiving a sufficiently accurate hypothesis. This card retains that oracle interface. Sampling distributions are generated by the reduction; the task does not give a practical learner arbitrary target membership queries.

The polynomial target-size exponent is fixed before the allowed output exponent. For each allowed output exponent the reduction may be different. Adaptive randomized Turing reductions are allowed; the card does not impose the additional deterministic, nonadaptive, witness-mapping or honesty conditions used in some of the source’s cryptographic consequences.

The June 2026 paper proves conditional hardness for a related full-support learning problem. It assumes a strong indistinguishability obfuscator and a lower-bound hypothesis for propositional proof systems. These are substantive assumptions, so the result does not by itself give the unconditional reduction asked for here.

cards.title: Quasipolynomial accuracy exponent for Gaussian agnostic halfspace learning
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C,K>0\) and one uniform randomized learner in the real-arithmetic model below such that, for every dimension \(n\ge2\), rational inverse excess error \(t\ge3\), and permitted Boolean target, its training cost plus output-evaluation cost is at most \[K n^{C\log_2 t}\] on every execution, and it succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\)? The target labels are deterministic: for every measurable \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\{-1,+1\}\), a learner sees independent \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\), and must output a predictor \(h\) such that \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{err}_f(h)\le\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)+\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23,\qquad \operatorname{err}_f(h)=\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)],\] where \[\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)=\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^n,\ b\in\mathbb R}\Pr_{x\sim\gamma_n}[\operatorname{sgn}(\langle w,x\rangle+b)\ne f(x)].\]
cards.definitions:
\(\gamma_n\) is the Borel probability measure on \(\mathbb R^n\) with density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\) with respect to Lebesgue measure; its coordinates are independent standard normal random variables. A halfspace predictor has the form \(x\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(\sum_i w_i x_i+b)\), with real coefficients and threshold and \(\operatorname{sgn}(z)=+1\) for \(z\ge0\), otherwise \(-1\). Constant predictors are allowed by \(w=0\). Affine halfspaces follow the source’s introductory definition, which includes a constant term; its later notation sometimes suppresses that term. No margin, bounded coefficient encoding, sparsity or homogeneity assumption is added. The infimum in \(\operatorname{OPT}_n(f)\) does not presume an available optimum or supply its value to the learner.

The unknown target \(f\) is any Borel-measurable Boolean function, fixed before the examples and learner coins are drawn. It need not itself be a halfspace. Each oracle request returns an independent Gaussian vector with its exact value under the same \(f\); the learner cannot choose the sampled point, inspect code for \(f\), ask for a label at a selected point, or query the optimum. There is no independent stochastic label distribution conditional on \(x\) in this literal target-function formulation. The outer success probability includes all sample draws and internal randomness; error is measured on a fresh Gaussian input. The learner may output an improper predictor. The source uses \(L^1\) notation: for \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued \(h,f\), \(\mathbb E|h-f|=2\operatorname{err}_f(h)\). Thus excess disagreement \(1/t\) is excess \(L^1\) loss \(2/t\), not \(1/t\). This exact factor is kept separate from asymptotic runtime notation.

Computational convention: use one finite uniform real-arithmetic register program, with rational constants in its fixed code, integer control and rational public parameters \(n,t\). It can copy real registers, apply \(+,-,\times,\div\) to a constant number of registers, compare their values, branch and generate a fair random bit, each at unit arithmetic cost. Division by zero must be handled by a comparison before division. Discrete control, register access and writing an output instruction each cost one step. Sampling and loading an \(n\)-coordinate labeled example costs \(n+1\) units. The oracle supplies exact real coordinates; no cost for internally generating a Gaussian real is attributed to the learner. There is no floor, digit-extraction primitive, arbitrary real advice, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or decision oracle for general properties of real numbers. Uniformity means the same finite program works for all \(n,t,f\), with no length-dependent constants or advice.

The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit on \(n\) real inputs, built from the same operations, Boolean choices and sign tests. Constants may be stored real values computed during training. It must define a total \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued predictor on every real input, with each division guarded when its denominator vanishes. Output writing and each stored real coefficient are charged one unit per written item. Evaluation cost is the number of circuit operations; it is included in the resource measure. Such circuits give measurable predictors and need no further examples or target access after training. There is no requirement that the output be a halfspace, and no fixed polynomial degree or circuit-size restriction beyond the stated time bound.

For a learner \(A\), let \(\tau_A(n,t)\) be the supremum over every allowed target, sample history and coin history of its training cost plus the evaluation cost of its output circuit, with nontermination or invalid output charged infinite cost. This exact-real arithmetic model is an explicitly stated convention completing the source’s continuous-example interface. It does not assert a theorem translating arbitrary real computations to the bit model. Exact Gaussian examples have no finite binary representation in general, and the 2014 question specifies neither a rounding oracle nor a coordinate-bit budget. A separate bit-complexity variant would need those definitions and a proof that rounding preserves the learning guarantee for arbitrary measurable targets. Numerical rounding is therefore not silently included as a free primitive in the present arithmetic target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that a single learner achieves the stated excess error with probability at least \(2/3\) within the joint training and evaluation bound \(Kn^{C\log_2 t}\). A refutation must exclude every proposed learner and pair of constants on the stated Gaussian model.
cards.why: Gaussian inputs remove many distributional complications, yet arbitrary labels can still make even the best linear predictor difficult to match. The question asks for the precise computational cost of decreasing excess error, allowing any output representation. It separates the number of examples needed for learning from the much larger time used by current algorithms.

cards.context:
A halfspace classifies points by which side of a hyperplane they occupy. In an agnostic task, the labels need not be linearly separable: the benchmark is the least disagreement achievable by a halfspace, plus a requested excess error. A regular Gaussian input marginal does not itself constrain the complexity of the labeling rule.

The 2014 paper contrasts the known \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}\) algorithmic scale with a sparse-noisy-parity-based conditional \(n^{\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))}\) obstruction. Its Question 3 asks for the optimal time and explicitly proposes \(n^{O(\log(1/\varepsilon))}\) as a possibility. The quoted lower scale comes from a reduction and a hardness premise; it is not an unconditional time lower bound.

Definition 4 of the source labels examples by a deterministic target function and states an L¹ approximation guarantee; its halfspace discussion also uses Boolean classification language. Later papers often start directly from an arbitrary joint distribution on features and labels. An upper guarantee for all such joint distributions includes deterministic labels as a special case. A lower bound for the larger family does not automatically apply to the deterministic subfamily.

COLT 2021 Diakonikolas–Kane–Pittas–Zarifis proves essentially matching \(n^{\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)}\)-scale statistical-query hardness for halfspaces in its general joint-distribution model. Statistical queries return approximate expectations of bounded test functions instead of the actual independent examples. This is an important optimality theorem for that restricted access model, not a lower bound for every sample-based learner in the present formulation.

ICML 2023 Diakonikolas–Kane–Ren gives a stronger related cryptographic obstruction. Its Corollary 3.2, under Assumption 2.3 on subexponential LWE hardness, excludes time \(n^{O((1/(\varepsilon\sqrt{\log n}))^\alpha)}\) for every fixed \(0<\alpha<2\), in its stated range \(c/(\sqrt n\log n)\le\varepsilon\le1/(\log n)^\gamma\), with \(\gamma>1/2\) and the specified sufficiently large constant \(c\). Both the logarithmic loss in the exponent and the error range are material. The theorem uses arbitrary joint labels and a computational cryptographic reduction; it is not an unconditional constant-factor characterization of this real-arithmetic deterministic-label problem.

The 2023 hard-instance construction contains residual random noise in the labels even after conditioning on the Gaussian feature vector, and its null case has independent fair labels. This review has not established a conversion of that construction into a fixed deterministic target with the same computational costs. Nor does a finite-bit cryptographic assumption by itself give a lower bound against unit-cost exact-real programs. Those interface gaps are stated explicitly rather than hidden by a claim that the original question is fully resolved.

Tikhonov–Vasilyan’s May 2026 Theorem 3.14 outputs an affine halfspace with error \(\operatorname{OPT}+\varepsilon\) and time \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon^2)}+(1/\varepsilon)^{O(1/\varepsilon^{2.5})}\) at constant confidence. Its general joint-label guarantee includes fixed deterministic targets, and proper output is allowed by an improper-learning task. The theorem advances proper learning and matches the known dimension exponent; its additional accuracy-only term and continuous computational conventions must remain visible in a joint optimal-time comparison. No finite-bit equivalence is claimed here.

The April 2026 Huang–Juba paper studies a further related problem with homogeneous halfspace output and general joint labels. Its LWE-based hardness is stated with those restrictions. Homogeneous proper learning is not substituted for unrestricted improper affine learning, and the computational assumption is not asserted true.

The original source does not fix coordinate precision or a universal elementary cost model for real samples. This card states a real-arithmetic convention so the resource question can be read precisely. Its current-status review remains uncertain: the inspected recent results explain substantial progress but do not certify a matching resolution with all the displayed label, computation and parameter conventions.

cards.formal: Resolve the following two distribution-specific questions, separately. For \(D_n=\gamma_n=N(0,I_n)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and for \(D_n=U_n\), the uniform measure on \(\{-1,+1\}^n\), does there exist a uniform randomized learner \(A_D\) and constants \(B_D,C_D\ge1\) such that, for all integers \(n,k\ge1\), \(t\ge3\), and all intersections \(f\) of at most \(k\) affine halfspaces, \(A_D(n,k,t)\), using only independent examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D_n\), outputs a predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23\] in total training, output-writing and evaluation cost at most \(B_D(n+k+t)^{C_D}\)? The Gaussian branch uses the explicit real-arithmetic convention below; the Boolean-cube branch uses bit computation. The learner may be improper. Both the number of halfspaces and inverse accuracy are variable parameters: a polynomial whose exponent depends on \(k\) or \(t\) does not answer either branch affirmatively. A full resolution reports an answer to each branch, rather than treating failure of one as a classification of both.
cards.definitions:
An affine halfspace has Boolean value \(+1\) when \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i+b\ge0\), and value \(-1\) otherwise, for arbitrary real \(w_1,\ldots,w_n,b\). Its boundary is included in the positive side. An intersection has value \(+1\) exactly when all its component inequalities hold; otherwise it has value \(-1\). The intersection with no components is the constant positive function. All coefficients and the number of nonredundant inequalities are hidden; only the upper bound \(k\) is supplied. No coefficient-size, margin, balance or homogeneity promise is added. On the cube, the function is simply the restriction of those inequalities to the finite domain; their real coefficients are not input strings whose sizes the learner must read.

\(\gamma_n\) has independent standard normal coordinates, with joint density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\). Under \(U_n\), each of the \(2^n\) sign vectors has mass \(2^{-n}\). The appropriate distribution is known to its learner, but the target is unknown. Each example is an independent draw with the exact noiseless target label. The learner cannot ask for labels at chosen points, inspect the target description, or query conditional distributions. The inner probability is disagreement on a fresh example; the outer probability includes training examples and the learner’s random coins. The error tolerance is \(\varepsilon=1/t\), with integer \(t\) supplied in unary together with \(n,k\). These reciprocal tolerances define arbitrary requested accuracy up to a constant factor without introducing an uncounted rational encoding length. Confidence is fixed at \(2/3\); neither branch promises perfect recovery of coefficients.

For the cube, \(A_U\) is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a source of independent fair bits and an example tape. Writing a labeled example costs \(n+1\) bit operations. The output is an ordinary finite acyclic Boolean circuit, using AND, OR and NOT gates and constants, evaluated on the input signs encoded as bits. Training, reading, output length, and worst-case output evaluation time are all counted. The polynomial bound must hold on every sample and coin history. The same program and constants must work for every \(n,k,t,f\), with no advice depending on input length.

For the Gaussian branch, use one finite real-register program whose fixed constants are rational. Copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division with an explicit zero-denominator guard, comparison, branching, and generating a fair bit have unit cost; discrete control, register access and output writing are also charged. Loading one exact labeled Gaussian vector costs \(n+1\) units. Integer control and the unary public parameters do not supply any infinite advice. There is no floor or digit extraction, optimization oracle, expectation oracle or oracle deciding general real-number properties. The output is a finite acyclic arithmetic-and-comparison circuit with constants computed during training and a total Boolean sign output. Every division must be guarded so evaluation is defined on every input. Its stored constants, instructions and worst-case evaluation operations are counted in the same polynomial bound; it requires no further target access. This permits any such efficiently evaluable predictor, including ones outside the intersection class. All these predictors are Borel measurable.

The real-arithmetic convention explicitly fills the source’s unspecified continuous-input cost interface. Exact Gaussian coordinates need not have finite binary representations, so this branch does not silently claim an equivalent finite-bit learning theorem. Conversely the discrete branch uses actual bit costs and Boolean outputs. A result stated in a different computational model must justify the transfer before it resolves the corresponding branch. Independent programs and constants for the two branches are allowed; each program must be uniform over its own parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Give Lean proofs deciding the displayed uniform-existence proposition for each of \(D=\gamma\) and \(D=U\). A positive proof supplies one learner, universal polynomial constants, termination/resource bounds, a valid finite predictor and the learning guarantee for every parameter and target. A negative proof negates that full existence statement: for every candidate learner and polynomial constants, show a violating parameter/target or resource requirement. A conditional lower bound proves only the corresponding implication unless its assumption is also established. A restriction to statistical-query learners, proper hypotheses, fixed \(k\), a positive margin or a different sample source does not by itself resolve these propositions. State the model transfer for any invoked bound. The answer is a pair of exact truth values; no numerical approximation or unspecified asymptotic exponent counts as a resolution.
cards.why: Simple independent input coordinates do not identify which inequality caused a negative label. The question asks whether that ambiguity creates a computational barrier even when the distribution is completely known. Its uniform dependence on the number of inequalities and desired accuracy separates practical polynomial learning from algorithms efficient only for fixed parameters.

cards.context:
The selected question is in the related-work discussion of the 2025 paper. Its antecedent distributions are Gaussian inputs and the uniform Boolean cube. The original card title mentioned factorizable distributions, which describe the surrounding paper’s main two-halfspace margin theorem; that title did not describe the selected question. The revised title restores the source scope.

An individual linear inequality is a simple classifier. An intersection accepts only points satisfying every inequality, while a rejected example does not say which condition failed. The desired learner receives labeled examples and may output any efficient predictor, rather than having to reconstruct the hidden inequalities.

The 2025 paper’s main result assumes two component halfspaces, a positive data margin, and a factorization relative to the subspace of relevant directions. Those are additional promises. Its theorem therefore does not resolve the separate question about a variable number of arbitrary affine halfspaces under the two known distributions.

Alman–Patel–Servedio’s 2026 Theorem 1 learns arbitrary Boolean functions of \(k\) halfspaces from random examples under any distribution in time \(\operatorname{poly}(2^{\sqrt n(\log n)^{O(k)}},1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta))\). The paper specifically notes the previously missing subexponential bound for two halfspaces on the uniform cube at \(\varepsilon=1/n\). This is substantial progress, but the displayed bound is not polynomial in \(n,k,1/\varepsilon\).

The STOC 2026 Gaussian sparsification theorem has learning applications for intersections with bounded geometric width, meaning the defining hyperplanes have a bounded distance from the origin in its stated representation. Its constants depend on width and accuracy. That result does not supply a single polynomial bound for arbitrary thresholds and arbitrary accuracy in the current question.

The May 2026 proper agnostic learner for Gaussian functions of halfspaces also includes realizable labels as a special case. However its dimension exponent depends on the number of halfspaces and inverse error, and it has an additional parameter-dependent term. The output restriction is stronger than needed here, but the running-time guarantee does not meet the fully polynomial target.

cards.title: Distribution-free improper learning of two unrestricted halfspaces
cards.formal: Is there a single randomized learner that, for every distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), every target \(f\) expressible as the intersection of two integer-weight halfspaces of total description length at most a supplied bound \(B\), and every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), uses only independent labeled examples from \(D\) to output a Boolean circuit \(H\) with \(\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in time polynomial in \(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\)?
cards.definitions: A halfspace is \(h(x)=1\) exactly when \(\sum_{i} w_{i} x_{i}\ge \theta\), with \(w_i,\theta\in\mathbb{Z}\) in signed binary; equality is positive. The target f is the conjunction of two such predicates. Its description length is the bit length of a list of both weight vectors and thresholds, using self-delimiting binary integers. The learner receives n and B in unary and a rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) in binary. It is promised that f has at least one such description of length at most B, but receives neither that description nor its weights. An example oracle returns independent pairs \((x,f(x))\) with x sampled from an arbitrary fixed distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). The learner receives only these labeled examples and its own independent fair coins. Each oracle call costs at least \(n+1\) steps to receive its bits; all further work is charged in Turing-machine bit steps. Membership queries, advice and descriptions or probability evaluations of D are absent. There must be a fixed polynomial P such that on every random tape the running time, and hence sample count and output length, are bounded by \(P(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon))\). Output a deterministic Boolean circuit \(H:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) in the explicit \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) basis. The success condition is \(\Pr_{\mathrm{samples,coins}}[\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon]\ge2/3\), uniformly over \(n,B,\varepsilon ,D\) and every promised f. Circuit evaluation costs polynomial time in its output encoding. The hypothesis need not be an intersection of halfspaces. Encoding an arbitrary deterministic polynomial-time evaluator by its Boolean circuit preserves this unrestricted efficient-output convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof constructing and bounding a learner under all the stated quantifiers, or a Lean proof that none exists. Proper-learning hardness and statistical-query lower bounds do not exclude all allowed learners. A margin promise, a restricted input distribution or membership queries would change the problem.

cards.title: Square-root multiclass regret from Littlestone dimension
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every pair of nonempty sets \(X,Y\), every nonempty class \(H\subseteq Y^X\) of Littlestone dimension at most \(d\), and all integers \(T\ge d\ge1\), the minimax expected regret satisfies \[R_T(H)\le C\sqrt{dT}?\] Infinite instance and label sets are allowed, and no regularity or computability restriction on the class is added. For the prediction game defined below, \[R_T(H)=\inf_A\ \sup_{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_T,y_T)\in X\times Y}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^T(1-p_t(y_t))-\min_{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1\{h(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right\}.\] Here \(p_t=A_t((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_{t-1},y_{t-1}),x_t)\) is a probability distribution on labels. The infimum ranges over all causal prediction rules, without computational restrictions.
cards.definitions: A hypothesis \(h\in H\) assigns a label from \(Y\) to each instance in \(X\). A depth-\(r\) Littlestone tree is a complete binary tree with an instance at each internal node and two distinct labels from \(Y\) on that node's outgoing edges; the pair of labels may vary by node. The tree is shattered if every root-to-leaf path has one fixed hypothesis agreeing with all its edge labels on its instance points. The dimension \(\operatorname{Ldim}(H)\) is the largest shattered depth, or infinity if depths are unbounded. On each round the adversary presents \(x_t\), the learner supplies \(p_t\), and the adversary then reveals \(y_t\). The learner observes the actual label before the next round and is charged expected zero-one loss \(1-p_t(y_t)\). It does not observe future instances. The adversary may react to \(p_t\); loss is the displayed expectation, not a reaction to a sampled label. The sequence need not be realizable by any hypothesis. The comparator is one fixed hypothesis chosen in hindsight, whose minimum loss exists since the possible losses are integers from zero to \(T\). A distribution here is a function \(p:Y\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(\sum_{y\in Y}p(y)=1\), with this sum defined as the supremum of sums over finite subsets. It automatically has at most countable positive support. This atomic convention does not increase the best possible regret relative to arbitrary probability measures with measurable singletons: any missing atom mass can be assigned to one fixed label, increasing no zero-one loss. All histories and rules are arbitrary set functions, so no topology or measurability structure on \(X,H\) is required. Rules may know \(H\) and \(T\), need not be proper, and have no runtime, memory, computability or finite-description bound. Infima and suprema need not be attained. Dimension zero means all hypotheses agree pointwise and zero regret is attainable. The range \(T\ge d\) avoids the separate saturation regime because cumulative regret cannot exceed \(T\). All requested comparison constants must be independent of the instance and label spaces, class, dimension and horizon.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that \(R_T(H)/\sqrt{dT}\) has a universal upper bound over the classes and horizons specified above, or prove that this ratio is unbounded on that domain.
cards.why: Would determine whether Littlestone dimension alone controls the exact minimax cost of multiclass sequential prediction, beyond the already known learnability characterization.

cards.context:
The learner sees the current instance and then receives the correct label after predicting. It can distribute its prediction among labels, and is scored by expected mistakes relative to the best fixed hypothesis. Labels can contradict every member of the class. The regret target is therefore different from a realizable mistake bound.

The 2023 paper proves that finite Littlestone dimension characterizes agnostic multiclass online learnability even for unbounded label spaces. This general learnability theorem does not require the separate minimax regularity assumption used in its sharper finite-label result. The remaining rate question asks how far a learner must fall behind the best fixed concept.

The unrestricted argument in §3 gives regret at most \(\operatorname{Ldim}(H)+\sqrt{(T/2)\operatorname{Ldim}(H)\ln(eT/\operatorname{Ldim}(H))}\) for positive dimension. In the stated horizon range this yields \(R(d,T)=O(\sqrt{dT\log(eT/d)})\). A universal lower scale is \(\Omega(\sqrt{dT})\). The logarithm is part of the unresolved gap and cannot be suppressed when asking for constant factors.

For a finite label set, Theorem 9 gives \(O(\sqrt{\operatorname{Ldim}(H)T\log|Y|})\) under the additional minimax regularity condition explicitly stated in p. 9 footnote 4 for those results. Under that condition a fixed label count yields the square-root scale, but the coefficient grows with the count. Even for two labels, removing the condition for unrestricted classes is a separate open issue recorded by the source and by the 2025 thesis.

The binary question restores the source’s square-root upper-bound conjecture. It retains arbitrary instance and label sets and does not add the regularity condition used in some sharper special-case theorems. The known lower scale motivates this endpoint; a complete determination of an alternative rate is not required.

The checked May 2026 oracle-complexity paper concerns binary classification and retains logarithmic factors in its dimension-dependent regret statement. It improves resource use within an online algorithm and does not resolve the unrestricted multiclass constant-factor rate.
