cards.title: Algorithmic threshold for the symmetric binary perceptron
cards.formal:
Does the Gaussian symmetric binary perceptron's polynomial-time search threshold satisfy
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\qquad\text{as }\kappa\downarrow0?\]
Precisely, are there constants \(C\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and \(\kappa_0\in(0,1/2]\) such that for every rational \(\kappa\in(0,\kappa_0]\),
\[\frac{\kappa^2}{C(\log(1/\kappa))^a}\ \le\ \alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)\ \le\ C\kappa^2(\log(1/\kappa))^a?\]
For fixed margin \(\kappa>0\) and density \(\alpha>0\), an instance is an \(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\)-by-\(n\) matrix \(G\) with independent standard Gaussian entries. A successful search returns \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n\) with
\[\max_{1\le i\le\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}\sigma_j\right|\le\kappa\sqrt n.\]
The threshold is the supremum of fixed rational densities at which a uniform polynomial-time algorithm succeeds with probability tending to one as \(n\to\infty\), in the real-arithmetic model specified below.

The polylogarithmic tolerance restores the tilde lost in the imported excerpt. To make the source's informal efficient-algorithm class definite on exact Gaussian inputs, this card explicitly selects rational-constant randomized real-arithmetic computation. It does not assert equivalence with every discretized or machine-specific version of the conjecture.
cards.definitions:
The dimension \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Margin \(\kappa\) and density \(\alpha\) are positive rational constants held fixed while \(n\) tends to infinity; write \(M=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\). The \(Mn\) entries of \(G\in\mathbb R^{M\times n}\) are mutually independent with probability density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-t^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). A feasible output is a full vector of \(n\) signs satisfying every displayed two-sided constraint. When \(M=0\), every sign vector is feasible. A failure symbol, a malformed vector or an infeasible vector counts as failure. No conditioning on satisfiability or planting of a hidden solution is performed.

The normalization is by \(\sqrt n\), the square root of the number of variables, and the density is constraints divided by variables. The symbol \(\kappa\) denotes the allowed absolute margin. All constraints are symmetric around zero; there is no one-sided inequality in place of the absolute value. This is the Gaussian version, not a matrix of independently uniform signs. For a nonzero row count the maximum is the usual infinity norm; the empty maximum is taken to be zero.

A permitted algorithm has a finite program with rational numerical constants and finite discrete control, real registers with exact arithmetic, and integer registers for array addresses and loop counters. It can read the supplied matrix, copy values, apply addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and branch on equality or order comparisons. Integer-address arithmetic is addition, subtraction and comparison; addresses used must be valid nonnegative integers. Each such instruction, register access, input access, output instruction and branch costs one operation. There is no floor, bit-extraction operation on a real register, arbitrary function oracle or infinite program-specific real constant. Division by zero must be handled by an explicit branch, not a source of extra computational power.

For internal randomness, the program may request independent fair bits or independent standard Gaussian real samples, each in one operation. These samples are independent of the input matrix and of all prior samples. The algorithm can be deterministic by making no random requests. There must be constants \(D>0\), \(d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) such that it halts after at most \(D(n+1)^d\) operations on every real input matrix of the required dimensions and every sequence of random choices, returning either a sign vector or failure. Space and all input inspection count through these operations. The finite program and constants may depend on the fixed rational pair \((\alpha,\kappa)\), but not on \(n\) or on the sampled matrix. No advice string depending on \(n\) is provided. Exact real arithmetic is a declared computational convention; operation count is not a bound on finite-precision bit complexity.

Let \(\mathcal D_\kappa\subseteq\mathbb Q_{>0}\) be the set of densities \(\alpha\) for which such an algorithm \(A\) exists with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{G,R}\bigl[A(G;R)\text{ returns a feasible sign vector}\bigr]=1.\]
Here the probability is over both the independent Gaussian entries and the algorithm's permitted internal randomness. The convergence need not have a supplied rate. The algorithm must be one uniform program for the full sequence of dimensions at the fixed parameter pair, rather than a different program at every dimension. Define
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\sup\bigl(\mathcal D_\kappa\cup\{0\}\bigr)\in[0,+\infty].\]
The supremum need not be attained; this definition does not assume an algorithm at the threshold or an all-input guarantee. The main conjecture includes a finite upper bound for sufficiently small margins. Showing algorithms whose densities approach a claimed lower endpoint can establish a lower bound on the supremum even if no endpoint algorithm exists.

In the displayed asymptotic claim, \(\log\) is the natural logarithm and \(\kappa\) approaches zero through positive rationals. The constants \(C,a,\kappa_0\) are chosen once before all those margins. The limit in \(n\) defining the threshold is taken first, separately for each fixed pair. No polynomial dependence of the running-time coefficient or exponent on \(1/\kappa\) is imposed. A statement for a shrinking margin \(\kappa(n)\), or for one fixed value such as \(\kappa=1\), is a different quantifier regime.

The two sides have different meanings: the lower side concerns the existence of successful algorithms at enough densities; the upper side bounds the success densities of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm. A geometric obstruction proved only for algorithms satisfying an additional stability property is not an upper bound for this unrestricted class. Failure to achieve success tending to one does not require success to tend to zero; there may be nonvanishing success or different subsequential behavior.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed two-sided polylogarithmic envelope for the defined threshold. A positive answer must establish both inequalities with one set of fixed constants in the declared computational, input-distribution and order-of-limits conventions. A refutation must exclude every permitted choice of those constants, rather than only a selected logarithmic exponent or the stronger claim with no logarithmic loss. Bounds restricted to stable algorithms, experiments, existence of solutions without efficient search, or a result conditional on an unproved lattice hardness assumption do not alone settle the statement. The benchmark target is the asymptotic conjecture, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its logarithmic-factor precision.
cards.why: The symmetric binary perceptron is a basic random constraint model in which many solutions can exist while known algorithms reach much smaller densities. Locating the small-margin search scale tests whether the observed computational obstruction captures all efficient algorithms or only particular algorithm families. Its links to discrepancy, random solution geometry and worst-case lattice hardness make the threshold a substantial average-case complexity question.

cards.title: Littlestone-dimension regret bounds for unrestricted classes
cards.formal: Do universal real constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) exist such that, for every nonempty set \(\mathcal X\), every nonempty Boolean concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\) of finite Littlestone dimension \(d\ge1\), and every integer horizon \(T\ge d\), the optimal adversarial online regret satisfies \[c\sqrt{dT}\le R_T(\mathcal H)\le C\sqrt{dT}?\] Here \[R_T(\mathcal H)=\inf_A\ \sup_{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_T,y_T)\in\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}}\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(p_t,y_t)-\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf1\{h(x_t)\ne y_t\}\right\},\] where \(p_t=A_t((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_{t-1},y_{t-1}),x_t)\in[0,1]\), \(\ell(p,0)=p\), and \(\ell(p,1)=1-p\). The infimum ranges over all such causal prediction rules. No restriction of countability, topology, compactness, or measurability is imposed on \(\mathcal X\) or \(\mathcal H\). The unresolved issue in the source is whether the upper bound holds with this full generality; the matching lower scale is already known.
cards.definitions: A concept \(h\) assigns one binary label to every instance. A complete binary tree of depth \(r\) has one instance from \(\mathcal X\) at each internal node and its outgoing edges labeled 0 and 1. The tree is shattered by \(\mathcal H\) if every root-to-leaf path has a concept whose labels on that path's nodes equal its edge labels. The Littlestone dimension \(d\) is the largest shattered depth. Each horizon-specific rule \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_T)\) is an arbitrary family of set functions from labeled histories and the current instance to \([0,1]\); it may depend on the whole class and on \(T\). The number \(p_t\) is a probability of predicting label 1, so \(\ell(p_t,y_t)\) is the expected zero-one mistake loss. No probability distribution on the arbitrary instance space is required: regret is defined directly by the displayed supremum of finite sums. Equivalently, the adversary presents \(x_t\), the learner chooses \(p_t\), and the adversary then supplies \(y_t\); the charged loss is \(\ell(p_t,y_t)\), not an adversary's reaction to a sampled binary prediction. The learner sees the label before the next round. Future instances and labels are unavailable. The sequence need not be realizable by any concept; comparison is to the best single concept in hindsight. The minimum comparator loss exists because the class is nonempty and losses are integers in \(\{0,\ldots,T\}\). The infimum over rules and supremum over sequences need not be attained. Running time, memory, computability, and finite descriptions of the class or rules are unrestricted; the predictor need not choose a concept from the class. The constants must be independent of the domain, class, dimension, and horizon, and logarithmic factors may not be hidden. The restriction \(T\ge d\) is essential to this square-root formulation because regret is at most \(T\); the omitted dimension-zero case has a single distinct concept and zero regret.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal two-sided statement, or its logical negation, in Lean under the stated arbitrary-set prediction model. For a positive answer, supply universal constants and prove both bounds, using any previously formalized lower-bound result with matching hypotheses. If an optimal rule does not attain the infimum, rules approaching the upper bound arbitrarily closely suffice. A negative answer must refute the existence of universal constants: for every proposed pair \(0<c\le C<\infty\), some class and allowed horizon violate a bound. In view of the known universal lower bound, the outstanding mathematical task is the upper bound or classes with unbounded ratio \(R_T(\mathcal H)/\sqrt{dT}\). A result with a class-dependent constant, an extra logarithmic factor, or an added regularity hypothesis does not settle the question. This is an exact constant-factor asymptotic claim, not an additive numerical approximation.
cards.why: Littlestone dimension already characterizes whether adversarial online classification is learnable. This question asks whether that single combinatorial number also controls the sharp regret for every class. Removing the remaining regularity assumption would complete that quantitative characterization; a counterexample would exhibit a genuine limitation of a purely dimension-based prediction theorem.

cards.context:
In agnostic online classification, labels can contradict every member of the reference class. Regret therefore subtracts the errors of the best fixed concept instead of requiring the learner to make few errors outright. Randomized predictions are represented by their probabilities, which gives the stated finite-sum game even when the instance set has no measurable structure.

Littlestone dimension measures how long a class can sustain every binary answer pattern along an adaptively chosen tree of instances. Finite dimension characterizes online learnability. Here the question is quantitative: can the optimal cumulative excess error always be bounded by a universal constant times the square root of dimension times horizon?

The standard unrestricted binary bounds have lower scale \(\Omega(\sqrt{dT})\) and an upper bound with an additional logarithmic factor. Alon and coauthors obtain the sharp square-root rate through a connection with sequential Rademacher complexity. The later sources explicitly point out that the minimax step supporting this connection assumes an additional regularity condition on the class.

The source paper studies self-directed learning, where the learner chooses the order of available instances. Its footnote asks a separate question about the ordinary adversarial game. This card preserves that footnote’s question: the adversary supplies each next instance, and the dimension is Littlestone dimension rather than the paper’s self-directed dimension.

The 2023 multiclass paper explicitly records the unresolved unrestricted binary question and carries the same regularity condition into its sharp finite-label bounds. Raman’s 2025 dissertation repeats that qualification. It would therefore be incorrect to treat the unrestricted-looking headline of the 2021 theorem as a checked unconditional resolution.

The theorem on randomized Littlestone dimension and nearly realizable sequences cites the same 2021 upper bound inside its proof. It supplies no independent justification for removing the regularity condition. Its different mistake-budget formulation is not silently substituted for the present arbitrary-sequence regret target.

The checked May 2026 work improves weak-consistency-oracle complexity and memory in agnostic online learning. Its dimension-dependent regret guarantee still hides logarithmic factors. Those resource improvements do not supply the universal constant-factor upper bound requested here.

cards.title: Sample-optimal Gaussian graphical model learning in polynomial time
cards.formal: Can general Gaussian conditional-independence graphs be learned in uniform polynomial time using, up to a universal constant factor, the information-theoretically optimal number of independent observations? For integers \(p\ge2\), \(1\le d\le p-1\), \(r\ge2\), and rational \(0<\kappa<1\), let \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) be the Gaussian family defined below and let \(m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\) be its minimax sample count for exact graph recovery with failure probability at most \(2^{-r}\), allowing unrestricted measurable estimators. Is there one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,B,a\ge1\) such that, for every parameter choice and every \(P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\), \(A(p,d,\kappa,r)\) returns its exact graph with probability at least \(1-2^{-r}\), draws at most \(\lceil C m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\rceil\) independent samples, and uses at most \[B\bigl(p+d+\lceil\kappa^{-1}\rceil+r+L\bigr)^a\] real-arithmetic operations, including sample loading and output, where \(L\) is the binary encoding length of \(\kappa\)? The exponent and constants must be independent of every parameter and of the unknown distribution. This retains the general sample-optimal computational question from the source’s conclusion; bounded-degree recovery is already treated there. The minimax definition does not presume that the commonly quoted \(d\log p/\kappa^2\) sample scale is sharp in all joint parameter regimes.
cards.definitions:
A member \(P\) of \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) is \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\), where \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\) is arbitrary, \(\Sigma\) is a real symmetric positive definite \(p\times p\) covariance matrix, and \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\) is its precision matrix. Its undirected graph has vertices \([p]=\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and an edge \(\{i,j\}\), for \(i\ne j\), exactly when \(\Theta_{ij}\ne0\). Every vertex has at most \(d\) neighbors, and every edge satisfies \[\frac{|\Theta_{ij}|}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\ge\kappa.\] This normalized precision entry is the magnitude of the corresponding partial correlation. For an empty graph the edge condition holds vacuously. The parameters are upper and lower promises, not assertions that degree equals \(d\) or minimum strength equals \(\kappa\). No eigenvalue, condition-number, variance, sign-pattern, incoherence, faithfulness, treewidth or walk-summability restriction is imposed. The learner is not given \(\mu,\Sigma,\Theta\), or a graph representation.

An observation is an entire vector \(X\in\mathbb R^p\) drawn from \(P\); observations are independent and identically distributed. The graph-recovery loss is zero exactly when all off-diagonal zero/nonzero decisions are correct, and one otherwise. Estimating covariance entries to a numerical tolerance is a different task. The probability in the guarantee includes the observations and internal randomness. The public failure tolerance is \(2^{-r}\); allowing all integers \(r\ge2\) keeps confidence variable. The graph output is its \(p\times p\) symmetric binary adjacency matrix with zero diagonal.

For a fixed \((p,d,\kappa,r)\), define \(m^*\) as the least nonnegative integer \(m\) for which some Borel-measurable randomized estimator from \((\mathbb R^p)^m\) to the finite set of labeled undirected graphs satisfies \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)}\Pr_{X_1,\ldots,X_m\sim P}[\widehat G(X_1,\ldots,X_m)=G(P)]\ge1-2^{-r}.\] Randomization is an independent infinite fair-bit sequence, and the estimator must be measurable jointly in data and that sequence. It may depend arbitrarily on the four public parameters and has no computation bound; this defines an information benchmark, not a computational oracle. If the set of such sample counts were empty, set \(m^*=+\infty\); known finite sample upper bounds exclude that case for this family. The target algorithm receives neither \(m^*\) nor an optimal estimator. Its sample limit must hold on every possible observation and coin history, even if it adaptively decides when to stop. Padding an early stop with unused observations makes comparison with fixed-size estimators unambiguous.

Computation uses an explicitly chosen standard exact-real arithmetic convention. One finite uniform register program has rational constants in its code, discrete control and fair random bits. Copying, \(+,-,\times,\div\), comparison, branching and each control or output operation cost one unit; any division must be guarded at a zero denominator. Loading one observed vector costs \(p\) units. The algorithm outputs only finite bits for the adjacency matrix. It has no access to conditional samples, a Markov transition trajectory, matrix entries of the unknown distribution, exact expectations, optimization oracles, arbitrary real advice, floor/digit extraction, or an oracle deciding general real-number properties. The positive integers \(p,d,r\) are public unary inputs and \(\kappa\) is supplied by positive coprime binary numerator and denominator, with total bit length \(L\). Reading and translating these inputs are counted. The displayed worst-case operation bound applies to all sample and random-bit histories, not just in expectation.

This convention makes the source’s continuous-observation computational question precise without asserting equivalence to finite-bit Gaussian data. Exact Gaussian coordinates are generally not finite binary strings; the source does not prescribe a rounding budget. In particular, allowing arbitrary condition numbers in the distribution is material to numerical implementation. Any finite-precision result, or computational hardness assumption in another machine model, needs a justified relation to this arithmetic convention before it resolves the displayed proposition. Polynomial time means a single fixed exponent for variable \(d\); \(p^{O(d)}\) is insufficient. Sample optimality means a universal multiplicative factor, with no suppressed dependence on \(d,\kappa,r\) or logarithmic loss.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the existence proposition or its full negation. An affirmative result must supply one uniform algorithm and constants, prove exact graph recovery over the entire promised Gaussian family, prove the universal constant-factor comparison with the defined information-theoretic minimum, and verify worst-case sample and arithmetic-time bounds. A negative result must rule out every such learner and constants on some allowed parameters or distribution. A conditional computational obstruction remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A \(p^{O(d)}\) method, a result only for a fixed degree, a polynomial-time method using more than a universal-factor sample overhead, or a theorem with extra spectral/sign assumptions does not suffice. Neither does learning from a Glauber trajectory establish the independent-observation guarantee. A closed form for \(m^*\) is useful but is not assumed in advance; any claimed closed form must be proved uniformly in its stated regime. The answer is an exact yes/no theorem, not a numerical estimate of a covariance matrix.
cards.why: Sparse conditional dependence can be statistically identifiable even when variables are extremely correlated. Recovering that graph from few observations is useful only if the necessary search is computationally affordable. The problem asks whether uniformly efficient computation must pay an extra sample cost without regularity assumptions on the covariance.

cards.context:
The graph records conditional dependence, not merely pairwise correlation: an edge is determined by a nonzero entry of the inverse covariance matrix. Strong correlations and poor conditioning are allowed. This explains why guarantees depending only on dimension, sparsity and normalized edge strength are stronger than many familiar covariance-estimation results.

The source’s DICE theorem gives exact recovery when \(m>2d+192\kappa^{-2}d\log p+64\kappa^{-2}\log(4d/\delta)\). Its neighborhood-search cost is \(O(p^{2d+1})\). Thus fixed-degree graphs have a polynomial-time guarantee, but the exponent is not uniform over growing degree.

The source explicitly qualifies statistical tightness when degree grows while minimum edge strength shrinks. Therefore its motivating abstract sentence cannot be read as an unresolved bounded-degree theorem, or its sample bound as a universally matching minimax formula. The current question retains the general computational issue using an explicit minimax benchmark.

Kelner–Koehler–Meka–Moitra provide fixed polynomial-time algorithms without condition-number bounds for attractive and walk-summable Gaussian models. These are genuine positive results for additional structural subclasses. Their assumptions do not cover every signed precision matrix in the present family.

COLT 2024 Kelner–Koehler–Meka–Rohatgi, Remark 43, gives conditional evidence of a sample-computation gap. Under its Conjecture 33 relating low-degree likelihood tests to polynomial-time detection for a spiked Wishart model, efficient general recovery would need nearly quadratic rather than linear dependence on sparsity in the relevant regime, even at constant normalized edge strength. The conjecture is not a proved theorem about arbitrary algorithms.

The hard family in that remark has covariance equal to identity plus a negative rank-one perturbation supported on a hidden sparse set. Exact graph recovery would distinguish it from the independent-coordinate null model. This is a stated reduction under a specific detection-hardness conjecture, not an unconditional archive-worthy impossibility. Its computational convention must also match any use against the real-arithmetic target.

The 2026 Shen–Wu–Majid–Moitra paper gives a polynomial-time method observing one Glauber trajectory, where coordinates are successively resampled conditional on the others. Its introduction still identifies efficient recovery from few independent samples as unresolved. A trajectory exposes update information that independent observations do not provide, so the newer theorem does not automatically answer the present question.

cards.title: Nontrivial agnostic membership-query learning of \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)
cards.formal: Can polynomial-size constant-depth modular circuits be agnostically learned under uniform inputs using membership queries in time \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\)? Precisely, for every fixed depth bound \(d\ge1\), fixed modulus \(m\ge2\), and fixed integer size exponent \(k\ge1\), do there exist one uniform randomized oracle Turing machine \(A_{d,m,k}\), an integer \(n_0\), and a saving function \(\sigma:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(\sigma(n)/\log_2 n\to\infty\) and the following holds? For every \(n\ge n_0\) and every joint distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\times\{-1,+1\}\) whose first marginal is uniform, \(A_{d,m,k}\), given \(1^n\) and the conditional-label oracle described below, runs in worst-case time at most \(2^{n-\sigma(n)}\) and outputs a hypothesis \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr\left[\operatorname{corr}_D(h)\ge \max_{c\in\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)}\operatorname{corr}_D(c)-2^{-n^{99/100}}\right]\ge\frac13,\qquad \operatorname{corr}_D(g):=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim D}[g(x)y].\] All machine coins and oracle responses are included in this probability. The success constant \(1/3\) is the literal consequence of the source’s full-learning convention \(1-\delta\) and its assignment \(\delta=2/3\); it is recorded explicitly rather than silently exchanged with the separate weak-learning convention.
cards.definitions:
An \(\operatorname{ACC}_{d,m,k}(n)\) circuit is a finite acyclic circuit with \(n\) input bits, constants, unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates, one-input NOT gates, and unbounded-fan-in \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gate returns one exactly when the number of its one-valued inputs is divisible by \(m\). There are at most \(d\) gates along each input-to-output path and at most \(n^k\) internal gates and wires in total. Its output bit is converted to \(-1,+1\) by \(b\mapsto2b-1\). Fix an effective binary encoding of gates and their ordered incoming wires. These fixed-depth, fixed-modulus, polynomial-size classes give the usual \(\mathrm{ACC}^0\) target when the fixed parameters vary. Gate-count versus wire-count conventions change polynomial size exponents only; the question quantifies over every exponent. The parameters are fixed before input length and may determine the learner and its saving; neither depth nor modulus grows with \(n\). Hidden comparator circuits may be chosen independently at different lengths and need not form a uniformly constructible family. No target circuit description is given to the learner.

The joint distribution \(D\) is otherwise arbitrary. For each chosen query \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\), the oracle returns one fresh label sampled from \(D(Y\mid X=z)\), independently of its earlier samples conditional on the submitted queries. Queries may adapt to previous answers, and repeated queries need not agree. The uniform marginal gives every \(z\) positive probability, so all conditional label distributions are defined. Labels may be deterministic, stochastic, noisy, or inconsistent with every comparator circuit; no realizability promise is made. The learner knows the uniform marginal and can itself draw uniform inputs. It has no sampler description for the label probabilities, equivalence oracle, circuit advice, or oracle access to an optimal comparator. Correlation lies in \([-1,1]\), and the maximum exists because the comparator set is finite and nonempty. For \(\{-1,+1\}\)-valued functions, zero-one error equals \((1-\operatorname{corr})/2\); thus the displayed correlation slack is excess prediction error at most \(2^{-n^{99/100}}/2\), rather than a multiplicative approximation to optimum error.

The output is a finite description of an ordinary Boolean circuit with AND, OR and NOT gates, interpreted as \(h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{-1,+1\}\). The hypothesis need not be an ACC circuit, have depth \(d\), or have size \(n^k\); this is improper learning. Its description is counted in the learner’s running time, and it is evaluated without further training queries. Using ordinary finite circuits makes the usual effectively evaluable hypothesis convention explicit. All query writing and reading, fair random bits, bit computation and output writing count toward worst-case running time; one submitted label is one oracle response, and the oracle’s internal generation cost is not charged. Consequently the number of queries is bounded by the same time. There is no real-arithmetic unit-cost computation in the learner. The exponential accuracy threshold is a mathematical success condition fixed by \(n\), not an exact irrational input that must be encoded or compared by the machine.

The expression \(2^n/n^{\omega(1)}\) means that a single learner for each fixed \((d,m,k)\) has a saving \(\sigma(n)\) whose ratio to \(\log_2 n\) tends to infinity: for every real \(B>0\), eventually \(\sigma(n)\ge B\log_2 n\). The saving is a runtime-bound witness, not an additional oracle or input. Finite exceptional lengths are allowed. A fixed-factor improvement or division by one fixed power of \(n\) is insufficient. Polynomial factors in an otherwise qualifying time can be absorbed into a smaller saving with the same limit. No efficient procedure for constructing the learner uniformly from the fixed depth, modulus and size exponent is additionally requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence statement, or of its full logical negation: some fixed \((d,m,k)\) admits no uniform learner with the stated eventual superlogarithmic saving and correlation guarantee simultaneously for all uniform-marginal label distributions. A positive answer must meet the specified shrinking accuracy, the literal full-learning success constant, the conditional-query interface and worst-case total time, including a finite evaluable output. Constant-error learning, realizable-only learning, a fixed polynomial-factor saving or a multiplicative optimum-error factor does not meet this agnostic target. A lower bound against a restricted query method or a conditional cryptographic obstruction is not the unconditional negation unless the additional assumption is also proved. This is an exact asymptotic yes/no statement, not a request to approximate a numerical quantity.
cards.why: Constant-depth circuits with modular gates are a central boundary class in circuit complexity. The question asks whether their predictive structure can be exploited even when labels need not come from that class and the learner may choose its queries. The requested saving must beat every fixed polynomial factor relative to the exponential scale while retaining the source’s high-accuracy guarantee.

cards.context:
Agnostic learning compares the returned predictor with the best member of a chosen circuit class, while allowing the observed labels to be generated by an arbitrary process. Membership queries let the learner choose which input is labeled; they do not reveal a target circuit or guarantee that an exact circuit representation exists. The original paper fixes both the extremely small correlation slack and the confidence parameter when defining its nontrivial-time problem.

The source explicitly states that the ACC⁰ problem is open even with uniform inputs and even without the agnostic requirement. This card retains the agnostic question selected in its title and records the source’s uniform-input version. It does not replace the comparator by only prime-modulus circuits or by a restricted family of symmetric-polynomial gates.

Carmosino–Impagliazzo–Kabanets–Kolokolova obtain quasipolynomial-time query learning for prime-modulus AC⁰[q] with a polylogarithmic multiplicative factor on optimum error. That is a meaningful earlier result, but both the restricted modulus and the multiplicative error criterion differ from full ACC⁰ agnostic learning with the additive slack specified here.

Karchmer’s positive results treat several circuit classes built from restricted low-degree threshold or symmetric-polynomial functions. Those classes include functions outside earlier families, but the published statement does not contain all polynomial-size ACC⁰ circuits. The paper separately identifies that missing full class as a frontier question.

The full-learning definition gives success at least 1−δ and then sets δ to 2/3. The separate weak-learner definition uses success at least 2/3. These are distinct displays in the source. This record preserves the literal full-learning guarantee 1/3 and marks the convention explicitly; it does not assume a typographical correction or silently use the weak definition as the target.

The original arXiv record still lists only its November 2023 version, and the checked published ALT 2024 text contains the question. Bounded later-work searches through September 2026 found no matching theorem, but that search is not a proof of continued openness. Current status is therefore recorded as uncertain.

cards.title: Linear conditional-information bounds for VC learning
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(c>0\) such that the following holds? For every nonempty Boolean hypothesis class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), and every integer \(n\ge d\), there is a proper randomized learner \(A:(X\times\{0,1\})^n\to H\) satisfying both \[\forall P,\quad \operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)\le cd\] and \[\forall s\in(X\times\{0,1\})^n,\quad \mathbb E_{W\sim A(s)}\widehat L_s(W)\le\inf_{h\in H}\widehat L_s(h)+c\sqrt{d/n}?\] The first quantifier ranges over all labeled-data distributions in the measurable model below, including nonrealizable distributions. The second ranges over every deterministic sample, including samples with conflicting labels. The same learner must satisfy both guarantees; it may depend on \(H,n\), but not on \(P\). This is the original source’s main agnostic Conjecture 6, recovered from the imported introduction excerpt, not its different realizable or improper variants.
cards.definitions:
A hypothesis is a total function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\). A finite set \(V\subseteq X\) is shattered if every map \(V\to\{0,1\}\) is the restriction of a hypothesis in \(H\); the VC dimension is the supremum of sizes of shattered finite sets. For a labeled sequence \(s=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n\), its empirical zero-one loss is \(\widehat L_s(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{h(x_i)\ne y_i\}\). Samples are ordered and may contain repeated points. Proper means that every output is a member of \(H\), rather than an arbitrary Boolean predictor. The expected empirical loss averages only the learner’s private randomness, with the input sequence held fixed. There is no running-time, finite encoding, efficient evaluation, or finite/countable-domain restriction.

The following explicit measurable-kernel convention makes the source’s probability notation meaningful. Equip \(X\) and the hypothesis space \(H\) with sigma-algebras for which evaluation \((h,x)\mapsto h(x)\) is jointly measurable; binary labels have all subsets. The statement quantifies over such measurable presentations of the classes. A randomized learner is a probability kernel from the product sample space into \(H\): for each input it assigns a probability distribution on \(H\), and probabilities of measurable output events vary measurably with the input. Deterministic learners are included. All distributions \(P\) on the labeled product space are allowed. This is a stated probability-interface convention, not a finite-domain specialization, a premise that a measurable empirical-risk minimizer exists, or a claim about nonmeasurable learning rules. It should be retained explicitly in a formalization.

For \(\operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)\), draw a supersample \(\widetilde Z=(Z_{i,b})_{1\le i\le n,\ b\in\{0,1\}}\) of \(2n\) independent labeled examples from \(P\), and independently draw a uniformly random selector \(B\in\{0,1\}^n\). Let \(\widetilde Z_B=(Z_{i,B_i})_{i=1}^n\), then draw \(W\) from the kernel \(A(\widetilde Z_B)\) using no access to the unselected examples. Define \[\operatorname{CMI}_{P}(A)=I(W;B\mid\widetilde Z)=n-H(B\mid W,\widetilde Z)\] in bits. Here \(H(B\mid W,\widetilde Z)=\mathbb E[-\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^n}p_b\log_2 p_b]\), where \(p_b=\mathbb E[\mathbf1\{B=b\}\mid\sigma(W,\widetilde Z)]\), and \(0\log_2 0=0\). This finite-selector definition uses conditional expectation and does not need pointwise conditional densities on arbitrary domains. The quantity lies between zero and \(n\). It measures the complete hypothesis-valued output \(W\) under its stated measurable structure, not merely the labels it predicts on the supersample and not the learner’s unreleased random seed. Changing logarithm base only rescales the universal constant. The learner cannot see \(P\), the supersample or selector as additional inputs. The accuracy slack and information constant are uniform over all classes, dimensions and sample sizes; a bound with an extra \(\log n\), or with a class-dependent constant, is a different assertion.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of Conjecture 6 in the explicitly stated probability convention, or prove its logical negation. A positive answer supplies one universal \(c\) and a proper probability kernel for every admitted \(H,n\), with the distribution-uniform CMI bound and pointwise empirical-loss bound both established. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(c>0\), some admitted class and sample size defeat every proper kernel: either some distribution violates the information bound, or some deterministic sample violates the expected empirical-loss bound. A counterexample only to exact consistency or to empirical loss \(O(d/n)\) does not refute the allowed \(O(\sqrt{d/n})\) slack here. A generalization bound using a different information quantity, an improper output, or a distribution-dependent learner does not prove this claim. The target is existence with universal constants, not a numerical quantity requiring additive approximation.
cards.why: Classical VC theory controls prediction error through the richness of a class. This question asks whether the same optimal scale can always be realized by a learner whose whole output reveals only a dimension-proportional amount about which examples were used. The joint information and empirical-accuracy requirements make it a statement about the learner itself.

cards.context:
Conditional mutual information exposes two candidates for each training position and measures what the final hypothesis reveals about which candidate was selected. Conditioning on both candidates avoids the unbounded information cost that can arise when an algorithm reveals a real-valued observation under ordinary mutual information.

The source’s Theorem 5 gives an empirical-risk minimizer with conditional information at most \(d\log n+2\), in its logarithm convention. Empirical-risk minimization chooses a hypothesis with the fewest training errors. Conjecture 6 permits a controlled excess in this empirical error while asking that the extra sample-size dependence disappear from the information bound.

The source also states Conjectures 7 and 8 for realizable samples. They demand expected empirical loss \(O(d/n)\), or zero, together with the linear information bound. Haghifam and coauthors’ Theorem 4.2 refutes those two proper-learning claims, even if the information bound is replaced by an arbitrary dimension-only function. Its smaller empirical-loss allowance is essential; that theorem does not supply a refutation of Conjecture 6 as displayed here.

The same lower-bound paper notes that chaining conditional-information analyses yields the optimal \(O(\sqrt{d/n})\) expected generalization scale. That fact concerns the resulting bound on prediction behavior. It does not assert that a single learner’s complete output has CMI at most \(cd\) while satisfying the present pointwise training guarantee.

The 2021 PAC-Bayes/CMI paper’s VC-class Theorem 13 retains an information term \(d\log(2n)\). This extends information-based generalization guarantees, but it does not remove the sample-size dependence required to answer Conjecture 6.

cards.title: PAC learning of finite automata under the uniform distribution
cards.formal: Are deterministic finite automata efficiently PAC learnable from independent uniformly distributed words and their acceptance bits? Use the ordinary finite-word, fixed-length uniform model. Does there exist one randomized classical Turing machine \(L\) and one polynomial \(p\) such that, for every alphabet size \(q\ge2\), word length \(n\ge1\), state bound \(s\ge1\), integers \(a,b\ge3\), and deterministic finite automaton \(M\) with at most \(s\) states over \(\Sigma_q=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), the following holds? Given \(1^q,1^n,1^s,1^a,1^b\) and access only to independent examples \((w,M(w))\) with \(w\sim U_{q,n}\), \(L\) runs in worst-case time at most \(p(q+n+s+a+b)\), and outputs a finite predictor \(h\) satisfying \[\Pr_{L,\,\mathrm{examples}}\left[\Pr_{w\sim U_{q,n}}[h(w)\ne M(w)]\le\frac1a\right]\ge1-\frac1b?\] The predictor may use any efficiently evaluable representation; it need not be an automaton. A 2021 theorem rules out this guarantee under a specified local-pseudorandom-generator assumption, already for binary alphabets. This card retains the unconditional algorithm-existence question, while recording that published conditional negative answer explicitly.
cards.definitions:
A deterministic finite automaton is a tuple \(M=(\Sigma_q,Q,q_0,F,\tau)\) with a nonempty finite state set \(Q\), \(|Q|\le s\), initial state \(q_0\in Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), and a total transition function \(\tau:Q\times\Sigma_q\to Q\). Starting at \(q_0\), it reads the letters of a finite word from left to right and updates its current state by \(\tau\); \(M(w)=1\) exactly when its final state lies in \(F\), and otherwise \(M(w)=0\). The target transition table, states and accepting set are hidden. The public value \(s\) is an upper bound on the number of states, not the full target description. The source’s size convention is state count. A complete transition-table encoding has length polynomial in \(s\) and \(q\), so the explicit polynomial dependence on both parameters accounts for that representation.

\(U_{q,n}\) assigns probability \(q^{-n}\) to every word in \(\Sigma_q^n\); equivalently its \(n\) letters are independent and uniform in \(\Sigma_q\). Each oracle request supplies a fresh independent word and its deterministic acceptance bit under the same fixed \(M\). The learner may request more independent examples adaptively but cannot select the word to be labeled. It sees neither the final state nor the sequence of intermediate states. There are no membership queries, equivalence queries, counterexamples, nonuniform advice or random-target assumption. The guarantee must hold for every automaton, including arbitrarily chosen transition graphs and accepting sets. Randomness in the outer probability comes only from examples and the learner’s independent fair coins; the inner probability is error on a fresh uniform word. This is the realizable PAC model with noiseless labels. Parameters \(1/a\) and \(1/b\) range over inverse integers, which suffice to express every desired positive accuracy and failure tolerance by rounding downward.

For a concrete hypothesis interface, encode each letter in \(\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits and let the output be an ordinary Boolean circuit on the resulting \(n\lceil\log_2 q\rceil\) bits. Its output on valid word encodings is \(h(w)\); values on unused letter codes are irrelevant. The circuit may use two-input AND/OR, one-input NOT and constant gates with a fixed effective binary encoding. Its description is written within the learning-time bound and is evaluated without examples or access to the target. This expresses unrestricted improper efficient prediction: the output is not constrained to at most \(s\) states or to a minimal consistent automaton. Uniformly polynomial-time evaluable finite predictors have ordinary polynomial-size circuit representations under the usual bit-computation convention. All bit operations, reading examples, fair random bits and output writing count toward the one polynomial bound, as does the number of example requests. The example oracle supplies the promised distribution; its own sampling computation is not charged. The same machine and polynomial work for all displayed parameters, lengths and targets.

Uniformity refers to words of the specified length, not to an impossible probability measure assigning equal mass to all of \(\Sigma_q^*\). The learner may depend on the public \(n\), and its guarantee is only over words of that length. Exact identification of the complete infinite regular language, prediction simultaneously at every length by one output, geometric length mixtures, and real-valued limit-average behavior on infinite words are different tasks. The arbitrary-finite-alphabet convention follows the source’s DFA and \(U^n\) definitions; the later hardness theorem applies already when \(q=2\). Computational efficiency is essential: the question does not merely ask for a finite or polynomial information-theoretic sample bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of \(L,p\) with the complete uniform guarantee in Lean, or prove its logical negation: for every proposed machine and polynomial, some allowed parameters and target violate the runtime, finite-output or PAC condition. A positive answer must allow every target automaton and observe only independent acceptance-labeled uniform words. A result for random transition graphs, additional state labels, membership queries or only a fixed bounded state count does not meet the statement. A negative answer under the local-PRG assumption is a conditional theorem and must retain that premise; it does not by itself prove the unconditional negation. Hardness of finding a smallest consistent DFA also does not exclude an arbitrary efficient predictor. The yes/no assertion has exact logical quantifiers and rational error/confidence tolerances; no numerical optimum is being approximated.
cards.why: Finite-state machines give very small descriptions of potentially complicated behavior on long strings. This question isolates whether uniformly random training words make that behavior computationally learnable from acceptance labels alone. It separates the simplicity of the sampling distribution from the difficulty of recovering a useful predictor.

cards.context:
The 2019 source studies weighted limit-average automata, but its related-work paragraph cites Pitt’s older question about ordinary deterministic automata. The imported card refers to that ordinary Boolean acceptance problem. The paper’s own infinite-word impossibility and minimization results concern a different model and do not answer the selected question.

Knowing that every finite automaton has a finite transition table does not imply a polynomial learning algorithm. There are only finitely many targets at a fixed state bound, but computationally finding a useful predictor is a stronger requirement than having enough examples to identify one statistically. The target permits improper prediction and therefore does not ask for minimum-state reconstruction.

Daniely–Vardi Theorem 12 proves a conditional obstruction substantially stronger than failure of high-accuracy PAC learning: for every constants c, η>0, no efficient learner achieves error at most 1/2−1/n^c for all n^η-state DFAs under the uniform distribution on n-bit words, under their Assumption 1. The learning model allows arbitrary efficiently evaluable hypotheses. Consequently the obstruction is not merely a lower bound for proper automaton reconstruction.

Assumption 1 is the existence of Goldreich-style local pseudorandom generators with every constant polynomial stretch: for each constant \(t>1\), some constant locality \(k\) and Boolean predicate \(P\) make the length-\(N^t\) output formed by applying \(P\) to independent random ordered \(k\)-tuples of distinct seed positions computationally indistinguishable from uniform with advantage at most \(1/3\). The chosen tuples are public to the polynomial-time distinguisher. This is an unproved computational assumption, not a consequence of merely defining a finite automaton or a uniform distribution. The exact security convention is the named Assumption 1 of the cited paper; it is not added as a premise of this card’s unconditional target.

The official ALT 2026 paper on learning regular expressions explicitly lists uniform-distribution DFA PAC hardness under its local-PRG Assumption C and attributes that result to Daniely–Vardi. Its additional regular-expression results concern a different succinct representation: equivalent languages can require exponentially different description sizes. Thus the 2026 table corroborates the conditional status rather than proving the cryptographic premise.

Angluin–Chen’s 2015 positive result assumes a random transition graph and access to information about the terminal state reached by a sampled word. The acceptance bit does not identify that state. Likewise, the known polynomial algorithms with membership and equivalence queries use more information than the sampling-only oracle in this card. These distinctions prevent positive results in richer observation models from being substituted for the target.

The historical source described the question as open in 2019; that summary is incomplete after the 2021 conditional hardness theorem. The present record makes this development prominent and keeps current unconditional status uncertain. It does not claim that an unproved local-PRG assumption has been established or that a bounded literature check proves continued unconditional openness.

cards.title: Minimax sample complexity of proper agnostic online reinforcement learning
cards.formal:
For proper agnostic online reinforcement learning in the finite episodic model below, determine \(N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)+1\) up to universal constant factors. Supply one function \(g\) of the given policy tables, layers, start state, horizon and accuracy, and constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) such that
\[c\,g(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\le N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)+1\le C\,g(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\]
for every legal finite instance description and every real \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). Here \(N\) is the minimax number of training episodes. This is the TCS500 benchmark’s quantitative finite-state version of the source question.
cards.definitions:
An instance description specifies a horizon \(H\ge1\), finite nonempty disjoint state layers \(S_1,\ldots,S_H\), a designated initial state \(s_0\) in \(S_1\), a fixed action set {0,1}, and a nonempty finite class \(\Pi\) of deterministic policies. A policy is a table assigning one action to every state; the layer identifies time. The learner receives all these tables. The unknown MDP has arbitrary stochastic transitions from layer h to h+1, and a terminal reward in [0,1] whose distribution depends on the last state and action. Earlier rewards are zero. All probability distributions may have arbitrary real probabilities. The value \(V(\pi)\) is expected terminal reward from \(s_0\).

Each episode starts afresh at \(s_0\) and follows the actual transitions for H steps. The learner observes visited states, chosen actions and the terminal reward. During training it may choose arbitrary randomized actions based on the entire history, including previous episodes. It cannot reset to an intermediate state, sample a chosen transition or inspect the transition/reward tables. There is no computation or policy-evaluation cost restriction: this is statistical complexity with measurable randomized learning rules.

\(N(\Pi,H,\varepsilon)\) is the least nonnegative integer N for which some such rule, after at most N complete episodes, outputs a member \(\hat\pi\) of \(\Pi\) with \(V(\hat\pi)\ge\max_{\pi\in\Pi}V(\pi)-\varepsilon\) with probability at least 2/3, for every MDP on these layers. The layer sets and start state are understood as part of \(\Pi\)’s description. N is finite, since testing every policy separately is allowed.

The required answer supplies an explicit expression or structural parameter g of the policy tables, layers, H and \(\varepsilon\), and universal constants c,C>0 with \(cg\le N+1\le Cg\) for every description. A definition merely repeating the optimization over learners and MDPs is not a determination. The added one handles classes learnable without samples. This narrows the broad characterization request to a specified minimax quantity; dependence on state count is not prohibited in the expression. It fixes proper output, binary actions and terminal rewards rather than silently treating all online RL models as equivalent.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked characterization by one explicitly described \(g\), with matching bounds for \(N+1\) and constants independent of the full instance and accuracy. A singleton policy class has \(N=0\), so the bounds must cover \(N+1=1\) there. Prove the upper bound using episodic online access and a policy in the given class. Prove the lower bound for every allowed learner. The local definitions specify which structural characterizations qualify.
cards.why: A structural characterization would distinguish statistically tractable online reinforcement learning from settings needing stronger access.

cards.title: Dimension complexity of distribution-independent SQ learning
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant \(C>0\) with the following property? For every nonempty set \(X\), every nonempty binary concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^{X}\), every integer \(m\ge1\), tolerance \(0<\tau<1\) and error \(0\le\varepsilon<1/4\), suppose a single randomized statistical-query learner makes at most \(m\) queries of tolerance \(\tau\) and, for every input distribution \(D\), target \(h\in\mathcal H\) and admissible oracle response rule, returns \(\hat h\) with \(\mathbb E[\Pr_{x\sim D}(\hat h(x)\ne h(x))]\le\varepsilon\). Must \(\operatorname{dc}(\mathcal H)\le C m/\tau^{2}\)? The learner is selected before the distribution, target and oracle replies. The constant is independent of all these objects and of the accuracy, domain size and class.
cards.definitions:
Use the discrete measurable structure \(2^{X}\) on an arbitrary domain, and quantify over all countably additive probability measures on it. A tolerance-\(\tau\) query is an arbitrary bounded function \(q:X\times\{-1,+1\}\to[-1,1]\); its answer is any real \(v\) satisfying \(|v-\mathbb E_{x\sim D}q(x,h(x))|\le\tau\). Queries may depend on previous answers and an internal random seed independent of the instance. A response rule can depend on the public history, including the current query, but observes the hidden seed only through that history. It must obey the tolerance at every history that can occur for the fixed distribution and target. The guarantee holds for every such rule, with expectation over the learner's seed. Require the interactions and their resulting loss to be measurable, so that the stated expectations exist. These measurable-interaction conventions specify the source's abstract oracle model. Query count is the resource: there is no restriction on computation between queries, description length, adaptivity, or the class containing the output predictor. There are no free samples or additional distribution information.

The dimension complexity is the least integer \(d\ge0\) for which there is one map \(\phi:X\to\mathbb R^{d}\) such that, for each \(h\in\mathcal H\), some \(w_h\in\mathbb R^{d}\) satisfies \(h(x)=\operatorname{sgn}_{+}(\langle w_h,\phi(x)\rangle)\) for every \(x\in X\). Here \(\operatorname{sgn}_{+}(z)=+1\) when \(z\ge0\), and \(-1\) otherwise, and the inner product is the sum of coordinatewise products. Put \(\operatorname{dc}=+\infty\) if no finite dimension works. The feature map is deterministic, shared by all targets, and independent of \(D\); no construction or efficiency requirement is imposed on it. Offsets require a coordinate of the feature map. The representation must be exact at every point, even though the learner's premise allows positive expected error.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal implication, or of its negation. A positive answer must supply a universal finite \(C\). A negative answer must show that no such constant works: for every \(C>0\), exhibit or prove the existence of a class and admissible learner parameters satisfying the premise but with \(\operatorname{dc}(\mathcal H)>Cm/\tau^{2}\). An infinite dimension example also qualifies. A result assuming extra rank, margin or distribution conditions, or allowing only approximate or random feature representations, does not establish the stated implication.
cards.why: This asks whether learning successfully from noisy expectation information under every distribution forces all targets to share a small linear representation. It connects a general information-access model with the geometric capacity of linear predictors, and tests whether known advantages of learned representations depend essentially on the input distribution.

The source poses separate questions about a specified neural-network training procedure and about statistical queries. This card selects its formal Open Question 2. The broader deep-learning motivation is retained here; the card does not assert that this SQ question is equivalent to the neural-network question.

Learning may choose different predictors after observing different distributions. A low-dimensional representation has a stronger order of choices: the same features must work before either the distribution or the target is selected. Exact representation also concerns points that may have negligible probability in a particular learning instance.

The statistical-query interface permits queries that depend jointly on the example and its label. Restricting queries to a label multiplied by an example function gives a different model. Similarly, replacing the requested bound by an unspecified polynomial, or adding dependence on the domain size, changes the question.

The August 2026 preprint gives a conditional polynomial dimension statement. It assumes a bound on the dimension of a space of averaged terminal predictions; that bound is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence established for arbitrary SQ learners. Its authors explicitly describe the remaining gap to the original question.

A low-dimensional representation has a stronger order of choices: the same features must work before either the distribution or the target is selected. Exact representation also concerns points that may have negligible probability in a particular learning instance.

The statistical-query interface permits queries that depend jointly on the example and its label. Restricting queries to a label multiplied by an example function gives a different model. Similarly, replacing the requested bound by an unspecified polynomial, or adding dependence on the domain size, changes the question.

The August 2026 preprint gives a conditional polynomial dimension statement. It assumes a bound on the dimension of a space of averaged terminal predictions; that bound is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence established for arbitrary SQ learners. Its authors explicitly describe the remaining gap to the original question.

cards.title: Recursive teaching dimension conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(K>0\) such that, for every finite set \(X\) and every finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\), \[\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)\leq K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)?\] Both dimensions are the combinatorial quantities defined below. The constant must be independent of the number of concepts, the domain size and the class itself.
cards.definitions: A concept is a function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\); repeated copies are not distinct concepts. A set \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every Boolean labelling of \(S\) is the restriction of some member of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the largest size of a shattered set, with value zero for the empty class. For a nonempty subclass \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C\) and \(h\in\mathcal D\), put \[t(h,\mathcal D)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \forall g\in\mathcal D,\ g|_S=h|_S\Rightarrow g=h\}.\] These are labelled teaching examples: the labels are those assigned by \(h\). The minimum exists, and for a singleton class it is zero. Set \(t_{\min}(\mathcal D)=\min_{h\in\mathcal D}t(h,\mathcal D)\), and define \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=\max_{\varnothing\ne\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C}t_{\min}(\mathcal D)\), with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\varnothing)=0\). Equivalently, repeatedly remove all concepts of minimum teaching-set size from the current class and take the largest such minimum encountered. No computational-efficiency, random-sampling or teacher-algorithm requirement is imposed. Restricting to finite \(X\) loses no instance for finite concept classes on an arbitrary domain: retain one domain point for each distinct vector of labels across the class. This preserves both dimensions and yields a finite domain.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal linear bound for some finite \(K\), or of its negation. A refutation must establish that for every \(K>0\) there is a finite class of positive VC dimension with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)>K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)\); one class with \(\operatorname{RTD}>\operatorname{VCdim}\) only rules out constant one. The optimal constant need not be determined. A quadratic upper bound, a result for special concept classes, or a lower bound for one teaching-set construction does not resolve the statement.
cards.why: A universal linear bound would connect sample-based combinatorial complexity with the number of examples needed for structured teaching. It asks whether recursive teaching can always be controlled at the same scale as VC dimension.

VC dimension measures how freely a class can realize labels on a chosen set of instances. Teaching instead allows examples tailored to one concept. Its failure would require ratios with no finite upper bound, while an affirmative result would uniformly connect two distinct notions of information needed for learning.

cards.title: Multiclass sample compression from binary compression
cards.formal: Is the following implication valid for every function \(f:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb N_0\)? Suppose every nonempty binary concept class \(B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{U}\) on every nonempty domain \(U\), with finite VC dimension \(v\), admits an exact realizable sample compression scheme of size at most \(f(v)\). Must there exist an integer \(A_f\ge1\) such that every nonempty multiclass concept class \(H\subseteq Y^X\), on arbitrary nonempty sets \(X,Y\) and with finite graph dimension \(d\), admits such a scheme of size at most \[A_f f(d)?\] The constant may depend on the chosen binary bound \(f\), but not on \(X,Y,H,d\), the sample size or the labels occurring in a sample. Label sets may be infinite. No properness, majority-vote form, stability, effectiveness or computational efficiency of the compression schemes is assumed. This restores the hypothesis omitted from the imported source sentence: the question concerns transfer of an arbitrary universal binary compression bound, not just existence of some graph-dimension bound.
cards.definitions: \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A concept is a function assigning a label to every instance. A finite labeled sample is a sequence \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\); repetitions and the empty sample are allowed. It is realizable by \(H\) if a single \(h\in H\) satisfies \(h(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\). A compression scheme for the fixed class is a pair of deterministic set functions \[\kappa:(X\times Y)^*\to(X\times Y)^*\times\{0,1\}^*,\qquad \rho:(X\times Y)^*\times\{0,1\}^*\to Y^X.\] Writing \(\kappa(S)=(S',b)\), every labeled record in \(S'\) must occur in \(S\). Following the source’s explicit convention that subset notation for sequences means inclusion of their underlying sets, the retained list may be reordered and may repeat a retained record. Every occurrence counts toward its length. No new or relabeled record may be introduced. The bit string \(b\) is auxiliary information. Size at most \(s\) means \(|S'|+|b|\le s\) on every finite input sample. The reconstruction receives only \(S',b\), not the original sample, its length, or the original positions of retained records. One retained labeled record costs one unit; one auxiliary bit costs one unit. Domain points and labels are mathematical objects, not charged by bit length. Exact realizable consistency means \(\rho(\kappa(S))(x_i)=y_i\) for every record of every realizable \(S\). The reconstructed function need not belong to \(H\), and no accuracy requirement is imposed on unrealizable samples. Both functions may depend on the complete class, but the same pair must work at all sample sizes. There is no randomness or failure probability. A binary class has VC dimension \(v\) when \(v\) is the largest size of a set of distinct domain points on which all binary label patterns occur. A multiclass class graph-shatters distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\) if there are reference labels \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\in Y\) such that every subset \(I\subseteq[r]\) has a hypothesis with \(h(x_i)=a_i\) exactly for \(i\in I\). The graph dimension is the largest such \(r\). Only classes of finite dimension enter the implication; dimension zero permits a size-zero scheme because all hypotheses agree pointwise. No monotonicity or computability assumption is placed on \(f\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication in Lean, or prove its logical negation. A positive answer must show that every binary bound satisfying the premise transfers with a constant \(A_f\) uniform over all multiclass classes and all sample sizes; an effective black-box procedure is not required. A negative answer must exhibit one function \(f\) that really bounds compression for every binary class as stated, and prove that for every integer \(A\ge1\) some finite-graph-dimension multiclass class admits no compression scheme of size at most \(Af(d)\). Merely showing failure of a particular reduction does not refute the implication. A result with an extra label-count factor, an added structural requirement on the binary reconstruction, or a substituted dimension does not settle this question. The assertion concerns exact consistency and constant-factor size transfer; there is no numerical error tolerance.
cards.why: A general transfer theorem would carry any improvement in binary sample compression to multiclass prediction without a penalty for the number of labels. It would separate the combinatorial difficulty of binary compression from additional requirements imposed by multiclass reconstruction. This matters even though bounded compression at an exponential graph-dimension scale is already known.

cards.context:
Sample compression retains a few labeled examples and a few auxiliary bits, from which a fixed reconstruction rule must recover a predictor agreeing with the entire original realizable sample. It compresses the information needed for consistency, not the literal binary encoding of all discarded data. The size bound must hold regardless of the original sample length.

VC dimension records which binary patterns a class can realize on a finite set. Graph dimension asks which agreement and disagreement patterns with chosen reference labels a multiclass class can realize. These dimensions coincide for binary classes. The target uses graph dimension, not the different dimension characterizing general multiclass learnability.

Theorem 4 of the proceedings paper transfers any binary bound \(f(d)\) to a finite-label multiclass bound \(O(f(d)\log|Y|)\). The question asks whether that extra label-count cost can be removed without assumptions on the binary compression scheme. In the April 2025 revision the same open question is numbered 3.3.

The source removes the extra factor if the available binary reconstruction is proper or is a finite majority vote of class members; that result also covers infinite label sets. Proper means that the reconstructed binary predictor belongs to the class, and majority vote means pointwise voting among finitely many members, with ties assigned zero. The existence of an unrestricted binary compression scheme does not supply either property.

A separate result removes the extra factor for finite label spaces if the binary compressor is stable: removing records outside its retained set leaves its compressed message unchanged. The source treats infinite labels in that direction using a stronger extension of compression to infinite samples. Those are extra premises, so none is silently inserted into this card’s general finite-sample question.

Finite graph dimension already guarantees bounded compression of size \(2^{O(d)}\), and the source also gives size one for graph dimension one. These results do not establish transfer of every potentially smaller binary bound. In particular, proving a new binary bound would answer this card only if its multiclass consequence preserved the requested order.

Pabbaraju’s counterexample concerns multiclass learnability with a different dimension and an infinite label space. The paper explicitly distinguishes finite graph dimension, where bounded compression is available. Thus the broad slogan that multiclass learnability does not imply compression does not refute this finite-graph-dimension reduction.

cards.title: Uniform convergence under Dobrushin dependence
cards.formal: For every \(a\in[0,1)\), does there exist a finite constant \(C_{a}\) such that the following holds uniformly? Let \(m\ge 1\), let H be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions on a measurable instance space X with finite VC dimension d, and let \(P_{m}\) be a joint law of \(S=(Z_{1},\ldots ,Z_{m}), Z_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i})\in X\times \{0,1\}\), whose marginals all equal D and whose total-variation Dobrushin coefficient is at most a. For every \(\delta \in (0,1)\), require \(\Pr _{S\sim P_{m}}[\sup _{h\in H}|L_{S}(h)- L_{D}(h)|>C_{a}\sqrt{(d+\log (2/\delta ))/m}]\le \delta\). Here \(L_{S}\) and \(L_{D}\) are zero-one losses and the conditional-kernel and measurability conventions below are part of the model. This card reads the source’s proposed extension quantitatively, using the iid-order finite-VC rate stated in equation (18) of its full version; it is not merely a claim that some unspecified convergence rate exists.

The admissibility promise is existence of such conditional-kernel versions with \(\max _{i} \sum_{j

Specifying versions on null configurations prevents undefined conditioning from deciding the promise. A finite \(F\subseteq X\) is shattered if every binary labeling of F is the restriction of a member of H. \(\operatorname{VC}(H)\) is the largest size of a shattered set, or infinity if these sizes are unbounded. The hypothesis \(d<\infty\) includes \(d=0\). The constant \(C_{a}\) may depend on the fixed upper bound a and may diverge as a approaches one, but must be independent of \(m,d,\delta ,X,H,D\) and \(P_{m}\). cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of such a constant for every fixed \(a<1\), uniformly over all the displayed models and parameters, or refute this quantified rate. A negative answer must defeat every proposed constant for some fixed \(a<1\). A family with its coefficient tending to one does not by itself suffice. Proving generalization only for a particular learner, a bound depending on the cardinality of H, a slower rate, or a result needing stronger log-influence assumptions does not establish the displayed extension.
cards.why: Would determine whether the standard weak-influence condition suffices for the uniform statistical guarantees that make finite VC dimension useful, beyond the already-known existence of a successful learner.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
cards.definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm{P}\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.
cards.why: One-way functions are a basic foundation for computational pseudorandomness and cryptography. This question asks whether a worst-case separation between decision and verification already forces a function whose efficiently generated outputs resist inversion on average, without a separate cryptographic assumption.
