cards.context:
A one-way function concerns the difficulty of reversing a computation on a randomly generated input. Key agreement concerns a joint distribution generated by two initially independent parties: they must learn the same string while a public observer cannot distinguish it from a fresh uniform string. Hardness of inversion by itself does not directly assert this joint secrecy property.

The secrecy experiment includes the candidate key as well as the transcript. A key can be difficult to recover in full while still revealing predictable bits, so mere resistance to complete key recovery is not the chosen definition. The saved card already required indistinguishability from uniform; this review preserves that stronger standard formulation and makes the probability spaces and adversary-dependent negligible bounds explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established an oracle world in which one-way permutations exist but secure key agreement does not. A one-way permutation is a length-preserving bijective special case of a one-way function. This separates the relativized primitives and obstructs reductions that continue to work in that world. It is not a proof that ordinary one-way functions exist without ordinary key agreement. The author manuscript checked here is dated 28 May 1994; the original conference publication was STOC 1989.

Black-box uselessness asks a further composition question: can adding a one-way-function primitive help obtain key agreement from some auxiliary primitive that did not suffice alone? Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody prove restricted forms, rather than the general statement. Their ITCS 2021 Theorem 17 uses infinitely-often security, perfect correctness and a constant bound on one party’s queries to the one-way-function oracle; the other auxiliary oracle is still available. These restrictions and the paper’s specified reduction notions are part of that theorem. They are not assumptions of this card.

Public-key encryption implies passive key agreement, whereas the target here permits a general polynomial amount of interaction. The two existence questions are therefore closely related but have different conclusions. The agreed key must remain secret only against an observer; this does not assert authentication or security against a party that replaces the messages. The absence of pre-existing shared information is an essential part of the question.

Brzuska, Couteau, Egger and Quach obtain key agreement from one-way functions in a bounded-storage model. Their publisher abstract describes a large public stream and an a priori storage restriction on the observer, and reports polynomial storage gaps. That additional physical resource restriction is absent here: a PPT observer may retain the entire honest transcript. The abstract and publication metadata were checked; this review does not claim to have verified the full bounded-storage construction.

Li, Li, Li and Liu’s August 2026 preprint states a many-round quantum random-oracle impossibility result. With independent initial private states, classical messages, a Boolean-output random oracle and perfect agreement, it claims a classical eavesdropper making \(O((q_A+q_B)^{5})\) oracle queries when the parties make \(q_A,q_B\) quantum queries. The observer is allowed unbounded other computation. The statement was checked in the paper, but its proof was not independently verified. Its oracle, perfect-correctness and query-cost conditions differ from this card’s classical, negligible-error, polynomial-time target.

Li, Ni and Zan’s 2023 preprint explicitly claims public-key encryption from one-way functions. If valid, this would also settle the key-agreement implication. This audit checked the claim but did not verify its proof or find a conclusive later assessment. Its presence therefore changes the recorded scientific status to uncertain; it does not justify archival.

cards.title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function secure against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary imply the existence of an efficiently generated public-key family of one-way permutations on full Boolean cubes, with the same adversary convention? Require a bijection on the entire cube for every key the generator can output, and negligible inversion probability averaged over an honestly generated public key and a uniform input. No trapdoor is required.
cards.definitions:
All inputs and outputs are finite binary strings. Uniform polynomial time means one finite classical Turing program with a polynomial worst-case bit-operation bound in its input length. Randomized programs use independent fair random bits within that bound. A nonuniform polynomial-size adversary is a family of polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with polynomially many random input bits allowed. Its description and any auxiliary advice have polynomial length in the security parameter and may depend on that parameter, but not on independently sampled secret experiment coins.

A function \(\mu:\mathbb N\to[0,1]\) is negligible if, for every integer \(a\ge1\), there exists \(N_a\) such that \(\mu(n)\le n^{-a}\) for all \(n\ge N_a\).

The premise is that a single deterministic polynomial-time program computes a family
\[
 f_n:\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{\ell(n)},
\]
where \(\ell(n)\) is a nonnegative integer, polynomially bounded and computable in polynomial time from \(1^n\), such that every nonuniform polynomial-size randomized family \(I_n\) has negligible success probability in the following experiment. Sample \(X\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), give \((1^n,f_n(X))\) to \(I_n\), and declare its output \(Z\) successful exactly when \(Z\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(f_n(Z)=f_n(X)\). Any preimage counts. The function's description is public, and no injectivity or subexponential hardness is assumed.

The desired permutation family consists of a fixed polynomially bounded integer function \(m(n)\ge n\), computable in polynomial time from \(1^n\), a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm \(\operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\to pk\), and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluation algorithm \(\operatorname{Eval}(1^n,pk,x)\). Let \(K_n\) be the support of Gen: the finite set of keys that occur with positive probability. For every \(n\ge1\) and every \(pk\in K_n\), evaluation on the whole input cube defines a map
\[
 \pi_{n,pk}:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n)},
 \qquad \pi_{n,pk}(x)=\operatorname{Eval}(1^n,pk,x),
\]
and this map must be a bijection. Equivalently, for each output in that cube there is exactly one input in the cube with that output. This is an exact structural property for every generated key, not a property permitted to fail on a negligible fraction of keys or inputs.

One-wayness requires that, for every nonuniform polynomial-size randomized adversary \(A_n\), the probability of the event
\[
 Z=A_n(1^n,pk,\pi_{n,pk}(X))\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \pi_{n,pk}(Z)=\pi_{n,pk}(X)
\]
is negligible in \(n\), where \(pk\leftarrow\operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\), \(X\) is independently uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), and adversary coins are independent. An incorrectly sized or malformed output fails. Each adversary may have its own polynomial resource bound and negligible success bound. The public key and all algorithm descriptions are available to the adversary; the generator's private coins are not supplied.

Full domain refers to each permutation's input and output sets, both the complete Boolean cube. It does not require \(K_n\) to contain all strings of some length, to have efficiently recognizable membership, or to be independent of the construction's building blocks. No requirement is imposed on bijectivity for keys outside \(K_n\), although the evaluation program must still terminate within its polynomial bound on all inputs. No inverse algorithm, secret trapdoor, key recovery or hardness for every individual key is demanded. A trapdoor construction would qualify if its public family has the required properties and satisfies the stated security.

All algorithms and security guarantees are classical. The implication is about existence in the ordinary model with no ideal oracles. It may use the full description of an underlying one-way function, and its polynomial bounds may depend on that function. It is not restricted to a black-box compiler or reduction and assumes no obfuscator, additional cryptographic primitive or stronger security level.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated existence implication, supplying uniform generation and evaluation, the length function, every-key bijectivity and the negligible inversion bound against all stated adversaries; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation in the ordinary computational model.

A restricted-domain permutation or merely injective length-expanding function does not satisfy the target. Additional assumptions must themselves be derived from ordinary one-way functions. An oracle separation or exclusion of a class of black-box constructions is a barrier, not a refutation of this unrestricted implication. Proving that ordinary one-way functions do not exist would establish the implication vacuously, not refute it. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.
cards.why: Determine whether basic average-case inversion hardness necessarily supports efficient bijections, a rigid primitive at the foundation of cryptographic constructions.

cards.context:
A general one-way function can merge distinct inputs and miss possible outputs. A permutation is exactly bijective; its average-case inversion hardness must coexist with a unique preimage for every output.

This target retains a publicly indexed family of permutations of complete Boolean cubes. Sparse input domains, an unkeyed single permutation family, and the distribution or recognition of valid keys are distinct conventions and must be identified when comparing results.

The historical thesis describes its original permutation barrier conditionally on a combinatorial conjecture. Its oracle method studies limits of techniques rather than the unrestricted ordinary-model implication.

Even injective one-way functions expanding their input by only one bit face a fully black-box barrier under the 2011 theorem. The result does not rule out every method that can inspect the underlying code.

The inherited paper has two separate conclusions: an OWF-only black-box barrier that permits domains to depend on the building blocks, and a barrier with oracle-aided obfuscation under a domain-invariance requirement. Combining them into an unrestricted nonexistence theorem would lose essential hypotheses.

The July 2025 theorem gives full-domain trapdoor permutations from subexponentially secure obfuscation and one-way functions. Its stronger output property does not remove either additional premise.

The 2025 paper explains compatibility with the older obfuscation barrier: full input domains do not imply that the valid-key domain is independent of the building blocks. This card places no such invariance condition on valid public keys.

cards.title: Collision-resistant hashing from one-way functions
cards.formal:
In the ordinary classical computational model, is the following existence implication true?
\[\bigl(\exists f\;\operatorname{OWF}(f)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(\exists\operatorname{Gen},H\;\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\bigr).\]
The predicates are defined below. The honest functions and algorithms are uniform and polynomial-time, and security is against every nonuniform family of polynomial-size classical Boolean circuits. The hash family has a freshly sampled public key \(k\) and maps \(H_k:\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\to\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) for every positive integer security parameter \(\lambda\). Both members of a proposed collision may be chosen after the key is known. The implication permits unrestricted constructions and proof techniques, including use of a one-way function's implementation.
cards.definitions:
Parameters and computation. All strings are finite binary strings. The security parameters \(n,\lambda\) range over the positive integers, and \(1^n\) denotes the unary string of \(n\) ones. Honest algorithms are ordinary Turing machines with one fixed finite program, no advice and no oracles. Deterministic algorithms have polynomial bit running time in the total input length. A probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm additionally uses independent fair random bits and has a polynomial running-time bound on every random tape; it therefore uses at most polynomially many random bits. The polynomial and its degree are fixed for each program, independent of the parameter and sampled inputs.

Adversaries. A nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) consists of finite acyclic Boolean circuits over AND, OR, NOT and constant gates, with fan-in at most two and unrestricted fan-out. Size counts all gates and input and output wires, including random input wires. There are constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) such that each size is at most \(C(n+1)^d\). A randomized circuit receives independent uniform bits on its random wires. Circuit descriptions may be arbitrary functions of the parameter and the fixed public honest programs; no algorithm generating the family is required. They are fixed before the fresh challenge or hash key is sampled. Each family has its own polynomial bound.

Finite-string encoding. To supply a string \(z\) of length at most an integer bound \(P\) to a fixed-width circuit, use \(\operatorname{enc}_P(z)\): the binary representation of \(|z|\), padded to exactly \(\lceil\log_2(P+1)\rceil\) bits, followed by \(z\) and enough zero bits to fill a \(P\)-bit data field. Bounds used below are positive integer-valued polynomials. This encoding reveals the string and its length and adds only polynomial overhead. In particular, variable-length function outputs and public keys are not supplied as a length-regularity promise.

Negligibility. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in the security parameter of each experiment.
The threshold may depend on the exponent and the adversary, as well as on the fixed primitive. Security must hold eventually for every parameter, not merely on an infinite subsequence. No fixed inverse-polynomial or constant error is allowed.

One-way function. A candidate \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) is total and uniformly deterministic polynomial-time computable. Fix a positive integer-valued polynomial \(p\) bounding \(|f(x)|\) whenever \(|x|=n\). In its inversion experiment, sample \(X\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^n\), independently sample the circuit's random wires \(R\), and compute exactly once
\[Y=A_n(1^n,\operatorname{enc}_{p(n)}(f(X));R)\in\{0,1\}^n.\]
Define \(\operatorname{Inv}_{f,A}(n)=\Pr[f(Y)=f(X)]\). Then \(\operatorname{OWF}(f)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted family \(A\). Any preimage of the challenge of length \(n\) is accepted; recovery of the original \(X\) is not required. Restricting the circuit output to \(n\) bits only removes invalid answers, which could always be replaced by a fixed \(n\)-bit candidate. The choice of the polynomial padding bound does not change security because valid encodings with different bounds can be converted in polynomial time.

Publicly keyed hash family. A candidate consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time generator \(\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda)\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(H(1^\lambda,k,x)\). There is a fixed positive integer-valued polynomial \(q\) such that every generated key has length at most \(q(\lambda)\). For every key in the support of the generator and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\), the evaluator outputs exactly \(\lambda\) bits. Write \(H_k(x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x)\) when the parameter is understood. No evaluator property is required for keys outside that support. The key need not be uniform over all strings; its actual distribution is the output of the generator. It is fully public, and evaluation needs no secret.

Collision experiment. Independently sample the generator's random tape \(S\) and the adversary's random wires \(R\), set \(k=\operatorname{Gen}(1^\lambda;S)\), and compute exactly once
\[(x,x')=B_\lambda(1^\lambda,\operatorname{enc}_{q(\lambda)}(k);R)\in\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\times\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}.\]
Define
\[\operatorname{Coll}_{\operatorname{Gen},H,B}(\lambda)=\Pr[x\ne x'\ \land\ H(1^\lambda,k,x)=H(1^\lambda,k,x')].\]
The predicate \(\operatorname{CRH}(\operatorname{Gen},H)\) means this probability is negligible for every permitted circuit family \(B\). The adversary can compute the public evaluator within its circuit budget and select both inputs as functions of the key. It does not receive the generator's private random tape. Fixed-width candidate outputs again lose no successful attacks.

Scope of the implication. Existence of any one-way function in this model is the only cryptographic hypothesis. The conclusion is existence of some secure hash family; it need not be a particular proposed transformation applied to every one-way function. There is no requirement that a single algorithm transform arbitrary program descriptions into hash-family descriptions. No random oracle, trusted setup, quantum computation, extra hardness assumption or stronger exponential-security requirement is supplied. The all-parameter, nonuniform security and exact factor-two compression conventions are retained from the inherited card.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish the existence of the specified public-key generator and evaluator from the one-way-function hypothesis alone, including uniform polynomial-time computability, exact compression for every generated key, and negligible collision success against every nonuniform polynomial-size circuit family. All transformations of parameters and security guarantees used in that proof must be justified. A proof may use function implementations and need not be black-box.

The logical negation requires proving both that a one-way function exists and that no hash family satisfying this model exists. For the latter assertion, every pair of uniform polynomial-time programs meeting the hash syntax must admit a permitted circuit family with nonnegligible collision probability. Equivalently, for each such pair there must be an adversary and a fixed \(c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\) whose success exceeds \(\lambda^{-c}\) for infinitely many \(\lambda\). Merely proving that a chosen construction fails, even for one secure one-way function, is insufficient.

An oracle world separating these primitives or an impossibility theorem restricted to black-box reductions establishes a barrier, not this ordinary-model negation. Target-collision resistance, resistance only to finding three or more colliding inputs, injective noncompressing functions, security only for uniform adversaries or only infinitely often, and constructions assuming quantitative product hardness do not meet the full conclusion. This is an exact yes-or-no implication, with no additive numerical tolerance on the security requirement.
cards.why: Determines whether a fundamental compressing cryptographic primitive needs assumptions beyond ordinary one-wayness, while exposing the gap between known black-box barriers and unrestricted constructions.

cards.context:
A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are \(2^{2\lambda}\) possible inputs and only \(2^{\lambda}\) outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi construct collision-resistant hashing under stronger assumptions on simultaneously inverting independently sampled challenges. Their Theorem I.5 uses symmetric injective two-product functions whose batch inversion probability is at most \(2^{-n-\omega(\log n)}\) for polynomial-time attackers; a separate theorem treats noninjective functions under stronger quantitative hardness. Ordinary one-wayness only requires a negligible single-challenge inversion probability. The product assumption is therefore additional structure and security, not an established consequence of the hypothesis on this card.

Collision finding is also a total search problem: an explicitly represented shrinking circuit always has two distinct inputs with the same output, and a proposed pair can be checked efficiently. The published ITCS 2024 paper of Folwarczný and coauthors extends separation results to a restricted class of reductions for total NP search. Its main condition permits a single call to a total-search solver and no query to the one-way function before that call. The result includes semi-black-box reductions, but is still a limitation on a specified reduction model.

Mao and Zhang's March 2026 manuscript, published on ECCC in April, reports a further black-box hierarchy: for every fixed \(K\ge2\), \(K\)-collision resistance cannot be constructed fully black-box from \((K+1)\)-collision resistance in their model. Here an attacker seeks \(K\) distinct inputs with one common hash value. In particular, hardness of finding a triple does not give a black-box construction of hardness of finding a pair. The paper also separates distributional collision resistance from three-collision resistance. These are barriers among weaker primitives; the ordinary unrestricted implication from one-way functions remains open in the introduction.

Rothblum's July 2026 manuscript reports interactive arguments for deterministic computations taking time \(T\) and space \(S\), assuming one-way functions. The communication is \(S\operatorname{poly}(\log T,\kappa)\), the verifier time is \((S+n)\operatorname{poly}(\log T,\kappa)\), and the number of rounds is polylogarithmic in \(T\). Soundness loses a factor polynomial in \(T\) in the adversary-size bound. This weakens assumptions for an interactive application; its use of target-collision-resistant hashing does not supply full public-key collision resistance.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

cards.title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply the existence of an IND-CPA-secure, compact, unleveled fully homomorphic bit-encryption scheme for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with the algorithms and security convention below?
cards.definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. A public-key bit-encryption scheme consists of \(Gen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,b)=c\) for \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\in \{0,1,\perp\}\). There is one negligible \(
u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))
e b]\le
u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. In the IND-CPA experiment Gen is run, the adversary receives pk and selects bits \(b_{0},b_{1}\) and a state, an independent uniform \( eta \in \{0,1\}\) is chosen, \(c=Enc(pk,b_{ eta})\) is returned, and the adversary outputs \( eta '\). Require \(|\Pr[ eta\prime= eta]-1/2|\) to be negligible. The adversary may perform any polynomial number of public encryptions on its own before and after the challenge. There is no decryption oracle. Bit encryption suffices; longer messages are represented by bit lists. For FHE, Gen outputs (pk,evk,sk); the evaluation key evk is public and is included with pk in the IND-CPA experiment. Gen receives no circuit size or depth bound. Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)) outputs one ciphertext for a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{t}	o \{0,1\}\), encoded as an acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuit with listed wires. For every polynomial s there is a negligible \(
u _{s}\) such that for every \(\lambda\), every such C of description length and input count at most \(s(\lambda )\), and every \(m\in \{0,1\}^{t}\), independently of the generated keys, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Eval}(evk,C,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_t)))
e C(m)]\le
u_s(\lambda)\). The probability includes key generation, fresh encryption coins for each bit, and evaluation coins. Eval’s time is polynomial in the entire supplied circuit and ciphertext encoding, with one algorithm for all C. There is one polynomial q, independent of C,t and s, bounding every evaluated ciphertext length and its decryption time by \(q(\lambda )\); keys also have polynomial length. The scheme must also correctly decrypt fresh encryptions. Multiple output bits mean separate output ciphertexts, so compactness scales linearly with output length. Only the usual one-evaluation correctness contract is required; no circuit privacy or additional guarantee for arbitrary malformed or previously evaluated ciphertexts is imposed. The assertion is an existence implication between these two primitives in the classical standard model; it permits non-black-box constructions and supplies no extra setup, ideal oracle, circular-security or number-theoretic assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the existence implication, including the specified correctness, security and circuit-independent compactness bounds, or a Lean refutation of that implication. The target uses no supplied depth bound at key generation. An extra cryptographic premise or a separation restricted to black-box constructions does not settle this unrestricted implication.

cards.title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
cards.definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count. These are the concrete synopsis, privacy and sample-size conventions already selected for this card in September 2026; they are not claimed equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order variant of the source question.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this existence statement or its logical negation in Lean. A positive answer must exhibit the fixed uniform machines, exponent, polynomial resource bounds and vanishing error function and prove both privacy and simultaneous accuracy on every valid database. A negative answer must exclude all such choices; hardness only under an unproved cryptographic assumption proves the corresponding conditional obstruction, not the unconditional negation. Fixed positive error, accuracy only for most queries or typical databases, a polynomial number of interactive queries, or a runtime polynomial in the exponential number of all query answers does not meet the stated criterion. The target is the existence of a vanishing-error polynomial-time synopsis, rather than a numerical value requiring additive \(1/100\) determination.
cards.why: Marginals are basic summaries of relationships among attributes. The question asks whether the large information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional data can be captured by a compact, efficiently evaluated object using polynomially many records. It isolates a statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete query family while allowing outputs more flexible than synthetic datasets.

cards.context:
A marginal measures how often a selected pattern occurs in a set of attributes. Low-order queries concern small attribute groups; this problem includes every order. There are exponentially many queries, but each query has a short description. Polynomial running time therefore requires a reusable compact synopsis with a query evaluator, rather than an explicit table of all answers.

Privacy and accuracy concern different quantifiers. Changing one person’s entire row must leave the output distribution nearly unchanged. For each fixed database, a single successful synopsis must answer every query accurately at once. Evaluating it after release accesses no additional records. A guarantee for each query separately with a fresh failure probability would not give the requested simultaneous event.

Vadhan’s 2017 open question asks for vanishing error with polynomially many records and polynomial computation. The current card retains the previously approved approximate-privacy parameters and a noninteractive binary synopsis. The survey’s alternative question about some growing but restricted order is not substituted for the all-orders requirement.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give a subexponential per-query algorithm on small databases. Theorem 1.1 handles a sequence of adaptively chosen marginal queries at fixed absolute error and its database-size guarantee depends on the length of that sequence. This is meaningful progress, but is not a polynomial-time construction of one synopsis answering all orders with vanishing error.

The survey’s synthetic-data hardness theorem assumes one-way functions and restricts the output to a new database, even for two-way marginals. It does not rule out an arbitrary synopsis: the survey explicitly contrasts that obstruction with efficient nonsynthetic answers to low-order marginals. The benchmark deliberately retains this broader output interface.

The checked December 2025 weighted-Fourier paper provides exact optimality for weighted or maximum noise variance within Gaussian factorization mechanisms. Its runtime is polynomial in the dataset and the explicit output/workload size. For the entire \(3^{d}\)-query family that size is exponential, and variance optimality within that mechanism class is not a general polynomial-synopsis theorem or impossibility result.

cards.title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme imply the existence of an IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption scheme in the plain model, with correctness and classical security as defined below, against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries? The sole premise is ordinary chosen-plaintext-secure public-key encryption, and the conclusion is full adaptive chosen-ciphertext security with no fixed bound on an attacker's polynomial number of decryption queries.
cards.definitions:
A public-key encryption scheme consists of one fixed triple of uniform classical algorithms
\[
 \operatorname{Gen}(1^n)\to(pk,sk),\qquad
 \operatorname{Enc}(pk,m)\to c,\qquad
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\to m\text{ or }\bot .
\]
Here \(n\ge1\) is a security parameter, and keys, messages and ciphertexts are finite binary strings. The symbol \(\bot\) is distinct from every message. Gen and Enc use independent fair random bits; Dec is deterministic. Each algorithm is a finite Turing program with worst-case time polynomial in its full input length, including \(n\), which may be included in the keys. In particular, Gen has polynomially bounded output length. Encryption supports arbitrary binary messages; decryption is defined and halts on every ciphertext string, with malformed encodings rejected. The algorithms use no external oracle or advice.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(n\). Correctness requires that, for every polynomial length bound \(p\), some negligible function \(\mu_p\) satisfies
\[
 \max_{|m|\le p(n)}
 \Pr_{(pk,sk)\leftarrow\operatorname{Gen}(1^n),\ \operatorname{Enc}}
 [\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m))\ne m]
 \le\mu_p(n).
\]
The maximum includes the empty message. Neither perfect correctness nor recovery of the encryption randomness is required.

An adversary is a nonuniform family of classical polynomial-size computations with polynomially many fair random bits and polynomial-size advice. Advice can depend on \(n\), but not on the independently sampled keys, challenge bit or honest encryption coins. Total running time, state, message lengths, oracle-query lengths and number of queries are bounded by some polynomial in \(n\) that may depend on the adversary. Equivalently, these are polynomial-size Boolean circuits with the specified adaptive oracle interfaces. Arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information independent of the fresh experiment is included in the advice.

In the IND-CPA experiment, generate \((pk,sk)\), give \((1^n,pk)\) to the first stage \(A_1\), and let it output two equal-length messages \(m_0,m_1\) and a state \(\sigma\). Choose an independent uniform bit \(b\), form \(c^*=\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_b)\) with fresh coins, and give \((1^n,pk,\sigma,c^*)\) to \(A_2\), which outputs a bit \(\widehat b\). Its advantage is
\[
 \left|\Pr[\widehat b=b]-\frac12\right|.
\]
The probability includes all key-generation, challenge-encryption, challenge-bit and adversary randomness. The quantification is over adversaries obeying the equal-length challenge rule and producing a bit; failures to follow this syntax may instead be defined to yield an independent fair guess. Both stages can compute arbitrary encryptions themselves using the public algorithm, so a separate encryption oracle is unnecessary. The scheme is IND-CPA secure if this advantage is negligible for every adversary just defined.

The IND-CCA2 experiment is the same except for adaptive decryption access. Before the challenge, \(A_1\) may query any ciphertext \(c\), receiving \(\operatorname{Dec}(sk,c)\). After it chooses the messages and receives \(c^*\), \(A_2\) has the oracle
\[
 \mathcal D_{sk,c^*}(c)=
 \begin{cases}
 \bot,&c=c^*\text{ as binary strings},\\
 \operatorname{Dec}(sk,c),&c\ne c^*.
 \end{cases}
\]
Every later query may depend on the challenge and all earlier answers. The exclusion applies only after the challenge is issued; it does not retroactively invalidate a pre-challenge query. Any different string is permitted, even if it encodes related data or decrypts to the challenge plaintext. The scheme is IND-CCA2 secure if the same advantage is negligible for every such two-stage adversary.

For each security notion, one fixed scheme must satisfy the definition for every polynomially bounded adversary. The scheme cannot be chosen after fixing a maximum number of decryption queries. Its negligible bound may depend on the adversary. All security is classical; no quantum adversary is requested.

The plain model provides no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, trusted hardware or separate setup. The recipient's own random key generation is allowed. The question is an implication between existence statements. A resulting scheme may use the descriptions of the starting algorithms, change all formats and incur any fixed polynomial overhead. No particular compiler, black-box access discipline or preservation of the starting efficiency is required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that an IND-CPA scheme implies an IND-CCA2 scheme satisfying the precise definitions, with proofs of uniform implementation, polynomial running time, correctness and security; or give a complete Lean-checked proof of the negation of this existence implication in the ordinary computational model.

Breaking a particular CPA scheme under chosen-ciphertext attack does not disprove the existence of a different secure scheme. A separation restricted to black-box constructions, or relative to an oracle, is not a negative resolution here. Additional trapdoor, proof-system, pseudorandomness or setup assumptions must themselves follow from the sole premise. Security only before the challenge, only against an a priori bounded number of decryption queries, or only against ciphertext modification without the stated decryption access is insufficient. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.
cards.why: Determine whether public-key confidentiality alone can always be strengthened to resist adaptive decryption attacks, without importing another cryptographic assumption.

cards.context:
Public encryption already permits arbitrary chosen plaintexts. The stronger game additionally returns decryptions of adaptively selected ciphertexts, including queries after the challenge. The exact challenge string is excluded because its decryption would reveal the challenge message directly.

The source asks whether some stronger scheme follows from the existence of a weaker one. An attack on an individual CPA-secure scheme does not settle that foundational implication.

The 2007 separation applies to a restricted black-box class in which the new decryption does not query the original encryption algorithm. It does not exclude unrestricted constructions.

The 2008 bounded-CCA result fixes the query bound before constructing the scheme. Here one scheme must handle every polynomial-time attacker, including attackers with a larger query polynomial.

Injective trapdoor functions suffice without the extra lossiness or correlated-product guarantees required in earlier approaches. An ordinary encryption scheme need not recover its encryption randomness or provide such an injective function.

A hinting pseudorandom generator supplies a stronger security property than ordinary pseudorandomness. The corresponding generic upgrade keeps that additional requirement.

The revised batch-argument result reduces the proof-length saving required of the extra argument system. It does not remove that additional resource.

The threshold-encryption transforms have different prerequisites: the route from arbitrary CPA security uses a random oracle, while the other route assumes stronger security and further proof-system resources. Neither primary abstract establishes the exact plain-model implication here.

cards.title: Pseudorandom functions from worst-case hardness of learning
cards.formal:
For every circuit class
\[
\mathcal C\in\{\mathrm{AC}^0,\ \mathrm{AC}^0[p]\ (p\text{ any fixed prime}),\
\mathrm{ACC}^0,\ \mathrm{TC}^0,\ \mathrm{NC}^1,\
\mathrm{Formula},\ \mathrm{Circuit}\},
\]
does the following implication hold?
\[
\neg\operatorname{Learn}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{PRF}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C).
\]
Here learning means uniform randomized polynomial-time improper learning under the uniform input distribution, with adaptive membership queries. The conclusion is a uniformly polynomial-time samplable family of functions computed by polynomial-size \(\mathcal C\)-circuits, secure against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time oracle distinguisher. Both notions are defined below.

The hypothesis is only worst-case failure of learning: each candidate learner may fail on its own target function. No efficiently samplable common distribution of hard targets is assumed.
cards.definitions:
All targets are Boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\), with \(n\ge2\). Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs with input bits, optional constants, and a single Boolean output. Size counts wires; depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. Negation gates have one input. General \(\mathrm{Circuit}\) uses AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two and NOT gates, with unrestricted depth. \(\mathrm{Formula}\) uses the same basis but has a tree of gates, with no reuse of a gate output. \(\mathrm{NC}^1\) uses that bounded-fan-in circuit basis with depth at most \(d\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) for a fixed integer \(d\).

For \(\mathrm{AC}^0\), AND/OR gates may have unbounded fan-in and depth is at most a fixed integer \(d\). The class \(\mathrm{AC}^0[p]\) additionally permits a gate testing whether the number of ones among its inputs is divisible by the fixed prime \(p\). For \(\mathrm{ACC}^0\) the same definition permits any fixed integer modulus \(m\ge2\); the modulus does not grow with \(n\). The class \(\mathrm{TC}^0\) instead additionally permits unweighted majority gates, which output one when at least half their inputs are one. Negations and constants are allowed in all classes. These conventions specify classes of target functions; targets need not themselves be uniformly generated.

A fixed polynomial subfamily is specified by an integer \(k\ge1\), the wire bound \(n^k\), and, where relevant, fixed \(d\) and \(m\). Write \(\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\) for the resulting set of \(n\)-input functions, where \(\theta\) collects these fixed constants. For \(\mathrm{AC}^0[p]\), \(p\) is fixed as part of the choice of class.

The assertion \(\operatorname{Learn}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)\) means that for every fixed \(\theta\) there is one probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(L_\theta\) and a polynomial \(P_\theta\) with the following property. For every \(n\ge2\), integer \(q\ge2\), and \(f\in\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\), the machine \(L_\theta^f(1^n,1^q)\) halts within \(P_\theta(n,q)\) steps on every execution and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs a finite ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) satisfying
\[
\Pr_{x\leftarrow\{0,1\}^n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le 1/q.
\]
It may adaptively query any \(n\)-bit input and receive its exact value under \(f\); writing queries and the hypothesis counts toward its time. The hypothesis need not belong to \(\mathcal C\), and the target circuit description is not supplied. The polynomial running-time bound also holds for every other Boolean oracle. There is no advice depending on \(n\). Negating this definition gives the hardness premise with its quantifiers, including the possibility that the hard target depends on the learner and on \(n\).

The assertion \(\operatorname{PRF}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal C)\) means that for some fixed \(\theta\), some polynomial-time computable seed length \(a(n)\le n^r\), and a single deterministic polynomial-time sampler \(S\), every \(S(1^n,s)\), \(s\in\{0,1\}^{a(n)}\), describes a circuit for a function \(f_{n,s}\in\mathcal C_{\theta,n}\). The sampler runs in polynomial time in \(n\), including writing its entire output. It may be a general polynomial-time algorithm; only the sampled functions are required to have the stated \(\mathcal C\)-circuits.

For every uniform probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(D\) running in polynomial time in \(n\), the advantage
\[
\left|
\Pr_{s\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{a(n)}}[D^{f_{n,s}}(1^n)=1]
-
\Pr_{g\leftarrow\mathcal F_n}[D^g(1^n)=1]
\right|
\]
is negligible in \(n\), where \(\mathcal F_n\) is the set of all Boolean functions on \(n\) bits with its uniform distribution. Both probabilities include \(D\)'s random bits. The same sampled function answers all queries consistently. The distinguisher may choose polynomially many queries adaptively but does not receive the seed or circuit description. A nonnegative function \(\eta(n)\) is negligible when for every integer \(j\ge1\), \(\eta(n)\le n^{-j}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Security is eventual at all lengths, not merely on an unspecified infinite subsequence.

The implication is asked in the ordinary, unrelativized model. It does not require a black-box construction or an algorithm that extracts a sampler from a description of a hardness proof. This card fixes the uniform polynomial-time meaning of the source’s broader question; its exponential and nonuniform theorem is recorded separately as context.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication for the specified classes and quantifiers. A proof must obtain the efficiently sampled same-class family from the stated learning-hardness premise alone. Assuming a samplable hard target distribution, proving only a nonuniform or exponential-time dichotomy, or supplying a conditional PRF candidate does not suffice. A refutation must establish a failure of this implication in the stated unrelativized model; a relativizing or black-box barrier alone is not a refutation. This is a binary implication question, with exact security and learning quantifiers; numerical \(1/100\) slack does not alter them.
cards.why: A function class may resist every efficient learner without coming with a usable way to sample difficult targets. Cryptographic pseudorandomness requires a single efficient sampling procedure whose outputs defeat every efficient observer. The question asks whether the first obstruction alone supplies the second object within the same class.

cards.title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[
\operatorname{NCP}_2\notin\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\forall D\in\mathrm{PPT}\ \forall c>0\ \exists n_0\ge9\ \forall n\ge n_0:
\quad n\text{ a square}\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Adv}_D(n)<n^{-c}.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is the unrestricted binary Nearest Codeword decision problem defined below. The distinguisher receives either \((A,As+e)\) or \((A,u)\), with a uniform \(n^2\times n\) binary matrix, independent uniform secret and comparison vector, and independent noise bits of probability \(1/\sqrt n\). The conclusion requires negligible advantage at all sufficiently large square dimensions for every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo two. For a binary vector \(v\), its Hamming weight \(\operatorname{wt}(v)\) is the number of its one coordinates. An instance of \(\operatorname{NCP}_2\) is an explicitly given binary matrix \(G\in\mathbb F_2^{a\times b}\), a binary vector \(y\in\mathbb F_2^a\) and an integer \(t\) with \(0\le t\le a\), where \(a,b\ge1\). It is a YES instance exactly when some \(z\in\mathbb F_2^b\) has \(\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t\). The input lists the dimensions, entries and threshold with delimiters, using binary integers and row-major matrix entries. Invalid encodings are NO instances. There is no rank, balance, noise-distribution or closeness promise, and the task asks for one decision bit, not a codeword.

A language is in BPP if a single probabilistic Turing machine halts within a polynomial in the total binary input length on every input and every random tape, and answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. Its fair random bits are private; no advice or oracle is supplied. The premise means that no such machine decides this entire Nearest Codeword language.

For the average-case experiments let \(n=q^2\) with an integer \(q\ge3\). Independently draw all entries of \(A\), all bits of \(s\), and all bits of \(u\) uniformly. In the noisy experiment draw \(e_1,\ldots,e_{n^2}\) independently with \(\Pr[e_i=1]=1/q\), also independently of \(A,s,u\). The noisy vector is \(As+e\), computed over \(\mathbb F_2\); the other experiment uses \(u\). The distinguisher receives \(1^n\), the row-major entries of \(A\), and the corresponding vector with fixed delimiters. The sample count is exactly \(n^2\). It receives neither \(s\) nor \(e\), and cannot request extra samples. Square dimensions make the noise probability exactly rational.

A distinguisher \(D\in\mathrm{PPT}\) is one classical probabilistic Turing machine outputting a bit in worst-case polynomial time in the encoded input length, on every random tape. On these inputs that is equivalent to a polynomial in \(n\). Its description is independent of \(n\), and it has no advice, oracle or preprocessing depending on the particular random matrix. The advantage is
\[
\operatorname{Adv}_D(n)=\left|\Pr[D(1^n,A,As+e)=1]-\Pr[D(1^n,A,u)=1]\right|,
\]
where both probabilities include all experiment randomness and the independent internal randomness of \(D\).

The conclusion is eventual negligible advantage along the square dimensions: for each fixed distinguisher and positive exponent there is a threshold beyond which every square dimension satisfies the displayed upper bound. Its failure means that some fixed distinguisher and exponent have inverse-polynomial advantage at arbitrarily large square dimensions. The formulation uses this stronger length convention on 18 September 2026. The unrestricted decision premise, exact sample count and exact noise rate remain editorial specifications of the broader source direction, rather than a theorem stated verbatim there.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. An affirmative proof must obtain eventual negligible advantage, including exclusion of a distinguisher that succeeds only on an unbounded subsequence of square dimensions. A sufficient route converts any such nonnegligible distinguisher into a BPP decider for the entire unrestricted Nearest Codeword language. A refutation must establish both the Nearest Codeword premise and a distinguisher violating the conclusion; an oracle separation or failure of a particular reduction is insufficient. An additional dual-code hardness assumption, a different sample/noise regime or only the exclusion of distinguishers successful at every sufficiently large length does not settle this target.
cards.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

cards.title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
cards.definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of a deterministic uniform polynomial-time many-one reduction satisfying both stated promises, or a Lean proof that such a reduction does not exist. The source’s complete-problem equivalence identifies these alternatives with equality or inequality of NISZK and SZK. Randomized reductions or computational zero knowledge concern different targets.
cards.why: Determine the intrinsic role of interaction in information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.

cards.title: One-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) from one-way functions
cards.formal:
Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) circuit family? With the definitions below, the proposition is
\[
\bigl[\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)\bigr]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl[\exists g\;\mathrm{OWF}(g)\land\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\bigr].
\]
Both sides require security against every nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit family. The conclusion asks for the existence of some such \(g\), with some constant depth and some polynomial bounds. These constants may depend on \(g\), but not on its input length or on an adversary. There is no additional assumption on the starting function's circuit depth, no requirement that \(f\) and \(g\) have the same input or output lengths, and no requirement of a black-box construction or an efficient compiler from descriptions of \(f\).
cards.definitions:
A candidate function is a family \(f=(f_n)_{n\ge1}\), with a length function \(m_f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N\) and total maps
\[
f_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m_f(n)}.
\]
The output length depends only on \(n\), and zero is an allowed length. Let \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) mean that there are a single deterministic machine \(M\) and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), the machine outputs exactly \(f_n(x)\) and halts within \(B(n+1)^k\) steps, with \(m_f(n)\le B(n+1)^k\). The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finitely many tapes, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary symbols, a separator and a blank, and one-cell head moves; each transition counts as one step. The input is the binary string on a read-only input tape with end markers, work tapes are initially blank, and output bits are written sequentially on an output tape. This fixes ordinary bit computation; the number of tapes, alphabet and program are fixed independently of \(n\). No advice, oracle or random coins are supplied to the evaluator.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose input nodes carry the input bits, whose constant nodes carry \(0\) or \(1\), and whose internal gates are binary AND, binary OR or unary NOT. Fan-out is unrestricted, and the same predecessor may occupy both input positions. Outputs are an ordered list of references to nodes, with repetitions allowed. Size is the number of nodes plus the number of output positions. Depth is the largest number of internal gates on a path from an input or constant node to an output. Circuit descriptions list the nodes in a topological order, with gate tags and predecessor indices, followed by the output indices; indices and list lengths are in binary with separators from a fixed finite alphabet. No gates for arbitrary functions or oracle evaluation are present.

For a candidate \(f\), an allowed inverter is any family \(A=(A_n)_{n\ge1}\) of Boolean circuits of this basis, together with integers \(r(n)\ge0\), such that
\[
A_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m_f(n)+r(n)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n},
\qquad
\exists C,c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1,
\quad\max\{\operatorname{size}(A_n),r(n)\}\le C(n+1)^c.
\]
No uniform procedure for producing \(A_n\) is required, and its depth is unrestricted. The input blocks are \(1^n\), a proposed function value, and \(r(n)\) independent fair random bits. Thus the security parameter is given in unary, the adversary may depend on the input length nonuniformly, and it is not restricted to shallow circuits. For independent uniform strings \(X\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(R\in\{0,1\}^{r(n)}\), put
\[
s_{f,A}(n)=\Pr\!\left[
f_n\bigl(A_n(1^n,f_n(X),R)\bigr)=f_n(X)
\right].
\]
Success means finding any preimage of the specified length \(n\), not necessarily the sampled \(X\). The function itself is deterministic; the probability is only over \(X\) and the adversary's coins \(R\). The negligible-success requirement is
\[
\forall A\text{ allowed}\ \forall a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists N\ge2\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad s_{f,A}(n)\le n^{-a}.
\]
The threshold \(N\) may depend on \(f,A,a\). Define \(\mathrm{OWF}(f)\) to mean \(\mathrm{PolyEval}(f)\) together with this requirement. Security holds at every sufficiently large length for each adversary and exponent, rather than merely on infinitely many lengths. There is no requirement of injectivity, length preservation, expansion, or any fixed ratio of output to input length.

The predicate \(\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\) means that there are a single deterministic circuit-generating Turing machine \(G\), integers \(B,k\ge1\), and an integer \(D\ge0\), such that for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\), the machine \(G\) outputs the full description of a circuit \(C_n\) in at most \(B(n+1)^k\) steps. That circuit has exactly \(n\) input bits, exactly \(m_g(n)\) outputs, size at most \(B(n+1)^k\), and depth at most \(D\), and satisfies \(C_n(x)=g_n(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). Generation uses the same deterministic bit-computation convention as above. The depth bound is a single constant for the entire family; in particular, every output depends on at most \(2^D\) input bits. The question places no bound on how many outputs a given input bit may influence. Circuit generation has no random setup, randomly chosen graph, public key or advice. The two existentially quantified functions may have different length functions and polynomial bounds.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed implication or of its logical negation, using exactly the evaluation, uniformity and nonuniform-security conventions above. A positive proof must establish the existence of a secure family with one constant depth bound from the sole assumption that a one-way function exists. A negative proof must establish both
\[
\exists f\;\mathrm{OWF}(f)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall g,\quad\mathrm{PUniformNC}^{0}(g)\Longrightarrow\neg\mathrm{OWF}(g).
\]
Equivalently, for every candidate \(g\) with such a uniform constant-depth implementation, it must establish an allowed polynomial-size inverter family \(A\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) with
\[
\forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N,\qquad s_{g,A}(n)>n^{-a},
\]
as well as the existence of an unrestricted one-way function. The inverter and exponent may depend on \(g\). A separation only relative to an oracle, an obstruction only to a selected kind of reduction, or failure of a particular local candidate does not prove this negation. A theorem under an additional computational assumption establishes only that conditional result.
cards.why: The question tests whether the minimal computational assumption underlying much of cryptography already guarantees functions with constant-depth local evaluation. A positive answer would make this extreme parallelism available under the general one-way-function assumption; a negative answer would separate local cryptographic hardness from unrestricted polynomial-time cryptographic hardness.

cards.title: Verifiable random functions from one-way functions alone
cards.formal: Does the existence of arbitrary one-way functions imply a standard-model verifiable random function on all \(\lambda\)-bit inputs with perfect correctness on honest evaluations, adaptive pseudorandomness and perfect uniqueness even for malformed public keys?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines. Security quantifies over nonuniform polynomial-size probabilistic circuits with polynomially many oracle queries. All message, instance and witness lengths in the experiment are polynomial in \(\lambda\). Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto). The model supplies no random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption.

Assume a uniform polynomial-time family \(f_\lambda:\{0,1\}^\lambda\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(\lambda)}\) with polynomially bounded output length. For uniform \(X\in\{0,1\}^\lambda\), every admissible adversary given \(\lambda\) and \(f_\lambda(X)\) has negligible probability of returning any \(\lambda\)-bit \(x'\) with \(f_\lambda(x')=f_\lambda(X)\). Collisions are allowed.

\(\operatorname{KeyGen}(1^\lambda)\) returns a public key pk and secret key sk. Deterministic Eval(sk,x) returns a \(\lambda\)-bit value for each x in \(\{0,1\}^\lambda\), and Prove(sk,x) returns a proof. Deterministic Verify(pk,x,y,pi) accepts or rejects. For every security parameter \(\lambda\ge1\), every pair \((pk,sk)\) that honest key generation can output, every \(x\in\{0,1\}^\lambda\), and every proof \(\pi\) that the honest prover can output on \((sk,x)\), require \[\operatorname{Verify}(pk,x,\operatorname{Eval}(sk,x),\pi)=1.\] This is the perfect provability condition in Definition 1 of Dodis and Yampolskiy. All sizes and runtimes are polynomial in \(\lambda\).

Perfect uniqueness requires that for every public-key string of the permitted polynomial length, every x, and any two pairs (y,pi),(y-prime,pi-prime) accepted by Verify, y=y-prime. A malformed key may reject everything. There is no requirement that the proof string itself be unique.

For pseudorandomness, an adversary receives an honest pk and adaptively queries an oracle returning (Eval(sk,x),Prove(sk,x)). It chooses a fresh challenge x-star not previously queried, receives either Eval(sk,x-star) or an independent uniform \(\lambda\)-bit string, and continues oracle queries excluding x-star. No proof for the challenge is supplied. Its distinguishing advantage must be negligible. The domain has \(2^\lambda\) inputs; weak security on randomly selected inputs is insufficient. Non-black-box techniques are allowed, and there is no setup beyond the individual generated key pair.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction with proofs of perfect honest correctness, perfect uniqueness and adaptive pseudorandomness from arbitrary one-way functions, or refute the unrestricted implication. A black-box separation alone does not rule out constructions using the one-way-function description.
cards.why: The question tests whether public verifiability requires stronger assumptions than ordinary private pseudorandomness.

cards.title: Blind signatures from one-way functions alone
cards.formal: Does the existence of arbitrary one-way functions imply a classical plain-model blind-signature scheme with concurrent blindness and one-more unforgeability, allowing polynomially many interaction rounds and non-black-box constructions?
cards.definitions:
The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines. Security quantifies over nonuniform polynomial-size probabilistic circuits with polynomially many oracle queries. All message, instance and witness lengths in the experiment are polynomial in \(\lambda\). Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto). The model supplies no random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption.

Assume a uniform polynomial-time family \(f_\lambda:\{0,1\}^\lambda\to\{0,1\}^{\ell(\lambda)}\) with polynomially bounded output length. For uniform \(X\in\{0,1\}^\lambda\), every admissible adversary given \(\lambda\) and \(f_\lambda(X)\) has negligible probability of returning any \(\lambda\)-bit \(x'\) with \(f_\lambda(x')=f_\lambda(X)\). Collisions are allowed.

KeyGen generates a signer key pair (pk,sk). A polynomial-round interactive protocol between Signer(sk) and User(pk,m) gives the user a signature sigma or an abort symbol. Deterministic Verify(pk,m,sigma) checks signatures. Messages have polynomial length. Honest executions yield accepted signatures except with negligible probability. The scheme has no CRS or globally accessible oracle.

Blindness is tested against a malicious signer that chooses a public key and two equal-length messages m0,m1. A hidden uniform bit b assigns mb to one honest-user session and m(1-b) to another. The signer interleaves both sessions arbitrarily with any further polynomially many sessions on messages of its own choice. If both challenge users finish, it receives their final signatures ordered by message (m0 first, m1 second), without session labels; if either aborts it receives only the common failure notification instead of either signature. Together with its entire interaction view, this must give only negligible advantage in guessing b. Honest users verify signatures before reporting success; malformed public keys may lead to abort.

For one-more unforgeability a malicious user interacts with an honest signer under an honest public key in any polynomial number q of sessions, scheduled concurrently. It wins by outputting q+1 accepted message-signature pairs with pairwise distinct messages. Here q counts all sessions initiated, including aborted sessions; no stronger completed-session accounting is required. The win probability must be negligible for every polynomial-size adversary. Signer sessions use fresh random coins. This fixes the session-count convention explicitly. Signatures need not be unique, and no ideal-world universally composable security or extraction is demanded.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and correctness, blindness and one-more-unforgeability reductions from arbitrary one-way functions, or refute the unrestricted implication. Black-box-only separations and constructions in a global random-oracle model do not settle the plain-model target.
cards.why: This asks how little computational hardness suffices for anonymous authenticated transactions.

cards.title: PZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{PZK}=\mathrm{SZK}\) for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems in the precise input-only simulation model below? Both classes use uniform polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible completeness and soundness errors, and zero knowledge against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier. Perfect simulation may output a failure symbol with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on success its distribution must be exactly correct. Statistical simulation permits negligible total variation distance.
cards.definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \(L=(Y,N)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). An interactive proof has a single computationally unbounded honest prover \(P\) and a uniform probabilistic Turing verifier \(V\), both receiving the common input \(x\). They exchange binary messages over an ordinary interactive channel. The verifier uses at most polynomially many random bits, computational steps and communicated bits, with a fixed polynomial in \(|x|\); its bound holds on every random tape and against every prover. A message or interaction exceeding the verifier's prescribed length or turn limit can be rejected. The prover has arbitrary computation and private randomness, but sees only the input and communicated history, not the verifier's private random tape.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(n\). There must be one negligible error bound with honest acceptance probability at least \(1-\varepsilon(|x|)\) for every \(x\in Y\), and acceptance probability at most \(\varepsilon(|x|)\) for every \(x\in N\) and every possibly unbounded cheating prover strategy. Soundness thus concerns proofs, not arguments secure only against computationally bounded provers. No correctness or simulation condition is imposed outside the promise. Completeness is not required to be perfect.

A malicious verifier \(V^*\) is any fixed uniform probabilistic polynomial-time interactive Turing machine, with polynomial worst-case bounds on its computation, random bits and communication on every interaction. The honest prover has a specified behavior on every received history, including malformed messages or early halting. The view \(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x)\) is the resulting finite record of \(x\), the verifier's random bits and all exchanged messages with their order and delimiters. Its output and final state are determined by this record and its program. Random tapes can be padded to the verifier's fixed polynomial bound. This fixes one finite binary encoding of views; the special simulator failure symbol \(\bot\) is not a view.

The promise problem belongs to SZK if it has such a proof \((P,V)\) and, for every \(V^*\), a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator \(S^*\) and a negligible function \(\mu_{V^*}\) such that for every \(x\in Y\),
\[
\operatorname{TV}\bigl(S^*(x),\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x)\bigr)\le\mu_{V^*}(|x|).
\]
For distributions on finite binary records, \(\operatorname{TV}(D,E)=\tfrac12\sum_z|\Pr[D=z]-\Pr[E=z]|\); the sum may include records given zero probability by one distribution. Any simulator output not encoding a real view counts in that distance.

PZK uses the same requirements on the proof but replaces the last simulation condition by
\[
\Pr[S^*(x)=\bot]\le\tfrac12,\qquad
\mathcal L(S^*(x)\mid S^*(x)\ne\bot)=\mathcal L(\operatorname{View}_{P,V^*}(x))
\]
for every \(x\in Y\). Here \(\mathcal L\) denotes the probability distribution, and equality requires equality of each record's probability. Nonfailure has positive probability, so conditioning is defined.

Every simulator has a strict polynomial bound on every input and random tape, rather than an expected-time bound. Its polynomial and description may depend on the fixed verifier \(V^*\), but not on \(x\). It receives \(x\) alone, with no witness, prover interaction, nonuniform advice or separate auxiliary input. It may use the fixed verifier's description internally; no black-box simulation requirement is imposed. There is no common random string, oracle, computational assumption or multiprover resource. This retains the saved input-only convention; an auxiliary-input or expected-time variant is not substituted.

Class equality quantifies over all promise problems and permits the perfect proof system to differ completely from the statistical one. PZK is contained in SZK under these conventions: repeat a perfect simulator independently polynomially many times, retain the first nonfailure output and use any fixed record if all runs fail. The latter event can be made negligible while preserving a strict polynomial bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that every promise problem in the stated SZK class also belongs to the stated PZK class, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it admits no PZK proof in this model. The positive direction need not be a uniform compiler from protocol descriptions. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP or multiprover protocol, or an honest-verifier-only result without a matching transformation does not resolve the unrelativized equality.
cards.why: Determine whether allowing any negligible statistical simulation error increases the expressive power of information-theoretic zero-knowledge proofs.

references.title: Perfect Zero-Knowledge PCPs for #P
references.authors: Tom Gur; Jack O’Connor; Nicholas Spooner
references.locator: Introduction, printed pp. 3–4: PZK=SZK remains unknown; PCP model distinction

cards.context:
Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.
