cards.title: Polynomial-time computationally sound verification of \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\)
cards.formal: Do there exist deterministic uniform algorithms \(P,V\), integers \(C>c\ge1\), and a constant \(K\ge2\) giving the following plain-model argument system for exact \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\), without unproved hardness assumptions? On a Boolean formula \(\Phi\) encoded in \(N\) bits, \(P\) produces a proof of length at most \((N+1)^C\) in time \(T_P(N)=2^{K(N+1)^c}\). The verifier runs in time \(K(N+1)^C\) and outputs either the exact number of satisfying assignments or the rejection symbol \(\bot\). Completeness requires \(V(\Phi,P(\Phi))=\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) on every valid formula. Soundness requires that every uniform randomized adversary running in any fixed polynomial in \(T_P(N)\) has only negligible probability, as a function of \(T_P(N)\), of generating a length-\(N\) formula and a proof on which \(V\) outputs an incorrect number. This card fixes the unconditional version of the source question; conditional constructions are recorded below.
cards.definitions:
Fix a polynomial-time parsable binary encoding of formulas over AND, OR and NOT. An instance lists its \(n\) variables explicitly, so \(n\le N\), and its formula is a finite tree with leaves among those variables and Boolean constants. The value \(\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) is the number of assignments in \(\{0,1\}^n\) on which the formula evaluates to one, including choices of any listed unused variables. The answer is written in binary and has at most \(n+1\) bits. Measuring resources in the full encoding length fixes the meaning of polynomial-size formulas and includes the cost of reading their descriptions.

The prover and verifier are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. The proof is one finite binary string; there is no interaction, oracle, common reference string, advice, secret setup or verifier randomness. The verifier rejects malformed instances and overlong proofs. It halts within its stated bound on every input, reading at most one symbol beyond the permitted proof length to detect excess input. Increasing the fixed constant \(K\) absorbs encoding and rejection overhead. The honest prover must construct its proof in the stated exponential time; mere existence of a proof with no bound on its production is insufficient.

More explicitly, for every uniform probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) whose worst-case runtime on \(1^N\) is at most \(T_P(N)^a\) for some fixed \(a\ge1\), and for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(N_{A,d}\) such that, for every \(N\ge N_{A,d}\),
\[\Pr_{(\Phi,\pi)\leftarrow A(1^N)}\bigl[\Phi\text{ is valid},\ |\Phi|=N,\ V(\Phi,\pi)\notin\{\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi),\bot\}\bigr]\le T_P(N)^{-d}.\]
Probability is over independent fair random bits used by \(A\). Any output that is not a valid formula/proof pair is a failed attack. The adversary chooses both the formula and its proof, knows \(P,V\), and has no nonuniform advice or auxiliary input. The polynomial exponent \(a\) may be arbitrarily large and is not fixed by the protocol. Negligibility is measured in the honest prover's time, rather than merely inverse polynomial in the formula length. The constants \(c,C,K\) and the two machines must be fixed before quantifying over adversaries and accuracy exponents.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a system exists, including all completeness, uniformity, running-time and soundness requirements, or prove that no such system exists. A positive answer must be unconditional. A construction assuming a conjectured hard function is progress but does not settle this selected version. Randomized verification, interaction, a setup string, soundness only against polynomial-in-input-length adversaries, or an unbounded honest prover changes the question.
cards.why: Exact counting requires certifying that no satisfying assignments were missed, as well as that counted assignments exist. This question tests whether computational soundness can give deterministic short verification of such global information while retaining an honest prover with a specified running time. It connects the power of proof systems with derandomization and the distinction between uniform computational attacks and arbitrary false witnesses.

references.title: Fiat-Shamir in the Plain Model from Derandomization (Or: Do Efficient Algorithms Believe that NP = PSPACE?)
references.authors: Lijie Chen; Ron D. Rothblum; Roei Tell
references.locator: Revision 1, 3 April 2025; Definition 1.1, Theorem 1.3/4.3, Assumption 4.1 and Section 3.4; conditional polynomial-time verification with exponential-time honest provers and stronger uniform adversaries.

cards.context:
Computational soundness permits incorrect proofs to exist, provided no adversary with the specified resources can generate a false instance together with an accepted proof. Ordinary NP soundness forbids every false proof. Allowing nonuniform advice would let an adversary hardwire a false pair at each input length, removing this distinction.

The honest prover is allowed exponential time, and the adversary is allowed every polynomial in that time. Requiring a polynomial-time honest prover would instead give a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm by composing prover and verifier. Allowing an arbitrarily stronger honest prover than the attacker would also distort the model; the later paper explains why.

The 2023 source gives, under strong assumptions, verification in time \(2^{\varepsilon n}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with an honest prover and adversaries using \(2^{O(n)}\) time. Its next question asks for a polynomial-time verifier.

The 2025 paper proves \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm{cs}\text{-}\mathrm{NP}\) under strong assumptions about functions that remain hard for small-space computation on efficiently samplable inputs. Its Definition 1.1 explicitly allows a polynomial-time verifier with an exponential-time honest prover. Applying its polynomial-space verification result to exact-count claims gives conditional progress on this card, since exact counting can be performed in polynomial space. The paper does not prove the required hardness assumptions.

cards.title: Efficient split-state non-malleable codes approaching capacity
cards.formal: Do uniform polynomial-time two-share nonmalleable codes exist with k message bits, equal share length \(\ell(k)\), negligible statistical error in k, and rate \(k/(2\ell(k))\) tending to 1/2 as k tends to infinity, against all independent tampering functions on the two shares?
cards.definitions:
For each positive integer \(k\), let \(S_k=\{0,1\}^{\ell(k)}\). The randomized encoder \(\operatorname{Enc}_k\) maps each \(k\)-bit message to a pair of shares \((L,R)\in S_k\times S_k\). The deterministic decoder \(\operatorname{Dec}_k\) maps every such pair into \(\{0,1\}^k\cup\{\bot\}\). The share length \(\ell(k)\) is polynomially bounded and computable in polynomial time. Both algorithms are uniform and run in polynomial time in \(k\) on every input and random tape. Honest decoding returns the message with probability one. The model provides no shared setup secret or computational hardness assumption.

There is one negligible function \(\eta\) such that for every \(k\) and every two deterministic maps \(f,g:S_k\to S_k\), there is a distribution \(D_{k,f,g}\) on \(\{0,1\}^k\cup\{\bot,\mathsf{same}\}\) with the following property for every message \(m\). Sample \((L,R)\) from \(\operatorname{Enc}_k(m)\). The total variation distance between \(\operatorname{Dec}_k(f(L),g(R))\) and the following simulated output is at most \(\eta(k)\). Draw \(d\) from \(D_{k,f,g}\), return \(m\) if \(d=\mathsf{same}\), and return \(d\) otherwise. The symbols \(\bot\) and \(\mathsf{same}\) are distinct and lie outside the message alphabet. The same distribution works for every \(m\) and need not be efficiently samplable. For every real \(c>0\), \(\eta(k)<k^{-c}\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).

Tampering maps may be computationally unbounded and know the public code but are fixed independently of the message and encoding randomness. Each sees only its own share; correlated choices of maps are covered by mixtures of deterministic pairs. The target is single-shot nonmalleability, not adaptive repeated tampering or leakage resilience. Rate counts both shares, and convergence to 1/2 is a single uniform family with \(\ell(k)=k+o(k)\), not a claim about an unbounded-time existential code.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked uniform code family with perfect correctness, the statistical simulation property and the limiting rate, or prove that no such efficient family exists. Computational nonmalleability, bitwise tampering or more than two shares does not answer this information-theoretic two-share question.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient split-state coding can reach its information-theoretic capacity.

cards.title: Unconditional zero knowledge for gap circuit complexity
cards.formal: Is there a fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) for which \(\mathrm{Gap}_{\varepsilon}\mathrm{MCSP}\) admits a computational zero-knowledge interactive proof system without a computational hardness assumption? Given the length-\(N=2^n\) truth table of a Boolean function, the promise distinguishes circuit size at most \(N^\varepsilon\) from size greater than \(N^{1-\varepsilon}\). This card selects the MCSP branch of the original question and the gap family used by Hirahara and Nanashima; it does not claim equivalence with every MINKT or other gap variant.
cards.definitions:
The common input is the full truth table \(x\) of a function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with \(n\geq1\) and \(N=2^n\). Let \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\) be its minimum Boolean circuit size. Fix the standard basis of binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with constant inputs available, arbitrary fan-out, one output, and size equal to the number of gates. Circuits are acyclic and compute every truth-table entry correctly.

A yes-instance satisfies \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)\leq N^\varepsilon\). A no-instance satisfies \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(f)>N^{1-\varepsilon}\). Inputs between these thresholds have no required decision outcome. The strict no-threshold follows the formal definition in the later source; the thresholds need not be integers. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, not supplied per instance. The task has both low-complexity and high-complexity promised inputs at arbitrarily large lengths.

An interactive proof has an honest prover \(P\) and a randomized verifier \(V\). Total communication, rounds and verifier computation are polynomial in \(N\), the explicit truth-table length. No computational bound is imposed on the prover. On every yes-instance, the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(2/3\). On every no-instance, every cheating prover, including an unbounded one, causes acceptance with probability at most \(1/3\). This is a proof system; soundness only against efficient provers would be an argument system.

Computational zero knowledge requires that for every randomized polynomial-time verifier \(V^*\), including one given arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information \(z\), there is a randomized polynomial-time simulator \(S_{V^*}\). Given only \(x,z\), it produces a distribution computationally indistinguishable from the entire view of \(V^*\) in the honest-prover interaction on \(x\). That view includes the common input, auxiliary information, verifier randomness, messages and final output. The simulator is not given a small circuit or other witness.

Indistinguishability is required on all yes-instances: every polynomial-size distinguishing circuit has only negligible advantage in \(N\), uniformly over these instances and polynomial-length auxiliary strings. Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(N\). The simulator and verifier use the ordinary polynomial-time convention of the later source. No setup, random oracle, trusted third party or hardness assumption is supplied.

The chosen circuit basis fixes a concrete representation. The existential constant-gap formulation tolerates constant-factor changes of standard finite bases by choosing a slightly wider gap and handling finitely many small lengths separately. It does not identify circuits with a shortest program: MINKT instead bounds the program length needed to print a string within a supplied time budget, and its gap parameters constitute a separate choice.

The target asks for one protocol meeting worst-case completeness, soundness and zero knowledge at every input length. A protocol that succeeds on most inputs from a particular distribution or only at infinitely many lengths is a weaker result.
cards.answer_criterion: Give some fixed admissible gap constant and a protocol with proofs of polynomial verifier and simulator cost, completeness, soundness against all provers, and computational zero knowledge against arbitrary efficient auxiliary-input verifiers, without assuming one-way functions or another hardness premise. A negative answer must rule out the specified protocols for every constant in this selected gap family. Failure for that family would not by itself refute all alternatives in the original broader question.
cards.why: Would provide a natural unconditional zero-knowledge protocol for a central problem about circuit descriptions. It probes the connection between worst-case complexity, average-case cryptographic hardness and verification that reveals no efficiently usable information beyond the claim.

The standard one-way-function theorem supplies zero-knowledge proofs for NP. The original question asks for an unconditional result; the case where the problem is worst-case hard but suitable cryptographic hardness is unavailable is not covered by that theorem.

cards.title: Sublinear communication for perfectly secure two-party computation
cards.formal: Is there a uniform two-party protocol in the trusted correlated-randomness model that perfectly computes every Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) with polynomial setup and computation, and online communication \(O(n+g(s))\) for some function \(g(s)=o(s)\), where \(s\) is the circuit's supplied size? More precisely, seek fixed algorithms, constants \(K,q\ge1\), and \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) with \(\lim_{s\to\infty}g(s)/s=0\), such that every circuit and every pair of inputs satisfy the correctness and privacy conditions below; dealer computation, total setup length and both parties' computation are at most \(K(n+s+1)^q\), while at most \(K(n+g(s))\) bits are exchanged online. The circuit is arbitrary, without a layering or depth restriction. The additive input-length term fixes the source's sublinearity question in a form that also covers circuits of linear size.
cards.definitions:
A circuit is an explicitly given finite directed acyclic graph with \(2n\) input vertices, Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one designated output. Fan-out is unrestricted. Let \(s\) count all vertices, including inputs and constants; in particular \(s\ge2n\). Gates and predecessors are encoded in topological order with binary indices. Both parties and the dealer know this public description. The inputs \(x_0,x_1\in\{0,1\}^n\) are private to their respective parties. The size in the bound is that of the supplied circuit; the protocol may optimize its computation, but cannot charge an artificially padded circuit to increase its communication allowance.

Before the parties receive their inputs, a trusted randomized dealer, given only \(C\), samples finite correlated strings \((r_0,r_1)\) and privately sends \(r_b\) to party \(b\). These strings may depend on \(C\) but not on either input. The dealer then takes no further part. Dealer randomness consists of independent fair bits; its computation and output length obey the polynomial bound on every run. Independent local random tapes can be included in these strings. After this phase the parties are deterministic machines on their input, setup string and message history. Their descriptions are fixed across all circuits and lengths, and their complete online runtimes obey the same polynomial bound. There is no other setup, oracle or computational hardness assumption.

The parties exchange binary messages and output private bits \(y_0,y_1\). Perfect correctness means
\[\Pr[y_0\mathbin\oplus y_1=C(x_0,x_1)]=1\]
for every input pair, where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The task uses the source's shared-output convention: neither party is required to learn the reconstructed answer. Perfect privacy against one passive corruption means that, for each \(b\) and each fixed \(C,x_b\), the distribution of party \(b\)'s entire view is identical for every choice of the other party's input. Its view includes \(r_b\), all sent and received messages and its output. A passive adversary follows the protocol and may inspect that entire view with unlimited computation; the parties do not collude. Privacy and correctness have zero error.

Online cost is the worst-case number of bits sent in both directions, over inputs and all dealer outcomes of positive probability. Message boundaries, control information and input-dependent stopping must be encoded in this communication; timing and silence are not free channels. There is no separate round bound beyond polynomial runtime. The dealer's private deliveries are excluded from online communication but included in the setup-length bound. For every family whose circuit size is polynomial in \(n\), the stated \(\operatorname{poly}(n+s)\) resource bound is polynomial in the input length, as required by the source. A single choice of algorithms, \(K,q,g\) must work for all such families, not only a fixed function or depth.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence, including perfect privacy, correctness, polynomial setup/computation and a uniform sublinear \(g\), or prove that no such protocol and resource bounds exist. A protocol for layered circuits only, a computationally secure construction, or a truth-table protocol using setup exponential in \(n\) does not settle this target. A negative answer must rule out all sublinear savings allowed above, rather than only exactly optimal or one-round online communication.
cards.why: Standard perfectly private evaluation pays communication proportional to circuit size, even after preprocessing. A general sublinear protocol would show that polynomial preprocessing can reduce this online cost without relying on conjectured cryptographic hardness. A lower bound would expose a fundamental limit on what preprocessing can achieve, beyond the extreme regime of exactly optimal communication.

cards.context:
The input-independent setup is a resource, not a free truth table of the function. Beaver-style evaluation uses linear-size correlated randomness and linear online communication. A one-time truth table can make communication linear in the input length, but its exponential setup falls outside this question.

Couteau gives perfect passive-security protocols for layered circuits with communication \(O(n+s/\log\log s)\) for a fixed number of parties and a constant-size output, using polynomial storage. In a layered circuit every edge joins consecutive layers. Transforming a general circuit into this form can increase its size and therefore does not automatically give sublinear cost relative to the original circuit.

The 2023 source proves exponential setup lower bounds when each party sends exactly as much information as its input, including a stronger bound for a single online round. Its functions have a two-bit shared output and input domain size \(N\); the lower bounds are in \(N\), which is exponential in input bit length. These endpoint results do not rule out \(O(n+g(s))\) communication with additional interaction.

Computationally secure protocols may replace large correlations by short pseudorandom descriptions under hardness assumptions. Perfect privacy here requires exact equality of view distributions even for an unbounded observer, so those constructions answer a different question.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\). The classical reduction requirement preserves the saved card’s variant; the cited survey’s standard formulation permits quantum reductions.
cards.definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
cards.why: This asks whether coarse average-energy estimation retains the full difficulty of verification with an arbitrary quantum witness. The per-term normalization prevents a numerical rescaling from creating the required gap. A positive result would give a robust quantum analogue of classical constraint-satisfaction hardness, with consequences for the computational structure of low-energy states. The saved classical-reduction version additionally requires that the hard physical instance be produced without quantum computation.

cards.context:
Editorial scope: the existing card explicitly chose deterministic classical reductions. This review preserves that mathematical target and qualifies the title. Aharonov, Arad and Vidick instead state their Conjecture 1.3 under quantum polynomial-time reductions, and explain that permitting quantum reductions is needed for the known equivalence with their proof-verification formulation. The stronger reduction requirement here is therefore not attributed to their conjecture as an established equivalent formulation.

The classical PCP theorem gives constant-gap hardness for constraint satisfaction. Quantum local Hamiltonians replace local Boolean penalties by local operators, while a global state may be entangled across all qubits. The quantum Cook–Levin theorem establishes QMA-completeness at inverse-polynomial relative precision. The constant relative gap asked for here remains an additional claim. The no case rules out low average energy for every state, rather than only product states or a specified family of trial states.

Anshu, Breuckmann and Nirkhe proved the no-low-energy-trivial-states theorem, first announced in 2022 and published at STOC 2023. Their families have bounded-size local interactions and a fixed positive energy-density threshold below which state preparation needs depth \(\Omega(\log n)\). Depth counts layers of disjoint bounded-size quantum gates, with no geometric restriction. This establishes a strong structural phenomenon in low-energy states, but is not a reduction proving QMA-hardness of distinguishing high and low ground energies. In particular, their theorem’s Hamiltonians are frustration-free: they have a common zero-energy state.

The games version also requires care. Natarajan and Nirkhe’s 2024 status note identifies an error in an earlier Natarajan–Vidick energy-amplification argument that invalidates its claimed games PCP for a QMA-complete problem. Their note distinguishes efficient honest provers from arbitrarily powerful entangled provers. Neither the old claim nor general results about interactive games supply the Hamiltonian statement on this card.

Buhrman, Helsen and Weggemans give a detailed quantum reduction between constant-query proof checking and local Hamiltonians, and clarify adaptive-query and multiple-prover variants. Their 2025 theorem controls approximation of a verifier’s acceptance probability by an energy and can produce a fixed classical Hamiltonian description with high probability. The reduction itself is quantum. These structural results do not establish that all QMA problems have constant-query proofs, or that the needed Hamiltonian descriptions can always be computed by classical reductions.

The October 2025 Bergamaschi–Metger–Vidick–Zhang preprint proves a gap-amplification result with an increase in the locality of the resulting Hamiltonian. Its locality-gap tradeoff does not preserve a constant locality throughout the full conjectured gap increase. Thus it is a distinct partial result even though its reductions can be deterministic.

Sun and Vidick’s June 2026 preprint gives interactive oracle proofs for QMA with polynomial total communication, polylogarithmic query and round counts, and a constant soundness gap. The interaction and nonconstant query bounds are part of the theorem. It does not assert the noninteractive, constant-locality Hamiltonian hardness asked for here. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Nguyen’s July 23, 2026 Simons talk abstract explicitly keeps the general quantum PCP question open and reports amplification of a combinatorial gap. The checked abstract does not assert the full normalized energy-gap theorem. A matching full paper or video proof was not verified in this review.

Bafna and Vyas’s August 19, 2026 preprint also explicitly describes quantum PCP as open. It concerns classical private PCPs for NP, with nonconstant query complexity and additional parameter improvements conditional on a product-expansion conjecture. Its classical result does not verify quantum witnesses or settle this Hamiltonian problem.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
cards.why: This asks whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable total problems beyond classical randomization. It identifies the exact classical lower bound needed to turn an efficient quantum decision algorithm into an unconditional separation of computational power.

cards.context:
Quantum computation evolves complex amplitudes, whose cancellations allow interference; a final measurement gives an ordinary random bit. Both classes on this card still require reliable membership decisions on every input. Efficient classical randomized computation is contained in the quantum class. The open issue is strictness of that containment, not whether one particular classical simulation has an exponential cost.

The fixed Hadamard, quarter-phase and controlled-NOT gates form a standard universal quantum basis. Boykin and coauthors establish universality for this finite set; the quarter-phase gate is exactly the T matrix in the definition. The model therefore does not supply infinitely many arbitrary gate parameters as free computational information.

Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, with polynomial measured in the input bit length. These are function tasks. Their algorithms alone supply neither a proof that every classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm fails nor the complete total-language separation requested here. The classical hardness needed for such a separation is not a conclusion of Shor’s theorem.

Raz and Tal prove that some oracle \(O\) satisfies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{PH}^{O}\), where the polynomial hierarchy \(\mathrm{PH}\) allows any fixed number of alternating polynomially bounded existential and universal quantifiers around a polynomial-time predicate. This implies \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}^{O}\). Both sides receive the same fixed black-box function, and the quantum machine may query it coherently on a superposition. The cost and power of that oracle are part of the changed model; the result does not itself separate the unrelativized classes.

Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication proves an unconditional sampling separation for shallow circuits. In Theorem 3 and Corollary 4, the classical circuits have fan-in two and at most \(n+n^\delta\) fair random inputs for fixed \(\delta<1\); approximating the stated distribution requires depth \(\Omega(\log\log n)\). Closeness is total variation distance, half the sum of absolute differences between outcome probabilities. The quantum constant-depth model permits arbitrary constant-size unitaries. These are explicit sampling and circuit-resource conditions, not an exclusion of arbitrary polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

A promise problem specifies disjoint yes and no sets and leaves other inputs unconstrained. Miloschewsky, Podder and Rudolph’s September 2026 preprint gives an oracle with \(\mathrm{BPP}^{O}=\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\) for total languages but \(\mathrm{PromiseBPP}^{O}\ne\mathrm{PromiseBQP}^{O}\). This shows, in a relativized setting, why a language equality cannot simply be substituted for the corresponding promise equality. It does not prove equality or separation of the ordinary total-language classes here.

source_formulation.text: The retained target is strict containment for total decision languages. In the inspected August 2019 edition of Wigderson, it is Conjecture 11.5, alongside Definition 11.1 and Theorem 11.2. Conjecture 11.4 in that edition concerns NP versus BQP; the older March 2018 numbering must not be carried over. The card keeps its finite H, T, CNOT basis and now gives explicit matrices, uniformity and measurement semantics.

cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states strict total-language containment as Conjecture 11.5. Primary oracle separations, the August 2026 shallow sampling publication and the September 2026 language/promise oracle example retain their specified model or output restrictions. Bounded searches located no full matching unrelativized separation or equality claim. An unverified claim that P differs from both BPP and BQP does not decide this comparison. This review checks statement and source scope; it does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all subsequent literature.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every choice of integers \(q\ge2\), \(r,g\ge1\) and real numbers \(J,\Delta>0\), does there exist a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta)\ge0\) with the following property? For every square-lattice size \(L\ge1\), every Hamiltonian satisfying the locality, norm, incidence, unique-ground-state and global-gap conditions below, and every subset \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), its ground state satisfies \[S(\rho_A)\le C\,|\partial A|.\] The constant must be independent of \(L\), the region and the particular interaction matrices. This is an entropy area law for general uniformly gapped two-dimensional local systems.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\Lambda_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^2\), with open boundaries and a copy of \(\mathbb C^q\) at each site. The full Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_L=\bigotimes_{x\in\Lambda_L}\mathbb C^q\), with the standard product basis and inner product \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian operator \(H=\sum_a h_a\), with a finite list of Hermitian interaction terms. Each term acts as identity outside a specified nonempty support \(X_a\subseteq\Lambda_L\). Its support has diameter at most \(r\) in the maximum-coordinate distance \(d_\infty(x,y)=\max\{|x_1-y_1|,|x_2-y_2|\}\). A one-site support has diameter zero. Each site belongs to at most \(g\) listed supports; terms with equal supports are counted separately. Every term has operator norm at most \(J\), where \(\|T\|=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Tv\|\) and \(\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}\). The terms need not be positive, commute, be translation invariant or admit a common energy-minimizing state.

List the eigenvalues of \(H\), with multiplicity, as \(E_0\le E_1\le\cdots\). Its lowest eigenspace is required to have dimension one and \(E_1-E_0\ge\Delta\). Choose a unit eigenvector \(\psi\) for \(E_0\). Uniqueness means uniqueness up to global phase, so \(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|\) is uniquely specified. The gap condition concerns the entire Hamiltonian only. No lower gap bound is assumed for subregions or subsets of its interaction terms. Both \(J\) and \(\Delta\) are in the same fixed energy units.

For \(A\subseteq\Lambda_L\), let \(A^c=\Lambda_L\setminus A\) and let \(\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_{A^c}(|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|)\). Partial trace is defined in product-basis indices by \[(\rho_A)_{u,v}=\sum_z\psi_{(u,z)}\,\overline{\psi_{(v,z)}},\] where \(u,v\) index basis configurations on \(A\), \(z\) ranges over configurations on \(A^c\), and tuples are placed in the original site order. This is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one. If its eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_D\), its entropy in bits is \(S(\rho_A)=-\sum_{j=1}^D\lambda_j\log_2\lambda_j\), with \(0\log_2 0=0\).

The geometric boundary \(\partial A\) consists of unordered nearest-neighbor lattice edges \(\{x,y\}\) with exactly one endpoint in \(A\), where \(|x_1-y_1|+|x_2-y_2|=1\). Its cardinality is measured in lattice units and is defined by geometry, even if a particular Hamiltonian has no term crossing an edge. No exterior vertices or periodic wrap-around edges are added. Regions may be disconnected or touch the exterior boundary. Empty and full regions have zero entropy and zero internal boundary. The interaction matrices may have arbitrary complex entries and may vary with location and with \(L\). There is no finite input encoding, state-preparation task, efficient computation requirement or frustration-free assumption. The question asks for a uniform mathematical entropy bound across all the specified finite systems.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal statement with the displayed order of quantifiers, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative answer fixes one choice of \(q,r,g,J,\Delta\) and shows that for every finite \(C\ge0\), there is an admissible system and region violating the bound. Equivalently, it may exhibit a sequence with these same fixed local parameters, unique ground states, gaps at least \(\Delta\), and unbounded ratios \(S(\rho_A)/|\partial A|\) on nontrivial regions. Allowing the gap to close, the interaction norm or local dimension to grow, or the lowest eigenspace to become degenerate does not refute this statement. A positive result for frustration-free or locally gapped systems, only one family of interactions, or an entropy bound with an unbounded extra logarithmic or subpolynomial factor does not prove it. No algorithm for finding the ground state is required. The statement is an exact yes/no bound; a fixed additive approximation to individual entropies is not a substitute.
cards.why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.

cards.context:
A region containing \(m\) sites has entropy at most \(m\log_2q\). For a square block with side length \(\ell\), this volume bound is quadratic in \(\ell\), while the conjecture permits only a constant times its boundary length. Fixing both interaction norms and the gap prevents rescaling an increasingly gapless family from appearing uniformly gapped.

Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped one-dimensional local systems. An interval has only a constant number of boundary edges, so its entropy stays bounded as the chain grows. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not give a constant independent of width: each grouped site has dimension \(q^L\).

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.

progress.text: Hastings proves the area law for gapped one-dimensional quantum systems; the bound depends on fixed local parameters.
Huang establishes QMA-completeness of two-dimensional local Hamiltonian problems even when ground states satisfy area laws, without claiming a uniform spectral gap.
Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar publish an area law for entanglement spread, rather than von Neumann entropy.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset give a nearly linear entropy bound for vertical cuts in locally gapped frustration-free systems. In arXiv version 3, the explicit bound is \(n^{1+O((\log  n)^{- 1/5})}\) at the end of §4.
Arad, Firanko, and Jain extend approximate-projector methods to mutual information of maximally mixed ground states; their theorem still requires a good approximate ground-space projector.
Garratt and Abanin derive entropy bounds from thermodynamic information and area laws for frustration-free systems with suitably bounded subsystem ground-space degeneracies.

sentences: An area law says that entanglement between a region and its surroundings grows with the region's boundary rather than its volume.
This problem asks for such a bound for the unique ground state of a general two-dimensional local Hamiltonian with a fixed positive spectral gap.
Interaction strength, local dimension, and interaction range are held fixed as the lattice grows.
Known routes involving frustration-free systems or additional conditions do not automatically establish the unrestricted statement recorded here.
A solution would clarify how strongly locality and an energy gap constrain many-body quantum states, without by itself supplying an efficient algorithm to find them.

problem_origin.note: The gapped two-dimensional area-law frontier was sharpened by Hastings’s one-dimensional theorem in 2007; area laws themselves have earlier physics roots.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal:
Can a completely classical verifier check arbitrary efficient quantum computation by interacting with one efficient quantum prover, with soundness against every computationally unbounded cheating prover?

The common input is an explicitly encoded quantum circuit \(C\) over \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), with all qubits initially zero and a designated output qubit. Write \(N\) for its description length and \(p(C)\) for the probability that measuring that output in the computational basis gives one. The promise is
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\iff p(C)\ge 2/3,\qquad C\in\mathrm{NO}\iff p(C)\le 1/3.\]
Does there exist one uniform interactive protocol \((P,V)\) and positive integer constants \(a,d\) with the following properties? The verifier \(V\) is a classical probabilistic machine; the honest prover \(P\) is a quantum machine with classical control. They exchange only classical messages with no setup or extra prover. Both honest computations, the verifier against every cheating strategy, the number of messages and total communication have the polynomial bounds specified below. For every promised circuit,
\[C\in\mathrm{YES}\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P\text{ on }C]\ge2/3,\]
\[C\in\mathrm{NO}\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall P^*\quad\Pr[V\text{ accepts in interaction with }P^*\text{ on }C]\le1/3.\]
Here \(P^*\) ranges over all adaptive response strategies, without any computational bound. The protocol and the constants precede the quantifiers over inputs and cheating strategies.
cards.definitions:
A circuit consists of \(q\ge1\) labelled qubits, an ordered list \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) of gates with \(m\ge0\), and an output index \(o\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). The one-qubit matrices and two-qubit action are
\[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|x,y\rangle=|x,x\mathbin\oplus y\rangle.\]
Here \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Each gate acts on its indicated qubit or ordered pair of distinct qubits and as the identity on the rest. Let \(U_C=g_m\cdots g_1\), with identity for an empty list. In the vector space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes q}\), set
\[p(C)=\sum_{\substack{z\in\{0,1\}^q\\z_o=1}}|\langle z|U_C|0^q\rangle|^2.\]
These gate entries and probabilities are exact mathematical quantities, not floating-point input data. No correctness condition is imposed when \(1/3<p(C)<2/3\).

For a concrete bit encoding, write \(q\) as \(1^q0\), followed by \(U(m),U(o)\) and every gate in sequence. The length-delimited integer code is \(U(b)=1^\ell0s\), where \(s\) is the canonical binary expansion of \(b\ge0\), \(\ell=|s|\), and zero has expansion 0. A gate uses a two-bit tag for H, T or CNOT, followed by the \(U\)-encoded target indices; the fourth tag is invalid. All indices must be within the declared range and CNOT indices must be distinct. No trailing bits are allowed. Thus \(q\le N\) and all gates are explicitly listed. Both parties receive the same classical description; neither receives an additional quantum input or witness. Malformed descriptions are rejected by the verifier.

The two algorithms have fixed finite classical control programs, independent of \(N\) and \(C\). The verifier has ordinary classical work tapes, private independent fair random bits, and a classical message interface. It has no quantum register, quantum channel or ability to prepare, transform or measure qubits. The honest prover starts with zero qubits, may create zero ancillas, apply H, T and CNOT gates, measure qubits in the computational basis, and use outcomes in subsequent classical computation. Measurements follow the squared-amplitude rule; a measured qubit may be discarded. Its classical controller may also toss fair coins. Gate addresses, classical arithmetic and generation of the next instruction are computed and charged. There is no input-dependent or length-dependent advice, precomputed advice state or uncharged oracle for either honest party.

Put \(R(N)=a(N+1)^d\). On every input and every branch of its private randomness, the verifier uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps, reads at most that many received bits, and halts with accept or reject. This clock holds against every possible sequence of replies. In an honest execution, the prover uses at most \(R(N)\) classical bit steps and elementary quantum operations in total, on every randomness and measurement branch. One elementary quantum operation acts on at most two addressed qubits; all classical bit operations and all written or read message bits are charged. The honest prover holds at most \(R(N)\) qubits. These bounds also apply to well-formed circuits outside the promise. The protocol allows at most \(R(N)\) messages and \(R(N)\) communicated bits in total; the verifier enforces the declared message lengths and aborts on a violation. A missing reply or an explicit abort is rejection. There is no constant-round requirement or uncharged preprocessing phase.

For soundness, an arbitrary prover strategy can be described by a conditional distribution on its next classical reply for each input and history of messages it has seen. It can have unlimited private memory and arbitrary input-dependent information, but cannot see the verifier's private coins except through sent messages. This description includes the observable behaviour of any quantum cheating prover through the classical interface; no bound on its computation, circuit size or internal state is assumed. Acceptance probabilities include all private randomness and measurement outcomes. There is no initial shared secret, correlated setup state, trusted third party, random oracle or enforced separation inside the single prover.

Completeness concerns the one fixed honest algorithm on all YES instances. Soundness concerns every strategy on each NO instance. The task is verification of this decision promise problem; it imposes no separate blindness, sampling-output or witness-preservation requirement. Fixed error constants are part of the specification, rather than a numerical approximation tolerance for the final answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a protocol or its full logical negation. A positive answer must give uniform algorithms and universal polynomial resource bounds, prove completeness on every YES circuit, and prove the stated bound against all unbounded response strategies on every NO circuit. A negative answer must rule out every protocol in this model: for each resource-bounded pair, some YES input violates completeness or some NO input and cheating strategy violate soundness. A cryptographic argument sound only against efficient attackers, a quantum verifier, extra isolated provers, an inefficient honest prover or an impossibility theorem restricted to particular protocols does not settle this proposition.
cards.why: The question isolates the resources needed for a classical user to trust a quantum answer. Known protocols obtain trust by giving the verifier some quantum capability, separating several devices, or assuming that particular computations are hard for an attacker. Resolving the stated conjunction would determine whether any of those additional resources is necessary when the honest server itself remains efficient.

cards.context:
The honest-prover condition matters as much as the classical-verifier condition. The standard containments of quantum polynomial time in polynomial space, and IP=PSPACE, provide classical interactive proofs with an unrestricted prover. They do not establish that the auxiliary answers needed by that prover can be generated by a quantum polynomial-time machine. A verification protocol that demands a substantially more powerful server would not meet this card.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev supply information-theoretically sound verification with an efficient quantum prover when the verifier retains a small quantum register. For a fixed error gap, a constant number of qubits suffices in their result. Although their class definition first restricts dishonest provers, they explicitly state that the protocol proof protects against unbounded provers. Eliminating the verifier’s remaining quantum capability is the open question highlighted in their §1.8.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani use separated entangled quantum subsystems. Their classical verifier can certify and control quantum operations under the noncommunication constraints of that model. A single freely communicating prover is allowed to coordinate its replies across all of its internal components, so combining the devices loses a condition used by the multiprover theorem.

Mahadev’s protocol achieves the classical verifier and single efficient quantum prover by using a computational assumption. The inspected version bases its construction on quantum hardness of Learning With Errors with the specified superpolynomial noise ratio. Its soundness quantifies over efficient quantum cheating algorithms. An unbounded strategy is outside that guarantee, even if the protocol is otherwise fully classical at the interface.

The February 2026 quantum-cat preprint addresses preservation of a quantum witness: the prover can reuse one copy while obtaining negligible errors. Its abstract retains the post-quantum LWE assumption. A QMA witness is an additional quantum input that is not present in the all-zero BQP computation here, and preserving it does not remove the computational soundness assumption.

Another February 2026 preprint gives a conditional barrier to quantum black-box reductions for non-interactive QMA verification from falsifiable assumptions. Its model has one message after instance-independent setup, and its premise is a QMA–QCMA gap problem. Both the task and the restrictions differ from this card’s arbitrary polynomial interaction for BQP. The checked abstract therefore supplies no general impossibility answer here.

The April 2026 paper proves \(\mathrm{BQP}^{O}\subseteq\mathrm{MIP}^{O}\) for every classical oracle \(O\). Its associated classical proof is exponentially long but checked at polynomially many adaptively chosen locations. The theorem concerns several classical provers without shared entanglement, and it does not promise that their honest work is quantum polynomial time. Section 2 separately asks for such an efficient-prover result. The paper presents relativization as a research perspective, not as an equivalence resolving single-prover verification.

The May 2026 trusted-gate article removes trusted state preparation and measurement from the client’s requirements while retaining trusted quantum transformations. Its first construction uses single-qubit rotations and bit flips; the inspected preprint explicitly sends qubits through the client. Removing two hardware capabilities is useful progress, but the client still has quantum operations and quantum communication. It is not the classical machine specified here.

For this question, “information-theoretic” is a quantifier about every cheating strategy. It does not require perfect completeness, zero soundness error, blindness or verification of an entire output distribution. Keeping these notions distinct prevents either a stronger unrelated task or a weaker computational guarantee from replacing the stated decision problem.

The May 2026 trusted-gate article removes trusted state preparation and measurement from the client’s requirements while retaining trusted quantum transformations. Its first construction uses single-qubit rotations and bit flips; the inspected preprint explicitly sends qubits through the client. Removing two hardware capabilities is useful progress, but the client still has quantum operations and quantum communication. It is not the classical machine specified here.

For this question, “information-theoretic” is a quantifier about every cheating strategy. It does not require perfect completeness, zero soundness error, blindness or verification of an entire output distribution. Keeping these notions distinct prevents either a stronger unrelated task or a weaker computational guarantee from replacing the stated decision problem.

cards.title: NPT bound entanglement
cards.formal: Does there exist a negative-partial-transpose state that is undistillable for every finite number of copies? Precisely, are there integers \(a,b\ge2\) and a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) such that \(\rho^{\Gamma_B}\) has a strictly negative eigenvalue and \[\langle\psi,(\rho^{\Gamma_B})^{\otimes k}\psi\rangle\ge0\] for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\otimes(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\) of Schmidt rank at most two across the displayed bipartition? The same dimensions and the same state must satisfy the condition for all \(k\).
cards.definitions:
All vector spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb C\). The inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j\), and a unit vector has \(\langle u,u\rangle=1\). A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(\langle v,\rho v\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. In the fixed standard product basis, with indices \(i,r\in\{1,\ldots,a\}\) and \(j,s\in\{1,\ldots,b\}\), its partial transpose on the second party is \[(\rho^{\Gamma_B})_{(i,j),(r,s)}=\rho_{(i,s),(r,j)}.\] This matrix is Hermitian but need not be positive semidefinite. Negative partial transpose, abbreviated NPT, means it has an eigenvalue strictly less than zero. Positive partial transpose, abbreviated PPT, means all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; zero eigenvalues do not make a state NPT. The \(k\)-fold tensor power is the Kronecker product of \(k\) copies of the same matrix. When evaluating the displayed expectation, regroup the tensor factors from \((A_1B_1)\cdots(A_kB_k)\) into \((A_1\cdots A_k)(B_1\cdots B_k)\), where \(A_j=\mathbb C^a\) and \(B_j=\mathbb C^b\). The corresponding permutation of basis vectors is part of this identification. Schmidt rank of \(\psi\) across these two groups is the least integer \(r\) such that \(\psi=\sum_{j=1}^r u_j\otimes v_j\), with \(u_j\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\) and \(v_j\in(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\). No independence or product condition is imposed between copies within either party.

A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination \(\sum_j p_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) of local density matrices, with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\); otherwise it is entangled. Every NPT state is entangled. The exact criterion used in this question defines \(k\)-copy distillability as existence of a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two unit vector with strictly negative displayed expectation. A state is distillable if such a vector exists for at least one finite \(k\); undistillable means none exists at any finite \(k\). This finite-matrix definition is the formal target. It agrees with the standard operational notion of obtaining entangled two-qubit states with positive probability from finitely many copies using local operations and classical communication, and hence of distilling Bell pairs at positive asymptotic rate. That interpretation allows two-way classical communication and local ancillary systems, but no quantum communication or extra shared entanglement. The card asks for mathematical existence, not efficient preparation or an algorithm acting on a finite encoding of \(\rho\); arbitrary complex matrix entries are allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of a single finite-dimensional state satisfying the NPT condition and every quantified rank-two inequality, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every finite \(a,b\) and every NPT density matrix \(\rho\), some finite \(k\) and eligible unit vector \(\psi\) give a strictly negative expectation. In the second outcome, \(k\) and the vector may depend on \(\rho\), and no universal copy bound is requested. Numerical checks, one fixed copy count, a restricted set of test vectors, or a sequence of different states depending on \(k\) do not establish the existential all-copy statement. Positivity and negativity are exact; this yes/no problem has no numerical approximation substitute.
cards.why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.

cards.context:
Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

In local dimension two, every bipartite vector has Schmidt rank at most two, so an NPT state is already one-copy distillable. The open problem therefore concerns larger local spaces. The formal statement still quantifies over all finite dimensions, with no promise that the state has a rational description, a symmetry, or an efficient preparation circuit.

DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal investigated NPT states whose one-copy behavior differs from their spectral negativity. Their evidence did not establish one fixed NPT state undistillable for every finite number of copies. The present question retains that full order of quantifiers.

The Werner family is \(\rho_{\mathrm W}(d,\alpha)=(I+\alpha F)/(d^2+\alpha d)\), for \(d\ge2\) and \(-1\le\alpha\le1\), where \(F(u\otimes v)=v\otimes u\) swaps the two local systems and \(I\) is identity. Its members are NPT exactly for \(\alpha<-1/d\), and one-copy distillable exactly for \(\alpha<-1/2\). Thus \(-1/2\le\alpha<-1/d\) is the NPT one-copy-undistillable interval when \(d\ge3\). This is a known subclass; the target is not restricted to Werner states.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(4,- 1/2)\). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

Bharti, Gajjala and Haug also obtain the two-copy threshold and several restricted finite-copy extensions, while explicitly leaving the general all-copy assertion open. A family of states indexed by the allowed number of copies does not give the single fixed state required by the existential target.

Wu and Zou prove three-copy endpoint nonnegativity for specified sectors, including normal rank-two coefficient operators. A coefficient operator is the matrix of a bipartite test vector in product bases; normal means that the matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose. Other rank-two matrices are allowed in the full criterion, so these sector results do not settle unrestricted three-copy distillability or the all-copy question.

cards.title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable stabilizer codes
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(r,\delta,s>0\) and positive integers \(w,b\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge1\), some stabilizer code on \(n\ge N\) qubits has an admissible list of checks as defined below and satisfies \[k\ge rn,\qquad d\ge\delta n,\qquad H\succeq\frac{s}{n}D_Q?\] Here \(k\) is its number of logical qubits, \(d\) its code distance, each listed check acts on at most \(w\) qubits, and each qubit occurs in at most \(b\) listed checks. All five constants are fixed for the unbounded family. This is the bounded-degree stabilizer version of asymptotically good quantum local testability.
cards.definitions:
The physical Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). In the standard one-qubit basis, \(X|0\rangle=|1\rangle\), \(X|1\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|0\rangle=|0\rangle\), \(Z|1\rangle=-|1\rangle\), and \(Y=iXZ\), where \(i^2=-1\). The Pauli group consists of tensor products of \(I,X,Y,Z\), multiplied by phases from \(\{1,-1,i,-i\}\). A Pauli's support is the set of positions with a nonidentity tensor factor, and its weight is the cardinality of that set; the scalar phase does not affect support.

An admissible stabilizer presentation is a finite nonempty list \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) of Hermitian Pauli checks of positive weight. Hermitian means \(S_j=S_j^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose. The checks commute pairwise, and the group they generate does not contain \(-I\). Its code space is \[Q=\{\psi\in\mathcal H_n:S_j\psi=\psi\text{ for every }j\}.\] This nonzero space has dimension \(2^k\); the target requires \(k\ge1\). The distance \(d\) is the minimum weight of a Pauli \(P\) that preserves \(Q\), meaning \(P(Q)=Q\), but whose restriction to \(Q\) is not a scalar multiple of identity. For a stabilizer code with \(k\ge1\), such logical Paulis exist. This distance concerns undetectable changes to encoded information. The rate is \(k/n\) and the relative distance is \(d/n\).

The checks need not be independent, and a list may contain repetitions. The bounds refer to that actual list: \(\operatorname{wt}(S_j)\le w\) for every \(j\), and each qubit belongs to the supports of at most \(b\) checks, counting repetitions separately. Both are maximum bounds, not average bounds. Define the normalized check Hamiltonian \[H=\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{I-S_j}{2}.\] Each summand is the orthogonal projection onto the failing eigenspace of one check. If a check is selected uniformly, the rejection probability on a unit vector \(\phi\) is \(\langle\phi,H\phi\rangle\); on a density matrix \(\rho\) it is \(\operatorname{Tr}(H\rho)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one.

For \(0\le t\le n\), let \(Q_t\) be the complex linear span of vectors \(E\psi\), where \(\psi\in Q\) and \(E\) ranges over Pauli errors of weight at most \(t\). Let \(\Pi_t\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(Q_t\). These spaces are nested, with \(Q_0=Q\) and \(Q_n=\mathcal H_n\). Define \[D_Q=\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(I-\Pi_t)=\sum_{t=1}^n t(\Pi_t-\Pi_{t-1}).\] The two expressions agree by telescoping. The eigenvalue \(t\) measures the error radius of the corresponding orthogonal layer. Using Pauli errors in the span is equivalent to using arbitrary operators supported on at most \(t\) qubits, since local Pauli products span all such operators. This is not trace distance between density matrices.

The inequality \(H\succeq(s/n)D_Q\) means its difference is positive semidefinite: \(\langle\phi,[H-(s/n)D_Q]\phi\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(\phi\in\mathcal H_n\), where \(\langle u,v\rangle=u^\dagger v\). Equivalently it holds in expectation for every density matrix. The number \(s\) is normalized soundness. The family may use an arbitrary unbounded sequence of lengths rather than every integer length. Checks may connect any qubits, without geometric locality. No CSS restriction, efficient construction, decoding algorithm or transversal-gate property is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that fixed constants and an unbounded family satisfying all conditions exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every \(r,\delta,s>0\) and positive integers \(w,b\), there is a finite length bound beyond which no admissible presentation satisfies all the conditions simultaneously. An existence proof need not provide a polynomial-time construction. A failure for one proposed family, one subclass such as CSS codes, or one geometry does not prove nonexistence. Inverse-polylogarithmic soundness or relative distance, a growing maximum check weight or incidence, and a soundness guarantee confined to selected error weights do not meet the target. The operator inequality must cover the entire physical Hilbert space. This is an exact existence question, not a numerical approximation task.
cards.why: A central missing object connecting quantum error correction to robust verification. It asks whether sparse quantum constraints can simultaneously protect a linear amount of information and detect global corruption with constant normalized soundness.
