cards.title: Exponential repetition of two-player entangled games
cards.formal: Does every finite two-player, one-round game \(G\) with entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)<1\) admit a constant \(c_{G}>0\) such that \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq \exp(-c_{G}n)\qquad\text{for every integer }n\geq1?\] The repetition uses the unchanged game and requires winning every coordinate. The 2016 paper proves convergence to zero at a polynomial rate; an August 2026 manuscript claims the exponential bound, with verification limits recorded below.
cards.definitions:
A game is specified by finite nonempty question sets \(X,Y\), finite nonempty answer sets \(A,B\), a probability distribution \(\mu\) on \(X\times Y\), and a winning predicate \(V:X\times Y\times A\times B\to\{0,1\}\). The referee samples \((x,y)\) from \(\mu\), sends \(x\) only to Alice and \(y\) only to Bob, and accepts their answers \(a,b\) exactly when \(V(x,y,a,b)=1\). The two questions may be correlated, and some pairs may have probability zero.

Before receiving their questions, the players may share any finite-dimensional bipartite quantum state \(\rho\) on \(\mathcal H_{A}\otimes\mathcal H_{B}\). On question \(x\), Alice applies a measurement \(\{E^{x}_{a}:a\in A\}\); on question \(y\), Bob applies \(\{F^{y}_{b}:b\in B\}\). Each measurement is a family of positive semidefinite operators summing to the identity. Their conditional answer probability is
\[\Pr[a,b\mid x,y]=\operatorname{Tr}\!\bigl(\rho(E^{x}_{a}\otimes F^{y}_{b})\bigr).\]
They cannot communicate after receiving the questions. Shared randomness is permitted and can be incorporated into the shared state.

The entangled value \(\omega^{*}(G)\) is the supremum of the winning probability over all such finite-dimensional states and local measurements. The dimensions have no fixed upper bound, and a strategy attaining the supremum need not exist. This is the finite-dimensional tensor-product model, not the possibly larger commuting-operator or general nonsignaling model. No efficiency restriction is placed on a strategy.

In \(G^{\otimes n}\), the referee samples \(n\) independent pairs from \(\mu\), sends the complete tuple of Alice's questions to Alice and the complete tuple of Bob's questions to Bob, and receives answer tuples in \(A^{n}\) and \(B^{n}\). Acceptance requires \(V(x_{i},y_{i},a_{i},b_{i})=1\) for every coordinate \(i\).

Each player may use one joint local measurement depending on their entire tuple. Their shared state and its dimension may depend on \(n\). Thus independent sampling by the referee does not force independent play. Product strategies give the lower bound \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\geq\omega^{*}(G)^{n}\); this is not the requested upper bound.

The constant \(c_{G}\) may depend on the entire fixed game, including its soundness gap \(1-\omega^{*}(G)\). It must be positive and independent of \(n\), the strategy and its dimension. No universal optimal exponent or algorithm for computing \(c_{G}\) is requested. A transformed game with added questions is a different game and cannot replace \(G\) in this statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal exponential upper bound in the stated strategy model, or exhibit one fixed finite game with value below one for which no positive \(c_{G}\) works. A sequence of different games with progressively slower exponential constants is not a counterexample. Polynomial decay, convergence to zero, exponential decay only for a special game family, or amplification after changing the game does not settle the conjecture.
cards.why: Determines how reliably independent challenges amplify soundness against quantum players who may coordinate across all copies. The universal question isolates the effect of entanglement without adding auxiliary tests or restricting the form of the game.

Theorem 1.1 and Definitions 2.1–2.2 were read; the proof was not independently verified. A claimed resolution, not certified here as an accepted theorem.

cards.context:
Yuen proves \(\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})=O_{G}(n^{-1/4}\log n)\) for \(n\geq2\). Hence the repeated value cannot stay bounded away from zero. The surrounding text explicitly leaves exponential decay as the full conjecture; the previous working summary conflated these two targets.

The source describes anchoring and fortification transformations that add auxiliary questions and give exponential decay for the resulting game while preserving quantum completeness. This supplies useful gap amplification but does not bound standard repetition of every original game.

Chapter 6, Theorem 1.1, claims a universal \(c>0\) with \[\omega^{*}(G^{\otimes n})\leq\exp\!\left(-c\,\frac{\varepsilon^{13}}{\varepsilon+\ln(|A||B|)}\,n\right),\qquad\varepsilon=1-\omega^{*}(G)>0.\] Its definitions allow arbitrary finite-dimensional joint strategies and correlated question distributions for the unchanged game. If valid, this resolves the displayed conjecture; the exponent \(13\) is not claimed optimal.

This review checked the manuscript’s version date, theorem and model against the original conjecture. It did not independently verify the proof or establish an independently reviewed publication of this result. The card therefore records an uncertain claimed resolution rather than labeling the conjecture securely open or verified resolved.

cards.title: Dihedral hidden subgroup problem in BQP
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), every integer \(\ell\ge1\), every subgroup \(H\le D_N\), and every function \(f:D_N\to\{0,1\}^{\ell}\) hiding \(H\) as defined below, the algorithm outputs a finite list generating exactly \(H\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+\ell+2)^c\) total operations? The only external quantum oracle is the reversible evaluation of \(f\). The bound is uniform over subgroup and hiding-function choices and includes both oracle calls and all other computation.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\) with addition modulo \(N\). The dihedral group \(D_N=\mathbb Z_N\times\{0,1\}\) has multiplication \[(x,b)(y,d)=\bigl((x+(-1)^by)\bmod N,\ (b+d)\bmod2\bigr).\] Its identity is \((0,0)\). A subgroup is a subset containing the identity and closed under products and inverses. For \(g\in D_N\), the left coset \(gH\) is \(\{gh:h\in H\}\). The hiding promise is \[f(g)=f(g')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad gH=g'H.\] Thus each coset has one label and distinct cosets have different labels; no structure in the label bits is promised. The classical input is \(N\) in binary and the register width \(\ell\) in unary, fixing input size at the parameter scale \(\log N+\ell\) used in the inherited bound. With \(m=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\), an element is encoded by \(m\) bits for \(x\), followed by one bit for \(b\). Bit strings with \(x\ge N\) are invalid element encodings. The oracle acts on a group register and an \(\ell\)-bit register by \[U_f|g,z\rangle=|g,z\mathbin\oplus f(g)\rangle\] for valid \(g\), extended linearly to superpositions, and acts as identity on invalid group encodings. Here the XOR acts coordinatewise. Each invocation costs one operation; it is self-inverse. The algorithm has no classical truth table of \(f\), subgroup description, coset-state preparation oracle, subset-sum oracle or uncharged random-access-memory service. It may implement additional operations using the allowed gates and controller, with their full cost charged. Output is a classical finite list of valid encoded elements; success means that the smallest subgroup containing all listed elements is \(H\). The empty list generates the identity subgroup. Writing the list is charged, so its length is automatically bounded by the running time. The algorithm may fail with probability at most \(1/3\), but its running-time guarantee holds on every execution. Probability is over its measurements and internal randomness for each fixed legal \(N,\ell,H,f\). When \(\ell\) is polynomial in \(\log N\), as in the usual succinct oracle setting, the requested time is polynomial in \(\log N\).

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with all stated guarantees, or of the logical negation ruling out every eligible uniform algorithm and polynomial total-work bound. An affirmative proof must establish exact subgroup-generation correctness with the specified probability for every legal hiding function. A negative proof must apply to the full model, not merely a particular sieve, measurement family or recently proposed procedure. Polynomial query complexity with superpolynomial postprocessing, a method requiring an additional oracle, or uncounted parallel work is insufficient. The target is a yes/no algorithm-existence statement; subgroup generators on each input must be exact, and numerical approximation of a group element is not an alternative answer.
cards.why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.

cards.context:
Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has \(H=H_{s}=\{(0,0),(s,1)\}\), with an unknown \(s\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\). The hiding promise says \(f(x,0)=f(x+s,1)\), and each restriction to \(b=0\) or \(b=1\) is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

In the reflection case, a coset sample is a state \((|0,x\rangle+|1,x+s\rangle)/\sqrt2\) with an unknown random \(x\). Its Fourier representation includes a known random label \(k\) and a qubit with relative phase \(e^{2\pi i ks/N}\), for a chosen Fourier-sign convention. This phase encodes information about \(s\); it is not a classical register containing \(ks\). The sample interface and the hiding-function oracle interface are distinct.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  N})}\). It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length \(n\approx \log  N\): the target here is \(n^{O(1)}\), not \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\).

Regev’s separate polynomial-space algorithm uses time \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N}))\). Improving quantum memory alone and obtaining polynomial total running time are different achievements.

Kuperberg’s later collimation algorithm attains \(\exp(O(\sqrt{\log N}))\) time with logarithmic quantum space and subexponential classical storage. The paper explicitly separates quantum-addressable classical memory from ordinary memory: Proposition 4.2 analyzes the former, while Corollary 4.3 gives an implementation without quantum memory access, with its additional work counted. No free memory-access primitive is included in this card’s target.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be \(N/2\), which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
cards.formal: Does the ordinary graph-isomorphism decision problem belong to \(\mathrm{BQP}\), bounded-error quantum polynomial time? That is, do there exist one uniform quantum algorithm and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, for every pair of finite simple graphs given by their complete binary adjacency matrices, the algorithm decides whether a vertex bijection preserves adjacency, with error at most \(1/3\), using at most \(C(n+2)^c\) total elementary operations, where \(n\) is the larger vertex count? No distributional or structural promise is imposed on the graphs.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(r\ge0\), write \([r]=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite simple graph on \([r]\) is an undirected graph with no loops or parallel edges. Its adjacency matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{r\times r}\) is symmetric with zero diagonal. Each input graph is encoded by its binary order with a self-delimiting length prefix, followed by all adjacency entries in row-major order; the two graph encodings are concatenated. A prefix can be encoded as \(1^t0\) followed by a \(t\)-bit binary order, using \(t\ge1\) and the usual minimal binary representation. Invalid encodings are rejected. Graphs of different orders are not isomorphic. If both have order \(r\), an isomorphism is a bijection \(\pi:[r]\to[r]\) such that \[A_{uv}=B_{\pi(u),\pi(v)}\qquad\text{for every }u,v\in[r].\] The two order-zero graphs are isomorphic. A yes-instance has at least one such bijection; a no-instance has none. The algorithm must accept every yes-instance with probability at least \(2/3\) and every no-instance with probability at most \(1/3\). Its probability is over its quantum measurement outcomes and any internal random bits, separately for each fixed input. It receives only the explicit classical input, with no witness, nonuniform advice, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle, promised rigidity, degree bound or typical-input assumption. Here GI denotes this ordinary permutation-based relation, not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory. The running time is polynomial in the graph order and hence in the explicit input length; malformed encodings must be rejected in time polynomial in their actual length.

The allowed elementary gates are \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \[H=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle.\] Here \(a,b\) are bits and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. A quantum register of \(r\) qubits has computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^r\}\); its pure state is a unit vector \(\sum_z\alpha_z|z\rangle\) with complex coefficients. Gates act by their specified unitary matrices on selected qubits and as identity elsewhere. A computational-basis measurement of a register has outcome probabilities given by the squared norms of its corresponding state components. All working qubits start at zero. Classical control is performed by one finite Turing program with no advice; each classical bit step, each elementary gate, and each measured or initialized qubit is charged. Fair random bits, if used, cost one step each. All executions halt within the displayed worst-case bound. This uniform circuit-and-control model charges total work, including input parsing, data preparation, classical postprocessing and output, rather than only circuit depth.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language lies in BQP, including uniformity, bounded error on every input and polynomial total work, or a complete Lean-checked proof that it does not lie in BQP. A classical polynomial-time algorithm is a valid affirmative solution because it can be implemented within the quantum model with polynomial overhead. A negative proof must exclude all uniform bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms, rather than only coset-state, Fourier-sampling or photonic-sampling methods. A necessary invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic graphs, an efficient fixed relaxation, or uncharged preparation of a helpful state does not establish membership. The output is a proof of the yes/no complexity statement, not an approximate isomorphism score.
cards.why: A canonical test of whether quantum computation can efficiently recognize equivalence of explicit combinatorial structures, beyond the algebraic problems already handled by standard period finding.

cards.context:
Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\) would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). cards.title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
cards.formal: For every finite pair of local dimensions \(d_A,d_B\ge2\) and every entangled state \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^{d_A}\otimes\mathbb C^{d_B}\), do there exist a finite integer \(k\ge1\), local filters with strictly positive joint success probability, and finite families of local measurements for which the successfully filtered state obtained from \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) has Bell-nonlocal correlations? Both filters act before the measurement settings are chosen. No auxiliary shared entangled state is supplied. The number of copies, filters, output dimensions and measurement families may depend on \(\rho\).
cards.definitions:
A density matrix is a Hermitian matrix \(X=X^\dagger\) with \(v^\dagger Xv\ge0\) for all complex vectors \(v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}X=1\). Dagger is conjugate transpose and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination of product density matrices; entangled means not separable. No purity, rational-entry or efficient-preparation promise is imposed. The \(k\) copies are independent copies of the same state. Regroup the tensor factors of \(\rho^{\otimes k}\) into Alice's \((\mathbb C^{d_A})^{\otimes k}\) and Bob's \((\mathbb C^{d_B})^{\otimes k}\); each party may act jointly on all of its own copies.

A successful local filter is specified by finitely many rectangular complex matrices \(A_j\) from Alice's input space to a finite output space \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\), with \(\sum_jA_j^\dagger A_j\le I\). It maps \(X\) to \(\mathcal F_A(X)=\sum_j A_jXA_j^\dagger\). Bob's filter \(\mathcal F_B\) is defined by matrices \(B_l\) and \(\sum_lB_l^\dagger B_l\le I\), with output \(\mathbb C^{r_B}\). Here \(S\le I\) means \(I-S\) is positive semidefinite. These are precisely finite-dimensional completely positive trace-nonincreasing maps. Their joint success probability and conditional output are \[q=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})\bigr]>0,\qquad \sigma=\frac{(\mathcal F_A\otimes\mathcal F_B)(\rho^{\otimes k})}{q}.\] No lower bound on \(q\) uniform over states or copy counts is required. The success flags may be compared before the measurement settings are chosen. The filters cannot depend on those settings. Local ancillary states are absorbed in the local maps; no entangled ancilla shared between the parties is permitted.

Let \(X,Y,O_A,O_B\) be finite nonempty sets of settings and outcomes. For each \(x\in X\), Alice's positive-operator-valued measurement is a family \((M_{\alpha|x})_{\alpha\in O_A}\) of positive semidefinite operators on \(\mathbb C^{r_A}\) summing to identity. Define Bob's \((N_{\beta|y})_{\beta\in O_B}\) similarly. The conditional correlation is \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\sigma(M_{\alpha|x}\otimes N_{\beta|y})\bigr].\] Measurement settings are independently selected after successful preparation; no communication is allowed after they are supplied. All outcomes are retained in this distribution, with no further postselection on outcomes or settings.

The correlation is Bell-local if there are a finite set \(L\), nonnegative weights \(w_\lambda\) summing to one, and normalized conditional probability distributions \(u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)\), \(v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\), such that \[p(\alpha,\beta\mid x,y)=\sum_{\lambda\in L}w_\lambda u_\lambda(\alpha\mid x)v_\lambda(\beta\mid y)\] for every setting and outcome. The weights cannot depend on \(x,y\). For finite settings and outcomes this includes all local hidden-variable models, since deterministic response tables have a finite convex hull. Bell-nonlocal means no such representation exists. Equivalently, the distribution violates some linear Bell inequality valid for all local distributions. The target permits every finite Bell scenario, not only two settings or the CHSH inequality. Public shared randomness may select local procedures, but cannot turn a convex combination of Bell-local correlations into a nonlocal one; existence can therefore be tested for fixed filters and measurements as above. There is no computation, sample or circuit-size bound on the chosen operations.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal finite-copy assertion, or of its logical negation: there is one finite-dimensional entangled state for which every finite \(k\), every allowed pair of filters with positive success probability, and every finite family of local measurements produces a Bell-local distribution. A positive proof need not bound \(k\), filter success probability or violation size uniformly over states. A one-copy local model, including a model surviving every one-copy filter, does not establish the negative all-copy assertion. Activation with a different auxiliary entangled state, a network with additional parties, or a test with quantum inputs does not establish the specified bipartite target. Bell violation and filter positivity are exact mathematical conditions; approximate numerical evidence alone is insufficient.
cards.why: A positive answer would give every entangled bipartite state an intrinsic Bell-nonlocal manifestation using only repeated access to that same state. A negative answer would exhibit entanglement that remains Bell-local under every finite collective local test and preliminary filter. This separates the mathematical resource of entanglement from the observable nonlocal correlations used in device-independent information tasks.

cards.context:
Entanglement describes the shared state. Bell nonlocality describes observed correlations that cannot be reproduced by local response functions and shared randomness. The source explicitly asks whether collective use of repeated copies and preliminary local filtering always connects these two notions.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove that entanglement can activate a Bell violation when combined with a suitable auxiliary state. That auxiliary resource need not be a copy of the state being tested, so the theorem leaves the question in this card open.

Hirsch and coauthors exhibit entangled two-qubit states remaining Bell-local after every local filter on one copy, including general positive-operator-valued measurements. Their theorem rules out a universal one-copy claim; it does not give a state remaining local after arbitrary numbers of copies.

The December 2025 broadcast result places the original source in a four-party experiment and rules out quantum-realizable broadcast explanations with a separable source across the original cut. Its additional parties and causal assumptions differ from the ordinary two-party local hidden-variable definition here. Its universal entanglement-certification result therefore does not settle this repeated-copy question.

The original source also distinguishes arbitrary Bell inequalities from the CHSH test. The repeated-copy filtered CHSH criterion is tied to distillability, while the present target allows every finite setting and outcome configuration. Restricting the output test to CHSH would change the question.

cards.title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
cards.formal: Determine the optimal polynomial separation exponent \[\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}=\inf\bigl\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall\text{ nonconstant }f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\ R(f)\le C\,Q(f)^a\bigr\}.\] Here \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) are randomized and quantum bit-query complexities with worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The constant \(C\) must be independent of both \(n\) and \(f\). The known range is \(3\le\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\le4\). This card makes the source's maximum-gap question precise at the level of its polynomial exponent; logarithmic factors are not part of this numerical target.
cards.definitions:
A total Boolean function assigns one output bit to every length-\(n\) bit string, with no promise restricting the inputs. Nonconstant means that both output values occur. A deterministic decision tree adaptively chooses an input coordinate, receives its bit, and ultimately outputs a bit. Its depth is the maximum number of queries on a root-to-leaf path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution over deterministic trees of depth at most \(T\). It must output \(f(x)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input \(x\). The least possible \(T\) is \(R(f)\); unlimited computation and storage between queries are free.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

Both complexities are positive integers for nonconstant functions and at most \(n\). The infimum takes all real nonnegative exponents with a universal multiplicative bound. An exponent at the infimum need not itself admit such a bound: logarithmic factors may prevent attainment. Removing constant functions avoids zero-complexity conventions. The approximation tolerance for \(\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\) concerns the exponent itself, not a relative approximation to a query count.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a_*\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a_*-\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) suffices via its midpoint. It must control the universal upper bound and the existence of sufficiently large separations to certify this accuracy; merely improving one currently known bound does not suffice. The benchmark does not require resolving logarithmic factors or proving that the infimum exponent is attained.
cards.why: This quantifies the greatest possible quantum query advantage when an algorithm must handle every input, without a promise. It tests a basic limitation on quantum speedups and distinguishes the role of classical randomization from that of deterministic computation.

cards.context:
Quantum algorithms can exploit a special promise to obtain enormous advantages over randomized algorithms. Total functions remove that freedom. Every input string must have a specified correct answer, so both the quantum algorithm and its classical competitors must handle adversarial inputs.

The quartic upper bound follows from \(R(f)\le D(f)=O(Q(f)^4)\), where \(D(f)\) is deterministic decision-tree depth. A matching separation between deterministic and quantum queries does not automatically give a matching separation against randomized algorithms.

The near-cubic lower-bound family comes from stronger promise-problem separations combined with a construction turning them into total functions. This establishes an exponent of at least three; it does not supply a quartic randomized separation.

The exponent formulation intentionally ignores subpolynomial factors. For example, an additional logarithmic factor in a universal cubic bound would still be compatible with exponent three. Establishing the exact bound with exponent three and no extra factor is a finer question.

cards.title: Quantum query-to-communication lifting
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge0\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), there is a total nonconstant Boolean communication gadget \(g_n:\{0,1\}^{a_n}\times\{0,1\}^{b_n}\to\{0,1\}\), with finite positive integers \(a_n,b_n\), for which every partial Boolean function \(f:D\to\{0,1\}\), \(D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), satisfies \[\frac{Q_{1/3}(f)}{C(\log_2n)^k}\ \le\ Q^*_{1/3}(f\circ g_n^n)\ \le\ C(\log_2n)^k Q_{1/3}(f)?\] Here \(Q_{1/3}\) is quantum query complexity and \(Q^*_{1/3}\) is two-party quantum communication complexity with unrestricted prior entanglement. Both have worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The gadget depends on \(n\), but not on \(D\) or \(f\), and the constants are common to the entire family.
cards.definitions: For \(z\in D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\), a query applies \(O_z:|i,b,w\rangle\mapsto|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}z_i,w\rangle\), where \(i\in[n]\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and \(w\) denotes an arbitrary finite workspace. A quantum query algorithm starts in an input-independent state, uses arbitrary input-independent local quantum operations and measurements between queries, and produces \(f(z)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every promised \(z\). \(Q_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum worst-case number of calls to \(O_z\), counting all branches. Computation between queries is free; there is no uniformity or finite-gate-set restriction. A function constant on its promise, including an empty promise, has query complexity zero. For the composed communication problem Alice receives \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) with \(x_i\in\{0,1\}^{a_n}\), Bob receives \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\) with \(y_i\in\{0,1\}^{b_n}\), and the promise is that \(z=(g_n(x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n\) belongs to \(D\). Bob must output \(f(z)\). A protocol has arbitrary finite-dimensional local registers and any finite-dimensional shared initial state independent of the inputs, with no bound on its entanglement. It may exchange messages in both directions, perform arbitrary local quantum operations and measurements depending on its own input and local history, and use shared or private randomness. All communicated qubits in both directions count; a classical bit sent as a message costs one qubit. Local computation, local memory, and the shared initial state are free. \(Q^*_{1/3}\) is the minimum worst-case total communication over protocols whose error probability is at most \(1/3\) for every promised input pair. The number of rounds is unrestricted, subject to finite protocol length; communication cost includes every branch. Query algorithms and protocols may depend on the particular finite function and promise and need not be uniformly constructible. The gadget family is existential: no efficient method to print its truth table, input-length bound on \(a_n,b_n\), or fixed gadget independent of \(n\) is required. Its communication cost is nevertheless constrained by the universal two-sided inequality, which includes coordinate functions \(f(z)=z_i\). All logarithms in the inequality are base two.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of this gadget family and common constants with both inequalities for all \(n,D,f\), or a complete Lean proof that no such family and constants exist. A theorem for a restricted class of outer functions, a fixed round bound, approximate polynomial degree instead of quantum query complexity, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not meet the stated affirmative target. The target is bounded-error lifting; a separate zero-error theorem is not also required.
cards.why: Quantum query complexity captures information obtainable from an oracle, while communication complexity measures information exchanged between separated parties. A universal lifting theorem would tightly connect these two models across all Boolean promise problems. The demand for only polylogarithmic loss is substantially stronger than transferring a weaker lower-bound measure or obtaining an arbitrary polynomial relation.

cards.title: Quantum versus classical nonuniform advice
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}=\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) as classes of languages without an oracle? Explicitly, for every language decidable by a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm supplied with a polynomial-size quantum advice state depending only on input length, does some uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm with polynomial-length classical advice decide the same language with error at most \(1/3\) on every input? The algorithm and polynomial advice bound may change. The reverse inclusion follows by encoding a classical advice string in the computational basis.
cards.definitions: A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\); here every binary string must be decided, with no promise excluding some inputs. For each \(n\ge0\), let \(m(n),a(n)\) be nonnegative integers bounded by a fixed polynomial. A single deterministic classical Turing machine, given an input string \(x\) of length \(n\), generates in polynomial time a quantum circuit \(U_x\) with an \(m(n)\)-qubit advice register, \(a(n)\) ancillary qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\), polynomially many gates, and one designated output qubit. The generating machine has no advice and no oracle. It uses the fixed exact gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), with \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\) and \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit outputs the computational-basis measurement of its output qubit. The quantum advice family is a sequence \((\rho_n)_{n\ge0}\) of density matrices on \(\mathbb C^{2^{m(n)}}\). A density matrix is positive semidefinite with trace one; positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho_nv\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\), and trace is the sum of diagonal entries. The probability of output 1 is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1U_x\bigl(\rho_n\otimes|0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a(n)}\bigr)U_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output 1 and is identity on the remaining qubits, and dagger denotes conjugate transpose. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\) if some such generating machine, polynomial bounds and advice family satisfy output-1 probability at least \(2/3\) for every \(x\in L\) and at most \(1/3\) for every \(x\notin L\). The same fixed \(\rho_n\) must work for all \(2^n\) strings of length \(n\). A fresh copy of that state is supplied for each independent computation; no cloning or repeated reuse of a consumed copy is promised. Advice is trusted: the requirement concerns the selected family, not all possible advice states. There is no computability or efficient-preparation requirement on the family, and its preparation cost is not charged. The language belongs to \(\mathrm{BQP/poly}\) if the advice can instead be a binary string \(b_n\in\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\), supplied as the basis state \(|b_n\rangle\). Its length may have a different polynomial bound and the circuit may be different, but \(b_n\) still depends only on \(n\), need not be computable, and must work for every length-\(n\) input. Both classes use uniform quantum computation in addition to the explicitly allowed nonuniform advice. BQP abbreviates bounded-error quantum polynomial time; poly and qpoly indicate classical-bit and quantum-qubit advice of polynomial length.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP/poly}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language has quantum advice as defined but no eligible classical-advice algorithm and family. An affirmative proof need not produce the classical advice efficiently, but must establish one length-indexed family and a uniform algorithm that work for all inputs. A negative proof must rule out every polynomial advice length, every classical advice family and every uniform quantum algorithm. A separation of promise problems alone does not automatically meet this card’s retained total-language target. Oracle separations, a difficult-to-describe state, or an advantage for advice selected after seeing the input do not suffice.
cards.why: This compares the computational value of quantum and classical information stored in advance for an entire input length. It asks whether a short quantum state can support useful computations that no polynomial-length classical record can support, even when preparing either kind of advice is free. The shared-advice requirement makes this a different resource comparison from per-instance witnesses.

cards.context:
Advice is fixed before the particular input is seen and is trusted to be the chosen length-specific information. It must support every input of that length. A witness, by contrast, may be selected for one instance and must be checked against dishonest alternatives. Neither comparison is obtained simply by changing the name of the auxiliary register.

Quantum advice is supplied as a fresh copy on each run. The definition does not assume the algorithm can clone an unknown state or preserve it for unlimited reuse. Classical advice can be copied, but the class comparison allows either algorithm to consume the supplied resource during its computation.

The advice families can be uncomputable in both models. The question concerns what polynomial-size information makes possible for the uniform computation, not how to construct that information. Allowing input-specific advice would remove the crucial requirement that one message works for all strings of a given length.

Aaronson proved \(\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}\subseteq\mathrm{PP/poly}\). PP permits polynomial-time classical randomized computation with acceptance probability strictly greater than one half on yes-inputs and at most one half on no-inputs, without an inverse-polynomial margin; poly again permits length-specific classical advice. This upper bound uses a different computation model from bounded-error BQP, so it is not the desired simulation in BQP/poly.

The 2007 quantum-oracle separation demonstrated an advice advantage when both computations share a quantum black box. This supplies evidence in that augmented computation model and retains the oracle as an essential part of its statement.

The 2024 result separates the advice classes with an oracle encoding a classical function, but restricts even quantum algorithms to classical queries. This is a genuine precursor to the later standard classical-oracle theorem. Permitting superposition queries gives the classical-advice algorithm more power, so the access conventions must not be conflated.

The February 2026 construction, checked in its April revision, separates the advice classes using a standard classical oracle that both quantum algorithms may query in superposition. It resolves that oracle question while leaving the ordinary language equality asked here unresolved.

cards.title: Classical hardness of approximate Boson Sampling
cards.formal: Is the following classical sampling impossibility statement true? There is no single probabilistic classical Turing machine \(M\) and polynomial \(p\) such that, for every valid ideal Boson Sampling input \(B\) defined below and every integer \(k\ge2\), the machine \(M(B,1^k)\) outputs an occupation vector with law \(Q_{B,k}\), always halts in at most \(p(|B|+k)\) steps, and satisfies \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q_{B,k},D_B)=\frac12\sum_{s\in\Omega_{m,n}}|Q_{B,k}(s)-D_B(s)|\le\frac1k?\] The target distribution is \[D_B(s)=\frac{|\operatorname{Per}(A_s)|^2}{\prod_{j=1}^{m}s_j!},\qquad A=\operatorname{GS}(B),\qquad \Omega_{m,n}=\{s\in\mathbb N_0^m:\sum_js_j=n\}.\] Thus the approximation must meet every requested error tolerance, in time polynomial in the explicit network description and the inverse tolerance. The claim is unconditional and concerns all valid inputs, rather than only typical random optical networks.
cards.definitions:
There are \(n\ge1\) indistinguishable photons and \(m\ge n\) modes. A mode is one orthogonal single-particle state. Initially each of the first \(n\) modes contains one photon and every other mode is empty. The network is ideal passive linear optics: it preserves photon number and acts on the single-particle mode space by an \(m\times m\) unitary matrix \(U\). It has no loss, noise, distinguishability of photons, intermediate measurements, adaptive feed-forward or postselection. The output records the photon count in every mode. Collisions, meaning two or more photons in a mode, are included.

Only the first \(n\) columns of \(U\) matter for this input. Write these columns as \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}\), so \(A^\dagger A=I_n\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. Any such column isometry can be completed to a unitary, and the distribution below is independent of that completion. The input therefore specifies this part of the optical network rather than an exponentially large many-photon transition matrix.

Here is an explicit finite encoding of the matrix convention in the source's footnote19. The input \(B\) contains \(m,n\) and every entry of an \(m\times n\) complex matrix. Real and imaginary parts are signed dyadic rationals, each stored as an integer numerator and a nonnegative denominator exponent in unary: \(a/2^b\). All numerator bits, signs, exponents and matrix entries count toward \(|B|\). Dimensions and lists are explicitly delimited. A valid input satisfies \[\|B^\dagger B-I_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac12,\] where the operator norm is \(\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Cv\|_2\). This promise ensures that the columns are linearly independent. It is a convenient fixed conditioning threshold for the finite encoding, not a physical noise parameter. Define the represented ideal isometry by exact ordered Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization: for the columns \(b_j\) of \(B\), set \[v_j=b_j-\sum_{i<j}a_i(a_i^\dagger b_j),\qquad a_j=v_j/\sqrt{v_j^\dagger v_j},\] using the positive square root, and let \(A=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\). These equations define the ideal mathematical distribution exactly; they do not give the classical sampler a real-arithmetic oracle or make numerical computation free. Finer explicit dyadic approximations can represent arbitrary optical isometries to arbitrary precision. The encoding spells out the source's correction of a finite-precision matrix to an isometry; its chosen threshold does not impose a restriction on the number of photons or on network depth.

For \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_m)\in\Omega_{m,n}\), form the square \(n\times n\) matrix \(A_s\) by repeating row \(j\) of \(A\) exactly \(s_j\) times, in increasing row order. For an \(n\times n\) matrix \(C\), its permanent is \[\operatorname{Per}(C)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n C_{i,\pi(i)},\] where \(S_n\) is the set of permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The factorial convention is \(0!=1\). The bosonic transition rule gives the displayed \(D_B\); because \(A\) is an isometry, these nonnegative probabilities sum to one. The output lists all \(m\) occupation numbers in binary. No requirement to enumerate the whole distribution or to estimate each exponentially small probability is imposed.

The classical machine is a uniform multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. It receives the complete explicit finite input, has no advice, quantum operations or oracle, and its polynomial runtime bound holds for every input and every random tape. Correctness is required only on valid matrices. For each such input, its output must lie in \(\Omega_{m,n}\). The law \(Q_{B,k}\) averages over all its random bits; there is no separate high-probability event certifying closeness. Total variation compares this full output law with the target distribution. The polynomial and machine are fixed independently of \(m,n,B,k\).

The unary accuracy input \(1^k\) requests error at most \(1/k\). This gives the arbitrary-error convention \(\varepsilon>0\) with runtime polynomial in input length and \(1/\varepsilon\): choose \(k=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\). It does not require polynomial dependence on \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). Every \(m\ge n\) is allowed, with its full matrix encoding charged; in particular the class includes the dilute, polynomially many-mode families used in the original hardness results. It does not claim that every individual network is hard. Easy subfamilies are compatible with the universal-sampler impossibility statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the impossibility statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation by a uniform classical probabilistic machine with one polynomial bound satisfying all input, output and accuracy quantifiers above. A positive answer must rule out every such machine without assuming a separation of complexity classes or an unproved permanent conjecture. A conditional polynomial-hierarchy consequence, hardness of computing an individual probability, an exact-sampling lower bound, a multiplicative-error result, a fixed numerical error guarantee, or experiments on finitely many networks do not settle this total-variation question. This is an exact yes/no question about arbitrarily requested sampling accuracy; the benchmark's numerical-value tolerance does not replace its quantified error requirement.
cards.why: This asks for an unconditional boundary between classical sampling and a concrete, restricted quantum optical experiment. It would clarify whether reproducing an entire physically defined distribution can require superpolynomial classical resources even when universal quantum computation is not part of the device model.

references.title: Exponential improvements to the average-case hardness of BosonSampling
references.authors: Adam Bouland; Ishaun Datta; Bill Fefferman; Felipe Hernandez
references.locator: v2, 4 September 2025; FOCS2025. Full introduction, Theorems1/3 and stated remaining accuracy gap checked; multiplicative-error sampling theorem is conditional and differs from total-variation sampling.

cards.context:
The overview presents Boson Sampling as a restricted quantum experiment whose output distribution is conjectured to be difficult to reproduce classically. Its source paragraph does not choose an error model. The formulation uses approximate sampling to every requested total-variation error with polynomial inverse-error cost; this card records that specialization explicitly. The exact version remains distinct source context, not an asserted equivalent formulation.

Passive optics acts linearly on the single-photon modes, but the output probabilities for several indistinguishable photons involve squared permanents and factorial collision factors. Sampling asks for one random occupation pattern with the right distribution, rather than a list of all probabilities. The two computational tasks cannot be identified merely from that formula.

The 2013 paper proves that an efficient exact classical sampler would entail a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. Its route to a corresponding total-variation statement additionally uses conjectures about average-case Gaussian permanents and anticoncentration. These are conditional consequences; neither the noncollapse of the hierarchy nor all the required permanent statements are unconditional theorems.

The 2025 work substantially strengthens average-case probability-estimation hardness and proves a conditional multiplicative-error sampling theorem. Its Theorem1 still has an accuracy gap relative to the permanent conjecture, while Theorem3 assumes noncollapse of the polynomial hierarchy and an anticoncentration conjecture. Multiplicative control of individual probabilities is stronger than the total-variation guarantee selected here.

The present claim concerns ideal indistinguishable photons and a sampler that works on every explicitly represented network. Typical-network hardness, constant-error hardness, loss-tolerant experiments and Gaussian Boson Sampling are separate variants. No measured experimental advantage or special family of classically simulable networks decides the stated universal-sampler question.

cards.title: Black-box unitary synthesis
cards.formal: Is there one polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum oracle circuits \(\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\)-qubit unitary matrix \(U\), some Boolean function \(f_U:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to\{0,1\}\) makes the channel implemented by \(A_n^{f_U}\) approximate \(\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger\) within diamond distance \(1/10\)? The oracle input length \(m(n)\), total number of qubits, number of ordinary gates, and number of oracle calls must all be bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). The circuit family is chosen before \(U\); only the Boolean oracle may depend on \(U\). This is the fixed-constant-error version of black-box unitary synthesis.
cards.definitions:
An \(n\)-qubit system has state space \(\mathbb C^{2^n}\). A unitary matrix satisfies \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. A density matrix is a positive semidefinite matrix with trace one and describes a possibly mixed quantum state.

Each circuit receives an arbitrary \(n\)-qubit input, initializes all additional qubits to zero, and outputs a specified \(n\)-qubit register. Other registers are discarded, inducing a quantum channel \(\Phi_{A_n^{f_U}}\). The ordinary gate set is Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT. Gates may act on any named wires. One oracle call applies \(|z,b\rangle\mapsto|z,b\mathbin{\oplus}f_U(z)\rangle\) to the address and answer registers, including on superpositions; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. All calls use the same fixed Boolean function. Oracle inputs and answer registers count toward the qubit bound. The oracle's own computation is uncharged, but every ordinary gate and each oracle call counts toward circuit size. General adaptive quantum computation is allowed through its equivalent coherent circuit representation with polynomially many ancillas.

Uniformity means that a single deterministic Turing machine, on input \(1^n\), outputs the complete gate and wire list in time polynomial in \(n\). It receives no description of \(U\). The oracle function may be arbitrary, and no efficient procedure for computing it or deriving it from \(U\) is required. No additional quantum advice, input-dependent initial ancilla, postselection, or other oracle is available.

For channels with \(n\)-qubit input and output, define their diamond distance by \[D_\diamond(\Phi,\Psi)=\tfrac12\sup_{\rho}\|((\Phi-\Psi)\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\rho)\|_1,\] where \(R\) is an untouched \(n\)-qubit reference register and the supremum ranges over density matrices on input and reference together. The trace norm is \(\|M\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{M^\dagger M}\). The desired inequality holds for every input, including one entangled with the reference. The constant \(1/10\) is the allowed channel-approximation error, not an acceptance-probability or heralded-success condition. Global phases of \(U\) are irrelevant to its channel.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a universal efficient oracle-circuit family exists, or a proof of its negation. A positive proof must supply the uniform circuit family and show the existence of a suitable Boolean oracle for every unitary while meeting all resource and diamond-distance bounds. A negative proof must rule out polynomially many sequential oracle calls with polynomial total computation. A lower bound restricted to one query, parallel queries, or a prescribed oracle encoding does not suffice.
cards.why: The question asks whether implementing arbitrary quantum transformations can be reduced efficiently to evaluating Boolean functions. A negative answer would establish a black-box obstruction to explaining all quantum transformation complexity through classical function computation, a central issue for unitary complexity and quantum cryptography.

cards.context:
Preparing a chosen state starts from a known blank input. Unitary synthesis must act correctly on an unknown state and preserve its coherent relationships with any external system. Preparing each output column of a matrix separately does not by itself implement the unitary on an arbitrary superposition.

The Boolean oracle is allowed to encode the desired transformation without a computational restriction. The difficulty lies in extracting and using that information through short coherent queries within polynomial total computation. Counting the number of possible ordinary circuits therefore does not alone refute this model.

Rosenthal gives an oracle implementation using time \(\widetilde O(2^{n/2})\), with exponentially small approximation error. This improves a more direct exponential construction but remains far above polynomial time. His matching lower bound is for a particular column-construction interface, not every possible Boolean oracle.

Lombardi, Ma and Wright rule out general one-query synthesis and the corresponding polynomial parallel-query setting with efficient resources. The July 2026 follow-up studies one-query separations for more structured unitary families. These results leave unrestricted polynomially many sequential queries as a different question.

cards.title: Efficient approximation of the optimal dihedral measurement
cards.formal: Can the specific pretty good measurement \(\{E_0,\ldots,E_{N-1},E_{\bot}\}\) defined below be approximated by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits to every requested inverse-polynomial accuracy? Precisely, does there exist one deterministic circuit generator and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), number of copies \(k\ge1\), and precision parameter \(m\ge2\), it runs in time at most \(p(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+k+m)\) and produces a circuit with at most that many gates and ancilla qubits whose output distribution satisfies \[\sup_{\sigma}\frac12\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z_N\cup\{\bot\}}\left|\Pr[C_{N,k,m}(\sigma)=j]-\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\right|\le\frac1m?\] The supremum ranges over all input density matrices on \((\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The circuit receives one such state and returns one classical outcome. The selected target concerns this concrete measurement, without requiring a particular unitary realization or a Subset Sum algorithm.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\mathbb Z_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\), with addition modulo \(N\). For a hidden shift \(s\in\mathbb Z_N\) and \(x\in\mathbb Z_N\), let \[|c_x^{(s)}\rangle=\frac{|0,x\rangle+|1,x+s\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad \rho_s=\frac1N\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_N}|c_x^{(s)}\rangle\langle c_x^{(s)}|.\] Thus \(\rho_s\) is the mixed state obtained by a uniform unknown coset offset. For \(k\) independent samples with the same shift, the state is \(\tau_s=\rho_s^{\otimes k}\) on \(\mathcal H_{N,k}=(\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^N)^{\otimes k}\). The discrimination ensemble assigns prior probability \(1/N\) to each shift \(s\). Both this prior and the average over coset offsets are part of the definition; neither \(s\) nor the offsets are supplied to the implementing circuit.

For this ensemble define \[G=\sum_{s\in\mathbb Z_N}\tau_s,\qquad E_s=G^{-1/2}\tau_sG^{-1/2},\qquad E_{\bot}=I-P_G.\] The inverse square root is the inverse on the support: if \(G=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda\) is its spectral decomposition, then \(G^{-1/2}=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1/2}P_\lambda\), with value zero on the kernel, and \(P_G=\sum_{\lambda>0}P_\lambda\). Every \(E_s\) is positive semidefinite and \(\sum_sE_s=P_G\). Adding \(E_{\bot}\) makes the sum the identity on the entire input space. A positive operator-valued measure is such a finite collection of positive semidefinite operators summing to identity; its outcome probabilities on state \(\sigma\) are \(\operatorname{Tr}(E_j\sigma)\). A density matrix is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one. Hermitian means \(\sigma=\sigma^\dagger\), with dagger conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\sigma v\ge0\) for all vectors \(v\). The above expression, including its kernel convention, fully specifies the measurement even when \(G\) is singular. On each \(\tau_s\), outcome \(\bot\) has probability zero. The source associates that complementary outcome with the trivial hidden subgroup, but optimality is asserted for the uniform ensemble of order-two subgroups.

The classical generator receives \(N\) in binary and \(k,m\) in unary. This makes the error tolerance \(1/m\) and the polynomial dependence on its reciprocal explicit. The target does not demand polynomial dependence on \(\log m\). Each \(N\)-dimensional register is embedded in \(q=\lceil\log_2N\rceil\) qubits by the binary basis encodings of \(0,\ldots,N-1\); the input therefore uses \(k(q+1)\) qubits. No correctness condition is imposed on states outside that valid encoded subspace. The given state can be mixed, entangled across copies, and unrelated to an actual hidden shift; the error bound specifies the measurement on its whole valid input space. The circuit receives no further copies or a state-preparation oracle. It may consume the input, and no condition is imposed on the remaining quantum state after it outputs the label. In particular, this is a guarantee for classical outcome distributions, not for a prescribed post-measurement state or a particular coherent circuit extension.

Ancillas start in zero, and the circuit uses the fixed gates \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] These act on the indicated wires and as identity elsewhere; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two and \(i^2=-1\). A final computational-basis measurement produces a binary outcome label, with \(0,\ldots,N-1\) interpreted as shifts and every remaining label mapped to \(\bot\). Ordinary finite gates and classical bit operations have unit cost, so no arbitrary real matrix is supplied as one free gate. There is no nonuniform advice, extra oracle, postselection or unbounded repeat-until-success loop. The displayed half-sum is total variation distance between the actual and specified outcome distributions; it is the largest difference in probabilities of an event defined by a set of labels. The requirement is uniform in the input state and every finite \(N,k,m\), with one polynomial and generator for the whole family. It asks for a sample from the distribution, not an explicit list of its \(N+1\) probabilities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the displayed uniform approximation family exists, including the circuit-generation and gate bounds and its total-variation guarantee, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such polynomially bounded family exists. A negative proof must cover all implementations of these outcome probabilities, not merely a prescribed subset-sum-basis unitary or a chosen extension to a larger Hilbert space. A different measurement with a good success probability for recovering the hidden shift does not by itself implement the specified POVM. Agreement only on the average success rate, or only on the coset ensemble without the uniform-input error guarantee, is insufficient for this precise implementation target. Exponential dependence on \(\log N\), \(k\), or the unary precision parameter does not meet the resource bound. This is a yes/no efficiency question with accuracy quantified in its definition, not a numerical output problem requiring only a fixed additive tolerance.
cards.why: This isolates the cost of extracting the information already present in dihedral coset states. An efficient implementation would turn a provably optimal measurement into an algorithmic resource, while a general impossibility theorem would distinguish measurement optimality from computational feasibility.

cards.context:
The imported card combined implementation of an optimal measurement with the broader relation between the dihedral problem and random Subset Sum at different densities. The formulation uses efficient approximation of the specific measurement. The present target records that narrowing and explicitly fixes its statistical error criterion and unary inverse-accuracy parameter. The wider reduction question is not claimed answered.

Bacon, Childs and van Dam prove that the displayed pretty good measurement maximizes the probability of identifying a uniformly random hidden shift from the coset-state ensemble. Optimality is an information-theoretic statement: it does not bound the number of elementary gates needed to carry out the measurement.

Their Theorem 2 gives success probability at least \(1/8\) once \(k\ge\log_2N+4\), and bounds it above by \(2^k/N\) for every \(N,k\). Thus enough copies can contain useful information even while extracting that information efficiently remains difficult. The chosen implementation target permits all copy counts and does not select a random Subset Sum density.

The earlier implementation analysis connects coherent uniform sampling of subset-sum solutions with an implementation of the optimal measurement. Its converse imposes a particular refinement and unitary realization. The 2016 source studies further restricted types of subset-sum-basis unitaries and derives consequences for subset-sum collision problems. Those statements do not prove a lower bound for every possible circuit with the same measurement statistics.

The later dihedral survey continues to separate the existence and success rate of an optimal measurement from its efficient implementation. Its exact-recovery no-go statements concern deterministic recovery from nonorthogonal samples, not approximation of the probabilistic measurement defined here.

The August 2026 semidirect-product algorithms apply under explicit restrictions on the abelian factor and the acting prime. For the dihedral action that prime is two, and the required ratio condition does not cover arbitrary cyclic order. Those results therefore do not supply this general measurement implementation.

cards.title: A finite quantum gate set with decision power strictly between P and BQP
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite set \(G\) of constant-arity unitary quantum gates with algebraic complex matrix entries such that
\[
\mathrm{P}\subsetneq Q_G\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP},
\]
and \(G\) is not contained in any common one-qubit conjugate of the Clifford gates? The bounded-error decision class \(Q_G\), the circuit interface, and the conjugation exclusion are defined below. Both strict containments are unconditional parts of the assertion.
cards.definitions:
A \(k\)-qubit gate is a \(2^k\)-by-\(2^k\) complex unitary matrix, for an integer \(k\ge1\). The set \(G\) is finite and independent of input length; its maximum arity is therefore a constant. Each matrix entry is algebraic over \(\mathbb Q\), and each gate can be specified exactly by its minimal polynomials and isolating data for the real and imaginary parts. These fixed descriptions are not input-dependent advice. Algebraicity is an explicit editorial finite-description convention.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) is in \(Q_G\) if one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, on each input \(x\), produces a polynomial-size circuit description \(C_x\) with polynomially many qubits, a computational-basis initial string \(b_x\), and one designated output qubit. Initialize the state to \(|b_x\rangle\). A gate from \(G\) may be applied to any ordered tuple of distinct qubits of the correct arity, with identity on all other qubits. There are no geometry or depth restrictions beyond the polynomial size bound. At the end, measure only the designated output qubit in the computational basis. Require
\[
x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr[C_x\text{ outputs }1]\ge2/3,
\qquad
x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr[C_x\text{ outputs }1]\le1/3.
\]
The generator and polynomial bound may depend on \(L\) and \(G\), but not nonuniformly on input length. They count all classical bit operations. The generator may prepare additional \(|0\rangle\) and \(|1\rangle\) qubits by specifying them in \(b_x\), but no other initial states. Wires may be named arbitrarily. Only gates listed in \(G\) are available: inverses, controlled variants, and arbitrary one-qubit gates are not free. Intermediate measurements, postselection, classically controlled quantum branches, quantum advice, and joint-output sampling followed by unrestricted classical postprocessing are not part of this interface. The final single-bit output convention makes the selected decision target precise.

Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). Define \(\mathrm{BQP}\) by the same uniform bounded-error circuit convention using the universal gates
\[
H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad
\operatorname{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle.
\]
Classical preprocessing and basis preparation imply \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq Q_G\). Fixed algebraic gates are efficiently approximable, so \(Q_G\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). The strictness requirements mean that some language in \(Q_G\) is not in \(\mathrm{P}\), and some language in \(\mathrm{BQP}\) is not in \(Q_G\). Merely failing to densely generate every unitary is insufficient, since encoded computation can still give full BQP power.

For the Clifford exclusion, let
\[
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
and let \(\mathcal P_k=\{i^j P_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P_k:j\in\{0,1,2,3\},\ P_i\in\{I,X,Y,Z\}\}\) be the Pauli group. The Clifford group consists of the unitaries \(V\) satisfying \(V\mathcal P_kV^\dagger=\mathcal P_k\); global phase is immaterial. Require that there is no one-qubit unitary \(U\) such that, for every \(g\in G\) of arity \(k\),
\[
U^{\otimes k}g(U^\dagger)^{\otimes k}
\]
is Clifford. The same \(U\) must be tested for all gates, but it may be any complex unitary, not only an algebraic one. The condition is a structural exclusion, not an additional allowed operation.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of existence of a finite algebraic gate set satisfying both strict decision-class containments and the common-conjugate Clifford exclusion. Conditional sampling hardness, universality only after postselection, a separation for nonuniform circuits, or physical nonuniversality alone does not settle the statement. A positive proof must establish both strictness assertions in the specified uniform single-output model.
cards.why: A genuine intermediate decision class generated only by a finite gate set would expose a computational regime beyond deterministic classical computation but below universal quantum computation. It would distinguish gate-induced limitations from restrictions on depth, state preparation or geometry.

cards.context:
The classical reversible-gate classification motivates a quantum analogue. The source distinguishes dense unitary generation from universality through an encoding, and asks whether other finite gate sets support intermediate computational behavior.

Conjugated Clifford circuits illustrate why the output interface matters: their full output distribution can be difficult to sample under complexity assumptions, while individual output-bit probabilities have an efficient classical strong simulation. They therefore do not supply the required decision separation in this card’s single-output model.

The October 2025 revision classifies weak multiplicative simulation for additional conjugated Clifford fragments, including commuting cases. Its quantum-advantage statements concern sampling and use a noncollapsing polynomial-hierarchy assumption; they do not establish either unconditional strict decision-class containment here.

A positive answer would in particular prove P distinct from BQP. Conversely, simply assuming that separation, excluding Clifford conjugates, or showing a generated group is not dense does not prove the displayed intermediate-class assertion.
