cards.title: Parity versus \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) with shallow quantum preprocessing
cards.formal: Does every polynomial-size constant-depth classical \(\mathrm{AC}^0\) circuit with polynomial-size constant-depth quantum preprocessing have asymptotically zero correlation with parity? Precisely, for every polynomial \(p\), constant \(d\in\mathbb N\), and sequence \((C_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the model and bounds below, is \[\left|2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\ \sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{n+m(n)}}\Pr[C_n(x)=y]f_n(y)(-1)^{\sum_{i=1}^nx_i}\right|\longrightarrow0\quad(n\longrightarrow\infty)?\] Here \(m(n)\le p(n)\) zero-initialized ancillary qubits are allowed, both circuit stages have depth at most \(d\), and both have polynomial size bounded by \(p(n)\). There is no geometric locality, uniformity or clean-ancilla condition.
cards.definitions:
For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), parity in the sign convention is \(\operatorname{Par}_n(x)=(-1)^{x_1+\cdots+x_n}\). The quantum circuit \(C_n\) begins in the computational-basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{m(n)}\rangle\). A qubit is a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and the full register has state space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes(n+m(n))}\). A gate is any unitary on one or two qubits, acting as identity on the others. Unitary means \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\). Gates are arranged in layers, with disjoint supports in each layer. The number of layers is the quantum depth, at most \(d\); the total number of nonidentity gates is at most \(p(n)\). Any two wires may interact. The ancillary count is separately bounded by \(p(n)\), including ancillary wires that are only measured.

All output wires are measured once in the computational basis. If the product of the layers is \(U_n\), the resulting bit string \(y\) has probability \[\Pr[C_n(x)=y]=|\langle y|U_n|x,0^{m(n)}\rangle|^2.\] There are no intermediate measurements, adaptive gate choices or postselection. No ancillary wire has to return to zero, and garbage is allowed. The initial ancillas are zeros, not arbitrary input-dependent advice states. Gates may depend on \(n\) and may have arbitrary complex entries satisfying unitarity: this is the source's nonuniform circuit lower-bound model, not a uniform algorithm with free real-number input. Consequently no fixed finite gate alphabet or efficient gate-description requirement is imposed.

The classical postprocessor \(f_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m(n)}\to\{-1,1\}\) is a finite Boolean circuit of unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and fan-in-one NOT gates, with constants permitted. Its underlying output bit \(b\) is interpreted as \((-1)^b\). Classical depth is the greatest number of gates on an input-to-output path and is at most \(d\). Its number of gates is at most \(p(n)\); repeated identical incoming wires can be omitted. Including wires in the size instead gives an equivalent polynomial-size family, since the vertex count is polynomial. There are no parity gates, arbitrary Boolean lookup-table gates, threshold gates or extra classical advice inputs. The entire classical circuit is allowed to depend nonuniformly on \(n\).

The two stages are composed once: measure the quantum output, then apply the deterministic classical circuit to that outcome. The correlation is the expectation of \(f_n(Y)\operatorname{Par}_n(X)\) when \(X\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings and, conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\) follows the Born probabilities above. There is no promise on the input Hamming weight. The average success probability at computing sign parity is \((1+\operatorname{Corr}_n)/2\). Correlation is signed; the displayed limit of its absolute value is equivalent to the source's limit \(\operatorname{Corr}_n\to0\). It also rules out a persistent advantage after negating the output.

The polynomial, depth and circuit sequence are fixed before taking the limit, but are otherwise arbitrary. Equivalently, for each such choice and every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there must be an \(N\) such that \(|\operatorname{Corr}_n|<\varepsilon\) for all \(n\ge N\). No particular rate of decay is requested. A refutation can consist of one polynomially bounded sequence and one \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(|\operatorname{Corr}_n|\ge\varepsilon\) at infinitely many input lengths; constant correlation at every length is sufficient but is not necessary for a negative answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified zero-correlation limit, or a complete Lean-checked refutation under the same gate, ancilla, depth, size and average-input conventions. A positive result must allow every polynomially bounded number of zero ancillas and every polynomial-size classical postprocessor. Ancilla-free preprocessing, linear-size classical circuits, geometric restrictions, uniform families, a finite restricted gate set or a worst-case statement about one input do not cover the whole conjecture. A negative result must supply a circuit sequence with a proved failure of convergence; search or sampling advantages for another task do not suffice. This is an exact asymptotic proposition, not a request to estimate a correlation at finitely many sizes.
cards.why: Parity is a basic test of global information processing. Resolving this conjecture would show whether very shallow quantum preprocessing can give weak classical decision circuits a persistent advantage on a canonical Boolean function, beyond known quantum search and sampling separations.

cards.context:
A single output qubit of a shallow bounded-fan-in quantum circuit depends on only a bounded number of input wires. The hybrid model instead measures all wires and lets the classical circuit use their joint outcome. The source asks whether this combination can overcome the classical constant-depth limitation on computing parity.

Conjecture3 is a correlation statement over uniformly random classical inputs and quantum measurement outcomes. It is stronger than ruling out exact computation. The source uses arbitrary two-qubit unitaries, polynomially many zero ancillas and no locality or clean-computation restriction; those choices are preserved here.

The source proves a bound of the form \(2^{-n/\operatorname{polylog}n}\) for ancilla-free preprocessing and general polynomial-size classical postprocessing. Its separate linear-classical-size theorem permits general shallow quantum preprocessing, even with quantum advice. Neither theorem covers both polynomially many ancillas and arbitrary polynomial-size classical postprocessing at once.

The ITCS2026 follow-up studies unconditional pseudorandomness against shallow quantum and hybrid circuits. Its introductory comparison repeats the ancilla-free and linear-classical-size parity results. Its broader ancilla allowance for QNC0 alone and its restricted-ancilla hybrid pseudorandomness theorem are different statements from this full parity-correlation conjecture.

This model does not insert unbounded quantum fanout or other large-arity quantum gates. Results about such QAC0 models cannot be substituted solely because both circuit families have constant depth. Likewise, a quantum advantage for a promise search relation does not directly supply a parity decision circuit.

Corollary 9 gives a Fourier-tail bound under the uniform input distribution for one designated output qubit. The multi-qubit readout allowed here applies an arbitrary classical AC⁰ function jointly to all the measurement results.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.
cards.why: Turing degrees encode relative computational power and have a highly non-linear structure. Martin’s conjecture asks whether invariance under mutual computability nevertheless forces every nontrivial operation into an ordered hierarchy once behaviour is compared on cones under determinacy. It gives a precise structural target behind the observed regularity of many degree operators, and connects computability with descriptive set theory and analogous hierarchies of logical strength.

cards.context:
A function can assign different output reals to equivalent inputs while still inducing a well-defined operation on degrees. This is the invariance required here. The operation itself need not be computable: the Turing jump is a central example. The conjecture concerns the organization of such operations rather than an algorithm for listing or calculating their values.

The two parts have separate content. Part I is a dichotomy for all invariant functions. Part II concerns the full collection already above the identity and asserts both a well-order after identifying cone-equivalent functions and an exact successor rule. In particular, strict increase under the jump alone is weaker than the assertion that its rank is the next ordinal. No continuity rule at limit ordinals is included in that successor clause.

Determinacy gives a zero-one law for invariant sets: each contains a cone or its complement contains one. Martin measure assigns these cases values one and zero. Thus the phrase almost everywhere in the cited formulation means on a Turing cone. It does not refer to the usual probability measure from independent bits, and a comparison base need not work for unrelated functions.

Uniform invariance requires one map \(u:\omega^2\to\omega^2\) that converts any pair of indices witnessing \(x\equiv_T y\) into a pair witnessing \(f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\), independently of the reals. Even this index map is not required to be computable in the survey’s definition. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the two parts for the uniform subclass. Ordinary invariance does not supply such a map.

The regressive case is already settled: if invariant \(f\) satisfies \(f(x)\leq_T x\) on a cone, then on a cone it is constant in degree or equivalent to the identity. Order preservation is a different restriction, namely \(x\leq_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq_T f(y)\). The saved full target includes neither restriction. Earlier extraction of only a regressive subcase was corrected before this audit; this review preserves the full conjecture.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and for all measure-preserving invariant functions. Here the latter means \(\forall a\;\exists b\;\forall x\geq_T b:\ a\leq_T f(x)\), with the base allowed to depend on the fixed target degree. Their Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 4.8 use determinacy and dependent choice for reals, which follow from this card’s stronger fixed background. The older Part II theorem for order-preserving functions retains a Borel restriction; Borel means inverse images of open sets belong to the sigma algebra generated by the finite-prefix open sets of Cantor space.

The background cannot be replaced by \(\mathsf{ZFC}\). Lutz and Siskind’s §6.4 supplies choice-based counterexamples, including an invariant order-preserving function that is neither constant nor above the identity on a cone. These do not satisfy the determinacy setting. A faithful proof-assistant treatment must keep that internal set universe distinct from any ambient use of choice.

The author erratum to the Marks–Slaman–Steel survey withdraws Theorem 1.8, an asserted equivalence whose argument fails at limit ordinals. This audit therefore uses the actual two-part conjecture and checked restricted theorems, without importing the withdrawn equivalence as a fact about arbitrary invariant Borel functions.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision studies conditional consequences of an unresolved decomposition question for Turing equivalence, including nonuniformity for functions whose outputs are compared by many-one reducibility. These are related structural results with a different output reducibility and an additional open premise. They do not claim a counterexample to the full conjecture stated here.

Walsh’s March 2026 journal survey states the full conjecture explicitly as open and distinguishes the order-preserving Part I theorem from the Borel order-preserving Part II theorem. This supplies a dated status source; the bounded September follow-up search is recorded separately from verification of the underlying proofs.

cards.title: Busy Beaver \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\)
cards.formal:
Determine the exact six-state binary Busy Beaver runtime \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=S(6)\) by giving a concrete machine \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\) and proving
\[M_*\text{ halts on the blank tape},\qquad
\forall M\in\mathcal M_6:\ M\text{ halts on the blank tape}\ \Longrightarrow\ T(M)\le T(M_*).\]
Here \(\mathcal M_6\) is the finite class of deterministic six-nonhalting-state, two-symbol Turing machines defined below, and \(T(M)\) is the number of transitions through the first entry into the separate halting state. The complete transition table of \(M_*\), together with proofs of its halting and universal maximality, specifies the answer exactly as \(S(6)=T(M_*)\).
cards.definitions:
Machine. Fix the nonhalting states \(Q=\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\), one additional halting state \(Z\notin Q\), and the tape alphabet \(\{0,1\}\). A machine is a total transition function
\[\delta:Q\times\{0,1\}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\times\{-1,+1\}\times(Q\cup\{Z\}).\]
Thus its description has exactly twelve entries. The three outputs specify the symbol to write, a move of exactly one cell left or right, and the next state, respectively. There are no stationary moves, extra tapes or transitions out of \(Z\). Unreachable states and entries are allowed. Different tables need not have different behavior; no symmetry reduction is imposed on the quantified class \(\mathcal M_6\).

Execution. The tape is indexed by all integers. A configuration consists of a state \(q\), a head position \(h\in\mathbb Z\), and a tape function \(\tau:\mathbb Z\to\{0,1\}\). At time zero, \(q=A\), \(h=0\), and \(\tau(i)=0\) for every integer \(i\). If \(q\ne Z\) and \(\delta(q,\tau(h))=(b,d,q')\), one transition replaces \(\tau(h)\) by \(b\), leaves every other tape cell unchanged, replaces the head position by \(h+d\), and enters \(q'\). Execution stops immediately on entering \(Z\); that final write-and-move transition is included in the count. Each transition costs one step, irrespective of head position or time elapsed. There is no external input, randomness or resource limit.

Halting time and maximum. A machine halts if its unique execution first enters \(Z\) at some positive integer time. Only for such a machine, \(T(M)\) denotes this least time. Let \(\mathcal H_6\subseteq\mathcal M_6\) be the halting machines. Define
\[S(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal H_6\}.\]
There are \(28^{12}\) tables in \(\mathcal M_6\), since each entry has \(2\cdot2\cdot7\) choices. The halting subset is nonempty, since a table can send \((A,0)\) directly to \(Z\). Hence the maximum exists as a finite positive integer. No value of \(T\) on a nonhalting machine is used in the statement or the submitted certificate.

Answer representation. The runtime of a specified, proved-halting table defines an exact integer through a terminating step-counting computation, even when actually evaluating it is infeasible. The accepted answer need not separately evaluate that computation. In this card, \(\mathrm{BB}\) always means the runtime maximum \(S\), not the distinct extremal function \(\Sigma\) that maximizes the number of ones on the final tape.

Notation in the context. For positive integer \(k\), \(2\uparrow\uparrow k\) is a tower of \(k\) twos, equivalently \(2\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2^{(2\uparrow\uparrow k)}\). Three arrows mean iteration of this tower operation: \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow1=2\) and \(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular \(M_*\in\mathcal M_6\), with complete mathematically correct proofs checked in Lean that it halts from the stated blank initial configuration and that every halting \(M\in\mathcal M_6\) has \(T(M)\le T(M_*)\). These two proofs must establish the exact equality \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=T(M_*)\). This is the exact witness criterion, superseding the default numerical tolerance for this card only.

The witness runtime is an accepted exact finite description of the integer. A simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. A candidate machine without both proofs, an estimated runtime, a one-sided bound, a list of undecided machines or a restatement of the defining maximum is insufficient. Any reduction to representative transition tables must itself be justified as covering the full stated class. A result for a different alphabet, state count, tape convention or final-tape score does not settle this target.
cards.why: The halting behavior of a finite set of exceptionally short programs is still beyond complete classification. This problem makes the boundary of current computability knowledge concrete: one additional nonhalting state separates the established five-state maximum from an unresolved maximum with enormous certified examples and difficult residual halting questions. A solution would give a universal exact upper bound for every halting program in this precisely fixed class.

cards.context:
Radó introduced Busy Beaver functions in 1962 as concrete examples of noncomputability. The runtime function takes a maximum over finitely many halting programs at each state count, but there is no algorithm computing all its values. That statement about the entire sequence does not make every individual value unknowable. The first five binary runtime values have now been determined.

Finiteness alone does not supply an effective stopping rule for the search: a machine still running may halt much later or may run forever. Conversely, a proved value of \(S(6)\) would decide blank-tape halting for every table in this finite class in principle, by checking whether it halts within that many steps. The enormous possible duration makes this a mathematical consequence, not a practical promise.

The collaboration proves \(S(5)=47{,}176{,}870\) in Coq, now called Rocq. Its 2026 revised paper proves coverage of the relevant five-state machines as well as their halting classifications. The total number of representatives examined by that proof is \(181{,}385{,}789\); it is not a count of six-state holdouts or of all syntactically distinct tables in this card.

The formal paper presents halting entries as undefined transitions. Its convention counts the final attempt to execute such an entry, so even an immediately halting machine takes one step. Replacing an undefined entry by a write/move transition into the separate state Z preserves its runtime exactly. The card retains total twelve-entry tables to make a submitted witness fully explicit.

For six states, the paper records the lower bound \(S(6)>2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow5\). Appendix B carefully separates two kinds of evidence: the champion’s halting is proved in Coq, while the stated enormous step lower bound is estimated mathematically from its verified abstract evolution rules. The paper does not claim a formally verified exact runtime for that champion or a proof of universal six-state maximality.

Runtime and final output are different objectives. The function \(\Sigma(n)\) maximizes the number of ones present when a machine halts; \(S(n)\) maximizes the duration. Even their maximizing machines need not coincide: the paper records this already for three states. Approximate final-output formulas in a champion table therefore cannot simply be used as an exact answer for runtime.

One unresolved six-state behavior is Antihydra. Its halting question has an equivalent arithmetic form: start at \(a_0=8\) and iterate \(a_{j+1}=\lfloor3a_j/2\rfloor\). It halts exactly when some finite prefix of \(a_0,a_1,\ldots\) contains strictly more than twice as many odd terms as even terms. This is a particular recurrence question; resemblance to the classical Collatz problem is not an equivalence with that conjecture.

The Antihydra page discusses a probabilistic model suggesting nonhalting. The machine itself is deterministic, and a heuristic probability is not a halting or nonhalting proof. More generally, the six-state project distinguishes proved halters from unresolved machines, including examples heuristically expected to halt. Those expectations cannot certify a Busy Beaver upper bound.

The holdout table records 964 remaining six-state representatives in the entry dated 8 September 2026, attributed to mxdys. Some equivalent machines are omitted. The page warns that contributed lists are not uniformly independently verified, and this particular entry does not yet link a downloadable list. The number is therefore a dated project progress report, not a checked exhaustion theorem.

Holdout counts need not decrease monotonically: when an incompletely specified representative reaches a previously undefined transition, further completions of its table may need to be considered. Counts also depend on which equivalences have been removed. A smaller list measures progress in classification but is neither the Busy Beaver value nor a substitute for a universal proof.

The accepted answer isolates exactly what must be established: one explicit halting machine attaining the maximum, with a proof that every halting machine in the stated class takes no more steps. It can name an integer far beyond feasible decimal expansion through that certified runtime. Neither the general noncomputability theorem nor speculation about axiomatic independence supplies this requested witness.

cards.title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
cards.formal:
Let \(D_T=\mathcal P(\mathbb N)/{\equiv_T}\) be the set of all Turing degrees, ordered by Turing reducibility. Is this order rigid? The exact assertion is
\[\forall\pi:D_T\to D_T,\quad \Bigl[\pi\text{ is bijective}\ \land\ \forall a,b\in D_T\,\bigl(a\le_T b\iff\pi(a)\le_T\pi(b)\bigr)\Bigr]\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall a\in D_T\,\pi(a)=a.\]
The domain is the full quotient of all subsets of the standard natural numbers. The quantifier over \(\pi\) ranges over arbitrary functions on this quotient in ordinary classical set theory, with ZFC as the set-theoretic background.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \(\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\) for its full power set, and \(\chi_A:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\) for a set's characteristic function. A deterministic oracle Turing machine is a finite program with ordinary unbounded work tapes and an additional operation that receives \(\chi_B(k)\) when it asks whether \(k\) belongs to the oracle set \(B\). Each terminating computation takes finitely many steps and makes finitely many queries; no uniform bound on their number, time or space is imposed. Natural inputs and queries have the usual finite binary encodings. Any fixed effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\mathbb N}\) of all such programs gives
\[A\le_T B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists e\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ \Phi_e^B(n)\text{ halts with output }\chi_A(n).\]
The same index must work on every input, but may depend on \(A,B\). Programs contain no additional oracle, infinite advice or noncomputable constants. All subsets are eligible oracle sets, including noncomputable ones.

Define \(A\equiv_T B\) by \(A\le_T B\) and \(B\le_T A\). A degree \([A]\) is the equivalence class of \(A\), and \([A]\le_T[B]\) means \(A\le_T B\); this is independent of the representatives. Equality of degrees is mutual reducibility, not equality of their representatives. The set \(D_T\) includes every degree, not just degrees containing computably enumerable sets, arithmetical degrees, or degrees below a selected bound. A set is computably enumerable if a program with no oracle lists exactly its members, with arbitrary repetition and delay allowed.

An order automorphism is a total injective and surjective map \(\pi:D_T\to D_T\) that preserves and reflects every reducibility comparison. It need not be computable, definable, continuous or induced by a prescribed operation on sets. A representation \(F:\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\to\mathcal P(\mathbb N)\), if used to specify it, must satisfy \([F(A)]=\pi([A])\) for every \(A\); the representation itself need not be bijective. The order language has only equality and \(\le_T\). Jump preservation is a known consequence of this order structure, not an extra assumption in the target.

For the dated context, \(\mathbf 0=[\varnothing]\). The join \([A]\vee[B]\) is \([A\oplus B]\), where \(A\oplus B=\{2n:n\in A\}\cup\{2n+1:n\in B\}\). Set \(A'=\{e:\Phi_e^A(e)\text{ halts}\}\); the Turing jump is \([A]'=[A']\), and \(\mathbf 0''=(\mathbf 0')'\). These degrees are independent of the chosen effective machine enumeration. The upper cone with base \(b\) is \(\{a:b\le_T a\}\). Its complement includes both degrees below \(b\) and degrees incomparable with \(b\).

The assertion concerns the degree order built from the full power set in the ambient universe, not a selected countable model's internally computed degrees. The continuum hypothesis and determinacy are not hypotheses of the target. There are no finite input sizes, efficiency bounds or numerical approximation parameters in this structural question.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed universal assertion or its exact negation. A positive answer must apply to every set-theoretic order automorphism of the entire \(D_T\). A negative answer must prove
\[\exists\pi:D_T\to D_T\ \exists a\in D_T,\quad\pi\text{ is bijective},\quad \forall b,c\in D_T\,\bigl(b\le_Tc\iff\pi(b)\le_T\pi(c)\bigr),\quad\pi(a)\ne a.\]
An existence proof is sufficient; no computable formula for the automorphism is required. A construction on representatives must establish that it descends to this full quotient and has all the stated properties. Proving rigidity only on a proper substructure or for a restricted family of maps does not meet the criterion. Nor does a non-surjective order embedding or a permutation of representatives that fixes every degree. Both answer directions retain the stated classical background without an unproved extra hypothesis; relative consistency or independence alone does not assert either of these two mathematical conclusions. All supporting formalized definitions and theorems needed for the chosen direction must be included or supplied by verified Lean libraries.
cards.why: Rigidity asks whether the entire ordering of relative computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. Its connection with intrinsic definability and second-order arithmetic makes it a central structural question in computability, beyond the classification of individual computable problems.

cards.context:
Two oracle decision problems represent the same Turing degree precisely when each can compute the other. Their degree records computational power without committing to a particular set of integers as its encoding. This question asks whether all degrees can be consistently relabeled, changing at least one point while preserving every reducibility comparison. A nontrivial symmetry must work simultaneously across the whole structure.

The computable degree \(\mathbf 0\) and the join operation are fixed by every order automorphism. Shore and Slaman proved the stronger fact that the graph of the Turing jump is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Thus \(\pi(a')=\pi(a)'\) for every degree \(a\), and all finite jumps of \(\mathbf 0\) are fixed. Preservation of the jump is an established restriction, not a proof of full rigidity.

Slaman and Woodin proved that every automorphism fixes every degree at least \(\mathbf 0''\); their automorphism group is also at most countable. These are statements about restrictions of global automorphisms. They do not assert that an arbitrary automorphism of the upper cone extends to the full structure, and they do not cover degrees incomparable with its base. The underlying set of all degrees has cardinality \(2^{\aleph_0}\).

The same structural analysis connects rigidity with the Slaman–Woodin bi-interpretability conjecture: the degree structure and full second-order arithmetic would recover one another through logical interpretations, with the correspondence to degrees definable without parameters. The survey states equivalence with rigidity in its precise sense of bi-interpretability. This concerns the expressive power of the whole order.

Rigidity does not mean that every degree has its own parameter-free first-order definition. There are only countably many finite formulas in this language and uncountably many degrees. Most degrees therefore cannot be individually defined that way, even if the entire order is rigid.

Kjos-Hanssen proves that a coordinate permutation \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), acting on characteristic sequences by \(F_p(A)(n)=A(p(n))\), can induce an automorphism of all Turing degrees only when that automorphism is the identity; in fact \(p\) must be computable. He also excludes nontrivial automorphisms induced by homeomorphisms of \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) preserving every Bernoulli product measure. Here the topology is generated by finite initial segments, and the measure with parameter \(t\in[0,1]\) makes coordinates independent bits with probability \(t\) of being one. These representation and measure restrictions are absent from the main question.

Slaman and Soskova study the separate structure of degrees at most \(\mathbf 0'\), equivalently the \(\Delta^0_2\) degrees. They prove that this local structure has a finite automorphism base: agreement on a fixed finite tuple determines an automorphism. They obtain a countable automorphism group and an equivalence between local rigidity and bi-interpretability with first-order arithmetic. None of these conclusions states that the group is trivial. Their local arithmetic comparison is distinct from the full structure’s second-order comparison.

Ongay-Valverde’s 2021 preprint gives restrictions on the action of a hypothetical automorphism on generic degrees under the continuum hypothesis \(2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1\). Theorem 7.4 additionally concerns families meeting a relative genericity condition above every degree, with jointly generic representatives for each degree and its image. Its Section 8 explicitly keeps the continuum-hypothesis assumption. This conditional restriction neither constructs a nontrivial automorphism nor proves that all automorphisms are trivial, even under that hypothesis.

Cooper’s 1999 Theorem 1.1 claims a nonidentity global automorphism fixing every degree at least \(\mathbf 0'\). This is a claim of a full negative answer, rather than merely a local example. The present review checked the statement in the author-uploaded text but did not verify its long construction.

Slaman’s later survey explicitly reports that Cooper’s construction had not been independently verified and treats the general problem as unresolved. The subsequent permutation paper also states the full question as open. The card therefore keeps the historical full-solution claim visible and uses uncertain status; it does not infer either correctness or a proved error from the announcement alone.

Slaman’s published survey states rigidity on the cone above \(\mathbf 0''\), countability of the automorphism group and equivalence between full rigidity and its bi-interpretability conjecture. It retains the global question as open.
Slaman and Soskova’s journal article gives finite automorphism bases and related definability results for \(D_T(\le_T\mathbf 0')\), without proving local or global rigidity.

Kjos-Hanssen’s preprint and later journal publication exclude nontrivial automorphisms induced by coordinate permutations or by homeomorphisms preserving all Bernoulli measures. The preprint record remains version 1.

Ongay-Valverde’s version 1 gives a conditional restriction on genericity of degrees and their images; Theorem 7.4 and its Section 8 consequences assume the continuum hypothesis. The complete proof was not independently certified in this review.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal:
Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random for the fair-coin product measure? In the precise model below, determine whether
\[\forall X\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N},\qquad
\operatorname{KLR}(X)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{MLR}(X).\]
The reverse implication is known, so this is equivalently equality of the two randomness classes. Betting strategies may choose fresh coordinates adaptively, need not visit every coordinate, and are ordinary partial computable procedures without an oracle.
cards.definitions:
Space and measure. Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Cantor space \(2^{\mathbb N}=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) consists of all functions \(X:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}\), including noncomputable ones. Let \(2^{<\mathbb N}\) be the finite binary strings. For a string \(\sigma\), its length is \(|\sigma|\), and its cylinder is
\[[\sigma]=\{X:\ X(i)=\sigma(i)\text{ for all }i<|\sigma|\}.\]
The fair-coin product probability measure \(\mu\) makes coordinates independent and assigns \(\mu([\sigma])=2^{-|\sigma|}\). No bias, alternative measure or oracle relativization is involved.

Martin-Löf tests. A uniformly effectively open family is specified by one ordinary Turing program enumerating a set \(W\subseteq\mathbb N_{\ge1}\times2^{<\mathbb N}\). Put
\[U_k=\bigcup_{(k,\sigma)\in W}[\sigma].\]
It is a Martin-Löf test when \(\mu(U_k)\le2^{-k}\) for every \(k\ge1\). This condition concerns the measure of the union, not the sum of cylinder measures when cylinders overlap. Repetitions in an enumeration are harmless, no disjointness or prefix-free presentation is required, and levels need not be nested. The measure bound is a mathematical condition on a test; the enumerating program is not required to certify it or compute the exact measure. Define
\[\operatorname{MLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{for every Martin-Löf test }(U_k)_{k\ge1},\quad X\notin\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k.\]
Uniform enumeration across all levels is mandatory.

Histories and betting procedures. A history is a finite ordered list
\[h=((j_0,a_0),\ldots,(j_{s-1},a_{s-1}))\]
with distinct \(j_i\in\mathbb N\) and \(a_i\in\{0,1\}\). It records precisely the coordinates already queried and their observed values, in query order. A strategy is a deterministic partial computable function \(S\) which, on such a history, either fails to return an action or returns
\[S(h)=(j,q),\qquad j\notin\{j_0,\ldots,j_{s-1}\},\quad q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,2].\]
Every returned action on a valid history must meet these conditions. Computability means a finite Turing-machine program operating on an effective finite encoding of this list, natural coordinates, and rational numerator/positive-denominator pairs. These encodings carry no resource bound. The program receives only the history; it cannot inspect any further bit of \(X\) before choosing its action, use an oracle, or use an uncomputable real parameter. Internal deterministic work and previously computed data can be recovered from the history and program. The equivalent history of observed bit values alone suffices when the query coordinates are reconstructed by rerunning that same strategy.

Run and capital. Start at empty history with capital \(C_0^S(X)=1\). If \(S(h_s)=(j_s,q_s)\) returns, reveal \(a_s=X(j_s)\), append \((j_s,a_s)\), and update
\[C_{s+1}^S(X)=\begin{cases}
C_s^S(X)q_s,&a_s=0,\\
C_s^S(X)(2-q_s),&a_s=1.
\end{cases}\]
The two possible multipliers average to one, so the bet is fair on a fresh unbiased bit. Capital is always nonnegative, with no borrowing or outside deposits; zero capital remains zero. The choice \(q_s=1\) reads a bit without risking capital. Coordinates may be arbitrarily large and need not increase. They cannot repeat, including after a zero wager. There is no requirement to query every coordinate even on an infinite run.

If the next computation diverges or returns no action, the run has no further completed bets and earns no further capital. Computation time itself does not increase capital. There are no time or space bounds. Let \(D_S(X)\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the finite or infinite initial segment of completed-bet counts, including zero. The strategy succeeds precisely when
\[\forall K\in\mathbb N\ \exists s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)>K.\]
This is unbounded supremum of capital, not a requirement that capital converge to infinity, grow at a computable rate, or exceed a single fixed threshold.

Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness. Let \(\mathcal S\) be the class of all strategies just specified. Define
\[\operatorname{KLR}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\quad C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The bound may depend on both \(S\) and \(X\), and no algorithm producing those bounds is required. Rational stakes and unit initial capital give the standard notion. Replacing partial computability by total computability gives the same randomness class, but requiring every coordinate to be visited is a separate condition and is not imposed here.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication or its negation, with these exact measure, effectiveness and betting conventions.

A positive answer must hold for every infinite binary sequence and every uniformly effective Martin-Löf test. Equivalently, prove that for each \(X\) failing some Martin-Löf test there exists an admissible computable strategy with unbounded capital on \(X\). That existential strategy may depend on \(X\); it must still be a finite oracle-free program. A uniform conversion of tests to a finite universal family of strategies is not an additional requirement.

A negative answer must prove the existence of one sequence \(X\) and one Martin-Löf test \((U_k)_{k\ge1}\) such that
\[X\in\bigcap_{k\ge1}U_k\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall S\in\mathcal S\ \exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall s\in D_S(X):\ C_s^S(X)\le K.\]
The same sequence must satisfy every test level and defeat every allowed strategy. A nonconstructive existence proof qualifies; an algorithm computing the bits of \(X\) is not required. Different sequences for different levels or strategies, a separation for fixed query orders, a generalized betting game, or a frequency-only stochasticity result does not settle the full target. Finite simulations or a one-sided known implication are insufficient.
cards.why: Determines whether adaptive computable fair betting detects every effective measure-theoretic failure of randomness in an individual infinite sequence. Equality or separation would connect two foundational ways to formalize unpredictability.

cards.context:
Martin-Löf randomness and betting randomness concern individual infinite objects. Effective tests describe events of arbitrarily small fair-coin probability, while a gambler uses observed bits to determine future bets. Neither definition is a confidence score for a finite sample. Every finite binary string can occur at the start of a Martin-Löf random sequence, so a finite unusual-looking prefix alone cannot settle membership in either class.

Adaptivity changes the information available to a strategy. It may inspect coordinate 100, then choose between coordinates 3 and 7 based on that value. Reading a bit with no money at risk still reveals it and makes it unavailable for later betting. The strategy must choose its next fresh position and wager using only its current history; otherwise it could exploit information it has not legitimately obtained.

The established implications are \(\operatorname{MLR}\subseteq\operatorname{KLR}\subseteq\operatorname{CR}\), where computable randomness \(\operatorname{CR}\) rules out successful total computable fair gamblers that read bits in their original order. The first inclusion is the known direction; the card asks whether it is equality. Kolmogorov–Loveland stochasticity instead controls limiting frequencies of adaptively selected bits and is a different, weaker requirement than defeating all fair betting strategies.

Partiality must be separated from which bits are eventually visited. The standard theory permits partial computations, and using total nonmonotonic procedures yields the same randomness class. However, a total procedure can still leave infinitely many coordinates unseen. Requiring a total strategy to visit every coordinate changes its power: the classical source shows that such a strategy can be matched by a monotonic gambler on every sequence where it succeeds.

Kastermans and Lempp separate Martin-Löf randomness from randomness against predetermined computable permutation orders, and against the more general predetermined computable injective orders. A permutation visits every position; an injection may omit positions. In both cases the query order is fixed independently of revealed bit values. These separations therefore do not decide what fully adaptive strategies can detect.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan show that a Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequence has Martin-Löf random subsequences on computable sets of coordinates with densities arbitrarily close to one. Their Theorem 12 says that splitting at any infinite co-infinite computable set leaves at least one Martin-Löf random part. These are substantial proximity results, but randomness of a subsequence does not establish randomness of the whole interleaving.

Petrović’s universal-pair result concerns a generalized half-betting game. Such games allow richer computable partitions of the remaining possible sequences than asking for the value of one fresh coordinate. A pair of generalized strategies can cover all failures of Martin-Löf randomness, but this theorem does not turn them into strategies in the more restricted query model of the card.

The 2025 open-set theorem is stronger than merely a statement about one finite family: it assigns bounds to all Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies and finds arbitrarily small effective open sets, each containing a sequence staying below every strategy’s bound. The witnessing sequence can depend on the open-set level. The result does not give one such sequence in every level of a single Martin-Löf test, and the paper leaves equality open.

The decisive quantifiers concern one infinite sequence at a time. For a negative answer, that sequence must fail an effective test and simultaneously evade every permitted computable gambler. For a positive answer, a successful gambler may be different for different nonrandom sequences. The mathematical question does not require one fixed gambler, a fixed finite family, or uniform speed of winning.

cards.title: Computability of the Mandelbrot set
cards.formal:
Is the Mandelbrot set a computable compact subset of the plane?

Precisely, does there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\) such that for every integer \(k\ge0\), \(A(k)\) halts and outputs a finite nonempty set \(S_k\) of points with dyadic rational coordinates satisfying
\[
d_H(S_k,M)\le 2^{-k},
\]
where
\[
M=\{c\in\mathbb C:\ (z_j(c))_{j\ge0}\text{ is bounded}\},\qquad
z_0(c)=0,\quad z_{j+1}(c)=z_j(c)^2+c?
\]
The assertion is unconditional and places no complexity bound on \(A\).
cards.definitions:
Identify \(\mathbb C\) with \(\mathbb R^2\) and use the Euclidean norm \(|\cdot|\). Boundedness of the orbit means that there exists a finite real \(R\ge0\), depending on \(c\), such that \(|z_j(c)|\le R\) for every integer \(j\ge0\). For this family, equivalently,
\[
M=\{c:\ \forall j\ge0,\ |z_j(c)|\le2\}.
\]
The set \(M\) is nonempty, closed and contained in the closed disk of radius two, hence compact.

A dyadic rational is an integer divided by a nonnegative integer power of two, encoded by signed binary integers for numerator and exponent. The output \(S_k\) is an explicit finite list of pairs of such numbers; repetitions may be removed. No bound on the list length is imposed. The accuracy input \(k\) has its ordinary finite binary encoding.

For two nonempty compact subsets \(X,Y\) of the plane, their Hausdorff distance is
\[
d_H(X,Y)=\max\left\{
\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{y\in Y}|x-y|,
\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}|x-y|
\right\}.
\]
Thus every reported point must be within the stated accuracy of \(M\), and every point of \(M\) must be within that accuracy of a reported point. A close picture on a selected finite grid without a proved global error guarantee is insufficient.

The machine is an ordinary algorithm operating on finite strings. It receives only \(k\); it has no oracle for complex numbers, set membership, the halting problem or a dynamical conjecture. One finite program must work at every precision, rather than a separately chosen program or advice string for each \(k\).

This is the standard computable-analysis notion for a fixed compact set. Equivalently, its distance function
\[
\operatorname{dist}(q,M)=\inf_{c\in M}|q-c|
\]
must be uniformly computable: a machine, given any rational point \(q\in\mathbb Q^2\) and \(k\ge0\), returns a rational number within \(2^{-k}\) of this distance. The equivalence uses the fixed compact bound on \(M\). The question does not ask for a total exact membership decision on arbitrary real inputs, for a polynomial running time, for the area of \(M\), or for its boundary alone.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of \(A\) with the stated all-precision Hausdorff guarantee. A positive answer must prove both termination and the approximation bound for every \(k\). A negative answer must rule out all ordinary Turing programs with this behavior. An implication from an additional unproved conjecture or an undecidability result for exact real membership does not settle the assertion. This is a binary computability question: a fixed numerical tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the requirement to handle every \(2^{-k}\).
cards.why: The defining iteration is simple and finite images are ubiquitous, yet those facts do not establish a uniform algorithm with certified error at every resolution. The problem tests whether the global geometry of a natural dynamical parameter set is effectively recoverable from its definition.

cards.context:
The source uses this question as motivation for computable geometry. Its main results concern semicomputable triangles, so the existence of that paper does not constitute progress resolving the Mandelbrot question.

The author’s later handout distinguishes one-sided information from a complete approximation algorithm: the exterior can be effectively enumerated as an open set, while the boundary and hyperbolic components satisfy other enumerability properties. These individual statements do not by themselves provide the target distance computation.

The relevant hyperbolicity conjecture asserts that every \(c\) in the interior of \(M\) gives a quadratic map with an attracting periodic cycle. Here a periodic point \(z\) of period \(r\) is attracting when \(|(f_c^r)'(z)|<1\), for \(f_c(z)=z^2+c\). Hertling shows that this conjecture would imply computability, including a stronger two-sided distance notion. The conjecture is not an assumption of this card.

The 2021 handout lists ordinary distance computability separately from the stronger two-sided assertion. Accordingly this card asks only for the ordinary compact-set approximation target and does not add a requirement to recognize the entire interior.

The 2025 escape-problem paper supplies an alternative conditional result for the quadratic family. Its Theorem 22 identifies the robust instances reached by its reduction and retains the hyperbolicity condition; it does not claim an unconditional approximation algorithm for the whole Mandelbrot set.

The 2025 paper also distinguishes the bit-based approximation question from exact membership in the Blum–Shub–Smale real-computation model. A negative result for the latter is not a negative answer to the finite Hausdorff-approximation question specified here.

cards.title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the \(\omega\)-jump
cards.formal:
Does the following formal provability statement hold?
\[
\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\ \vdash\
\forall X\,\exists Y\,
\bigl[Y_0=X\ \wedge\ \forall j\,(Y_{j+1}=Y_j')\bigr].
\]
Here \(\mathrm{HT}\) is Hindman's theorem for every finite coloring of the positive integers and all nonempty finite sums of distinct members of one infinite set. The conclusion says that every set has its coded \(\omega\)-jump. Equivalently, does full Hindman's theorem imply \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) over \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\)?
cards.definitions:
Use classical two-sorted first-order logic, with number variables, set-of-number variables, equality, membership, \(0\), successor \(S\), addition and multiplication. Set equality is extensional. Models may have nonstandard numbers, and their set sort need not contain every subset of their number domain. Thus the logical semantics is Henkin semantics, not full second-order semantics.

The number axioms are Robinson arithmetic: \(Sx\ne0\), \(Sx=Sy\Rightarrow x=y\), \(x\ne0\Rightarrow\exists y\,x=Sy\), \(x+0=x\), \(x+Sy=S(x+y)\), \(x\cdot0=0\), and \(x\cdot Sy=x\cdot y+x\). Write \(1=S0\), define \(x<y\) by \(\exists z\,x+S(z)=y\), and define \(x\le y\) by \(x<y\) or \(x=y\).

A bounded arithmetic formula has only number quantifiers bounded by number terms; set membership and free set parameters are allowed, but quantified set variables are not. A \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula consists of a finite block of existential number quantifiers followed by a bounded formula; a \(\Pi^0_1\) formula uses a universal block instead. The base theory \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\) adds the universal closures of the following schemes, allowing number and set parameters. For every \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \(\varphi(n)\), it includes
\[
[\varphi(0)\wedge\forall n(\varphi(n)\Rightarrow\varphi(Sn))]
\Rightarrow\forall n\,\varphi(n).
\]
For every \(\Sigma^0_1\) formula \(\varphi(n)\) and \(\Pi^0_1\) formula \(\psi(n)\), it includes
\[
[\forall n(\varphi(n)\leftrightarrow\psi(n))]
\Rightarrow\exists Z\,\forall n\,[n\in Z\leftrightarrow\varphi(n)],
\]
where \(Z\) is not free in either defining formula. This is \(\Delta^0_1\) comprehension.

Functions and finite sequences are represented by their usual arithmetic codes. Fix the pairing \(\langle j,e\rangle=(j+e)(j+e+1)/2+e\), whose division is exact, and a standard effective coding of finite sequences and oracle Turing computations. All statements about a coded finite computation or sequence are interpreted inside the theory. In particular, finite lengths and color counts range over its number sort, rather than only over externally standard integers.

In \(\mathrm{HT}\), quantify over every number \(k\ge1\) and every set coding the graph of a total function \(c:\mathbb N_{>0}\to\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\). There must exist a set \(H\subseteq\mathbb N_{>0}\) and a number \(i<k\) such that \(\forall b\,\exists h>b\,(h\in H)\) and
\[
c(h_0+\cdots+h_{r-1})=i
\]
for every coded strictly increasing finite sequence \(h_0<\cdots<h_{r-1}\) from \(H\) with \(r\ge1\). There is no fixed bound on \(r\), no repeated summand and no extra separation condition on the binary supports of the integers in \(H\).

Fix a standard enumeration of oracle Turing machines. For a set \(A\), the notation \(A'\) denotes the halting set
\[
\{e:\text{the }e\text{-th machine with oracle }A\text{ halts on input }e\}.
\]
The assertion \(B=A'\) is the arithmetic formula saying that membership of \(e\) in \(B\) is equivalent to existence of a coded finite halting computation using the answers supplied by \(A\). It does not assume that the jump set already exists in the model. For a single set \(Y\), define its sections by \(Y_j=\{e:\langle j,e\rangle\in Y\}\). The target requires one such \(Y\) simultaneously recording every finite jump iterate, beginning with \(Y_0=X\). The theory \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) is \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\) plus this closure axiom.

The symbol \(\vdash\) means existence of a finite formal derivation in a sound and complete classical two-sorted first-order proof calculus using the stated axioms and schemes. Equivalent standard encodings of syntax and computation do not alter the question. This is an exact provability proposition, with no bound on proof length or computational resources.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that a finite formal derivation of the displayed closure axiom exists from \(\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such derivation exists. For the latter, a fully verified Henkin model of \(\mathrm{RCA}_0+\mathrm{HT}\) omitting the coded \(\omega\)-jump of some set suffices, together with the soundness argument. A model with standard natural numbers is sufficient but is not required.

Proving the closure axiom in the ambient logic of Lean without verifying the restriction to the stated object theory does not prove this reversal. Neither the known \(\mathrm{ACA}_0\) lower bound, the known \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\) upper bound, nor a claim about one computable coloring decides it. A negative answer need not establish equivalence with \(\mathrm{ACA}_0\); any valid separation from the displayed closure axiom settles the question.
cards.why: The problem asks how much set existence is forced by a basic theorem about finite sums. A reversal would identify unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity with closure under all finite Turing jumps recorded in one set; a separation would show that this known upper theory is stronger than necessary.

cards.context:
A finite coloring may be arbitrary. Hindman’s theorem supplies one infinite set whose single elements, pair sums, triple sums and every larger finite sum all have the same color. The theorem itself is established; this card asks which axioms its assertion forces.

The classical bounds are \(\mathrm{ACA}_0^+\Rightarrow\mathrm{HT}\Rightarrow\mathrm{ACA}_0\) over \(\mathrm{RCA}_0\). Ordinary arithmetic comprehension gives each set its next Turing jump. The stronger closure principle collects all finite iterates into one set.

Restricted sum lengths can have different strengths. The inherited paper obtains the arithmetic-comprehension lower bound already for sums of at most two elements. Such a lower bound does not supply the whole coded sequence of jumps required here.

Liu and Patey prove that, for every non-arithmetical set \(C\) and every arithmetical finite coloring, some full Hindman solution \(H\) satisfies \(C\not\le_T H\). Here arithmetical means definable using only number quantifiers, and \(C\le_T H\) means computable with oracle \(H\). In particular, an individual such coloring cannot force every solution to compute \(\emptyset^{(\omega)}\).

The same authors explicitly state that this does not rule out equivalence with omega-jump closure through multiple applications of Hindman’s theorem. Their result does not construct a model closed under every required instance while omitting the target jump.

The July conservation paper concerns a different one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle. Its introduction distinguishes the additional block-order condition associated with Hindman’s theorem, so its weaker axiomatic bounds do not settle this card.

cards.title: Unconditional coding theorem for randomized Kolmogorov complexity
cards.formal:
Is the following coding statement true without a computational hardness or derandomization assumption?
\[
\forall D\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ \exists c,d\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\ge2\ \forall x\in\operatorname{supp}(D_n):
\quad
\mathrm{rK}^{(n+2)^d}(x)
\le
\left\lceil\log_2\frac1{D_n(x)}\right\rceil
+c\left\lceil\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil .
\]
Here \(D=\{D_n\}_{n\ge2}\) ranges over uniformly polynomial-time samplable distributions on \(n\)-bit strings, and \(\mathrm{rK}^t\) uses private random bits and success probability at least \(2/3\), as defined below. The constants \(c,d\) may depend on the fixed sampler but must work for every length and every string in its support.

The target is existence of short polynomial-time randomized descriptions. No efficient algorithm for finding a description from \(x\) is required.
cards.definitions:
Fix one standard efficiently universal probabilistic Turing machine \(U\), with a binary program, a one-way tape of independent fair random bits and an output tape. Its simulation of any fixed machine has polynomial time overhead and a constant program-description overhead. The program receives no input string, length, advice, shared random tape or oracle for the sampler's distribution.

For \(t\in\mathbb N\), define
\[
\mathrm{rK}^{t}(x)=
\min\left\{
 |p|:
 \Pr_{r\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{t}}
 [U(p;r)\text{ halts within }t\text{ steps with output exactly }x]
 \ge\frac23
\right\}.
\]
A computation uses at most \(t\) random bits in \(t\) steps; unused bits are ignored. Failure to halt in time or outputting another string is failure. The minimum is \(+\infty\) if there is no such program. The same program \(p\) must succeed for the indicated fraction of random tapes. It may depend on \(D,n,x\), but it is chosen before the random tape. A description can encode the length and a sampler description within its counted program bits.

Membership \(D\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) means that there is one deterministic algorithm \(S\), a polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer function \(a(n)\), and a polynomial time bound, such that for every \(n\ge2\) and every \(r\in\{0,1\}^{a(n)}\), the computation \(S(1^n,r)\) outputs exactly \(n\) bits within that bound. The law of \(S(1^n,R)\) for uniform \(R\) is \(D_n\). Thus \(D_n(x)\) is an exact rational probability and \(\operatorname{supp}(D_n)=\{x:D_n(x)>0\}\). The sampler is uniform and has no length-dependent advice.

The expression \(\log_2(1/D_n(x))\) is the information content, in bits, of the particular string. The inequality is pointwise on the entire support, including very unlikely strings. It is not only an expected-length bound or a guarantee outside a small exceptional set. There is one polynomial decoding-time exponent and one logarithmic-overhead constant for the whole sampler family.

For comparison, probabilistic complexity \(\mathrm{pK}^{t}(x)\) permits the short deterministic program to be chosen after seeing public random bits: its quantifiers have the form \(\Pr_r[\exists p\text{ short}:U(p;r)=x]\ge2/3\). That is a different measure from the single-program private-randomness measure in the question. Likewise, an efficient coding theorem would additionally require an efficient encoder that finds a short description; this card does not impose that requirement.

No assumption about one-way functions, average-case hardness or circuit lower bounds is part of the statement. The fixed universal-machine convention is harmless for this existential polynomial-time and logarithmic-overhead target, since the constants and exponent may change.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal coding statement. An affirmative answer must cover every uniformly polynomial-time sampler and every supported string with the stated quantifier order. A negative answer must establish a sampler family for which no pair of constants \(c,d\) works. A conditional result, a coding theorem only for public-randomness complexity, an expected-length bound, or a theorem allowing exceptional strings does not suffice. This is a binary question; numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not relax the coding inequality or its universal quantifiers.
cards.why: A sampler may assign a string high probability without providing an obvious short description that a fast decoder can use. The question asks whether information content nevertheless always predicts description length, allowing private randomness and logarithmic overhead. A resolution would clarify a recurring gap between information-theoretic coding and computational descriptions.

cards.context:
The classical coding principle bounds description length by information content when no decoding-time restriction is imposed. The card asks for a polynomial-time private-randomness version for arbitrary efficient samplers.

Public-randomness descriptions may choose a different short program after seeing the shared random tape. The cited literature supplies stronger coding results in that model; they do not give the single fixed randomized program required here.

The source proves efficient coding for next-bits predictable distributions, where conditional next-bit probabilities can be estimated to arbitrarily small inverse-polynomial accuracy. An efficient sampler alone is not that additional prediction guarantee.

Theorems I.1–I.2 give conditional and average-case coding consequences under the non-existence of infinitely-often one-way functions. Their assumptions and allowance of exceptional instances differ from the unconditional pointwise statement.

Theorem I.7 identifies a cryptographic obstruction to efficient encoding for all samplable distributions. It does not show that short descriptions fail to exist when the encoder is unrestricted.

The December 2025 boundary-hardness paper still identifies the unconditional theorem for every string in the sampler support as missing, and explains why an average-case coding result does not supply that requirement.

cards.title: Mortality of \(2\times 2\) integer matrix semigroups
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite list \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{m}\) of \(2\times 2\) integer matrices, halts and correctly decides whether there exist \(\ell\ge 1\) and indices \(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{\ell}\in \{1,\ldots ,m\}\) with \(A_{i_{1}} A_{i_{2}} \cdots  A_{i_{\ell}}=0_{2}\)?
cards.definitions: The input explicitly gives \(m\ge 0\) and all four entries of each \(A_{i}\) as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: \((AB)_{r,s}=\sum _{t=1}^{2} A_{r,t}B_{t,s}\). The target \(0_{2}\) is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length \(\ell\) is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of \(0_{2}\) in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.
cards.why: A minimal-dimensional undecidability frontier for matrix products and discrete dynamical systems.

references.locator: 16 April 2026. Full abstract and Introduction read. New word representations and embedding results for complex matrix structures do not give a general integer-mortality decision procedure; this source is subsequent scope checking, not a fresh explicit mortality-status assertion.

cards.context:
A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

Let \(A=[[1,0],[0,0]]\) and \(B=[[0,0],[1,0]]\). Neither is the zero matrix, but \(AB=0_{2}\), so the list \((A,B)\) is mortal. Reversing the order gives \(BA=B\), showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.

cards.title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(b\ge 2\) and every real \(x\in[0,1)\), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
cards.definitions: Write \(x=\sum _{n\ge 1}d_{n} b^{- n}\), where \(d_{n}\in \{0,\ldots ,b- 1\}\), using the unique expansion that is not eventually all \(b-1\). A terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means \(x=p/q\) for integers p,q with \(q\ne 0\). Algebraic means \(P(x)=0\) for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant \(C\ge 1\) such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing \(t_{n}\) for the step at which \(d_{n}\) appears, \(1\le t_{n+1}- t_{n}\le C\) for every \(n\ge 1\). The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.
cards.why: A proof would impose a strong arithmetic restriction on numbers generated at the fastest possible asymptotic output rate. The checked 2024 source also records that the conjecture would rule out linear-time integer multiplication on multitape Turing machines.

cards.context:
For example, \(1/7=0.142857142857\ldots\) in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, \(\sqrt{2}- 1\) is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies \(x^{2}+2x- 1=0\). The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from \(b^{n}\) supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.
