cards.title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space
cards.formal:
Does there exist one computable compiler \(\mathcal C\) that maps every deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) to a reversible multitape machine \(R=\mathcal C(M)\) with the following simultaneous guarantees? For every \(M\), there are a constant \(c_M\ge1\) and an integer \(d_M\ge1\) such that, on every input \(x\) on which \(M\) halts, \(R\) halts with exactly the output pair \((x,M(x))\), clears its auxiliary tapes, and satisfies
\[S_R(x)\le c_M S_M(x),\qquad T_R(x)\le c_M T_M(x)^{d_M}.\]
On every input on which \(M\) does not halt, \(R\) must also fail to halt. The same \(R\) must meet both bounds on every halting input. This is the previously selected polynomial-time, linear-space version of the source's broader simulation tradeoff question.
cards.definitions:
Each machine has a finite transition table, finitely many states, a finite tape alphabet containing 0, 1, a blank and delimiters, and a fixed finite number of two-way tapes with one head per tape. A transition reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Tapes are indexed by integers, and all heads initially sit at a designated origin. The machine description lists these finite objects explicitly in a fixed effectively decodable binary syntax. Alphabet size, tape count and states may depend on the fixed machine but not on its input. There are no oracle, advice, random or external-storage tapes.

Initially the binary input \(x\), with fixed delimiters, occupies consecutive cells of one tape; all other cells are blank. A halting run has a finite designated binary output \(M(x)\), with delimiters on an output tape. A transition is a partial deterministic function on full configurations; a configuration with no next transition is terminal. The full configuration includes the state, every tape's contents and every head position. A simulator must implement the stated terminal-output convention on its intended input runs.

A machine is reversible if its partial one-step map is injective on its entire configuration space: whenever transitions from configurations \(u\) and \(v\) produce the same configuration, \(u=v\). Thus no step may merge two different predecessor configurations. This property concerns the finite machine's full transition semantics, not just the particular run from a blank workspace. Halting states have no outgoing step; injectivity does not require every configuration to have a predecessor. Reversibility is logical reversibility of a classical machine, not a physical energy model or a quantum operation.

For a halting run, \(S_M(x)\) is the number of distinct tape cells initially occupied or visited during the entire run, summed over all tapes, with a minimum of 1. A cell still counts if it is later erased. Input, output, delimiter, history and work cells all count. Let
\[T_M(x)=\max\{1,|x|,\text{number of transitions before halting}\}.\]
Define \(S_R,T_R\) in exactly the same way. This is a per-input resource comparison, not a comparison of unrelated worst-case inputs of a given length. Finite control is part of the fixed machine description, while every tape cell used at run time is included. No additional initially full catalytic tape is supplied for free.

At termination, the simulator has two designated output tracks or tapes containing the original \(x\) and \(M(x)\), with the fixed delimiters, and all auxiliary tape contents are blank. Retaining \(x\) is essential: different inputs can yield the same \(M(x)\), but a reversible computation cannot merge their histories into an identical final configuration. The output pair is required exactly; leaving a computation-history string as garbage is not accepted. The simulator need only preserve the partial function in this input-preserving sense, rather than reproduce each intermediate configuration of \(M\).

The compiler is a single total deterministic computable function on valid machine descriptions; its compilation time is unrestricted. It outputs a finite reversible machine description, with no dependence on the later input \(x\). Neither the compiler nor the simulator is given the eventual halting time or space use as an extra input. The constants \(c_M,d_M\) may depend on \(M\), but are fixed before quantifying over all \(x\). No halting-time or resource bound is required on divergent runs beyond preservation of nontermination. A simulator chosen separately for every individual input would not satisfy the compiler requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of this compiler. A positive answer must establish total computability of compilation, reversibility of every output machine on its full configuration space, preservation of the partial function and nontermination behavior, clean input-preserving output, and the two simultaneous per-input resource bounds. A negative answer must prove that no compiler can satisfy these requirements for all machines and inputs; failure of one known construction does not suffice. Separate simulators achieving the time and space bounds independently do not settle the conjunction. A lower bound only for reversible pebble games, an oracle-relative simulation model or circuits does not refute unrestricted reversible multitape simulation. The resource requirements are exact asymptotic claims, without additive numerical tolerance.
cards.why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

cards.context:
An irreversible computation may overwrite information that is no longer needed. A reversible machine must retain enough information elsewhere to make each transition invertible on its image. The question asks whether doing so can always preserve the original storage scale while incurring only polynomial time overhead.

Input preservation and clearing auxiliary tapes specify what counts as a completed simulation. They prevent two easy ambiguities: erasing distinct inputs that have the same answer, and treating a large retained execution history as an acceptable final result.

Bennett’s simulations establish polynomial-time reversible computation with space \(O(S\log(T+2))\), among other tradeoffs. The logarithmic multiplier is not bounded by one machine-dependent constant as the input grows, so this bound does not establish the card’s \(O(S)\) requirement.

Lange, McKenzie and Tapp show that deterministic space can be preserved by reversible computation. The general construction can take exponential time, so space preservation alone does not imply the required polynomial overhead in the original running time.

Buhrman, Tromp and Vitányi give intermediate time-space tradeoffs and discuss how to remove an advance bound on the simulated running time. Their result bridges the classical extremes but does not give the required simultaneous polynomial-time and constant-factor-space guarantee for every machine.

Reversible pebble games model a particular style of simulation, with memory snapshots represented by pebbles. A lower bound for that model need not apply to all reversible machines. The space-preserving theorem itself demonstrated that general simulation can escape restrictions of that particular model.

The 2026 catalytic-computation paper studies an additional tape initialized with arbitrary contents that must be restored. Its reversible-space lemma has no general polynomial-time-overhead guarantee. Both its separate catalytic resource and the missing time bound matter: it is related progress, not a solution to the total-storage target here.

Logical reversibility is relevant to the information erased during computation, but this card does not set an energy bound for hardware. Its mathematical success criterion is entirely the classical compiler, correctness, time and space statement.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
cards.definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
cards.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

cards.context:
Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\). cards.title: Existence of p-optimal proof systems
cards.formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation \(t_{Q}\) satisfying \(P(t_{Q}(\pi ))=Q(\pi )\) for every finite binary proof string \(\pi\)?
cards.definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function \(P:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\mathrm{TAUT}\), computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string \(\pi\) proves formula F when \(P(\pi )=F\). Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as \(x_{1}\lor \neg x_{1}\). A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on \(\pi\). The order is \(\exists P \forall Q \exists t_{Q} \forall \pi\). No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in \(|\pi |\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.
cards.why: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.

cards.context:
Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\).

Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from \(P=\mathrm{NP}\). Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.

cards.title: Frege versus Extended Frege
cards.formal:
Does ordinary Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege in proof size? For the two fixed systems and binary size convention below, determine whether
\[\exists C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \forall\varphi\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow\exists\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\land |\rho|\le C(|\pi|+2)^{k}]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over all finite propositional formulas in the ordinary variables, and \(\pi,\rho\) range over finite binary strings. The constants are independent of the formula and of both proofs. This asks for existence of short Frege proofs of the same conclusions; it does not require a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them. Equivalently, for every tautology \(\varphi\), is its minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) bounded by one fixed polynomial in its minimum Extended Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varphi)\)?
cards.definitions:
Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by ordinary variables \(x_i\), temporary extension variables \(e_i\), negation \(\neg A\), and material implication \(A\to B\), with \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). Ordinary formulas contain no \(e_i\). A Boolean assignment gives each variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses this value and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and consequent false. A tautology is an ordinary formula true under every assignment to its ordinary variables. Every syntactic occurrence is written separately: a formula is a tree, not a circuit with shared subformulas.

The fixed Frege calculus has precisely these three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each occurrence of a scheme uses a consistent substitution of formulas for its metavariables \(A,B,C\). The only inference rule is modus ponens, deriving \(B\) from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\). A Frege proof is a nonempty finite sequence of ordinary formulas, each justified by an axiom instance or modus ponens, with the last formula its conclusion. There are no hypotheses, extension axioms or separate rules that substitute into an already derived line. Any earlier line may be reused arbitrarily often. Auxiliary ordinary variables not occurring in the conclusion are permitted.

Extended Frege uses the same schemes and modus ponens, and additionally permits a consecutive pair of extension lines \(e_i\to\theta\) and \(\theta\to e_i\). At this introduction, \(e_i\) has not occurred in any earlier line and does not occur in \(\theta\) or in the final conclusion. The formula \(\theta\) may contain any ordinary variables and extension variables from completed earlier pairs, but no other extension variables. Both lines are written explicitly. After the pair, \(e_i\) may occur in later axiom instances, modus-ponens lines and definitions. Every extension variable in any line must be introduced this way; the final conclusion contains none. Definitions are thus acyclic, and cannot assert arbitrary assumptions about the ordinary variables. There is no bound on formula depth, proof depth, number of extensions, or reuse of earlier lines. No tree-like restriction is imposed on the proof sequence.

Use the following fixed prefix-free binary encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), where concatenation is intended. A formula uses tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(x_i\), tag 01 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(e_i\), tag 10 followed by the child encoding for negation, and tag 11 followed by the antecedent and consequent encodings for implication. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then consists of a three-bit justification tag and its entire formula encoding. Tags 000, 001 and 010 specify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be an instance of the specified scheme. Tag 011 specifies modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): for line number \(j\), the indices satisfy \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) is \(A\), and line \(b\) is exactly \(A\to B\) where the current formula is \(B\). Tags 100 and 101 specify the first and second lines of an extension pair. They must occur consecutively with exactly the two formulas and freshness conditions above; no additional data are implicit. The other tags and all malformed encodings are invalid. Frege permits only the first four tags and no extension variables. The size \(|\pi|\) is the bit length of this entire string, including every formula occurrence, variable index, line count and inference reference.

The predicates in the question mean validity under these syntactic rules with the specified final formula, not mere semantic validity of an unverified proof string. The displayed finite calculus is a standard complete classical Frege presentation; the explicit pair convention, auxiliary-variable convention and binary annotations fix ordinary polynomially equivalent presentations of the source systems. In particular, the bit cost is not merely the number of inference steps. The minimum sizes are defined for tautologies, all of which have finite Frege proofs. A size simulation alone is the target; the stronger notion of p-simulation additionally requires a polynomial-time proof translation.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation for the fixed systems and encoding. A positive answer must establish one pair of constants \(C,k\ge1\) that works for every valid Extended Frege proof and supplies the existence of a Frege proof of exactly the same ordinary conclusion with the required size. A negative answer must establish
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi,\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\land\forall\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\rho|>C(|\pi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
The formula and Extended Frege proof may depend on \(C,k\); no additional uniform construction of a separating family is imposed. All validity, size and quantifier claims must be justified in Lean. Conditional comparisons, a particular expensive expansion, restricted proof systems, a quasipolynomial simulation, or a polynomial-time proof-search lower bound alone do not meet this criterion. This is a binary asymptotic proof-size comparison, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its polynomial bound.
cards.why: This asks whether naming and reusing intermediate formulas can shorten rigorous propositional proofs by more than every polynomial factor. It is a central comparison between strong proof systems and between reasoning with formula trees and shared circuit representations. A separation would yield superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege; an equivalence would show that the extension rule changes shortest-proof lengths by at most polynomial factors.

references.locator: TR26-166: submitted 4 September, published 5 September 2026; Definition 1.1 pp. 6–7, Theorem 1.2 p. 7 and Theorem 1.3 p. 8; §2.3 Definitions 2.6–2.8 pp. 17–18; no later revision listed on 15 September

cards.context:
Frege proofs model a finite list of ordinary propositional deductions. Extended Frege adds named definitions, allowing a long expression to be referenced by a variable after paying for its definition. Chains of these definitions describe shared Boolean circuits. Every assignment to the ordinary variables extends uniquely through an acyclic sequence of definitions, so the extension rule preserves truth of conclusions that contain no extension variables. This explains the systems' common set of theorems while leaving their proof lengths potentially different.

Proof reuse and subformula sharing are different resources. Both systems may cite an earlier proof line many times; ordinary Frege still pays for every occurrence inside each newly written formula. Extended Frege also has names for intermediate expressions. This representational distinction does not itself show that any tautology lacks a short Frege proof. The question compares the best proofs available in the two systems, irrespective of how those proofs were discovered.

The usual robustness theorem compares finite sound and complete Frege presentations with polynomial overhead. Cook and Reckhow also define fresh extension variables and establish the analogous robustness of Extended Frege. The card preserves the saved size-simulation target while making its syntax and bit accounting explicit. It restores the source convention allowing auxiliary ordinary variables; restricting such variables to those of the conclusion gives a polynomially equivalent convention. A bounded-depth, tree-like or otherwise restricted Frege system would be a different question.

A polynomial bound on the existence of translated proofs is distinct from a polynomial-time translator. Buss's work separates these notions and relates size simulation to short finite consistency proofs. His 1991 result characterizes Frege simulation of Extended Frege by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the corresponding partial EF consistency statements: finite propositional assertions that a contradiction has no proof up to a specified length. Frege already has polynomial-size partial self-consistency proofs. This comparison is a stated theorem about the systems, not a resolution of Frege versus EF. The current review checked the author and publisher abstracts; the author's downloadable copy is headed 11 July 2002, although the journal publication is from 1991.

Buss's Stanford tutorial of 27 February 2014 explicitly presents the formula-versus-circuit proof comparison as a longstanding open question. Its discussion of proposed separating principles is historical context, not a current lower-bound theorem. Quasipolynomial upper bounds for particular families must remain distinct both from polynomial upper bounds and from a separation of the unrestricted systems.

A concrete example is the Kneser–Lovász coloring principle. The graph has the \(k\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) as vertices and joins disjoint subsets; for \(n\ge2k\), its propositional principle rules out a proper coloring with \(n-2k+1\) colors. Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs for each fixed \(k\). Constants and exponents may depend on that fixed parameter. Their 2015 conference version states these as Theorems 4 and 5; the 2018 expanded journal abstract retains the fixed-parameter condition. These are upper bounds for particular tautologies, not a superpolynomial Frege lower bound or a uniform bound with both parameters growing.

Krajíček's 11 June 2026 preprint describes circuit-equivalence reasoning by local circuit rewrites. Its relation is polynomial-time recognizable, and each rewrite may delete gates and add at most seven; a short EF proof yields a polynomially bounded chain. The intermediate objects retain circuit sharing. The concluding discussion also distinguishes existence of a small chain from a polynomial-time construction of it by the presented proof. This normal-form statement therefore supplies neither the polynomial-size formula proof nor the polynomial-time translator that could be mistakenly inferred from the abstract.

The September 2026 report by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay states a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted Ideal Proof System over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\), the field with two elements. Certificates are algebraic formulas. The original variables are divided into two groups, noncommuting within a group and commuting across groups; Definition 1.1 separately specifies the noncommuting placeholder variables and included Boolean and commutator axioms. Theorem 1.2 concerns refutations of unsatisfiable CNFs in that model. Its certificate restrictions and quasipolynomial overhead both prevent it from answering the unrestricted EF question. The report and theorem scope were checked; its complete new proof was not independently verified.

An EF proof includes its final formula, so a superpolynomial separation from Frege would imply superpolynomial Frege proof-size lower bounds as a function of formula length. The converse need not follow: a family hard for Frege might also require long EF proofs. Likewise, the separate question whether EF is polynomially bounded asks whether every tautology has a short EF proof, rather than whether Frege can match EF's shortest proofs. The present card makes no assumption that \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) and does not identify a computation-class separation with this proof-system comparison.

The original variables are divided into two groups, noncommuting within a group and commuting across groups; Definition 1.1 separately specifies the noncommuting placeholder variables and included Boolean and commutator axioms. Theorem 1.2 concerns refutations of unsatisfiable CNFs in that model. Its certificate restrictions and quasipolynomial overhead both prevent it from answering the unrestricted EF question. The report and theorem scope were checked; its complete new proof was not independently verified.

An EF proof includes its final formula, so a superpolynomial separation from Frege would imply superpolynomial Frege proof-size lower bounds as a function of formula length. The converse need not follow: a family hard for Frege might also require long EF proofs. Likewise, the separate question whether EF is polynomially bounded asks whether every tautology has a short EF proof, rather than whether Frege can match EF's shortest proofs. The present card makes no assumption that \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) and does not identify a computation-class separation with this proof-system comparison.

cards.title: Weak automatability of Resolution
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in \(|F|+s\), that on input a CNF formula \(F\) and a unary proof budget \(1^{s}\) distinguishes the following two promised cases: \(F\) is satisfiable, or \(F\) has a Resolution refutation with at most \(s\) clauses?
cards.definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated deterministic polynomial-time separator, or prove that no such separator exists. If a lower bound assumes a complexity separation, that separation must also be proved to settle the negative answer. Hardness of finding a Resolution refutation, estimating its minimum length, or solving unrestricted SAT does not establish hardness of this particular promise separator without a reduction that respects its two promised cases.
cards.why: Asks whether the existence of a short familiar refutation can make unsatisfiability efficiently recognizable even when finding a refutation in that same calculus is hard. This isolates an unresolved limitation of proof search and the theoretical analysis of SAT solvers.

cards.title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege lower bounds
cards.formal:
For every prime integer \(p\), does there exist a single polynomial-time constructible family of DNF tautologies \((\tau_{p,n})_{n\ge1}\) of length polynomially related to \(n\), such that its proofs in the fixed modular Frege calculus below exceed every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth? Precisely, require for each \(p\) a finite deterministic machine \(M_p\) and integers \(C_p,k_p\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) the machine outputs a DNF \(\tau_{p,n}\) within \(C_p(n+2)^{k_p}\) bit steps, this formula is a tautology, and
\[n\le |\tau_{p,n}|\le C_p(n+2)^{k_p}.\]
The required lower bound is
\[\forall d,r,N\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists n\ge N\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau_{p,n})\Rightarrow |\pi|>n^r\bigr).\]
The machine and the family may depend on \(p\) but not on \(d,r,N\); the witness \(n\) may depend on all three. No effective procedure producing \(M_p\) from \(p\) is required. The family consists of genuine tautologies, not formulas whose lack of short proofs might be due to falsity. The lower bound is infinitely often, not necessarily eventually for every \(n\).
cards.definitions:
Fix a prime \(p\ge2\). Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees built from constants \(0,1\), variables \(x_i\) for \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), unary \(\neg\), binary \(\land,\lor\), and gates \(\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(A_1,\ldots,A_t)\) for \(0\le j<p\) and any finite arity \(t\ge0\). Under an assignment of Boolean values to the variables, the usual connectives have their ordinary truth tables, and a modular gate is true exactly when the number of its true arguments is congruent to \(j\) modulo \(p\). A tautology is true under every assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation. A DNF is a finite disjunction of finite conjunctions of literals, written as a binary formula with any parenthesization; an empty conjunction is \(1\), an empty disjunction is \(0\), and a singleton conjunction or disjunction is its sole member. Target DNFs contain no modular gates.

The notation \(A\Rightarrow B\) is an abbreviation for \(\neg A\lor B\), and \(A\Leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((A\Rightarrow B)\land(B\Rightarrow A)\). Both are expanded fully before checking syntax, depth or size. Fix the following finite ordinary Frege axiom schemes, in the order displayed:
\[\begin{gathered}
 A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow A),\\
 (A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow C))\Rightarrow((A\Rightarrow B)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow C)),\\
 (\neg B\Rightarrow\neg A)\Rightarrow(A\Rightarrow B),\\
 (A\land B)\Rightarrow A,\qquad (A\land B)\Rightarrow B,\\
 A\Rightarrow(B\Rightarrow(A\land B)),\\
 A\Rightarrow(A\lor B),\qquad B\Rightarrow(A\lor B),\\
 (A\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow((B\Rightarrow C)\Rightarrow((A\lor B)\Rightarrow C)),\\
 1,\qquad \neg0.
\end{gathered}\]
The metavariables \(A,B,C\) may be replaced consistently by arbitrary formulas of the full modular language. The sole inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\Rightarrow B\), infer \(B\). There are no hypotheses. Besides these eleven schemes, allow the modular axioms
\[\operatorname{MOD}_{p,0}(),\qquad \neg\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}()\quad(1\le j<p),\]
and every instance of
\[\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(\Gamma,A)\Leftrightarrow
 \bigl((\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}(\Gamma)\land\neg A)\lor
 (\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j-1}(\Gamma)\land A)\bigr),\]
where \(\Gamma\) is any finite ordered list of formulas, including the empty list, and \(j-1\) is reduced modulo \(p\) to \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\). These are the modular schemes of the cited source, attached to the specified finite complete classical Frege basis. An axiom line must match its indicated scheme syntactically after expansion, using the same substituted formula at each occurrence of a metavariable. A proof is a nonempty finite sequence of axiom or modus-ponens lines ending with the claimed formula. Earlier lines may be reused without restriction. There are no extension-variable definition axioms, no separate substitution rule for previously derived lines, and no restrictions of regularity or tree shape.

Define the logical depth \(\delta\) of constants and variables to be zero. Negation has depth \(1+\delta(A)\), and a modular gate has depth \(1+\max(0,\delta(A_1),\ldots,\delta(A_t))\). For a conjunction, flatten its maximal connected subtree of conjunction nodes and collect the boundary subformulas whose roots are not conjunctions; its depth is one plus the maximum depth of those subformulas. Use the same rule for disjunctions. Flattening does not cross a negation, modular gate or different Boolean connective. It defines the depth measure only: the actual binary syntax tree is still written and counted in full. A depth-at-most-\(d\) proof must have \(\delta\le d\) for every line, including instantiated axioms and the conclusion. This bounds individual formulas, not the length of an inference path in the proof graph. Such paths and the total number of lines are unrestricted.

All sizes are bits in a fixed prefix encoding. For \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), using concatenation. Formula tags 000 and 001 encode constants \(0\) and \(1\); 010 followed by \(E(i)\) encodes \(x_i\); 011 followed by the child encodes negation; 100 and 101 followed by both child encodings encode conjunction and disjunction. Tag 110 followed by \(E(j)E(t)\) and all \(t\) ordered child encodings represents \(\operatorname{MOD}_{p,j}\). Tag 111 is invalid. The prime is fixed by the system, not supplied as an oracle. A proof starts with \(E(m)\), its positive number of lines. Each line contains \(E(q)\) followed by its complete formula encoding. Rule labels \(q=1,\ldots,11\) refer to the ordinary schemes in their displayed order; labels 12, 13 and 14 refer respectively to the empty-zero-residue, empty-nonzero-residue and recursive modular schemes. Label 15 denotes modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): on line \(j\), require \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a=A\) and line \(b=A\Rightarrow B\), with the current line exactly \(B\). Other rule labels and malformed strings are invalid. The length \(|\pi|\) includes every variable index, gate, repeated formula occurrence, line count and inference reference. Formula length uses the same formula encoding. Nothing is given by a compressed circuit, advice or a program for generating a larger proof.

The predicate \(\operatorname{Proof}_{p,d}(\pi,\tau)\) means validity under all these rules, conclusion \(\tau\), and line depth at most \(d\). Construction time for the target family is measured on a standard deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite number of tapes and a finite alphabet containing input/output bits and blank. A transition reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell; all transitions and output writes count. Each \(M_p\) is one finite program, with no oracle or length-dependent advice. Its constants \(C_p,k_p\) may depend on that program and the fixed prime. The formula-size lower bound \(|\tau_{p,n}|\ge n\) and polynomial upper bound make size in \(n\) polynomially comparable with size in the conclusion. Quantifying over positive integer exponents \(r\) is equivalent to exceeding every polynomial bound, including bounds with arbitrary fixed multiplicative constants.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the stated families, their construction machines and bounds, together with a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that all outputs are DNF tautologies and that the displayed lower-bound quantifiers hold for every prime and every fixed line depth. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of the logical negation: some prime \(p\) has no family satisfying all the stated requirements. Equivalently, for that prime, every polynomial-time constructible DNF tautology family of the prescribed length scale has some fixed depth \(d\), exponent \(r\) and threshold \(N\) for which every \(n\ge N\) admits a valid depth-\(d\) proof of size at most \(n^r\). A negative answer does not require an efficient proof-finding algorithm. Unproved tautologicity, one fixed polynomial lower bound, a bound only at restricted derivation depth, or a result for only one prime does not establish the full positive claim. All assumptions, construction bounds, depth and size conventions must match the card. This binary asymptotic claim retains its polynomial precision; the numerical 1/100 tolerance is not a replacement for a proof-size lower bound.
cards.why: This is a central unresolved comparison between the expressive power of shallow formulas and the length of rigorous deductions. Ordinary bounded-depth Frege lower bounds are known, but modular gates permit compact reasoning about arithmetic counts, including parity. Proving the stated lower bounds would move a major proof-complexity frontier beyond shallow reasoning without modular counting.

cards.context:
A modular gate states that a count has a particular residue. The case \(p=2\) includes parity, while other primes give other fixed modular tests. A bounded-depth proof may make arbitrarily many deductions, each of which uses only a bounded number of logical layers. Krajíček's §5 explicitly defines the modular recurrence axioms and the depth convention that flattens consecutive conjunctions or disjunctions. The card fixes a finite ordinary basis and a complete binary encoding within that presentation.

The saved benchmark asks for one efficiently generated DNF family for each prime that defeats all fixed line depths, with the same family at every exponent. This explicit construction and quantifier order are retained as the card's chosen formulation of the broad modular-Frege frontier; they are not silently replaced by a family chosen separately for each depth. A method for selecting the program uniformly from the prime is not an additional requirement. Hard instances may occur on different infinite subsequences at different depths and exponents.

Without modular gates, the bounded-depth comparison has established lower bounds. Ajtai's 1988 work proves superpolynomial bounds for propositional pigeonhole formulas, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo's 1993 paper strengthens them to exponential-type size bounds at each fixed depth. These are statements about ordinary bounded-depth Frege. Adding all modular axiom instances enlarges the set of possible proofs, so an ordinary-Frege lower bound does not itself establish the present one.

Circuit lower bounds and proof lower bounds measure different things. Prime-modulus circuit lower bounds concern nonconstant Boolean functions that cannot be computed by small circuits. Every tautology in this card instead computes the constant true function. The object required to be large is a syntactically verified deduction of that tautology in a fixed calculus. The February 2026 source explicitly retains modular Frege lower bounds as open while distinguishing the circuit results.

Resolution over parities permits disjunctions of linear equations modulo two as proof lines. It is a restricted proof system within the modular-Frege setting. Efremenko and Itsykson's CCC 2025 Theorems 3 and 4 give a tree-like lifting statement and a size-versus-derivation-depth tradeoff, respectively. For their lifted Tseitin family with \(m\) variables, the latter requires either size \(2^{\Omega(m/\log m)}\) or derivation depth \(\Omega(m\log m)\). These results leave open proofs of polynomial size with sufficiently long inference paths; the present card permits such paths.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov's February 2026 result gives a stronger tradeoff for parity resolution. After the specified fixed-gadget lifting, resolution width \(w\) of the original CNF forces derivation depth \(\Omega(w^2/\log S)\) in a size-\(S\) parity-resolution refutation, and also an unconditional size bound \(\Omega(w^2)\). Here width is the maximum number of literals in a clause, minimized over ordinary resolution refutations. The construction and gadget conditions remain part of the source theorem. The depth tradeoff and quadratic bound each fall short of a superpolynomial bound on unrestricted derivation size.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret's full version states in Corollary 5.7 that, for every prime, an explicit DNF sequence has no polynomial-size modular Frege proofs. Crucially, the same corollary describes the formulas' validity as unknown. A false formula has no proof in a sound calculus, so lack of short proofs alone cannot certify a hard tautology. The ITCS 2026 published abstract retains this distinction and discusses conditional evidence for tautologicity. Those conditions have not become unconditional theorems in the versions checked here.

Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret's May 2026 report states exponential-type lower bounds for actual Boolean CNF instances in \(\mathrm{roABP}\text{-}\mathrm{IPS}_{\mathrm{LIN}}\), where the algebraic certificate representation is restricted to read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs in the linear-certificate model. The stated bound holds for every variable order and every field. It is stronger in instance scope than earlier purely algebraic examples, but it retains its restriction on certificate representation. It therefore does not supply lower bounds against arbitrary modular-Frege deductions. The report's new complete proof was not independently verified in this card review.

The target excludes hardness arising merely from an enormous conclusion or an unbounded search for its description: every output has polynomial length and a polynomial-time construction, and its truth must be proved. It also excludes confusing a fixed bound such as \(n^{10}\) with growth beyond every polynomial. The depth, prime and uniform-family conventions are part of the mathematical question rather than implementation details that can be decided after submitting a proof.

It also excludes confusing a fixed bound such as \(n^{10}\) with growth beyond every polynomial. The depth, prime and uniform-family conventions are part of the mathematical question rather than implementation details that can be decided after submitting a proof.

cards.title: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic
cards.formal:
Are there integers \(i>j\ge1\) and a closed first-order arithmetic sentence \(\theta\) such that
\[T_2^i\vdash\theta\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_2^j\nvdash\theta?\]
The theory \(T_2^r\) is BASIC together with induction for every \(\Sigma_r^b\) formula in the language defined below. The question asks for a separation as sets of provable sentences, with no assumed separation of computational complexity classes and no additional oracle symbols. One pair of levels is enough; it need not be fixed in advance, and proving strictness at every pair is not required.
cards.definitions:
Use classical first-order logic with equality and the one-sorted language \(L=\{0,1,+,\cdot,H,\ell,\#,\le\}\). Here \(H\) and \(\ell\) are unary, \(+\), \(\cdot\), \(\#\) are binary, and \(\le\) is a binary predicate. Terms are the finite expressions formed from variables, these constants and these function symbols. Atomic formulas are equalities or inequalities between terms. The logical operations are negation, conjunction, disjunction and first-order universal/existential quantification; implication and equivalence abbreviate their usual Boolean expansions. The successor notation \(Sx\) abbreviates \(x+1\), \(2\) abbreviates \(1+1\), and \(2x\) means \(2\cdot x\).

The intended standard structure has domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), its usual addition, multiplication and order, \(H(x)=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1\) for \(x>0\), and \(x\#y=2^{\ell(x)\ell(y)}\). This interpretation explains the symbols; the theory's nonlogical axioms are exactly the following finite BASIC list and the specified induction scheme, rather than all sentences true in this standard structure. Every free variable in the following displays is universally quantified.

The order and successor axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a\le b\ \to\ a\le b+1,\qquad a\ne a+1,\qquad 0\le a,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ a+1\le b,\qquad a\ne0\ \to\ 2a\ne0,\\
a\le b\lor b\le a,\qquad (a\le b\land b\le a)\ \to\ a=b,\\
(a\le b\land b\le c)\ \to\ a\le c,\qquad a\le a+b,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]
The addition and multiplication axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\
a\cdot0=0,\qquad a\cdot(b+1)=a\cdot b+a,\qquad a\cdot b=b\cdot a,\\
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c),\\
1\le a\ \to\ ((a\cdot b\le a\cdot c)\leftrightarrow(b\le c)).
\end{gathered}\]
The length, halving and smash axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
\ell(0)=0,\qquad \ell(1)=1,\qquad a\le b\ \to\ \ell(a)\le\ell(b),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\
\ell(a\#b)=\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)+1,\qquad 0\#a=1,\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]
These are the 32 axioms in Krajíček's Definition 5.2.1, regrouped by operation, with \(H\) and \(\ell\) replacing the printed halving and length notation. No sequence function or oracle predicate is added.

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. They are sharply bounded when the bound is explicitly \(\ell(t)\). The bound may contain other free variables. Let \(\Sigma_0^b=\Pi_0^b\) be all formulas built from atomic formulas using Boolean operations and only sharply bounded quantifiers. Recursively, \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b,\Pi_{r+1}^b\) are the smallest pair of classes satisfying: both contain \(\Sigma_r^b\cup\Pi_r^b\); both are closed under conjunction, disjunction and both sharply bounded quantifiers; \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded existential quantification; \(\Pi_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded universal quantification; and negation sends either class into the other. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

For a set \(T\) of closed axioms, \(T\vdash\theta\) means that the closed sentence \(\theta\) has a finite proof in classical first-order logic with equality from those axioms. Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

For each integer \(r\ge1\), \(T_2^r\) has the displayed BASIC axioms and, for each \(\varphi(x,\vec a)\in\Sigma_r^b\), the universal closure over all parameter variables \(\vec a\) of
\[\bigl(\varphi(0,\vec a)\land\forall x(\varphi(x,\vec a)\to\varphi(x+1,\vec a))\bigr)\ \to\ \forall x\,\varphi(x,\vec a).\]
Parameters are allowed and are not required to be numerals. There are no induction axioms for formulas outside the specified class unless they are consequences of these axioms. Since the formula classes are nested, \(T_2^j\subseteq T_2^i\) in deductive strength when \(j<i\). A positive answer therefore gives a strict inclusion. The separating sentence may have unrestricted first-order quantifiers; no complexity or syntactic bound on that witness sentence is part of the target.

The indices, finite formulas and finite proofs in the question range over ordinary standard mathematical objects. The nonprovability claim is external: it means that no finite proof from the weaker theory exists, rather than asking the weaker theory itself to prove its inability. A countermodel for the weaker theory and the sentence is an equivalent way to certify that nonprovability. A positive answer must be unconditional in the usual mathematical metatheory; adding an unproved complexity assumption changes the requested statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existential separation. A positive answer must establish one pair of standard integers \(i>j\ge1\), a closed sentence provable in \(T_2^i\), and its nonprovability in \(T_2^j\); the latter can equivalently be proved by a model of \(T_2^j\) falsifying the sentence. A negative answer must establish equality of the deductive closures for every pair \(i>j\ge1\). A difference between axiom lists, a lower bound on the shortest proof of a still-provable sentence, a relativized separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved complexity conjecture does not settle this target.
cards.why: These theories organize arithmetic reasoning by the logical complexity permitted in induction hypotheses. Showing that even two positive levels prove different sentences would establish an unconditional difference in the strength of those reasoning principles. It would clarify how computational complexity is reflected in provability, beyond the known conditional connections.

cards.title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)\) lower bounds
cards.formal:
Is resolution over parities not polynomially bounded on unsatisfiable Boolean CNF formulas? Precisely, is the following proposition true?
\[
\forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists F\quad
\bigl[F\text{ is an unsatisfiable CNF}\ \land\
L_{\oplus}(F)>C\bigl(N(F)+1\bigr)^k\bigr].
\]
Here \(L_{\oplus}(F)\) is the minimum number of lines in any unrestricted \(\mathrm{Res}(\oplus)\) refutation of \(F\), with the rules below, and \(N(F)\) is its full combinatorial input size. Earlier proof lines may be reused arbitrarily. There is no restriction on depth, width, regularity or space.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) has addition and multiplication modulo two. A Boolean assignment to \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) is an element of \(\mathbb F_2^n\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\); a clause is a finite set of literals interpreted as their disjunction, with the empty clause false. A CNF formula \(F\) is a finite conjunction of clauses. It is unsatisfiable if no assignment makes every clause true. Relabel its distinct occurring variables consecutively as \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\); no unused declared variables are counted. Put
\[
N(F)=n+\#\{\text{clauses of }F\}+
       \sum_{D\text{ a clause of }F}|D|.
\]
The empty conjunction and empty clauses are allowed. Clauses are listed explicitly, with signs and binary variable indices. This input measure is polynomially equivalent to the length of this ordinary explicit binary encoding, so the existence of a polynomial bound does not depend on that encoding choice.

A linear form is \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i\), with \(a_i\in\mathbb F_2\), including the zero form. A linear equation is \(f=b\), for \(b\in\mathbb F_2\). A linear clause is a finite disjunction of these equations, again allowing the empty disjunction. Its truth value is given by evaluating all equations over \(\mathbb F_2\). Ordinary positive and negative literals are represented respectively by \(x_i=1\) and \(x_i=0\).

A refutation is a finite sequence of linear clauses ending with the empty clause. Each line is either an input clause of \(F\), translated as above, or follows from earlier lines by one of exactly these rules:

Parity resolution:
\[
\frac{A\vee(f=0)\qquad B\vee(f=1)}{A\vee B},
\]
where \(A,B\) are linear clauses and \(f\) is any linear form in the input variables. Disjunction is taken modulo order and repeated identical disjuncts.

Semantic weakening: from a linear clause \(A\), infer any linear clause \(B\) such that
\[
\forall x\in\mathbb F_2^n,\quad A(x)=1\Longrightarrow B(x)=1.
\]
This rule is implication from one previous line, not arbitrary implication from all input clauses jointly.

All equations use only the variables of \(F\); there are no extension variables, additional axiom schemes or unlisted inference rules. A previous line can serve as a premise arbitrarily many times, giving a directed acyclic proof graph. Size is the total number of lines, including occurrences of input clauses and weakening steps. It is not the sum of the lengths of the equations. Define \(L_{\oplus}(F)\) as the minimum such size. Every unsatisfiable CNF has a refutation since the system contains ordinary resolution.

The constants \(C,k\) are proposed universal bounds; the witnessing formula may depend on both. The question imposes no separate running-time condition on constructing these witnesses and fixes no particular family of formulas. It asks for unconditional non-polynomial boundedness of this fixed proof system, not for a conditional statement assuming a complexity separation.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its negation. An affirmative answer must rule out every uniform polynomial line-count upper bound for unrestricted refutations. A negative answer must prove that there are fixed \(C,k\ge1\) such that every unsatisfiable CNF \(F\) has a refutation of at most \(C(N(F)+1)^k\) lines; no efficient proof-finding algorithm is additionally required. Lower bounds confined to tree-like, regular, reversible or bounded-depth proofs do not meet the affirmative target, and a conditional lower bound does not settle the unconditional proposition. No additive numerical tolerance changes this binary asymptotic claim.
cards.why: A central lower-bound challenge for a small extension of resolution that can reason directly about parity. Resolving it would establish whether this algebraic ability suffices to give short refutations of every unsatisfiable CNF, or whether even unrestricted reuse of parity information leaves an unavoidable superpolynomial proof-size barrier.

cards.title: \(PV_1\) nonprovability of polynomial-time SAT solvers
cards.formal: Is it true that, for every unary function symbol \(g\) in the syntactically generated language \(L_{PV}\) below, \[PV_1\not\vdash\Phi_g,\qquad \Phi_g=\forall F\,\forall a\bigl(\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\to\operatorname{Sat}(F,g(F))\bigr)?\] The theory, admissible symbols and arithmetic formula \(\operatorname{Sat}\) are fixed in the definitions. This is an unconditional assertion about finite first-order proofs.
cards.definitions:
The theory is one-sorted classical first-order arithmetic with equality. We use Jeřábek's explicit presentation of \(PV_1\), cited as an alternative axiomatization by the source survey. Its base language is
\[
L=\{0,S,+,\cdot,\le,\#,\operatorname{len},M\}.
\]
In the intended structure on the nonnegative integers, \(S(x)=x+1\), \(\operatorname{len}(x)=\lceil\log_2(x+1)\rceil\), \(M(x,y)=\lfloor x/2^y\rfloor\), and \(x\#y=2^{\operatorname{len}(x)\operatorname{len}(y)}\). In particular \(\operatorname{len}(0)=0\). Write \(1=S(0)\), \(2=S(S(0))\), \(H(x)=M(x,1)\), and \(x<y\) for \(x\le y\land x\ne y\). These intended interpretations do not supply additional axioms.

The base theory has the universal closures of the following arithmetic axioms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x+0&=x,& x+S(y)&=S(x+y),\\
x\cdot0&=0,&x\cdot S(y)&=x\cdot y+x,\\
0&\le x,& S(y)\le x&\ \longleftrightarrow\ y<x,\\
M(x,0)&=x,&
M(x,y)&=2M(x,S(y))\ \lor\ M(x,y)=S(2M(x,S(y))),\\
\operatorname{len}(0)&=0,&
x\ne0&\ \longrightarrow\ \operatorname{len}(x)=S(\operatorname{len}(H(x))),\\
0\#1&=1,&
x\ne0&\ \longrightarrow\
\bigl(x\#1=2(H(x)\#1)\ \land\
y\#x=(y\#1)(y\#H(x))\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
It also has ordinary induction
\[
[A(0,\vec z)\land\forall x(A(x,\vec z)\to A(S(x),\vec z))]
\to\forall x\,A(x,\vec z)
\]
for every base-language formula \(A\) all of whose quantifiers are sharply bounded. A sharply bounded quantifier is \(\forall v\le\operatorname{len}(t)\) or \(\exists v\le\operatorname{len}(t)\), where \(t\) has no free occurrence of \(v\). A bounded universal quantifier expands to an implication, and a bounded existential quantifier to a conjunction. All induction parameters \(\vec z\) are universally closed.

Generate \(L_{PV}\) syntactically from \(L\) by finitely iterating two rules. For every existing term \(t\) with free variables among \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\), add an \(r\)-ary symbol \(f_t\). For every tuple of existing symbols \(g(\vec x),h_0(\vec x,y,z),h_1(\vec x,y,z),b(\vec x,y)\), add a new symbol \(R_{g,h_0,h_1,b}(\vec x,y)\). Arity is finite, the parameter tuple may be empty, and distinct construction trees are distinct symbols even when their intended functions agree. Include the universal closure of \(f_t(\vec x)=t(\vec x)\). For each recursion symbol, abbreviating it by \(R\), include exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(\vec x,y)&\le b(\vec x,y),\\
g(\vec x)\le b(\vec x,0)&\to R(\vec x,0)=g(\vec x),\\
y\ne0\land h_0(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y))\le b(\vec x,2y)
&\to R(\vec x,2y)=h_0(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y)),\\
h_1(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y))\le b(\vec x,S(2y))
&\to R(\vec x,S(2y))=h_1(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y)).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are bounded-recursion constraints; no unconditional recursion equation is added when its bounding test fails.

Finally include polynomial induction
\[
[A(0,\vec z)\land\forall x(A(H(x),\vec z)\to A(x,\vec z))]
\to\forall x\,A(x,\vec z)
\]
for every quantifier-free \(L_{PV}\)-formula \(A\). Together with the base theory and the symbol axioms, these schemes define \(PV_1\) here. A proof is a finite derivation in classical first-order logic with equality from finitely many instances of these schemes. No true-universal arithmetic sentences, consistency assumptions, or external correctness axioms are added. The outer quantifier over unary symbols \(g\) ranges over their finite syntactic construction trees, not over an oracle for deciding which arbitrary programs run in polynomial time.

The SAT relation is fixed arithmetically, rather than by selecting an unspecified polynomial-time evaluator symbol. All abbreviations in this paragraph and below expand into formulas of the base language \(L\). Set \(\ell=\operatorname{len}(F)\), and define
\[
\operatorname{Bit}(x,i)\ \longleftrightarrow\
M(x,i)=2M(x,S(i))+1.
\]
Every auxiliary quantifier over a node, field, index or width is bounded by \(\ell\), with any smaller displayed bound imposed as a guard. Thus these quantifiers are sharply bounded. The one truth-table witness below has a separate bound.

The natural number \(F\) encodes an ordinary propositional formula tree whose nodes are numbered \(0,\ldots,m-1\), with children before their parents. Its variables are \(x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}\), with unused variables allowed. To define \(\operatorname{Form}(F,w,d,m)\), require \(w,d,m\le\ell\), \(w\ge2\), \(m\ge1\), \(w+d=\ell\), and
\[
\ell=w+2+(1+3m)w.
\]
The least significant \(w\) bits of \(F\) are all one and bit \(w\) is zero. Starting at bit \(w+1\) are \(1+3m\) fields of \(w\) bits, followed by the high sentinel bit one; the exact bit-length equality enforces that sentinel and forbids further bits. Put \(P=M(1\#F,d)\), whose intended value is \(2^w\). Field \(j\) has value \(r\) exactly when
\[
D(F,w,d,j,r)\ \longleftrightarrow\
r<P\ \land\
M(F,w+1+jw)=P\,M(F,w+1+(j+1)w)+r.
\]
Require field zero to have value \(m\). For each node \(i<m\), its fields \(1+3i,2+3i,3+3i\) have values \(\tau_i,u_i,v_i\), respectively. This notation abbreviates existentially quantified numbers at most \(\ell\) satisfying their three \(D\) relations, not new function symbols. Every record must satisfy exactly the relevant one of these four cases:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\tau_i & \text{record restrictions} & \text{meaning}\\
0 & u_i<m,\ v_i=0 & x_{u_i}\\
1 & u_i<i,\ v_i=0 & \neg\text{ child }u_i\\
2 & u_i<i,\ v_i<i & \text{child }u_i\land\text{child }v_i\\
3 & u_i<i,\ v_i<i & \text{child }u_i\lor\text{child }v_i .
\end{array}
\]
Every node \(i\) with \(S(i)<m\) must occur in exactly one child slot of all records, and the node \(r\) with \(S(r)=m\) in no child slot. Specifically, slot \((j,0)\) contains \(i\) when \(j<m,\tau_j\in\{1,2,3\},u_j=i\); slot \((j,1)\) contains \(i\) when \(j<m,\tau_j\in\{2,3\},v_j=i\). Denote this relation by \(C(j,s,i)\), with other slot values false. Exactly one means
\[
\exists j,s\le\ell\
[C(j,s,i)\land
\forall k,t\le\ell\,(C(k,t,i)\to(k=j\land t=s))].
\]
Together the record restrictions, field conditions and child-slot conditions define \(\operatorname{Form}\). In particular this encodes a tree, with no shared subtrees or circuit gates.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(F,a,v,w,d,m)\) by requiring, at every node \(i<m\), the following biconditional for the indicated record type:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\tau_i & \operatorname{Bit}(v,i)\text{ is equivalent to}\\
0 & \operatorname{Bit}(a,u_i)\\
1 & \neg\operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\\
2 & \operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\land\operatorname{Bit}(v,v_i)\\
3 & \operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\lor\operatorname{Bit}(v,v_i).
\end{array}
\]
Here \(v\) is the numeric table witness and \(v_i\) the second child field; their names designate different bound variables when the abbreviations are expanded. Now set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\ \longleftrightarrow\
\exists w,d,m,e\le\ell\ \exists v<1\#F\
[&\operatorname{Form}(F,w,d,m)\land e+m=\ell\\
 &\land a<M(1\#F,e)
 \land\operatorname{Eval}(F,a,v,w,d,m)\\
 &\land\exists r\le\ell\,(S(r)=m\land\operatorname{Bit}(v,r))].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a\) is an assignment of \(m\) bits, allowing leading zeroes, and the first \(m\) bits of \(v\) are the values of the formula nodes with true root. The bound \(1\#F\) is \(2^\ell\), so the table has only linearly many bits in the input bit length. Malformed formula codes make \(\operatorname{Sat}\) false. No unrestricted exponentiation symbol or semantic SAT predicate is added to the theory.

For each syntactically generated unary symbol \(g\), let
\[
\Phi_g=\forall F\,\forall a\,
(\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\to\operatorname{Sat}(F,g(F))).
\]
It asserts search correctness on every satisfiable formula. It imposes no required output on an unsatisfiable formula. The claim concerns absence of finite \(PV_1\) proofs of these sentences, not absence of semantically correct polynomial-time solvers as a separate assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that no generated unary symbol has a finite first-order derivation of its displayed SAT-search correctness sentence from the stated PV1 axioms, or a complete Lean proof of the negation, exhibiting a particular symbol and a valid finite derivation. The formalization must implement the stated syntactic theory and arithmetic SAT relation; any substitute SAT encoding or axiomatization must be proved to preserve the relevant provability claim. Neither assuming P differs from NP, adding all true universal arithmetic axioms, checking finitely many proofs, nor proving only a conditional statement settles this target.
cards.why: The question isolates whether reasoning restricted to efficiently computable concepts can certify a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-complete search task. It is a foundational test of the strength of feasible mathematics and separates the truth of an algorithmic assertion from the existence of a proof in a particular theory.

Open Problem 5.3 states this nonprovability schema using polynomial-time symbols and a standard SAT verifier. It is a formal weakening of the conjecture that polynomial-time algorithms cannot solve SAT: even if a solver existed, the theory might fail to prove its correctness. cards.title: Lovász–Schrijver simulation of Cutting Planes
cards.formal:
Does the basic Lovász–Schrijver system \(\mathrm{LS}\) polynomially simulate Cutting Planes \(\mathrm{CP}\) in the following real-coefficient, line-count sense?

There exist a real constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), every \(m\ge0\), every finite initial system
\[
\Phi=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}x_j\ge b_i:1\le i\le m\right\},
\qquad a_{ij},b_i\in\mathbb R,
\]
and every CP refutation \(\Pi\) of \(\Phi\), there is an LS refutation \(\Lambda\) of the same initial system satisfying
\[
|\Lambda|\le C\bigl(n+m+|\Pi|+1\bigr)^k.
\]
All variables are Boolean. The proof systems and the length measure are defined below. The constants are independent of the initial coefficients and both proofs.
cards.definitions:
A line is an inequality \(f(x)\ge0\). Polynomials are over \(\mathbb R\) in the original variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\); algebraically identical polynomials are identified by collecting coefficients. The initial lines are the members of \(\Phi\), written with the right-hand side moved to the left. Boolean axioms \(x_j\ge0\) and \(1-x_j\ge0\) are available. The harmless constant axioms \(0\ge0\) and \(1\ge0\) are also permitted; they can be derived from the Boolean axioms with constantly many steps.

Both systems permit nonnegative linear combination: from earlier lines \(f\ge0\) and \(g\ge0\), derive \(\alpha f+\beta g\ge0\) for any \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Coefficients are exact real numbers. Combining any finite number of earlier lines instead of two changes length by at most a polynomial factor, so the binary version fixes a definite convention.

CP contains only affine-linear lines. Its additional rounding rule is
\[
\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_jx_j\ge d}
{\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_jx_j\ge\lceil d\rceil},
\qquad c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb Z,\ d\in\mathbb R.
\]
The rounding premise must have integer variable coefficients; the right side and intermediate combination coefficients may be real. Rounding is justified by the Boolean, hence integer, values of the variables.

Basic LS contains lines of degree at most two. In addition to the common rules and axioms it permits both \(x_j^2-x_j\ge0\) and \(x_j-x_j^2\ge0\). From an earlier affine-linear inequality \(f\ge0\), it may derive \(x_jf\ge0\), or \((1-x_j)f\ge0\), as one line each. Multiplication is permitted only for an affine-linear premise. Nonnegative combination may combine linear or quadratic lines. The source’s linear weakening rule \(a\cdot x\ge d\Rightarrow a\cdot x\ge d'\) for \(d'\le d\) is permitted; it is also obtainable by adding a nonnegative multiple of \(1\ge0\). There is no unrestricted multiplication rule, no rule freely adding arbitrary squares, and no rounding rule in LS. Boolean reduction of quadratic monomials must be justified by the displayed axioms; equality merely on Boolean assignments is not free algebraic rewriting.

A refutation is a finite sequence of justified lines ending with \(-1\ge0\), equivalently \(0\ge1\). Any negative constant conclusion can be normalized by a positive scalar in one further step. An earlier line may be used any number of times: proofs are directed acyclic graphs, not necessarily trees. There are no auxiliary extension variables. Length \(|\Pi|\) is the number of listed lines, counting each occurrence of an initial inequality or axiom that appears, and each derived line. Reuse adds no copy unless a new line is written.

No bound is imposed on the magnitude or bit representation of real coefficients, and no effective transformation from \(\Pi\) to \(\Lambda\) is requested. The statement quantifies mathematically over finite systems of real inequalities; its size parameters count variables, initial inequalities and proof lines. This is the convention, not a bit-size or polynomial-time simulation assertion.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the uniform polynomial line-count assertion. A positive answer must prove the existence of the LS refutation bound for every allowed CP refutation and initial system. A negative answer must show that every candidate polynomial bound fails for some allowed initial system and CP proof. A lower bound restricted to tree-like LS, a simulation only with restricted coefficients, or the already known separation in the opposite direction does not decide this statement. No numerical \(1/100\) tolerance applies to this binary assertion.
cards.why: Cutting Planes derives integer consequences by rounding, while LS derives consequences using Boolean identities and quadratic inequalities. Establishing or separating their remaining simulation direction would clarify whether the latter rules can always match concise arguments based on rounding. The known reverse separation makes this a concrete boundary between major proof systems.

cards.context:
An inconsistent zero-one system has no assignment of zeros and ones satisfying all its inequalities. A refutation proves this by deriving an impossible inequality. Two complete systems may both refute every inconsistent system while requiring very different numbers of steps.

The systems exploit integrality differently. CP rounds a lower bound upward when its left side is integer-valued. LS uses products with a variable or its Boolean complement, together with the identities for zero-one values. Keeping all intermediate degrees at most two is part of the basic LS model.

The paper gives systems with polynomially many LS proof lines but superpolynomial CP length. Therefore CP cannot polynomially simulate LS. That theorem addresses the opposite direction from this card and does not show whether LS always matches short CP proofs.

Pitassi and Segerlind separate tree-like LS+, even with extra square axioms, from tree-like CP. In a tree proof a derived result cannot be shared freely between branches. The present target permits sharing through a general directed acyclic graph, so the tree restriction is material.

Counting lines ignores the cost of writing or manipulating their coefficients. The formulation uses this measure with real coefficients. A proof of an efficient algorithm translating finite rational encodings would be a stronger kind of result; this card requires only the quantified existence of short proofs.

The September 2026 hereditary-property paper studies how geometric cutting-plane closures interact with faces of convex sets. Properties of closure rounds and faces do not by themselves bound the length of a DAG refutation in the specified syntactic systems. Its abstract contains no resolution of this simulation question.
