cards.title: Polynomial resolution length from logarithmic clause space
cards.formal:
Does logarithmic clause space imply polynomial refutation length for every fixed input clause width in general resolution?

Precisely, for every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and real constant \(a>0\), do there exist constants \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), depending only on \(k,a\), such that every unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\) satisfies
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(F)\le B\,N(F)^d?\]
Here \(N(F)=2+|F|+\sum_{C\in F}|C|\) is formula size, \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\) is the minimum number of clauses simultaneously retained in a resolution refutation, and \(L(F)\) is its minimum number of axiom downloads and inference steps. These two minima are taken independently over all general resolution refutations. The short refutation whose existence is requested has no space restriction.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, and a clause is a finite set of literals interpreted as their disjunction. Clauses contain no repeated literal and no complementary pair \(x,\neg x\). The empty clause \(\bot\) is false. A CNF formula is a finite set of clauses interpreted as their conjunction; it is unsatisfiable if no assignment to its variables makes every clause true. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals in every input clause. The fixed input-width parameter \(k\) does not bound clauses derived during a proof.

The variable universe for a proof is the finite set of variables occurring in \(F\). Renaming these variables has no cost. The size \(N(F)\) counts input clauses and literal occurrences, with the added constant two ensuring that its logarithm is positive. Input clauses are a set, so padding by duplicate clauses does not change the formula or its size. If a concrete binary encoding is needed, number the occurring variables consecutively, encode each literal by its index and sign, and list clauses with delimiters. For fixed \(k\), this encoding and the stated combinatorial size are polynomially related; the logarithmic-space versus polynomial-length question is invariant under this choice of size convention.

A resolution refutation is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal D_0,\ldots,\mathcal D_T\), each a set of clauses over the input variables. Initially \(\mathcal D_0=\varnothing\), and the final configuration contains \(\bot\). Each step performs exactly one of the following operations. It may download one input clause \(C\in F\) into memory, adding it to the current set. It may erase one currently retained clause. It may add a resolvent \(C\cup D\) from two currently retained premises \(C\cup\{x\}\) and \(D\cup\{\neg x\}\), where neither \(C\) nor \(D\) contains the pivot variable and the resolvent is non-tautological. It may also weaken a retained clause by adding literals, provided the result is a clause over the same variables. These are the ordinary syntactic resolution and weakening rules. Arbitrary semantic consequence is not an additional inference rule.

Premises must be present before an inference, and they remain present after it unless erased in subsequent steps. An inference adds its conclusion before any such erasure, so the temporary memory needed to hold the conclusion is counted. An erased clause must be downloaded or derived again before reuse. The input formula itself is available for downloads without occupying working memory. Resolution proofs may share intermediate results arbitrarily; neither the tree-like restriction nor the regularity restriction forbidding repeated pivots on a proof path is imposed. No extension variables, stronger proof rules, randomization or error are allowed.

For a refutation \(\pi\), define
\[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}|\mathcal D_t|,\]
and let \(L(\pi)\) be its number of axiom-download and inference steps, with repetitions counted. Erasures are not counted in length. One can instead count all steps without changing polynomial-length bounds, because useful erasures can be bounded by the number of additions. Clause space counts each stored clause as one object regardless of its width. It is different from total literal space \(\max_t\sum_{C\in\mathcal D_t}|C|\), from the number of distinct variables in memory, and from the number of stored bits.

For an unsatisfiable formula, resolution completeness guarantees that the following finite integer minima exist:
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}\operatorname{Sp}(\pi),\qquad L(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}L(\pi).\]
The refutation attaining the first minimum may have very large length. The question is whether a possibly different refutation of polynomial length must nevertheless exist whenever that minimum space is logarithmic.

The full quantifier order is \(\forall k\ge1\;\forall a>0\;\exists B>0,d\ge1\;\forall F\). The exponent \(d\) may depend on the input-width bound and the constant multiplying the logarithm, but not on the individual formula or its size. The proposition does not demand one exponent uniform in all \(k,a\), a procedure finding the short proof, or a transformation that keeps the original space bound.

A negative answer means that for some fixed \(k\) and \(a>0\), no polynomial bounds the minimum length throughout this class: for every \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), some unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF \(F\) has \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\) but \(L(F)>B N(F)^d\). Thus it must establish genuinely superpolynomial unrestricted resolution length despite the small-space refutation. Merely proving that all proofs which retain small space are long does not refute the proposition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified implication. A positive answer must establish a polynomial length bound for all promised formulas, with its dependence on fixed \(k,a\) explicit or provably existent. A negative answer must prove the stated logical negation against all polynomial length bounds, including unrestricted-space refutations. A quasipolynomial upper bound, a theorem for constant clause space only, a result for tree-like resolution only, or a simultaneous length–space tradeoff does not settle the target. The statement is an exact asymptotic proposition; additive numerical tolerance is inapplicable.
cards.why: The question asks whether a resolution proof that can be checked with only logarithmically many retained clauses necessarily has a short certificate somewhere in the same proof system. Resolving it would sharpen the relation between proof memory and proof length beyond the known constant-space case, without conflating proof existence with an efficient search algorithm.

cards.context:
Resolution combines clauses to certify that a Boolean formula is inconsistent. Its proof length is a basic lower bound on the work needed by resolution-based proof search, while clause space records how many learned facts must be retained together.

The memory measure here treats a clause as one object even when it is long. This makes logarithmic clause space fundamentally different from logarithmic bit space of an ordinary machine computation; a small number of clauses may encode many bits.

For constant-width input CNFs, the known space-to-width relation and the width counting bound imply \(L(F)\le N(F)^{O(\operatorname{Sp}(F)+k)}\). In particular, constant clause space implies polynomial length, whereas logarithmic clause space gives only a quasipolynomial bound \(N(F)^{O(\log N(F))}\). The question asks whether that remaining gap can always be removed.

The reverse implication behaves differently: the survey documents families with short refutations but large minimum clause space. Those examples do not decide whether small clause space forces short refutations.

A simultaneous-resource question asks whether a single proof can be both short and economical in memory. This card asks only whether a short proof exists at all. A tradeoff forcing a memory-limited proof to be long is compatible with a polynomial proof that uses more memory.

The 2023 work organizes connections among clause space, other space measures and tree-like proof size, and leaves major simultaneous-resource questions open in its concluding section. Those developments supply recent structural context but are not a solution or a newly restated confirmation of the precise logarithmic-space implication in this card.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

cards.context:
Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.

Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.

progress.text: Lovász and Saks pose the relation between real matrix rank and deterministic communication, as traced in the checked source papers.
Lovett establishes the general upper bound \(O(\sqrt r\log(r+2))\), substantially improving the linear-rank upper bounds.
Göös, Pitassi and Watson prove a nearly quadratic lower bound in log-rank. Their Theorem 2 first concerns one-sided partition number, with the real-rank consequence stated separately.
Sudakov and Tomon obtain \(D(f)=O(\sqrt{r(f)})\). The preprint dates from November 2023, the article appeared online in July 2024, and the journal volume is dated 2025.

Song reports \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) for an explicit construction. This is a preprint claim with a specific quantitative comparison, not an independently verified catalogue assertion of the strongest bound over all constructions.
The checked third revision of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley proves the signed-rectangle decomposition theorem and equivalent formulations, and explicitly retains the general conjecture as open.

The conjecture asks whether their minimum worst-case deterministic communication is bounded by one universal polynomial in logarithmic real matrix rank.
The protocol may use arbitrary interaction and local computation, but all input pairs must be handled correctly.
A refutation must defeat every universal polynomial, rather than a single proposed constant or exponent.
Known square-root-rank upper bounds, nearly quadratic logarithmic lower bounds and signed-partition equivalences leave the central gap unresolved.

cards.title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist one finite real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every positive integer \(n\) and every function \(f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}\), \[H(f)\le C I(f),\] where \(H(f)\) is the Shannon entropy in bits of the squared Fourier spectrum and \(I(f)\) is total influence for uniformly distributed inputs? The same \(C\) must work for all dimensions and all Boolean functions.
cards.definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and give each \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) probability \(2^{-n}\). For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\), with empty product one, and \[\widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x),\qquad q_S=\widehat f(S)^2.\] These are real coefficients and \(\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}q_S=1\). Define \(\eta(0)=0\) and \(\eta(t)=t\log_2(1/t)\) for \(0<t\le1\), where \(\log_2 t=\ln t/\ln2\). Then \[H(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\eta(q_S).\] The sum includes the empty set and is not conditioned on nonempty spectral subsets or divided by the variance. For each \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) negate coordinate \(i\) and retain all other coordinates. Set \[I_i(f)=2^{-n}\bigl|\{x\in\{-1,1\}^n:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}\bigr|,\qquad I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n I_i(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|q_S.\] Influence uses an actual bit flip, with no additional probability of leaving that coordinate unchanged. All scalar Boolean functions are allowed; no balance, monotonicity, circuit-size, degree or efficient-computability promise is imposed. Constant functions satisfy \(H(f)=I(f)=0\). The inequality is non-strict, so it includes them.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal inequality for some positive finite constant, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must use the specified uniform measure, full squared spectrum, base-two Shannon entropy and total bit-flip influence for every \(n\) and every scalar Boolean function. A negative proof must establish \[\forall C>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\},\quad H(f)>C I(f).\] The dimension and function may depend on \(C\); equivalently, the entropy-to-influence ratios of nonconstant Boolean functions must be unbounded. Defeating one numerical constant or checking finitely many truth tables is insufficient. No optimal value of \(C\), algorithm for finding counterexamples or numerical approximation is required.
cards.why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.

cards.context:
A Fourier coefficient records correlation with a parity of selected input bits. Squaring these correlations gives a probability distribution on subsets of the coordinates. Its Shannon entropy measures dispersion among subsets; total influence is the expected cardinality of a subset from that distribution. The conjecture asks whether being the spectrum of a Boolean-valued function forces a universal linear relation between these two quantities.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy \(\log _{2} n\) but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function \(g(x)=(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/\sqrt{n}\), which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

If FEI holds with constant \(C\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\), some family \(\mathcal T\) of at most \(2^{CI(f)/\delta}\) subsets satisfies \(\sum_{S\notin\mathcal T}q_S\le\delta\). Equivalently, retaining those Fourier coefficients approximates \(f\) with mean squared error at most \(\delta\) under the uniform measure. The support bound depends on the accuracy parameter; a guarantee independent of accuracy is not being asserted.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou prove FEI for symmetric Boolean functions, which are invariant under every permutation of coordinates, and for read-once decision trees, where the variables used in the two branches at each query are disjoint. The read-once condition is stronger than merely avoiding a repeated query along each path. Their application to a disjunction of \(m\ge2\) conjunctions of literals uses \(I(f)=O(\log m)\): FEI would give concentration on \(m^{O(1/\delta)}\) Fourier coefficients for each fixed error \(\delta\). This is a version of Mansour’s conjecture, not its stronger proposed logarithmic dependence on inverse error. It concerns uniform-measure spectral concentration and the associated query-learning setting.

Han’s Theorem 1 bounds \(H(f)\) by an absolute constant times \(I(f)+\sum_i I_i(f)\log_2(1/I_i(f))\), with zero terms when \(I_i(f)=0\). The journal version appeared online on 20 December 2024 in Combinatorica volume 45 (2025). The 10 December 2025 arXiv revision adds an acknowledgement of related prior work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. The extra coordinate-entropy term can exceed a constant times total influence, so this bound leaves FEI open.

The earlier Keller–Mossel–Schlank paper already gives \(H(f)\le\sum_i h_2(I_i(f))\) in Claim 4.1, where \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) with zero endpoint terms. The claim supplies the same general kind of coordinate-entropy control and applies beyond Boolean-valued spectra after normalization. This is why a later proof or refinement of that weaker bound must be distinguished from resolving FEI. Min-entropy, \(-\log_2\max_S q_S\), concerns just the largest coefficient and is a different, weaker target than Shannon entropy.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s revision of 9 June 2026 reports FEI for the defined \(\delta\)-tribes class and for classes with recursive separation properties. The separation theorems retain hypotheses on their terminal functions and constants; they are not assertions for all monotone functions or unrestricted decision trees. The paper also exhibits failure of a stronger inequality involving a prescribed splitting coordinate. Those examples satisfy FEI, so that failure is not a counterexample to this card’s target.

Slote’s 2 August 2026 preprint reports a counterexample to the quantum extension, whose inputs are Hermitian unitary operators and whose coefficients come from tensor products of Pauli matrices. Theorems 1 and 5 give operators supported on degree-\(d\) Pauli terms with entropy \(\Theta(d^2)\) and influence \(d\). Classical Boolean functions form a restricted diagonal case of that operator setting. The operators constructed in the theorem therefore do not supply scalar Boolean counterexamples. The full new construction was not independently verified in this review.

A follow-up by Slote, Volberg and Zhang, revised 6 August 2026, also treats quantum counterexamples. Its §6.6 reports Hermitian involutions with total influence below two and spectral entropy \(\log_2 n+O(1)\) in its family parameter. The underlying auxiliary scalar functions take complex values of modulus one, rather than only the real values \(-1\) and \(1\). That domain change is essential, and §6 still describes classical FEI as open. These theorem scopes were checked without independently certifying the full proofs.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.

If FEI holds with constant \(C\), then for every \(0<\delta<1\), some family \(\mathcal T\) of at most \(2^{CI(f)/\delta}\) subsets satisfies \(\sum_{S\notin\mathcal T}q_S\le\delta\). Equivalently, retaining those Fourier coefficients approximates \(f\) with mean squared error at most \(\delta\) under the uniform measure. The support bound depends on the accuracy parameter; a guarantee independent of accuracy is not being asserted.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou prove FEI for symmetric Boolean functions, which are invariant under every permutation of coordinates, and for read-once decision trees, where the variables used in the two branches at each query are disjoint. The read-once condition is stronger than merely avoiding a repeated query along each path. Their application to a disjunction of \(m\ge2\) conjunctions of literals uses \(I(f)=O(\log m)\): FEI would give concentration on \(m^{O(1/\delta)}\) Fourier coefficients for each fixed error \(\delta\). This is a version of Mansour’s conjecture, not its stronger proposed logarithmic dependence on inverse error. It concerns uniform-measure spectral concentration and the associated query-learning setting.

Han’s Theorem 1 bounds \(H(f)\) by an absolute constant times \(I(f)+\sum_i I_i(f)\log_2(1/I_i(f))\), with zero terms when \(I_i(f)=0\). The journal version appeared online on 20 December 2024 in Combinatorica volume 45 (2025). The 10 December 2025 arXiv revision adds an acknowledgement of related prior work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. The extra coordinate-entropy term can exceed a constant times total influence, so this bound leaves FEI open.

The earlier Keller–Mossel–Schlank paper already gives \(H(f)\le\sum_i h_2(I_i(f))\) in Claim 4.1, where \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) with zero endpoint terms. The claim supplies the same general kind of coordinate-entropy control and applies beyond Boolean-valued spectra after normalization. This is why a later proof or refinement of that weaker bound must be distinguished from resolving FEI. Min-entropy, \(-\log_2\max_S q_S\), concerns just the largest coefficient and is a different, weaker target than Shannon entropy.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s revision of 9 June 2026 reports FEI for the defined \(\delta\)-tribes class and for classes with recursive separation properties. The separation theorems retain hypotheses on their terminal functions and constants; they are not assertions for all monotone functions or unrestricted decision trees. The paper also exhibits failure of a stronger inequality involving a prescribed splitting coordinate. Those examples satisfy FEI, so that failure is not a counterexample to this card’s target.

Slote’s 2 August 2026 preprint reports a counterexample to the quantum extension, whose inputs are Hermitian unitary operators and whose coefficients come from tensor products of Pauli matrices. Theorems 1 and 5 give operators supported on degree-\(d\) Pauli terms with entropy \(\Theta(d^2)\) and influence \(d\). Classical Boolean functions form a restricted diagonal case of that operator setting. The operators constructed in the theorem therefore do not supply scalar Boolean counterexamples. The full new construction was not independently verified in this review.

A follow-up by Slote, Volberg and Zhang, revised 6 August 2026, also treats quantum counterexamples. Its §6.6 reports Hermitian involutions with total influence below two and spectral entropy \(\log_2 n+O(1)\) in its family parameter. The underlying auxiliary scalar functions take complex values of modulus one, rather than only the real values \(-1\) and \(1\). That domain change is essential, and §6 still describes classical FEI as open. These theorem scopes were checked without independently certifying the full proofs.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.

cards.status_note: Open in the checked classical primary literature, explicitly reiterated in both August 2026 quantum papers. Bounded searches and version checks through 15 September 2026 found no proof or refutation of the universal scalar Boolean Shannon-entropy inequality. The June separated classes impose extra hypotheses, the coordinate-entropy estimates retain an extra term, and the August counterexamples are operator-valued or use non-Boolean complex phases. Li–Han’s December 2025 weaker-bound preprint was withdrawn for prior appearance of its result. Complete new preprint proofs were not independently verified.

cards.title: Mansour’s conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal:
Does there exist an absolute real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), integer \(s\ge2\), function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, and real \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\), there is a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) for which
\[
 |\mathcal F|\le\left\lceil s^{C\log_2(1/\varepsilon)}\right\rceil,
 \qquad
 \sum_{S\subseteq[n],\ S\notin\mathcal F}\widehat f(S)^2\le\varepsilon?
\]
The coefficients are the ordinary Walsh–Fourier coefficients under the uniform distribution. The same constant \(C\) must work for every dimension, term count, formula and accuracy.
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(2^{[n]}\) be its set of subsets. A literal is either the condition \(x_i=1\) or the condition \(x_i=-1\). A term is a conjunction of literals; a disjunctive normal form (DNF) is an OR of terms. Its represented function has value \(+1\) when at least one term is satisfied and \(-1\) otherwise. The number of terms, rather than the total number of literal occurrences, is the size parameter \(s\). Each term may contain any number of variables; variables may occur in arbitrarily many terms, and terms may overlap. Empty conjunctions and an empty disjunction have their usual constant meanings. The statement asks only for existence of some representation with at most \(s\) terms.

For every \(S\subseteq[n]\), define the parity character and its coefficient by
\[
 \chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_i,\qquad \chi_{\varnothing}(x)=1,
 \qquad
 \widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x).
\]
These characters form an orthonormal basis for real functions on the uniform Boolean cube, with inner product \(\mathbb E[g(X)h(X)]\) for uniform \(X\). In particular,
\[
 f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat f(S)\chi_S(x),
 \qquad \sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat f(S)^2=1.
\]
The empty-set coefficient is included in these sums and may belong to \(\mathcal F\).

Keeping the coefficients indexed by \(\mathcal F\) gives the real multilinear polynomial
\[
 g_{\mathcal F}(x)=\sum_{S\in\mathcal F}\widehat f(S)\chi_S(x),
\]
whose mean squared error is exactly
\[
 \mathbb E[(f(X)-g_{\mathcal F}(X))^2]
   =\sum_{S\notin\mathcal F}\widehat f(S)^2.
\]
Thus \(\varepsilon\) measures discarded squared Fourier mass, without an additional normalization factor. The approximant need not be Boolean-valued. The bound concerns the number of retained characters, not their maximum degree, pointwise error or disagreement probability.

The family \(\mathcal F\) may depend on the function and on \(\varepsilon\). No efficient algorithm for discovering it, producing the coefficients or learning the function is required. There is no promise on a DNF’s read number, which is the maximum number of its terms containing any one variable, and no random distribution on formulas. The only input distribution in the approximation is uniform on \(\{-1,1\}^n\).

This is the strong accuracy-dependent form of the conjecture. Allowing \(s^{K(\varepsilon)}\) characters for an arbitrary function \(K\) of the error would be a weaker target. Here that exponent must be bounded by one constant times \(\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\), uniformly even when \(\varepsilon\) decreases with \(n\) or \(s\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed statement with one universal \(C\), or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation.

A negative answer must show that for every \(C>0\) there are admissible \(n,s,\varepsilon,f\) for which every family of at most \(\lceil s^{C\log_2(1/\varepsilon)}\rceil\) characters leaves discarded squared mass greater than \(\varepsilon\). Defeating only one proposed constant does not refute existence of another. A theorem only for random DNFs, bounded-read formulas, fixed width or a different input distribution does not cover the target. A polynomial concentration bound with unspecified dependence of its exponent on \(\varepsilon\) establishes only the weaker form. This is an exact universal proposition; the benchmark’s numerical \(1/100\) tolerance is not a replacement for its full range of error parameters.
cards.why: A fundamental bridge between short logical formulas, sparse spectral representations, and learning with queries. The strong accuracy parameter makes the question a precise test of how much analytic structure small DNF size forces.

cards.title: Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal:
Does there exist a positive integer \(C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\), every integer \(1\le d\le n\), and every real multilinear polynomial \(f\) in \(n\) variables of degree at most \(d\),
\[\bigl[\forall x\in\{-1,1\}^n,\ 0\le f(x)\le1\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists i\in[n]:\ \operatorname{Inf}_i(f)\ge\left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f)}d\right)^C?\]
Variance and squared \(L_2\) influence use the uniform distribution on the entire Boolean cube, with the normalization below. The same exponent \(C\) must work for all dimensions, degrees, coefficients and variances.
cards.definitions:
Polynomials and domain. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j\) for \(S\subseteq[n]\), with \(\chi_{\varnothing}=1\). A real multilinear polynomial is a finite sum
\[f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}a_S\chi_S(x),\qquad a_S\in\mathbb R.\]
Multilinear means that each variable has exponent at most one in each monomial. Degree at most \(d\) means \(a_S=0\) whenever \(|S|>d\). The range restriction \(0\le f(x)\le1\) is required at every one of the \(2^n\) sign vectors. No range condition away from this cube is imposed.

Uniform averages and Fourier coefficients. For any real-valued function \(h\) on the cube, define \(\mathbb E h=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}h(x)\). The characters \(\chi_S\) give the unique multilinear representation on the cube, with
\[\widehat f(S)=\mathbb E[f(x)\chi_S(x)]=a_S.\]
In particular \(\widehat f(\varnothing)=\mathbb Ef\). Variance is
\[\operatorname{Var}(f)=\mathbb E[(f-\mathbb Ef)^2]=\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq[n]}\widehat f(S)^2.\]
For the stated range, \(0\le\operatorname{Var}(f)\le1/4\).

Influence. Let \(x^{\oplus i}\) be obtained from \(x\) by negating its \(i\)-th coordinate and leaving all others fixed. Set
\[D_if(x)=\frac{f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i})}{2},\qquad \operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=\mathbb E[(D_if)^2]=\frac14\mathbb E[(f(x)-f(x^{\oplus i}))^2]=\sum_{S\ni i}\widehat f(S)^2.\]
This is a mean squared difference, not the probability that the two function values differ, their mean absolute difference, or the maximum change over inputs. All sums and expectations in the target use this same uniform measure.

Scope and quantifiers. Coefficients are arbitrary real numbers, without a rationality, description-length or computability restriction. The statement is an existence inequality, not a demand for an algorithm finding the coordinate. The coordinate may depend on the whole polynomial. No sparsity, block decomposition, common coefficient magnitude, Boolean-output, nonnegativity-of-coefficients or realizability-by-quantum-algorithms promise is present. There is no positive lower threshold on variance. Constant polynomials have zero variance and all influences zero, so every coordinate satisfies the inequality for them. The degree parameter is a positive upper bound, so division by zero never occurs.

Normalization of the exponent. Allowing any real \(C\ge1\) gives an equivalent assertion: for \(0\le v/d\le1/4\), increasing the exponent to a positive integer only decreases the right-hand side. A bound of the usual form \(c\,\operatorname{Var}(f)^a/d^b\), with fixed positive constants \(c,a,b\), also yields this formulation after increasing \(C\). Thus the one-exponent statement records polynomial dependence without selecting a particular best exponent or a hidden constant depending on \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must prove one exponent works simultaneously for every allowed \(n,d,f\), including arbitrarily small positive variance. No optimal exponent or algorithm for computing an influential coordinate is required.

A negative answer must prove that for every positive integer \(C\) there exist integers \(n\ge1\), \(1\le d\le n\), and an admissible polynomial of positive variance such that
\[\forall i\in[n],\quad\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)<\left(\frac{\operatorname{Var}(f)}d\right)^C.\]
The dimension, degree and polynomial may depend on \(C\). A rigorously specified family with those properties qualifies; a counterexample to just one proposed exponent does not negate the existence of another universal exponent. Numerical estimates must be certified strongly enough to establish the exact pointwise range and strict influence inequalities they assert.

A theorem only for Boolean-valued outputs, completely bounded forms, boundedly many quantum-query rounds, or a positive fraction of randomly restricted functions does not by itself cover the full polynomial class. An exponential dependence on degree is also weaker than the requested polynomial bound. This is a yes-or-no conjecture with an exact inequality, not a numerical target subject to additive 1/100 tolerance.
cards.why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.

cards.context:
A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider \(f(x)=1/2+(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/(2n)\). This degree-one polynomial always lies in \([0,1]\), but \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=1/(4n)\) and each coordinate has influence \(1/(4n^{2})\). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

A \(t\)-query quantum algorithm has acceptance probability represented on the Boolean cube by a real polynomial of degree at most \(2t\), with values in \([0,1]\). Aaronson and Ambainis prove that the influence conjecture would imply a classical estimate of this probability within additive \(\varepsilon\) on at least a \(1-\eta\) fraction of uniformly distributed inputs using \(\operatorname{poly}(t,1/\varepsilon,1/\eta)\) queries. The classical algorithm may depend on the quantum algorithm. This gives a concrete reason why a dimension-independent inequality for bounded polynomials matters to quantum computation.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

Complete boundedness imposes more than scalar boundedness. In a block-multilinear polynomial, each monomial contains at most one variable from each of several fixed blocks. Replace variables by square matrix contractions, meaning matrices whose Euclidean operator norm is at most one, and multiply factors in block order. The completely bounded norm is the supremum of the resulting operator norm over all such matrices and dimensions. Requiring this norm to be at most one can support influential-variable theorems, but it is an extra hypothesis not imposed on the polynomials in this card.

The published ITCS 2025 restriction theorem assumes \(d\ge2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\ge1/d\). Each coordinate is independently left free with probability \(\log(d)/(C_1d)\), and otherwise fixed to an independent uniform sign. For universal positive constants \(C_1,C_2\), the resulting function has a coordinate with influence at least \(\operatorname{Var}(f)^2/d^{C_2}\) with probability at least \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\log(d)/(50C_1d)\). These are influences of the restricted function. The March 2026 revision retains both the restriction and original-variance assumptions; it does not establish the unrestricted claim.

Blanc, Docter, Strassle and Tan’s August 2026 theorem concerns quantum query rounds. A round applies parallel input queries between input-independent operations; the number \(r\) of rounds is distinct from the total \(t\) queries and from polynomial degree. Their classical query bound is \(2^{O(r^2)}(t\log(1/\eta)/\varepsilon)^{O(r)}\) for approximation error \(\varepsilon\) outside an \(\eta\) fraction of inputs. This is polynomial for fixed \(r\), but its exponent is not uniform over an unbounded number of rounds. The theorem neither treats every scalar bounded polynomial nor proves the full influential-variable conjecture.

The September 2026 theorem gives \(\sum_i\sqrt{\operatorname{Inf}_i(a)}\le t\|a\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\) for a polynomial with \(t\) blocks, summed over all variables. The constant is optimal, and the result permits nonadaptive classical queries in the associated restricted simulation. The authors expressly retain the unrestricted scalar conjecture as open. A small scalar norm does not supply the completely bounded norm hypothesis, so this sharper inequality is not a general resolution.

The 2019 Keller–Klein preprint once claimed a general proof, but the authors withdrew it on 2 December after a flaw in Lemma 5.3 invalidated the argument. The original abstract still contains the affirmative claim; its withdrawal notice is the controlling status information. It is not evidence that the conjecture has been established.

It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

A \(t\)-query quantum algorithm has acceptance probability represented on the Boolean cube by a real polynomial of degree at most \(2t\), with values in \([0,1]\). Aaronson and Ambainis prove that the influence conjecture would imply a classical estimate of this probability within additive \(\varepsilon\) on at least a \(1-\eta\) fraction of uniformly distributed inputs using \(\operatorname{poly}(t,1/\varepsilon,1/\eta)\) queries. The classical algorithm may depend on the quantum algorithm. This gives a concrete reason why a dimension-independent inequality for bounded polynomials matters to quantum computation.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

Complete boundedness imposes more than scalar boundedness. In a block-multilinear polynomial, each monomial contains at most one variable from each of several fixed blocks. Replace variables by square matrix contractions, meaning matrices whose Euclidean operator norm is at most one, and multiply factors in block order. The completely bounded norm is the supremum of the resulting operator norm over all such matrices and dimensions. Requiring this norm to be at most one can support influential-variable theorems, but it is an extra hypothesis not imposed on the polynomials in this card.

The published ITCS 2025 restriction theorem assumes \(d\ge2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\ge1/d\). Each coordinate is independently left free with probability \(\log(d)/(C_1d)\), and otherwise fixed to an independent uniform sign. For universal positive constants \(C_1,C_2\), the resulting function has a coordinate with influence at least \(\operatorname{Var}(f)^2/d^{C_2}\) with probability at least \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\log(d)/(50C_1d)\). These are influences of the restricted function. The March 2026 revision retains both the restriction and original-variance assumptions; it does not establish the unrestricted claim.

Blanc, Docter, Strassle and Tan’s August 2026 theorem concerns quantum query rounds. A round applies parallel input queries between input-independent operations; the number \(r\) of rounds is distinct from the total \(t\) queries and from polynomial degree. Their classical query bound is \(2^{O(r^2)}(t\log(1/\eta)/\varepsilon)^{O(r)}\) for approximation error \(\varepsilon\) outside an \(\eta\) fraction of inputs. This is polynomial for fixed \(r\), but its exponent is not uniform over an unbounded number of rounds. The theorem neither treats every scalar bounded polynomial nor proves the full influential-variable conjecture.

The September 2026 theorem gives \(\sum_i\sqrt{\operatorname{Inf}_i(a)}\le t\|a\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\) for a polynomial with \(t\) blocks, summed over all variables. The constant is optimal, and the result permits nonadaptive classical queries in the associated restricted simulation. The authors expressly retain the unrestricted scalar conjecture as open. A small scalar norm does not supply the completely bounded norm hypothesis, so this sharper inequality is not a general resolution.

The 2019 Keller–Klein preprint once claimed a general proof, but the authors withdrew it on 2 December after a flaw in Lemma 5.3 invalidated the argument. The original abstract still contains the affirmative claim; its withdrawal notice is the controlling status information. It is not evidence that the conjecture has been established.

source_formulation.text: The inherited ITCS 2025 Conjecture 4 and Aaronson–Ambainis’s original Conjecture 6 ask for polynomially large influence in terms of variance and inverse degree. The original source uses the bit cube and omits the factor 1/4 in its influence; changing cube coordinates preserves degree and this fixed normalization factor is absorbed by the unspecified exponent. Restricting the exponent to positive integers is equivalent, not an additional mathematical restriction.

cards.title: Interactive compression with logarithmic input-length overhead
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) such that every two-party protocol \(\pi\) on \(n\)-bit inputs, under every joint input distribution \(\mu\), has a simulation \(\rho\) with distributional error at most \(1/100\) and worst-case communication at most
\[
K\bigl(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1\bigr)\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil\quad\text{bits}?
\]
Here \(n\ge1\), the protocol and simulation model, internal information cost \(I_{\mu}\), and joint-transcript error are defined below. There is no restriction on the finite communication cost of \(\pi\), and \(K\) must be independent of \(n,\mu,\pi\).

This is an explicitly selected editorial version of the source's proposed logarithmic-loss question. The source's surrounding paragraph concerns two-party internal information, despite the article's multiparty title. It already reports that compression without an overhead is impossible. The particular logarithmic factor, constant error, additive regularization and worst-case transcript-simulation guarantee below are specified here rather than attributed verbatim to its informal sentence.
cards.definitions:
Alice has \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), Bob has \(y\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), and the pair \((X,Y)\) has an arbitrary probability distribution \(\mu\) on this finite product. The inputs may be correlated. Both parties know \(n\), the description of \(\pi\) and \(\mu\). Neither party is initially given the other party's realized input. No promise is placed on the support of \(\mu\).

A protocol uses one finite string \(R\) of shared fair random bits and two finite strings \(R_A,R_B\) of private fair random bits. The three strings are mutually independent and independent of \((X,Y)\). Their finite lengths may depend on the protocol and are not charged as communication. A length of zero is allowed. For each fixed public string, the protocol is a finite rooted binary communication tree: every internal node designates Alice or Bob, and the selected player sends one bit determined by their own input, private string, public string and the earlier messages. That bit selects the next child. A leaf terminates communication. The owner of the next message and termination are therefore determined by the public string and common message history, rather than by an uncharged timing channel. The transcript of communicated bits is \(M\), and the augmented transcript is \(T=(R,M)\). Both parties observe every communicated bit. A protocol is defined on every input pair and every coin choice. Its worst-case communication \(\operatorname{CC}(\pi)\) is the maximum number of transmitted bits over all these executions; it is finite but may be arbitrarily large.

All local computation, protocol descriptions and shared randomness are free. There is no restriction on the number of rounds or the local running time, and no privacy requirement. No advice depending on the other party's realized private input or quantum resources are supplied; all initial resources are exactly those specified above. Protocols for different \(n,\mu,\pi\) may be unrelated. This is an existence statement about finite communication protocols, not an efficient compiler for producing one from a table of \(\mu\).

For a finite random variable \(U\), its base-two Shannon entropy is
\[
H(U)=-\sum_{u}\Pr[U=u]\log_2\Pr[U=u],
\]
where \(0\log_2 0=0\). Conditional entropy \(H(U\mid V)\) is the average of \(H(U\mid V=v)\) weighted by \(\Pr[V=v]\), with zero-probability terms omitted. The conditional mutual information is
\[
I(U;W\mid V)=H(U\mid V)-H(U\mid V,W).
\]
The internal information cost in bits is
\[
I_{\mu}(\pi)=I(X;T\mid Y)+I(Y;T\mid X).
\]
All variables use the joint law of \(\mu\) and the three independent coin strings of \(\pi\). Including \(R\) in \(T\) accounts for public randomness; private coins are not included in that transcript. This is internal information, not the external quantity \(I(X,Y;T)\), and not the distinct multiparty public-information measure introduced in the source. The quantity is finite, nonnegative and at most \(2n\).

A simulation \(\rho\) is another finite protocol in the same model, with its own independent shared and private fair coins. At its terminal leaf Alice outputs a value \(T_A\) determined by her local view and Bob outputs \(T_B\) determined by his. These values lie in the finite set of augmented transcripts possible for \(\pi\), together with a failure symbol \(\bot\). Output descriptions and their lengths are not communication costs. The simulated public string of \(\pi\) is part of these output values; it need not equal \(\rho\)'s actual public string.

Let \(P\) be the law of \((X,Y,T,T)\) produced by drawing \((X,Y)\sim\mu\) and executing \(\pi\). Let \(Q\) be the law of \((X,Y,T_A,T_B)\) produced by drawing the same input distribution and executing \(\rho\). Regard both as distributions on the same finite product space, assigning zero mass to impossible original outcomes and to original failures. The simulation error is their total variation distance
\[
\operatorname{err}_{\mu}(\rho,\pi)=
\frac12\sum_{x,y,t_a,t_b}|P(x,y,t_a,t_b)-Q(x,y,t_a,t_b)|.
\]
Thus the requirement preserves correlation with the inputs and agreement between the parties' reconstructed transcripts, except for total variation at most \(1/100\). It is stronger than reproducing only an output bit of a particular function or only the unconditioned marginal law of \(T\). Error is averaged under \(\mu\) and the coins, whereas communication is worst case over every input pair and every coin string, including pairs of \(\mu\)-probability zero. There is no joint simulation of many independent copies. The \(+1\) in the cost bound avoids a zero-information boundary convention, and the logarithm is of the input bit length \(n\), not the number of possible inputs, the transcript length or the number of rounds.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the universal compression statement or its full negation. Equivalently, a positive answer gives one absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) and proves
\[
\forall n\ge1\ \forall\mu\ \forall\pi\ \exists\rho:\quad
\operatorname{err}_{\mu}(\rho,\pi)\le\frac1{100}
\ \land\
\operatorname{CC}(\rho)\le
K(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.
\]
A negative answer must prove that for every proposed \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\), there are \(n,\mu,\pi\) in the stated domain for which every simulation with error at most \(1/100\) has communication strictly larger than that bound. A positive theorem only for product input distributions or public-coin original protocols does not cover the universal domain, although a matching lower bound within either subclass can refute the universal statement. Refuting only constant-overhead compression does not refute the logarithmic allowance. An expected-communication upper bound must be converted to the specified worst-case guarantee; error slack and an increased absolute constant can permit such a conversion. A theorem for external or multiparty public information must establish the claimed conclusion for the internal-information measure defined here to qualify. Likewise, failure of one simulation construction is not a lower bound for all simulations. The chosen constant simulation error is part of the mathematical proposition; the benchmark asks for a proof of that proposition or negation, rather than an approximate numerical verdict.
cards.why: The question asks how much communication is forced by interaction beyond the information actually transferred. A general small-overhead simulation would strengthen the connection between information-theoretic lower bounds and communication complexity, with consequences for direct-sum phenomena. A matching obstruction would show why correlated inputs prevent a near-information-cost account of interactive communication.

Interactive information measures what two participants learn about each other’s inputs during a conversation. The number of transmitted bits can be much larger. The source asks whether most of that discrepancy can always be removed while retaining the relevant behavior.

Reading the complete source paragraph changes the interpretation of the imported excerpt. It discusses the two-party question and says that compression with no loss is already ruled out. The open direction permits a small loss, giving logarithmic input-size dependence as an example.

The paper subsequently introduces a different public-information measure for multiparty computation and proves a compression theorem for it with logarithmic factors. That theorem cannot be substituted for a solution to the preceding two-party internal-information question.

Internal simulation reconstructs the original transcript for both participants while retaining its joint distribution with their inputs. cards.title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Are randomized classical and entanglement-assisted quantum communication polynomially related for every total Boolean function? Precisely, do universal constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that \[R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\le C\bigl(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1\bigr)^k\] for every pair of nonempty finite sets \(X,Y\) and every function \(F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\)?
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and Bob must output \(F(x,y)\). A protocol is agreed in advance for the entire function \(F\). Local computation and storage are unrestricted and free; only communication is charged. The protocol may depend on \(F\), but its shared resources are independent of the actual inputs. In the classical model the parties exchange bits and may use shared public randomness and private randomness. In the quantum model they exchange qubits, may use arbitrary finite-dimensional local quantum operations and measurements, and may start with any finite-dimensional shared entangled state independent of \((x,y)\). There is no fixed upper bound on the amount of this prior entanglement; its preparation is not charged. Local quantum operations are completely positive trace-preserving maps, with measurement outcomes retained in local registers, and the final output is a two-outcome measurement at Bob. Classical bits sent by a quantum protocol count as transmitted qubits. Neither model receives free input-dependent advice or any communication through timing, message length, silence or postselection. One may use a fixed finite alternating schedule of transmissions, padding unused transmissions; local branches cannot signal through the schedule. Arbitrarily many rounds are allowed, with no input-length-dependent round restriction imposed by the question. The cost is the worst-case total number of bits or qubits transmitted, including all rounds and all randomness or measurement branches. In either model the output must equal \(F(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every pair \((x,y)\). The quantities \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\) and \(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)\) are the least costs among protocols with this guarantee. Total means that all of \(X\times Y\) is the correctness domain; no additional joint promise is allowed. The additive one in the polynomial handles zero-communication functions. The constants \(C,k\) must be independent of the function, the domains, any bit encoding of the inputs, and the amount of shared entanglement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal polynomial bound or of its negation. A negative answer must show that for every \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\), some finite total Boolean function satisfies \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)>C(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1)^k\). A superpolynomial separating family can witness this; one fixed polynomial separation cannot. A bound with an extra input-length factor, a promise-problem or relation separation, or a comparison imposing a fixed round limit does not resolve the stated all-functions, unrestricted-round target.
cards.why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

cards.context:
Communication complexity isolates the information that must cross between two parties who already have unlimited ability to process their own inputs. A quantum advantage in this setting is therefore a saving in transmitted information, rather than a faster local computation. The shared entanglement in the quantum model is a free, input-independent resource.

For a total function, every combination of an Alice input and a Bob input must be handled. Promise problems may omit difficult combinations, and relations may accept several different answers. These distinctions prevent the known much larger advantages for those models from automatically providing a counterexample here.

The polynomial has to be the same for all functions. Examples in which the classical cost is a fixed power of the quantum cost are compatible with the conjecture, even if that power exceeds two. The negation requires advantages that defeat every fixed polynomial bound.

Bhattacharya and coauthors state this as the Log-Equivalence Conjecture, attributed to Shi and Zhu. Their earlier 2026 paper explicitly retains the general total-function question and studies a restricted composed family.

For \(F(x,y)=f(x_1\land y_1,\ldots,x_n\land y_n)\), their revised Theorem 1.2 gives \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}(F)=O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F))^7\log^2 n)\), where \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}\) denotes exact deterministic communication. This restricted AND-composition result, with its additional input-length factor, differs from the universal polynomial in quantum cost alone.

Hasegawa and Le Gall’s August 2026 preprint obtains a polynomial quantum advantage for a total function using a constant number of quantum communication rounds. Its improvement concerns interaction: the size of the communication gap remains polynomial. It therefore does not refute the general polynomial-relation conjecture.

Resolving the conjecture would determine whether total Boolean communication imposes a general limit on quantum savings. The comparison permits arbitrary prior entanglement and unrestricted interaction, so such a limit would apply beyond particular algorithms or graph-like compositions.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint claims an explicit total-function family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and randomized classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the input length of each party. The stated quantum protocol has two transmissions and no prior entanglement; the classical lower bound permits any number of rounds. Polynomial growth in \(N\) defeats every fixed power of its logarithm, so this would refute the displayed conjecture if the proof is correct.

Le Gall's preprint of 15 September 2026 claims \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum communication and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized communication with two quantum messages, and \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) classical cost for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\) with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Section 2 explicitly uses public randomness, unrestricted classical rounds, worst-case message costs and error at most \(1/3\) per input. These are total Boolean functions, not promise problems or relations. The full proof has not been independently verified here.

The new claims also apply to the comparison with free prior entanglement: a protocol using no prior entanglement is admissible when that resource is permitted. A protocol whose final receiver is Alice can send its output bit to Bob, adding at most one to the communication cost without changing the error probability. These model correspondences establish a match to the stated target; they do not certify the new lower-bound arguments.

For a total function, every combination of an Alice input and a Bob input must be handled. Promise problems may omit difficult combinations, and relations may accept several different answers. These distinctions prevent the known much larger advantages for those models from automatically providing a counterexample here.

The polynomial has to be the same for all functions. Examples in which the classical cost is a fixed power of the quantum cost are compatible with the conjecture, even if that power exceeds two. The negation requires advantages that defeat every fixed polynomial bound.

Bhattacharya and coauthors state this as the Log-Equivalence Conjecture, attributed to Shi and Zhu. Their earlier 2026 paper explicitly retains the general total-function question and studies a restricted composed family.

For \(F(x,y)=f(x_1\land y_1,\ldots,x_n\land y_n)\), their revised Theorem 1.2 gives \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}(F)=O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F))^7\log^2 n)\), where \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}\) denotes exact deterministic communication. This restricted AND-composition result, with its additional input-length factor, differs from the universal polynomial in quantum cost alone.

Hasegawa and Le Gall’s August 2026 preprint obtains a polynomial quantum advantage for a total function using a constant number of quantum communication rounds. Its improvement concerns interaction: the size of the communication gap remains polynomial. It therefore does not refute the general polynomial-relation conjecture.

Resolving the conjecture would determine whether total Boolean communication imposes a general limit on quantum savings. The comparison permits arbitrary prior entanglement and unrestricted interaction, so such a limit would apply beyond particular algorithms or graph-like compositions.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint claims an explicit total-function family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and randomized classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the input length of each party. The stated quantum protocol has two transmissions and no prior entanglement; the classical lower bound permits any number of rounds. Polynomial growth in \(N\) defeats every fixed power of its logarithm, so this would refute the displayed conjecture if the proof is correct.

Le Gall's preprint of 15 September 2026 claims \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum communication and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized communication with two quantum messages, and \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) classical cost for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\) with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Section 2 explicitly uses public randomness, unrestricted classical rounds, worst-case message costs and error at most \(1/3\) per input. These are total Boolean functions, not promise problems or relations. The full proof has not been independently verified here.

The new claims also apply to the comparison with free prior entanglement: a protocol using no prior entanglement is admissible when that resource is permitted. A protocol whose final receiver is Alice can send its output bit to Bob, adding at most one to the communication cost without changing the error probability. These model correspondences establish a match to the stated target; they do not certify the new lower-bound arguments.

cards.title: Asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every \(1\le d\le n\), and every Boolean function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\) represented as the sign of a real polynomial of degree at most \(d\), \[I(f)\le C d\sqrt n?\] Here \(I(f)\) is total influence, the expected number of input coordinates whose flip changes the output at a uniformly random input. The precise polynomial and tie conventions are defined below. The same constant must work for growing degrees as well as fixed degrees.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) denote the polynomial threshold functions specified below, and let \(M(n,d)=\max_{f\in\mathcal F_{n,d}}I(f)\). 

Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A real multilinear polynomial of degree at most \(d\) has the form
\[p(x)=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]\\|S|\le d}}a_S\prod_{i\in S}x_i,\qquad a_S\in\mathbb R,\]
with empty product \(1\). All coefficients are unrestricted reals; there is no bound on their magnitude, bit length, the number of nonzero monomials, or the minimum nonzero value of \(|p|\) on the cube. Require \(p(x)\ne0\) at every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\). Its threshold function is \(f(x)=+1\) when \(p(x)>0\), and \(f(x)=-1\) when \(p(x)<0\). The class \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) contains every function with at least one such representation, not just those whose least possible threshold degree is exactly \(d\). Starting with arbitrary real polynomials gives the same class: reducing powers using \(x_i^2=1\) preserves the cube values and does not increase degree. Excluding zeros fixes the tie convention; any representation using one fixed value of sign at zero can be perturbed by a sufficiently small constant to remove its cube zeros without changing the function.

Choose \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) cube points, with independent equally likely coordinates. For \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) have coordinate \(-x_i\) at \(i\) and agree with \(x\) elsewhere. Define
\[\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=2^{-n}|\{x:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}|,\quad s_f(x)=|\{i\in[n]:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}|,\]
\[I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Inf}_i(f)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}s_f(x).\]
Thus total influence is average sensitivity, not maximum pointwise sensitivity and not influence divided by \(n\). There is no biased input distribution or additional probability over polynomials. The maximization is over Boolean functions; different coefficient choices representing the same function have the same influence. It is a maximum rather than merely a supremum because only finitely many Boolean functions exist on a fixed cube, and \(\mathcal F_{n,d}\) is nonempty. Constants belong to the class with influence zero, while a dictator \(f(x)=x_1\) has influence one; hence \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain.

The constants in the answer must be absolute: they cannot depend on degree, dimension, a representation, or an asymptotic path through the parameter pairs. The estimates must hold throughout the domain, including small dimensions and growing degrees; finite exceptional cases must be covered by the proved constants. This is a mathematical extremal-growth problem, with no evaluation-time requirement or finite encoding assumption for real coefficients. The omitted degree-zero case has value zero, and degrees larger than \(n\) give no additional Boolean functions, so the displayed domain covers all nontrivial regimes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that \(I(f)/(d\sqrt n)\) is bounded by one universal constant on the stated class of polynomial threshold functions, or show that this ratio is unbounded when \(n\) and \(d\) may vary.
cards.why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.

cards.context:
The selected target is the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture \(I(f)=O(d\sqrt n)\), uniformly in dimension and degree. It is distinct from the stronger, disproved assertion that one particular symmetric function is an exact maximizer.

A polynomial threshold function evaluates a real polynomial and keeps its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority and weighted voting rules; degree two also permits pairwise interactions. Threshold degree measures the degree needed to represent the sign pattern, rather than the degree needed to equal the Boolean function numerically on every input.

Total influence is the expected number of sensitive coordinates at a uniformly random input. If \(D(f)\) is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2^{1-n}D(f)\). By contrast, the probability that flipping one uniformly chosen coordinate changes the output is \(I(f)/n\). The normalization in the target is the former, which ranges from zero to \(n\).

For odd \(n\), majority has \[I(\operatorname{MAJ}_n)=n\,2^{1-n}\binom{n-1}{(n-1)/2}\sim\sqrt{2n/\pi}.\] Thus influence already grows with dimension at degree one. At the opposite endpoint, parity \(f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\) has degree \(n\) and influence \(n\), so \(M(n,n)=n\).

The classical symmetric examples change sign across consecutive central Hamming layers. Their total influence has order \(\min\{n,d\sqrt n\}\), with constants uniform in the two parameters. This supplies the standard lower scale, including saturation at large degree. Gotsman and Linial conjectured that such an example actually maximizes influence exactly; the remaining asymptotic question permits different maximizers.

Chapman’s counterexamples refute that exact assertion for \(d=2\) in every odd dimension \(n\ge5\), and for \(n\ge7\) with \(3\le d\le n-3\). They do not rule out a universal \(O(d\sqrt n)\) upper bound. Combined with the elementary upper bound \(I(f)\le n\) and the standard lower scale, that surviving conjecture would give \(M(n,d)=\Theta(\min\{n,d\sqrt n\})\).

The common constants are part of the mathematical target. Bounds \(M(n,d)\le C_d\sqrt n\) with an unspecified degree-dependent constant \(C_d\) do not determine the joint dependence on \(n,d\). Nor does an estimate only as \(n\to\infty\) with \(d\) fixed cover sequences of increasing degree. The requested bound must also cover the transition to influence of order \(n\).

Kane’s Theorem 2 gives \(I(f)\le\sqrt n\,(\log n)^{O(d\log d)}2^{O(d^2\log d)}\) for \(d\ge2\). For every fixed degree this has the correct power of \(n\), up to logarithmic factors. Those factors still grow with dimension, and the bound’s dependence on degree is much larger than linear, so it does not give matching universal factors in the requested joint regime.

For quadratic threshold functions, Kim, Maldonado and Wellens study the graph whose edges mark nonzero coefficients of pairwise monomials. Their Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 give bounds in terms of the graph’s fractional chromatic number and its number of edges. These are structural estimates for a prescribed representation, not a matching bound for all dense quadratic representations.

The April 27, 2026 revision by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a fixed-degree polylogarithmic bound on Boolean surface area, defined by \(\operatorname{BSA}(f)=\mathbb E_x\sqrt{s_f(x)}\). Its Theorem 1.1 has constants depending on degree. The paper explicitly distinguishes this fractional sensitivity moment from total influence \(\mathbb E_x s_f(x)\).

A proof or refutation of this universal upper bound answers the card. Determining the full extremal function after a refutation is not required.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision establishes a polynomial relationship between rational degree and ordinary degree. Its §5.2 restates the asymptotic influence conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue. Neither that main degree theorem nor the proposed weaker conjecture determines the maximum influence of arbitrary polynomial threshold functions.

A matching joint bound would quantify how strongly a low-degree sign representation constrains the edge boundary of a Boolean function. This connects algebraic representation to sensitivity, noise behavior and learning-theoretic complexity. A solution may establish the surviving conjectured scale or a different scale, but disproving one particular candidate without determining the extremal growth does not complete the task.

cards.title: Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on \([n]\) to \(\{0,1\}\) that is invariant under every permutation of \([n]\) and monotone under adding edges, is \(D(f)=n(n- 1)/2\), where \(D(f)\) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(U_{n}=\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n\}\). A graph is an arbitrary edge set \(E\subseteq U_{n}\), with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means \(E\subseteq F\) implies \(f(E)\le f(F)\). Invariance means \(f(\pi (E))=f(E)\) for every permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), where \(\pi (E)=\{\{\pi (i),\pi (j)\}:\{i,j\}\in E\}\). A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in \(U_{n}\) and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output \(f(E)\) for every \(E\subseteq U_{n}\). The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives \(D(f)\le |U_{n}|\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(D(f)=|U_{n}|\) for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most \(|U_{n}|- 1\). A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.
cards.why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.
