cards.context:
Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\) is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning \(n=p^{k}\) for a prime p and an integer \(k\ge 1\). Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.

Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning \(n=p^{k}\) for a prime p and an integer \(k\ge 1\). Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.

cards.title: Constant-factor randomized direct sums for total Boolean functions
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) such that, for every pair of nonempty finite input sets \(X,Y\), every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), \[R_{1/3}(f^{\otimes k})\ge c\,k\,R_{1/3}(f),\] where communication is public-coin, worst-case and measured with one global error probability?
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know \(f\) and the finite domains. A public-coin protocol selects a deterministic binary communication tree using a finite string of independent shared fair random bits, independent of the inputs. At a node, the designated player sends one bit determined by that player’s own input, the public string and the transcript so far. At termination Bob outputs a bit determined by his input, the public string and transcript. The worst-case cost is the maximum number of communicated bits over all inputs and public strings. Local computation and the public random string are free; its finite length may depend on the protocol. There is no message to reveal the public seed, no advice depending on private inputs and no restriction to one-way communication. The complexity \(R_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum cost of a protocol whose output equals \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input pair. It is finite because Alice can send an encoding of her input. Protocols may depend nonuniformly on the finite function; no uniform construction from its truth table is requested. For \(f^{\otimes k}:X^k\times Y^k\to\{0,1\}^k\), Alice and Bob receive their full tuples and Bob must output \((f(x_1,y_1),\ldots,f(x_k,y_k))\). Success probability at least \(2/3\) concerns the entire vector simultaneously on every tuple pair. The inputs need not be independent draws from a distribution: the cost and error guarantees are worst-case. The protocol may communicate across coordinates in any way. The constant \(c\) must work for all domains, functions and copy counts; a different constant for each fixed function is insufficient. Zero-communication functions impose the vacuous lower bound zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the universal constant-factor inequality, or a Lean proof of its negation: for every positive proposed constant there are a total Boolean function and copy count violating it. Refuting a version for relations, partial functions, distributional inputs or per-coordinate error alone does not refute this selected assertion. Expected communication is not the cost used here.
cards.why: Direct sums ask whether communicating about many tasks together can save a substantial fraction of the single-task cost. They connect communication lower bounds with interactive compression and the distinction between information revealed and bits transmitted. The exact error and task conventions determine which savings are possible.

cards.title: Fixed-player number-on-forehead disjointness exponent
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the communication exponent \[x_{\mathrm{NOF}}(k)=\inf\{a\ge0:R(n,k)=O_k(n^a)\text{ as }n\to\infty\}.\] Here \(R(n,k)\) is the minimum worst-case public-coin randomized communication for deciding whether \(k\) subsets of \([n]\) have empty common intersection, with error at most \(1/3\); player \(i\) sees every set except the \(i\)-th. The full interactive broadcast model and asymptotic quantifiers are below.
cards.definitions:
The universe \([n]\) is \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Each \(S_j\) is represented by its characteristic vector \(x^{(j)}\in\{0,1\}^n\), where \(x^{(j)}_t=1\) means \(t\in S_j\). There is no restriction on set sizes, intersections, repeated sets, or the number of players relative to \(n\). In particular, \(k\) can exceed \(n\). The predicate asks for an empty intersection of all sets, not pairwise disjointness. Equivalently, the complementary predicate asks whether some row of the \(n\)-by-\(k\) incidence matrix is all ones; complementing the common output leaves the communication complexity unchanged.

All players know \(n,k\), their labels and the protocol. Player \(i\)'s initial view is the ordered tuple \((x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(i-1)},x^{(i+1)},\ldots,x^{(k)})\). No player initially sees its missing column. This is the number-on-forehead model; it is different from giving player \(i\) only \(S_i\).

A deterministic protocol is a finite binary tree. An internal node specifies which player broadcasts the next bit. That bit can be any function of that player's visible input and the preceding public transcript. The bit is written once on a blackboard and is seen by all players; broadcasting one bit costs one bit, not \(k\) bits. Each leaf specifies a common output bit. The speaker and the decision to stop are determined by the public node, so they cannot transmit an uncharged input-dependent signal. The players may speak in any order prescribed by the tree and may return arbitrarily often; neither the number of rounds nor the number of messages is separately bounded.

A public-coin randomized protocol is a distribution over deterministic protocols, selected using shared randomness independent of the inputs. Its cost is the maximum depth of any tree in the support. This bound is over all inputs and all random outcomes, not an expectation. For every full input tuple, the probability that the common output equals \(\operatorname{DISJ}_{n,k}\) must be at least \(2/3\). No private communication, pre-shared secret or quantum resource is provided.

Local computation, storage and the complexity of the protocol description are free. Protocols may be chosen independently for each pair \((n,k)\); there is no uniform algorithm for generating them or local running-time requirement. The model therefore asks about communication alone.

Define \(R(n,k)\) to be the least integer \(d\ge0\) for which such a randomized protocol of cost at most \(d\) exists. This set of costs is nonempty: one player can transmit a missing column to another, who can broadcast the answer, using at most \(n+1\) bits. Both output values occur for every allowed \((n,k)\), so a zero-communication output independent of the input cannot attain error \(1/3\) on all inputs. Thus \(1\le R(n,k)\le n+1\).

For each fixed integer \(k\ge2\), define \[x_{\mathrm{NOF}}(k)=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ R(n,k)\le Cn^a\}.\] The constant and threshold may depend on \(k\) and \(a\). The elementary bounds above ensure \(0\le x_{\mathrm{NOF}}(k)\le1\). The infimum need not be attained. The target does not require matching logarithmic factors, a uniform constant as \(k\) grows with \(n\), or a single protocol generator. Lower bounds must apply to all permitted randomized interactive protocols.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply one explicitly described real-valued function \(a\) on all integer player counts \(k\ge2\). Prove in Lean that \(|a(k)-x_{\mathrm{NOF}}(k)|\le1/100\) at every point of that domain. A pair of [certified bounding functions](definitions.html#numerical-answers) \(L,U\) also qualifies if \(L(k)\le x_{\mathrm{NOF}}(k)\le U(k)\) and \(U(k)-L(k)\le1/50\) everywhere, with \(a=(L+U)/2\). At each fixed player count use the specified public-coin, worst-case communication measure.
cards.why: Each player knows almost the entire input, which makes communication lower bounds much harder than in the ordinary split-input model. Set disjointness gives a concrete way to measure how this overlap and additional players change the power of randomized interaction. A full answer would clarify a basic limitation used in several connections between communication, circuits and proofs.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width \(q\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\) but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions:
Use the shared [bounded-width CNF encoding and rate \(s_q\)](definitions.html#sat-encoding). The exponential term uses the number of distinct variables \(n(F)\). The polynomial factor uses the full input length \(N(F)\), including every repeated clause. The decider may depend on the fixed width \(q\).

The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(N(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected \(\varepsilon\). There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.
cards.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

cards.context:
Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports randomized bounds \(O^*(1.306969598^n)\) for Unique-3-SAT and \(O^*(1.307031578^n)\) for general 3-SAT, where \(O^*\) suppresses polynomial input factors. These are stated preprint results whose proof and numerical certification have not been independently verified here. In either case, fixed width three and internal randomness differ from a deterministic saving that holds at every fixed width.

The 2015 textbook explicitly cautions that its limiting-rate definition is more precise than the informal question about one unrestricted CNF-SAT algorithm. A negative answer may consist of separate algorithms for all fixed widths, sharing one positive saving in the exponential rate but not necessarily a uniform generator or a common polynomial input factor.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic algorithms for 3SUM
cards.formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.
cards.definitions:
The size parameter \(n\ge2\) bounds the length of each of the three lists. Repeated values are allowed and do not affect the answer; each chosen value comes from its prescribed list. A triple may contain equal numerical values from different lists. There is no single-list distinctness condition. Integers are supplied explicitly in signed binary and fit in one word of
\[w=\left\lceil(B+3)\log_2(n+1)\right\rceil\]
bits. The target equation is equality of ordinary integers, not congruence modulo the word size.

For each fixed \(B\), a uniform word-RAM algorithm has a finite program independent of \(n\) and of all list contents. Its memory cells contain \(w\)-bit words and are addressed by words. Initially only the input and its lengths are present; other cells are zero. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing a word, copying, comparing, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by a word-specified amount; a shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Division by zero can be defined to return zero. The program may obtain an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word at unit cost. There is no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, real-number operation, oracle or nonuniform lookup table. Any table construction, sorting and preprocessing count toward the runtime. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented by these instructions.

Las Vegas means that the program halts with probability one and every output produced is correct; randomization affects its runtime, not its answer. The required bound means that for each \(B\) there are \(K_B,n_B\) such that the expected number of instructions is at most \(K_B n^{2-\varepsilon}\) on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_B\). Expectation is over the program's random words, followed by a worst case over the input lists. All smaller valid instances must also be decided correctly with finite expected time. No average-case input distribution or reusable preprocessing is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence claim, including one positive exponent saving uniform over every fixed \(B\), correctness, almost-sure termination and the expected instruction bound; or prove its negation. Negation means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed polynomial universe admits no algorithm meeting that saving. An improvement by logarithmic factors alone, a fast data-structure query after expensive preprocessing, a restricted comparison-tree lower bound, or a Monte Carlo algorithm without the stipulated zero-error guarantee does not settle this selected target.
cards.why: 3SUM is a central test of whether apparently quadratic search over pairs can admit a fixed polynomial improvement. Its conjectured hardness supports fine-grained lower bounds for many geometric, graph and data-structure problems. The exact model matters: removing a logarithmic factor, changing integer size or omitting preprocessing costs can make a result look stronger than the improvement asked for here.

cards.title: Subexponential-time Circuit-SAT
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), an integer \(d\ge1\), a constant \(K\ge1\), and a function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(\lim_{n\to\infty}g(n)/n=0\), such that \(A\) decides satisfiability of every explicitly given Boolean circuit with \(n\ge1\) input variables and \(s\ge0\) gates in at most
\[
K\,2^{g(n)}(N+1)^d
\]
Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(N\) is the full binary encoding length, gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT, and depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The output must be correct on every circuit. The requested bound is abbreviated \(2^{o(n)}\operatorname{poly}(N)\); its exponential parameter is the number of input variables, not the number of gates or encoding bits.
cards.definitions:
Use the [De Morgan circuit basis](definitions.html#boolean-circuits) with \(n\) input variables, free constants 0 and 1, and one designated output. A supplied circuit has size \(s\), the number of its operation gates. An input, constant or gate may serve as the output. Depth, fan-out and the growth of \(s\) with \(n\) are unrestricted. The polynomial overhead exponent \(d\) is fixed across all these sizes.

For an assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\), evaluate gates in topological order using ordinary Boolean operations. Satisfiability means that at least one such assignment gives output 1. The algorithm returns exactly this yes/no answer; it need not count or enumerate satisfying assignments. All declared input nodes are explicitly listed and included in \(n\), even if some are unused.

Use the [self-delimiting integer code](definitions.html#sat-encoding). List the codes of \(n,s\), then \(n\) input-node markers, and then the \(s\) gates in a topological order. Number the constants 0 and 1 first, the inputs next and the gates last. Each gate has a two-bit type tag and coded predecessor indices, all smaller than its own index. Finish with the coded output-node index, with no trailing data. Invalid encodings are outside the domain. The total length \(N\) is \(O((n+s)\log(n+s+2))\); the polynomial factor pays for processing the entire explicit description.

The algorithm is one classical deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice, no oracle and no random bits. All input processing, intermediate bit computation and output are charged. The constants, function and program are chosen before the input: the quantifier order is \(\exists(A,d,K,g)\;\forall C\), subject to the displayed limit on \(g\). In particular, \(g\) depends only on \(n\), and \(d\) cannot grow with circuit size or an accuracy parameter. The limit means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an integer \(N\) such that \(g(n)\le\varepsilon n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Thus one fixed saving \(2^{(1-\delta)n}\) for a constant \(0<\delta<1\) does not by itself meet this target.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must supply a single deterministic algorithm, prove exact decision correctness on every encoded circuit, and prove the full charged running-time bound with fixed \(d,K\) and \(g(n)/n\to0\). A negative answer must unconditionally rule out every such algorithm and bound; a lower bound conditional on another conjecture establishes only that conditional statement.

An algorithm restricted to linear-size circuits, bounded depth, formulas or a fixed clause width does not establish this universal target. A running time subexponential only in \(N\) or \(n+s\), or a fixed positive saving in the coefficient of \(n\), also does not suffice. This is a genuine existence question, not a numerical request to approximate an infimum running-time exponent.
cards.why: Determining whether general circuit satisfiability admits a vanishing exponential rate would identify a fundamental boundary of exact algorithms, beyond fixed improvements to exhaustive search or restrictions to simple circuit families.

cards.context:
Circuit satisfiability asks whether a Boolean computation accepts any assignment to its inputs. The 2013 Dagstuhl report distinguishes its exponential-time behavior from that of formulas whose clauses have bounded width, despite their polynomial-time equivalence.

Williams proves conditional connections between satisfiability running times at different circuit sizes, including consequences giving subexponential algorithms for smaller circuits. These are implications from algorithmic assumptions, not an unconditional algorithm meeting this card.

This target implies the positive answer to TCS-7270, which asks only for a fixed exponential saving at each fixed linear gate density. The converse is not asserted: the present question requires a vanishing exponential rate and covers general gate counts.

An October 2026 OpenAI preprint claims subexponential counting for each fixed clause width. That theorem is stated for formulas in conjunctive normal form, meaning conjunctions of clauses that are disjunctions of literals (variables or their negations). It is not stated for general circuits measured by their original input variables. Introducing a variable for each gate can increase the variable count to \(n+s\), so that conversion alone does not establish the bound requested here. The preprint is recorded as a claim; its proof and formalization were not independently audited in this addition.

cards.title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a constant \(K>0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) with the following property? For every integer \(n\ge2\), every Boolean matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\), and every sequence \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n\) supplied online, the algorithm outputs each \(Mv_t\) before receiving \(v_{t+1}\), and outputs \(Mv_n\) at the end, using at most
\[
 K n^{3-\varepsilon}
\]
word-RAM instructions in total on every execution, including preprocessing of \(M\), with probability at least \(2/3\) that all \(n\) output vectors are correct? Products are over the Boolean semiring:
\[
 (Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j\bigr).
\]
The OMv conjecture asserts a negative answer.
cards.definitions:
The input initially supplies \(n\) and all \(n^2\) entries of the fixed matrix \(M\), in row-major order. After the algorithm's initial preprocessing, vectors arrive one at a time in the order \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). Each vector is an arbitrary length-\(n\) bit string. The next vector is unavailable until the algorithm has finished returning the current vector's complete answer. The algorithm may preserve its computed state and earlier vectors, but cannot postpone an output to use future inputs. There is no per-query time bound beyond the total bound and these deadlines.

Both the matrix bit string and each input vector are explicitly packed into consecutive words with known zero padding. An output vector contains its \(n\) bits in coordinate order; an explicit array with one Boolean value per word is an allowed canonical output representation. Returning an implicit circuit, a pointer to uncomputed answers, a count of nonzero entries or just one queried coordinate is insufficient. All input access and output writes are charged. The matrix never changes. The operations \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) mean Boolean AND and OR; this is neither arithmetic multiplication over the reals nor multiplication over the field of two elements.

The computation is a sequential word RAM with
\[
 w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil
\]
bits per word and one fixed finite program for all \(n\). Memory cells, registers and addresses are word-sized. Unit-cost instructions are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) positions return zero. Multiword computations cost their component instructions. An independent uniform random \(w\)-bit word can be generated in one instruction. This permits deterministic algorithms as a special case. There are no quantum instructions, nonuniform advice, free precomputed tables or input-dependent oracles. Unused memory initially contains zero.

All instructions are counted, including construction of auxiliary tables, allocation or initialization performed by the program, preprocessing before the first vector, work between vectors, generation of random words, copying and output. There is no separate allowance for an arbitrary polynomial preprocessing phase. Space has no additional sublinear or near-linear restriction, but every address must fit in a word and writing any used state costs instructions. Only the currently supplied input is made available by the online interface; it supplies no information about a future vector.

For the success guarantee, the matrix and complete vector sequence are fixed independently of the algorithm's randomness. The probability is over the program's random words, and the successful event requires every bit of every output to be correct. A separate success probability of \(2/3\) for each individual query is not the specified joint guarantee. The time bound holds for every random execution, including erroneous executions. Every output deadline and eventual termination must likewise be met on every execution.

The constants \(\varepsilon,K,B\) and the program are chosen once, independently of the input dimension and contents. Any fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) suffices. A merely logarithmic or subpolynomial improvement in total time is not a fixed exponent saving. No restriction to combinatorial algorithms is imposed: every algorithm implementable by the specified word-RAM instructions is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated algorithm exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist.

A positive answer must establish the fixed exponent saving after charging preprocessing and all input/output work, the online deadlines, and joint success for every fixed input. It refutes the OMv conjecture in this model. A negative answer must exclude every admissible uniform randomized program, every fixed word-size constant and every positive exponent saving. It proves the conjecture in this model and cannot assume the conjecture itself or another unproved hardness hypothesis.

An algorithm for structured matrices, an offline matrix product, a query bound after uncharged preprocessing, or a cell-probe bound with free computation does not meet the target without a proved extension. Neither does a speedup of the form \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}\), which supplies no fixed positive saving in the exponent.
cards.why: The conjecture supports many precise lower bounds for dynamic graph and data-structure problems. A general truly subcubic online algorithm would overturn these conditional barriers, while an unconditional lower bound would explain a shared obstacle to faster dynamic algorithms.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic exact edit distance
cards.formal: For the binary alphabet \(\Sigma=\{0,1\}\), do there exist constants \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), \(C>0\) and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(x,y\in\Sigma^n\), the algorithm outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) in at most \(C(n+1)^{2-\varepsilon}\) operations?
cards.definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has \(w=\operatorname{ceil}(4 \log _{2}(n+2))\) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) bound for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.
cards.why: A fundamental quadratic barrier for string comparison and a principal example in fine-grained complexity.

references.title: Approximation Schemes for Edit Distance and LCS in Quasi-Strongly Subquadratic Time
references.locator: 31 March 2026 abstract; accepted to STOC 2026. Randomized (1+η)-approximation for fixed η>0, with a quasi-polynomial factor saving, not exact deterministic edit distance.

cards.context:
The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes \(O(n^{2})\) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log  n\) is smaller than \(n^{2}\) but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) with one \(\varepsilon >0\) that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every \(\delta >0\) there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in \(O(2^{(1- \delta )N} \operatorname{poly}(L))\) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation for each fixed \(\eta >0\), with running time \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega}(1) n}\). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on \(\eta\) cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

cards.title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is it true that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\ \text{no allowed algorithm solves bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors in }O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\text{ time}\]
for all integers \(n\ge2\) on two lists of \(n\) vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), where \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\)? An allowed algorithm is a uniform randomized classical word-RAM program in the model below. Its running-time bound is worst-case over both inputs and random choices, and its answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. The dimension constant \(c\) may depend on the proposed exponent saving \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed as \(n\) grows.
cards.definitions:
Decision problem. For \(n\ge2\), the input consists of ordered lists \(A=(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(n)})\) and \(B=(b^{(1)},\ldots,b^{(n)})\) of binary vectors of common dimension \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\). Repeated vectors, zero vectors and overlap between the lists are allowed. Output YES exactly when
\[\exists r,s\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad\sum_{j=1}^{d}a^{(r)}_j b^{(s)}_j=0.\]
The sum is an ordinary nonnegative integer sum. Equivalently, the two supports are disjoint. Orthogonality modulo two is a different predicate. The selected pair must come from opposite lists, but the task only asks for a decision bit, not for a witness. There is no promise on Hamming weights, intersections, number of solutions or input distribution.

Words and encoding. A machine fixes an integer \(\lambda\ge2\) and uses unsigned words of
\[w=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+d+2)\rceil\]
bits. Input headers supply \(n,d\), followed by the two lists in order. Each vector occupies \(\lceil d/w\rceil\) consecutive words, with its coordinates packed from least to most significant bit and unused final bits zero. Thus for fixed \(c\) one vector occupies a constant number of words as \(n\) grows. The input is explicit, not supplied by a membership or inner-product oracle. Changing between ordinary explicit bit arrays and this packing costs at most a logarithmic factor; the stated acceptance bound itself uses the packed model.

Instruction set and cost. The program is finite and independent of \(n\). It has word registers and random-access memory addressed by single words. One step may read or write a constant number of addressed words; perform addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\); perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; apply bitwise AND, OR, XOR or NOT; shift logically left or right; compare words; or branch using a comparison. Shifts discard overflow and give zero when their shift count is at least \(w\). A fresh uniform random \(w\)-bit word costs one step and is independent of all previous random words. A compound operation on several words must be built from these instructions and charged accordingly. There is no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic, real arithmetic, vector instruction of input-dependent width, or additional oracle.

Uniformity, memory and preprocessing. Outside the explicit input, memory initially contains only zeros. Programs may contain fixed finite constants, but receive no advice, precomputed tables or extra data depending on \(n\). Any such tables must be produced during the charged computation. The program and \(\lambda\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), as may constants in the running-time bound; none may vary with \(n\). Single-word addressing bounds available memory by \(2^w\) words. Reading input, constructing tables, preprocessing either list, generating randomness and producing the answer are all charged. There is no separate free preprocessing phase.

Time and error. To solve the problem, the program must halt with a decision bit on every allowed input and random execution. For each fixed input, over its independent internal random words, the bit must equal the predicate above with probability at least \(2/3\). Either type of error is allowed within this bound. The claim \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) means that there exist a real \(K>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge2\) such that every input of every size \(n\ge n_0\), and every sequence of random choices, takes at most \(K n^{2-\varepsilon}\) steps. An expected-time or average-input bound is not itself this worst-case guarantee. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring the random instruction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this lower-bound proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every allowed uniform randomized program in the specified instruction model, with the quantifier order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) and the per-input success requirement. A proof conditional on an unproved version of the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis is evidence for the conjecture, not an unconditional resolution.

A refutation must establish
\[\exists\varepsilon\in(0,1)\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists A_c,\lambda_c,K_c,n_{0,c}:\quad A_c\text{ meets the stated time and correctness conditions}.\]
The same positive saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every fixed \(c\). The programs, word-size constants, multiplicative constants and asymptotic thresholds may depend on \(c\). Each \(A_c\) must be uniform in \(n\); no additional uniform algorithm taking \(c\) as input is demanded. A deterministic family would also refute the randomized hypothesis.

An exponent saving \(\varepsilon_c>0\) that shrinks with \(c\), a bound for a fixed small dimension, logarithmic improvements over quadratic time, success only on random instances, or a lower bound restricted to monotone circuits, formulas or branching programs does not settle the full proposition. A fast online query bound with separate preprocessing must satisfy the total charged offline time before it qualifies. This is an asymptotic yes-or-no claim, with no additive numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.

cards.context:
Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are \(n^{2}\) possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on \(c\) is the main subtlety. Abboud, Williams and Yu’s SODA 2015 algorithm runs in \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) time in the relevant large-\(c\) regime. Thus a positive exponent saving is already known for every fixed dimension constant, but the saving decreases as that constant increases. This is compatible with the hypothesis, which excludes one positive saving shared by all constants. The conference year is 2015, even though some later bibliographies label the paper 2014.

Randomness is not necessary for the existing dimension-dependent saving. Chan and Williams’s SODA 2016 result obtains deterministic \(n^{2-1/O(\log c)}\) time, including counting orthogonal pairs and batched bichromatic detection. It still allows the saving to decrease with \(c\). The hypothesis therefore does not assert that randomization is the only obstacle to a universal subquadratic algorithm.

The ICALP 2026 algorithm has a one-sided-error running-time bound \(\widetilde O(1.25^d n)\), with a reported computer-aided improvement to \(O(1.16^d n)\). Here the tilde suppresses logarithmic factors in the input size, including polynomial factors in \(d\) in the stated logarithmic regime. The finite parameter evaluation was not independently rerun in this review. Exponential dependence on dimension becomes a power of \(n\) after substituting \(d=\lceil c\log_2n\rceil\), so this bound does not give the uniform exponent saving excluded by the hypothesis.

For example, substituting \(c=2\) into \(1.25^{d} n\) gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, \(n^{1+2 \log _{2} 1.25}\), whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies this randomized OV hypothesis through the standard satisfiability reduction and sparsification. That supplies a conditional explanation for the proposed barrier, not an unconditional lower bound. A deterministic-only satisfiability assumption cannot by itself rule out randomized OV algorithms. The current primary literature continues to separate these assumptions from the restricted-model theorems it proves.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.

The May 2026 online-OV paper deterministically refutes a different conjecture about preprocessing space and later query time. Its logarithmic-dimensional query saving depends on \(c\), and preprocessing has its own stated cost. The offline decision problem here is charged for both lists and every preprocessing step. The word “refutation” in that paper consequently does not mean the present OV hypothesis was refuted.

source_formulation.text: Rohatgi’s inherited source states a randomized OV conjecture for a superlogarithmic dimension function. The existing card selected the standard logarithmic-dimension formulation with the order “for every exponent saving, some fixed dimension constant”; July 2026 Conjecture 1 states exactly that order and explicitly includes randomized algorithms. This review retains that selected variant, bichromatic lists, packed inputs, worst-case running time, category and importance 96. It makes the word-RAM operations and parameter dependencies explicit, without claiming that the different dimension formulations are identical solely by renaming parameters.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. July 2026 Conjecture 1 explicitly retains the unrestricted randomized OV hypothesis while proving circuit, formula and branching-program restrictions. Deterministic and randomized dimension-dependent algorithms remain compatible with its quantifier order. The May online-OV refutation addresses a different space/query conjecture, and average-case algorithms do not cover every input. No matching unrestricted resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; external proofs were not independently formalized.

The retained hypothesis says that every proposed fixed saving over quadratic time fails at some fixed logarithmic-dimension constant.
It concerns uniform randomized word-RAM algorithms with all preprocessing charged, worst-case running time and bounded error on every input.
A complete Lean refutation must provide one positive exponent saving valid for every dimension constant, although its individual programs and time constants may depend on that constant.
Known deterministic and randomized dimension-dependent savings, average-case improvements and restricted-model lower bounds leave this full hypothesis unresolved.

cards.title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
cards.formal:
For each fixed integer \(k\ge3\), let \(\tau(k)\) be the infimum worst-case time exponent for uniform classical randomized algorithms deciding whether an \(n\)-vertex graph contains a \(k\)-clique, in the word-RAM model defined below. Let \(\omega\) be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over \(\mathbb C\). Is
\[
 \liminf_{k\to\infty}\frac{\tau(k)}{k}=\frac{\omega}{3}?
\]
The input size \(n\) tends to infinity with \(k\) fixed when defining \(\tau(k)\); only afterwards does \(k\) grow in the displayed limit inferior.
cards.definitions:
A graph is simple and undirected, with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge k\), and an explicitly given symmetric Boolean adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. Its \(n^2\) entries are stored in row order, one per word, together with \(n\). A \(k\)-clique is a set of \(k\) distinct vertices with all pairs adjacent. The algorithm outputs a YES or NO bit; it is not asked to list or count cliques.

For fixed \(k\), call a real \(a\ge0\) admissible if there exist a finite uniform randomized program, an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), real \(C>0\) and integer \(N\ge k\), such that for every graph on \(n\ge N\) vertices every execution takes at most \(Cn^a\) instructions and the answer is correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The program must also terminate and meet the same probability guarantee on each valid smaller input. Constants and program may depend on \(k\) and \(a\), but not on \(n\) or the graph. Define
\[
 \tau(k)=\inf\{a\ge0:a\text{ is admissible for }k\}.
\]
Exhaustive enumeration makes this set nonempty. Its infimum need not itself be achieved. There is no requirement for an efficient compiler taking \(k\) to its program; uniformity here means one program handling every \(n\) for each fixed \(k\).

At size \(n\), words contain \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. One instruction may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, perform addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\), divide two unsigned words with nonzero divisor and return quotient or remainder, apply a bitwise Boolean operation, shift a word, compare two unsigned words, or branch. Logical shifts discard bits beyond the word; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word may also be obtained in one instruction. All other memory is initially zero, and every preprocessing operation is charged. No nonuniform advice, free table depending on \(n\), arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic or external oracle is allowed. The constant \(B\) may be chosen with the algorithm so that its polynomially many addressed cells fit in a word. The time bound holds on every random tape, not only in expectation, while success probability is over that tape on each fixed graph.

To define \(\omega\), for each integer \(N\ge1\) let \(M(N)\) be the smallest number of binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates in an arithmetic circuit over \(\mathbb C\) that computes every entry of the product of two formal \(N\)-by-\(N\) matrices. The \(2N^2\) entries of those matrices are independent indeterminates. Circuits may share intermediate results and use arbitrary complex constants, but not division or branching; they must compute the required polynomial identities exactly. Put
\[
 \omega=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\ \forall N\ge N_0,
                       \ M(N)\le CN^a\}.
\]
This is the characteristic-zero arithmetic exponent, not a particular currently published numerical upper bound. The complex constants used to define it are not free constants or arithmetic oracles supplied to the word-RAM graph algorithm.

For a real sequence \(u_k\), its limit inferior is \(\sup_K\inf_{k\ge K}u_k\). Thus the question concerns the leading coefficient of clique size in the optimal exponent. The standard matrix-multiplication benchmark gives the upper asymptotic coefficient \(\omega/3\); the hypothesis asserts the matching lower coefficient. The inherited leading-exponent formulation does not separately assert the precise optimum for each small fixed \(k\). Nor does it invoke an informal restriction to algorithms described as combinatorial: all classical algorithms in the specified machine model are included.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed equality or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation, with exactly the models and order of limits defined above.

In view of the matrix-multiplication upper benchmark, an affirmative result must establish that for every real \(\delta>0\) there is \(K\) such that \(\tau(k)\ge(\omega/3-\delta)k\) for every integer \(k\ge K\). A negative result can establish one fixed positive saving \(\delta\) for arbitrarily large clique sizes, with proved algorithms and resource bounds, so that the limit inferior is strictly smaller than \(\omega/3\).

An improvement confined to a single fixed \(k\), logarithmic factors in \(n\), or an additive \(o(k)\) saving in the exponent does not by itself refute this formulation. Beating an outdated numerical upper bound on \(\omega\) is also insufficient. Lower bounds only for a restricted algorithm family, or only conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis, do not prove the unrestricted proposition. This is an exact yes-or-no hypothesis about exponents; numerical accuracy within \(1/100\) is not a substitute for the equality or its negation.
cards.why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.

cards.context:
The hypothesis concerns the exponent of a polynomial-time problem for each fixed clique size. Ordinary NP-hardness when the clique size varies with the input does not give the requested sharp leading coefficient.

Matrix multiplication supplies the asymptotic benchmark. Divisibility by three and rectangular refinements affect individual clique sizes, so the source’s leading-coefficient target should not be silently replaced by a stronger statement for every small size.

The 2024 graph-detection improvements save logarithmic factors. Those do not change the leading coefficient tested here; its hypergraph and clique-listing results concern different tasks.

The August 2026 preprint reports \(\omega<2.371177\). Such progress improves the matrix-based upper benchmark but does not prove its optimality for clique decision. The target uses the true exponent, with no numerical estimate substituted.

The source applies clique hardness to dynamic Boolean-formula problems. A precise form of the assumption therefore matters beyond clique detection itself. Conditional applications and exponent-preserving reductions are not unconditional proofs of the hypothesis.

cards.title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), input arrays \(A=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1})\) and \(B=(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1})\) are explicitly listed. Output all \(2n-1\) integers \(c_{k}=\min\{a_{i}+b_{j}:0\le i,j<n,\ i+j=k\}\), for \(0\le k\le2n-2\). Inputs need not be sorted or monotone. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) is common to all fixed magnitude exponents \(a\); the program, word-size constant and hidden time constant may depend on \(a\). Signed entries and exact output sums use a constant number of words.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) permits the stated family of uniform algorithms for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), with worst-case time and whole-output success guarantees, or prove the logical negation in Lean. In the negation, every proposed saving \(\varepsilon\) fails for at least one fixed \(a\), allowing all permitted algorithms and their constants. Neither a conditional hardness implication nor a theorem for monotone inputs proves that negation.
cards.why: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.

references.title: Necklaces, Convolutions, and \(X+Y\)
references.authors: David Bremner; Timothy M. Chan; Erik D. Demaine; Jeff Erickson; Ferran Hurtado; John Iacono; Stefan Langerman; Mihai Pătraşcu; Perouz Taslakian
references.locator: Algorithmica 69, 294–314; introduction and section 3.

cards.context:
Min-plus convolution combines two cost profiles: entry \(c_k\) is the cheapest way to split the total index \(k\) between them. For \(A=(3,1)\) and \(B=(4,2)\), the output is \((7,5,3)\). The middle entry compares two different splits, while an endpoint has only one. All output positions are required simultaneously.

The direct computation checks every pair of input entries, producing a quadratic amount of work for a linear-size output. Unlike ordinary convolution, replacing sums of products by minima of sums changes the algebraic operation. The hypothesis is a computational barrier for this exact cost-combination primitive.

The 2026 paper records an unrestricted upper bound \(n^2/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\), obtained from earlier results. This is an improvement over quadratic time, but its exponent saving tends to zero with input length. The requested algorithm must save a fixed positive exponent, not merely a growing subpolynomial factor.

The same paper gives \(n^{1.5+o(1)}\) deterministic time when the arrays are monotone and their values obey the specified bounded-range condition. Neither monotonicity nor that special linear range is assumed by this card. Structured convolution is therefore a restricted positive result rather than an unrestricted resolution.

The established hypothesis name predicts a negative answer to the displayed algorithm-existence question. The card fixes a precise polynomially bounded integer formulation: one exponent saving works for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), while the implementation and constants may depend on \(a\). There is no claim about arbitrary real-number inputs or bit lengths growing faster than \(O(\log n)\).

The probability guarantee is for the entire output on each fixed input. A small error probability for each entry separately would not automatically give that guarantee for the full array. Likewise, average performance over an input distribution is different from the worst-case time and per-input correctness requirements.

cards.title: Randomized APSP hypothesis for polynomial integer weights
cards.formal: Is the following hypothesis true? \[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \neg\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] Here \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) means that a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the entire exact distance matrix of every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^c,n^c]\) and no negative-weight cycle, succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input, and has worst-case time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) over all inputs and coin sequences. The word model and the quantifiers hidden in this definition are specified below. The weight exponent \(c\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This makes explicit the weaker quantifier order stated in the 2026 source; the 2018 source's phrase about sufficiently large \(c\) did not specify that dependence.
cards.definitions:
For fixed integers \(n\ge2\) and \(c\ge1\), the vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input is \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order, with a presence flag for each ordered pair and, for each present edge, a signed integer weight \(w(u,v)\) satisfying \(|w(u,v)|\le n^c\). There is at most one edge per ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges are indicated by their flags. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle with negative total weight. Negative edges, zero-weight cycles and ties between shortest paths are allowed. For vertices \(u,v\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the minimum total weight of a finite directed walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or a separate unreachable symbol \(+\infty\) if there is no such walk. The empty walk has weight zero. Under the promise every reachable minimum is attained, \(d_G(u,u)=0\), and each finite distance has absolute value at most \((n-1)n^c\). The output consists of these \(n^2\) exact integers or unreachable flags in vertex-pair order; listing all path vertices is not required.

The machine is a word RAM with one fixed finite program. For a fixed integer \(a\ge c+4\), its word length on \(n\)-vertex inputs is \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each memory address and memory cell is one word. The input is one word for n followed in row-major order by two words for each matrix entry: its zero-or-one presence flag and its signed weight, with zero in the weight word when the flag is zero. The output uses the same row-major order and two words per entry: a zero-or-one finite-distance flag and its signed distance, with zero in the second word for unreachable pairs. Signed integers use two's-complement encoding; distances fit in a constant number of words. Word load, store, copy, comparison, conditional branch, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) each cost one step. Unsigned quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step. Division by zero is invalid; shifts by at least \(b(n)\) positions return zero. Algorithms may use several words for larger quantities, charging all operations. All accessed addresses must fit in a word. Work memory initially contains zero, and no input-dependent precomputed tables, advice or oracle are supplied. All preprocessing, table construction, memory operations and output writing count toward the time bound. One random instruction yields one fresh independent fair bit in one step. The input graph is fixed before the coins are drawn. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring random bits.

Precisely, \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) asserts the existence of a finite program \(A\), an integer word-size factor \(a\ge c+4\), and an integer constant \(C\ge1\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) and every promised graph, every run halts within \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps, and with probability at least \(2/3\) its entire output matrix equals \((d_G(u,v))_{u,v\in[n]}\). Correctness is joint for the matrix, rather than a separate bound for each entry. The program, \(a\) and \(C\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\) or the input graph. There is no requirement to classify or detect inputs that violate the promise. The exponent in the time bound concerns the number \(n\) of vertices; the input has \(\Theta(n^2)\) words and \(O(n^2\log n)\) bits for each fixed \(c,a\). Rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\) capture every possible fixed positive exponent saving.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed hypothesis, or of its full logical negation \[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] A refutation must therefore establish one common positive exponent saving for every fixed polynomial weight bound; programs and runtime constants may depend on \(c\). A proof of the hypothesis must rule out all uniform randomized algorithms in the specified model for a suitable \(c\) at each saving \(\varepsilon\). A deterministic-only lower bound, a barrier for a particular algorithm or reduction technique, or a truly subcubic algorithm only for one restricted weight regime does not settle the statement. Neither do approximate distances, random input distributions, single-source bounds, distributed round bounds or extra accurate predictions. A subpolynomial-factor improvement over cubic time alone is insufficient. This yes/no target concerns exact APSP algorithms; an unproved APSP hypothesis cannot be assumed as the proof of itself.
cards.why: The randomized APSP hypothesis is a principal foundation of fine-grained complexity. Resolving it would determine whether exact distances in general integer-weighted graphs admit a fixed polynomial improvement over cubic time, and would affect a large network of conditional bounds for graph, matrix, sequence and dynamic problems.

references.title: Truly Subquadratic 3SUM and Truly Subcubic APSP via Triangles in Sparse Lopsided Graphs
references.authors: Josh Alman and Virginia Vassilevska Williams
references.locator: Abstract and main APSP theorem for directed graphs with polynomially bounded integer weights.

cards.context:
The 2018 survey treats APSP as one of the central hypotheses used to explain polynomial-time barriers. Its model permits randomization and logarithmic machine words, and its graph weights are polynomially bounded signed integers with no negative cycle.

Fischer's 2026 formulation explicitly places the requested exponent saving before the weight exponent: for every saving there is a polynomial weight range that remains hard. Its footnote distinguishes the stronger hypothesis with one absolute weight exponent for all savings. The paper uses nonnegative weights and explicitly states equivalence with the signed, no-negative-cycle convention retained here.

Williams gives a randomized word-RAM algorithm for nonnegative integer weights bounded by \(M\) in time \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}+n^{2+o(1)}\log M\). For polynomial \(M\), this achieves a substantial improvement over cubic time while the saving remains subpolynomial in \(n\), so it does not provide a fixed exponent improvement.

The 2025 few-weights algorithms exploit a bound on the number of distinct edge weights associated with each vertex. Their truly subcubic results concern those restricted instances, whereas this hypothesis imposes no such bound.

The 2026 universe-reduction paper connects APSP to stronger hypotheses for small-weight and unweighted graphs. Its full equivalence is conditional on the matrix-multiplication exponent being two and on an additional algorithmic assumption from additive combinatorics; it proves neither the APSP hypothesis nor its negation.

The August 2026 lower bound concerns a class of black-box triangle reductions. It limits those reductions' ability to preserve precise running-time exponents, and does not establish a general lower bound for APSP algorithms.

A direct truly subcubic algorithm also satisfies the fine-grained Turing reduction from integer APSP to 3SUM. It computes the answer using zero oracle queries.

cards.title: Hitting Set conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Sets are supplied explicitly as \(d\)-bit incidence vectors; lists may contain repetitions and empty sets. Equivalently, the answer is yes if some vector \(a\in A\) has integer inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^d a_j b_j>0\) with every \(b\in B\). The coordinate sum is over integers, not modulo two. The dimension constant \(c\) is fixed independently of input size.

Use a word RAM with word length
\[
w=\max\!\left\{\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil,\ \lceil\log_2(2nd+n+d+8)\rceil\right\}.
\]
The second term ensures that the full explicit input and its headers fit in the address universe even for small \(n\) and a large fixed dimension constant \(c\). For every fixed \(c\), it is eventually dominated by the first term, so this finite-input correction leaves the stated asymptotic time hypothesis unchanged. Incidence vectors are packed into consecutive words, with unused bits zero. A machine has a finite program independent of \(n\), word-addressed memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, copies, comparisons, branches, arithmetic addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero may return zero. A uniformly random independent \(w\)-bit word is available at unit cost. Memory initially contains only the instance; any further preprocessing or lookup-table construction is charged. There are no oracles, advice or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily long integers.

A bounded-error algorithm must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input. Its runtime bound applies to every random tape and every input, not only in expectation. For fixed \(\varepsilon,c\), a forbidden algorithm would have constants \(K,n_0\) such that it takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) instructions for every \(n\ge n_0\); the constants and program may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\). Finite smaller instances must also be decided correctly within finite time.

The order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) is essential. Refutation requires one \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every fixed \(c\) there is an algorithm with that same exponent saving; it does not require the same program or multiplicative constant for all \(c\). Conversely, a faster algorithm at one small dimension constant does not refute the conjecture. Choosing integral \(c\) is harmless because extra zero coordinates pad smaller dimensions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated bounded-error word-RAM model. A refutation must supply a common positive exponent saving across all fixed dimension constants. A proof conditional on another unproved hypothesis is not a proof of this conjecture. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a restricted instruction set, or an isolated value of \(c\) does not suffice.
cards.why: This hypothesis captures a quadratic barrier with an existential choice followed by a universal test. It supports fine-grained lower bounds for graph radius, centers and quantified geometric problems where the more familiar two-existential-quantifier orthogonal-vectors hypothesis does not directly match the task. Settling it would clarify the role of quantifier order in fine-grained complexity.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm{P}.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). The deterministic program and its fixed time bound may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or length. All input access, arithmetic and output count in the [bit model](definitions.html#bit-model).

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm{P}.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: This asks whether independent random bits increase the set of total decision problems solvable efficiently. An equality would identify deterministic and randomized polynomial-time decision power; a separation would exhibit an inherent benefit of randomness even when a different deterministic algorithm is allowed.
