cards.context:
A randomized answer is allowed to be wrong with probability at most one third on any specified input. For example, correctness on 99% of all strings of each length would still fail this definition if a remaining string were always answered incorrectly. The uncertainty belongs to the machine’s internal choices, not to which inputs the user may supply.

Adleman’s theorem gives \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) allows a separate polynomial-size Boolean circuit at each input length, without requiring one efficient procedure that constructs these circuits. This is a nonuniform existence statement; the target requires one finite deterministic program for all lengths.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove a conditional equality: if a Boolean function computable in deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) has worst-case circuit complexity at least \(2^{\varepsilon n}\), for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and all sufficiently large \(n\), then \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\). Circuit complexity here counts gates of unrestricted nonuniform Boolean circuits over a fixed complete finite basis that compute the function correctly on every input of that length. The exponential lower-bound hypothesis is part of the theorem; this is not an unconditional equality or a theorem assuming only \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh and Zuckerman’s May 2026 preprint obtains finer conditional derandomization bounds for algorithms with a specified insensitivity property. For each fixed input, changing one uniformly chosen coin coordinate of a correct tape must rarely make the answer incorrect. Their two-sided version additionally constrains incorrect tapes that have a correct neighbor. Theorem 9.10 retains explicit circuit-hardness, insensitivity and error assumptions; these structural conditions are not properties required of every BPP program. The paper distinguishes hitting-set and pseudoentropy generators from general pseudorandom generators.

Tianrong Lin’s July 2026 revision states a direct claim of \(\mathrm{P}\subsetneq\mathrm{BPP}\) in Theorem 1.1, with additional claimed separations. That would answer this card negatively if its proof were valid. This review read the claimed theorem and checked its version history, but has not certified its proof or located independent primary validation in the bounded searches. It is therefore recorded as an unverified claim, and the card retains uncertain status.

cards.title: L versus BPL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, is it true that
\[\forall S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \Longrightarrow\ S\in\mathrm{L}?\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPL}\) consists of total decision languages recognized with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by one uniform randomized machine using logarithmic work space and polynomial time on every input and every random tape. The target is a uniform deterministic logarithmic-work-space decider for each such language.
cards.definitions:
A language \(S\) is a set of finite binary strings; put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). A machine has a finite program, one two-way read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input head cannot move outside the endmarkers. Work tapes are semi-infinite; their heads move by at most one cell per step. Space is the sum of the numbers of distinct work-tape cells visited, including blank cells. The read-only input and finite control are excluded from this count; all stored counters, arithmetic operands, history and auxiliary data are included. Acceptance or rejection is a halting control state, not an additional readable output tape.

A randomized transition can obtain at most one fresh independent fair bit. Past bits cannot be revisited unless retained in counted work space. There is no random-tape address, free clock, oracle, advice, or additional uncounted storage. A deterministic machine has the same tape model and no coin transitions. One ordinary machine transition costs one time step.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{BPL}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and positive integers \(K,C,d\) such that for every input \(x\) and every realization of its random choices, \(R\) visits at most
\[K\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\]
work cells and halts with a bit in at most \(T(n)=C(n+2)^d\) steps. In addition, for every \(x\),
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf 1_S(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
The probability is only over internal coins. Exactly, supply a uniform string \(u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}\), consuming one bit whenever requested and ignoring the unused suffix; the success requirement is
\[3\bigl|\{u\in\{0,1\}^{T(n)}:R(x;u)=\mathbf1_S(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{T(n)}.\]
This finite counting formula defines the probability; it is not an extra operation available to the machine. The space and time bounds hold on every random string, not merely in expectation. Success is required separately on every member and nonmember, not only for a typical input distribution. No promise excludes inputs with intermediate acceptance probability: a valid decider for \(S\) must meet the appropriate bound on every binary string.

Membership \(S\in\mathrm{L}\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(D\) and a positive integer \(K'\) such that for every \(x\), \(D\) halts with \(\mathbf1_S(x)\) and visits at most \(K'\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. In this bounded-input-head model there are only polynomially many configurations at a fixed input length. A halting deterministic run cannot repeat a configuration, so a separate polynomial time guarantee follows. The program and its constants may depend on \(S\), but not on the particular input or its length.

The deterministic machine may have a different space constant, time exponent and computation from the randomized decider. Uniformity means a single finite program serves all input lengths, without length-dependent advice. Deterministic machines are a special case of randomized machines, so \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{BPL}\). The question asks for the reverse inclusion of languages; it does not prescribe a pseudorandom-generator construction or a compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the inclusion in the statement, or of its logical negation
\[\exists S\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad S\in\mathrm{BPL}\ \land\ S\notin\mathrm{L}.\]
A positive proof must establish a uniform deterministic decider with one logarithmic work-space bound for every language satisfying the full randomized definition. A negative proof must establish one fixed total language with a valid bounded-error randomized decider and exclude every deterministic decider with every constant logarithmic space bound for that language.

Extra polylogarithmic space, a rereadable uncounted random tape, advice, an oracle, a promise-problem separation, or correctness only at selected lengths does not meet this target. A failed generator construction or a lower bound for a restricted family of simulations does not rule out all deterministic deciders. Unproved hardness assumptions yield conditional results only. This is a yes/no class-comparison question with an exact probability threshold, not a numerical approximation target.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness adds computational power when an algorithm can remember only logarithmically many bits of an arbitrarily long input. An equality would permit deterministic bounded-memory decision whenever bounded-error randomized decision is possible; a separation would show an inherent memory advantage of randomness.

cards.context:
Logarithmic memory is enough for a constant number of input-position counters but not for storing an arbitrary long random history. Fresh coins can guide the computation without remaining available afterward. Allowing the machine to freely revisit an entire random string changes the resource model, which is why the random-access convention is part of the question.

Saks and Zhou obtained deterministic simulation in \(O((\log n)^{3/2})\) space. Hoza’s Theorem 1.6 improves this to
\[O\!\left(\frac{(\log n)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{\log\log n}}\right)\]
as \(n\to\infty\). This remains larger than \(O(\log n)\). These are space bounds; they do not assert that the improved-space simulation also runs in polynomial time.

A read-once branching program is a finite layered computation: each newly read random symbol selects a transition to the next layer, and a designated final state determines the answer. Its width is the number of states per layer and its length is the number of symbols read. This represents the random part of a bounded-space computation after the ordinary input is fixed. Restricted transition structures or unusually short programs need not capture every BPL computation.

An ordinary pseudorandom generator approximates acceptance probabilities using a genuine distribution generated from a short uniform seed. A weighted generator instead associates possibly negative real weights with seeds and approximates acceptance through a signed weighted average. Such estimates can be useful for derandomization, but they are not themselves sampling probabilities. Improving weighted generators does not automatically supply an ordinary generator with identical parameters.

Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction into weighted generators, including dependence on the alphabet size. The revision explicitly attributes the relevant earlier arity/error implication to Cheng and Hoza. It retains the general BPL versus L question as open; neither its weighted output nor the conditional implication supplies the equality here.

Cheng and Wu’s July 2026 version gives \(O(\log w)\)-space derandomization for regular branching programs of width \(w\), length at most \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log w})}\), binary alphabet, and inverse-polynomial additive error. Regularity means that every consecutive-layer transition graph has the same incoming and outgoing degree at every vertex. Both regularity and the short-length regime are genuine hypotheses. The result does not cover arbitrary polynomial-length, polynomial-width programs representing general BPL computations.

Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction into weighted generators, including dependence on the alphabet size. The revision explicitly attributes the relevant earlier arity/error implication to Cheng and Hoza. It retains the general BPL versus L question as open; neither its weighted output nor the conditional implication supplies the equality here.

Cheng and Wu’s July 2026 version gives \(O(\log w)\)-space derandomization for regular branching programs of width \(w\), length at most \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log w})}\), binary alphabet, and inverse-polynomial additive error. Regularity means that every consecutive-layer transition graph has the same incoming and outgoing degree at every vertex. Both regularity and the short-length regime are genuine hypotheses. The result does not cover arbitrary polynomial-length, polynomial-width programs representing general BPL computations.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic finite-program algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,D\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n,w\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\), all integers, the algorithm specifies an integer seed length \(s=s(n,w,p)\ge0\) and a function
\[G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\]
with \(s\le Cq\), where \(q=\lceil\log _2 n\rceil+\lceil\log _2 w\rceil+p\), such that every length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program \(B\) satisfies
\[\left|\Pr_{u\sim U_s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\sim U_n}[B(z)=1]\right|\le 2^{-p}?\]
Here \(U_k\) is the uniform distribution on the \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). Require \(A\) to compute both \(s(n,w,p)\) and any requested bit \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), in at most \(Dq\) work bits and \((nw2^p)^D\) steps per call, in the model below. The same algorithm, constants and generator family must work for every parameter triple and every permitted program.
cards.definitions:
A length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program consists of nonempty finite layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_n\), each of size at most \(w\), a start state in \(V_0\), an accepting subset of \(V_n\), and functions \(\delta_{i,b}:V_{i-1}\to V_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\). On input \(z\), the state is updated by \(\delta_{i,z_i}\) at step \(i\); \(B(z)=1\) exactly when the final state is accepting. The bit order is \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\). Transitions may merge states, including two equally labeled edges from distinct states; no regularity or permutation promise is imposed. The transition tables, start state and accepting subset are arbitrary finite, possibly nonuniform data. The generator receives none of them.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and a mode flag. In the seed-length mode its input is \((n,w,p)\) and its output is \(s(n,w,p)\) in binary. In the bit mode its input is \((n,w,p,u,i)\) and it outputs exactly one bit before halting. Integer parameters use canonical binary notation with separators; the seed is its full binary string, with leading zeroes retained. Inputs occupy read-only tapes whose heads are bounded by endmarkers. There is a fixed finite number of initially blank, semi-infinite work tapes over \(\{0,1,\square\}\), with heads moving by at most one cell per transition. Each distinct work-tape cell visited is charged two work bits, including blank cells. This fixed encoding of tape symbols only fixes a constant in the space bound. All counters, arithmetic, stored history and preprocessing are charged; output is write-only and cannot serve as storage. There is no advice, oracle, external clock or other uncounted memory. Each transition costs one time step. The required bounds hold on every valid call, for every seed and requested index. Only the requested bit must be output in bit mode; there is no requirement to store the whole length-\(n\) string.

Probabilities are exact uniform finite averages. In particular, a seed always has weight \(2^{-s}\), even if several seeds produce the same string; signed weights and externally assigned coefficients are not permitted. The parameter \(p\) controls additive error, not failure probability of a randomized construction: \(A\) itself is deterministic. With \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\), the target is \(O(\log n+\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) seed length and work space. Ceiling conventions change only constants. Arbitrary \(0<\varepsilon<1\) can be covered by a dyadic tolerance no larger than \(\varepsilon\). No compression requirement \(s<n\) is imposed in parameter regimes where the displayed allowance is already at least \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existential proposition above or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a single finite program and universal constants, formalize its seed-length and bit computations, establish the stated worst-case resource bounds, and prove the additive-error inequality for every permitted program and every parameter triple. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform program and choice of constants; a limitation of one construction, one analysis or one restricted generator class is insufficient. The theorem must use the stated ordinary uniform-seed distribution and arbitrary merging transitions. A result solely for weighted generators, hitting sets or a restricted branching-program subclass does not meet this target.
cards.why: A solution would give a uniform optimal-seed pseudorandom distribution for arbitrary small-memory computations and imply L = BPL. It would close the central gap between the existence of short seeds and their computation in small space, beyond the structural restrictions and weighted approximations covered by current results.

cards.context:
A branching program models a stream computation that remembers only its current state. Its width \(w\) permits roughly \(\log_2 w\) memory bits, while its length \(n\) counts inspected input bits. The quantifiers require one distribution that works simultaneously for every allowed transition table. Computing a favorable distribution after seeing a particular table would answer a different question.

Short-seed distributions exist nonconstructively; in particular, seed length \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) is known for width-\(n\), length-\(n\) programs. The unresolved issue is explicit computation with the required space bound. An optimal ordinary generator of the kind requested here would imply \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\), the equality of deterministic and bounded-error randomized logarithmic-space decision classes. The card does not assert the converse implication.

The classical general bound is \(O(\log n\cdot\log(nw/\varepsilon))\) seed bits. For polynomial width and constant error, this becomes \(O(\log^2 n)\), whereas the requested bound is \(O(\log n)\). The September 2026 RANDOM paper still identifies this general gap, while distinguishing improvements in special width/length regimes.

Weighted generators approximate the acceptance probability by an average \(\mathbb E_u[\rho(u)B(G(u))]\), where \(\rho\) may take negative values. Hoza’s Theorem 1.5 obtains seed length \(O(\log(wn)\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) for this relaxed object. Such weights are useful for deterministic estimates but do not define the ordinary sampled distribution required in this question.

Cheng–Wu’s July 2026 version improves weighted constructions across several parameter regimes. Its optimal-space simulation theorem concerns regular programs in a short-wide regime, not arbitrary programs. A regular program has equal incoming and outgoing degree at each state of each consecutive-layer graph; general transitions in this question can concentrate many incoming edges at one state.

Chen and coauthors improve weighted error reduction and alphabet dependence in the September 2026 proceedings version. Its separate ordinary-generator implication assumes an ordinary PRG with stronger parameter dependence; the weighted theorem does not supply that assumption. The paper credits the earlier Cheng–Hoza result for this connection.

A hitting set guarantees at least one accepting output whenever the uniform acceptance probability exceeds a specified threshold. It need not approximate that probability. Cheng–Hoza prove that a logarithmic-space hitting set for polynomial-width programs would nevertheless imply \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\). Their conclusion about class derandomization does not itself produce the ordinary generator required by this card.

For permutation programs, each symbol acts bijectively between consecutive layers of equal size. Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber’s July 2026 theorem gives an ordinary generator with seed \(O((\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\log n)\), including arbitrary accepting subsets. The structural promise and remaining product of logarithms distinguish it from the general target.

Krak’s September 2026 preprint states a hitting-set result with seed \(O(\log(n/\varepsilon))\) for ordered width-three programs. The theorem is both a hitting guarantee and a constant-width result; its definition of explicitness requires polynomial time rather than the logarithmic workspace imposed here. This scope review does not independently certify the new proof.

cards.title: AM versus NP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm{AM}=\mathrm{NP}\)? Equivalently, does every language having an Arthur–Merlin protocol admit polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically in polynomial time?

For a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), an Arthur–Merlin protocol is specified by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and polynomially bounded lengths \(p(n),q(n)\). Arthur draws a uniform public string \(r\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\); after seeing \(x\) and \(r\), Merlin may choose a reply \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\). With \(n=|x|\), require
\[x\in L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\ge\tfrac23,\]
\[x\notin L\Longrightarrow\Pr_r[\exists y:\ V(x,r,y)=1]\le\tfrac13.\]
Must there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\) and a polynomially bounded length \(s(n)\) such that, for every binary string \(x\),
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(|x|)}:\ W(x,z)=1?\]
The resulting verifier and its polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but must work uniformly at all input lengths.
cards.definitions:
Languages are subsets of the finite binary strings. Every input string is either a yes-instance in the language or a no-instance outside it; the target is an equality of ordinary language classes. There is no omitted promise domain. Input size \(n\) is the full bit length of \(x\), and the empty input is allowed.

Use classical uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions. A polynomial time bound means \(C(n+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(a\ge0\). In a verifier taking several strings, time is polynomial in their total encoded length; the stated polynomial message bounds make this polynomial in \(n\) on protocol inputs. The verifier terminates on every such tuple, including misleading messages. It has no advice depending on the input length, oracle or quantum operation. All communication consists of ordinary binary strings.

The functions \(p,q,s:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) are computable in polynomial time and bounded by fixed polynomials. They may be taken to be integer-coefficient polynomial bounds, with unused bits ignored. Messages have the indicated exact lengths. Permitting shorter messages with a length encoding and padding gives the same class. Malformed messages are rejected according to the chosen verifier; they cannot provide an extra form of communication or uncounted computation.

The protocol has two messages: Arthur’s random challenge followed by Merlin’s reply. Arthur samples \(p(n)\) independent fair bits, so each challenge has probability \(2^{-p(n)}\). All of these bits are public before Merlin replies. The verifier’s final computation \(V(x,r,y)\) is deterministic; there is no additional hidden random tape. A zero-length challenge or reply is permitted. The polynomial defining each length is fixed for the protocol, not chosen separately for individual inputs.

Merlin is computationally unbounded. He knows the entire input and challenge and may choose a different reply for every pair \((x,r)\). Thus the existential quantifier over \(y\) is inside the probability over \(r\). Completeness says that on each yes-instance an accepting reply exists for at least two thirds of the challenges. Soundness says that on each no-instance an accepting reply exists for at most one third of them, even with an unbounded dishonest prover. Randomizing Merlin’s reply cannot increase the set of challenges for which some accepting reply exists.

These two probability conditions define \(\mathrm{AM}\). They are per-input guarantees. Neither the inputs nor Merlin’s strategy are averaged over an external distribution. The soundness bound is information-theoretic: it is not limited to efficient cheating provers. The fixed gap between two thirds and one third is part of the chosen standard definition; ordinary amplification yields equivalent constant-gap conventions. Perfect completeness is not an added requirement of this card.

The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages with a verifier \(W\) and certificate length \(s\) satisfying the displayed exact equivalence. On yes-instances at least one certificate is accepted, and on no-instances every certificate is rejected. The verifier is deterministic and has no random challenge. The certificate itself need not be found in polynomial time. A proof of AM containment in NP must establish existence of these certificates and their efficient verification, not efficient deterministic decision or witness generation.

The inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{AM}\) is immediate by letting the AM verifier ignore its challenge. Thus equality asks for the converse inclusion. A positive answer must cover every AM language. A negative answer must exhibit, or prove the existence of, an AM language that has no polynomially bounded deterministic certificate system. Failure of one proposed verifier, one circuit family or one polynomial exponent does not establish such a separation.

The quantifier order is \(\forall L\in\mathrm{AM}\;\exists W\;\exists s\;\forall x\), with a fixed polynomial running-time bound for each \(W\). There is no common required exponent for all languages. Equality of language classes does not additionally require a computable compiler from protocol descriptions to NP verifiers, although a proved general transformation would suffice. A certificate system whose exponent changes with the individual input is not polynomially bounded in this sense.

The related class \(\mathrm{MA}\) reverses the message order: Merlin supplies a certificate before Arthur’s fresh random choices. Moving \(\exists y\) outside the probability changes the condition and must not be done here. Standard results identify AM with constant-round interactive proofs, but the explicit two-message public-coin definition above is the target model. Protocols with an input-dependent polynomial number of rounds are not the target.

A promise problem consists of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), with no correctness requirement outside \(Y\cup N\). The notation \(\mathrm{prAM}\) refers to the analogous promise-protocol class. A claim that every promise-AM problem has a separating NP language is stronger than the ordinary language inclusion asked here and is not assumed equivalent. This distinction matters for the neighboring targeted-generator question TCS-1135 and for several recent derandomization theorems.

Graph nonisomorphism is an example consequence, not a completeness reformulation. A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges; two such graphs are isomorphic if some bijection between their vertex sets preserves adjacency. Graph nonisomorphism asks whether no such bijection exists, for explicitly encoded graph pairs. An NP certificate for nonisomorphism would be a polynomial-length binary witness of that negative assertion checked in polynomial time. Since graph nonisomorphism has an AM protocol, AM equality with NP would supply such certificates. Solving only that graph problem would not establish the full class equality without an additional proved completeness reduction.

For the conditional progress cited below, \(\mathrm{NE}=\bigcup_{c\ge1}\mathrm{NTIME}(2^{cn})\) and \(\mathrm{coNE}\) is its complement class. A single-valued nondeterministic Boolean circuit has ordinary input bits, auxiliary choice bits, and two outputs: a flag and a value bit. For every input some choice must set the flag to one, and every choice with flag one must give the correct value of the function. Choices with flag zero are ignored. Circuit size counts gates in a fixed fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT basis, together with auxiliary input bits. Circuits may vary nonuniformly with the input length. An exponential lower bound means that some \(\alpha>0\) requires size at least \(2^{\alpha n}\) for every sufficiently large length \(n\). This hardness hypothesis belongs to the cited conditional result and is not a premise of the question.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\mathrm{AM}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that some language lies in \(\mathrm{AM}\setminus\mathrm{NP}\), with the specified verifier, message-order, uniformity and probability conventions. Equality must supply the existence of polynomial-length certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification for every AM language on every input. It need not supply a deterministic decision algorithm or an efficient way to find the certificates. A separation must rule out every NP verifier and polynomial certificate bound for the chosen language. Conditional collapses, oracle results, simulations with advice, average-input correctness, larger time bounds and a certificate system only for graph nonisomorphism do not settle the unconditional class comparison. The default numerical approximation tolerance does not apply to this exact proposition.
cards.why: This asks whether short randomized interaction gives more verification power than static certificates. It is a fundamental derandomization question beyond decision algorithms, with consequences for certifying graph nonisomorphism and with close links to nondeterministic circuit hardness.

cards.context:
An NP proof is one static certificate that a deterministic verifier can check. In an Arthur–Merlin protocol, the prover first sees a fresh public challenge and can tailor the proof to it. The question asks whether this additional use of randomness and interaction changes which languages have efficient proofs.

The placement of the existential reply inside the probability is the defining feature. Different challenges may need different valid replies. A deterministic certificate system must verify the same membership claim without asking for that random challenge, while retaining polynomial certificate length and verification time.

Graph nonisomorphism illustrates why this matters. A relabeling certifies that graphs are isomorphic, while certifying that no relabeling works is a different verification task. The known AM protocol for nonisomorphism gives an interactive justification; equality with NP would guarantee static, efficiently checkable certificates.

Miltersen and Vinodchandran show that an exponential lower bound against single-valued nondeterministic circuits for a language in the intersection of nondeterministic and co-nondeterministic exponential time implies AM equality with NP. The published theorem weakens earlier circuit-hardness hypotheses, but does not establish the required hardness premise.

The 2025 work of van Melkebeek and Mocelin Sdroievski develops conditional connections between Arthur–Merlin derandomization and uniform hardness or constructive refutation. Its main near-equivalences carefully distinguish ordinary protocols from promise protocols and account for advice. These are refinements of the conditions under which derandomization follows, not an unconditional collapse.

The same paper gives an unconditional weaker simulation in a different resource model: it uses a second-level quantified machine, subexponential time and a short advice string, and is guaranteed on most inputs at infinitely many lengths. Its theorem therefore leaves several requirements of ordinary NP verification unmet, including the time bound, lack of advice and correctness on all inputs.

A positive answer would eliminate random interaction as a source of additional polynomial-time proof power for this class. It would not make NP membership efficiently decidable. A negative answer would establish that some efficiently verifiable interactive claims inherently lack static polynomial-time certificates.

context_blocks.text: An NP proof is one static certificate that a deterministic verifier can check. In an Arthur–Merlin protocol, the prover first sees a fresh public challenge and can tailor the proof to it. The question asks whether this additional use of randomness and interaction changes which languages have efficient proofs.

The placement of the existential reply inside the probability is the defining feature. Different challenges may need different valid replies. A deterministic certificate system must verify the same membership claim without asking for that random challenge, while retaining polynomial certificate length and verification time.

Graph nonisomorphism illustrates why this matters. A relabeling certifies that graphs are isomorphic, while certifying that no relabeling works is a different verification task. The known AM protocol for nonisomorphism gives an interactive justification; equality with NP would guarantee static, efficiently checkable certificates.

Miltersen and Vinodchandran show that an exponential lower bound against single-valued nondeterministic circuits for a language in the intersection of nondeterministic and co-nondeterministic exponential time implies AM equality with NP. The published theorem weakens earlier circuit-hardness hypotheses, but does not establish the required hardness premise.

The 2025 work of van Melkebeek and Mocelin Sdroievski develops conditional connections between Arthur–Merlin derandomization and uniform hardness or constructive refutation. Its main near-equivalences carefully distinguish ordinary protocols from promise protocols and account for advice. These are refinements of the conditions under which derandomization follows, not an unconditional collapse.

The same paper gives an unconditional weaker simulation in a different resource model: it uses a second-level quantified machine, subexponential time and a short advice string, and is guaranteed on most inputs at infinitely many lengths. Its theorem therefore leaves several requirements of ordinary NP verification unmet, including the time bound, lack of advice and correctness on all inputs.

A positive answer would eliminate random interaction as a source of additional polynomial-time proof power for this class. It would not make NP membership efficiently decidable. A negative answer would establish that some efficiently verifiable interactive claims inherently lack static polynomial-time certificates.

cards.title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. An algorithm decides \(L\) if it halts and outputs one exactly on inputs in \(L\), and zero on all other inputs. Use uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. One transition costs one time unit. A randomized machine may additionally request independent unbiased bits, at unit cost per bit. It has no advice, oracle or preprocessing that depends on input length without being computed by the machine.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there are such a randomized machine \(M\) and constants \(a,C\ge1\) with worst-case runtime at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every length-\(n\) input and every random tape, and with
\[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3.\]
This is a class of total decision problems. The acceptance-probability gap holds on every input; it is not a promise that an external user must supply.

The notation \(L\in\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{1/k}})\) means that a deterministic machine decides \(L\) and has worst-case runtime at most \(C_k\lceil2^{n^{1/k}}\rceil\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some fixed \(C_k\). All finitely many smaller inputs must also be decided correctly and with termination. Requiring every integer \(k\) is equivalent to requiring time \(O(2^{n^\varepsilon})\) for every fixed real \(\varepsilon>0\). The machine is allowed to change with the exponent; an effective compiler taking \(M,k\) and producing the simulator is not an additional requirement.

This definition of SUBEXP is the source's intersection of subpower-exponential time classes. A single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time bound, such as \(2^{n/\log n}\), need not meet it. Likewise, correctness only on most inputs, or on infinitely many input lengths, is insufficient. The simulator must decide the same language exactly on all strings.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion or its negation. A positive proof must cover every BPP language and every fixed exponent \(1/k\), without a hardness assumption, oracle or advice. A negative proof must establish a language in BPP that is outside one of the deterministic time classes in the displayed intersection. A conditional simulation, a simulation for a particular randomized problem, or a heuristic correct on almost all inputs does not settle the question.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness can provide a much larger speedup than the usual derandomization conjectures predict, even after allowing deterministic time far beyond polynomial. An unconditional simulation would move the general worst-case upper bound into the source’s much smaller subexponential class. A counterexample would establish a major separation between randomized and deterministic computation.

cards.context:
Enumerating every random tape gives a deterministic simulation in \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\) time. A polynomial-time randomized algorithm can use polynomially many random bits, so this direct simulation gives EXP rather than the displayed SUBEXP target.

If \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{P}\), the desired inclusion follows. The converse is not asserted: a subexponential simulator may still take much more than polynomial time.

Known hardness-versus-randomness theorems yield much stronger derandomization under suitable circuit lower-bound assumptions. For example, the Impagliazzo–Wigderson theorem derives BPP = P from exponential circuit hardness for a language computable in single-exponential time. Those hardness hypotheses are part of the conditional theorem and cannot be removed by citing it.

Fixing a good random tape separately for each length gives a nonuniform object. Uniformity requires a finite deterministic algorithm that computes its behavior; a sequence of good tapes supplied for free does not meet the target.

cards.title: Pseudorandom generators from hitting-set generators
cards.formal:
Does the existence of a polynomial-time hitting-set generator secure against all polynomial-size Boolean circuits imply the existence of a polynomial-time pseudorandom generator secure against all such circuits, in the cryptographic regime defined below? In symbols, decide
\[
\bigl(\exists H\;\operatorname{HSG}(H)\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\bigl(\exists G\;\operatorname{PRG}(G)\bigr).
\]
Both generators must be uniform, have a seed shorter than their output, and meet their respective security conditions with negligible error. Their seed lengths, negligible functions and polynomial running-time bounds may differ. This is an implication between existence statements; it does not require an algorithm that compiles a given hitting-set generator into a pseudorandom generator.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(m\ge 0\), let \(U_m\) denote the uniform distribution on the \(2^m\) binary strings of length \(m\). Output lengths are integers \(N\ge 2\). An admissible generator family \(F=(F_N)_{N\ge 2}\) has a seed-length function \(s:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to\mathbb N\) with \(1\le s(N)<N\) and maps \(F_N:\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\to\{0,1\}^{N}\). One deterministic multitape Turing machine computes \(s(N)\) from \(1^N\), and another computes \(F_N(z)\) from \((1^N,z)\) for every seed \(z\). Here \(1^N\) is the unary encoding of \(N\). There are constants \(A,b\ge 1\), depending only on the family, such that each computation takes at most \(A(N+1)^b\) steps. In particular, time is polynomial in the output length. A machine has finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes with a fixed finite alphabet. In one step each head reads and may move by at most one cell, each work head may write one symbol, and at most one output bit may be appended. All tapes start at their first cell and are indexed by nonnegative integers; a left move at zero stays at zero. The generator input is the literal string \(1^N\#z\), and the seed-length output is the binary encoding of \(s(N)\). The machine programs and tape counts are independent of \(N\). These machines receive no advice, oracle or randomness. The output need not contain the seed, and different seeds may have the same output.

A test at length \(N\) is an arbitrary deterministic Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^{N}\to\{0,1\}\), with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one, constant gates, unrestricted fan-out and unrestricted depth. Its size is its number of gates, excluding the input nodes. There is no uniformity requirement on tests at different lengths. Security against polynomial-size circuits means the quantifier \(\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\) followed by a threshold length that may depend on \(c\), and then a guarantee for every circuit of size at most \(N^c\) at every larger length.

Use the [negligible-function convention](definitions.html#crypto) in \(N\). The functions here take values in \((0,1]\) for \(N\ge2\). No computability assumption is imposed on a security-bound function.

For an admissible family \(H\) with seed length \(s\), the property \(\operatorname{HSG}(H)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists N_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge N_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\ge\varepsilon(N)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{s(N)}\; C(H_N(z))=1.
\]
The hit is an existence guarantee; it need not occur with any specified fraction of seeds.

For an admissible family \(G\) with its own seed length \(t\), the property \(\operatorname{PRG}(G)\) means that there exists a negligible function \(\eta\) such that
\[
\forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\ \exists M_c\ge 2\ \forall N\ge M_c\ \forall C\text{ of size at most }N^c,
\]
\[
\left|\Pr_{z\sim U_{t(N)}}[C(G_N(z))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_N}[C(x)=1]\right|\le\eta(N).
\]
Thus generated outputs are sampled by a uniform seed, with multiplicity when seeds collide. The same generator and the same negligible function must serve every circuit-size exponent. In the implication, all generator, seed-length, time-bound and security-bound witnesses are existentially quantified separately on the two sides.
cards.answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the stated existence implication or of its negation. A positive answer must establish the existence of a generator satisfying the full PRG definition whenever a generator satisfying the HSG definition exists. A negative answer must establish that an HSG as defined exists while no PRG as defined exists, in the stated ordinary model. A theorem restricted to a smaller test class, additional hardness assumptions, infinitely many lengths, or the impossibility of a particular conversion method does not decide this implication.
cards.why: This asks whether hitting dense sets and reproducing acceptance probabilities have the same existential power when a uniform efficient generator must withstand arbitrarily stronger polynomial-size tests. Pseudorandom generators are foundational cryptographic objects connected to one-way functions, while the weaker hitting guarantee arises naturally from errorless average-case hardness. A resolution would clarify whether these two notions represent distinct assumptions about computational randomness, rather than merely improve the parameters of one construction.

cards.title: Explicit near-optimal vertex expanders
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every rational \(\delta>0\), there exists an integer \(d_0\ge3\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge d_0\), there exist a rational \(\eta\in(0,1/2)\), real \(K>0\), integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) which, for every integer \(j\ge1\) supplied in unary, outputs a finite simple undirected \(d\)-regular graph \(G_j\) within \(K(j+1)^a\) bit operations, with strictly increasing vertex counts \(n_j=|V(G_j)|\), and such that \[|\Gamma_{G_j}(S)\setminus S|\ \ge\ (d-2-\delta)|S|\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V(G_j)\text{ with }1\le |S|\le\eta n_j?\]
cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has no loops or multiple edges. It is \(d\)-regular if each vertex has exactly \(d\) distinct neighbors. Its labeled vertex set is \([n_j]=\{1,\ldots,n_j\}\). For \(S\subseteq[n_j]\), define
\[
\Gamma_{G_j}(S)=\{v\in[n_j]:\ \exists u\in S,\ \{u,v\}\in E(G_j)\}.
\]
The left side in the target counts distinct neighbors outside \(S\), not edges leaving \(S\), not neighbors counted with multiplicity, and not neighbors inside \(S\). The cutoff \(\eta n_j\) is a real number; the condition is imposed on every integer set size satisfying the displayed inequality. Empty sets impose no requirement. The same positive \(\eta\) works for the entire family at the fixed values of \(\delta,d\).

The output of \(A\) is \(n_j\) in binary followed by an explicit list of the edges, each an unordered pair of distinct binary vertex labels, with delimiters. Isolated vertices would still be specified by \(n_j\), although none occur for \(d\ge3\). Reading the unary index, all computation and every output bit count in the bound. The machine has a finite program, no random bits, advice, oracle or uncharged preprocessing. It must work on every \(1^j\), not merely on infinitely many selected indices. The integers \(n_j\) must increase strictly, so the construction gives arbitrarily large graphs; an allowed family need not contain every admissible vertex count.

The degree threshold \(d_0\) may depend on \(\delta\). After \(d\) is fixed, the machine \(A\) and constants \(\eta,K,a\) may depend on both \(\delta,d\), but not on \(j\) or \(S\). No algorithm uniform in \(\delta,d\) is required. The construction requirement is the survey's mild explicitness convention, polynomial time in the family index, with full output charged. It does not additionally require computing one neighbor in time polynomial in \(\log n_j\). Restricting positive \(\delta\) and the small-set fraction to rationals loses no expansion guarantee: a smaller positive rational tolerance or fraction can be chosen when needed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the entire proposition, including the explicit algorithm families, their cost bounds and the expansion inequality for all indicated sets, or a complete Lean proof of its negation. Random existence alone is insufficient. A construction with a relative loss tending to zero as degree grows does not meet this additive-loss target without a proof of the displayed bound with the stated quantifier order. A result for one degree or a one-sided bipartite expansion promise does not by itself establish the proposition.
cards.why: Random regular graphs have almost the largest possible external neighborhood for every small set. Matching that additive guarantee by deterministic constructions would sharpen a central benchmark for expanders, with consequences for combinatorial structures underlying coding, routing and pseudorandomness.

cards.context:
The saved survey explicitly asks for \(d-2-\delta\) external vertex expansion for every sufficiently large degree, with a positive small-set fraction depending on \(d,\delta\). This card preserves that additive target. Definitions 2.3 and 4.6 supply the mild explicitness and external-neighborhood conventions; it does not replace the question by a relative \((1-\varepsilon)d\) target.

Theorem 4.16 shows that random regular graphs have the displayed small-set expansion asymptotically. This establishes the combinatorial feasibility of the bound, not a deterministic polynomial-time family.

Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner and Zhang give explicit lossless expanders: for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large degrees admit a \((1-\varepsilon)d\) distinct-neighbor guarantee. Their introduction cites the survey question as a longstanding problem addressed by their construction.

The two quantitative formulations are not identical. A degree threshold depending on \(\varepsilon\) does not by itself justify taking \(\varepsilon\) proportional to \(1/d\) at the same degree. Moreover, counting all distinct neighbors and counting only external neighbors differ. The review therefore does not infer the exact additive \(d-2-\delta\) proposition from the stated relative-loss theorem.

The November 2026 construction adds a full-rank adjacency guarantee. Its expansion theorem still fixes the relative loss in advance, and gives degrees depending on that choice.

cards.title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
cards.formal:
Does there exist an integer \(C\ge0\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) defining functions
\[
E_n:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}\qquad(n\ge1)
\]
such that, for every \(n\) and every two independent probability distributions \(X,Y\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\) with
\[
H_\infty(X),H_\infty(Y)\ge\log_2 n+C,
\]
we have
\[
\left|\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]-\frac12\right|\le\frac1{100}?
\]
The algorithm receives only \(n\) and the two strings. The same additive constant, finite program and polynomial running-time bound must work for all lengths and all eligible distributions.
cards.definitions:
Write \(S_n=\{0,1\}^n\) for all binary strings of length \(n\). A probability distribution on this finite set is any function \(p:S_n\to[0,1]\) with real values and \(\sum_xp(x)=1\). Its min-entropy is
\[
H_\infty(p)=-\log_2\!\left(\max_{x\in S_n}p(x)\right).
\]
Thus the required entropy condition means \(p(x)\le 1/(2^C n)\) for every string \(x\). Distributions need not be uniform on their support, rational, computable or efficiently samplable. Independence means that the joint distribution is \(\Pr[X=x,Y=y]=p(x)q(y)\). The output probability in the question is the finite sum
\[
\Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]=\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\,\mathbf1_{\{E_n(x,y)=1\}}.
\]
The indicator is one when its subscripted condition holds and zero otherwise. For a single output bit, the displayed bias is its statistical distance from the uniform bit, where statistical distance between distributions \(r,s\) on a finite set is \(\frac12\sum_z|r(z)-s(z)|\). There is no conditioning on either source in this guarantee.

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and fixed finite tape alphabet. Its read-only input is \(1^n\#x\#y\), where \(|x|=|y|=n\), and its work tapes initially contain blanks. One transition reads and writes at most one symbol on each tape and moves each tape head by at most one cell, costing one step. There are no random coins, oracle calls, auxiliary seed, advice or length-dependent precomputed tables. The machine must halt and output exactly one bit on every such input. There must be integers \(K,d\ge1\) such that this takes at most \(K(n+1)^d\) transitions for all \(n,x,y\), including inputs at lengths with no eligible sources. The input contains no distribution description or samples other than \(x,y\); \(C,K,d\) and the machine are fixed existential choices, independent of both distributions and of \(n\). Let \(\mathcal A\) be the class of all machines meeting this total polynomial-time evaluation condition, and write \(E^A_n\) for the function computed by a member \(A\).

Only the probability bound concerns the random choice of the two input strings; the evaluator itself is deterministic. When \(\log_2n+C>n\), no eligible distribution exists, so the extraction requirement at that length is vacuous. Using a nonnegative integer for the existential additive constant fixes a harmless convention: any fixed real constant can be increased to such an integer. The task has one output bit and fixed error \(1/100\); it does not demand arbitrarily small error, more output bits or resilience to tampering.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence proposition, including one finite machine, its uniform polynomial-time bound and the probability guarantee for all eligible distributions. Alternatively, give a complete Lean proof of its logical negation: for every integer \(C\ge0\) and every \(A\in\mathcal A\), there exist \(n\ge1\) and distributions \(p,q\) on \(S_n\), each having min-entropy at least \(\log_2n+C\), for which
\[
\left|\sum_{x,y\in S_n}p(x)q(y)\mathbf1_{\{E^A_n(x,y)=1\}}-\frac12\right|>\frac1{100}.
\]
In this negation the length and distributions may depend on the machine and additive constant. A construction requiring \(c\log_2n\) entropy for an unspecified constant \(c>1\), nonuniform existence alone, or a conditional implication does not establish the displayed unconditional target.
cards.why: The additive threshold asks whether polynomial-time evaluation can match the entropy scale available without an efficiency restriction, including its leading coefficient. It is a basic question about converting two independent imperfect sources into a nearly unbiased bit and has consequences for explicit Ramsey constructions.

cards.title: Seeded extraction with constant total entropy loss
cards.formal:
Do there exist an explicit family of ordinary seeded extractors and absolute constants \(C,\Delta\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge2\) and \(0\le k\le n\), the family supplies a function
\[\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{d(n,k)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m(n,k)}\]
with
\[d(n,k)\le C\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad 0\le k+d(n,k)-m(n,k)\le\Delta,\]
and, for every distribution \(X\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) with min-entropy at least \(k\),
\[\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\operatorname{Ext}_{n,k}(X,U_{d(n,k)}),U_{m(n,k)}\bigr)\le1/100?\]
The seed is uniform and independent of \(X\). Explicitness means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(n\), with the same algorithm and polynomial for all \(n,k\). This is the constant-total-entropy-loss question in Vadhan's Open Problem 6.41.
cards.definitions:
All lengths \(n,k,d,m\) are integers measured in bits, with \(d,m\ge0\), and logarithms have base two. For a finite random variable \(X\),
\[H_{\infty}(X)=-\log_2\max_x\Pr[X=x].\]
Thus the source promise is \(\Pr[X=x]\le2^{-k}\) for every \(n\)-bit string \(x\). The source may have arbitrary dependencies between its coordinates and need not be samplable by an efficient algorithm. The extractor receives a sample string, not a description of its distribution. \(U_t\) denotes the uniform distribution on all \(t\)-bit strings, including the unique empty string when \(t=0\). For distributions \(P,Q\) on the same finite set,
\[\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|.\]
The condition is statistical and quantifies over every promised source, with no computational restriction on a test of the output.

A family is explicit if there are two fixed deterministic multitape Turing machines and integers \(K,q\ge1\): a parameter machine on \((1^n,k)\), with \(k\) in binary, outputs \(d(n,k),m(n,k)\) in binary; an evaluation machine on \((1^n,k,x,y)\) outputs the entire \(m(n,k)\)-bit string. Both halt within \(K(n+1)^q\) steps on all valid inputs. All preprocessing and output writing are counted. There is no advice, oracle, randomized construction or length-dependent table supplied for free. The machines, \(C,\Delta,K,q\) are chosen before \(n,k\) and before the source distribution.

Total entropy loss means \(k+d-m\): it counts the source's guaranteed entropy together with all perfect seed bits consumed. This ordinary extractor requirement concerns the output distribution alone. It does not require that the output remain uniform when the seed is separately disclosed. A strong extractor, whose output is uniform jointly with a disclosed seed, may be converted to an ordinary one by including its seed in the total output, but those seed bits must then be counted in \(m\). The convention \(m\le k+d\) is harmless output truncation for this error level. Integer entropy thresholds suffice for the stated additive-constant target; rounding down a real threshold changes the loss by less than one bit.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform construction claim. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and universal constants and prove the extraction guarantee, logarithmic seed bound, constant total loss and polynomial evaluation time throughout the parameter domain. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform family. An existence proof without efficient evaluation, a loss growing with \(n\) or \(k\), or an output bound that ignores consumed seed entropy does not meet the criterion.
cards.why: This asks whether an efficient general randomness purifier can preserve all but a constant number of the available random bits while using only a logarithmic seed. In applications that enumerate seeds or pay exponentially for entropy loss, the additive loss determines a multiplicative cost. Resolving the question would distinguish information-theoretic feasibility from the achievable efficiency of explicit extraction.

cards.title: Subpolynomial-seed pseudorandom generators for \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\)
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), is there an unconditional, mildly explicit generator family
\[
G_{k,m}:\{0,1\}^{d_k(m)}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{m}\qquad(m\ge1)
\]
whose integer seed length satisfies \(d_k(m)=m^{o(1)}\), and which fools every depth-at-most-\(k\), size-at-most-\(m\) \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[2]\) circuit on \(m\) input bits with error at most \(1/4\)?

Precisely, for every such circuit \(C\),
\[
\left|\Pr_{s\sim U_{d_k(m)}}[C(G_{k,m}(s))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_m}[C(x)=1]\right|\le1/4.
\]
The generator for a given \(k,m\) must work simultaneously for all the indicated circuits and cannot depend on \(C\). “Mildly explicit” means uniform deterministic evaluation in time polynomial in \(m\) and \(2^{d_k(m)}\), with the polynomial permitted to depend on \(k\).
cards.definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output bit. Input nodes carry literals \(x_i\), their negations \(\neg x_i\), or constants \(0,1\), for \(1\le i\le m\). Every computation node is an AND, OR or parity gate with arbitrarily many predecessors. AND is one exactly when all its input bits are one; OR is one exactly when at least one is one; parity is the sum of its inputs modulo two. For no predecessors, AND is one and OR and parity are zero. Fan-out is unrestricted. Gates may be used at any depth, and parity gates may feed other parity gates or either Boolean gate type.

Size counts computation nodes only. Input literals and constants are free input nodes. Depth is the maximum number of computation nodes along a directed path from an input to the output; a literal or constant output has depth zero. There is no restriction on wires beyond a finite circuit description, and no requirement that the testing circuit descriptions be generated uniformly over lengths. Negations are available at inputs as in the source definition. Allowing complemented parity outputs or internal NOT gates gives the same all-fixed-depth target after routine constant changes in resources, but the formal statement uses the specified basis.

For an integer \(\ell\ge0\), \(U_\ell\) is the uniform distribution on all \(\ell\)-bit strings; \(U_0\) is concentrated on the empty string. Randomness consists only of the uniformly chosen seed. The generator is a deterministic map, may have collisions and outputs exactly \(m\) bits. The two probabilities use independent draws from the stated uniform domains.

For each fixed \(k\), a single function \(d_k:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb N_{\ge0}\) must satisfy
\[
\forall a>0\ \exists M_{k,a}\ \forall m\ge M_{k,a}:\ d_k(m)\le m^a.
\]
This defines the subpolynomial seed requirement. It does not ask merely for one fixed sublinear power, nor permit choosing a different generator family separately for each \(a\).

Uniform mild explicitness requires deterministic algorithms for computing \(d_k(m)\) and evaluating \(G_{k,m}(s)\). There are constants \(A_k\ge1,b_k\ge1\) such that on input \(1^m\) the first algorithm outputs the binary encoding of \(d_k(m)\), and on input \((1^m,s)\), with \(|s|=d_k(m)\), the second outputs \(G_{k,m}(s)\), each within
\[
A_k\bigl(m+2^{d_k(m)}+1\bigr)^{b_k}
\]
steps. Use the ordinary uniform deterministic multitape Turing model: finitely many tapes and finite alphabets, initially blank work tapes, and one-cell head moves per transition. Input access and output writing are charged. There is no advice, random construction, oracle, unbounded unit-cost arithmetic or assumed computational hardness. The programs and constants may depend on the fixed \(k\); no efficient procedure producing them from \(k\) is required. A fully explicit polynomial-in-\(m\) evaluation algorithm also qualifies, but is not required.

The size parameter is the source's number of computation gates and is set equal to the output length. The requested error bound is the absolute difference of acceptance probabilities, with no averaging over circuits. It must hold at every positive \(m\); only the seed-length estimate is asymptotic.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction or a proof that the asserted family cannot exist. A positive answer must prove the uniform evaluation bound, the subpolynomial seed condition and the \(1/4\) fooling guarantee for every fixed depth and every circuit in the stated class. A construction using a hardness assumption, treating only one depth, restricting the locations or number of parity gates, or providing only a fixed sublinear seed exponent does not suffice. This is an existence question with its own exact error threshold; numerical \(1/100\) answer tolerance does not replace the \(1/4\) pseudorandomness condition.
cards.why: Adding parity gates is a basic step beyond constant-depth AND/OR circuits, yet existing worst-case lower bounds do not supply the strong average-case guarantees used by standard generator constructions. A generator with the requested seed would permit deterministic seed enumeration in subexponential time for the entire fixed-depth class. The question probes a central gap between proving circuit lower bounds and turning them into useful pseudorandomness.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. Use [FPT and FPT many-one reductions](definitions.html#parameterized). Here the parameter is the requested clique size \(k\). The languages reducible to this parameterized Clique problem form \(\mathrm{W}[1]\). Hence an FPT algorithm for Clique is equivalent to \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

cards.context:
For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions:
Use the shared [bounded-width CNF encoding and rate \(s_q\)](definitions.html#sat-encoding). The exponential term uses the number of distinct variables \(n(F)\). The polynomial factor uses the full input length \(N(F)\), including every repeated clause. The decider may depend on the fixed width \(q\).

This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(N(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from \(\varepsilon\) to a machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

references.title: Mind the Gap? Not for SVP Hardness Under ETH!
references.authors: Divesh Aggarwal; Rishav Gupta; Aditya Morolia; Chuanqi Zhang
references.locator: ICALP 2026, Article 8, published 1 July 2026; Definition 2.10 distinguishes deterministic/randomized ETH, Definition 2.11 separates Gap-ETH, and Theorems 1.1–1.2 specify the different lattice consequences.

cards.context:
NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.

cards.title: Set Cover conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
cards.definitions:
Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\). Each set is represented by its sorted list of distinct element indices in binary; the family is an explicitly supplied list without duplicate sets. Empty sets and an empty family are allowed. Write \(m=|\mathcal F|\). For fixed \(d\),
\[m\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(d,n)}\binom nj\le(n+1)^d,\]
so the entire valid input has length polynomial in \(n\), with its degree allowed to depend on \(d\). The threshold can be capped at \(n\), since any cover contains a subcover of at most \(n\) sets. The question counts the universe size, not the number of available sets or selected sets, in the exponential part of the time bound.

Use a uniform random-access machine with finite program, binary words of length \(w=\lceil4(n+\log_2(m+2)+1)\rceil\), and word-addressed memory. This allows the usual exponential-size dynamic-programming tables while keeping each word polynomially many bits long. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copies, branches, comparisons, addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer division with remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and obtaining a uniformly random independent word. Shifts by at least \(w\) and division by zero may return zero. Initially memory holds only the input and otherwise zeroes. Every table construction and preprocessing operation is counted. The machine has no oracle or nonuniform advice, and no operation acts on an exponentially long bit string as one word. Charging polynomial bit cost for scalar word operations only alters the allowed polynomial factor.

A randomized algorithm must return the correct decision with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input and halt within its asserted time bound on every random tape. The bound means that for a fixed \(d,\varepsilon\), there are constants \(K,r,n_0\) for which runtime is at most \(K(2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\) whenever \(n\ge n_0\). All finite smaller valid instances must also be correctly decided. These constants and the program may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but not on \(n,\mathcal F,t\).

The negation is a single \(\varepsilon>0\) that works for every fixed \(d\), allowing a different algorithm and polynomial factor for each \(d\). An improved base for one particular set-size bound does not refute the conjecture. The decision version used here and the source's minimum-cover optimization version have the same exponential base: searching thresholds and recovering a cover uses only polynomially many calls for fixed \(d\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated randomized computational model. A refutation must give a uniform positive improvement of the exponential base across every fixed maximum set size. Proving a lower bound assuming SETH or another conjecture, restricting to deterministic algorithms, improving one bounded-size case, or counting only arithmetic operations on unbounded-size objects does not settle this target.
cards.why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.
