cards.title: Strictness of the W-hierarchy
cards.formal:
Is the \(W\)-hierarchy strict at every positive level?
\[
\forall\,t\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad
W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1].
\]
The classes use uniform deterministic fixed-parameter many-one reductions and exact-weight satisfiability of bounded-depth Boolean circuits, as defined below. Equivalently, for every \(t\ge1\), is there a parameterized decision problem in \(W[t+1]\) that does not belong to \(W[t]\)?
cards.definitions:
A parameterized decision problem is a set \(P\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\times\mathbb N\). An input is a finite binary string \(x\) together with a nonnegative integer \(k\), its parameter. The input length \(L\) includes both \(x\) and the binary encoding of \(k\), with delimiters. Membership is an exact yes/no question.

Use [FPT many-one reductions](definitions.html#parameterized) in the deterministic [bit model](definitions.html#bit-model). Both the input and output parameters belong to the encoded pairs. Time includes writing the target instance.

A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with at least one input node and a designated output node of outdegree zero. Nodes of indegree zero are distinct Boolean input variables. Each other node is either a NOT gate of indegree one or an AND or OR gate of indegree at least two, with the usual Boolean semantics. Gates have unrestricted fan-out. A gate is large if its indegree exceeds two. The depth of the circuit is the maximum number of edges on a path from an input node to the designated output. Its weft is the maximum number of large gates on such a path. Unused input nodes are allowed and still count among the input variables.

For an explicit encoding, order all \(N\) nodes topologically, put the \(n\) input nodes first, and give the integers \(n,N\) and the output-node index, followed by each remaining gate's type, indegree and list of distinct predecessor indices. Predecessors must have smaller indices. Encode each integer \(u\ge0\) by \(1^{h}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary representation of \(u+1\) and \(h=|w|\); encode gate types NOT, AND, OR by integers \(1,2,3\). All listed integers use this code, and there are no trailing bits. Invalid encodings are no-instances in the circuit problems below.

For fixed integers \(t,d\ge1\), let \(\operatorname{WCS}_{t,d}\) be the parameterized problem consisting of pairs \((C,k)\) where \(C\) is an encoded circuit of weft at most \(t\) and depth at most \(d\), and some assignment to its input nodes has exactly \(k\) ones and makes its output one. The parameter is \(k\) alone. Circuits exceeding either structural bound, or having fewer than \(k\) input nodes, are no-instances.

Define
\[
W[t]=\{P:\ \exists\,d\ge1\text{ such that }P
\text{ has a fixed-parameter many-one reduction to }
\operatorname{WCS}_{t,d}\}.
\]
The integer \(d\) may depend on the problem \(P\) and level \(t\), but it is a fixed constant independent of the input and its parameter. The reduction may also depend on \(P,t,d\). This quantifier does not allow depth growing as a function of \(k\).

The inclusions \(W[t]\subseteq W[t+1]\) follow directly from the weft bounds. Strict inclusion means that at least one problem belongs to the larger class and not the smaller one. The formal target quantifies over all fixed positive integers \(t\); it does not require an algorithm that constructs witnesses from \(t\).

Separating \(\mathrm{FPT}\) from \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) would leave the requested adjacent-level separations to be proved.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof that \(W[t]\subsetneq W[t+1]\) for every integer \(t\ge1\), with the classes and reductions above; or supply a complete Lean-checked refutation, proving \(W[t]=W[t+1]\) for at least one particular \(t\ge1\). A proof for just finitely many strict inclusions does not establish the universal positive answer. Completeness or hardness for one of these classes, an oracle-relative separation, or a separation conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not settle the target. No claim about collapse of all other levels is required for a negative answer.
cards.why: Parameterized completeness places many natural problems into different levels of a common hierarchy, but a level label alone does not prove a difference in computational power. Establishing strictness would show that these levels capture distinct forms of parameterized intractability. An equality would instead identify a new general reduction principle connecting problems currently treated as having different complexity.

cards.title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
cards.formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
cards.definitions:
An input graph is a finite undirected unweighted loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\). Vertices are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\); edges are an explicitly listed sequence of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Parallel edges are distinct listed objects, each costing one deletion. The terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) consists of distinct designated vertices. The budget \(k\ge0\) is an integer in binary. Encode \(n\) in unary, the edge-list length and endpoints in a self-delimiting binary format, the terminal set as an \(n\)-bit membership vector, and \(k\) in self-delimiting binary. The total encoding length \(N\) includes every listed edge, vertex and terminal and the budget. The output uses the same format; succinct circuits, binary edge multiplicities and binary weights are not allowed.

A cut is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of edge identities with \(|F|\le k\). The graph \(G-F\) retains every vertex and terminal. It must contain no path between any two distinct terminals. Terminals cannot be deleted, and terminal labels carry no further pairing data: every terminal must be separated from every other. Disconnected graphs, empty graphs, zero budgets and fewer than two terminals are included. The kernel need only preserve the decision answer, not the optimum cut value or every terminal-partition cut. It may relabel vertices and change the terminal set and budget.

The multigraph convention permits the contractions used in kernelization. It does not change polynomial-kernel existence relative to explicit simple graphs: replacing every edge by its own two-edge path through a fresh nonterminal gives a simple graph of polynomial encoding size with the same minimum number of edge deletions needed to separate terminals. Either part of such a path can be deleted at unit cost, while deleting both never helps beyond deleting one.

Use a uniform multitape probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits and one transition per time unit, charging for writing the output. There is no advice, oracle or separately provided preprocessing. Runtime, output-format and size guarantees hold on every random tape. The probability of preserving equivalence is at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input, with two-sided error permitted. This explicitly fixes the saved card's allowance of randomized preprocessing; deterministic or one-sided-error polynomial kernels also qualify. The failure probability is not averaged over a distribution of graphs.

A polynomial kernel has size bounded solely by a fixed polynomial in \(k\), even when the original graph and terminal set are much larger. A bound such as \(k^{|T|+1}\) does not satisfy this condition, since its exponent changes with the input. A size bound \(k^{\log^{O(1)}k}\) is quasipolynomial and is likewise insufficient. Both bounds use the full encoding length, not just the number of vertices while ignoring labels, edges or weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the randomized polynomial-kernel claim. A positive proof must provide the preprocessing algorithm and verify the all-tape polynomial runtime, output size and parameter bounds, and per-instance equivalence probability for arbitrary terminal sets. A negative proof must rule out every algorithm in this model. A kernel for a fixed number of terminals, a reduction to a different decision language, quasipolynomial preprocessing or output size, or a conditional exclusion relying on an unproved complexity assumption does not by itself settle the stated unconditional claim.
cards.why: Kernelization asks whether the information relevant to a small cut budget can be compressed before solving the remaining hard instance. Edge Multiway Cut is a central test of that principle because it combines many terminal-separation requirements while parameterizing only the number of removed edges. A polynomial kernel would replace arbitrarily large graphs by uniformly small equivalent instances without fixing the number of terminals.

cards.title: Polynomial compression versus polynomial kernelization
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed parameterized language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\) such that its unary-parameter encoding \(\widetilde Q\) is NP-complete and \[\operatorname{PC}(Q)\ \land\ \bigl(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\bigr)?\] Here \(\operatorname{PC}\) means deterministic polynomial compression to an arbitrary fixed language, and \(\operatorname{PK}\) means deterministic polynomial kernelization back to \(Q\), with the exact definitions below. Thus the requested compression is unconditional, while its separation from kernels uses the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\).
cards.definitions:
The parameter \(k\) is a nonnegative integer supplied in unary. Encode a pair \((x,k)\) by
\[
\langle x,k\rangle=1^{|x|}0\,x\,1^k,
\qquad
\widetilde Q=\{\langle x,k\rangle:(x,k)\in Q\}.
\]
The prefix determines the end of the binary string \(x\); the remaining symbols must all be one. Strings that fail this syntax are outside \(\widetilde Q\). Input length is \(2|x|+k+1\), equivalent within fixed constants to \(|x|+k+1\).

The property \(\operatorname{PC}(Q)\) holds when there exist a fixed language \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a constant \(C\ge1\), and integers \(a,b\ge1\), such that for every binary string \(x\) and every \(k\ge0\), \(A\) on \(\langle x,k\rangle\) halts within \(C(|x|+k+2)^a\) bit steps and outputs a binary string \(y\) satisfying
\[
|y|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad
(x,k)\in Q\ \longleftrightarrow\ y\in R.
\]
The target language \(R\) is fixed across all inputs and parameters. No decidability or NP-membership condition is imposed on \(R\). The compressor has no membership oracle for \(R\); it only computes the string. The machine, exponents and constants may depend on the selected \(Q\) and compression scheme, never on \(x,k\).

The property \(\operatorname{PK}(Q)\) holds when there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(B\), a constant \(D\ge1\), and integers \(c,d\ge1\), such that, for every \((x,k)\), \(B\) outputs an encoded pair \(\langle x',k'\rangle\) within \(D(|x|+k+2)^c\) bit steps, with
\[
|x'|+k'\le D(k+1)^d,\qquad
(x,k)\in Q\ \longleftrightarrow\ (x',k')\in Q.
\]
The output language is the same \(Q\), and the bound includes the new parameter in unary. In both definitions all input reading, computation and output writing count. Algorithms have finite fixed programs, no advice, no oracle and no randomness. They must be correct on every valid pair, without a promise on \(x\) beyond the language membership being decided.

For completeness, a binary language \(L\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and a polynomial bound \(p\) such that
\[
x\in L\ \longleftrightarrow\
\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}\ V(x,z)=1.
\]
The notation \(\{0,1\}^{\le r}\) denotes all binary strings of length at most \(r\). A language \(L\) is in \(\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(W\), a polynomial bound \(p\), and a sequence of advice strings \((\alpha_n)_{n\ge0}\) with \(|\alpha_n|\le p(n)\), such that
\[
x\in L\ \longleftrightarrow\
\forall z\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}
\ W(x,\alpha_{|x|},z)=1.
\]
Advice may depend on input length but not on the particular input, and need not be computable. It belongs only to this comparison class, not to the compression or kernel algorithms. Each language may have its own verifier, polynomial and advice sequence. The inclusion \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) means every NP language belongs to that advice class.

A language is NP-complete when it belongs to NP and every NP language reduces to it by one deterministic polynomial-time many-one map preserving membership. This is ordinary polynomial-time completeness of the unary-encoded language \(\widetilde Q\), not parameterized hardness of \(Q\).

The main proposition quantifies over a single fixed \(Q\), with an unconditional compression scheme and the displayed implication for every possible polynomial kernel. It does not require proving the hypothesis that NP is not contained in the advice class. It also does not assert unconditional nonexistence of a kernel. The informal adjective “natural” is not a further uncheckable requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the language and encoding, prove NP-completeness of its unary form, establish an unconditional deterministic compression with all size and running-time guarantees, and prove that any deterministic polynomial kernel would imply the displayed complexity-class inclusion. Absence of a known kernel, a randomized compression alone, or an output language merely not known to belong to NP does not establish the proposition. The lower-bound implication must be proved; the assumed noninclusion itself need not be proved.
cards.why: Kernelization asks whether small equivalent instances can remain in the original problem language, while compression permits a different representation. A separation would expose a fundamental limit of preprocessing back into the same NP-complete problem even when short decision-equivalent information is computable.

cards.context:
The textbook asks for a separation on “natural problems” without defining a mathematical class for that adjective. The formulation uses a precise NP-complete source-language branch. This card records that selection and uses the usual conditional kernel-lower-bound interpretation with the displayed advice-class assumption. This is a documented formulation of the research direction, not a claim that NP-completeness is equivalent to the original informal requirement.

Definition 15.8 permits an arbitrary compression target, including languages not known to be decidable. Restricting the target to NP would materially change this question. The algorithms themselves are ordinary effective polynomial-time machines and receive no target-language oracle.

The kernelization monograph proves that an NP-hard unary source language has a polynomial kernel whenever its polynomial compression targets a language in NP. The unresolved comparison therefore concerns the possibility of more general compressed representations.

For a nontrivial NP source language, proving unconditional absence of polynomial kernels would in particular prove that P differs from NP, since a polynomial-time decider could output fixed yes and no instances. The selected implication gives the conventional conditional distinction without importing that stronger demand.

cards.title: General Formula-SAT with a fixed exponential saving
cards.formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), constants \(K\ge1\), an integer \(d\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that every explicitly given Boolean formula \(F\) over AND, OR and NOT is correctly decided for satisfiability in at most
\[
K\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}\bigl(N(F)+1\bigr)^d
\]
Turing-machine bit steps? Here \(n(F)\) is the number of distinct variables occurring in \(F\), \(N(F)\) is its full binary encoding length, and no restriction is placed on its size or depth. The same algorithm, positive saving and constants must work for every formula.
cards.definitions:
Use the explicit [SAT formula tree](definitions.html#sat), with binary AND and OR, unary NOT and constants 0 and 1. All declared variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) must occur, and \(n=0\) is permitted. The input permits repeated occurrences, arbitrary depth and arbitrary negations. Every occurrence is written in full.

The output is one bit indicating whether an assignment makes the root true. A formula with no variables has its ordinary Boolean constant value.

Use the [self-delimiting integer code](definitions.html#sat-encoding). Begin with \(\operatorname{code}(n)\), then traverse the tree in preorder. Each node has a three-bit tag specifying constant zero, constant one, variable, NOT, AND or OR. A variable tag is followed by \(\operatorname{code}(i)\), \(1\le i\le n\); other tags determine their arity and have no extra payload. There must be exactly one complete tree, no unused tags or trailing bits, and all declared variables must occur. The full length of this encoding is \(N(F)\). This includes every copy of a repeated subexpression. A succinct generator, truth-table oracle or circuit with shared gates is not an alternative input encoding.

The algorithm is one fixed finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes and finite tape alphabets. One transition reads or writes only the cells under its heads and moves each head by at most one cell; its cost is one bit step up to a fixed machine-dependent factor. It halts on every input, rejects malformed encodings in polynomial time in their length and returns the exact satisfiability answer for every valid formula. Parsing, input access, preprocessing and internal computation are included in the runtime. There is no advice, randomness, oracle, quantum computation or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. No separate workspace restriction is imposed.

The quantifier order is \(\exists(\varepsilon,K,d,A)\,\forall F\). In particular, neither the exponent saving nor the polynomial exponent may deteriorate with formula size, depth, variable-occurrence count or a chosen size bound. The target includes formulas of every polynomial size as well as larger explicit formulas; their input length remains charged through the displayed factor. For a fixed polynomial relation \(N\le n^q\), any polynomial overhead is absorbed into a smaller fixed exponential saving for sufficiently large \(n\), but no separate size-dependent algorithm is substituted for the single program demanded here.

Exhaustive evaluation gives a bound \(2^n\operatorname{poly}(N)\). The question asks to replace its exponential base by some fixed smaller value. A bound \(2^{n-n^\alpha}\operatorname{poly}(N)\), \(0<\alpha<1\), or a polynomial-factor improvement over \(2^n\) does not meet the target: its saving divided by \(n\) tends to zero. No particular numerical saving is prescribed. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1)\) preserves existence of a positive fixed saving.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must supply an exact deterministic decision algorithm and a fixed positive saving valid for every allowed formula, with all input and computation costs counted. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms and constants in the proposition unconditionally; a lower bound assuming SETH, ETH or another unproved hardness hypothesis is only a conditional result.

Results restricted to fixed clause width, bounded variable occurrences, linear-size or subcubic-size formulas do not establish the universal positive answer. A counting algorithm could establish it only if it satisfies the full stated size, time and machine requirements. There is no additive numerical tolerance or minimum required saving of one hundredth.
cards.why: Boolean formulas are more general than bounded-width CNF instances while still lacking arbitrary circuit sharing. A fixed exponential saving across all formula sizes would reveal algorithmic structure beyond exhaustive search and would also improve every fixed-width SAT problem with one common saving.

cards.title: Single-exponential Directed Feedback Vertex Set
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm and constants \(A,c>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which decide Directed Feedback Vertex Set on every \(n\)-vertex directed graph and deletion budget \(0\le k\le n\) within \(A\,2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) bit-computation steps? The answer must be YES exactly when deleting at most \(k\) vertices makes the graph acyclic. The exponential dependence is solely on the solution-size budget, and the polynomial exponent is independent of \(k\).
cards.definitions: The input digraph is \(D=([n],E)\), \(n\ge1\), with \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\). Self-loops and opposite arcs are allowed; repeated copies of an arc are not represented and have no effect. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_1,\ldots,v_t\), \(t\ge1\), with arcs \((v_j,v_{j+1})\) for \(j<t\) and \((v_t,v_1)\). Thus self-loops are cycles of length one, and opposite arcs give a cycle of length two. For \(S\subseteq[n]\), the remaining graph is the induced digraph \(D[[n]\setminus S]\). A feedback vertex set is a set \(S\) for which this remaining digraph contains no directed cycle. Its cost is the cardinality \(|S|\); no vertex weights are present. There are no promises of planarity, bounded degree, bounded treewidth, a supplied solution or bounds on cycle length. Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one finite program for all \(n,k,D\), no advice and no random bits. A valid input consists of the prefix \(1^n0\), followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row-major order, followed by exactly \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits encoding \(k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) in most-significant-bit-first binary. The machine must halt and return the correct decision on every valid input. Each Turing-machine transition costs one step, including all input processing and preprocessing. No running-time condition on malformed strings is part of the target. The fixed encoding has length polynomial in \(n\), so ordinary polynomial-time changes of explicit graph encoding only alter the permitted polynomial factor. The quantified constants \(A,c,d\) are independent of \(n,k,D\). The target is worst-case exact decision, including NO instances; it requires neither an optimal deletion set nor enumeration of all solutions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the specified deterministic algorithm with its correctness and \(A2^{ck}(n+1)^d\) worst-case bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm and constants exist. A \(2^{O(k\log k)}n^{O(1)}\) algorithm, an exponent depending on \(k\) in the polynomial input-size factor, an approximation, or a result for restricted graph classes is insufficient for the affirmative answer. A lower bound conditional on an additional unproved hypothesis establishes only that conditional version of the negative statement.
cards.why: Deleting a small number of vertices to destroy every directed cycle is a basic model of repairing cyclic dependencies. Fixed-parameter algorithms make small deletion budgets tractable in principle, but the known factorial dependence is much larger than a fixed exponential base. The target asks whether directed cycle structure inherently causes that additional parameter cost.

cards.title: Exact recognition of bounded clique-width
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A_{k}\) and constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\ge 1\) such that \(A_{k}\) decides whether \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) for every finite simple undirected graph G in at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps, where N is the bit length of G’s adjacency-matrix encoding?
cards.definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\). It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph \(G, \operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The input contains \(n\ge 0\) and the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal \(0/1\) adjacency matrix for the graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. \(A_{k}\) outputs YES exactly when \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists A_{k},C_{k},c_{k} \forall G: k\) is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each \(A_{k}\) is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language \(\{G:\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\}\) has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. An expression with more than k labels does not establish a YES answer; failure of one construction does not establish NO. Variable-k NP-hardness, or fixed-k hardness under an unproved assumption, does not alone unconditionally refute this proposition.
cards.why: Tests whether a major dense-graph width parameter admits efficient exact recognition at every fixed value.

cards.context:
Clique-width counts reusable labels in a construction, not the size of a largest clique. Every nonempty edgeless graph has width 1. Complete graphs with at least two vertices have width 2, regardless of their size. Thus even very dense graphs can have small clique-width; the parameter captures how uniformly groups of vertices can be assembled.

Fellows and coauthors prove NP-completeness when both G and k are input. The present statement allows a different polynomial bound for each fixed k. For example, a hypothetical bound \(N^{k+2}\) would be polynomial for each such threshold, while not giving a polynomial bound when k grows with N. The source lists fixed-threshold recognition separately from the stronger FPT question, which asks for one algorithm with runtime \(f(k)N^{c}\) and c independent of k.

Polynomial-time recognition is known through \(k=3\), with the full three-label algorithm published by Corneil and coauthors in 2012. The cited sources retain \(k=4\) as the first unresolved threshold. A solution only for four labels would still leave the card’s quantification over every fixed k.

A procedure that returns an expression with \(f(k)>k\) labels for graphs of width at most k can enable other graph algorithms, yet leave the exact threshold undecided. Likewise, the July 2026 feedback-vertex-set result assumes a k-expression is already supplied. These results explain the usefulness of clique-width without providing the recognizer requested here.

cards.formal:
Is there one uniform deterministic algorithm that computes the chromatic number of every \(n\)-vertex finite simple undirected graph in time \(O^{*}(2^n)\) and polynomial space?

Precisely, do there exist a deterministic machine \(A\) and fixed integers \(K\ge1,c,d\ge0\) such that, for every such graph \(G\), the machine outputs \(\chi(G)\), halts after at most
\[
K\,2^n(n+1)^c
\]
transitions, and uses at most
\[
K(n+1)^d
\]
work-tape cells throughout its computation? The graph encoding and computation model are defined below. Both bounds must hold for the same algorithm on the same input.
cards.definitions:
The input graph has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge0\), and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops, parallel edges, weights or promises about the graph class. The input consists of \(1^n0\), followed by one adjacency bit for each pair \((i,j)\) with \(1\le i<j\le n\), in lexicographic order. Thus it has \(n+1+\binom n2\) bits. There are no trailing bits.

A proper \(q\)-coloring is a map \(h:[n]\to[q]\) such that \(h(i)\ne h(j)\) whenever \(\{i,j\}\) is an edge. The chromatic number is the least integer \(q\ge0\) for which such a map exists. In particular, \(\chi(G)=0\) for the empty graph and \(1\le\chi(G)\le n\) for a nonempty graph. The output is the ordinary binary encoding of this integer, using the string \(0\) for zero. A coloring itself is not required as output.

The computation model is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and finitely many tapes over fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape, initially blank work tapes and a write-only output tape. Heads start at cell zero; a transition reads or writes only the cells under the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. Tapes have nonnegative cell indices, with left moves at zero staying there. The time bound counts all transitions, including parsing, input access, arithmetic and output writing. Work space counts the total number of work-tape cells visited; the finite alphabets make this equivalent to bits up to a constant factor. The output tape is append-only and cannot serve as extra readable memory. The read-only input has polynomial length and does not affect the polynomial-space requirement.

There is no random source, advice depending on input length, oracle, unbounded-integer unit-cost operation or uncharged preprocessing. Malformed encodings must be rejected in time polynomial in their length. Constants and the machine are fixed once for all graphs and all \(n\). The bounds are worst-case bounds, not expected or average-case guarantees.

The notation \(O^{*}(2^n)\) suppresses only a factor polynomial in \(n\). A factor \(2^{o(n)}\) is not automatically permitted: for example, \(2^{n+\sqrt n}\) does not meet the displayed bound. A smaller exponential base does qualify if the same algorithm uses polynomial space.

The task is to determine the unrestricted chromatic number, so the number of colors may grow with \(n\). Separate algorithms for every fixed color count, with resources or advice depending on that count, do not by themselves give the required uniform bound. A procedure outputting a rational approximation to \(\chi(G)\) with proved absolute error at most \(1/100\) also yields an exact integer output by rounding; if it meets the stated resource bounds, this conversion incurs only polynomial overhead.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of exact correctness, the \(K2^n(n+1)^c\) time bound and the \(K(n+1)^d\) space bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Correctness must cover every finite simple graph, including inputs whose chromatic number grows with their size. A fixed-color algorithm, a randomized algorithm with possible error, an exponential-space construction, or a result conditional on an unproved hypothesis does not meet the target. The question asks for the existence of an algorithm with simultaneous resource bounds; approximate experimental running times or sampled graph tests are insufficient.
cards.why: Fast exact coloring algorithms illustrate the power of storing information for all vertex subsets, but that table has exponential size. The question asks whether the time advantage survives when the algorithm can retain only polynomially many bits. A resolution would clarify a central time-space tradeoff in exact algorithms for graph partitioning problems.

The 2026 fixed-color algorithms improve the running-time base separately for each constant number of colors and use randomness. Their guarantees do not provide one deterministic algorithm with the requested memory bound for arbitrary chromatic number.

The latest checked fixed-color paper explicitly lists removing randomness and achieving fast polynomial-space computation as further questions.

cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\), there exists an integer \(q\ge2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish the following two classes of explicitly listed Unique Games instances over the alphabet \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\):
\[\text{YES: }\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad \text{NO: }\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta.\]
NP-hardness here means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT with the completeness and soundness guarantees defined below. The alphabet size and the reduction may depend on the two constants but must be fixed before the input size grows. The target is this hardness proposition itself, without assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).
cards.definitions:
Instance and value. An instance has a finite vertex set \(V=[n]\) with \(n\ge2\), an ordered nonempty list of \(m\ge1\) directed edges \((u_j,v_j)\) with distinct endpoints in \(V\), and a permutation \(\pi_j:[q]\to[q]\) for each edge index \(j\in[m]\). Repeated directed edges, including repeated constraints or different constraints on the same ordered pair, are allowed and counted separately. There is no restriction on degree, expansion, connectedness or bipartiteness, and isolated vertices are allowed. A permutation is a bijection: each label occurs exactly once among its \(q\) images. A labeling is one map \(\ell:V\to[q]\), with no probabilistic or quantum strategy. Edge \(j\) is satisfied when \(\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\). Define
\[\operatorname{val}(G)=\max_{\ell:V\to[q]}\frac{|\{j\in[m]:\pi_j(\ell(u_j))=\ell(v_j)\}|}{m}.\]
The finite maximum is attained and lies in \([0,1]\). All edge occurrences have equal weight. Reversing an edge would require using the inverse permutation; its stored direction fixes the equation used here. The two promised classes are disjoint because \(\delta<1-\varepsilon\). Instances with \(\delta<\operatorname{val}(G)<1-\varepsilon\) are outside the promise.

Explicit encoding. Vertex labels and all integers are written in binary with length prefixes. Concretely, a nonnegative integer \(z\) may be encoded by \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(z+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(z+1)\rfloor+1\). A game encoding lists \(q,n,m\), all \(n\) vertex labels in order, and for each edge its two endpoints followed by the entire table \(\pi_j(1),\ldots,\pi_j(q)\). Tables are not circuits or oracles representing longer objects. Input and output lengths count every listed bit. This convention fixes a finite-string model; polynomially interconvertible standard explicit encodings give the same hardness question.

Reduction and source problem. A 3CNF formula \(\varphi\) is an explicitly listed conjunction of clauses, each an ordered disjunction of three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable \(x_i\) or its negation. Repeated literals are allowed. List the variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_s\) and the clauses, recording literal signs as bits and indices and list lengths with the integer encoding above. The empty conjunction is allowed and is true. A satisfying assignment is a map from these variables to \(\{0,1\}\) making every clause true. Let \(|\varphi|\) be the full bit length of this encoding. For fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta,q\), the required reduction is a single deterministic Turing-machine program \(F\) for which some constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) bound its time by \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\) on every valid formula. Time includes writing the output. On each such formula it must output one valid game \(G=F(\varphi)\) over exactly \([q]\), satisfying
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\ge1-\varepsilon,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow\operatorname{val}(F(\varphi))\le\delta.\]
Thus both kinds of formulas map into the promise. A multi-tape deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes suffices as the computation model; each transition reads and writes one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. No advice, randomness or oracle is allowed. Behavior on malformed formula strings is immaterial. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is the meaning of NP-hardness used here; no decision algorithm for the game is part of the requested reduction.

Parameter quantifiers. The order is \(\forall(\varepsilon,\delta)\ \exists q\ \exists F,C,k\ \forall\varphi\). The machine, alphabet, time exponent and constant may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but not on the formula. The parameters are not growing input variables, and no common polynomial exponent or effective procedure selecting reductions for all parameters is additionally required. Restricting the gap parameters to positive rationals loses none of the usual real-parameter conjecture: smaller rational errors give the required inclusions of the real-parameter YES and NO classes. The usual one-error formulation is equivalent by taking the smaller of the two errors.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the entire quantified hardness proposition, including the deterministic reductions, polynomial output/time bounds, valid permutation constraints, and both implications for every formula, or prove its logical negation. A negative answer must identify fixed rational \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) with \(\varepsilon+\delta<1\) such that no alphabet \(q\ge2\) admits the required reduction. Equivalently, for each \(q\) and every deterministic polynomial-time candidate program, some valid 3CNF formula has an invalid output or violates its applicable YES/NO guarantee. This is a statement about all reductions, not just a failed construction or a particular alphabet. No unproved complexity assumption may replace the requested conclusion. A polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm alone does not logically refute the NP-hardness proposition without an appropriate separation such as \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Hardness with completeness bounded away from one, perfect satisfiability testing, a restricted graph class, or a result for many-to-one constraints does not by itself settle this target.
cards.why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

cards.context:
Each constraint is locally reversible: either endpoint label fixes exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Despite this simplicity, the conjecture asks whether an almost perfectly consistent collection is NP-hard to distinguish from one for which every labeling violates almost all constraints. This is a promise decision gap, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum.

For example, with two labels an identity permutation asks for equal labels, while a transposition asks for different labels. Three transposition constraints on the edges of a triangle have value \(2/3\). This illustrates how individually consistent requirements can conflict globally; the conjecture quantifies over larger alphabets and much more extreme gaps.

Exact satisfiability, meaning \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\), is polynomial-time decidable in this explicit model. The positive completeness error \(\varepsilon\) is therefore an essential feature of the conjecture. A uniformly random labeling satisfies an expected fraction \(1/q\) of the edges, so every instance has value at least \(1/q\). In particular, if \(\delta<1/q\), there are no NO instances. The alphabet cannot be fixed in advance of all soundness thresholds.

Raghavendra’s 2008 theorem ties Unique-Games-based hardness to a general semidefinite-programming framework for constraint satisfaction over a fixed finite domain. Under UGC, its approximation guarantees are optimal up to arbitrary fixed accuracy, with the usual consequence for polynomial-time algorithms requiring a complexity separation. This explains why one apparently narrow family of permutation constraints governs many approximation thresholds.

Arora, Barak and Steurer’s 2010 theorem gives, for an absolute \(\alpha>0\), an \(\exp(qn^{\varepsilon^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm returning a \((1-\varepsilon^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling on an \(n\)-vertex, \((1-\varepsilon)\)-satisfiable instance. For fixed \(q\) and sufficiently small fixed \(\varepsilon\), this is subexponential but does not give polynomial time. Its dependence on completeness is compatible with reductions whose polynomial exponent depends on the desired gap.

The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies that, for every fixed positive soundness threshold, Unique Games is NP-hard with completeness \(1/2\). Khot’s exposition states this as Theorem 2.20. The conclusion leaves the near-one completeness in UGC unresolved. The 2025 journal publication of one part of the proof sequence records the historical role of its conditional intermediate theorem and still states full UGC separately as Conjecture 1.4.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims the \(4\)-to-\(1\) Games Conjecture with perfect completeness. Its constraints are projections in which each right-hand label has four preimages, rather than bijections. Theorem 1.6 is a major related hardness claim, with graph-coloring consequences, but does not prove the permutation-constraint UGC. The same introduction retains UGC as Conjecture 1.4 and identifies completeness \(1/2\) as the existing Unique Games hardness frontier. Its full proof has not been independently verified in this review.

Yoshida’s May 2026 tolerant-testing preprint concerns adjacency-list queries and distinguishes small from larger optimum violation fractions. Its Theorem 1.1 requires \(\varepsilon\log n\le c_q\rho^4\), where \(\rho\) is the larger violation threshold and \(c_q>0\) depends on the fixed alphabet. For the UGC gap, \(\rho=1-\delta\); the displayed assumption does not hold for every input size when the positive errors and alphabet are fixed. Thus the tester’s sublinear query bound does not refute this fixed-parameter, all-instance hardness statement.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute \(\alpha >0\), an \(\exp (q n^{\varepsilon ^{\alpha}})\)-time algorithm finding a \((1- \varepsilon ^{\alpha})\)-satisfying labeling in a \((1- \varepsilon )\)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-\(\varepsilon\) regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness \(1/2\) and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.
Yoshida reports a sublinear-query tolerant tester with the additional condition \(\varepsilon\log n\le c_q\rho^4\); this is not the unrestricted fixed-gap UGC regime.

Fei–Minzer–Wang claim perfect-completeness hardness for 4-to-1 games and consequent coloring hardness. Their introduction still separates full UGC as a conjecture; no independent certification of the new proof is asserted here.

UGC asks for NP-hardness of distinguishing almost completely satisfiable instances from those with arbitrarily small optimum value.
The alphabet and deterministic reduction may depend on the fixed gap parameters, but must be independent of the growing input formula.
A complete Lean proof must establish the full reduction statement or its negation over every alphabet and polynomial-time candidate reduction.
The September 2026 perfect-completeness 4-to-1 claim and the known half-completeness Unique Games theorem do not establish this near-one-completeness permutation-constraint conjecture.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Does Densest \(k\)-Subgraph have a deterministic polynomial-time constant-factor approximation on all explicitly given finite simple undirected unweighted graphs?

For \(n\ge1\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). If \(G=([n],E)\) and \(1\le k\le n\), define
\[e_G(S)=|\{\{u,v\}\in E:u,v\in S\}|,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max_{\substack{T\subseteq[n]\\|T|=k}}e_G(T).\]
The proposition is that there exist one real constant \(C\ge1\), positive integer constants \(D,d\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\) such that, on every encoded input of length \(L\), \(A\) halts within \(D(L+1)^d\) bit steps, and on every valid \((G,k)\) it outputs an explicitly represented set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfying
\[|S|=k\qquad\text{and}\qquad C\,e_G(S)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(G,k).\]
The same algorithm, constants and polynomial clock must work for all \(n,G,k\).
cards.definitions:
The graph has exactly the labelled vertices \([n]\), including isolated vertices. Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices, with no repetitions, loops, weights or directions. Its input is \(U(n)U(k)\) followed by the \(n(n-1)/2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of pairs \((u,v)\) with \(u<v\). Here \(U(a)=1^\ell0b\), where \(b\) is the canonical binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(a\), \(\ell=|b|\), and zero uses \(b=0\). The code must have precisely the indicated number of adjacency bits, with \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le k\le n\). Invalid encodings may be rejected; the clock applies to them too. This dense explicit encoding is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. A succinct circuit or edge oracle is not an input representation for this card.

The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector. A one at position \(i\) means vertex \(i\) belongs to \(S\), and exactly \(k\) bits must be one. The objective counts each internal edge once. The maximum exists because the family of \(k\)-subsets is finite and nonempty. An estimate of the optimum without an accompanying vertex set does not satisfy the output requirement.

Running time counts ordinary bounded-symbol Turing-machine steps, including reading input, arithmetic and writing all output bits. The machine has one fixed finite program and a fixed finite number of tapes. The constants cannot depend on graph size, \(k\), edge density or any promise about the input. No advice, randomness, quantum operations or uncharged oracle is supplied. A running time whose polynomial exponent increases with \(k\) does not meet the clock.

The approximation is purely multiplicative and holds on every valid input, with no additive loss, input-distribution exception or probability of failure. When \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=0\), the inequality is automatic but the output must still be a valid \(k\)-set. This includes \(k=1\), edgeless graphs and \(n=1\). The case \(k=n\) is included. The quantifier over \(C\) could equivalently use a positive integer, since rounding an admissible real factor upward preserves the guarantee.

Exactly \(k\) vertices is part of the target. On these feasible sets, maximizing internal edge count, average degree \(2e_G(S)/k\), or edges per vertex \(e_G(S)/k\) gives the same approximation ratio. If the number of selected vertices is allowed to vary, these objectives are no longer interchangeable. A guarantee for at least \(k\) vertices, a special graph class, a planted input distribution or a randomized algorithm is a different statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this proposition or of its full logical negation. A positive answer must specify one deterministic algorithm and universal constants, prove the global polynomial clock, and prove both exact output cardinality and the approximation inequality on every valid graph and parameter. A negative answer must exclude every such constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm. Equivalently, for every deterministic polynomial-time machine that always outputs a valid \(k\)-set and every fixed \(C\ge1\), some valid input must satisfy \(C e_G(A(G,k))<\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)\). A lower bound conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis, or a limitation of a specified relaxation or algorithm family, does not by itself prove the full negation.
cards.why: Densest k-Subgraph asks whether a prescribed number of vertices can capture a constant fraction of the greatest possible internal connectivity. Its approximation landscape is a central gap between available algorithms, conditional hardness and what follows from the usual P-versus-NP assumption. The answer also matters for several graph optimization objectives linked to its approximability.

cards.context:
The exact cardinality makes the objective distinctive. A large region of moderate density can be an excellent answer when size is unrestricted or only bounded below, yet it need not contain a k-vertex region with a comparable fraction of the optimum for exactly k. The card asks for the actual selected vertices, so evaluating a continuous objective or estimating an optimum is insufficient.

Bhaskara and coauthors give an \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in \(n^{O(1/\varepsilon)}\) time for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Their paper includes a deterministic combinatorial algorithm. Its title’s \(O(n^{1/4})\) endpoint requires quasipolynomial \(n^{O(\log n)}\) time in that analysis. The 2026 AAAI paper still describes the quarter-power-plus-epsilon bound as the general polynomial-time benchmark; neither bound is a universal constant.

Manurangsi proves that the Exponential Time Hypothesis rules out polynomial-time approximation within \(n^{1/(\log\log n)^c}\) for some universal \(c>0\). The paper states ETH as the absence of a deterministic \(2^{o(m)}\)-time algorithm for 3SAT with \(m\) clauses. Its hard YES instances contain a \(k\)-clique, a property called perfect completeness. The result already excludes every fixed approximation constant if ETH holds, but ETH is an unproved assumption stronger than \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

The corresponding conclusion under only P≠NP remains a different issue. The May 2026 at-least-k paper explicitly says that even NP-hardness of a 1.001 approximation for Densest k-Subgraph is not known. This is consistent with the ETH lower bound: different hypotheses support different conclusions. A proof of conditional hardness is significant evidence, but does not establish the unconditional negative answer required by the card.

Chuzhoy and coauthors propose a Low-Degree CSP conjecture. Together with \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), it would exclude a polynomial-time \(2^{(\log n)^\varepsilon}\)-approximation for some \(0<\varepsilon\le1/2\). Their stated consequence uses Cook-type reductions, which may make multiple oracle queries. The work also connects graph partitioning, dense coloring and other graph objectives, sometimes with quasipolynomial reductions. These are qualified conditional relationships rather than constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences.

The 2012 integrality gaps demonstrate limitations of specified strong semidefinite relaxations. They exhibit a separation between what a relaxation permits and the objective attained by genuine selected vertices. Such a separation constrains approximation arguments based on that relaxation; it does not rule out every polynomial-time algorithm.

Jones and coauthors give further Sum-of-Squares lower bounds in a planted-subgraph distinction model for \(k\le\sqrt n\). Their Theorem 1.1 constructs high-degree pseudoexpectations on random graphs, with approximately correct first-moment cardinality and normalization. These are the theorem’s particular relaxation constraints; they should not be silently replaced by all exact cardinality identities. This adds evidence about a broad algorithmic framework without proving unrestricted constant-factor hardness.

The AAAI 2026 continuous formulation is exact in a different sense. Under a sufficient penalty, its global optima correspond to the combinatorial problem, with an additional local-optimum correspondence. The accompanying convergence result controls a criticality residual under its stated algorithmic conditions. It does not guarantee a global optimum or a fixed approximation ratio on every input. Practical optimization progress can therefore coexist with the unresolved worst-case target.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi show that the absence of every constant-factor DkS approximation would rule out a \((3/2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for the at-least-k density problem, for each \(\varepsilon>0\). Their latter objective is edges per selected vertex and permits more than \(k\) vertices. Its known constant-factor algorithms do not solve the exactly-k problem.

The August 2026 preprint of Grigorescu and Taziki claims a linear-time approximation scheme for the unrestricted density objective. It also gives a near-linear-time at-least-k result with value at least \((1/2-\varepsilon)\) of that objective’s optimum. Both statements permit a different feasible cardinality from this card. They are relevant recent progress, but neither is a claimed resolution of its constant-factor question.

cards.title: Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every rational constant \(\eta \in (0,1/2)\), is there a rational constant \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with \(\delta n\) an integer, distinguish YES: some \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\le \eta\), from NO: every \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\ge 1- \eta\).
cards.definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs \(G=([n],E), n\ge 2\) and \(d\ge 1\), given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty \(S, \partial _{G} S\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(\Phi _{G}(S)=|\partial _{G} S|/(d|S|)\). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants \(\eta ,\delta\) are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For \(\delta =a/b\) in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since \(\eta <1/2\); inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each \(x\in L\) to a YES graph and each \(x\notin L\) to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on \(\eta\) and its chosen \(\delta\). The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every \(\eta\) by choosing \(\delta\) and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed \(\eta\). Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed \(\delta\) at that \(\eta\) would refute the hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

references.title: The Condition-Number Barrier in Sparse Least Squares
references.authors: Honghao Lin, Vahab Mirrokni and David P. Woodruff
references.locator: 3 August 2026 abstract: conditional hardness using a randomized exact-volume weighted regular-graph SSE assumption. Neither an unconditional SSE theorem nor a refutation.

cards.context:
Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly \(\Phi _{G}(S)\). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

If \(\delta =1/1000\), the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: \(\delta\) may depend on the desired expansion gap \(\eta\), and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion \(48/49\), and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(a,C,K,q\) and one uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A\) such that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance \(I\) of encoding length \(N\) with \(k\ge1\) terminals, every execution halts within \(K(N+1)^q\) bit steps and outputs a feasible arc subset \(F\), and
\[\Pr\!\left[c(F)\le a\bigl(\log_2(k+2)\bigr)^C\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right]\ge\frac23?\]
The probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness, separately for each input. The graph is arbitrary and directed, with exactly represented nonnegative rational arc costs. All four constants and the program must be independent of the instance.
cards.definitions:
Instance. The vertex set is \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge2\). A finite list of \(m\) indexed arcs specifies their tails and heads in \(V\); different indices denote different arcs even when their endpoints coincide. Loops and parallel arcs are allowed. The root is \(r\in V\), and the terminal set is \(T\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\), with \(k=|T|\ge1\). Every arc \(e\) has cost \(c_e=u_e/v_e\), where \(u_e\) is a nonnegative integer and \(v_e\) a positive integer, both supplied in binary. Zero costs and arbitrarily long cost descriptions are allowed. There is no planarity, acyclicity, degree, treewidth, depth or metric promise.

Reachability and feasibility. A directed path follows arc orientations from its first vertex to its last; it may be taken without repeated vertices. The input is promised feasible: every terminal is reachable from \(r\). A feasible output is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of arc indices such that the subgraph \((V,F)\) has a directed \(r\)-to-\(t\) path for every \(t\in T\). Nonterminal vertices may be used freely as intermediate vertices. Arc cost is paid once, regardless of how many terminal paths use it:
\[c(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c_e,\qquad\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min\{c(F):F\subseteq E\text{ is feasible}\}.\]
The minimum exists because there are finitely many subsets and at least one is feasible. It may equal zero. The name “tree” does not impose an additional output-syntax condition: a feasible directed subgraph qualifies. Nonnegative costs also permit deletion of redundant arcs to obtain a rooted outward branching without increasing cost. Terminals are not required to be leaves.

Encoding and size. The graph, root, terminal list and every arc cost are explicit. One fixed encoding lists \(n,m,r,k\), all vertex labels \(1,\ldots,n\), the \(k\) distinct terminal labels in increasing order, and, for each indexed arc in order, its tail, head, numerator and denominator. Encode each nonnegative integer by its binary expansion preceded by its length in unary and a zero delimiter; the expansion of zero is the single bit zero. Let \(N\) be the total bit length. In particular \(N\ge n\), and every bit of every cost contributes to \(N\). Output identifies the selected arc indices, or equivalently their \(m\)-bit indicator vector.

Computation and randomness. Use an ordinary uniform multitape Turing machine with a finite program, read-only input, initially blank work tapes and a write-only output tape. A step reads and updates a constant number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; a random step additionally supplies one independent fair bit. Reading the input, writing the entire solution, exact rational arithmetic and all preprocessing count in the bit time. No nonuniform advice, free optimization oracle, supplied fractional solution or unit-cost exact-real operation is available. The required bound holds for every random bit sequence, not just on average.

Guarantee. On each feasible input, every execution must return a feasible subset; on an event of probability at least \(2/3\), its cost must also satisfy the displayed ratio. On other executions the cost may be larger but feasibility is still required. When \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\), the successful output must have cost zero; an additive positive error is not allowed. The \(k+2\) convention makes the factor defined and positive also at one terminal. Choosing positive integer constants rather than arbitrary real constants at least one does not change existence, since the logarithm is greater than one and rounding constants upward only relaxes the bound. No behavior is prescribed on malformed encodings; infeasible well-formed instances may be detected and reported in polynomial time before applying the feasible-instance algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, specify an algorithm and fixed constants, and prove its bit running time on every execution, feasibility of every output, and the per-instance probability and cost bound throughout the full class. The proof must account for binary rational costs and zero optimum. A procedure with a variable time exponent depending on \(k\), or with uncharged access to a special fractional solution, does not meet the statement.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed power \(C\) of \(\log_2(k+2)\), every factor \(a\), every polynomial time bound and every permitted randomized program. For example, for every uniformly polynomial-time program that always returns feasible outputs and for every \(a,C\), it suffices to prove the existence of a feasible instance on which the probability of the requested ratio is less than \(2/3\). A lower bound for deterministic programs alone is insufficient. A conditional hardness theorem must identify its unproved assumptions and does not by itself give an unconditional negative answer.

A polylogarithmic ratio in quasipolynomial time, an \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) ratio for each separately fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a theorem for planar graphs, or an integrality gap for one chosen relaxation is partial progress. Hardness below a particular logarithmic power leaves larger fixed powers possible. Expected-time or expected-cost analyses must be converted into the stated execution-time and success guarantees in the checked proof; they cannot simply replace those requirements.
cards.why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.

cards.context:
The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting \(\varepsilon\) to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li prove a randomized \(O(\log^2 k/\log\log k)\) approximation with running time \(n^{O(\log^5 k)}\), in the asymptotic range where this expression is used. This is quasipolynomial: its exponent grows with the input parameter. The target here permits a larger fixed power of the logarithm, but requires one polynomial time exponent for every instance. The old classical paper’s original quasipolynomial \(O(\log^2 k)\) claim was corrected to \(O(\log^3 k)\) because of a height-reduction lemma; the 2019 paper explicitly records that correction.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity \(x_{e}\) for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most \(x_{e}\) on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including \(\Omega (\sqrt{k})\) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The December 2024 general approximation claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, calls itself a rectification and assumes access to a relatively integral solution of a strengthened relaxation: for each terminal and arc, its flow is either zero or the whole purchased capacity. Theorem 1 states an expected-polynomial-time rounding result under this extra hypothesis. This is neither an algorithm that supplies the needed solution on every ordinary input nor a proof for arbitrary standard flow-LP optima. The live record still carries the reachability-proof withdrawal comment. The restricted result is recorded as a reported claim, not an independently verified general approximation.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time \(O(\log  k)\)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by \(O(\log ^{2} k)\). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s length-constrained work appeared on arXiv in July and was published on 9 September 2026. The published introduction still explicitly identifies the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic DST question as open. For planar graphs, Theorem 2 gives logarithmic cost approximation with logarithmic length slack, while Theorem 3 gives a log-squared bound against a fractional relaxation with the same length slack. Removing the path-length constraint does not remove their planarity assumption. The related directed-forest theorem has multiple source–sink demands, a different target from one-root DST.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Do there exist real constants \(C\ge1\) and \(K>0\), an integer constant \(d\ge1\), and one uniform classical randomized Turing machine \(A\) with the following property? For every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge2\) vertices, every execution halts within \(K(n+1)^d\) bit operations and outputs a nonempty proper vertex set \(S\). For each fixed input graph,
\[
 \Pr\!\left[\varphi_G(S)\le C\operatorname{OPT}(G)\right]\ge\frac23,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{OPT}(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne T\subsetneq V(G)}\varphi_G(T),
 \qquad
 \varphi_G(T)=\frac{|E(T,V(G)\setminus T)|}{|T|\,|V(G)\setminus T|}.
\]
The same machine and constants must work for all these graphs.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \(V(G)=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input consists of \(n\) in binary and the explicit symmetric \(n\times n\) Boolean adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. Each edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices and has unit capacity; there are no parallel edges, additional weights or demand inputs. All finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge2\) are allowed, including disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and graphs with no edges.

For a set \(T\), the boundary \(E(T,V(G)\setminus T)\) consists of the edges with exactly one endpoint in \(T\). Every edge is counted once. The denominator counts unordered vertex pairs separated by the cut, each with demand one. It is positive for every allowed nonempty proper set. Thus all objective values and the minimum are well-defined nonnegative rational numbers. The word uniform refers to these equal pair demands, not to equal degrees or to a random input graph.

The output is the length-\(n\) Boolean membership vector of \(S\). On every execution it must encode a nonempty proper subset. The approximation guarantee, which may fail with probability at most \(1/3\), is required separately for each input graph; it is not an average over graphs. Since every output is feasible, its value is automatically at least the optimum. If the graph is disconnected, the optimum is zero, so success requires an output cut with no crossing edge, not merely an additive approximation. There is no balance requirement on the sizes of the two sides, and either a set or its complement represents the same cut value.

The machine uses independent unbiased random bits and otherwise has a fixed finite deterministic program. The total bit-operation bound holds on every possible random tape and includes reading the input, generating and processing random bits, all numerical computations and preprocessing, and writing the membership vector. There is no advice, oracle, uncharged preprocessing, exact real-arithmetic primitive or quantum computation. Intermediate numbers must have finite encodings and their manipulation is charged. The polynomial bound in \(n\) is equivalent to a polynomial bound in the specified explicit input length. All constants are absolute and independent of the input; the target does not prescribe their numerical values.

The output requirement is a cut, not merely an estimate of its optimum value. The denominator is the product of cardinalities above; replacing it by degree volumes gives a different objective. General unequal pair demands, a promised balanced cut and restrictions to regular, dense or algebraically structured graph families are not part of this input model.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a machine and constants exist, including output feasibility, the per-input approximation probability and the worst-case bit-time bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of their logical negation.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed finite approximation factor and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm in this model. A growing integrality gap for one linear or semidefinite relaxation does not by itself do this. Conditional inapproximability under an unproved complexity hypothesis establishes only that conditional assertion, with its assumptions and randomized-algorithm implications stated explicitly.

A factor growing with \(n\), an additive-error estimate, a number without a cut, or a result only on a special graph class does not establish the positive target. Results for arbitrary weighted capacities or demands must be shown to cover the selected unweighted uniform instances; hardness for a broader class alone is insufficient.
cards.why: A constant approximation would bound the quality loss for finding sparse graph separations independently of graph size, addressing a central question connecting approximation algorithms and metric geometry.
