cards.title: Vertex Cover approximation below factor two
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Do there exist a rational constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), and integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, on every explicitly encoded finite simple undirected graph \(G\) of input bit length \(N\), the algorithm halts within \(B(N+1)^k\) Turing-machine steps and returns a vertex cover \(S\) satisfying
\[|S|\le(2-\varepsilon)\tau(G),\qquad
\tau(G)=\min\{|T|:T\subseteq V(G),\ T\text{ is a vertex cover of }G\}?\]
The same positive improvement \(\varepsilon\) and the same algorithm must work for graphs of all sizes, with no structural promise. Vertices have unit cost. The question asks for an unconditional algorithm-existence theorem or its unconditional negation.
cards.definitions:
Graphs and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V,\ u\ne v\}\). For \(n=0\), the vertex set and edge set are empty. Edges are unordered pairs, with no loops or multiplicities. A set \(S\subseteq V\) is a vertex cover if every \(\{u,v\}\in E\) has \(u\in S\) or \(v\in S\). The quantity \(\tau(G)\) is the minimum cardinality of such a set; the minimum exists because the finite set \(V\) itself covers every edge. All vertices have weight one, so the cost is the number selected. If \(E=\varnothing\), then \(\tau(G)=0\), and the approximation inequality requires the output \(S=\varnothing\). Isolated vertices are allowed. The class includes disconnected, bipartite, nonbipartite, sparse and dense graphs without imposing any of those promises.

Input and output. The input is the full \(n\)-by-\(n\) binary adjacency matrix, preceded by a self-delimiting binary encoding of \(n\). One fixed encoding is \(1^b0\) followed by the \(b\)-bit binary expansion of \(n+1\), where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(n+1)\rfloor+1\), followed by the matrix entries in row order. A valid input has a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal, and entry \((u,v)\) equals one exactly when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). Its bit length is \(N=n^2+2b+1\). This explicitly includes all vertices, including isolated ones; there is no succinct matrix generator or graph oracle. The output is an \(n\)-bit indicator vector, with entry one exactly at selected vertices. Reading the input and writing this output count toward time. No guarantee is required on malformed encodings. Every labeling of the vertices by \([n]\) is a valid input order on which the guarantees must hold.

Computation. The algorithm is one deterministic Turing-machine program with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of tapes. Each step reads and writes one symbol on each tape, changes finite control and moves each head by at most one position. Work tapes are initially blank. No randomness, oracle, nonuniform advice or uncharged preprocessing is allowed. Integer or rational arithmetic, if used internally, is performed on finite binary representations with all bit operations charged. The time bound is worst-case over every valid input, rather than expected or amortized time. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once with the algorithm, not supplied as a graph-dependent accuracy parameter.

Quantifiers and accuracy. The order is
\[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)\ \exists A\ \exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G.\]
The time constants may depend on this chosen algorithm and improvement but not on the input graph. Requiring a rational improvement does not change the original real-constant question: any positive real improvement implies a smaller positive rational one. The objective inequality is multiplicative, with no additive error, asymptotic slack or exceptional small graphs. A guarantee strictly below two separately on each finite graph, such as \(2-1/n\), does not give one improvement valid for all sizes. The numerical benchmark tolerance of 0.01 is not an additive tolerance on this approximation-ratio existence question.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the formal statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), one deterministic program and common polynomial time constants, and prove termination, valid-cover output and \(|S|\le(2-\varepsilon)\tau(G)\) on every valid adjacency-matrix input, including empty and edgeless graphs. A negative answer must prove that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every deterministic program having a polynomial running-time bound on all valid inputs, some graph produces an invalid cover encoding, an uncovered edge, or a cover larger than \((2-\varepsilon)\tau(G)\). It must rule out all such algorithms, not merely one rounding scheme or restricted family. A conditional result under UGC, \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), ETH or another unproved hypothesis does not establish this unconditional negation. A vanishing improvement, experiments, an estimate of the optimum without a cover, or an algorithm restricted to a graph class does not meet the stated universal guarantee.
cards.why: Vertex Cover is a basic covering problem with a long-standing gap between its factor-two algorithmic benchmark and known unconditional hardness thresholds. A fixed improvement would distinguish the true computational limit from a barrier shared by many methods. Ruling out every such algorithm would require an unconditional complexity separation, so the logical strength of the chosen question must remain explicit.

cards.context:
A cover chooses vertices so that every edge is touched. A star with many leaves has optimum one, while a triangle has optimum two. The complement of a vertex cover is an independent set, but the identity between their optimum sizes does not preserve multiplicative approximation factors. This card uses unit vertex costs, retaining the unweighted target selected at admission.

The original seminar source discusses weighted Vertex Cover, its factor-two approximation, and its role in the primal-dual framework. The event was on 11 December 2000, and the online account is a summary by Claire Kenyon. It motivates the approximation barrier; it does not supply a contemporary status check or specify the full deterministic bit model used here.

Polynomial-time approximation bounds of the form \(2-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\log n})\) improve on two at each sufficiently large fixed size. The improvement nevertheless tends to zero as \(n\) grows. Karakostas’s result therefore does not answer whether one fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) works on all inputs. The present deterministic target also requires the stated worst-case bit-time and output guarantees.

The 2-to-2 Games line of work proves NP-hardness of approximation within \(\sqrt2-\eta\) for every fixed \(\eta>0\). The 2025 Khot–Minzer–Safra journal account explains how later work proved the combinatorial hypotheses in its original reduction. This hardness gives an algorithmic impossibility consequence under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), but leaves a gap up to two and does not unconditionally rule out the algorithms quantified here.

Khot and Regev prove NP-hardness below every fixed factor \(2-\varepsilon\), assuming the Unique Games Conjecture. Thus UGC together with \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would imply a negative answer to this card. Conversely, a deterministic improvement would contradict that conjunction; it would not by itself unconditionally refute UGC. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), an exact polynomial-time cover algorithm would give a positive answer.

Claimed improvements require version and quantifier checks. The latest Salvador preprint, version 3 posted 6 July 2026, labels its universal \(7/4\) ratio as Conjecture 1, supported by finite experiments. The earlier version’s asserted \(7/5\) theorem is not the current conclusion. The latest version therefore supplies no proved fixed improvement for every graph.

The inspected March 2026 Hallelujah preprint states \(|S|<2\tau(G)\) for each finite nonempty graph, not a graph-independent positive gap. Its explicit lexicographic selection rule also has a direct limiting example: on \(K_{r,r}\) with the two parts labeled by alternating odd and even numbers, all degrees tie and the selected union has \(2r-1\) vertices while the optimum is \(r\). Its ratio is therefore \(2-1/r\). This observation concerns that preprint’s stated rule; the separately published version was accessible only through its abstract. Neither this pointwise claim nor its stated UGC interpretation certifies the target here.

The 6 September 2026 Karthik–Minzer preprint reports stronger NP-hardness for vertex cover in hypergraphs: factor \(1+\sqrt2-\eta\) for three-element edges, and \(k-\eta\) for fixed edge size \(k\ge4\). Ordinary graphs have two-element edges and are outside those new parameter ranges. The recent perfect-completeness four-to-one-games result likewise continues to list \(\sqrt2\) as the graph Vertex Cover hardness frontier in its introduction.

sentences: A vertex cover selects at least one endpoint of every edge of a finite simple undirected graph.
The problem asks whether one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm always finds a cover within a fixed factor strictly below two of the minimum size.
The positive improvement must be independent of graph size, and the output and worst-case bit-time guarantees apply to every explicitly listed graph, including edgeless ones.
A complete Lean proof must establish such an algorithm or unconditionally rule out every polynomial-time candidate, rather than assume an unproved hardness hypothesis.
Known vanishing improvements, Unique-Games-based hardness, recent hypergraph results and the checked heuristic claims do not provide the required unconditional fixed-gap resolution.

cards.title: Unconditional NP-hardness at the Goemans–Williamson Max-Cut threshold
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Let
\[
 \alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}=
 \min_{0<\theta\le\pi}\frac{2\theta}{\pi(1-\cos\theta)}.
\]
Is the following statement true? For every rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon<1-\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\), there exist rational constants \(0<b<a\le1\), with
\[
 \frac ba<\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon,
\]
and a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction \(R_\varepsilon\) from 3-SAT to simple unweighted Max-Cut such that, for every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\), its output graph has at least one edge and satisfies
\[
 \varphi\text{ satisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow
       \operatorname{val}(R_\varepsilon(\varphi))\ge a,
 \qquad
 \varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\ \Longrightarrow
       \operatorname{val}(R_\varepsilon(\varphi))\le b?
\]
The statement assumes no hardness conjecture.
cards.definitions:
A graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple and undirected: there are no loops, parallel edges or edge weights. Write \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and \(m=|E|\ge1\). A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), representing the bipartition \((S,V\setminus S)\). Its size is the number of edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). Define the normalized optimum by
\[
 \operatorname{val}(G)=\frac1m\max_{S\subseteq V}
       |\{\{u,v\}\in E:|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}|.
\]
The constants \(a\) and \(b\) are fractions of all edges, not numbers of edges. The gap promise consists of YES graphs with value at least \(a\) and NO graphs with value at most \(b\). A procedure distinguishing these cases has no required behavior on graphs with value strictly between \(b\) and \(a\). The reduction must map every input formula into one of the two promised cases according to its satisfiability.

A 3-CNF formula is an explicit finite conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three Boolean literals, with each literal a variable or its negation. Satisfiability means that some assignment of Boolean values makes every clause true. Empty clauses are false and an empty conjunction is true. Variables and signs are listed in a standard binary encoding; let \(N\) be the full encoding length. Equivalent explicit encodings related by polynomial-time translations give the same reduction notion.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the reduction is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program, uniform over all input lengths. There must exist constants \(K\ge1\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) such that it halts within \(K(N+1)^d\) bit operations on every valid formula. It outputs the graph explicitly, for example by its vertex count and binary adjacency matrix. Thus its output size is also polynomial in \(N\). A single output graph is required; oracle calls, a randomized reduction and a succinct implicit graph do not meet this definition.

The rationals \(a,b\), the program and its polynomial bound may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(\varphi\) or \(N\). The question does not require one reduction with polynomial dependence on the bit length of \(\varepsilon\), or an algorithm that constructs the reduction from \(\varepsilon\). Once chosen, each reduction itself is uniform and efficient in its formula input.

The constant \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\) is defined by the exact real expression above, with angles in radians and the usual constants \(\pi\) and cosine. Its approximate value \(0.878567\) is only explanatory; substituting a rounded decimal does not define the target. A multiplicative retained-fraction guarantee \(r\) for this maximization problem means a cut of size at least \(r\) times the optimal size. A gap with \(b/a<r\) separates satisfiable and unsatisfiable reductions for such a guaranteed approximation.

Here NP-hardness means precisely the displayed reduction from 3-SAT. It is a claim about the existence of polynomial-time reductions, not an assumed inequality between complexity classes. Proving those reductions does not itself prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). The Unique Games Conjecture, Gap-ETH and other unproved hardness assumptions are not premises of the proposition.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or of its logical negation.

A positive answer must establish the reduction for every specified rational \(\varepsilon\), with rational thresholds, polynomial output size, deterministic polynomial bit complexity, and both correctness implications for all formulas. If an intermediate construction uses weighted graphs, parallel edges or a different constraint problem, its conversion to the required simple unweighted graph must be included with the required gap bound.

A negative answer must prove that some rational \(\varepsilon\) in the stated interval admits no pair of thresholds and deterministic polynomial-time reduction satisfying all the conditions. It is not enough to refute one proposed reduction or one conjecture used by a known construction.

An implication conditional on an unproved Unique Games assumption does not settle the unconditional proposition. An integrality gap for a particular relaxation, or an approximation algorithm without the further theorem needed to exclude NP-hardness, likewise does not alone establish either answer. No fixed additive numerical tolerance replaces the universal epsilon quantifier.
cards.why: An unconditional reduction at this threshold would explain the limit of a landmark semidefinite approximation algorithm using ordinary NP-hardness, without adding a separate hardness conjecture.

cards.title: Four-thirds approximation for metric TSP
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, on every symmetric rational metric TSP instance \(I\) defined below, always returns a feasible tour and satisfies \[\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I))]\le\frac43\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\] Running time must be polynomial in the full distance-matrix encoding length on every random execution. The guarantee is against the optimum integral tour, with no restriction to a particular linear relaxation or rounding method.
cards.definitions:
An input \(I\) consists of an integer \(n\ge3\) and the full explicitly listed matrix \(d\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), with
\[
 d(i,i)=0,\qquad d(i,j)=d(j,i)>0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad
 d(i,k)\le d(i,j)+d(j,k)\quad(i,j,k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}).
\]
Integers are binary encoded, and a rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. Let \(L(I)\) be the full binary encoding length, including all entries and their delimiters. There is no promise of an embedding, a graph representation, bounded aspect ratio or a restricted metric family.

A feasible output is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its tour cost includes the closing edge:
\[
 \operatorname{cost}_I(\pi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(\pi(i),\pi(i+1)),
 \qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).
\]
The positive number \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum of this cost over all permutations.

An algorithm is one uniform classical randomized Turing machine with independent fair random bits. For some polynomial \(p\), on every valid input and every random tape it halts within \(p(L(I))\) steps and outputs a feasible tour. Its program is finite and independent of the input length; no input-length advice, external oracle or uncharged real arithmetic is available. The runtime bound is worst-case over the coins, although approximation quality is measured in expectation over those coins. Deterministic algorithms are included.

A real number \(r\ge1\) is achievable if there exist such an algorithm \(A\) and polynomial bound \(p\) with
\[
 \mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_I(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)
 \quad\text{for every valid }I.
\]
The algorithm and its polynomial may depend on the fixed value \(r\), but not on the particular input or its unknown optimal tour. There is no requirement of an effective procedure that takes \(r\) and produces the algorithm. The set \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty by known constant-factor algorithms, so its infimum is a finite number at least one. The infimum need not itself be achievable.

This quantity compares efficient algorithms with the integral tour optimum. It is distinct from the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the optimum of the subtour linear program. An integrality-gap example is not by itself a lower bound against every algorithm. A result for one rounding method, a bounded number of vertices, graph metrics, Euclidean metrics or a special class of fractional solutions does not determine this unrestricted algorithmic infimum.

For the context, put \(\rho_{\mathrm{TSP}}=\inf\mathcal R\), where \(\mathcal R\) is the set of achievable factors defined above. No complexity assumption is imposed. A hardness argument conditional on an unproved assumption does not by itself refute the algorithmic assertion.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm always outputs a feasible tour and has expected cost at most \(4\operatorname{OPT}/3\) on each input, or refute the existence of such an algorithm.
cards.why: Determine the fundamental efficient-approximation limit of the canonical routing problem, beyond the guarantees of any one linear relaxation or rounding algorithm.

cards.context:
The 2021 breakthrough establishes a universal expected approximation strictly below \(3/2\), after decades at that threshold. Its theorem compares the returned tour with the optimal integral tour, matching this card’s denominator.

The later derandomization gives a deterministic guarantee below \(3/2\). Thus the current progress is not confined to algorithms with only an expected runtime bound.

The 2024 analysis records the explicit ratio \(3/2-2.18\cdot10^{-34}\). This improves a universal upper bound, but does not determine the best achievable ratio to absolute precision \(1/100\).

Approximating within any fixed factor strictly below \(123/122\) is NP-hard in the cited theorem. Such a hardness statement does not itself prove an unconditional numerical lower bound on the infimum over randomized polynomial-time algorithms.

The July 2026 \(10/7\) guarantee applies to half-integral cycle-cut instances. It does not give that ratio for every metric in this card.

A September 2026 preprint claims a larger universal saving above \(2.05522\cdot10^{-30}\) below \(3/2\). Its statement was checked, but its proof and numerical certificate were not independently audited. Even the claimed upper bound is far from a two-sided determination within \(1/100\).

cards.title: Factor-two subtour-LP gap for asymmetric TSP
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\le2\,\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) for every integer \(n\ge2\) and every nonnegative directed metric \(c\) on \(n\) vertices with \(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)>0\), using the Hamiltonian-tour objective and degree-constrained subtour linear program below? Equivalently, is the universal integrality gap \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{ATSP}}=2\), since the matching lower bound is known? This is an existence inequality; no efficient rounding algorithm is required.
cards.definitions:
A directed metric is a function \(c:V	imes V	o\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(c(i,i)=0\) and \(c(i,k)\le c(i,j)+c(j,k)\) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc \((i,j)\) for each \(i
e j\) and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) is the minimum over all such cycles. For \(S\subseteq V, \delta ^{+}(S)=\{(i,j):i\in S,j
otin S\}\) and \(\delta ^{-}(S)=\{(i,j):i
otin S,j\in S\}\); for a set of arcs F write \(x(F)=\sum_{(i,j)\in F} x_{ij}\). \(\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\) minimizes \(\sum_{i
e j} c(i,j)x_{ij}\) over real variables \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) subject to \(x(\delta ^{+}(\{v\}))=x(\delta ^{-}(\{v\}))=1\) for every v, and \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))\ge 1\) for every nonempty proper \(S\subsetneq V\). The degree equalities imply \(x(\delta ^{+}(S))=x(\delta ^{-}(S))\), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. Zero-LP instances are excluded from the ratio; they also have zero tour optimum. Indeed, the positive support of a zero-cost feasible solution is strongly connected by the cut constraints, and directed triangle inequalities then give zero distance between every ordered pair. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)/\mathrm{LP}_{\mathrm{ATSP}}(c)\), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path. The supremum is over every finite size and is not required to be attained. The usual factor-two conjecture asserts \(\Gamma _{\mathrm{ATSP}}=2\), taking account of known approaching lower-bound families.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the integral-tour optimum is at most twice the positive subtour-LP optimum for every directed metric in the stated domain, or exhibit such a metric with ratio strictly greater than two.

cards.context:
The selected binary question is the factor-two subtour-LP integrality-gap conjecture. A proof of the universal inequality or one instance with a strictly larger ratio answers it; a complete determination of any alternative gap is not required.

A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The quantity measures the largest possible multiplicative loss when converting fractional cost into an actual tour; the classical conjecture sets that loss at two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in \(\{0,1/2,1\}\). An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical \(4/3\) conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

cards.title: Deterministic k-server conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite or infinite metric space \((M,d)\) with at least \(k+1\) points, and every initial configuration \(C_0\in M^k\), do there exist a deterministic online rule \(A\) and a finite \(\beta\ge0\) such that \[\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma;C_0)\le k\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\] for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\)? Both parties have exactly \(k\) servers and start at \(C_0\); movement cost is the sum of distances in the model below. The rule and additive constant may depend on the metric and initial placement, but not on the future requests.
cards.definitions:
For every integer \(k\ge1\), define the universal deterministic competitive-ratio infimum
\[R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where
\[\mathcal R_k=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\ \forall(M,d)\in\mathcal M_k\ \forall C_0\in M^k\ \exists A\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\ \forall\sigma\in M^{<\omega},\quad
\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma;C_0)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite or infinite metric spaces having at least \(k+1\) points, \(A\) is a deterministic online rule in the serving model below, and \(M^{<\omega}\) is the set of all finite request sequences, including the empty sequence. 

A metric space here consists of a set \(M\) and a function \(d:M\times M\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with finite values, satisfying \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The space is known to the rule. It need not be finite, bounded, discrete, complete, compact, or given by computable distances. The quantifier ranges over ordinary set-based metric spaces.

There are exactly \(k\) servers with equal movement costs. For precise bookkeeping label them by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and write a configuration as a tuple \(C=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M^k\). Several servers may occupy the same point. Labels only identify which server moves and confer no different costs or service capabilities; the physical configuration is a multiset. The initial tuple \(C_0\) is specified before the first request and is identical for the online rule and the offline comparator.

For a request sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\), request \(q_t\) must be served before \(q_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay put and the cost of that step is zero. Otherwise the rule chooses one index \(i_t\in[k]\), moves that server from its current position \(x_{i_t,t-1}\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_{i_t,t-1},q_t)\). All other positions remain unchanged. Let \(\delta_t\) denote this step cost. The total cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\). These are lazy moves; for the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances objective, the classical laziness lemma shows that this restriction does not worsen the attainable competitive guarantees.

A deterministic online rule is a function assigning a legal next move to each nonempty revealed request prefix, with the current configuration determined recursively from earlier moves. On two sequences with the same prefix it must make the same decisions through that prefix. It may use the known metric, \(k\), the initial tuple, and the whole revealed history. No random bits, future-dependent advice, request horizon or next request are provided. All finite sequences are included, of arbitrary length; the definition also covers requests chosen adaptively from the rule's past moves. Covered requests may remain in the remembered history.

This is a question about existence of online decision rules, without any time, space, computability, finite-program or finite-precision restriction. In particular, a rule on a specified real metric is an abstract function; no unmentioned representation of all real distances is required. The ratio \(r\) depends only on \(k\). The chosen rule and finite constant \(\beta\) may depend on \(k,r,(M,d),C_0\), but neither may be chosen after seeing the future sequence. The same \(A,\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all sequence lengths and contents on that metric and initial placement.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)\) is the minimum total cost of all legal lazy move sequences serving \(\sigma\) from \(C_0\), with all requests known in advance. There are at most \(k^T\) choices of server indices, so the minimum is attained and finite even when \(M\) is infinite. Both costs are zero for the empty sequence. There is no final return requirement and no prescribed terminal configuration. The competitive inequality is used directly, including when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\); it is not a quotient by a possibly zero cost.

Movement costs and \(\beta\) have the same distance units, while \(r\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\) are dimensionless. Multiplying all distances by a positive constant rescales costs and the allowed additive constant, but does not change the competitive ratio. No normalization of metric diameter is imposed.

The known universal upper bound gives \(2k-1\in\mathcal R_k\), so this set is nonempty and its real infimum exists; the deterministic lower bound gives \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The infimum need not be attained. For \(u\ge1\), an upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u\) means that for every \(\eta>0\), the ratio \(u+\eta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_k\). The selected rules and additive constants may depend on \(\eta\). A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that for every \(r\in[1,\ell)\) there exist a metric and initial placement such that every online rule and every finite additive constant fail the competitive inequality on some finite sequence. The obstructing metric may depend on \(r\); no single metric witnessing attainment of a supremum is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that for each \(k\), metric and initial configuration, a deterministic online rule and a finite additive constant give the stated \(k\)-competitive bound on every sequence. To refute it, fix one such setting and defeat every rule and additive constant.
cards.why: The k-server problem measures the movement cost of responding to demand without knowing future requests. It includes paging and serves as a basic problem in competitive analysis, with the same number of resources available to the online rule and the offline optimum.

cards.context:
On the uniform metric, where every two different points have distance one, the covered points represent pages currently in a cache. A request at an uncovered point incurs a page replacement. General metrics permit different movement costs between different demand locations. The comparison here always gives exactly \(k\) servers to both parties.

Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator prove the deterministic lower bound \(k\) and a matching algorithm for two servers. Their original paper also handles metrics with exactly \(k+1\) points. The lower-bound argument permits an offline starting-position change at a finite additive cost, so requiring the same initial placement does not remove the asymptotic obstruction. Together with the direct one-server case, the established initial values are \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(1)=1\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(2)=2\).

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou establish a universal \((2k-1)\)-competitive deterministic rule, the work-function algorithm. Their manuscript explicitly allows infinite metrics and repeated server locations. As the classical bound before the September 2026 claim, this yields \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The result concerns competitive movement cost; it does not supply a polynomial running-time guarantee, and the present target does not require one.

The selected target is the classical conjecture asserting an actual \(k\)-competitive rule. It implies \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\), but an infimum value alone need not give endpoint attainment. The September 2026 preprint claims the actual competitiveness statement; its proof-review caveat is retained below.

Chrobak and Larmore obtain the optimal factor \(k\) on tree metrics, whose distances are the lengths of unique connecting paths in an edge-weighted tree. This covers the line as a special case. It is a guarantee for that geometry rather than for every metric.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle. For circumference \(L>0\), this metric is \([0,L)\) with \(d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,L-|x-y|\}\). Their separate computer-assisted limitation concerns a precisely defined family of potential certificates under a specified universal condition. It does not disprove 3-competitiveness of all online rules or exclude every proof for the work-function algorithm. The inspected text is the 2022 preprint; the journal article appeared in 2024.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani give metrics on \(k+1\) points with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). This refutes the randomized \(O(\log k)\) conjecture. Their ratio compares expected movement cost to the offline optimum with a sequence-independent additive constant. It neither refutes the deterministic factor \(k\) nor determines the deterministic infimum function.

Frei and coauthors' ISAAC 2025 result has a deterministic lower bound \(2k-1\) for a different objective: each request costs the maximum simultaneous server movement, rather than the sum of movements. That time objective can reward moving several servers at once, so the lazy distance model in this card is not an interchangeable formulation. The new lower bound is not a matching lower bound for \(R_{\mathrm{det}}\).

The April 2026 k-server-bench preprint evaluates candidate proof certificates on finite instances, including four-server circle instances. It explicitly distinguishes passing those finite checks from a proof covering all configurations and request sequences. Its reported experiments do not resolve the remaining general case.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 theorem gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on \(n\)-point metrics. Its reduction uses few random bits, but does not eliminate randomness. A separate deterministic consequence supplies advice that depends on the instance. Neither extra input nor randomization is present in this card, so these computational improvements do not determine its universal deterministic ratio.

Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński's preprint submitted on 14 September 2026 states in Theorem 1.2 that, for every metric and every finite request sequence,
\[\operatorname{WFA}_{C_0}(\sigma)\le k\operatorname{OPT}_{C_0}(\sigma)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}d(s_i,s_j).\]
Here \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) are the initial server locations. The additive term is finite and depends only on the initial placement, as permitted here. The paper explicitly handles coincident positions with distinct location labels and a pseudometric, and states the theorem for any metric space. Its lazy implementation agrees with the serving convention of this card. The matching claim changes the current status to uncertain pending verification; this review has not independently certified the whole proof.

Neither extra input nor randomization is present in this card, so these computational improvements do not determine its universal deterministic ratio.

Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński's preprint submitted on 14 September 2026 states in Theorem 1.2 that, for every metric and every finite request sequence,
\[\operatorname{WFA}_{C_0}(\sigma)\le k\operatorname{OPT}_{C_0}(\sigma)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}d(s_i,s_j).\]
Here \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) are the initial server locations. The additive term is finite and depends only on the initial placement, as permitted here. The paper explicitly handles coincident positions with distinct location labels and a pseudometric, and states the theorem for any metric space. Its lazy implementation agrees with the serving convention of this card. The matching claim changes the current status to uncertain pending verification; this review has not independently certified the whole proof.

Its scope covers the retained model, including repeated initial locations via distinct labels. Combined with the established lower bound, the claimed theorem would give R_det(k)=k for every k and establish the binary k-competitiveness assertion selected here. The full PDF, model, theorem and proof organization were inspected, but the complete proof is not independently certified or Lean-checked here. Status is uncertain pending verification, superseding the previous source-open assessment.

cards.title: Matroid secretary conjecture
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), there is a randomized online selection strategy \(\mathcal A_M\) satisfying
\[\forall w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0},\qquad
\mathbb E_{\pi,U}\!\left[\sum_{e\in S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)}w(e)\right]
\ge\frac1C\max_{I\in\mathcal I}\sum_{e\in I}w(e)?\]
The element weights are fixed adversarially before a uniformly random arrival permutation \(\pi\) and the strategy's independent randomness \(U\) are chosen. Each acceptance decision is irrevocable and must preserve independence. The same \(C\) must work for all matroids and all weights.
cards.definitions:
A finite matroid consists of a finite ground set \(E\) and a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\) of independent sets with two properties. First, \(B\subseteq A\in\mathcal I\) implies \(B\in\mathcal I\). Second, if \(A,B\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|B|\), some \(e\in B\setminus A\) satisfies \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). In particular, \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\). Loops, zero weights, ties and the empty ground set are allowed. The matroid rank is \(\max_{I\in\mathcal I}|I|\).

The strategy knows \(E\) and \(\mathcal I\) in advance, including all element identities and \(n=|E|\), but has no information about the weights of unarrived elements. At step \(t\), it sees the identity \(\pi(t)\) and its finite real weight \(w(\pi(t))\). Before the next arrival, it chooses to accept or reject that element. Its decision may use only the known matroid, the revealed prefix, its previous decisions and its random seed. An accepted element cannot subsequently be discarded, and a rejected element cannot subsequently be accepted. Every accepted prefix must belong to \(\mathcal I\), for every input, arrival order and seed. The notation \(S_{\mathcal A_M}(w,\pi,U)\) denotes the final accepted set.

A randomized strategy is a measurable nonanticipating decision rule; one may model its private randomness by \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\), independent of \(\pi\). The permutation is uniform among the \(n!\) permutations of \(E\) and independent of the fixed weight assignment. Expectations include these two sources of randomness. For every fixed assignment the optimum is finite, so the expected reward is well-defined and finite. If all feasible weights are zero, the inequality still applies with a zero right-hand side.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C\;\forall M\;\exists\mathcal A_M\;\forall w\). A strategy cannot be selected after seeing the weight assignment. The guarantee has no additive loss, no dependence of \(C\) on size or rank, and no high-probability requirement beyond the stated expectation. There is no restriction on computation, preprocessing or independence queries. This is the competitive-existence question in the known-matroid model, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights; no finite encoding or polynomial running time is appended.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed constant-competitiveness proposition, or of its full logical negation. A positive proof must give a finite universal constant and admissible strategies with the expected guarantee for every matroid and weight assignment. A negative proof must show that for every proposed finite constant some matroid defeats every admissible strategy on some fixed nonnegative weight assignment. A result for a restricted matroid family, randomly assigned weights, or a constant depending on rank does not settle this target. A newly posted proof claim is not itself a Lean-checked answer.
cards.why: This is a central question about the power of random arrival order in online selection under general independence constraints. A universal bound would apply across all matroids and is equivalent, through established reductions, to a general random-order contention-resolution guarantee.

references.title: The Matroid Secretary Conjecture is True
references.locator: Version 1 submitted 13 September 2026; PDF title-page date 15 September. §3 Theorem 3.1 and model; §4 separately announced extensions and unverified constant improvement. Fresh proof claim, not independently certified here.

cards.context:
The classical secretary task chooses one item whose unknown value is revealed on arrival. Matroids extend the feasibility rule to collections of items. For example, a uniform matroid permits any set up to a prescribed size, while a graphic matroid permits sets of edges containing no cycle. The offline optimum knows every weight; the online strategy sees only a random prefix at each decision.

Random arrival order and random assignment of weights are distinct sources of information. In the random-assignment variant, a multiset of weights is distributed uniformly among ground-set elements. Santiago, Sergeev and Zenklusen obtain a constant guarantee for that variant even without advance knowledge of the matroid. Their May 2023 preprint explicitly leaves the adversarial-assignment conjecture open. Its theorem cannot by itself justify the general claim here.

Before the new September claim, the cited general guarantee was \(O(\log\log r)\), with the small-rank cases treated separately, where \(r\) is the matroid rank. A growing rank-dependent factor differs from a universal constant, even though many particular matroid classes already admit constant guarantees.

Dughmi proves that a competitive secretary algorithm implies random-order contention resolution for arbitrarily correlated active sets, losing only the same multiplicative factor relative to the best offline guarantee. The later equivalence theorem establishes the converse at the level of universal constants. This connection concerns a known probability distribution and an information-theoretic guarantee; it does not require the distribution to be a product law.

Singla's preprint submitted on 13 September 2026 states in Theorem 3.1 that each element of a canonical offline optimum is accepted with probability at least \(1/4\), while the selected set is always independent. This would imply the displayed target with \(C=4\). The stated theorem allows fixed nonnegative values and needs only the ground-set size and independence queries on already arrived elements. Those assumptions are compatible with, and more restrictive than, this card's advance matroid knowledge.

The fresh preprint is recorded as a matching solution claim, pending independent verification. Its full PDF and theorem scope were inspected, but this review does not certify the complete proof. Section 4 separately announces extensions and defers their detailed proofs; those announcements are not treated as already established results. The paper also distinguishes the original constant-factor conjecture from the stronger proposed factor \(e\), where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm.

cards.title: Square-root-dimensional Euclidean convex body chasing
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge1\), some deterministic online strategy \(A_d\) for convex body chasing in \(\mathbb R^d\) satisfies \[\operatorname{cost}_{A_d}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\le C\sqrt d\,\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\] for every finite sequence of nonempty compact convex request sets? The strategy starts at the origin, sees each set before choosing its next point in that set, and pays Euclidean movement. The same strategy must work for every horizon; requests need not be nested, and no additive cost is allowed.
cards.definitions:
An online strategy starts at \(x_0=0\), sees a nonempty compact convex set \(K_t\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) at round \(t\), and must immediately choose \(x_t\in K_t\) using only \(K_1,\ldots,K_t\). Its cost on a finite request sequence is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|x_t-x_{t-1}\|_2\). Let
\[\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)=\min_{y_t\in K_t,\ y_0=0}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|y_t-y_{t-1}\|_2\]
and define
\[\mathcal C(d)=\inf\left\{c\ge1:\ \exists A\ \forall T\ge1\ \forall K_1,\ldots,K_T,\quad\operatorname{cost}_A(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\le c\,\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\right\}.\]


The Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_j^2)^{1/2}\). A request set is nonempty, compact and convex: it is closed and bounded, and contains \((1-\lambda)u+\lambda v\) whenever \(u,v\) lie in it and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). Lower-dimensional sets, including points and faces of polytopes, are allowed. There is no common diameter bound, containment relation or promise that consecutive requests intersect. In particular, the sequence need not be nested.

A deterministic online strategy is a sequence of maps \(A_t\), one for every positive integer \(t\), taking every length-\(t\) request history to a point in its final set. These maps jointly specify one causal strategy: two request sequences with the same prefix have the same choices on that prefix, irrespective of their eventual lengths or later requests. Its own previous locations are determined by that history. The full current set is available before choosing the current point; no future set, horizon, forecast, advice or random choice is supplied.

This is the information-theoretic model of competitive analysis used in the sources. Strategies are mathematical maps on convex sets, with unrestricted computation; a finite input encoding, polynomial-time evaluator or bounded number of membership queries is not an extra requirement. An answer must specify its strategy well enough to prove feasibility and cost, but the benchmark measures movement, not computational time.

The offline comparator starts at the same origin, knows the whole finite sequence, and may choose a different feasible point at every round. Compactness makes its displayed minimum attainable. There is no required return to the origin and no additional service cost or cost for reading a request. Competitiveness is a purely multiplicative guarantee on every finite sequence, with no additive constant. If OPT is zero, the online strategy must also incur zero cost; the definition uses an inequality to avoid division by zero. Requests may be selected adversarially after previous moves, since the guarantee covers every finite request history for a deterministic strategy.

The infimum is over all qualifying ratios and strategies in each dimension; it need not be attained. Its value is finite by the known dimension-dependent upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one constant \(C\) bounds the competitive ratio by \(C\sqrt d\) for a deterministic strategy in each dimension, starting at the origin, for every horizon. A refutation rules out every proposed \(C\) on some dimension.
cards.why: Convex body chasing isolates the movement cost of maintaining feasibility when constraints arrive without advance notice. The optimal dependence on dimension measures how much geometric complexity alone can penalize online decisions, independently of computational efficiency. Matching bounds would resolve a central quantitative gap between what convexity permits offline and what an online strategy can guarantee.

cards.context:
The 2025 source lists an \(O(d)\) upper bound for general convex body chasing and an \(\Omega(\sqrt d)\) lower bound in Euclidean space. It separately lists the stronger upper bound for nested requests; the saved card concerns the unrestricted sequence problem.

Sellke proves a competitive ratio of \(d\) for convex body chasing in an arbitrary \(d\)-dimensional normed space. That dependence is tight for the maximum-coordinate norm, but the corresponding general Euclidean lower bound is only of order \(\sqrt d\). A worst-case norm cannot be substituted for the fixed Euclidean norm here.

For Euclidean requests of horizon \(T\), Sellke also proves an \(O(\sqrt{d\log T})\) guarantee. Combining it with the dimension-only bound helps at shorter horizons, but it does not yield a sublinear-in-d bound uniformly over arbitrary \(T\).

The nested problem adds \(K_{t+1}\subseteq K_t\). Its \(O(\sqrt{d\log d})\) Euclidean upper bound is nearly the square-root lower bound, but that extra containment hypothesis is not available in this card. Recent applications to shrinking feasible regions therefore do not by themselves close the general chasing gap.

cards.title: Breaking factor two for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and one uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm that, on every valid unrelated-machine scheduling instance \(I\) defined below, outputs a feasible schedule \(\sigma\) with \[C_{\max}(\sigma)\le(2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(I)?\] The machine count is part of the input, and \(\varepsilon\) is independent of it and of all processing times. No complexity assumption is included.
cards.definitions:
For offline makespan minimization on unrelated parallel machines, define the real number
\[\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R,\qquad \mathcal R=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\exists A\ \exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\ \begin{array}{l} A(I)\text{ halts in at most }c(N(I)+2)^k\text{ bit steps,}\\ A(I)\text{ outputs a feasible schedule }\sigma_I,\\ C_{\max}(\sigma_I)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\end{array}\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal I\) is the full class of finite rational processing-time matrices defined below, \(N(I)\) is the full binary input length, and \(A\) ranges over finite deterministic Turing-machine programs. 

An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(N(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same approximation-ratio infimum.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside \(\mathcal I\). The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

For each fixed achieved ratio \(r\), the same program and constants \(c,k\) must work for all \(m,n,p\). They may depend on \(r\), but \(r\) is not additional advice or an input to the program. A different program for each input length is not allowed. The set \(\mathcal R\) concerns an absolute multiplicative guarantee on each instance, with no additive slack and no asymptotic or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; no quotient by zero is used. All these conventions include empty instances.

The ratio is dimensionless. The established factor-two algorithm gives \(2\in\mathcal R\), so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). The infimum need not be attained: \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\), for \(u\ge1\), means that for every \(\eta>0\) some program achieves a ratio at most \(u+\eta\), without requiring one program to attain \(u\) or one uniform procedure generating all these programs. A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that no program achieves any fixed \(r\in[1,\ell)\) on every instance.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm attains factor \(2-\varepsilon\) for one fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) on all unrelated-machine instances, or refute the existence of every such algorithm and improvement.
cards.why: This is a central approximation question for allocating heterogeneous work to heterogeneous machines. The long gap between achievable guarantees and conditional hardness also has formal consequences for max-min fair allocation, making its resolution informative beyond scheduling.

references.locator: Version 2, 19 June 2026, first posted 11 December 2024; introduction, Section 4.1 Theorem 1 and Remark 4.1 pp. 8–9; AAAI 2025 39(13):13839–13846, DOI 10.1609/aaai.v39i13.33513; inspected revised preprint distinguishes optimal initial input from polynomial transformation

cards.context:
The selected target restores the original source question: a polynomial-time \((2-\varepsilon)\)-approximation for one fixed universal \(\varepsilon>0\). It does not request a numerical determination of the full approximation-ratio infimum.

Unrelated machines need not have any common ranking by speed. A job can be fast on one machine and slow on another, while a second job has the reverse pattern. The makespan measures when all work has finished, so a schedule must balance indivisible loads rather than minimize their sum. Eligibility restrictions are included by forbidding selected assignments.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos prove a polynomial-time factor-two approximation and show that every fixed ratio below \(3/2\) would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Their hardness already uses a finite positive-integer subcase. Thus the unconditional bounds here are \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\); assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), they become \(3/2\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), the finite rational scheduling optimization admits exact polynomial-time search and \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=1\). The hardness assumption cannot be omitted from the lower endpoint.

Shchepin and Vakhania achieve ratio \(2-1/m\) for \(m\) machines. The same formula is below two for each finite \(m\), but its supremum over all machine counts is two. It therefore gives no fixed universal improvement. Likewise, the polynomial approximation scheme of Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos fixes the number of machines in advance; its running-time dependence is different from the single polynomial required for unbounded \(m\).

For a target time \(T\), the configuration linear program has one nonnegative variable \(y_{i,S}\) for each machine and each job subset \(S\) whose total processing time on that machine is at most \(T\). It requires \(\sum_S y_{i,S}=1\) for each machine and total fractional coverage one for every job. Verschae and Wiese show that the supremum of the integral optimum divided by the least feasible relaxation time is two, even when each job has at most two eligible machines with potentially different processing times. This is a statement about that relaxation, not an impossibility result for every polynomial-time algorithm.

Restricted assignment requires a job to have the same processing time on every eligible machine. The SODA 2024 work of Bamas and coauthors gives a \((7/4+\delta)\)-approximation for its two-size subcase. For general two-value matrices with entries in \(\{u,w,\infty\}\), it gives \(2-1/n^{\delta}\) for every fixed \(\delta>0\), where \(n\) is the number of jobs. The exponent is on \(n\), not on the whole ratio. These guarantees preserve their restrictions and instance-size dependence.

The same paper proves that a polynomial-time \((2-1/\alpha)\)-approximation for unrestricted makespan, for any fixed \(\alpha\ge2\), yields a polynomial-time \((\alpha+\delta)\)-approximation for general Santa Claus allocation for every fixed \(\delta>0\). In that problem indivisible items have nonnegative player-dependent values, and the objective is to maximize the minimum total value received by a player. The reduction preserves the algorithmic significance of any fixed improvement here; the paper’s converse equivalence is confined to the two-value variants.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint supplies an additional predicted partial job assignment. Its guarantee improves when prediction errors relative to an optimum are small and retains a worst-case factor two. The stated running time has a factor \((mn)^K\), so the search budget \(K\) must remain fixed for its polynomial-time claim. The inspected model uses positive processing times; neither good predictions nor a growing budget are supplied by the classical target.

The \(3/2\) result in Proportionally Fair Makespan Approximation concerns a mechanism’s fairness guarantee using an optimal initial allocation. The June 2026 revision explicitly states that its transformation is polynomial time given an allocation, while obtaining an optimal initial allocation is NP-hard. Consequently this existence result does not establish \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le3/2\). Fairness or incentive constraints and their separate existence bounds must be distinguished from computing a schedule with the complete polynomial-time guarantee in this card.

cards.title: Squared-logarithmic randomized k-server competitiveness
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(k\ge2\), every finite metric \((X,d)\) with at least \(k+1\) points, and every initial configuration \(C_0\), there are a randomized online strategy \(\mathcal A\) and a finite \(\beta\ge0\) with \[\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_{\mathcal A}(\sigma;C_0)]\le C\bigl(\log_2(k+1)\bigr)^2\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\] for every finite request sequence fixed independently of the strategy’s randomness? The strategy and \(\beta\) may depend on the metric and initial placement; \(C\) may not. The number of metric points is unbounded relative to \(k\).
cards.definitions:
For each integer \(k\ge2\), define
\[R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where \(\mathcal R_k\) is the set of real \(r\ge1\) such that
\[\forall (X,d)\in\mathcal M_k\;\forall C_0\in X^k\;\exists\mathcal A\;\exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\;\forall\sigma\in X^{<\omega},\qquad
\mathbb E_U[\operatorname{cost}_{\mathcal A}(\sigma;C_0,U)]
\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite metric spaces with at least \(k+1\) points, and \(\mathcal A\) is an online randomized strategy as defined below. 

A metric on a finite set \(X\) is a finite-valued function \(d:X\times X\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry and the triangle inequality. The number \(n=|X|\) is unbounded relative to \(k\). The strategy knows the full metric and initial configuration before any request. Distances may be arbitrary real numbers: no rational encoding, finite-precision cost or computability restriction is imposed on this information-theoretic question.

Exactly \(k\) identical servers serve the requests. For bookkeeping write a configuration as a tuple \((x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in X^k\); repeated locations are allowed and the labels confer no different costs. A finite sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\) is revealed one request at a time. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay and this step costs zero. Otherwise the strategy chooses one server, moves it from its current position \(x_i\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_i,q_t)\). All other servers stay. The total cost is the sum over the \(T\) steps. This lazy convention has the same attainable competitive guarantees as the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances model. It is not a simultaneous maximum-movement objective.

An online strategy is a measurable rule whose move depends on the known metric, \(k,C_0\), the revealed request prefix, its past choices and its private randomness. One may model the randomness by a uniform seed \(U\in[0,1]\). It must make a legal move for every prefix and seed, and serve the current request before observing the next. No future request, request horizon, prediction or advice depending on the sequence is supplied. There is no time, space, number-of-random-bits or finite-program bound. The same seed law and nonanticipating rule serve all finite sequences on the chosen instance.

The adversary is oblivious: each sequence \(\sigma\) in the guarantee is fixed independently of \(U\). It may know the strategy and its distribution, but may not choose the next request from observed random moves. Expectation is over \(U\), for that fixed sequence. Every finite-sequence cost is bounded by \(T\) times the finite metric diameter, so the expectation is finite. The offline comparator starts at the identical tuple \(C_0\), knows all of \(\sigma\), and minimizes total movement under the same serving convention. This minimum exists because there are finitely many possible server choices for a finite sequence. The empty sequence has online and offline cost zero.

For fixed \(k,r\), the strategy and finite additive term \(\beta\) may depend on the metric and initial tuple, but neither may depend on the future sequence or its length. The ratio \(r\), and ultimately the comparison constants \(a,b\), cannot depend on \(n\), distances or initial placement. The same chosen strategy and \(\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all lengths and contents. Classical deterministic bounds imply \(1\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le2k-1\), so the infimum is a finite dimensionless number. No strategy attaining the infimum is presumed to exist.

An upper bound on this infimum need not give an algorithm attaining its endpoint: for every positive slack, strategies with ratios at most the proposed upper bound plus that slack suffice on every metric and initial placement. A lower bound must exclude every smaller universal ratio; for such a smaller ratio some metric and initial placement must defeat every eligible strategy and every fixed additive constant on a sequence independent of the realized seed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one constant \(C\) bounds the expected competitive ratio by \(C(\log_2(k+1))^2\) under the stated additive allowance for all fixed request sequences. A refutation must address randomized strategies against that same oblivious adversary.
cards.why: A surviving central problem in randomized competitive analysis, beyond the refuted logarithmic k-server conjecture.

references.title: The k-server conjecture is true
references.authors: Christian Coester; Elias Koutsoupias; Marek Zbysiński
references.locator: Version 1 submitted 14 September 2026, PDF dated 15 September; §1.1 Theorem 1.2. Claimed deterministic factor k with initial-configuration additive term; no determination of the randomized asymptotic optimum.

cards.context:
On the uniform metric, all distances between distinct points equal one, and the server positions represent pages held in a cache. General metrics give different costs for replacing one location by another. Randomization can protect an online strategy from a fixed request sequence, but the comparator sees the whole sequence and has the same number of servers.

The old randomized conjecture proposed an \(O(\log k)\) ratio on every metric. Bubeck, Coester and Rabani refute it with \((k+1)\)-point metrics requiring \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\) randomized competitiveness. Their definition permits an arbitrary fixed additive constant and compares expected online cost to offline cost, matching the relevant convention here. The obstruction still leaves possible larger polylogarithmic ratios.

The \((k+1)\)-point special case has order \(\Theta(\log^2 k)\) through its connection with metrical service and task systems. This does not determine the card's function, which takes the worst case over every finite number of metric points. Allowing \(n\) much larger than \(k\) is an essential part of the remaining target.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 paper gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on hierarchically separated trees. These are a structured class of leaf metrics of weighted rooted trees whose edge scales decrease geometrically by a fixed factor along root-to-leaf paths. Theorem 1 also bounds the amount of randomness independently of request-sequence length. The geometry restriction matters to the competitive guarantee.

Their Corollary 2 gives \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\) competitiveness on arbitrary \(n\)-point metrics. This is a computational improvement, but the factor \(\log n\) cannot be hidden in a universal function of \(k\). The same paper explicitly states that even an \(o(k)\) ratio on arbitrary metrics remains open. Its separate advice-assisted consequence has additional future-dependent information and is not the oblivious randomized model here.

The classical deterministic upper bound is linear in \(k\), while the general randomized lower bound is \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). The selected binary question asks whether that lower scale is achievable on all finite metrics.

The September 2026 preprint by Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński claims that the deterministic work-function algorithm attains ratio \(k\) on every metric. If correct, it also gives \(R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le k\); it does not supply a randomized lower bound of \(k\), or improve the order \(O(k)\). Its theorem therefore does not settle the selected squared-logarithmic randomized upper bound. The new proof has not been independently certified in this review.

The weaker sublinear-ratio milestone formerly indexed as TCS-4983 would follow from the squared-logarithmic target. Its model is the same oblivious-adversary model with sequence-independent additive cost, rather than a request for computational efficiency.

source_formulation.text: The saved September 12 quantitative formulation broadened the polylogarithmic-in-k question to the asymptotic order of the universal randomized competitive ratio. That constant-factor target is retained, including finite known metrics, oblivious adversaries, no computation restriction and sequence-independent additive cost. The September deterministic conjecture claim does not replace this randomized question.

cards.title: Near-optimal dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb N_0\) such that the one-point adversarial bandit convex-optimization minimax regret defined below satisfies \[R^*(d,T)\le C d\sqrt T\bigl(\log_2(d+T+2)\bigr)^a\qquad(d,T\in\mathbb N_{\ge1})?\] Losses take values in \([0,1]\), the adversary is oblivious, and the learner observes only the exact value of its current action. The guarantee is uniform over all normalized convex bodies in the stated model; no smoothness or computation-time restriction is imposed.
cards.definitions: Let \(d,T\ge 1\) be integers and \(B_{2}^{d}=\{x\in R^{d}:\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}\le 1\}\). A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of \(R^{d}\) satisfying \(B_{2}^{d}\subseteq K\subseteq dB_{2}^{d}\); the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write \(F(K)\) for the Borel-measurable convex functions \(f:K\to [0,1]\), where convexity means \(f(\lambda x+(1- \lambda )y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1- \lambda )f(y)\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}\in F(K)\), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses \(X_{t}\in K\), incurs \(f_{t}(X_{t})\), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history \((X_{1},f_{1}(X_{1}),\ldots ,X_{t- 1},f_{t- 1}(X_{t- 1}))\). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define \(R_{K}(T)=\inf _{\pi} \sup _{f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}} E_{\pi}[\sum_{t} f_{t}(X_{t})- \inf _{x\in K}\sum_{t} f_{t}(x)]\), with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally \(R*(d,T)=\sup _{K} R_{K}(T)\), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that there are universal \(C,a\) giving the displayed regret upper bound for every \(d,T\), or prove that for every proposed pair the bound fails at some \(d,T\) in the stated one-point feedback model.
cards.why: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.

cards.context:
On the interval \([- 1,1]\), the convex losses \(f(x)=(1+x)/2\) and \(h(x)=(1- x)/2\) both equal \(1/2\) at \(x=0\), but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order \(d^{5/2}\sqrt{T}\), apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as \(d\sqrt{T}\). The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in \([0,1]\); an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.
