cards.title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every \(\varphi \ge 1/2\) and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on \([- 1,1]\) with probability densities bounded by \(\varphi\), the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most \(C(n+1)^{a}(1+\varphi )^{b}\)?
cards.definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density \(f_{e}\) for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each \(f_{e}\) is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on \([- 1,1]\), and is at most \(\varphi\) almost everywhere; weights \(w_{e}\) are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), with value \(W_w(S)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E,\;|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1}w_{\{u,v\}}\). A legal step replaces S by \(S\triangle \{v\}\) for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define \(L(G,w)\) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set \(L=0\) if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so \(L\le 2^{n}- 1\) and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on \(E_{w}[L(G,w)]\), or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.

cards.context:
The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut \(\{1,2\}\) has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut \(\{1,3\}\) has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by \(\varphi\) prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most \(\varphi h\). Larger \(\varphi\) permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with \(\varphi\).

The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\) for fixed \(\delta >0\); arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

Michel and Scott show superpolynomial smoothed behavior for 3-FLIP, where a step may move up to three vertices together. Their single-FLIP exponential examples instead concern the setting without random perturbations. Neither statement refutes polynomial expected length for the single-vertex, independently perturbed model here.

cards.title: Asymptotically optimal algorithms for random three-dimensional assignment
cards.formal: Is there a uniform polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) and a deterministic sequence \(\eta_n\ge0\) with \(\eta_n\to0\) such that, for an \(n\times n\times n\) array of independent mean-one exponential costs, \(A\) returns permutations \(\pi,\sigma\in S_n\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n C_{i,\pi(i),\sigma(i)}\le(1+\eta_n)\operatorname{OPT}(C)\right]\longrightarrow1?\] The dimension is exactly three and the assignment is axial, as defined below.
cards.definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(S_n\) for its permutations. The \(n^3\) input coordinates \(C_{ijk}\) are mutually independent with \(\Pr[C_{ijk}>t]=e^{-t}\) for \(t\ge0\). A feasible assignment is the set of \(n\) triples \((i,\pi(i),\sigma(i))\); each label in each coordinate position occurs once. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(C)=\min_{\pi,\sigma\in S_n}\sum_i C_{i,\pi(i),\sigma(i)}\). It is positive with probability one. The question concerns approximation to the realized optimum of the same array, not to its expectation.

The array is explicitly accessible in random-access memory, with each real entry read at unit cost. Use exact real arithmetic with addition, subtraction, multiplication, nonzero division and comparison, ordinary indexing and fair random bits, each at unit cost. No unit-cost operation exposes infinitely many bits of an input real. A finite program must run in at most \(Cn^c\) operations on every nonnegative input and every random tape, for some absolute constants \(C,c\). Polynomial time in \(n\) is also polynomial in the array length \(n^3\). The algorithm always returns two permutations; its approximation guarantee is only probabilistic. This explicitly chosen arithmetic model does not claim a bit-complexity result for finitely rounded costs.

Probability is jointly over the independent input array and any internal coins, taken independently. No success guarantee is required for each individual array. The same algorithm works for all \(n\); \(\eta_n\) is independent of the realized costs and no particular convergence rate is prescribed. Thus a scheme giving a separate algorithm for every fixed accuracy does not by itself state the required single polynomial-time, vanishing-relative-error guarantee.

The planar three-dimensional assignment problem imposes one chosen entry on each axis-parallel line and selects \(n^2\) entries. That is a different feasible set. This card instead imposes one entry in each coordinate plane and selects \(n\) entries.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked affirmative proof supplying the algorithm, polynomial bound, vanishing error sequence and probability limit, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists in the stated model. Bounding the optimum's expected value, giving a constant approximation factor, or obtaining an \(n^{o(1)}\) factor does not suffice for a factor tending to one. A runtime or quality guarantee confined to the planar variant does not answer this axial question.
cards.why: Random multidimensional assignment is a canonical test of how distributional structure changes optimization complexity.

cards.title: Polynomial-time exact optimization of random asymmetric TSP
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform algorithm \(A\) and absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for the complete directed graph on \([n]\), with mutually independent costs \(w_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) for \(i\ne j\), the probability that \(A\) returns an exactly minimum-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle within \(Cn^c\) arithmetic operations tends to one as \(n\to\infty\)? The algorithm must be correct whenever it terminates and terminate almost surely on this input distribution.
cards.definitions:
For \(n\ge2\), the graph has every ordered edge \((i,j)\) with distinct endpoints. Opposite directions receive independent costs; no metric or triangle inequality is promised. A directed Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of all vertices, of cost \(\sum_{t=1}^n w_{v_t,v_{t+1}}\), where \(v_{n+1}=v_1\). Cyclic rotations represent the same tour. The optimum is the minimum of these finitely many sums. The output is a tour, not a rounded estimate of its value.

The explicit real-valued edge array is the input. Use a uniform real RAM with exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, nonzero division, comparisons, register accesses, ordinary indexing and optional fair random bits at unit cost. There is no unit-cost binary-digit extraction from a real. Exactness therefore means correctness of comparisons and of the chosen tour in this arithmetic model, rather than a claim about storing a continuously distributed input in finitely many bits.

Let \(T_A(w,\rho)\) be the operation count, allowing infinity for a nonterminating run, where \(\rho\) is an internal random tape independent of \(w\). Require zero-error output: every terminating run on an eligible edge array returns an optimum tour. Require \(\Pr[T_A<\infty]=1\) under the product input-and-coin law for each \(n\), and \(\Pr[T_A\le Cn^c]\to1\). Deterministic algorithms are included. Slow exceptional runs are allowed; a bound on expected runtime is not imposed. These conventions make the imported high-probability exact-computation question explicit.

The algorithm need not use branch and bound or any particular relaxation. The assignment relaxation permits several directed cycles instead of a single cycle; solving that relaxed problem exactly is not the same task. Likewise, an asymptotically negligible additive tour-cost error does not establish exact optimality.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated algorithmic existence and probability limit, or its logical negation in the specified arithmetic model. The proof must establish exact output correctness and one fixed polynomial runtime threshold holding with probability tending to one. A quasi-polynomial bound, approximate tours, or polynomial behavior only under a discrete small-integer cost distribution does not suffice. A lower bound for a particular branch-and-bound implementation does not refute the existence of all algorithms allowed here.
cards.why: This asks whether random instances remove the worst-case obstacle to exact asymmetric traveling-salesman optimization.

cards.title: Average-case optimality of standard Shellsort
cards.formal: Does there exist a choice, for every \(n\ge2\), of a finite deterministic increment list \(h^{(n)}=(h_1,\ldots,h_p)\), with \(1\le h_i<n\) and \(h_p=1\), such that standard Shellsort with these increments uses at most \(Cn\log n\) key comparisons on average over a uniformly random permutation of \([n]\), for one absolute constant \(C\)? The list may depend on \(n\) but not on the input permutation.
cards.definitions:
The array has positions \(0,\ldots,n-1\) and contains distinct keys of ranks \(1,\ldots,n\). At a pass with increment \(h\), split positions into residue classes modulo \(h\). In each residue class, process entries from left to right by ordinary insertion sort: compare the key being inserted with preceding keys, shift larger keys one position right in that subsequence, and stop at the first preceding key no larger than it or at the beginning. Count every actual comparison between two keys, including the final unsuccessful comparison when it occurs. Index and loop-bound tests are not key comparisons.

Passes execute in the prescribed order. The terminal increment one guarantees sorting for every input. The definition permits any fixed list of valid increments, not an input-dependent choice or randomized compare-exchange pattern. No monotone-decreasing restriction is silently added to the imported question. A sequence with redundant passes still pays for all their comparisons.

Let \(C(h,\pi)\) be the total number of key comparisons on permutation \(\pi\). The requested bound is \(n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}C(h^{(n)},\pi)\le Cn\log n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); changing the logarithm base changes only the constant. This is a comparison-count existence question, with increments prescribed independently for each size. It imposes no separate bound on computing or describing those increments, and does not claim an overall RAM-time bound that includes generating them.

The input distribution is uniform over all rank permutations, not a random gap list or independent continuous key magnitudes with ties. Average-case success here is a bound on work: standard Shellsort still sorts every permutation exactly.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a family of increment lists exists and has the stated uniform expectation bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its negation. A randomized modification of Shellsort, a bound on a restricted input distribution, or empirical comparison counts do not settle this deterministic-increment question. A lower bound for a single proposed sequence does not exclude all families.
cards.why: This would determine whether the original increment-based sorting method can be average-case optimal.

cards.title: Asymptotic random-order ratio of Best Fit bin packing
cards.formal: Determine the asymptotic random-order ratio \[R_{\mathrm{BF}}=\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_{I:\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge M}\frac{\mathbb E_{\pi}[\mathrm{BF}(I^\pi)]}{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}\] of the Best Fit bin-packing algorithm. Benchmark acceptance requires absolute error at most \(1/100\) in this dimensionless constant; exact determination also qualifies.
cards.definitions:
An instance \(I=(s_1,\ldots,s_N)\) is any finite nonempty labelled list of real item sizes in \((0,1]\). A bin has capacity one. A packing assigns every item to a bin with total assigned size at most one, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the minimum number of nonempty bins over all packings. There is no bound on the number of distinct sizes or a positive lower bound on the smallest size.

Best Fit starts with no bins. For an arriving item of size \(s\), among all existing bins of load at most \(1-s\), it selects one of maximum load and puts the item there. It opens a new bin only if none can accommodate the item. Equal-load ties are broken by the bin's creation order, earliest first. Items are never moved afterward. \(\mathrm{BF}(I^\pi)\) is the final bin count when labels arrive in the order specified by \(\pi\), uniformly distributed over all \(N!\) permutations. Repeated sizes still have distinct labels. The only randomness is this permutation; the adversary fixes the entire list before it is sampled.

For every positive integer \(M\), the supremum ranges over lists of arbitrary length whose optimal bin count is at least \(M\). These tail suprema are nonincreasing and bounded, so the displayed limit is well defined. Equivalently it is the limsup, as \(m\to\infty\), of the largest expected ratio among instances with optimum exactly \(m\). It is not the supremum over all finite optimum sizes: that latter absolute random-order ratio can differ. Nor is it the ratio of two expectations over independently sampled item sizes. Expectations here condition on a fixed adversarial multiset, whose optimum is deterministic.

The scientific target is the asymptotic constant, with vanishing additive effects measured relative to the optimal bin count. The numerical benchmark tolerance is an acceptance rule for that constant, not a multiplicative relaxation of the packing algorithm or a proof of an exact conjectured value.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a mathematically specified real number \(a\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-R_{\mathrm{BF}}|\le1/100\). A proved interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies by its midpoint, and an exact value qualifies. Write \(r(I)=\mathbb E_\pi[\mathrm{BF}(I^\pi)]/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). An upper bound \(U\) must cover every sufficiently large optimum: for every \(\eta>0\) there is an \(M\) such that \(r(I)\le U+\eta\) whenever \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge M\). For a lower bound \(L\), for every \(\eta>0\) and integer \(M\ge1\) it suffices to exhibit a list with \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\ge M\) and \(r(I)\ge L-\eta\). Experiments, a distribution-specific ratio, an absolute-ratio example with bounded optimum, or a certified interval wider than the stated tolerance are insufficient.
cards.why: The target measures how much a random arrival order improves a classical greedy packing rule.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,c>0\) such that for every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) with \(n\ge1\) vertices and maximum degree \(\Delta\), and every integer \(q\ge\Delta+2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper labelled \(q\)-colourings satisfies \[t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^c?\] The constants must be independent of the graph, its degree and the number of colours. This retains the previously selected degree-uniform polynomial target; the time unit is one vertex update, not a sweep or a bit operation.
cards.definitions:
Let \(V(G)=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E(G)\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or parallel edges. Set \(N_G(v)=\{u:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\) and \(\Delta=\max_v|N_G(v)|\). The state space is \[\Omega_{G,q}=\{\sigma:[n]\to[q]:\sigma(u)\ne\sigma(v)\text{ for every }\{u,v\}\in E(G)\},\] where \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\). Colours are labelled and may be unused. There is no constraint on colour-class sizes, and no prescribed partial colouring or vertex-specific list. The state space is nonempty for the stated colour range.

At each discrete step, choose \(v\) uniformly from \([n]\). Given the current state \(\sigma\), form the available set \[A_\sigma(v)=[q]\setminus\{\sigma(u):u\in N_G(v)\}.\] Choose a colour uniformly from \(A_\sigma(v)\), assign it to \(v\), and leave every other vertex unchanged. The set has at least \(q-\Delta\ge2\) elements and includes the current colour; staying in the same colouring is allowed. The choices at successive steps are made from these conditional distributions. Let \(P\) be the resulting finite stochastic matrix and let \(P^t(\sigma,\tau)\) be its \(t\)-step transition probabilities, with \(P^0\) the identity matrix. The chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi(\sigma)=1/|\Omega_{G,q}|\), the uniform law on all proper labelled colourings. In this range it is irreducible and has self-loops, so that this stationary law is approached from every state.

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\), over every proper initial colouring. Denote it by \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\). The chain is ergodic in the stated range.

A step updates one vertex. No factor of \(n\) is absorbed into the time unit, and uniform sampling from a potentially large colour set is part of the mathematical transition rule. Thus the statement concerns the convergence rate of a specified chain, not an implementation bound polynomial only in \(n\) for operations on \(\log q\)-bit colour names. If a graph is encoded for formalization, use its explicit vertex and edge lists and the binary integer \(q\); no succinct graph representation is intended.

The bound is simultaneous for all finite degrees and all \(q\ge\Delta+2\), including \(q\) unbounded as a function of \(n\). A theorem of the form \(C_{\Delta,q}n^{c_{\Delta,q}}\) for each fixed pair of parameters does not automatically meet it. No girth, treewidth, chordality, planarity, expansion or random-graph assumption is imposed. Girth is the shortest cycle length, with infinity for a forest. A fixed multiplicative slack \(q\ge(1+\delta)\Delta\), with \(\delta>0\), does not cover \(q=\Delta+2\) uniformly as \(\Delta\) increases.

The heat-bath convention differs from proposing a uniformly random colour from all \([q]\) and rejecting a conflict, often also called Glauber or Metropolis dynamics. In the heat-bath chain, every proposed colour is available; in the latter chain, unsuccessful proposals contribute further holding probability. Flip dynamics can recolour an entire two-colour component and is a third chain. Related results must retain their update convention and comparison costs. The present question fixes the heat-bath chain exactly.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed uniform polynomial bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its failure. An affirmative proof must supply absolute \(C,c\) working for every graph, degree, colour count and initial proper colouring in the definition. A negative answer must show that for every proposed \(C,c\) there are eligible \(n,G,q\) with \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)>Cn^c\); one slow instance does not refute every polynomial. Polynomial mixing only for each fixed degree with an uncontrolled exponent, larger multiplicative palette slack, restricted graphs, a different dynamics, or an unspecified faster sampler is not the required bound. This is an exact asymptotic proposition about the specified chain, not a request to approximate a finite mixing time to the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: This tests whether the simplest local update rule samples proper colourings efficiently throughout the full range where it is guaranteed to move between all solutions. It connects random sampling, approximate counting and antiferromagnetic spin systems at a longstanding boundary for general graphs.

cards.context:
The source poses polynomial mixing at the degree-plus-two threshold. This card retains the already adopted heat-bath update rule and the explicit requirement of one polynomial for all degrees and palettes. The source’s initial update description uses proposal-and-rejection; that clock is stated separately rather than silently identifying its transition matrix with this one.

At one fewer colour, a clique on Δ+1 vertices can be frozen: every vertex already sees every other colour. Thus ergodicity itself can fail at q=Δ+1. At q≥Δ+2 the basic chain is ergodic, but eventual convergence alone supplies no polynomial bound on how long it takes.

The2020 source proves polynomial mixing for bounded-treewidth graphs at the additive threshold and for chordal graphs with fixed multiplicative slack. Its treewidth-dependent exponent and the extra hypotheses do not establish the all-graph uniform statement.

The2024 flip-dynamics theorem applies for Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ. cards.title: Polynomial mixing of critical three-dimensional Ising dynamics
cards.formal:
For the zero-field nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on the three-dimensional box \(V_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^{3}\) with free boundary conditions, at the infinite-lattice critical inverse temperature \(\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) defined below, is the worst-initial-state total-variation mixing time of random-site heat-bath dynamics polynomial in \(L\)? Precisely, do there exist constants \(C,a>0\) such that
\[\forall L\in\mathbb N,\ L\ge1,\qquad t_{\mathrm{mix}}(L,1/4)\le C(L+1)^a?\]
Time is counted in individual site-update attempts. The critical parameter is fixed independently of \(L\), and the target is the exact critical point, not a subcritical parameter approaching it at an unspecified rate.
cards.definitions:
Let \(E_L\) contain each unordered pair of vertices of \(V_L\) at lattice distance \(\|u-v\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{3}|u_i-v_i|=1\), once. A configuration is \(\sigma\in\Omega_L=\{-1,+1\}^{V_L}\). At inverse temperature \(\beta\ge0\), the Gibbs probability is
\[\pi_{L,\beta}(\sigma)=Z_{L,\beta}^{-1}\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right),\]
where \(Z_{L,\beta}\) is the sum of the displayed weight over all configurations. Each interaction strength is one, there is no external magnetic field, and free boundary means there are no interactions with vertices outside \(V_L\). Boundary vertices inside the box are updated just like other vertices.

To specify the critical inverse temperature without a numerical approximation, let \(B_R=\{-R,\ldots,R\}^{3}\subset\mathbb Z^3\), for integers \(R\ge1\). Define \(\mu^+_{R,\beta}\) on spins in \(B_R\) by fixing all neighboring exterior spins to \(+1\): its weight is proportional to
\[\exp\!\left(\beta\left[\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\subset B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\sigma_v+\sum_{\substack{u\in B_R,\ v\notin B_R\\\|u-v\|_1=1}}\sigma_u\right]\right).\]
Internal unordered edges and crossing edges are each counted once. Set
\[m_+(\beta)=\inf_{R\ge1}\mathbb E_{\mu^+_{R,\beta}}[\sigma_0],\qquad\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)=\inf\{\beta\ge0:m_+(\beta)>0\}.\]
The monotone limit of finite-volume plus-boundary magnetizations gives this standard infinite-lattice critical value, which is finite and positive. Plus boundaries are used only in defining the infinite-volume threshold; the finite chain being tested has free boundaries.

In one discrete step, choose a vertex \(v\) uniformly from the \(L^3\) sites, independently of previous choices. With \(h_v(\sigma)=\sum_{u:\{u,v\}\in E_L}\sigma_u\), redraw its spin as \(+1\) with probability
\[\frac{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))}{\exp(\beta h_v(\sigma))+\exp(-\beta h_v(\sigma))},\]
and as \(-1\) otherwise, leaving all other spins unchanged. Choosing its existing value still counts as one step. Set \(\beta=\beta_c(\mathbb Z^3)\) and denote the resulting transition matrix by \(P_L\). This finite chain is irreducible and aperiodic and has stationary measure \(\pi_L=\pi_{L,\beta_c}\).

Use [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) at tolerance \(1/4\) for \(P_L\) with law \(\pi_L\), from every initial spin configuration. One step is one site update. A continuous-time clock of rate one per site has a different normalization. The target concerns the defined transition law with its exact probabilities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the polynomial mixing bound or its negation for this exact model. A positive proof must establish finite constants independent of \(L\), with the critical parameter, free boundaries, update rule, worst initial state and distance threshold specified here. A negative proof must show that no fixed polynomial bounds this sequence of mixing times. Results at a tree threshold, in another lattice dimension, below criticality, with different boundaries or from a restricted initialization do not meet the criterion.
cards.why: This is a basic question about whether a standard local sampling dynamics remains efficient at a phase transition in three dimensions. The equilibrium system has correlations on many scales, so high-temperature mixing guarantees do not directly apply. A polynomial bound or a superpolynomial obstruction would clarify the computational cost of critical fluctuations in one of the central lattice models.

cards.title: Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(K,c>0\) exist such that, for all \(r,s\ge 1\) and all nonnegative integer margins \(a\in \mathbb{N} ^{r},b\in \mathbb{N} ^{s}\) with a nonempty realization set \(\Omega (a,b)\), the lazy switch chain below satisfies \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le K(r+s)^{c}\)?
cards.definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.
cards.why: A general guarantee for a basic sampler that preserves individual degrees, with applications to network and fixed-margin statistical models. The reported solution would close the gap between eventual convergence and a uniform polynomial sampling bound.

cards.context:
Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le \operatorname{binom}(r,2)\operatorname{binom}(s,2)(rs \ln  2+\ln  4)\), which implies a universal polynomial bound in \(r+s\). The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing \([[1,0],[0,1]]\) by \([[0,1],[1,0]]\) changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.

cards.title: Cutoff for bounded-degree transitive expanders
cards.formal:
Does every sequence of bounded-degree vertex-transitive expander graphs exhibit total-variation cutoff for lazy simple random walk? More precisely, consider any sequence \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) of finite connected undirected simple graphs, with \(N_k=|V(G_k)|\to\infty\). Assume each \(G_k\) is vertex-transitive, that there is a fixed integer \(D\ge3\) with \(3\le d_k\le D\) for its vertex degree \(d_k\), and that the lazy-walk spectral gaps satisfy \(\gamma_k\ge\delta\) for some constant \(\delta>0\) independent of \(k\). Must
\[\forall\varepsilon\in(0,1/2),\qquad\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{t_k(\varepsilon)}{t_k(1-\varepsilon)}=1?\]
The transition rule and worst-start mixing times \(t_k\) are defined below. The constants \(D\) and \(\delta\) may depend on the sequence. No quantitative cutoff window or common leading constant for different sequences is demanded.
cards.definitions:
A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. Vertex-transitive means that for any vertices \(x,y\) there is a bijection of the vertex set preserving adjacency in both directions and mapping \(x\) to \(y\). Consequently all its vertices have the same degree \(d_k\). The graph sequence is deterministic and need not come from a particular construction or a random-graph model.

One lazy-walk step stays at the current vertex with probability \(1/2\), and otherwise chooses a neighbor uniformly and moves there. Its transition matrix is
\[P_k(x,y)=\begin{cases}1/2&y=x,\\1/(2d_k)&\{x,y\}\in E(G_k),\\0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
The stationary probability is \(\pi_k(y)=1/N_k\). List the real eigenvalues in decreasing order as \(1=\lambda_{1,k}>\lambda_{2,k}\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_{N_k,k}\ge0\), and set \(\gamma_k=1-\lambda_{2,k}\). A uniformly positive lower bound on \(\gamma_k\), together with bounded degree, is the expander assumption used here. Laziness includes bipartite graphs without periodicity problems.

At an integer time \(t\ge0\), let
\[d_k(t)=\max_{x\in V(G_k)}\frac12\sum_{y\in V(G_k)}\left|P_k^t(x,y)-\frac1{N_k}\right|,\qquad t_k(\eta)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:d_k(t)\le\eta\}\quad(0<\eta<1).\]
The maximum is over every starting vertex. Times count discrete lazy steps, including steps that stay put. For a fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), the denominator \(t_k(1-\varepsilon)\) is positive for all sufficiently large \(k\); the limit uses this eventual tail. The displayed ratio condition defines total-variation cutoff. It asks that the transition between distance near one and distance near zero occupy a vanishing fraction of the mixing time.

The source first states the question with one fixed degree. Allowing degree to vary in a fixed finite range is equivalent at the level of this universal conjecture: each degree occurring infinitely often gives a fixed-degree subsequence. Neither degrees growing without bound nor expansion constants tending to zero are admitted.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that every sequence satisfying the hypotheses has the displayed cutoff property, or a Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must establish a sequence satisfying every hypothesis for which the ratio limit fails for at least one fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\). A single finite graph cannot refute an asymptotic cutoff statement. Logarithmic mixing-time bounds alone, cutoff in a different distance, or a result only for a special class of expanders do not meet the criterion.
cards.why: Expanders combine sparse connectivity with fast random-walk mixing and are central objects in algorithms and pseudorandomness. This conjecture asks whether spatial symmetry forces their approach to equilibrium to be abrupt. A resolution would separate the role of expansion in the speed of mixing from the role of symmetry in the shape of convergence.

The textbook asks this question for a fixed degree and explicitly chooses lazy random walk. The card retains that walk and the total-variation meaning of cutoff, while making the graph-sequence and uniform-gap quantifiers explicit.

Salez’s 2025 notes state the vertex-transitive expander conjecture as Problem 2.3. The notes explain that expansion already gives mixing time of logarithmic order in the graph size; cutoff asks for substantially finer asymptotic information.

cards.title: Stationary-start cover-time lower bound
cards.formal: For every finite irreducible reversible discrete-time Markov chain on \(n\ge2\) states started in stationarity, does its cover time \(C\) satisfy \[\mathbb E_\pi[C]\ge(n-1)\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac1j\,?\]
cards.definitions:
The transition matrix \(P\) has nonnegative real entries and each row sums to one. Irreducibility means that for every \(i,j\) there is \(t\ge0\) with \((P^t)_{ij}>0\). Its unique stationary distribution \(\pi\) has positive entries and satisfies \(\pi P=\pi\). Reversibility requires \(\pi_i P_{ij}=\pi_j P_{ji}\). Self-loops and periodic chains are allowed.

Draw \(X_0\sim\pi\) and evolve using \(P\). The cover time \(C=\min\{t\ge0:\{X_0,\ldots,X_t\}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\}\) counts transitions. The initial state counts as visited at time zero, and the expectation includes the choice of \(X_0\). The bound is required at each finite \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated proposition or its negation for the specified model.
cards.why: An exact extremal bound would identify how quickly a reversible exploration process can cover its state space.

cards.title: A single hard-core uniqueness threshold on the square lattice
cards.formal: Is there a finite \(\lambda_c>0\) such that the hard-core model on \(\mathbb Z^2\) has a unique Gibbs measure for every \(0<\lambda<\lambda_c\) and more than one for every \(\lambda>\lambda_c\)?
cards.definitions:
Join vertices of \(\mathbb Z^2\) at Manhattan distance one. A configuration \(\eta\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z^2}\) is admissible if adjacent vertices are never both occupied. Given a finite \(\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^2\) and an admissible exterior configuration \(\tau\), assign each compatible interior configuration \(\xi\) probability \(\lambda^{\sum_{v\in\Lambda}\xi(v)}/Z_{\Lambda,\tau}\), where the normalizing factor sums these weights. Incompatible configurations have probability zero.

A Gibbs measure is supported on admissible configurations and has these conditional laws almost surely for every finite \(\Lambda\). Uniqueness and multiplicity range over all Gibbs measures, including measures without translation invariance. The question leaves behavior at \(\lambda=\lambda_c\) open and asks only for existence of the threshold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated proposition or its negation for the specified model. A numerical estimate of a candidate transition point, or separated small-activity and large-activity theorems, does not establish the single-threshold statement.
cards.why: The lattice transition organizes the behavior of independent-set sampling and spatial correlations.

cards.title: Polynomial mixing of the self-avoiding-walk pivot chain
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that \[t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\le Cn^a\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge1?\] The chain below acts on rooted \(n\)-step self-avoiding walks in the square lattice, uses the five specified pivot symmetries, and counts every attempted pivot including rejection. Mixing means total-variation distance at most \(1/4\) from the uniform law, from every starting walk.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge1\), the finite state space \(\Omega_n\) consists of sequences \(\omega=(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_n)\) in \(\mathbb Z^2\) such that \(\omega_0=(0,0)\), \(\|\omega_{i+1}-\omega_i\|_1=1\) for \(0\le i<n\), and \(\omega_i\ne\omega_j\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Here \(\|(x,y)\|_1=|x|+|y|\). Walks are ordered, rooted at the origin and not identified under rotation, reflection or reversal. There is no confining box or additional energy weight. Let \(\pi_n\) give equal probability \(1/|\Omega_n|\) to each walk.

In one step independently choose \(k\) uniformly from \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\) and \(S\) uniformly from these five maps:
\[(x,y)\mapsto(y,-x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y),\quad(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y).\]
These are the three nontrivial quarter-turn rotations and the two coordinate-axis reflections in Example B.5. Propose
\[\omega'_i=\begin{cases}\omega_i&i\le k,\\\omega_k+S(\omega_i-\omega_k)&i>k.\end{cases}\]
If the proposal belongs to \(\Omega_n\), accept it; otherwise keep \(\omega\). In either case the time increases by one. Fresh choices are independent at subsequent steps. In particular \(k=n\) always leaves the walk unchanged. Denote this transition matrix by \(P_n\).

The proposal maps occur with the same probabilities as their inverses, so the chain is reversible for \(\pi_n\). The irreducibility established in the source, together with the positive holding probability, gives a unique stationary law and convergence to it. Write \(t_{\mathrm{pivot}}(n)\) for the [worst-start total variation mixing time](definitions.html#probability-distance) of \(P_n\) at tolerance \(1/4\), over every walk in \(\Omega_n\).

The clock counts proposals rather than CPU operations or accepted pivots. Testing whether a proposed walk intersects itself is part of implementing a transition, but its computational cost is not multiplied into this mathematical mixing time. The textbook’s instruction to repeat after rejection is interpreted as proceeding to the next proposal with the old state retained, as explicitly specified in Clisby’s standard pivot dynamics. Discarding all rejected attempts from the clock would define a different chain and is not the convention here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that the worst-start mixing time of the specified pivot chain is bounded by one polynomial in the walk length, or prove that every such bound fails. Count rejected pivots as steps when establishing either result.
cards.why: The pivot algorithm is a major sampling method for self-avoiding walks, a basic model of polymers with excluded volume. Its practical efficiency makes the absence of a matching rigorous convergence analysis especially consequential. Determining its mixing order would quantify when samples have forgotten an arbitrary initial shape, beyond the behavior of a few measured observables.

cards.title: Weakly negatively regressive sampling of matroid bases
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every finite matroid \(M\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) given by an independence oracle and every rational point \(p\) of its base polytope, samples a basis \(B\) with exact marginals
\[\Pr[i\in B]=p_i\quad(i\in[n])\]
and a weakly negatively regressive output distribution, in expected time polynomial in \(n\) and the binary encoding length of \(p\)?

Here weak negative regression (WNR) requires, simultaneously for every \(i\in[n]\) and every increasing function \(f:2^{[n]\setminus\{i\}}\to\mathbb R\),
\[\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{i\in B\}} f(B\setminus\{i\})]\le p_i\,\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})].\]
The algorithm receives no objective function \(f\). One output law must satisfy all these inequalities.

This card selects WNR, the weakest of the three alternative dependence requirements in the source question. Negative association or negative regression would also suffice by implying WNR. The independence-oracle, rational-input and exact expected-time sampling conventions below make the source's efficiency question precise; they are explicit editorial conventions.
cards.definitions:
A matroid \(M=([n],\mathcal I)\), with \(n\ge1\), consists of a nonempty family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^{[n]}\) of independent sets. If \(A\in\mathcal I\) and \(A'\subseteq A\), then \(A'\in\mathcal I\). If \(A,D\in\mathcal I\) and \(|A|<|D|\), some \(e\in D\setminus A\) has \(A\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). A basis is an inclusion-maximal member of \(\mathcal I\); all bases have the same cardinality. Let \(\mathcal B(M)\) be their family, including the singleton family containing the empty set for a rank-zero matroid.

The base polytope is
\[P_B(M)=\left\{\sum_{B\in\mathcal B(M)}\lambda_B\mathbf 1_B:\lambda_B\ge0,\ \sum_B\lambda_B=1\right\},\]
where \(\mathbf 1_B\in\{0,1\}^n\) is the incidence vector. This is the convex hull of bases, as specified by the source's maximal-independent-set convention. It is distinct from the convex hull of all independent sets.

An oracle query supplies an \(n\)-bit incidence vector for a set \(A\) and receives the exact bit indicating whether \(A\in\mathcal I\). The oracle is fixed throughout a run and is promised to describe a matroid. The input gives \(n\) in binary and \(p_i=a_i/b_i\), with binary integers \(0\le a_i\le b_i\) and \(b_i\ge1\). Let \(L\) be their total encoding length. The promise is \(p\in P_B(M)\); membership testing is not an additional required output. A convex decomposition of \(p\), an explicit list of bases and a sampling oracle are not supplied.

Use a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with this independence oracle and independent fair random bits. All ordinary bit operations, random-bit generation, oracle-query preparation and output writing count toward time; obtaining the answer to a completed oracle query costs one additional step. There must be fixed constants \(C,d\) such that expected total work is at most \(C(n+L+1)^d\) on every promised input and every matroid oracle. These constants and the machine are independent of the instance. No arbitrary real-arithmetic operations or nonuniform advice are available.

The machine must halt with probability one, and every terminating run must output the incidence vector of a basis. Its probability law over outputs must have the exact stated marginals and satisfy WNR without an additive tolerance. There is no failure output or exceptional probability on which feasibility or the distributional guarantees may fail. Expected time permits exact sampling with rational probabilities whose denominators are not powers of two. Independent invocations use fresh random bits; a joint coupling across different inputs is not required.

Increasing means \(f(A)\le f(D)\) whenever \(A\subseteq D\). The domain is finite, so each real-valued \(f\) has finite expectation. For \(0<p_i<1\), the displayed WNR inequality is equivalent to
\[\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})\mid i\in B]\le\mathbb E[f(B\setminus\{i\})\mid i\notin B].\]
For \(p_i=0\) or \(p_i=1\), the unconditional inequality is automatically an equality and does not invoke undefined conditional probabilities. WNR concerns all increasing functions of the remaining coordinates, not just pairwise covariances or linear functions.

For context, a set function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular when \(F(A)+F(D)\ge F(A\cup D)+F(A\cap D)\) for all sets \(A,D\). Submodular dominance at marginals \(p\) means \(\mathbb E[F(B)]\ge\mathbb E[F(R_p)]\) for every such \(F\), where \(R_p\) includes each element independently with probability \(p_i\). This consequence of WNR is not a substitute for the stronger specified distributional target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement in the declared oracle and bit-computation model. A positive answer must establish one uniform sampler, exact feasibility and marginals, all WNR inequalities, almost-sure termination and the expected polynomial resource bound for every promised input. A negative answer must prove that no such sampler exists; it need not show that a WNR law is nonexistent for any individual input. A theorem that only supplies a distribution nonconstructively, approximate marginals, pairwise negative correlation, submodular dominance, or a sampler for a restricted class of matroids does not by itself meet the full criterion.
cards.why: Randomized rounding must reconcile combinatorial feasibility with the dependence created by exact marginal requirements. This question asks whether every matroid base point has an efficiently accessible law controlling all monotone effects of conditioning on one coordinate. Such a general sampling theorem would support objective-independent rounding and strong guarantees for nonlinear submodular objectives, beyond the linear expectations fixed by marginals alone.

cards.context:
The 2022 question asks about sampling for arbitrary matroid marginals with WNR, negative association or negative regression. The latter two properties each imply WNR. This card adopts the first listed branch and retains arbitrary matroids; it does not impose one particular rounding procedure.

WNR implies submodular dominance: every submodular objective has expectation at least that under independent inclusion with the same marginals. Matching marginals alone fixes linear objectives, but does not establish this nonlinear guarantee.

The source reports a gap in an earlier claimed negative-association sampler for general matroids. It also observes that maximum-entropy matroid distributions need not have the required negative dependence, because even uniform distributions can have positively correlated coordinates.

The 2026 journal paper proves dimension-free submodular lower-tail bounds under one-negative association, equivalent to WNR for binary variables. Its introduction continues to flag the gap in the earlier general-matroid sampling claim and leaves the dependence properties of standard matroid rounding procedures open. These are conditional consequences of the dependence property, not a construction for every matroid.

The 2026 correlated-sampling paper gives cardinality-constrained rounding with preserved marginals and submodular dominance. Its discussion of negative association includes a known hypersimplex sampling law, and the introduction mentions a partition-matroid extension. Cardinality and partition constraints are special cases of matroids; the paper does not establish the arbitrary-matroid target here.

cards.title: Exact uniform spanning-tree sampling in linear time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every connected simple unweighted undirected graph G with m edges, outputs an exactly uniform spanning tree in expected \(O(m)\) total time?
cards.definitions:
The graph has n≥1 labelled vertices and is supplied by adjacency lists with every undirected edge represented at both endpoints. For n=1 the algorithm returns the empty tree in O(1) time; the asymptotic bound is O(m+1). A spanning tree is an acyclic connected subset of n−1 input edges. Let T(G) be the finite set of all such subsets. Exact uniformity means that for every H∈T(G), the output probability equals 1/|T(G)|.

Use a uniform word RAM with word width \(w=\Theta(\log(n+2))\) large enough for graph addresses. Use the [integer word instructions](definitions.html#ram) at width \(w\). A fresh independent uniform word costs one step. Unbounded exact real arithmetic is unavailable. The algorithm terminates almost surely, always returns a valid spanning tree, and has expected cost at most C(m+1) on each fixed input, for one absolute C. Reading or transforming the graph, preprocessing, random-number generation and writing all tree edges are charged. Rejection sampling is allowed and its work is counted. There is no total-variation tolerance, failure symbol or conditioning on successful runs in the output specification. Weighted graphs are outside this card’s target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked sampler with proofs of exact uniformity, almost-sure termination and the expected linear bound, or a complete impossibility proof in this model. An almost-linear m^(1+o(1)) runtime is insufficient. A distribution within small total variation distance is also insufficient, even if its computational bound is linear.
cards.why: This asks whether exact random generation can match the cost of reading the graph.

cards.title: Deterministic approximation scheme for graph cover times
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time approximation scheme for the expected cover time of simple random walk from a specified starting vertex of an arbitrary finite connected undirected simple graph? Specifically, does there exist one deterministic algorithm \(A\) such that, for every integer \(q\ge2\), there are constants \(C_q,a_q>0\) for which every allowed \(n\)-vertex input \((G,v,q)\) is processed within \(C_q(n+1)^{a_q}\) bit operations and the output rational number \(\widehat C\ge0\) satisfies
\[\left|\widehat C-C(G,v)\right|\le\frac{C(G,v)}q?\]
Here \(C(G,v)\) is defined below. The runtime is polynomial in graph size for every fixed accuracy \(1/q\); its exponent may depend on \(q\). This restores the relative-approximation question actually stated by Aldous and Fill, rather than the unsupported exact-output wording in the imported draft.
cards.definitions:
The input graph has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge1\), and no loops, parallel edges or edge weights. It is promised connected. Its encoding consists of \(n\) in unary followed by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix, a binary starting label \(v\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the integer accuracy parameter \(q\ge2\) in binary, with standard self-delimiting integer fields. All graph families and degrees are allowed; in particular there is no bounded-degree or rapid-mixing promise.

For \(n\ge2\), let \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) be the discrete-time walk with \(X_0=v\). At each step it independently chooses a uniformly random neighbor of its current vertex. It has no added holding probability. Define
\[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\{X_0,\ldots,X_t\}=V(G)\},\qquad C(G,v)=\mathbb E_v[\tau_{\mathrm{cov}}].\]
The initial vertex is already visited at time zero, and time counts edge traversals. There is no requirement to return to \(v\) after the last new vertex is visited. For \(n=1\), put \(C(G,v)=0\). Connectedness guarantees finite expectation. The quantity \(\max_v C(G,v)\), often called the graph’s cover time, is related but is not substituted for the supplied-start expectation.

The algorithm is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no random bits, advice or sampling oracle. Input processing, rational arithmetic and output writing count toward the runtime. Its output is a pair of binary integers representing a nonnegative rational with positive denominator. The required inequality holds for every input, not merely with high probability. When \(n=1\), it requires output zero.

The integer \(q\) represents reciprocal relative accuracy. This discretization covers any fixed requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) by taking \(q\ge\max\{2,1/\varepsilon\}\). The constants \(C_q,a_q\) are independent of the graph and the starting vertex. No polynomial dependence on \(q\) is demanded; that would be the stronger fully polynomial scheme. Nor is an exact numerator and denominator for the unknown expectation demanded.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that an algorithm with the displayed correctness and runtime guarantees exists, or a Lean-checked proof of the negation of that existence statement. A positive answer must work at arbitrarily fine fixed relative accuracy on every allowed graph and starting vertex. A constant-factor estimate, a randomized approximation, a theorem restricted to trees or a promise on hitting times, and a procedure that computes only the worst-start maximum do not establish the stated scheme. An exponential-time exact formula by itself does not establish the polynomial-time guarantee.
cards.why: Cover time is a global measure of how efficiently a random walk explores a network. It is readily estimated by randomized simulation, while deterministic evaluation must account for the distribution of entire exploration histories. A scheme for arbitrary graphs would resolve a concrete derandomization question about an important graph parameter, with accuracy beyond universal constant-factor estimates.

cards.title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform probabilistic algorithm \(A\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every finite undirected simple graph \(G\) and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(A(G,\varepsilon)\) halts on every random tape within
\[C\bigl(N+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and outputs a nonnegative rational \(\widehat Z\) satisfying
\[\Pr\bigl[(1-\varepsilon)Z(G)\le\widehat Z\le(1+\varepsilon)Z(G)\bigr]\ge\frac34?\]
Here \(Z(G)\) is the number of perfect matchings, \(N\) is the complete input bit length defined below, and, whenever \(Z(G)=0\), every run must output zero. This is the existence question for a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme on general unweighted graphs.
cards.definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge0\), a graph has labeled vertex set \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and an arbitrary subset of the unordered pairs of distinct vertices as its edges. It has no loops, parallel edges or weights. A matching is a subset of edges with pairwise disjoint endpoints; it is perfect when every vertex is incident to exactly one of its edges. Each such edge set is counted once, regardless of order or orientation. Thus \(Z(G)\in\mathbb N\), an odd-order graph has count zero, and the empty graph has count one, from its empty matching. The domain includes disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles and arbitrarily large degrees, with no bipartiteness, density, planarity, expansion, or existence promise.

Use the following explicit finite encoding. The graph is encoded by \(1^{n}0\) followed by one adjacency bit for each pair \(0\le i<j<n\), in lexicographic order. This includes the full vertex set even when there are no edges and is polynomially equivalent to an explicit vertex-and-edge list. Write \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms with integers \(0<r<s\). Let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer, with \(b(0)=0\), and let \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Append \(E(r)E(s)\) to the graph encoding. The total length is \(N\); the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\), not just the length of its encoding, may enter the time bound. The output has the form \(E(u)E(v)\) with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), meaning \(\widehat Z=u/v\); reduction to lowest terms is not required.

An algorithm is one finite multitape probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, and an output tape. Each ordinary transition and each newly requested independent fair bit costs one step. Its probability space is the infinite product of fair bits, and the clock bound must hold on every tape for every valid input. Reading, arithmetic, storage operations and writing the whole rational output are all charged. There is no advice, oracle, nonuniform dependence on the graph or accuracy, or unit-cost operation on unbounded integers. No guarantee is needed on malformed inputs. The same \(A,C,k\) must work for all graphs and all valid accuracies; success is per input and is not an average over a graph distribution.

The estimate has relative multiplicative error. In particular, an additive error guarantee on the raw count or on its logarithm is a different condition. Requiring deterministic zero output when no perfect matching exists is a harmless normalization of the usual FPRAS question because perfect-matching existence on general graphs is deterministically decidable in polynomial time. The probability \(3/4\) is fixed, and no random output is required to be an actual matching. This card asks whether the approximation algorithm exists; it does not ask for the numerical value of a fixed graph’s count at the catalogue’s default absolute tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition above or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite uniform algorithm and constants \(C,k\), and prove its every-random-tape clock, output encoding, exact zero behavior and per-input relative-error probability for every graph and rational accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm and every such polynomial bound; it need not consist of a single finite counterexample graph. Failure or slow mixing of a particular algorithm family does not prove that negation. A conditional impossibility theorem is only a conditional result unless its hypothesis is also proved. Exact exponential-time counting, constant-factor approximation without arbitrary requested accuracy, algorithms only for bipartite or dense graphs, and approximation of the total number of all matchings do not meet the target.
cards.why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.

cards.context:
Finding a perfect matching is possible in deterministic polynomial time on general graphs, but exact counting is #P-complete even on bipartite graphs. A relative approximation can be much easier than exact counting, as the permanent demonstrates. This question asks whether that distinction persists on all simple graphs, making it one of the central missing cases in the theory of randomized approximate counting.

For an \(m\times m\) nonnegative matrix \(B\), its permanent is \(\operatorname{per}(B)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{m}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}B_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(S_{m}\) is the set of permutations. When \(B\) is a zero–one bipartite adjacency matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings between the two specified vertex classes. Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda prove an FPRAS for every nonnegative permanent, solving the bipartite matching case. Their theorem does not require the matrix entries to be strictly positive.

For a general graph on an even number of vertices, the corresponding expression is the hafnian of its symmetric adjacency matrix: the sum, over partitions of the vertices into unordered pairs, of the product of the selected entries. It is different from the permanent of that same square matrix. For example, \(K_{4}\) has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine, because the latter also counts directed cycle covers. This example identifies the mathematical distinction between the two targets.

Jerrum and Sinclair’s 1989 Corollary 4.5 gives an FPRAS for the number of matchings of all sizes in arbitrary unweighted graphs. The related weighted monomer–dimer statement has a weight-encoding qualification; no unrestricted binary-weight theorem is needed here. Total matching count can differ exponentially from perfect-matching count: a disjoint union of \(j\) edges has \(2^{j}\) matchings but only one perfect matching. Thus the two quantities are not interchangeable even on elementary graphs.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes identify a precise obstruction for a family of chains on perfect and near-perfect matchings. A near-perfect matching leaves exactly two vertices uncovered, and its hole pattern records those vertices. For the specified JSV-type transitions and any weighting depending only on the hole pattern, their Theorem 2.2 gives graphs on which either perfect matchings have exponentially small stationary probability or the mixing time is exponential. The disjunction matters: the theorem does not assert slow mixing for every weighting, nor impossibility of every FPRAS. Their positive result treats bounded ear complexity of factor-critical subgraphs; a factor-critical graph remains perfectly matchable after deleting any one vertex, and ear count is not its vertex count.

The relevance extends to statistical counting models. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s Proposition 1.2 recalls that, for fixed rational equal interaction parameters \(\beta=\gamma<-1\), approximation of the corresponding two-state spin partition function is equivalent to general perfect-matching approximation under reductions preserving the existence of an FPRAS. The source states this equivalence in both directions and explicitly identifies the perfect-matching question as open. Its other tractable parameter regimes therefore do not settle this one.

Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s preprint of 27 August 2026 reports an improved permanent FPRAS. For an \(m\times m\) zero–one matrix with \(m\ge2\), its Theorem 1 states time \(O(m^{6}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{5}m\log(2/\delta))\) for relative error \(\varepsilon\) and failure probability \(\delta\); the trivial and zero-permanent cases are handled separately. The state space remains bipartite. This is a reported preprint running-time improvement within the solved neighboring case, not a general-graph theorem; its full proof and bit-level implementation were not independently verified here.

Zihong Yi’s preprint of 3 September 2026 claims a deterministic approximation scheme for weighted hafnians when the support graph has minimum degree at least \((1/2+\gamma)n\) and nonzero weights lie in \([\theta,1]\), for fixed \(\gamma>0\) and \(\theta>0\). The unweighted case takes \(\theta=1\), but it still has the fixed density margin. The polynomial’s exponents depend on these fixed margins. The paper explicitly retains the general nonbipartite FPRAS question as open and separately discusses its limitations at the exact Dirac threshold. The reviewed statement does not cover every graph, and the full new proof has not been independently verified.

A positive answer would extend a landmark success of randomized counting beyond bipartiteness. A negative answer would establish a separation between the ease of finding these objects and the existence of arbitrarily accurate relative estimates of their number. The source-specific Markov-chain obstruction explains part of the difficulty without deciding this algorithm-independent question.

cards.title: FP versus #P
cards.formal:
Is every function in \(\#\mathrm{P}\) computable exactly in deterministic polynomial time? With the numerical function convention defined below, the proposition is
\[\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N},\]
equivalently \(\#\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). Each function may have its own fixed machine and polynomial running-time bound. The output is the exact nonnegative integer in binary.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\{0,1\}^*\) for all finite binary strings, including the empty string, and \(|x|\) for their bit length. Natural numbers include zero. A polynomial witness bound is a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients; allowing any polynomial-time computable, polynomially bounded integer length gives the same class by unique zero padding. A verifier \(V(x,y)\) is a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine returning a bit on every pair of strings within polynomially many bit steps in \(|x|+|y|\). The class \(\#\mathrm{P}\) consists of the total functions
\[f_{V,p}(x)=\left|\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\right\}\right|.\]
Each distinct witness string is counted once. If several witnesses describe the same combinatorial object, their multiplicity is retained. The witness length is exactly the displayed length; shorter witnesses are not additionally counted. Equivalently, these functions count accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines with binary choices and an explicit machine convention preserving path counts.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to nonnegative integers for which some deterministic multitape Turing machine outputs the canonical binary representation on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps. Here \(C,d\) are fixed positive integers, the representation of zero is the single bit 0, and positive outputs have no leading zeros. All computation and output writing are charged. Machines have finite programs, no advice and no oracle. No error probability or approximation is allowed. The constants and program may depend on the function but never on the input. There is no requirement of a common exponent or a uniform compiler taking arbitrary verifiers as input.

Every \(\#\mathrm{P}\) value is at most \(2^{p(|x|)}\), so its binary representation has at most \(p(|x|)+1\) bits. The question does not request output in unary, listing all witnesses, or a time bound polynomial in the value of the count. Conversely, if a numerical function has a polynomial-time exact algorithm, choose a polynomial \(q\) longer than its output bit bound and accept a \(q(|x|)\)-bit witness precisely when its numerical value is smaller than \(f(x)\). Exactly \(f(x)\) witnesses are accepted. Thus \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm{P}\), which justifies writing equality rather than only the displayed inclusion. The source writes FP for this numerical interpretation of polynomial-time string functions.

For the comparisons below, \(\mathrm{P}\) is the class of languages decided by deterministic machines in polynomial time, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages of the form \(\{x:f_{V,p}(x)>0\}\). Use the shared definition of [PSPACE](definitions.html#space). A polynomial-time Turing reduction to a numerical function may make adaptively chosen exact queries, charging query writing and answer processing, while receiving the binary answer from its oracle. Counting completeness mentioned below uses this convention unless a stronger count-preserving reduction is stated.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of \(\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\), or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must supply existence of an exact uniform polynomial-time machine for every fixed verifier and witness bound; it suffices to solve an appropriately proved counting-complete problem exactly in polynomial time. A negative proof must establish a \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function admitting no such machine. A conditional separation assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), a lower bound for one restricted algorithm, or an efficient relative approximation does not by itself settle the unconditional proposition. Computing only whether the count is zero is also insufficient.
cards.why: This is the fundamental exact-counting analogue of P versus NP. It asks whether every efficiently checkable family of witnesses also admits efficient evaluation of its full multiplicity, and connects counting satisfiability, permanents and many discrete partition functions under one computational boundary.

cards.context:
A verifier checks one proposed witness quickly. Its counting function asks how many witnesses pass. The count can be exponentially large while its binary representation remains polynomially short, so the difficulty is not simply the time needed to write the answer.

Exact counting immediately decides whether any witness exists. Consequently, an affirmative answer implies P = NP, and a proof that P differs from NP would give a negative answer here. The converse implication is a separate question: efficient existence tests do not automatically evaluate the full count.

Counting satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula is a representative complete problem. The usual verifier-to-formula construction can retain one satisfying assignment per accepted witness by forcing the values of auxiliary computation variables. Therefore a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm for those formulas would evaluate every function in the class.

Some counting-complete problems have easy existence tests. For a zero-one matrix, its permanent counts perfect matchings in the associated bipartite graph; testing whether such a matching exists is polynomial-time solvable. Counting completeness here is under polynomial-time oracle reductions, and does not mean a count-preserving reduction from satisfiability.

A polynomial-space computation can enumerate all witnesses while keeping only a polynomial-length counter. The textbook therefore notes that P = PSPACE would imply a positive answer. This stronger hypothesis is distinct from P = NP, and the brute-force counting procedure itself generally takes exponential time.

Relative approximation allows a nonzero error proportional to the count. When the count is exponential, even a very small inverse-polynomial relative error can hide many integers. An approximation algorithm whose running time is polynomial in inverse accuracy can need exponential time at the precision that distinguishes adjacent counts.

cards.title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
cards.formal:
Does there exist one finite deterministic algorithm \(D\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), every explicitly encoded matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}^{n\times n}\), and every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), \(D(A,\varepsilon)\) halts within
\[C\bigl(N+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+1\bigr)^{k}\]
Turing-machine steps and returns a nonnegative rational \(z\) satisfying
\[(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{per}(A)\le z\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{per}(A)?\]
Here \(N\) is the full binary input length, and the permanent is defined below. The guarantee must hold on every input without randomness.
cards.definitions:
Let \([n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and let \(S_{n}\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. For a nonnegative rational matrix define
\[\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}A_{i,\pi(i)}.\]
Zero entries, zero rows, reducible matrices and arbitrarily large or small positive rational entries are permitted. There is no density, expansion, degree, rank, stochastic-scaling, or positive-entry lower-bound promise. This is the usual unsigned permutation sum, not the determinant or the hafnian. For a zero–one matrix it counts perfect matchings in the bipartite graph having one vertex for each row and each column, with an edge exactly where the entry is one. For a weighted matrix, each matching contributes the product of its edge weights.

For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its ordinary binary expansion, with \(b(0)=0\), and set \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Encode \(n\) as \(E(n)\), then encode all \(n^{2}\) entries in row-major order. Each entry is a reduced pair \(u/v\), with integers \(u\ge0,v\ge1\), encoded by \(E(u)E(v)\). Encode \(\varepsilon=r/s\) in lowest terms, \(0<r<s\), by appending \(E(r)E(s)\). The length of this complete string is \(N\). It is not a succinct circuit or oracle description of a larger matrix. Output \(E(p)E(q)\), with \(p\ge0,q\ge1\), represents \(z=p/q\); the output need not be reduced.

Computation uses one finite deterministic multitape Turing machine, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes over fixed finite alphabets and an output tape. Each transition costs one step, including all arithmetic, reading, writing, storage and output costs. There are no random bits, advice strings, oracles or unit-cost exact-real operations. The machine and the two clock constants are independent of the dimension, entries and requested accuracy. The exponent is fixed independently of \(\varepsilon\); polynomial dependence on the numerical value of \(1/\varepsilon\) is permitted in addition to dependence on its encoding length. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

The approximation is relative to the permanent itself, not additive relative to \(n!\), a matrix norm, or a rescaled quantity. Nonnegativity makes the permanent positive precisely when the positive-entry bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. Thus the zero case is deterministically recognizable in polynomial time, and the displayed inequality requires \(z=0\) exactly in that case. Arbitrarily small positive permanents must still receive the same relative guarantee. This is a genuine algorithm-existence question, not a numerical-value target at the catalogue’s absolute \(1/100\) tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify the finite deterministic machine and constants \(C,k\), and prove termination, the full bit-cost bound, the rational output and both inequalities for every valid nonnegative rational matrix and every valid accuracy. A negative answer must rule out every such machine and clock, rather than just one approximation formula or family of algorithms. A conditional lower bound remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A randomized FPRAS, a scheme restricted to positive dense matrices, a fixed dimension-dependent approximation factor, or running time \(n^{h(1/\varepsilon)}\) with an unbounded accuracy-dependent exponent does not qualify. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a negative answer: an exponentially small requested error may legitimately require exponential time under an FPTAS clock.
cards.why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.
