cards.context:
The permanent is a basic counting polynomial whose nonnegative entries remove cancellation. Its zero–one specialization counts bipartite perfect matchings, while weighted inputs total the contributions of all such matchings. Existence of a matching and accurate estimation of their total weight are different tasks. The input’s full bit encoding matters when weights vary over many orders of magnitude; floating-point proximity to zero is not a substitute for the required relative guarantee.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda establish a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for all nonnegative matrices. This makes the permanent a particularly explicit test of the power of randomness: the desired relative approximation is already possible with bounded error, and the question asks whether it can always be obtained deterministically with the same fully polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy.

Anari and Rezaei prove the tight comparison \(\operatorname{Bethe}(A)\le\operatorname{per}(A)\le2^{n/2}\operatorname{Bethe}(A)\). Here the Bethe permanent is a particular variational estimate over nonnegative matrices with all row and column sums equal to one. Block diagonal matrices with \(2\times2\) all-ones blocks attain the factor. This proves a limitation of that estimate, not a lower bound on all deterministic approximation algorithms. The result was first posted in 2018 and presented at FOCS 2019; the journal’s later issue date does not make it a new 2025 algorithm.

Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s 27 August 2026 preprint reports an improved permanent FPRAS, with \(O(n^{6}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^{5}n\log(2/\delta))\) time for zero–one inputs of dimension at least two, where \(\delta\) is the failure probability. The theorem also states an extension to nonnegative matrices. This is a reported improvement on the randomized side; it does not remove randomness or establish this deterministic target.

Anari’s preprint, first posted on 28 August 2026 and revised on 1 September, claims a deterministic polynomial-time factor \(c^{n}\) for an absolute \(c<\sqrt2\). Its main theorem explicitly treats rational matrices, with zero entries and certified finite precision discussed in Appendix A. Narang and Perkins independently claim the same type of improvement in their 31 August preprint. These are bounds for estimates different from the unmodified Bethe value, so they do not contradict its tight example. The new proofs and any associated formalization were not independently checked in full by this review.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint states a stronger general result: positive rational endpoints \(L_{A}\le\operatorname{per}(A)\le U_{A}\), after separate zero detection, with
\[\log(U_{A}/L_{A})=O\!\left(\frac{n(\log\log n)^{2}}{\log n}\right)\]
as \(n\to\infty\), using a polynomial number of bit operations on arbitrary nonnegative rational inputs. This is a subexponential multiplicative interval width, not subexponential running time. Its Theorem 1.2 makes the error/time tradeoff explicit, and the introduction still distinguishes its guarantee from a fully polynomial relative approximation scheme. The full new proof has not been independently verified here.

Yi’s preprint of 3 September 2026 claims a deterministic FPTAS on another substantial subdomain: nonzero matrix entries must lie in \([\theta,1]\), and every row and column of the support must contain at least \((1/2+\gamma)n\) nonzero entries, for fixed \(\theta>0\) and \(\gamma>0\). Its polynomial exponents may depend on those margins. The statement includes some matrices with zeros, but it does not cover unrestricted rational inputs or margins that shrink with the input size. Its full proof was not independently verified in this review.

The remaining question is a uniform relative approximation guarantee with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent and arbitrary requested accuracy. Improving an exponential factor, making its logarithm sublinear in dimension, and solving a restricted dense case are all meaningful advances, but none of their stated guarantees is the full requirement. A resolution would settle a central concrete derandomization problem in approximate counting.

cards.title: FP = #P from \(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold for ordinary uniform Turing computation?
\[\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\#\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}.\]
The conclusion means exact deterministic polynomial-time computation of every polynomially verifiable witness count, output as a binary nonnegative integer. Since \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm{P}\) holds unconditionally, the conclusion is also written \(\#\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\).
cards.definitions:
All language inputs are finite binary strings, of bit length \(n=|x|\). A deterministic polynomial-time machine has a finite program and halts on every input within \(C(n+1)^d\) steps of a multitape Turing machine, for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Each tape read, write and head move is charged; writing an output is part of the bound. There is no advice, randomness or oracle. The program and constants may depend on the fixed problem, but not on the input. A language belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\) when such a machine outputs its exact membership bit.

For a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients and a deterministic verifier \(V(x,y)\) running in time polynomial in \(|x|+|y|\), put
\[W_{V,p}(x)=\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\},\qquad f_{V,p}(x)=|W_{V,p}(x)|.\]
The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages \(\{x:W_{V,p}(x)\ne\varnothing\}\). The class \(\#\mathrm{P}\) consists of the total numerical functions \(f_{V,p}\). The verifier is required to halt on every pair of binary strings. Witnesses have exactly the specified length; each distinct witness string contributes one, even when several describe the same object. The hypothesis \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) asserts equality of these language classes, with a separate polynomial-time decider permitted for each language.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) computed by deterministic polynomial-time machines under the same bit-cost convention. The output is the exact binary integer, with 0 represented by a single zero and no leading zeros for positive integers. Every \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function satisfies \(f_{V,p}(x)\leq2^{p(n)}\), so polynomially many output bits suffice. Conversely, a polynomial-time numerical function is in \(\#\mathrm{P}\): choose a fixed polynomial witness length longer than its output bound, regard witnesses as binary integers, and accept exactly those smaller than its value. This explains the numerical FP equality convention in the source.

In the conclusion the quantifiers are \(\forall V,p\ \exists M,C,d\ \forall x\): one exact counting program for every fixed witness-counting function. No common exponent or effective transformation from arbitrary existence deciders to counting machines is required. The proposition is an implication about these unrelativized classes. It does not assert that P = NP actually holds, introduce access to a SAT oracle, or restrict the algorithms to a specified proof technique.

The logical negation of the target is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) together with \(\#\mathrm{P}\not\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). In particular, a proof of \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would prove the implication through its false antecedent, not refute it. Here and below exact computation differs from relative approximation: an approximation \(a\) with parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1\) need only satisfy \(|a-f(x)|\leq\varepsilon f(x)\), which forces \(a=0\) when the count is zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication, or of its logical negation. A direct affirmative proof may assume \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) and derive an exact deterministic polynomial-time counting machine for every fixed verifier; a proof of \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) also settles the literal implication affirmatively. A negative answer must establish both \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) and a \(\#\mathrm{P}\) function outside numerical FP. An oracle-relative counterexample, a limitation of one proposed reduction, or an error in a claimed affirmative proof does not establish that negation. Approximation, finding a single witness and time polynomial in the numerical count do not meet the exact-computation conclusion.
cards.why: The implication isolates the computational gap between learning that solutions exist and determining their exact number. A proof from the decision-collapse hypothesis would connect two central forms of computational tractability, while a negative answer would show that exact counting can remain hard even after all NP existence problems become easy.

references.title: Topological Collapse: P = NP Implies #P = FP via Solution-Space Homology
references.locator: Preprint v1, 23 March 2026; §2.4 p. 3 defines the complex from satisfying assignments; §3.2 p. 4 asserts that a family with positive second Betti number contains UNSAT instances. Checked directly on 16 September 2026; claimed resolution is not accepted by this review.

cards.context:
The known reverse implication is immediate: an exact count decides whether a witness exists by testing whether the value is positive. This card asks whether decision tractability forces counting tractability as well. It is separate from the unconditional question whether all counting functions are already efficiently computable.

Under P = NP, one can find a witness by fixing its bits successively and testing whether each chosen prefix still extends to an accepted witness. The number of prefix queries is polynomial. Running that process for every witness can still require exponential time, because polynomial-time verification allows exponentially many witnesses.

A tempting binary search asks whether \(f(x)\geq k\), with \(k\) encoded in binary. Listing \(k\) distinct witnesses certifies the threshold only at a cost proportional to \(k\), which can be exponential in the input length. Therefore this certificate does not place all binary-threshold questions in NP. An efficient threshold procedure would recover the count with polynomially many comparisons, but P = NP alone does not supply that procedure.

The source and Aaronson’s survey record a substantial weaker consequence: P = NP gives polynomial-time relative approximation at every fixed inverse-polynomial accuracy. Such accuracy need not distinguish adjacent exponential-size counts. Requesting exponentially small relative error can destroy a running-time guarantee polynomial in inverse accuracy, so this known result does not settle exact computation.

The stronger hypothesis P = PSPACE suffices for exact counting. Here PSPACE means decision problems solvable with polynomial working space: exhaustive counting stores a witness and a binary counter of polynomial length, and individual output-bit questions use only polynomial space. The source explicitly separates this implication from the P = NP question.

A March 2026 preprint claims the affirmative implication. A direct editorial check finds an internal obstruction: §2.4 defines \(S(F)\) using precisely the satisfying assignments of a formula, so an unsatisfiable formula gives the empty complex and has \(\beta_2(S(F))=0\), where the second Betti number is the dimension of second homology. Yet §3.2 uses unsatisfiable instances in a family with \(\beta_2=2^{\Omega(N)}>0\). That step cannot hold under the stated definition. This identifies a defect in the presented argument; it neither disproves the implication nor substitutes for a community assessment of the preprint.

cards.title: Deterministic relative counting for DNF
cards.formal:
Is there a deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the number of satisfying assignments of an arbitrary explicitly given DNF formula? In the precise reciprocal-integer accuracy convention used here, do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and positive integers \(C,a\) such that for every DNF formula \(\varphi\) of encoding length \(N\) over its declared \(n\) variables, and every integer \(q\ge2\), the algorithm outputs a nonnegative rational number \(\widehat Z\) with
\[|\widehat Z-Z(\varphi)|\le Z(\varphi)/q,\qquad Z(\varphi)=|\{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\varphi(x)=1\}|,\]
and halts within \(C(N+q+1)^a\) steps? The guarantee must hold on every input without randomness, advice or an oracle. There is no bound on term width or on the number of occurrences of a variable other than the explicit input length.
cards.definitions:
A literal is a declared variable \(x_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), or its negation. A term is a finite conjunction of literals; a DNF formula is a finite disjunction of terms. All literal occurrences and all terms are listed explicitly. Empty conjunctions evaluate to true and the empty disjunction evaluates to false. Repeated literals or terms are allowed, and a term containing both signs of one variable is false. A variable assignment specifies every declared variable, including unused ones; every satisfying assignment is counted once regardless of how many terms it satisfies.

Use an explicit encoding consisting of \(1^n\), a self-delimiting binary term count, and for each term its self-delimiting literal count followed by variable indices in binary and one sign bit per literal. Thus the declared variable set is part of the input, \(n\le N\), and arbitrary circuits or compressed representations of an exponentially larger DNF are excluded. Valid formulas with \(n=0\) are included and are evaluated on the unique empty assignment. Malformed encodings may be rejected in polynomial time and are not counted as instances of the formula problem.

The accuracy parameter \(q\) is given in binary. Computation uses a fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine; one transition costs one step, and writing the output is counted. Represent \(\widehat Z\) by a binary nonnegative numerator and positive denominator. They need not be in lowest terms. The constants in the running-time bound are independent of the formula, its width, its variable occurrence counts and \(q\). All preprocessing is included.

The target is relative error \(1/q\). This is the usual fully polynomial accuracy convention: an arbitrary requested \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) can be met by taking \(q=\max\{2,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\}\), with the time to read that request also counted. The runtime is polynomial in the reciprocal accuracy, not merely its bit length. If \(Z=0\), the output must equal zero exactly. If \(Z>0\), it must lie between \((1-1/q)Z\) and \((1+1/q)Z\). Additive error \(2^n/q\) is a different and potentially much weaker guarantee when satisfying assignments are rare. The algorithm is allowed to output a rational estimate; exact integer counting is not required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence or nonexistence of this deterministic approximation scheme. A positive answer must specify the algorithm and prove its relative-error and fully polynomial-time guarantees for all formulas and all \(q\ge2\), including zero counts. A negative answer must rule out every such uniform deterministic scheme. Randomized high-probability estimates, an additive-error approximation alone, quasipolynomial runtime, or polynomial algorithms restricted to bounded-width or bounded-occurrence formulas do not settle the full target.
cards.why: DNF counting is a canonical approximate-counting problem for which randomization gives an efficient relative approximation even when direct random assignment sampling rarely finds a solution. A deterministic scheme would remove randomness from this basic union-counting task across all formula widths and occurrence patterns. It would strengthen the explicit derandomization tools available for both complexity theory and probabilistic data processing.

cards.context:
The source’s randomized Algorithm 2.35 gives a relative approximation in time polynomial in formula size and reciprocal accuracy. Open Problems 2.36 and 7.32 ask for deterministic polynomial time, with the latter discussion supplying a quasipolynomial-time derandomization baseline.

Overlaps between terms are essential: adding the numbers of assignments satisfying the individual terms can count the same assignment many times. The problem counts the size of their union, with all declared variables included.

Trevisan gives deterministic multiplicative approximation in time linear in formula length and polynomial in reciprocal accuracy when term width is a fixed constant. Its dependence on that width does not provide a uniform polynomial bound for arbitrary DNF inputs.

Servedio and Tan study formulas in which each variable occurs at most k times, a restriction different from term width. Their relative-error algorithms have explicit dependence on k and accuracy; their results do not furnish the all-occurrence fully polynomial bound required here.

cards.formal: Do a deterministic Turing algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every explicitly given finite hypergraph \(H\), \(A\) outputs every inclusion-minimal transversal exactly once and terminates within \(C(N(H)+N_{\mathrm{out}}(H)+1)^c\) bit steps? Here \(N(H)\) and \(N_{\mathrm{out}}(H)\) are the encoded input and total output lengths.
cards.definitions: \(H=([n],E), n\ge 0\), is supplied as the explicit vertex list and a finite list of edges \(e\subseteq [n]\), each edge an increasing list of binary vertex identifiers. Repeated edges have no effect. \(N(H)\) is the bit length of this input including delimiters. A transversal is a set \(T\subseteq [n]\) intersecting every \(e\in E\); it is inclusion-minimal when no proper subset has this property. Output each such T as an increasing list of its binary vertex identifiers with a delimiter, in arbitrary order; no duplicate, nonminimal or incomplete output is allowed. \(N_{\mathrm{out}}(H)\) is the sum of the bit lengths of these records, counting one delimiter even for \(T=\varnothing\). If E is empty, the unique minimal transversal is \(\varnothing\). If E contains \(\varnothing\), there is no transversal and \(N_{\mathrm{out}}=0\). Time includes all computation, output and termination detection. The polynomial and algorithm are independent of n, E, edge size and output size; there is no separate delay or workspace bound, advice, oracle or randomization. Use the [explicit encoding convention](definitions.html#encoding).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of a single algorithm meeting the total output-polynomial bound, including completeness, uniqueness and termination on every finite hypergraph, or a Lean proof that none exists. The target imposes no polynomial-delay or polynomial-space bound. A lower bound for one enumeration algorithm does not establish nonexistence of all algorithms.
cards.why: This central enumeration question governs the complexity of converting a hypergraph into the family of all its minimal hitting sets and underlies many enumeration reductions.

cards.title: Output-polynomial vertex enumeration
cards.formal:
Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every rational matrix \(M\) and rational vector \(b\) for which
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Mx\leq b\}
\]
is bounded, \(A\) lists every vertex of \(P\) exactly once and halts in at most \(p(N+S)\) bit operations? Here \(N\) is the complete binary input length and \(S\) is the length of the required exact vertex list in the canonical encoding below. The dimension \(d\) is part of the input. Empty, lower-dimensional and degenerate polytopes are included.
cards.definitions:
The input consists of integers \(m,d\geq1\), an explicitly listed matrix \(M\in\mathbb Q^{m\times d}\) and vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\). The inequality \(Mx\leq b\) is coordinatewise. Every rational is represented by a signed integer numerator and a positive denominator in binary, in lowest terms, with no leading zeros; zero has numerator zero and denominator one. Fixed delimiters separate dimensions, entries and rows. The input length \(N\) includes all these symbols. Dimensions are unbounded, and no rank, sparsity, integrality or conditioning restriction is imposed.

A polyhedron is a set described by finitely many closed linear inequalities. The promise here is that it is bounded: there exists a finite real number \(B\) such that \(\|x\|_2\leq B\) for every \(x\in P\). An empty set satisfies this promise. The number \(B\) is neither supplied nor assumed to have a given value. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope. Redundant inequalities, repeated inequalities and a non-full-dimensional affine hull are allowed; no nondegeneracy or general-position promise is made.

A vertex is an extreme point. A vector \(v\in P\) is a vertex if, for all \(x,y\in P\), the equality \(v=(x+y)/2\) implies \(x=y=v\). Every vertex of a rational polyhedron is rational. The output must contain the coordinate vector of each distinct vertex, exactly once, in arbitrary order, with all \(d\) coordinates in the same reduced rational encoding. It ends with a fixed end marker. An empty polytope produces only that marker. A singleton produces its unique point even if its affine dimension is zero.

Define \(S\) as the sum of the canonical lengths of the distinct required coordinate vectors, including fixed separators and the end marker. Permuting the list does not change its length. Extra padding, duplicate vectors, alternative descriptions of the same vertex and extraneous certificates do not enlarge \(S\). At a vertex, a full-rank selection of active equations determines its coordinates; Cramer’s rule bounds their binary lengths by a polynomial in \(N\). Thus every individual output has polynomial length even though the number of outputs can be exponential.

Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with bit-operation cost, no advice and no oracle. The same finite program and the same polynomial \(p\) must work for every input satisfying the boundedness promise. Arithmetic precision, preprocessing, writing all coordinates, duplicate handling and the final termination signal are charged. The bound is on total time from start to termination. No polynomial-delay, incremental-polynomial-time or input-polynomial-working-space requirement is added. The algorithm may use space up to its total time bound. Its behavior outside the boundedness promise is immaterial; malformed encodings can be rejected.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm and polynomial exist, or a proof in Lean of their nonexistence. A positive proof must establish exactness of every rational output, completeness, absence of duplicates, termination and one uniform \(p(N+S)\) bit bound for all bounded rational input polyhedra, including the empty and lower-dimensional cases.

A negative proof must rule out every correct uniform deterministic enumerator with every polynomial total input-plus-output bound. It is not enough to exhibit an input on which a particular pivot rule or intermediate-representation algorithm is slow. A conditional hardness theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional existence question. Approximate vertices, a fixed dimension, bounded branch-width, nondegeneracy, or enumeration measured against all bases or all arrangement intersections does not meet the full criterion.
cards.why: This is a basic unresolved question about converting between implicit and explicit representations of convex feasible regions. A general output-polynomial algorithm would make degeneracy and intermediate representation growth manageable at the level of total complexity, while an impossibility result would separate efficient linear optimization from full exact enumeration.

references.title: An Efficient Algorithm for Vertex Enumeration of Arrangement
references.authors: Zelin Dong; Fenglei Fan; Huan Xiong; Tieyong Zeng
references.locator: Version 2, 25 March 2025; first version 30 January 2024. Abstract and §1 concern all arrangement vertices, a different output set from the vertices of one inequality-defined polytope.

cards.context:
An inequality system describes a convex region implicitly, while its vertices describe the extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without listing every vertex. The question asks whether converting the whole description requires only polynomial overhead beyond the size of the answer.

A polytope can have exponentially many vertices, so polynomial time in the input alone is not the intended goal. Output-polynomial time allows this unavoidable output cost. It still demands fast termination on instances whose final vertex list is short, even when a natural algorithm encounters a large collection of intermediate objects.

One direct method chooses sets of tight inequalities, solves the resulting linear systems and tests feasibility. Degeneracy can make many different sets identify the same vertex. The total number of bases examined can therefore be much larger than the number of distinct vertices. A total-polynomial bound in the number of such bases would not establish the required output-polynomial bound.

Reimers and Stougie obtain a total-polynomial algorithm when a branch-width parameter of the linear matroid of the constraint matrix is bounded by a fixed constant. This parameter measures how the columns can be recursively divided while limiting the overlap of the spans on either side. Their result supplies a structural tractable case, while their introduction explicitly retains the general bounded-polytope question.

The same source recalls that total-polynomial vertex enumeration for arbitrary unbounded polyhedra would imply P equals NP. Boundedness is therefore a substantive promise. Intersecting an unbounded polyhedron with a large box can introduce additional vertices; the number of these new outputs is not automatically controlled by the original required list, so this operation does not simply transfer the unbounded lower bound.

The arrangement paper, revised in March 2025, enumerates intersections arising throughout a family of hyperplanes. Most such intersections may be infeasible for the chosen orientations of the corresponding inequalities. Its output count can thus be much larger than the number of vertices of one polytope, so enumerating the entire arrangement and filtering it does not give the claimed bound in this card’s output size.

The numerical coordinates are part of the computational model. Their polynomial bit-length bound permits exact rational output and prevents an apparently short geometric answer from hiding unbounded precision costs. Conversely, no compact symbolic description of a vertex replaces the explicitly required coordinate vector.

cards.title: Incremental polynomial-time binary-matroid circuit enumeration
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given binary matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{r\times m}\), enumerates all circuits of its column matroid exactly once in incremental polynomial time while using space polynomial only in the input length? Equivalently, does binary-matroid circuit enumeration belong to \(\mathrm{IncP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\) under the source’s conventions? The target permits any fixed polynomial exponent in the number of outputs; retaining the known quadratic incremental exponent is a stronger variant distinguished in the later source.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) has addition and multiplication modulo two. The input matrix has nonnegative dimensions \(r,m\), represented by unary dimension headers followed by its \(rm\) entries in row order. Its encoded length \(L\) is of order \(r+m+rm+1\), including isolated zero columns and zero-dimensional cases. Malformed encodings are rejected in polynomial time. Column indices are distinct ground-set elements, even if their vectors coincide.

The column matroid has ground set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). A subset is independent exactly when its columns are linearly independent over \(\mathbb F_2\). A circuit is a nonempty inclusion-minimal dependent subset: \(C\subseteq[m]\) is a circuit if \(\operatorname{rank}(A_C)<|C|\) and every proper subset of \(C\) is independent. Equivalently over this field, the columns in \(C\) sum to zero and no nonempty proper subset has zero sum. A zero column gives a singleton circuit; two equal nonzero columns give a two-element circuit. A circuit is not required to have globally minimum cardinality.

The output for each circuit is its \(m\)-bit characteristic vector. Every circuit must occur once, no other set may be output, the order is unrestricted, and enumeration must halt. Let \(N(A)\) be the number of circuits, which can be exponential in \(L\). If there are no circuits, the algorithm must halt in polynomial time. The output stream is write-only and cannot be read back as free external memory. Registers or buffers retaining previously emitted vectors count toward working space.

Use the source’s deterministic random-access machine convention: finite programs, integer registers, basic arithmetic consisting of addition, subtraction and multiplication, with arithmetic cost proportional to operand bit lengths and unit-cost register access and other basic instructions. Working space counts the bits in all stored integers, including retained outputs and register addresses needed to access them. Output uses designated registers; its polynomial-length encoding may be charged explicitly without changing the class. There is no advice or randomness. The matrix is read-only input and contributes polynomially many bits even if copied into memory.

Incremental polynomial time means that there are fixed positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that, on every valid \(A\) and for every \(1\leq k\leq N(A)\), the time from the start through the \(k\)-th distinct output is at most \(C(L+1)^b(k+1)^a\). Preprocessing is included. Total time through termination is at most \(C(L+1)^b(N(A)+1)^a\), enlarging constants or exponents if necessary. Polynomial working space means that fixed positive integers \(D,c\) bound space at every moment by \(D(L+1)^c\), independently of \(k\) and \(N(A)\). All constants are uniform over matrices and dimensions. These are class-membership bounds, not a prescribed delay exponent or an order requirement.

The cited original circuit-enumeration algorithm also accepts a matroid through an independence oracle. On the promise that the matroid is binary, that representation and an explicit binary matrix are interchangeable with polynomial overhead: greedily find a basis \(B\), make its columns unit vectors, and for every \(e\notin B\) set its coordinate at \(b\in B\) to one exactly when \((B\setminus\{b\})\cup\{e\}\) is independent. In a binary matroid these are the unique fundamental-circuit coordinates and give a representing matrix with at most \(m\) rows. This uses polynomially many queries and polynomial space. Conversely, Gaussian elimination simulates independence queries from a matrix. Oracle queries are exact, and writing their \(m\)-bit sets is charged; the equivalence uses the binary promise and does not apply to arbitrary matroids.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm exists, or that no such algorithm exists. A positive proof must establish completeness, absence of duplicate outputs, termination, one uniform incremental polynomial bound and one simultaneous polynomial working-space bound for every binary matrix. A negative proof must rule out all algorithms meeting these bounds, not merely show that the known saturation algorithm stores exponentially many circuits. Polynomial total time without the prefix guarantees, unrestricted output-sized memory, enumeration with repeated circuits, or bounds only for graphic matroids do not settle the target. A conditional lower bound under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional question.
cards.why: This is a concrete test of whether the storage used by saturation-based enumeration is intrinsically necessary. A polynomial-space incremental algorithm would make all minimal binary linear dependencies accessible in output-sensitive time without retaining an exponentially large history, and could suggest methods for other closure-based enumeration problems.

references.locator: Computational Complexity 35, article 6, published 20 July 2026; introduction pp. 3–6 distinguishes saturation and duplicate storage from polynomial-space regularization. Also checked author preprint arXiv:2108.10208v2, 2 September 2024.

cards.context:
Circuits are the minimal linear dependencies among columns. Enumerating all subsets and testing rank uses little memory but can waste exponential time before finding early circuits. At the other extreme, storing the whole discovered family can support efficient generation but violates the requested space bound when the family is large.

The known algorithm generates circuits in incremental polynomial time by repeatedly using closure relations among circuits already found. The publisher’s original abstract states the result even for general matroids given by independence queries. The source singles out binary matroids for the additional polynomial-space question.

A zero-sum subset of binary columns need not be a circuit: it may contain several smaller dependencies. Gaussian elimination readily tests whether a proposed subset is a circuit, but this membership test does not by itself provide a way to visit all minimal dependencies with the required output-sensitive time bound.

For graphic matroids, represented by graph incidence matrices over the two-element field, circuits correspond to simple graph cycles. Binary matroids include more than this graphic subclass. An algorithm specialized to graph cycles therefore supplies an example of tractability without settling all binary representations.

Rerunning an enumeration to recognize duplicate outputs can trade additional incremental time for reduced storage when the underlying generator already has polynomial space. It does not automatically remove the large stored family that a saturation generator needs to create its future outputs. This distinction is why eliminating duplicate filters and eliminating the saturation memory are separate tasks.

The later WEPA formulation records a known bound quadratic in the number of generated circuits, times an input polynomial, and asks both whether that exponent can be retained in polynomial space and whether any polynomial incremental exponent can be obtained. This card keeps the latter class-membership target stated by the imported card, while recording the stronger timing question.

The 2026 regularization theorem turns polynomial-space linear incremental algorithms into polynomial-space polynomial-delay algorithms. Its input algorithm must already have polynomial space. Thus it resolves a buffering issue but does not directly compress the circuit family stored by the known saturation procedure. The paper’s black-box lower bounds likewise do not rule out a new algorithm exploiting the matrix.

cards.title: Edge-exchange Gray codes for directed spanning trees
cards.formal: For every finite loopless simple directed graph and root r admitting an out-arborescence, do all spanning out-arborescences admit an arc-exchange listing?
cards.definitions: A directed graph has a finite nonempty vertex set V and arcs (u,v) with u≠v, at most one arc for each ordered pair; opposite arcs may both occur. The root r∈V is fixed. An out-arborescence is an arc set of size |V|−1 in which r has indegree zero, every other vertex has indegree one, and every vertex is reachable from r along chosen arcs. The graph is promised to contain at least one such set. A listing contains every such arc set exactly once, and consecutive sets differ by deleting one arc and inserting one other arc. There is no last-to-first requirement and no bound on computation. The one-vertex case has the single empty arborescence.

cards.title: Exact counting of linear extensions below base two
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\), constants \(K>0\) and \(1<c<2\), and an integer \(n_0\), such that, for every \(n\ge n_0\) and every partial order \(P\) on \([n]\), \(A\) outputs the exact number \(e(P)\) of linear extensions using at most \(Kc^n\) bit-cost random-access steps? It must also terminate correctly on every smaller valid input. There is no restriction on the width, height, dimension, sparsity or a graph parameter of \(P\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\ge0\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A partial order \(\le_P\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive binary relation on \([n]\). The input consists of binary \(n\) and its explicit \(n\times n\) Boolean relation matrix in row-major order. A list of comparable pairs or a Hasse diagram can be converted to this representation in polynomial time. Invalid matrices may be rejected in polynomial time; the time bound ranges over valid posets.

A linear extension is a permutation \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of the distinct labels such that \(x\le_P y\) and \(x\ne y\) imply that \(x\) precedes \(y\). The integer \(e(P)\) counts these permutations. Elements with identical comparabilities remain distinct. The empty poset has one linear extension, and \(1\le e(P)\le n!\) for every finite poset. The required algorithm outputs this exact integer in binary; a sample, relative approximation or count modulo one prime is insufficient.

Use a uniform deterministic random-access machine with finite binary-string registers. Reading and writing a register charges for its address and data bits. Comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and elementary integer arithmetic charge for all operand and output bits using standard polynomial bit-cost arithmetic algorithms. No arithmetic on arbitrarily large integers is a unit-cost operation. Time includes reading the input and writing the output, and is worst-case over all \(n\)-element input posets. There is no additional polynomial-space requirement. This makes the source's exponential-time convention explicit; the reviewed construction uses polynomial-bit addresses and counters and polynomial work per state.

The constants \(K,c,n_0\) and the finite algorithm are fixed before the input is chosen. A bound \(O(b^n n^d)\) with fixed \(b<2\) and \(d\) answers the question: any fixed \(c\) between \(\max\{1,b\}\) and two absorbs the polynomial factor for sufficiently large \(n\). A \(2^{n-o(n)}\) bound does not suffice. The task asks for existence of a strict constant-base improvement, not determination of the optimal base. The second question in the same source passage, about treewidth of the Hasse diagram, is distinct.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked affirmative answer must specify one algorithm and prove exact correctness and termination for every finite input poset, together with the uniform worst-case bound for fixed \(c<2\) in the stated model. A negative answer must prove the full negation of this existence claim. This is an algorithm-existence proposition requiring exact output; numerical benchmark tolerance does not replace exact counting by approximation. A citation or finite collection of tests is not a substitute for the Lean theorem.
cards.why: The target asks whether a canonical exact counting problem can beat the all-subsets exponential barrier on every input, despite the ease of finding one feasible ordering. It connects precedence counting with the structure of exact exponential algorithms. The original target is retained historically because a checked 2026 preprint now answers it.

cards.context:
A partial order specifies precedence constraints while allowing incomparable elements. Counting compatible total orders measures the number of full rankings or schedules consistent with those constraints. This differs fundamentally from finding one compatible ordering, which is possible in polynomial time.

The 2013 question concerns unrestricted inputs. Earlier improvements for sparse or two-dimensional posets did not alone answer that worst-case question. The separate treewidth question concerns a different parameterized bound.

Oka’s August 2026 preprint proves deterministic exact \(O^{*}(1.89^n)\) counting on arbitrary posets. Absorbing the polynomial overhead into a slightly larger fixed base below two answers the selected target. The complete proof received the bounded review recorded here; peer review and Lean verification are not claimed.

cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every integer \(n\ge1\), every simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every integer \(t\ge1\), if \(\chi(G)\ge t\), then \(G\) contains \(K_t\) as an ordinary graph minor. Equivalently, \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every such graph, where \(h\) is the Hadwiger number defined below.
cards.definitions: The edge set of \(G\) is any set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices in \([n]\); there are no loops or parallel edges. For an integer \(r\ge1\), a proper \(r\)-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least such \(r\); it exists and lies between \(1\) and \(n\). The graph \(K_t\) has \(t\) vertices and every possible edge. A \(K_t\) minor in \(G\) means that there are \(t\) pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) with both of the following properties: for every \(i\), any two vertices of \(B_i\) are joined by a finite path of edges of \(G\) whose vertices all lie in \(B_i\); and for every \(i<j\), some edge of \(G\) has one endpoint in \(B_i\) and one in \(B_j\). A singleton is connected. The branch sets may have any sizes, need not cover all vertices, and have no restrictions on extra internal edges or on parity. This is equivalent to obtaining \(K_t\) by vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions, discarding loops and merging parallel edges after contraction. It is neither an induced-minor nor an odd-minor requirement. The Hadwiger number \(h(G)\) is the largest \(t\) admitting these branch sets, so \(1\le h(G)\le n\). For \(t\ge2\), the proposition equivalently says that absence of a \(K_t\) minor implies a proper \((t-1)\)-coloring; the \(t=1\) assertion holds automatically for a nonempty graph. Relabeling vertices has no effect. The quantifiers impose no connectedness, degree, order or other restriction on \(G\), and no running-time bound on finding a coloring or a minor.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition for all finite nonempty simple undirected graphs and all integers \(t\ge1\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: existence of a finite graph \(G\) and integer \(t\ge1\) with \(\chi(G)\ge t\) and no \(t\) branch sets satisfying the definition. A counterexample must certify both the chromatic lower bound and absence of the ordinary clique minor. A proof of \(h(G)\ge\chi(G)\) for every graph is an equivalent positive answer. No efficient algorithm is required. A constant-factor or asymptotic coloring bound, a finite list of established values of \(t\), a restricted graph class, or a counterexample only to the odd-minor variant does not cover the target.
cards.why: Hadwiger’s conjecture proposes an exact relation between two basic graph parameters: the number of colors needed and the size of a complete graph obtainable by contraction. It extends the Four-Color Theorem and would turn exclusion of a complete minor into the sharp universal coloring bound. Its significance comes from this structural connection across all finite graphs, rather than from an algorithmic requirement in the question.

references.title: Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture
references.authors: Marcus Kühn; Lisa Sauermann; Raphael Steiner; Yuval Wigderson
references.locator: Version 1, 23 December 2025; full PDF §1, ordinary Conjecture 1.1 on page 1, branch-tree odd-minor definition, Conjecture 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 on page 2. Still sole arXiv version on 14 September 2026; construction proof not independently certified.

cards.context:
A complete minor can be much larger than any complete subgraph: contraction groups connected regions into single vertices. Hadwiger asks whether the resulting complete graph can always have as many vertices as the original graph needs colors. For every \(t\ge2\), the graph \(K_{t-1}\) has no \(K_t\) minor and needs exactly \(t-1\) colors, so the conjectured bound for the excluded-minor class is sharp.

The exact cases through \(t=6\) are known. The \(t=5\) case is equivalent, via Wagner’s theorem, to the Four-Color Theorem for planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour and Thomas established the \(t=6\) case: without assuming four-colorability, their structural result makes a minimal counterexample apex, meaning that deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. The Four-Color Theorem then gives five colors for that graph. Their paper indexes the conjecture by the allowed number of colors, one less than the clique-minor order used on this card.

Kostochka and Thomason obtained an \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) bound on degeneracy, where a graph is \(d\)-degenerate if every nonempty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most \(d\). Such a graph is \((d+1)\)-colorable. The order of this degeneracy bound is tight, but that fact is not a chromatic lower bound of the same order and does not disprove Hadwiger. Delcourt and Postle’s Theorem 1.5 gives \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors for arbitrary \(K_t\)-minor-free graphs; its quantification has no bound on the number of vertices.

Liu and Luo’s version 2, submitted on 9 September 2026, states in Theorem 1.1 that an absolute constant \(C\) satisfies \(\chi(G)\le Ct\log\log\log t\) for every integer \(t\ge16\) and every \(K_t\)-minor-free graph. Their logarithms are natural. This is recorded as a recent preprint claim whose proof has not been independently verified here. It does not establish either the weakening \(\chi(G)=O(t)\) or the exact bound \(t-1\); the introduction still identifies clique-minor orders starting at seven as open.

For the odd-minor variant, the disjoint branch trees must each have a proper two-coloring, with an edge joining vertices of the same color between every pair of trees. Forgetting these extra requirements yields an ordinary minor, so absence of an ordinary minor implies absence of an odd minor; the reverse implication need not hold. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s December 2025 preprint states that for each fixed \(\delta>0\) and every sufficiently large \(t\), some graph has no odd \(K_t\) minor and has \(\chi(G)\ge(3/2-\delta)t\). This refutes the stronger odd-minor conjecture. Odd-minor absence by itself does not certify the ordinary-minor absence required for a negative answer here.

progress.text: Hadwiger’s original conjecture is restated in the introduction of the cited modern paper; the 1943 original was not inspected in this review.
Kostochka and Thomason establish the \(O(t\sqrt{\log t})\) degeneracy bound, summarized in Theorem 1.3 of Delcourt and Postle. Its tightness concerns degeneracy, not the conjectured chromatic bound.

Robertson, Seymour and Thomas establish the structural result that, with the Four-Color Theorem, proves five-colorability of \(K_6\)-minor-free graphs. The institutional abstract and publication metadata were checked.
Delcourt and Postle obtain \(O(t\log\log t)\) colors. The first preprint was submitted on 3 August 2021, the inspected version 5 on 5 March 2024, and the journal article appeared in 2025.

Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner and Wigderson’s Theorem 1.3 disproves the odd Hadwiger conjecture; their ordinary-minor Conjecture 1.1 remains a separate target. The preprint result is also cited in Liu and Luo’s September 2026 introduction.

Liu and Luo’s version 2 claims \(O(t\log\log\log t)\) colors in Theorem 1.1 and explicitly retains the ordinary Hadwiger conjecture as open. The arXiv version history still lists version 2 as latest on 14 September 2026; the proof was not independently verified.

Such a minor consists of disjoint nonempty connected vertex sets with an edge between every pair of sets.
There are no parity requirements, restrictions on the sizes of these sets, or algorithmic running-time requirements.
The conjecture would extend the Four-Color Theorem to an exact relation between coloring and clique minors in all finite graphs.
A solution must prove the full assertion or certify a finite counterexample in Lean; the recent coloring improvement and the disproof for odd minors do not settle this target.

cards.title: Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
cards.formal: For each integer \(h\ge 2\) and each undirected simple graph \(H\) on \([h]\), is there a real constant \(c_H>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every undirected simple graph \(G\) on \([n]\) containing no induced copy of \(H\), \[\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}\ge n^{c_H}?\] The exponent is chosen after the entire forbidden graph \(H\) and before the host graph \(G\); the assertion must hold for all such \(H\).
cards.definitions: Write \([m]=\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}\). A simple undirected graph on \([m]\) is a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation on this set; it has no loops or multiple edges. An induced copy of \(H\) in \(G\) is an injection \(f:[h]\to[n]\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent in \(H\) if and only if \(f(u)\) and \(f(v)\) are adjacent in \(G\), for every distinct \(u,v\in[h]\). Both edges and nonedges must be preserved. A clique is a vertex subset in which every distinct pair is adjacent, and an independent or stable set is one in which every distinct pair is nonadjacent. The integers \(\omega(G)\) and \(\alpha(G)\) are their respective maximum cardinalities; a homogeneous set in this card means a clique or an independent set. The right side \(n^{c_H}\) is an ordinary positive-real power, and the integer on the left is compared as a real number. The constant \(c_H\) may depend on all of \(H\), but not on \(G\) or \(n\). There is no additional degree, density, dimension or algorithmic promise. All positive host sizes, including \(n<h\), are included. This is an existence statement, with no required algorithm for computing \(c_H\) or finding the homogeneous set. A hereditary graph class is closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs; a proper such class omits some finite graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer proves existence of a positive exponent for every finite forbidden graph and the homogeneous-set guarantee for every permitted host graph. A negative answer proves that there is one fixed graph \(H\) with \(|V(H)|\ge2\) such that, for every real \(c>0\), some positive integer \(n\) and some \(H\)-free graph \(G\) on \([n]\) satisfy \(\max\{\alpha(G),\omega(G)\}<n^c\). The witness host graph may depend on \(c\), but the forbidden graph must be the same for all \(c\). Failure of one proposed exponent or verification of finitely many host sizes does not establish this negation. No numerical approximation to an optimal exponent is being requested.
cards.why: This central conjecture asks whether every proper hereditary restriction forces a polynomial-size clique or independent set, far beyond the logarithmic scale possible in arbitrary graphs. It would provide a common structural guarantee across all forbidden-induced-subgraph classes and clarify the relation between local exclusions, large nearly uniform vertex sets and neighborhood complexity. These are basic objects in structural and algorithmic graph theory; the assertion itself is an existence theorem, not an efficient clique or independent-set algorithm.

cards.context:
Ramsey theory guarantees homogeneous sets on the logarithmic scale in arbitrary graphs, and random graphs show that a polynomial guarantee is impossible without restrictions. The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture asks whether excluding any one fixed induced pattern always changes that scale to \(n^{c_H}\) for some positive constant. A proper hereditary class omits a graph \(H\) and hence every induced copy of it, so the conjecture is equivalently a polynomial homogeneous-set guarantee for every proper hereditary class.

The conjecture is traced to 1977 in the checked modern primary papers, and Erdős and Hajnal developed it in their 1989 Ramsey-type paper. Their general bound is \(2^{a_H\sqrt{\log_2 n}}\) for a suitable positive constant. Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improved this to \(2^{b_H\sqrt{\log_2 n\,\log_2\log_2 n}}\) for all \(n\ge2\). Their journal article appeared online on 6 May 2024. This still has a sublinear exponent in \(\log_2 n\) and does not yield a fixed positive power of \(n\).

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour proved the conjecture for the five-vertex path \(P_5\), whose only edges join consecutive vertices of a path. The preprint began in December 2023; the checked accepted revision is from 23 February 2026, and the journal publication is dated 23 March 2026. Together with the earlier bull and five-cycle cases and the known preservation properties, it completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices. The theorem concerns every \(P_5\)-free graph, with one positive exponent independent of its size.

The separate all-path theorem gives the following weaker guarantee: for every fixed path \(P\) and every real \(d\) with \(0<d<1\), there is \(a_{P,d}>0\) such that every \(P\)-free graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices has a homogeneous set of size at least \(2^{a_{P,d}(\log_2 n)^d}\). The constant can depend on both the path and \(d\). This explains the source notation \(2^{(\log n)^{1-o(1)}}\); its assertion for all fixed \(d<1\) does not include the required fixed-power case \(d=1\).

The 31 August 2026 revision by Huang, Ju and Zhou reports two further six-vertex cases. Both can be specified using the path \(a-b-c-d-e\) and a sixth vertex \(f\): the E-graph adds only \(cf\), while the Bird adds only \(bf\) and \(cf\). These definitions match Figures 4 and 5 of that revision. Each forbidden graph contains an induced \(P_5\), so its exclusion allows a larger host class than excluding \(P_5\). Theorems 1.10 and 1.11 concern these particular patterns, not every six-vertex graph.

Tran and Nguyen posted a further case on 28 August 2026. cards.title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\) admit an orientation \(D\) of all its edges and a function \(f:E\to\{1,2,3,4\}\) such that, at every vertex \(v\in V\), \[\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{head}_D(e)=v}f(e)=\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{tail}_D(e)=v}f(e)\] as an equality of integers?
cards.definitions: A finite loopless undirected multigraph has a finite vertex set \(V\) and a finite set \(E\) of distinct edge identities, each assigned an unordered pair of two distinct vertices. Multiple edges with the same pair of endpoints are allowed and counted separately in every sum. Two vertices lie in the same connected component when a finite sequence of incident edges joins them; a vertex is joined to itself by the empty sequence. A bridge is an edge whose deletion, with the vertex set retained, increases the number of connected components. Bridgeless means that no edge has this property. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and the graph with no vertices are allowed. An orientation chooses, for each edge, one endpoint as its tail and the other as its head. The orientation and all values are chosen together for the whole graph; conservation must hold at all vertices simultaneously. Empty sums equal zero. For an integer \(k\ge2\), a nowhere-zero \(k\)-flow in this convention has the same conservation law and values in \(\{1,\ldots,k-1\}\). Thus a 5-flow uses four possible positive integer values; it may use any subset of them. Equivalently, after fixing an arbitrary reference orientation, signed integer values \(z(e)\) with \(1\le|z(e)|\le4\) may be used: a negative value is represented by reversing that edge and taking its absolute value. Values are scalar integers, not vectors, and conservation is exact, not merely a congruence. There are no sources, sinks, externally prescribed demands, capacities, embedding, degree restrictions or construction-time requirements. The proposition is universal over finite graphs, with the orientation and values allowed to depend on the graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this universal existence proposition, or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G\) such that for every orientation \(D\) and every assignment \(f:E(G)\to\{1,2,3,4\}\), at least one vertex violates the integer conservation equality. A negative answer must prove both the graph hypotheses and the nonexistence of every permitted flow; failure of one orientation, one search method or a finite collection of trial assignments is insufficient unless it establishes that universal nonexistence. A positive answer must cover every size and all allowed parallel edges and components. A 6-flow, an assertion only for graphs with an additional restriction, or a statement conditional on an unproved conjecture does not settle this target. An alternative formulation can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication establishing the exact proposition or its negation. No efficient procedure for constructing the witness is required.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether the necessary absence of bridges always permits bounded nonzero integer circulation, with the universal value limit improved from five to four. It connects flow existence with graph coloring through planar duality and has a quantitative consequence for packing sets of arcs that meet every directed cut.

references.title: 5-flow conjecture
references.locator: Preserved discovery provenance from the card’s 11 September 2026 review; this pass grounds the formulation and current-status account in the primary papers above, not a fresh inspection of this community page.

cards.context:
Flow conservation models circulation with no accumulation at any vertex. If an edge is a bridge, summing conservation on one side of that bridge would force its value to be zero. Bridgelessness is therefore necessary. The issue is whether it is sufficient with the fixed range \(1,2,3,4\), independently of graph size. Components can be treated separately, and edgeless components satisfy conservation with the empty assignment. This extends the connected formulation in Conjecture 3 without changing the mathematical target.

Seymour’s 1981 6-flow theorem supplies values in \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) for every bridgeless graph. Younger’s 1983 work gives a polynomial-time construction, as recalled in Theorem 5 of the 2025 paper. The missing assertion is the universal reduction of the maximum value from five to four. The construction-time improvement in the known theorem is additional to the existence requirement on this card.

Tutte’s integer/group-flow theorem equates existence of a nowhere-zero integer 5-flow with existence of a flow over \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\), the residues modulo five, using nonzero values and conservation in that group. This equivalence is an existence theorem; simply interpreting the same residues as positive integers need not preserve integer conservation. Theorem 2.3 in the 2026 reconfiguration paper recalls the lifting statement.

For a connected bridgeless graph drawn in the plane without crossings, the dual graph has a vertex for each face and an edge crossing each original edge between its incident faces. Tutte’s duality identifies existence of an integer \(k\)-flow with a proper \(k\)-coloring of that dual: adjacent dual vertices receive different colors. This explains why flow questions extend coloring phenomena beyond graphs with a planar embedding.

A directed cut consists of all arcs crossing a nontrivial vertex partition when every crossing arc points in the same direction; a dijoin is a set of arcs meeting every such cut. Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi’s Theorem 3 implies that, when the underlying graph admits a 5-flow, a digraph with finite minimum directed-cut size \(\tau\ge2\) contains \(\lfloor\tau/5\rfloor\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins. The established 6-flow theorem yields \(\lfloor\tau/6\rfloor\). The 5-flow conjecture would improve this guarantee without asserting Woodall’s full packing equality.

Li and Su’s 2025 publisher abstract reports a 5-flow for every bridgeless graph of Euler genus at most 20. Euler genus is the least surface parameter admitting a crossing-free drawing: twice the number of handles for an orientable closed surface, or the number of crosscaps for a nonorientable one. This is a restricted graph class; no uniform bound on genus is assumed here. The present review inspected that abstract, not the full proof.

Esperet and coauthors’ July 2026 revision gives a graph with existing nowhere-zero 5-flows that cannot all be connected by steps changing a flow only along a cycle, while keeping every intermediate flow nowhere zero. Their Theorem 3.4 refutes this reconfiguration property in both the integer and modulo-five settings. It does not refute existence of a 5-flow; their introduction retains Tutte’s conjecture and the 6-flow theorem as the general benchmark.

Li, Li, Luo and Su’s January 2026 paper defines flows with vector values in several real dimensions and proves bounds on their norms. Its Conjecture 1.3 separately states the ordinary one-dimensional 5-flow question. A higher-dimensional flow has additional freedom and does not itself supply the scalar integer assignment required here.

cards.title: Erdős girth conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(k\ge 1\), do there exist constants \(c_{k}>0\) and \(N_{k}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge N_{k}\), some simple undirected graph G on exactly n vertices has at least \(c_{k} n^{1+1/k}\) edges and contains no cycle of length less than \(2k+2\)? Equivalently, is \(M_{2k+2}(n)=\Omega _{k}(n^{1+1/k})\) for every fixed k, where \(M_{s}(n)\) is the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no cycle shorter than s?
cards.definitions: A simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and repeated edges are not allowed. A cycle of length \(\ell\ge 3\) has \(\ell\) distinct vertices and the edges joining them cyclically. The girth is the length of the shortest cycle, and is +∞ for a forest. Thus “girth at least \(2k+2\)” forbids every cycle of lengths \(3,\ldots ,2k+1\), including non-induced cycles. \(M_{s}(n)\) is a maximum over all such graphs on the vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); connectedness, regularity and efficient construction are not required. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists c_{k},N_{k} \forall n\ge N_{k} \exists G\). Constants may depend on k, but not on n; k remains fixed as n tends to infinity. The target is the stated constant-factor asymptotic density, not merely \(n^{1+1/k- o(1)}\), nor a claim for an arbitrarily sparse subsequence of n. This at-least-girth convention reproduces the source’s definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence claim for every fixed integer k, or refute it for at least one fixed k. Refutation means that no positive \(c_{k}\) and threshold \(N_{k}\) work at that k; a construction for only selected k or a smaller exponent does not settle the universal conjecture.
cards.why: A central extremal graph question with direct consequences for compact routing and graph sparsification: it asks whether the standard density obstruction from short cycles is asymptotically tight at every fixed scale.

cards.context:
Known extremal upper bounds give \(M_{2k+2}(n)=O_{k}(n^{1+1/k})\). The conjecture asks whether forbidding all these short cycles still permits that many edges up to a constant factor.

Using threshold \(2k+1\) instead of \(2k+2\) gives an equivalent asymptotic conjecture: a graph has a bipartite subgraph with at least half its edges, and that subgraph has no odd cycles. This equivalence changes neither the exponent nor the fixed-k target.

The cases \(k=1,2,3,5\) are known. The July 2026 spanner paper still lists exactly those cases; the next missing parameter \(k=4\) asks for \(\Omega (n^{5/4})\) edges with girth at least 10.

The source uses these graphs to establish conditional lower bounds on the memory needed by routing schemes with small stretch. More generally, the conjecture controls sharpness of size-versus-stretch bounds for graph spanners.

The 2026 preprint removes this assumption for a particular model of spanners tolerating edge failures of bounded degree. It explicitly distinguishes that result from constructing graphs of the girth and density required here.

This additional occurrence comes from the same compact-routing paper. The retained formal statement fixes its own girth threshold and graph-size quantifiers; a differently quantified girth conjecture is not automatically identified with it.

cards.title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
cards.formal:
Is the following proposition true? For every finite nonempty tree \(T\) and every integer \(r\ge1\), there exists an integer \(B\ge0\) such that every finite simple undirected graph \(G\) satisfies
\[\bigl(\omega(G)\le r\ \land\ G\text{ has no induced copy of }T\bigr)
\ \Longrightarrow\ \chi(G)\le B.\]
The quantifier order is \(\forall T\,\forall r\,\exists B\,\forall G\). The bound may depend on the entire tree \(T\) and on \(r\), but must be independent of the number of vertices and every other parameter of \(G\). No rate of growth or computational requirement on \(B\) is prescribed.
cards.definitions:
Graphs and trees. A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops or multiple edges. A path has distinct vertices, with adjacent consecutive vertices; a cycle has at least three distinct vertices with consecutive and last-to-first adjacency. A tree is a nonempty connected graph containing no cycle. Connected means that each pair of vertices is joined by a path. The one-vertex tree is allowed. Host graphs need not be connected and may have no vertices. Equivalently, one may quantify over graphs with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) for every integer \(n\ge0\), with \([0]=\varnothing\); labels have no mathematical significance.

Induced exclusion. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the graph \(G[S]\) has vertex set \(S\) and exactly the edges of \(G\) with both ends in \(S\). An induced copy of \(T\) is an injective map \(\varphi:V(T)\to V(G)\) such that for all distinct \(u,v\in V(T)\),
\[\{u,v\}\in E(T)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in E(G).\]
A graph is \(T\)-free when no such map exists. The requirement preserves nonedges as well as edges. It is different from excluding an ordinary subgraph, a minor or a subdivision of \(T\). Edges from the image to vertices outside it are unrestricted.

Clique and chromatic numbers. A clique is a vertex subset whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. Its maximum possible size is \(\omega(G)\). A proper \(k\)-colouring is a map \(c:V(G)\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). The least nonnegative integer \(k\) admitting such a map is \(\chi(G)\). Thus both parameters are zero for the empty graph, and every nonempty edgeless graph has both equal to one. The bound \(\omega(G)\le r\) is equivalent to excluding a clique on \(r+1\) vertices. Colour classes are independent sets, meaning subsets with no adjacent pair. Colouring here is ordinary vertex colouring, without lists, weights, fractional assignments or edge orientations.

Scope of the bound. Both the tree and the clique bound are fixed before the host graph varies. There is no maximum-degree, girth, geometric-representation, size or other promise on the host. The integer \(B=B(T,r)\) may grow arbitrarily quickly with its two allowed parameters. The target asks for existence of a finite bound, not its minimum value, a polynomial in \(r\), a computable function, or a procedure finding a colouring. There is consequently no input encoding, algorithmic running time or random-error parameter in the proposition.

Equivalent terminology. A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs. The \(T\)-free graphs form such a class. Saying it is \(\chi\)-bounded means that there is a function \(f_T:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(\chi(G)\le f_T(\omega(G))\) for every graph in the class. The conjecture asserts this for every nonempty tree; there is no requirement that the same function work for all trees. A negative answer means there are one fixed tree \(T\) and one fixed integer \(r\ge1\) for which chromatic numbers of the permitted hosts have no finite upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its negation. A positive answer must establish a finite \(B(T,r)\) for every permitted pair and prove the bound for every finite host graph. A nonconstructive existence proof is sufficient; neither a sharp formula nor an efficient colouring algorithm is required.

A negative answer must specify a single finite tree \(T\) and a single integer \(r\ge1\) and prove
\[\forall k\ge1\ \exists G:\quad G\text{ is finite and }T\text{-free},\qquad
\omega(G)\le r,\qquad\chi(G)\ge k.\]
Equivalently, supply such a family \((G_k)_{k\ge1}\) with verified unbounded chromatic number. Changing the excluded tree or clique bound as \(k\) grows does not refute the proposition. One finite example can invalidate a proposed numerical bound but cannot rule out a larger bound.

Bounds depending on host size, special tree families, additional host promises, path-induced copies, or a different colouring parameter do not resolve the full statement. Nor does disproving only a polynomial or computable strengthening refute the unrestricted finite-bound target.
cards.why: Would characterize induced forests as the single forbidden patterns capable of bounding ordinary chromatic number in terms of clique number, clarifying a central structural obstruction to graph colouring and large independent sets.

cards.context:
A large clique forces many colours, but it is not the only obstruction: triangle-free graphs can also require arbitrarily many colours. The conjecture says that each fixed induced tree must eventually appear in every sufficiently high-chromatic graph with a fixed clique bound. Its force lies in independence from graph size; adding vertices cannot keep increasing the required palette while avoiding the same tree.

Ordinary and induced copies encode different restrictions. A triangle contains a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but does not induce that path because its endpoints are adjacent. More generally, a complete graph contains every tree on at most its number of vertices as an ordinary subgraph, but no induced tree on three or more vertices. The clique restriction alone does not solve the issue: the conjecture must hold for every fixed clique bound, including triangle-free hosts.

The forest boundary has a precise reason. Graphs can have arbitrarily high chromatic number and girth, where girth is the length of a shortest cycle. If an excluded graph contains a cycle, sufficiently large girth avoids that graph while still allowing unbounded chromatic number and no triangles. The nonempty-forest version of the conjecture is equivalent to the all-trees version: every finite forest is an induced subgraph of some finite tree.

Important tree families are known. Kierstead and Penrice proved the radius-at-most-two case in 1994; radius at most two means that some vertex has distance at most two from every other vertex. Scott and Seymour’s later Theorem 1.6 controls chromatic number polynomially in the part size of an excluded complete multipartite ordinary subgraph, for a fixed number of parts and a fixed radius-two tree. Its polynomial statement in that parameter is not a proof of polynomial dependence on clique number for every tree.

The inherited Nguyen–Scott–Seymour paper proves a weaker embedding theorem for every rooted tree: sufficiently high chromatic number at fixed clique bound forces a path-induced copy. Each root-to-vertex path has no extra edge among its own vertices. Edges between separate branches remain possible, so the entire image need not be an induced tree. Its main theorem therefore does not prove the conjecture stated here.

Their near-linear-stable-set theorem applies to every fixed forest and clique bound: an \(n\)-vertex permitted graph has an independent set of size \(n^{1-o(1)}\) and chromatic number \(n^{o(1)}\). In particular, for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), the chromatic bound is eventually at most \(n^\varepsilon\). This is much smaller than any fixed positive power, but can still diverge; \(\log n\) illustrates that distinction.

The same paper bounds fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, obtained by identifying the roots of paths with extra leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring permits weighted independent sets covering every vertex to total weight at least one; ordinary colouring requires an actual partition. General multibrooms remain an open case of the latter statement in that source.

Davies and Yuditsky’s April 2026 journal theorem treats intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in \(\mathbb R^d\), for each fixed dimension \(d\). Vertices represent boxes and adjacency means nonempty intersection. Excluding a fixed induced forest then gives a polynomial bound in clique number, but the polynomial may depend on both the forest and \(d\). This extra dimension parameter prevents the theorem from giving the unrestricted bound in the card.

The conjecture concerns existence of colourings and has consequences for independent-set size, because one colour class must contain at least the number of vertices divided by the number of colours. It does not automatically provide an efficient algorithm for finding either object. Separating the structural assertion from its possible computational refinements keeps the benchmark focused on the established conjecture.

A September 2026 paper studies a tournament analogue using directed clique and chromatic parameters. These differ from the ordinary undirected parameters in this card.

A June 2026 paper instead studies domatic number, which partitions vertices into dominating sets. The shared conjecture name does not make that parameter ordinary chromatic number.

sentences: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture asks whether excluding any fixed induced tree makes chromatic number bounded at each fixed clique bound.
The host is an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph, and the bound may depend on the tree and clique bound but not on host size.
An accepted answer requires a complete Lean proof, or one fixed tree and clique bound supporting graphs of unbounded chromatic number.
Path-induced copies, fractional colouring and subpolynomial size-dependent bounds are distinct from the selected ordinary-colouring statement.
The conjecture would identify forests as the precise single forbidden-pattern boundary for this form of hereditary graph colouring.

cards.title: Vertex reconstruction conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 3\) and every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G,H on n vertices, does equality \(D(G)=D(H)\) of their vertex decks imply that G and H are isomorphic?
cards.definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge of G if and only if \(\{f(u),f(v)\}\) is an edge of H. Write \([G]\) for its isomorphism class. For \(v\in V(G), G- v\) is the induced graph on \(V(G)\setminus \{v\}\): remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define \(D(G)\) to be the multiset \(\{[G- v]:v\in V(G)\}\), with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus \(D(G)=D(H)\) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on \(n- 1\) vertices, the number of vertices v with \([G- v]=K\) equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every \(n\ge 3\), or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge 3\) and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether all overlapping one-vertex views determine an entire graph. It tests how much structural information survives deletion and loss of labels, and connects graph structure to reconstruction and isomorphism problems.
