cards.context:
Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If \(n\ge 3\), every original edge appears in exactly \(n- 2\) members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by \(n- 2\). Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.

cards.title: List edge-coloring conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite loopless multigraph G and every assignment L of finite sets of colors to its edges with \(|L(e)|\ge \chi ' (G)\) for every edge e, does there exist a proper edge coloring c with \(c(e)\in L(e)\) for every e? Equivalently, is \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)=\chi ' (G)\) for every such G?
cards.definitions: A finite loopless multigraph consists of finite sets V and E and a map \(\partial\) assigning to each edge \(e\in E a\) two-element subset \(\partial e\subseteq V\). Distinct edges may have the same endpoints and are still distinct objects. Two distinct edges are adjacent if their endpoint sets intersect. A proper edge coloring assigns different colors to any two adjacent edges. For an integer \(k\ge 0\) let \([k]=\{1,\ldots ,k\}\), with [0] empty; \(\chi ' (G)\), the chromatic index, is the least k admitting a proper map \(E\to [k]\). A list assignment is a function \(e\mapsto L(e)\) where each \(L(e)\) is a finite subset of the positive integers, used only as distinct color names. Lists may differ, overlap arbitrarily and have an arbitrarily large finite union. The list chromatic index \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is the least \(k\ge 0\) such that every assignment with \(|L(e)|\ge k\) admits a proper edge coloring from those lists. Both indices are zero when E is empty and are at most |E| otherwise; hence these minima exist. Requiring lists of exactly k colors is equivalent, since larger lists can be restricted to k colors. Any finite collection of abstract colors can be renamed by distinct positive integers without changing feasibility. Isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and arbitrary parallel-edge multiplicities are allowed. The maximum degree \(\Delta\) counts edges incident with a vertex, including parallel copies separately, and is zero for an empty vertex set. The target concerns existence, with no required algorithm, running time or bound on color-name bit lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated universal list-colorability assertion, or refute it. A finite counterexample can specify a multigraph with ordinary chromatic index k and lists of k colors on every edge, together with a proof that no proper coloring from those lists exists. Equality only up to a vanishing relative error, a result for a restricted graph class, or successful coloring of selected list assignments does not resolve the universal claim.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether local restrictions on available edge colors ever increase the number of choices each edge must receive beyond the optimum with a shared palette. It tests whether ordinary scheduling feasibility is robust to arbitrary per-job availability, across all finite loopless multigraphs.

cards.context:
Think of an edge as a job requiring its two endpoint resources at the same time, and a color as a time slot. Jobs sharing a resource must use different slots. Ordinary edge coloring offers every job the same collection of slots. List edge coloring lets each job have its own availability restrictions and asks for a compatible schedule.

For two edges sharing one endpoint, ordinary edge coloring needs two colors. Lists {red,blue} and {blue,green} still each have size two, although their union has size three; choosing red for the first edge and blue for the second is valid. The conjecture compares the number of choices available to each edge, not the total number of distinct color names used across all lists.

Identical lists are permitted, so \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\) is always at least \(\chi ' (G)\). The question is whether arbitrary overlaps among different lists can ever create an additional obstruction. An ordinary coloring alone does not answer this, since a color assigned to an edge may be absent from that edge’s list.

The reference quantity is the chromatic index, rather than just maximum degree. A triangle has maximum degree two but needs three edge colors. If each of its three edges is doubled, the multigraph has maximum degree four, yet all six edges are pairwise adjacent and need six colors. Allowing parallel edges therefore matters to the target.

Galvin proves the conjecture for every bipartite multigraph, whose vertices split into two parts with all edges crossing between them. In that class both indices equal maximum degree. The theorem permits arbitrary lists and parallel edges; restricting lists to one shared palette would miss its main content.

Kahn’s theorem settles the general multigraph question asymptotically. In particular, for every \(\varepsilon >0\), all multigraphs of sufficiently large maximum degree satisfy \(\chi ' _{\ell}(G)\le (1+\varepsilon )\chi ' (G)\). This leaves the exact question intact: a relative gap tending to zero can still allow an extra color.

The August 2026 preprint of Jafari claims exact equality for the complete graphs \(K_{p- 1}\) and \(K_{2p}\) whenever p is an odd prime; \(K_{r}\) denotes the simple graph with every pair of its r vertices adjacent. The respective claimed values are \(p- 2\) and \(2p- 1\). These are specific families, and the paper itself leaves the general even-order complete-graph case open. Its proofs have not been independently verified in this review.

cards.title: Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(n\ge2\), every integer \(r\) with \(1\le r\le n-1\), and every simple loopless digraph \(D=(V,A)\) on \(n\) vertices, does
\[\bigl(\forall v\in V:\ d_D^+(v)\ge r\bigr)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bigl(\exists\text{ a directed cycle of length }\ell\le\lceil n/r\rceil\bigr)\]
hold? Opposite arcs are allowed, and a pair of opposite arcs counts as a directed cycle of length two. The bound is exact, for every permitted pair \((n,r)\), with no additive error.
cards.definitions:
A simple loopless digraph consists of a finite set \(V\), with \(|V|=n\), and an arc set
\[A\subseteq\{(u,v)\in V\times V:u\ne v\}.\]
There is at most one copy of each ordered pair; both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) may occur. Relabeling the vertices by \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) changes no requirement. The out-neighborhood and outdegree of a vertex are
\[N_D^+(v)=\{w\in V:(v,w)\in A\},\qquad d_D^+(v)=|N_D^+(v)|.\]
The minimum outdegree is \(\delta^+(D)=\min_{v\in V}d_D^+(v)\). Every vertex must meet the lower bound; an average-degree bound or a condition on only some vertices is not the hypothesis.

A directed cycle of length \(\ell\) is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1}\), where \(2\le\ell\le n\), such that \((v_i,v_{i+1})\in A\) for \(0\le i<\ell-1\) and \((v_{\ell-1},v_0)\in A\). It need not be induced: additional arcs among these vertices are allowed. Length counts arcs, equivalently the number of distinct vertices on the cycle. The closing return to \(v_0\) is not counted as an additional vertex. A repeated-vertex closed walk is not the cycle witness specified here.

The directed girth \(g(D)\) is the minimum length of a directed cycle, with value \(+\infty\) if there is none. Under the positive minimum-outdegree hypothesis it is finite. The ceiling is the least integer at least the real quotient \(n/r\); equivalently, \(\lceil n/r\rceil=\lfloor(n+r-1)/r\rfloor\) for the positive integers used here. Thus the target can also be written
\[g(D)\le\lceil n/r\rceil,\quad\text{or equivalently}\quad n\ge r(g(D)-1)+1.\]
It does not assert \(g(D)\le n/r\) without rounding.

No lower bound on indegree is imposed. In particular, a graph need not be regular, strongly connected, vertex-transitive, planar or randomly generated. An oriented graph is the restricted case with no opposite pair of arcs. The target includes oriented graphs and all the other simple loopless digraphs above. This is a finite extremal existence statement, with no construction, search-algorithm, encoding or computational resource requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover all integers \(n,r\) in the stated ranges and all eligible digraphs, producing a cycle with the exact ceiling bound. A negative answer may specify finite \(n,r\) and a finite arc set, but must prove in Lean both the minimum-outdegree condition and the absence of every directed cycle of lengths \(2,\ldots,\lceil n/r\rceil\). A proof of the full logical negation without an explicitly listed counterexample also qualifies. An asymptotic estimate, an additive-constant relaxation, a special degree value, or an extra regularity, indegree or forbidden-subgraph hypothesis settles only a restricted statement.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether a lower bound on every vertex’s number of outgoing neighbors forces a cycle at the sharp possible length. It would determine the exact universal relation between a local directed-degree condition and global cyclic structure. Even the dense regime that should force a directed triangle remains a major unresolved case, despite broad approximate bounds and results for symmetric graph classes.

cards.context:
Positive minimum outdegree already guarantees that some directed cycle exists. The content of the conjecture is its exact length guarantee as the degree grows. Requiring the bound at every vertex matters: many arcs in total can coexist with acyclicity if vertices near the end of a directed ordering have small outdegree. There is no corresponding escape from the positive minimum-degree assumption.

The ceiling is essential, and the conjectured bound is sharp for every allowed \((n,r)\). The standard extremal digraph has vertices modulo \(n\), with arcs from \(i\) to \(i+1,\ldots,i+r\), using residues modulo \(n\). Its outdegree is \(r\) and its directed girth is exactly \(\lceil n/r\rceil\). These are existing extremal examples, rather than evidence that all digraphs obey the bound.

Two uses of the parameter must be distinguished. The fixed-degree case \(r=3\) is known, but the triangle-forcing regime \(r\ge n/3\) is not thereby settled. In the latter regime the degree grows with the number of vertices. For an oriented graph the conjecture predicts a directed triangle at minimum outdegree at least \(n/3\); in the more general model of this card a directed two-cycle is also an acceptable outcome.

Hladký, Král’ and Norin establish a directed triangle at minimum outdegree at least \(0.3465n\) in an oriented graph. Their paper explicitly forbids opposite arcs in its definition of “digraph.” This is a published advance toward the \(n/3\) threshold, rather than the threshold itself. The April 2026 paper still cites it as the best known partial result for this regime.

The conjecture is known for fixed minimum-degree thresholds \(r=1,2,3,4,5\), and for vertex-transitive digraphs, where an arc-preserving permutation can send any chosen vertex to any other. These successes cover substantial families but do not impose the required conclusion on an arbitrary nonsymmetric digraph. A regular graph, whose indegrees and outdegrees are all the same, need not be vertex-transitive.

Approximate girth estimates also leave a genuine exact question. Hompe and Huynh recall Shen’s universal bound \(\lceil n/r\rceil+73\). Their own 2025 article proves an additive-constant result for the stronger rainbow-cycle setting, with an error depending on the fixed color-class size. Neither additive relaxation supplies the exact ceiling required here.

A rainbow cycle has no repeated edge color. Aharoni’s conjecture asks for a short rainbow cycle in an edge-colored graph with as many color classes as vertices and sufficiently many edges in each class; the general rainbow conjecture would imply the directed conjecture. The implication is not an equivalence assertion, and a theorem for a restricted family of color classes does not establish the universal directed result.

Guo’s 2026 journal article obtains logarithmic rainbow girth when a positive fraction of the color classes have specified non-star structure, under its size conditions. An edge set is a star when all its edges meet at one vertex. Such extra structure excludes the all-star configurations relevant to the extremal directed examples. The paper explicitly retains both the directed and general rainbow conjectures as open.

Steiner’s April 2026 preprint proves a different conjecture about regular digraphs: the number of directed cycles through a common vertex, disjoint away from that vertex, must grow at least linearly with the common degree. It also proves a directed tree-width result. The introduction separately states that the exact degree–girth conjecture remains open even for regular digraphs. Counting many overlapping cycles does not itself give the sharp shortest-cycle length in this card.

The 28 July 2026 revision of the DeVos and coauthors paper retains the exact rainbow theorem for color classes of size at least two. The arXiv revision note concerns a correction in a later matroid theorem. It should not be mistaken for a newly proved all-degree Caccetta–Häggkvist theorem merely because the paper reappeared among recent revisions.

A 2008 preprint claims a complete proof, but its stated labeling lemma does not establish the required universal path bound: a small digraph passing its degree and labeling conditions violates that bound. The review records the explicit check. The later primary papers inspected here continue to state the general conjecture as open; the historical proof claim is not treated as a verified resolution.

cards.title: Seese’s conjecture
cards.formal:
For every isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, does
\[
\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)\ \text{decidable}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists k\ge1\ \forall G\in\mathcal C,\quad\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k
\]
hold?

The language \(\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)\) contains exactly the encoded vertex-set monadic second-order sentences satisfied by at least one graph in \(\mathcal C\). The bound \(k\) may depend on the whole class but must hold for every graph in it.
cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. There are no loops, multiple edges, labels or additional relations in the logical vocabulary. The empty graph is allowed. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) contains only such graphs and is closed under isomorphism: renaming vertices does not change membership. It may be empty, finite or infinite, and no hereditary, degree, minor or forbidden-subgraph restriction is imposed. Equivalently, classes can be viewed as arbitrary collections of finite graph isomorphism types.

The logic \(\mathrm{MSO}_1\) has individual variables \(x,y,\ldots\) and vertex-set variables \(X,Y,\ldots\). Its atomic formulas are \(x=y\), \(E(x,y)\) and \(x\in X\). Formulas are finite expressions built from these atoms using Boolean connectives and existential or universal quantification over either sort. Set equality, when used, is shorthand for equality of membership at every vertex. A sentence has no free variables. On a finite graph, individual quantifiers range over \(V\) and set quantifiers over all subsets of \(V\), with the ordinary truth conditions. There is no vertex order, arithmetic relation, edge-set quantifier, cardinality predicate or modular counting extension.

Fix an effective, uniquely parsed finite-string encoding of this syntax, with binary variable indices and symbols for the finitely many logical operations. Define
\[
\operatorname{Sat}_{\mathrm{MSO}_1}(\mathcal C)
=\{\operatorname{enc}(\varphi):
\varphi\text{ is an }\mathrm{MSO}_1\text{ sentence and }
\exists G\in\mathcal C\ (G\models\varphi)\}.
\]
Decidable means that some deterministic Turing machine halts on every string, rejects malformed encodings and answers membership in this language correctly. That machine may depend on \(\mathcal C\); its only input is the sentence encoding. The class is not supplied as another input or as an oracle, and no running-time bound is imposed. No effective presentation of the class is assumed separately from this decidability premise. By negation of sentences, the premise is equivalent to decidability of the theory consisting of sentences true in every graph of \(\mathcal C\). It is not the model-checking problem in which a particular finite graph is also supplied.

For a positive integer \(k\), a \(k\)-expression is a finite term constructing a graph with temporary vertex labels in \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Its permitted operations are creation of a single vertex with any one label; disjoint union of two previously constructed labelled graphs; relabelling every vertex with label \(i\) to label \(j\); and, for distinct labels \(i,j\), adding every missing edge between a vertex labelled \(i\) and a vertex labelled \(j\). Vertices and existing edges are never deleted. Repeated edge additions have no further effect. The labels are forgotten in the final graph and are not extra relations available to the logic.

For a nonempty graph \(G\), the clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the minimum positive \(k\) for which a \(k\)-expression yields a graph isomorphic to \(G\). Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing)=0\). Every finite graph has finite clique-width, but bounded clique-width of a class requires a single \(k\) independent of its members and their orders. For the empty class the conclusion is vacuous.

The quantifier order is: for every class, if some class-specific sentence decider exists, then some class-specific finite width bound exists. The proposition does not demand one decider for all classes, a method to extract \(k\) from machine code, or an algorithm producing clique-width expressions. It is an exact universal implication, not a request for a numerical estimate of a width.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every stated graph class. Alternatively, specify one isomorphism-closed class \(\mathcal C\), a total sentence-deciding machine, and complete Lean-checked proofs of its correctness and of
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \exists G\in\mathcal C,\qquad\operatorname{cw}(G)>k.
\]
A single finite graph cannot refute a class-wide boundedness claim. Decidability for a restricted set of sentences, model checking on a given graph, a theorem with parity or edge-set quantification in the premise, or a result for only specially restricted graph classes does not establish the full target.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether decidability of an expressive graph language forces a uniform structural restriction. It connects computability of theories to finite graph construction with a bounded number of labels, without assuming an efficient decision procedure or a restricted graph class.

cards.context:
A finite graph can be checked against any one MSO sentence by exhaustive evaluation. The difficult premise here concerns a whole class: the algorithm must decide whether any member, of any size, satisfies the input sentence.

Clique-width measures how many temporary vertex labels suffice to build a graph with repeated disjoint unions, complete joins between labels and relabellings. The conjectured bound concerns every member of a class together; individual finiteness of clique-width is automatic.

Courcelle and Oum prove the implication when the language additionally tests whether a vertex set has even cardinality. Deciding that larger language is a stronger premise than deciding ordinary MSO, so the theorem does not prove the card’s assertion.

The inherited ICALP paper concerns shrub-depth and expressiveness and ends with a stronger conjecture about MSO dependence. Its discussion explicitly presents Seese’s conjecture as an unresolved consequence, rather than a theorem established in that paper.

Dawar and Sankaran establish results for specified hereditary families and analyze a stronger grid-interpretation conjecture. Their title does not mean that all hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width have already been covered.

The July 2026 theorem gives bounded clique-width for hereditary classes that are 2-WQO: after arbitrary two-colour vertex labellings, every infinite sequence contains an earlier graph embedded as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. That hypothesis is different from a decision procedure for the plain MSO theory.

cards.title: Excluded-grid treewidth exponent
cards.formal: Determine the excluded-grid exponent \(x_{\mathrm{grid}}\) to absolute error at most \(1/100\). For each integer \(r\ge2\), let \[f(r)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:\forall G,\ \operatorname{tw}(G)\ge t\Longrightarrow Q_r\text{ is a minor of }G\},\] where \(G\) ranges over finite simple undirected graphs and \(Q_r\) is the \(r\)-by-\(r\) square grid. Define \[x_{\mathrm{grid}}=\inf\{a\ge0:f(r)=O(r^a)\}.\] The precise asymptotic quantifiers, treewidth and ordinary graph-minor model are given below. The parameter \(r\) is grid side length, not its \(r^2\) vertices. Logarithmic factors are outside the requested precision.
cards.definitions:
Graphs and grids. A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set and an edge set consisting of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; there are no loops or parallel edges. The vertex set of \(Q_r\) is \(\{1,\ldots,r\}^2\), and two vertices \((i,j)\) and \((i',j')\) are adjacent exactly when
\[|i-i'|+|j-j'|=1.\]
Thus \(r\) counts the side length, while the grid has \(r^2\) vertices. Host graphs may be disconnected and have arbitrary order, degree and genus.

Minor containment. A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if there are nonempty vertex subsets \((B_v)_{v\in V(H)}\) of \(V(G)\) such that they are pairwise disjoint, each induced graph \(G[B_v]\) is connected, and for every edge \(uv\in E(H)\) an edge of \(G\) joins \(B_u\) to \(B_v\). These subsets are called branch sets. Extra edges inside or between branch sets are allowed. Equivalently, one may delete vertices and edges and contract edges, then remove loops and merge parallel edges. This is ordinary minor containment, with no prescribed roots, induced-subgraph condition or topological-minor requirement.

Treewidth. A tree decomposition of \(G\) consists of a finite nonempty tree \(T\) and bags \(X_t\subseteq V(G)\) for its nodes such that every vertex lies in a bag, both endpoints of every edge lie together in a bag, and for each vertex the nodes whose bags contain it form a nonempty connected subtree of \(T\). A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph. The decomposition width is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|X_t|-1\). The treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum width over all such decompositions. In particular, the empty graph has treewidth \(-1\) under this convention and has no effect on thresholds \(t\ge0\).

Extremal threshold. The qualitative Grid-Minor Theorem ensures that the defining set of thresholds is nonempty. Since treewidth is integer valued,
\[f(r)=1+\max\{\operatorname{tw}(G):G\text{ is a finite simple undirected graph with no }Q_r\text{ minor}\}.\]
This maximum exists: its set of integer values is nonempty and bounded above by the qualitative theorem. It is a maximum of widths, not a bound on the number of vertices of a grid-excluding graph. Arbitrarily large trees, for example, do not contain \(Q_r\) for \(r\ge2\).

Exponent convention. Define \[x_{\mathrm{grid}}=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists C>0\ \exists r_0\ge2\ \forall r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge r_0},\ f(r)\le Cr^a\}.\] The known polynomial Grid-Minor Theorem makes this set nonempty; the cited ninth-power bound with polylogarithmic overhead gives \(x_{\mathrm{grid}}\le9\), and the quadratic-logarithmic lower bound gives \(x_{\mathrm{grid}}\ge2\). The exponent is equivalently the limit superior of \(\log f(r)/\log r\); no ordinary limit or attainment of the infimum is assumed. In particular, exponent two permits a growing logarithmic factor and does not assert \(f(r)=O(r^2)\). Constants may depend on a chosen positive slack in the exponent, but not on the grid side length or host graph. This is a structural existence exponent, not a running-time exponent for finding a grid.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply \(a\) and prove \(|a-x_{\mathrm{grid}}|\le1/100\) in Lean. The growth parameter in both bounds is the side length \(r\) of the grid minor. A [certified enclosing interval](definitions.html#numerical-answers) of width at most \(1/50\) also suffices via its midpoint.
cards.why: The Grid-Minor Theorem connects an abstract measure of graph connectivity with a concrete planar pattern. Its quantitative loss controls the strength of many structural and parameterized-algorithm results. Determining the optimal loss would identify how much treewidth is inherently needed to force a grid in unrestricted graphs, including whether the remaining logarithmic obstruction captures the whole difficulty.

cards.context:
Treewidth records the smallest possible largest bag in a tree decomposition, minus one. Many graph algorithms can process small bags efficiently even when the whole graph is large. A grid is a canonical obstruction to small treewidth. The qualitative theorem says that sufficiently large treewidth forces any fixed grid as a minor; the unresolved issue is the optimal dependence on grid size.

The grid \(Q_r\) itself has treewidth \(r\), but this does not imply a linear threshold for arbitrary host graphs. The complete graph on \(r^2-1\) vertices has treewidth \(r^2-2\), yet cannot contain a minor with \(r^2\) vertices. Thus \(f(r)\ge r^2-1\). Branch sets can contract large parts of a host, but they must remain pairwise disjoint and nonempty.

The established lower bound is stronger: \(f(r)=\Omega(r^2\log r)\). The cited work attributes it to Robertson, Seymour and Thomas using constant-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs combine treewidth proportional to their order with long shortest cycles; a large grid minor forces many disjoint cycles in the host. The extra logarithmic obstruction survives even for sparse graphs.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy first made the relationship polynomial. Their theorem is stated in the reverse direction: treewidth \(k\) guarantees grid side length at least a constant times \(k^{1/98}\) divided by a fixed power of \(\log k\). Equivalently, it gives an upper bound \(f(r)=O(r^{98}\operatorname{polylog}r)\). Confusing side length with vertex count, or the threshold with this inverse guarantee, changes the exponents.

The selected numerical exponent distinguishes polynomial scales while ignoring logarithmic factors. In particular, a proved \(r^2\operatorname{polylog}r\) upper bound together with the known lower bound would give exponent exactly two and answer this card.

Chuzhoy and Tan prove \(f(r)\le Cr^9(\log r)^c\) for absolute constants \(C,c>0\). Together with the quadratic-logarithmic lower bound, this places the requested exponent in \([2,9]\). These are bounds recorded in the cited literature; the present formulation review does not certify a fresh catalogue-wide status audit.

Robertson, Seymour and Thomas predicted growth \(\Theta(r^2\log r)\), whereas Demaine and coauthors predicted cubic growth. These predictions would yield numerical exponents two and three respectively. Determining the exponent to absolute error \(1/100\) is the selected target; settling lower-order factors is not required.

The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited gives a finer structural description: graphs excluding a fixed planar graph embed as subgraphs of clique blow-ups of graphs of controlled treewidth. A clique blow-up replaces each vertex by a fixed-size complete graph and every original edge by all edges between the corresponding cliques. The factor controlling the clique size may depend on the excluded graph, so the theorem does not determine this card’s optimal numerical dependence on grid side length.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs proves that excluding both a fixed graph \(H\) and \(Q_r\) gives treewidth \(O(g_H r+t^{2304})\), where \(t=|V(H)|\) and \(g_H\) is the Euler genus of \(H\). Euler genus is the minimum value \(2-\chi\) of a closed connected surface admitting an embedding, with \(\chi\) its Euler characteristic. Since \(g_H=O(t^2)\), the paper also gives \(O(t^2r+t^{2304})\). For fixed \(H\), the dependence on \(r\) is linear.

The additional exclusion in that theorem matters. General host graphs do not avoid a common fixed \(H\). Choosing \(H=Q_r\) is allowed for a grid-excluding graph, but then \(H\) varies with \(r\) and \(t=r^2\); it cannot yield a linear universal threshold. This distinction prevents a sharp special-class result from being mistaken for a solution of the all-graphs problem.

The ICALP 2026 paper studies a designated set of vertices and grid models whose every branch set meets that set. It obtains polynomial bounds for the corresponding structural decomposition. Those bounds concern an annotated generalization and are not a matching estimate of the ordinary threshold defined here. Additional structure in a decomposition and an optimal numerical treewidth bound are different conclusions.

The May 2026 disjoint-paths preprint sharpens bounds for vital linkages and for vertices whose deletion preserves bounded-size rooted-minor information. Its parameters include the number of terminals and the size of a grid rooted on an annotated set. Despite the phrase “Optimal Bounds” in the title, its theorems do not claim a constant-factor characterization of the unrestricted excluded-grid threshold.

Sharper general grid bounds affect the quantitative consequences of routing, packing-versus-covering results and parameterized algorithms. Their role is to turn sufficiently large treewidth into a usable grid, or to bound treewidth when such a grid is absent. Matching lower bounds would also identify an unavoidable limitation of that structural implication.

cards.title: Lovász conjecture
cards.formal:
Does every finite nonempty connected vertex-transitive simple undirected graph have a Hamiltonian path? With the definitions below, prove or refute
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\quad
\bigl(\operatorname{Connected}([n],E)\land
\operatorname{VertexTransitive}([n],E)\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\exists p\in S_n\ \forall i\in[n-1]\quad
\{p(i),p(i+1)\}\in E.
\]
There is no restriction on the number of vertices, degree, automorphism group or representation as a Cayley graph. The required spanning object is a path; its endpoints need not be adjacent. This is an existence assertion without a computational time bound or a requirement to find the path efficiently.
cards.definitions:
Let \(\mathbb N_{\ge1}=\{1,2,\ldots\}\), and write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A finite nonempty simple undirected graph is a pair \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\) and \(E\) is a set of two-element subsets of \([n]\). Vertices \(u,v\) are adjacent when \(\{u,v\}\in E\). Thus there are no loops, parallel edges, orientations or weights. Using labeled vertices loses no generality because every finite graph is isomorphic to one on \([n]\). A finite representation consists of \(n\) and the \(\binom n2\) adjacency bits in lexicographic order of unordered pairs; no algorithmic constraint depends on this representation.

The graph is connected if for every \(u,v\in[n]\) there are an integer \(m\ge0\) and vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_m\in[n]\) such that \(v_0=u\), \(v_m=v\), and \(\{v_{j-1},v_j\}\in E\) for every \(1\le j\le m\). A sequence of length zero is permitted when \(u=v\).

Write \(S_n\) for the set of all bijections \([n]\to[n]\). An automorphism of \(G\) is a bijection \(\sigma\in S_n\) with
\[
\forall x,y\in[n]\quad
\bigl(\{x,y\}\in E\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \{\sigma(x),\sigma(y)\}\in E\bigr).
\]
The graph is vertex-transitive if for every ordered pair \(u,v\in[n]\) there exists an automorphism \(\sigma\) with \(\sigma(u)=v\). The automorphism may depend on the pair. Equal vertex degrees alone are not the condition.

A Hamiltonian path is a permutation \(p\in S_n\) such that consecutive vertices in \(p(1),\ldots,p(n)\) are adjacent. Bijection ensures that every vertex occurs exactly once. For \(n=1\), the adjacency requirement ranges over the empty set \([0]\), so the single vertex is a Hamiltonian path. No closing edge from \(p(n)\) to \(p(1)\) is required. A cycle discussed in the context is a cyclic sequence of at least three distinct vertices with edges between consecutive vertices and from the last back to the first; its length is its number of vertices. Such a cycle is Hamiltonian only if it contains every vertex.

For the restricted results mentioned below, a Cayley graph has the elements of a finite group as its vertices and joins \(g\) to \(gs\) for elements \(s\) of a fixed inverse-closed set of nonidentity group elements. A connected Cayley graph is an example of a connected vertex-transitive graph, but the conjecture includes all graphs satisfying the stated symmetry condition. A directed graph instead has ordered edges; results about paths or cycles required to follow those directions concern a different class of objects.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal assertion, or of its full logical negation, using the finite graph and permutation definitions above.

A positive answer must show that for every \(n\ge1\) and every connected vertex-transitive graph \(([n],E)\), some permutation has all its consecutive pairs in \(E\). It may establish existence without providing a uniformly efficient construction.

A negative answer must establish
\[
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists E\subseteq\binom{[n]}2\quad
\operatorname{Connected}([n],E)\ \land\
\operatorname{VertexTransitive}([n],E)\ \land\
\forall p\in S_n\ \exists i\in[n-1]\quad
\{p(i),p(i+1)\}\notin E.
\]
This requires one finite graph satisfying both hypotheses and a proof that every ordering of its vertices fails to be a Hamiltonian path. Existence of the counterexample can itself be proved; an efficient search procedure is not an additional requirement. An arbitrarily long nonspanning path, a spanning result for one subclass, or a counterexample to a directed or cyclic variant does not establish either required conclusion. The target is exact, so numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not relax it.
cards.why: A resolution would settle a central connection between graph symmetry and spanning structure. A proof would show that connectedness and vertex symmetry suffice for a spanning path across every finite simple undirected graph, beyond particular group constructions. A counterexample would identify an obstruction that survives complete vertex symmetry. The existence question remains meaningful without asking for a fast algorithm.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. Use the shared definition of [P](definitions.html#p-np). Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm{P}\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.
cards.why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

cards.context:
The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform deterministic comparison-RAM algorithm that, for every finite connected simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with arbitrary real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(n+m)\) worst-case total time, where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\)? The graph is explicitly listed, and weights are opaque keys that may only be copied and compared. The machine, output and quantifier conventions are fixed below; the bound counts all computation, not only weight comparisons.
cards.definitions:
Instance and objective. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with \(G=(V,E)\) connected. Write \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). Each \(e\in E\) has a weight \(w(e)\in\mathbb R\), with no integrality, magnitude, distinctness or sign promise. A spanning tree is a set \(T\subseteq E\) for which \((V,T)\) is connected and has no cycle; necessarily \(|T|=n-1\). Its weight is the finite real sum \(W(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\). A minimum spanning tree satisfies
\[\forall T'\subseteq E\text{ that is a spanning tree}:\quad W(T)\le W(T').\]
Connectedness ensures a spanning tree exists, and the finite collection of trees has a minimum. For \(n=1\), the graph has no edges and the required output is the empty tree. Equal or negative edge weights are allowed, and any minimizing tree is accepted. The algorithm need not output the numerical sum.

Explicit input and output. Input records give \(n,m\), the list of vertex labels, and an ordered list of \(m\) edge records. Edge \(j\), for \(1\le j\le m\), has endpoints \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and a handle for its opaque weight key. Pairs are not repeated, but their list order is arbitrary. The index \(j\) is the edge's distinct identifier. The input occupies \(\Theta(n+m)\) constant-size records. It is a full graph description rather than a circuit or oracle generating a larger graph. A weight key is supplied as an abstract atom, not a finite precision approximation or a binary expansion of its real value. The output lists exactly \(n-1\) distinct valid edge identifiers forming a minimum tree, in any order. No behavior is required on malformed or disconnected inputs.

Weight access. A weight handle can be stored, copied or retrieved in constant time. An instruction given two such handles returns their exact three-way real comparison: less, equal or greater. That instruction costs one operation independently of the real numbers. These are the only observations of weight values available to the algorithm. Weight handles identify their edge records; their numerical identifiers encode no information about the values. The program cannot inspect a weight's bits, add or subtract weights, multiply them, convert them to integers, hash their numerical representations, or compare arithmetic expressions involving weights. Copying a handle does not manufacture a new numerical key. The sum \(W(T)\) defines mathematical correctness, not an allowed machine instruction.

Nonweight machine operations. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\), and for input parameter \(N\) uses unsigned words of
\[\ell=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits for vertex labels, edge identifiers, counters and memory addresses. A word represents an integer from zero to \(2^\ell-1\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially zero; weight-key storage can equivalently keep the corresponding input handles. The input is read-only, and output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction touches a constant number of words or handles. Reading, writing, copying, comparing nonweight words and conditional branching cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^\ell\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, and bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT are also unit-cost. Logical shifts by fewer than \(\ell\) positions discard bits outside the word and fill with zeros; a shift by at least \(\ell\) returns zero. Larger integer calculations require multiple words and their operations are charged. The program may use \(\ell\) as the machine word length. Word arithmetic is not arithmetic on the represented real weights.

Uniformity and time. There is no random input, random instruction, input-size advice, free preprocessing table or external computational oracle. The same finite program and word constant are used on every instance and edge-list order. All initialization it performs, comparisons, ordinary computation, generated tables and writing every output identifier count. Let \(T_A(G,w)\) be the number of these operations, with the edge-list representation understood as part of the input. The algorithm must halt with a correct tree on every valid instance. The time requirement is
\[\exists C>0\ \exists N_0\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall(G,w)\text{ with }n+m\ge N_0:\quad T_A(G,w)\le C(n+m).\]
The constants are independent of the graph, weights, density and representation order. This is deterministic worst-case sequential time. It is not an expectation over random graphs or over random choices, and an unbounded slowly growing extra factor does not count as linear.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic program and fixed word constant and prove termination, spanning-tree feasibility, exact minimum total weight and the displayed total-time bound for every connected simple graph and all real weight assignments. The proof must cover repeated and negative weights and the single-vertex case. If it uses decision trees or lookup tables, all work needed to produce and use them must be included.

A negative answer must rule out every correct deterministic program in the specified comparison-RAM model. Equivalently, for every word constant and every program that halts with a minimum tree on every valid input, prove that for each \(C>0\) and each \(N_0\) there is a valid instance and edge-list order with \(n+m\ge N_0\) on which the time exceeds \(C(n+m)\). A lower bound for one particular algorithm, one data structure, or a stricter pointer-only model does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound must identify its unproved assumption and is not an unconditional resolution.

Expected-linear randomized algorithms, deterministic integer-weight algorithms that inspect weight bits, restricted graph classes and a linear number of comparisons with superlinear control overhead do not alone meet the target. Optimality relative to an unknown decision-tree complexity must include a linear bound on that complexity and the necessary implementation overhead to establish an affirmative answer. This card requires an exact minimum tree and an actual linear bound, with no numerical approximation tolerance.
cards.why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

cards.context:
A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is a basic optimization problem used in network design and clustering. The optimum can already be found in polynomial time; the unsettled issue is whether its exact deterministic computational cost can be only a constant multiple of the \(n\) vertex records and \(m\) edge records in the input.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for classical algorithms, but produces more information than the requested output. If the input graph is already a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of the weight order. For a triangle, omitting any largest-weight edge gives a minimum tree. The comparison lower bound for sorting all keys therefore does not automatically give a superlinear lower bound for this graph problem.

The optimum edge set can be identified using the order of the weights, even though its correctness is defined by a sum. The classical cut and cycle characterizations explain why numeric weight arithmetic is unnecessary. With ties there may be several minimum trees, all acceptable here. Distinct edge identifiers allow algorithms to impose a consistent order among equal keys, without imposing distinctness as an input promise.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle's deterministic comparison algorithm runs in \(O(m\alpha(m,n))\) time, apart from the trivial one-vertex case, where \(\alpha\) is an inverse-Ackermann function. It can be implemented on a pointer machine and assumes no numerical representation of the weights. Although its extra factor grows extremely slowly, the worst-case factor is unbounded asymptotically. The question asks for a constant overhead over input size, rather than a bound that is effectively small on practical instances.

Pettie and Ramachandran relate total deterministic computational cost to the optimal worst-case edge-comparison decision-tree complexity of the minimum spanning forest problem. Their construction is uniform: the cost of building and using small optimal decision trees is part of the analysis. For the present connected-graph problem, input reading and explicit output also remain charged. The resulting optimality theorem does not determine whether the worst-case bound is linear or slightly superlinear.

Eisenstat and coauthors distinguish two different girth restrictions. Girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with acyclic graphs assigned infinite girth. Their conditional reductions show equivalence of the unrestricted linear-time question with its restriction to any fixed lower bound on girth, and also with a suitably sparse family having at most \(3n/2\) edges. Their actual linear-time theorem assumes a girth threshold that grows with \(n\), according to an inverse-Ackermann variant. That size-dependent restriction leaves the general question unresolved.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

Pettie and Ramachandran also give randomized linear-time algorithms consuming far fewer random bits than the original sampling method. Reducing the number of random choices while preserving an expected time bound does not provide one deterministic program with a linear worst-case guarantee.

Doron and coauthors use minimum spanning tree as a motivating example in their May 2026 work on pseudorandomness for insensitive algorithms. Section 10.1 explicitly says that the existing deterministic near-linear MST algorithms are more efficient than the derandomizations expected from their results. The paper therefore supplies recent context on randomness reduction, not a new deterministic linear-time MST theorem.

It can be implemented on a pointer machine and assumes no numerical representation of the weights. Although its extra factor grows extremely slowly, the worst-case factor is unbounded asymptotically. The question asks for a constant overhead over input size, rather than a bound that is effectively small on practical instances.

Pettie and Ramachandran relate total deterministic computational cost to the optimal worst-case edge-comparison decision-tree complexity of the minimum spanning forest problem. Their construction is uniform: the cost of building and using small optimal decision trees is part of the analysis. For the present connected-graph problem, input reading and explicit output also remain charged. The resulting optimality theorem does not determine whether the worst-case bound is linear or slightly superlinear.

Eisenstat and coauthors distinguish two different girth restrictions. Girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with acyclic graphs assigned infinite girth. Their conditional reductions show equivalence of the unrestricted linear-time question with its restriction to any fixed lower bound on girth, and also with a suitably sparse family having at most \(3n/2\) edges. Their actual linear-time theorem assumes a girth threshold that grows with \(n\), according to an inverse-Ackermann variant. That size-dependent restriction leaves the general question unresolved.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

Pettie and Ramachandran also give randomized linear-time algorithms consuming far fewer random bits than the original sampling method. Reducing the number of random choices while preserving an expected time bound does not provide one deterministic program with a linear worst-case guarantee.

Doron and coauthors use minimum spanning tree as a motivating example in their May 2026 work on pseudorandomness for insensitive algorithms. Section 10.1 explicitly says that the existing deterministic near-linear MST algorithms are more efficient than the derandomizations expected from their results. The paper therefore supplies recent context on randomness reduction, not a new deterministic linear-time MST theorem.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized sequential word-RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph \(G\), terminates almost surely, always outputs a valid matching when it terminates, and outputs a maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\), with expected running time
\[(n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?\]
Here \(n=|V(G)|\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and the precise machine, input, probability and asymptotic conventions are below. In particular, the same program must meet every positive exponent slack; an algorithm chosen separately for each fixed slack is not the stated target.
cards.definitions:
Graph and optimum. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles, the empty graph and the edgeless graph are included. Put \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). A matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E\) such that no vertex belongs to two selected edges. Its cardinality is \(|M|\), and
\[\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\]
The empty matching is allowed, so this finite maximum exists on every input. The problem is unweighted. The algorithm must return the selected edges, not only the number \(\nu(G)\), a fractional solution, or a certificate that a perfect matching exists. Any maximum matching is acceptable.

Explicit representation. Use an edge list with headers \(n,m\), the vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), and then \(m\) indexed pairs \((u_j,v_j)\) with \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and no repeated pair. Edge indices are \(j=1,\ldots,m\); their order is arbitrary. Each integer occupies one machine word, so the entire input has \(2+n+2m\) words. Isolated vertices count in \(n\). The graph is a full list, not a succinct circuit or query oracle. The output consists of its cardinality \(t\) and a list of \(t\) distinct valid edge indices, in any order. Ordinary explicit adjacency lists can be converted to this form in \(O(n+m)\) word operations, preserving the target time scale. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

Machine. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\) and, on inputs of size parameter \(N\), uses words of exactly
\[w=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits. A word represents an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of word registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially all zero. The input is read-only and the output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction operates on a constant number of words. Reading or writing an addressed word, copying, comparing, branching, bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT, and arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\) cost one operation. Integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor also cost one operation. A left or right shift by fewer than \(w\) positions discards bits outside the word and fills with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger exact integers use multiple words, and their processing is charged. A random instruction supplies one fresh uniform \(w\)-bit word, independent of all previous random words. There are no exact-real primitives, oracle calls, nonuniform advice, or precomputed tables supplied at no cost. The program may use \(w\) as the machine word length. Preprocessing, input access, initialization it performs and writing every output word are included in time.

Randomness and correctness. For a fixed valid input, the probability space is the infinite sequence of independent uniform random words used by the machine. Let \(T_A(G,R)\) count its operations, with value \(+\infty\) on a nonterminating execution. For every input, termination must have probability one. On every terminating execution, including those outside the success event, the output indices must represent a matching. On each input separately,
\[\Pr_R[\text{the output matching has cardinality }\nu(G)]\ge2/3.\]
The output may be suboptimal on other executions, but it must remain feasible. No distribution over input graphs is assumed, and success is not merely an expectation bound on matching size. A single program is used for every graph and edge-list order.

Almost-linear expected time. The expectation is over the algorithm's random words, with the input fixed. The notation in the question means that this same algorithm and word constant satisfy
\[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \exists N_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G\text{ with }N\ge N_\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_R[T_A(G,R)]\le C_\varepsilon N^{1+\varepsilon}.\]
Constants and the threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and on the fixed algorithm, but not on the graph, its density, its edge order or its random choices. The slack \(\varepsilon\) is not an input selecting a different program. This is a worst-case-over-inputs bound on expected time, not a bound on every individual random execution. The claim covers sparse and dense graphs simultaneously and allows subpolynomial overhead beyond polylogarithmic factors.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a uniform finite program and a fixed word constant, prove almost-sure termination and feasibility on every terminating execution, prove per-input success probability at least \(2/3\), and establish the displayed expected-time bound for every positive exponent slack. All preprocessing, arithmetic and explicit output costs must fit that proof. A deterministic exact algorithm meeting the time bound is also a positive answer.

A negative answer must rule out all algorithms in the allowed randomized model. Equivalently, for every fixed word constant and program satisfying the termination, feasibility and success requirements, prove that there is some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every size threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid graph encoding with \(N\ge N_0\) and \(\mathbb E[T_A]>C N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The exponent slack may depend on the program. A conditional running-time lower bound must name its unproved assumptions and does not alone establish this unconditional negation.

Algorithms only for bipartite graphs, a near-linear maximal matching, a fixed-accuracy approximation, the optimum size without an output matching, and average performance on random input graphs do not meet the full target. Bounds for pointer machines, parallel rounds, catalytic space or restricted algorithmic techniques must not be substituted for the permitted word-RAM expected time. No additive numerical tolerance applies to either exact optimality or the asymptotic exponent.
cards.why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.

cards.context:
Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Classical exact algorithms use alternating paths to increase the size of a matching and blossoms to represent the odd-cycle structure of general graphs. Micali and Vazirani's 1980 algorithm has an \(O(m\sqrt n)\) RAM bound on its matching computation, or \(O(n+m\sqrt n)\) when reading all listed isolated vertices is included. Vazirani's later proof distinguishes this from an additional inverse-Ackermann factor in the pointer model. The historical bound is not evidence that such an overhead is necessary for every algorithm.

Bipartite maximum matching reduces to integral unit-capacity maximum flow with \(O(n+m)\) vertices and edges. Chen and coauthors explicitly obtain an almost-linear bipartite matching consequence from their exact flow theorem. Integrality in that setting yields an actual optimum matching. The reduction does not establish the same result on arbitrary undirected graphs, where no bipartition is available and odd-set constraints matter.

A triangle illustrates the integrality issue. Assigning value \(1/2\) to each edge respects a unit bound on the sum incident to every vertex, but has total value \(3/2\), whereas an integral matching has size at most one. For every odd vertex set \(S\), an integral matching contains at most \((|S|-1)/2\) edges entirely inside \(S\). These additional inequalities distinguish the general matching polytope from the simpler bipartite constraints.

Mucha and Sankowski construct maximum matchings by randomized algebraic computation in \(O(n^\omega)\) time for an available matrix-multiplication exponent \(\omega>2\); their Remark 1.1 records an extra logarithmic factor if the exponent is exactly two. Their finite-field arithmetic uses polynomially sized fields. This improves the classical bound on dense graphs, but even a quadratic-in-vertices bound does not approach the explicit input size on sparse graphs.

Duan, Pettie and Su prove a \((1-\delta)\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta^{-1}\log\delta^{-1})\) time, so the graph-processing time is linear for fixed \(\delta\). Unit edge weights give the cardinality case, with an additional \(O(n)\) cost for the explicit vertex list. Fixed positive relative error can still allow the loss of many matching edges as \(n\) grows. Making the allowed loss less than one when the optimum is proportional to \(n\) requires inverse-linear accuracy, for which that running-time expression is no longer almost linear.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

A 2011 preprint by Jindal, Kochar and Pal has an abstract claiming \(O(m\log^2 n)\) maximum matching via Glauber dynamics. Its current official arXiv record also contains the authors' correction: the coupling has incorrect marginals, so the mixing-time bound and the main result do not hold. The retained abstract must not be treated as a valid resolution of this target.

cards.title: Near-linear-time short cycle decomposition
cards.formal:
Can short cycle decomposition be computed in near-linear time with only polylogarithmic losses in cycle length and the number of uncovered edges?

Precisely, put \(h(n)=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). Do there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C,a,b,c,q\), with \(q\ge2\), such that the following holds for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\ge1\), and \(m=|E|\)?

On the explicit input defined below, using words of \(q h(n)\) bits, every execution of \(A\) halts within
\[
C(n+m)h(n)^a
\]
operations. With probability at least \(2/3\), it outputs simple cycles \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_t\) and an edge set \(R\) satisfying
\[
E=R\;\dot\cup\; E(Q_1)\;\dot\cup\;\cdots\;\dot\cup\; E(Q_t),
\qquad
|R|\le C n h(n)^c,
\qquad
|E(Q_i)|\le C h(n)^b\quad(1\le i\le t)?
\]
Here \(\dot\cup\) denotes disjoint union: no edge may appear in two output pieces. Distinct cycles may share vertices. All constants, logarithmic exponents, and the program are chosen before the input graph.
cards.definitions:
The graph has no loops or parallel edges. Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. The input gives \(n,m\) and an array of \(m\) distinct unordered pairs of different vertex labels, with each pair written in increasing order. These array positions identify the edges; their order is arbitrary. Input entries are binary integers stored in machine words. The algorithm must handle every valid such representation. The additive \(n\) in the time bound includes the cost of processing the vertex set, even when \(m<n\).

A simple cycle is a cyclic list \((v_0,\ldots,v_{\ell-1})\) of \(\ell\ge3\) distinct vertices such that every consecutive pair, including \(\{v_{\ell-1},v_0\}\), is an input edge. Its length is its number \(\ell\) of edges. Each output cycle is written explicitly as this vertex list. The remainder \(R\) is written as a list of input edge indices. The number \(t\) of cycles may be zero. The displayed partition covers every input edge exactly once; the remainder has no additional structural requirement. Every listed cycle must use only edges of the original graph, without adding shortcut edges, contracting vertices, or reusing an edge in multiple cycles.

The word RAM is a sequential random-access machine with one finite program independent of \(n\). Its word length is \(w=q h(n)\) bits. It has a fixed finite number of registers and a word-addressed memory with \(2^w\) cells. Each register and memory cell holds a word-sized unsigned integer; addresses occupy one word, and work memory is initially zero. Reading or writing one word, copying, comparison, conditional branching, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by fewer than \(w\) positions each cost one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, also cost one operation. Shifts discard bits outside the word. Fresh independent unbiased random bits are available at unit cost per bit. Input access, workspace operations, and writing every output word count toward running time. There is no oracle, nonuniform advice, unbounded-precision arithmetic, or free graph preprocessing.

Probability is over the algorithm's independent random bits for a fixed input. The entire output must simultaneously satisfy all the stated conditions with probability at least \(2/3\). On other runs it may report failure or produce an invalid output, but the same worst-case time bound still applies. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case.

In this card, a polylogarithmic factor means at most a fixed power of \(h(n)\), up to a fixed multiplier. The three exponents may differ but cannot grow with \(n\). Near-linear time means the displayed \((n+m)\)-times-polylogarithmic bound, rather than a bound allowing an arbitrary subpolynomial factor.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement above or its logical negation. A positive result must specify one uniform algorithm and fixed constants, prove the running-time bound on every random tape, and establish the joint success probability for every valid input graph. A negative result must rule out every choice of program and fixed constants in this model; an explicitly conditional lower bound alone does not establish the unconditional negation.

Existence of the decomposition without the required construction time is insufficient. An almost-linear-time result, or a near-linear algorithm whose cycle length or uncovered-edge bound has an arbitrary \(n^{o(1)}\) loss, qualifies only if its actual bounds meet the fixed logarithmic powers required here. This is a binary algorithm-existence target, not a request to approximate a running-time exponent numerically.
cards.why: A fast decomposition into short, edge-disjoint cycles is a reusable primitive for graph compression that preserves information lost by independent edge sampling. The question asks whether this primitive can match the near-linear running times of other basic graph routines.

cards.title: Deterministic Exact Matching
cards.formal:
Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(d\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with an even number \(n\ge0\) of vertices, every red-edge subset \(R\subseteq E\), and every integer \(0\le k\le n/2\), the machine halts within \(K(N+1)^d\) steps and outputs YES exactly when
\[
 \exists M\subseteq E:\qquad
 \bigl(\forall v\in V,\ |\{e\in M:v\in e\}|=1\bigr)
 \quad\text{and}\quad |M\cap R|=k?
\]
Here \(N\) is the input bit length under the explicit encoding below. No bipartition is promised.
cards.definitions:
Vertices are labelled \(1,\ldots,n\), and an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Loops and parallel edges are excluded. Every edge is either red, meaning it belongs to \(R\), or blue, meaning it belongs to \(E\setminus R\). The graph, all its edges and their colours are given explicitly, not through an oracle or a succinct circuit. One fixed encoding uses a length-prefixed binary header and a list of adjacency records, one for each vertex including isolated vertices, with neighbour labels and colour bits; each undirected edge has consistent entries at both endpoints. The integer \(k\) is in binary. The encoding contains all \(n\) vertex records, so its length is at least \(n\); a binary header alone does not describe exponentially many unlisted vertices.

A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share a vertex. It is perfect if every vertex belongs to one of its edges, equivalently the degree condition in the formula. Every perfect matching then has \(n/2\) edges. The requested count is exactly \(k\) red edges, rather than at least \(k\), at most \(k\) or a count congruent to \(k\) modulo an integer. On the empty graph, the empty matching is perfect and the allowed input \(k=0\) has answer YES.

The machine is one uniform finite classical multitape Turing program; all bit operations, reading, auxiliary computation and output count toward its running time. It has no random bits, nonuniform advice or external oracle. The same \(A,K,d\) must work on every input size, colour pattern and allowed \(k\), with no error. Malformed encodings, odd vertex counts and out-of-range values of \(k\) can be rejected as invalid inputs in polynomial time. The graph may be disconnected, nonplanar and nonbipartite, with arbitrary degrees.

The required output is a decision bit; computing the number of matchings is not requested. Polynomial time means membership of this explicitly encoded decision language in the class \(\mathrm{P}\). Only sequential polynomial time is sought; a polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithm is not required. The statement is unconditional: no computational hardness or derandomization assumption is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the stated deterministic algorithm and common polynomial bound exist, or a complete Lean-checked proof that this decision language does not belong to \(\mathrm{P}\).

A positive answer must cover both YES and NO instances on all finite simple graphs. A randomized polynomial-time procedure, nonuniform circuit family, special graph class, exact-parity test or algorithm with a small red-count or matching-size error does not by itself suffice. A conditional lower bound or a barrier to one algebraic approach is not an unconditional negative answer. No numerical approximation tolerance applies.
cards.why: Determine whether randomness can be removed from a basic exact constraint on perfect matching. The problem connects combinatorial derandomization with algebraic algorithms while keeping a short, directly checkable input and feasibility condition.

cards.context:
An ordinary perfect matching covers every vertex once. The exact colour constraint asks for one specified attainable count, which is not determined merely by optimizing the count upward or downward.

On a six-cycle whose edge colours alternate red and blue, the two perfect matchings have zero and three red edges. Counts one and two are absent even though they lie between the minimum and maximum. This elementary obstruction already occurs on bipartite inputs.

Randomized methods place the problem among natural candidates for studying the power of randomness in efficient computation. A matching witnesses a YES answer, but the target requires a deterministic polynomial-time decision on NO instances as well.

The August 2026 revision tests all red counts simultaneously in matrix-multiplication time measured in finite-field operations. Its decision algorithm still uses randomness, and the introduction explicitly leaves derandomization open.

The April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic algorithm only for bipartite graphs. Its Appendix A records eight unproved structural inputs in the Lean formalization. This review does not certify those inputs or the full proof; even a verified bipartite theorem would require a further general-graph argument to settle this card.
