cards.title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A_a\), integers \(B_a\ge a+3\), \(k_a\ge0\) and \(C_a\ge1\) with the following property? On every explicitly represented directed graph \(G\) with \(n\ge2\) vertices, \(m\) arcs, distinct terminals \(s,t\), and integer arc capacities
\[0\le u_e\le n^a,\]
the algorithm uses words of \(w=B_a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, halts on every random execution within
\[C_a(m+n)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^{k_a}\]
word operations, and outputs an exact integral maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow with probability at least \(2/3\)?
The output must give a flow value on every original arc. The algorithm, constants and logarithmic exponent may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph, its capacities, its terminal choices or its input ordering. The complete graph, flow and machine conventions are specified below.
cards.definitions:
Graph and representation. The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An ordered arc list \((e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) consists of distinct ordered pairs \(e_j=(x_j,y_j)\in[n]^2\) with \(x_j\ne y_j\), so \(0\le m\le n(n-1)\). Opposite arcs may both occur and have independent capacities; parallel copies of the same ordered pair and loops are excluded. The graph may be disconnected and may contain isolated vertices and zero-capacity arcs. The terminals \(s,t\in[n]\) are distinct. The input is an array of machine words containing the header \((n,m,s,t)\), the list \(1,\ldots,n\) of vertices, and the triples \((x_j,y_j,u_{e_j})\) in the given arc order. Correctness and time bounds hold for every ordering. Capacities and labels are unsigned integers, each in one word. The explicit vertex list fixes the \(m+n\) convention even when \(m=0\). There is no succinct representation, adjacency oracle or precomputed index.

Feasible flow and optimum. A flow is a list \(f=(f_{e_1},\ldots,f_{e_m})\) of integers with \(0\le f_e\le u_e\) on every arc and
\[\sum_{e=(x,v)}f_e=\sum_{e=(v,y)}f_e\qquad\text{for every }v\in[n]\setminus\{s,t\}.\]
Each sum ranges over the arcs actually present. Its value is the net flow leaving the source,
\[\operatorname{val}(f)=\sum_{e=(s,y)}f_e-\sum_{e=(x,s)}f_e.\]
Incoming arcs at \(s\), outgoing arcs at \(t\), and circulations are allowed. Conservation implies that this equals the net flow entering \(t\). Define \(F(G,u,s,t)\) as the largest value among the feasible integral flows. The set of such flows is finite and nonempty because the all-zero list is feasible, so the maximum is attained and nonnegative. Also \(F\le(n-1)n^a\). The usual integral-flow theorem identifies this optimum with the real-valued maximum flow for integral capacities. A successful output is the list of exactly \(m\) integers in original arc order that forms a feasible flow with value \(F\). No prescribed tie-breaking between different optimal flows is required. If \(m=0\), the empty list is the correct output.

Machine model. Put \(L_n=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), so each word contains \(w=B_aL_n\) bits. A word stores an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The random-access machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite set of registers and word-addressed memory; input words occupy the initial array and other memory is initially zero. Each executed instruction costs one operation. Allowed instructions are word reads and writes, moves, conditional branches, comparisons, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and unsigned integer division with a nonzero divisor. A logical shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A memory address must fit in one word. Input, output and all memory used must fit within the address space, with \(B_a\) chosen as part of the algorithm's fixed constants. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented using these operations and charged accordingly. Exact real arithmetic is not a unit-cost instruction.

Randomness and resources. A random-word instruction returns a fresh independent uniform element of \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\) at cost one; equivalently its bits are independent fair bits. The success probability is over this sequence for each fixed valid input. A run outside the successful event may return a failure marker or an incorrect result, but must obey the same time bound. All graph preprocessing, memory accesses, random generation and writing of output words are charged. The bound is on the total running time of every run of this one static computation, not merely on expected time or on typical executions. An amortized analysis of internal operations is permitted if it establishes this total bound. There are no oracles, quantum operations, input-dependent advice or free preprocessing. Behavior outside the stated input promises is unrestricted.

Uniformity and quantifiers. For each fixed \(a\), one finite program works for all \(n,m,G,u,s,t\); it cannot contain a table or different advice indexed by \(n\). The quantifier order is
\[\forall a\ge1\ \exists A_a,B_a,k_a,C_a\ \forall(G,u,s,t).\]
The selected target does not additionally require an effective procedure that constructs \(A_a\) from \(a\), a common logarithmic exponent for all \(a\), or a bound polynomial in \(a\). For each fixed \(a\), however, \(k_a\) is a single integer independent of input size. The explicit running-time expression is precisely the meaning of the title's \(O((m+n)\operatorname{polylog}n)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, for each fixed capacity exponent \(a\), one program and fixed constants satisfying both the every-run time bound and the per-input success probability, including exact integral feasibility and optimality of all output arc values. A deterministic algorithm with that bound also qualifies. A negative proof must establish a fixed \(a\ge1\) for which every uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm in this model having any such fixed-polylogarithmic worst-case bound has some valid instance with success probability strictly below \(2/3\). A lower bound for one flow framework, an oracle-only algorithm, or a conditional conjecture does not prove that universal negation. A \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximate flow, the optimum value alone, an algorithm for a restricted graph class, or a bound of \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) without the required fixed logarithmic overhead is insufficient. The algorithmic exact-flow requirement is retained; numerical benchmark tolerance does not replace its output specification.
cards.why: Maximum flow is a central primitive for routing, cuts and combinatorial optimization. Almost-linear algorithms have already removed a polynomial overhead. This question asks whether exact directed flow can be computed with only a fixed power of a logarithm beyond explicit input size, on all polynomial-capacity instances and with a complete flow as output.

cards.context:
Capacity constraints bound how much can travel along each arc, while conservation couples choices throughout the network. Exactness asks for the largest transferable amount, not merely a feasible routing. Because capacities are integral, an integral optimum exists, but the algorithm still has to find an optimal routing among many interacting possibilities.

The logarithmic overhead is the unresolved guarantee. For example, \(h(n)=2^{\sqrt{\log_2(n+2)}}\) satisfies \(h(n)=n^{o(1)}\), yet exceeds \((\log_2(n+2))^k\) for every fixed \(k\) once \(n\) is sufficiently large. Thus almost-linear and fixed-polylogarithmic time bounds are different. In this simple directed-graph format, \(n\le m+n\le n^2\), so logarithms of input word count and vertex count differ by only a constant factor.

Chen and coauthors’ 2022 breakthrough computes exact maximum flow in \(m^{1+o(1)}\log U\) time with high probability for integral capacities bounded by \(U\). For \(U\le n^a\), the capacity term is logarithmic, while the subpolynomial graph-size overhead remains. Their analysis uses fixed-point quantities with polynomially many logarithmic bits; charging multiword arithmetic does not turn that overhead into a fixed logarithmic power.

The 2023 deterministic algorithm of van den Brand and coauthors also obtains exact almost-linear flow. The 2024 duality paper further improves the stated static bounds: its Theorem 6.17 gives randomized \(m\,2^{O((\log m)^{3/4}\log\log m)}\) time and deterministic \(m\,2^{O((\log m)^{5/6}\log\log m)}\) time for polynomially bounded integral minimum-cost flow. These are still guarantees with subpolynomial overhead, rather than the fixed logarithmic bound requested here.

Li and Wice’s August 2026 manuscript removes the outer interior-point loop from another almost-linear maximum-flow framework. Its deterministic pseudo-circulation subroutine is combined with a randomized balanced-graph flow routine, and the stated final result remains almost-linear. The deterministic nature of an intermediate step does not make the full reduction deterministic, and removing the outer loop does not itself establish fixed-polylogarithmic overhead.

The ICALP 2026 algorithm of Fleischmann, George Z. Li and Jason Li has fixed-polylogarithmic overhead for constant-accuracy approximate flow on undirected graphs. Both qualifications matter: the present task concerns arbitrary directed graphs and exact integral output, and that approximation theorem has additional inverse-error dependence. It does not directly establish the target here.

An approximation with a fixed relative error need not determine an integer optimum whose magnitude grows with the input. Likewise, finding only an optimal value does not fulfill the requested output list. Polynomially bounded capacities ensure each input capacity and output arc value fits in a logarithmic number of bits; the question does not hide arbitrarily long integers behind unit-cost input access.

cards.title: Almost-linear triangle detection
cards.formal: Does one uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm exist that, for every finite simple undirected graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges given by explicit adjacency lists, returns whether a triangle exists with probability at least \(2/3\), while every execution takes at most \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\) word instructions? The running-time guarantee must cover all graph densities, all valid adjacency-list orders and every random tape.
cards.definitions:
Let \(n\ge0\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of unordered pairs of distinct elements of \(V\). Set \(m=|E|\). There are no loops or multiple edges. A triangle is a set \(\{u,v,z\}\) of three distinct vertices for which all three pairs are edges. The output is YES exactly when such a set exists, and NO otherwise; the algorithm need not output a witness or list triangles.

The input supplies \(n,m\), an array of \(n+1\) list offsets, and a contiguous array of \(2m\) vertex labels. The segment for vertex \(v\) contains precisely its neighbors, in an arbitrary order. Each undirected edge occurs once in each endpoint's list. Validity of this representation is promised. Vertex labels, counts and offsets occupy single words. Thus the input occupies \(O(n+m+1)\) words. Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed; graphs with fewer than three vertices are legitimate NO-instances.

The word length is
\[
 w=\left\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil.
\]
Memory consists of addressable \(w\)-bit words; addresses are unsigned words. Input is initially stored in its specified arrays, and other memory is initially zero. A fixed finite program may read or write one addressed word, copy a word, compare unsigned words, branch, perform bitwise Boolean operations, shift logically, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or take the integer quotient and remainder of unsigned division by a nonzero word, at unit cost per instruction. A shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. It may also obtain one independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word in one instruction. Longer integers and algebraic operations must be implemented using these instructions. There is no unit-cost arbitrary-precision arithmetic, matrix-product oracle, input-dependent advice or free precomputed table. All input access and preprocessing count toward time. The fixed word length permits the explicit graph representation at every \(n\).

Precisely, set \(S=n+m+2\). The algorithm must halt on every valid graph and every random tape. For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there must be an integer \(S_\varepsilon\) such that, on every valid input with \(S\ge S_\varepsilon\), every execution uses at most \(S^{1+\varepsilon}\) instructions. The same program works for every \(\varepsilon\); it does not receive \(\varepsilon\) as input. This convention absorbs fixed multiplicative constants and defines the displayed almost-linear bound. Thresholds may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and the program, but not on the graph, its list order or the random tape.

For each fixed input separately, the probability over internal random words of a correct YES/NO output must be at least \(2/3\). There is no average-case input distribution, degree bound, forbidden-subgraph promise, triangle-count promise or restriction to combinatorial methods. Algebraic algorithms are allowed with their actual implementation cost. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked construction and proof of an algorithm satisfying the exact uniformity, word model, all-input time and per-input probability guarantees; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists in this model.

A bound with any fixed exponent greater than one is insufficient. A quadratic bound in \(n\) alone need not be almost linear on sparse inputs. Restricted graph classes, counting or listing results, average-case guarantees, and conditional lower bounds do not settle the target by themselves. An expected-time or high-probability-time result needs a proved conversion to the stated all-tapes bound and success guarantee. A separate program for each exponent slack requires a justified uniform combination. The negation of this target need not supply one common positive exponent gap against every algorithm. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to the decision.

cards.context:
The output is only one bit. The large number of triangles in a dense graph therefore creates no output-size lower bound for this question. Correctly rejecting graphs with no triangle remains part of the requirement.

The classical sparse bound has exponent \(2\tau/(\tau+1)\) in the edge count for an available matrix-multiplication exponent \(\tau\), plus input reading. This is an upper bound, not a proof that a better unrestricted algorithm is impossible.

Arboricity-sensitive listing takes \(O(m\,a(G))\) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where \(a(G)\) is the minimum number of forests covering the edges. Bounded arboricity gives useful special cases but is not promised here.

The 2026 weighted improvement and restricted-graph dichotomies answer related questions. They do not supply the required almost-linear algorithm on every explicit graph.

In Lemma 7.1 the relevant neighbors must have identical length-r prefixes to participate in the same canonical class. For two fixed neighbors this has probability 2⁻ʳ. At the chosen level r this probability can shrink with the degree, even when both edges were retained. Lemma 7.2 repeats bucket probes within that class, using the same prefixes.

The 2024 combinatorial proposal was withdrawn after an invalid case analysis was identified. It is not an established upper bound.

The older parent-edge rule fails on the path \(0,1,2,3,4,5,6\) with added edges \(\{0,3\},\{3,6\},\{0,6\}\). Its only triangle uses none of the path’s DFS tree edges. This counterexample concerns the stated 2025 rule, not every subsequent implementation.

The replacement posted on 14 September 2026 claims an expected \(O(n^{2.5}\log n)\) dense bound with separate sparse processing. Even a verified result at that bound would not provide the target all-density almost-linear guarantee; its proof was not independently certified.

cards.status_note: Solution assessment on November 23, 2026. Step (b) of Lemma 7.1 assumes a constant chance that two prescribed triangle neighbors share the canonical prefix class. Their pairwise-independent keys agree on r specified prefix bits with probability 2⁻ʳ. At the chosen level this can tend to zero as the anchor degree grows. All bucket groups reuse those prefixes. cards.title: Linear-time directed shortest paths with nonnegative real weights
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), an absolute constant \(K>0\), and one uniform deterministic comparison-addition RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly given simple directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\) arcs of arbitrary nonnegative real lengths, and every specified source vertex, outputs all exact source distances within \(K(n+m)\) instructions? The model below charges control, memory access, preprocessing and output as well as operations on real values.
cards.definitions:
The graph has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Input consists of \(n,m\), a source \(s\in[n]\), and an arbitrary-order explicit list of all arcs, each with its two integer endpoints and one exact real length \(w_e\ge0\). There is no bound on real magnitudes or rationality. Zero lengths, zero-length cycles, disconnected graphs and vertices unreachable from the source are allowed.

A directed walk from \(s\) to \(v\) follows arcs in their given directions and has length equal to the sum of their lengths. The empty walk has length zero. For a reachable vertex, its distance is the minimum of these lengths; nonnegative weights allow repeated vertices to be removed without increasing length, so a minimum is attained by a simple path, or by the empty path when \(v=s\). An unreachable vertex has distance \(+\infty\). The output is an array indexed by \([n]\), containing each exact finite distance or a distinct infinity marker. No sorted order of distances is requested, and an unevaluated implicit distance expression is not the output.

The machine has integer control words of \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits and separately typed exact-real cells. Integer addresses must fit a word. An instruction can read or write one cell, copy a value, compare values of the same type and branch. Integer instructions also include Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and quotient or remainder by a nonzero word. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Multiword computations pay for their constituent instructions.

Real instructions are copying, comparison, addition and subtraction, each of unit cost. Finitely many rational program constants are allowed. There is no real multiplication or division, rounding, floor, access to digits or bits, or conversion of an input-dependent real value to an integer. Real values cannot serve as addresses. Integer instructions cannot inspect real encodings. The saved subtraction convention can be represented with pairs of sums and comparisons of such pairs; it does not supply multiplication or encoding access. The infinity output is a separate tag and is not treated as a real operand.

One finite program and the constants \(B,K\) work for all \(n,m,s\), graphs and real inputs. There are no random bits, advice strings, precomputed input-dependent tables or free oracles. Every executed instruction counts, including graph preprocessing, initialization of working storage, control and address arithmetic, and writing the \(n\) outputs. Table construction is charged. Time is worst-case over all inputs, and includes every operation needed to choose the next real comparison or sum; bounding only the number of real arithmetic operations is insufficient. The algorithm must halt correctly on every allowed input. The linear bound is uniform over real edge values and graph density.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a program and constants with the stated all-input bound, or prove its logical negation in exactly this model. A one-sided improvement above linear time, a result only for undirected graphs or integer weights, or a bound that excludes control and preprocessing time does not suffice. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion unless the condition is also proved.
cards.why: An optimal linear algorithm would determine whether directed shortest paths with general nonnegative numerical lengths can be computed at the cost of reading the graph.

cards.title: Deterministic almost-linear vertex connectivity
cards.formal:
Do there exist one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer word-size constant \(d\ge4\), and a function \(h:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log h(N)}{\log N}=0
\]
such that, for every explicitly given simple unweighted undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=[n]\), \(n\ge2\), \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m\), the algorithm uses at most \(KNh(N)\) instructions and outputs both
\[
 \kappa(G)=\min\bigl\{|S|:S\subseteq V,
 G[V\setminus S]\text{ is disconnected or }|V\setminus S|\le1\bigr\}
\]
and a set \(S\) attaining this minimum?

The machine has word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) and the operations and charged costs below. No randomness is allowed.
cards.definitions:
An edge is an unordered pair of distinct labelled vertices. Loops, parallel edges, edge weights and vertex weights are absent. The input explicitly lists all \(n\) vertices, including isolated ones, and the \(m\) edges as pairs of endpoint labels, with length headers. It occupies \(\Theta(n+m)\) words; a small binary header cannot stand for an unlisted exponentially large set of vertices. Edge order is arbitrary.

The induced graph \(G[V\setminus S]\) deletes every vertex of \(S\) and all its incident edges. A graph with at least two vertices is disconnected when some two of them have no path between them. The separate at-most-one-vertex clause defines the degenerate endpoint. In particular, \(\kappa(G)=0\) for an initially disconnected graph and \(\kappa(K_n)=n-1\) for a complete graph. There is always an attaining set. The requested output lists its vertices explicitly without repetitions, together with its integer size. Any minimum set is allowed; no canonical choice is prescribed.

This is global vertex connectivity: no distinguished source or sink is part of the input. The measure counts deleted vertices, not deleted edges. Every graph is allowed, including disconnected, dense and complete graphs, with connectivity possibly growing linearly in \(n\). A fixed-parameter running time whose hidden coefficient depends on \(\kappa(G)\) does not automatically give the stated uniform bound.

The uniform sequential word RAM is a fixed finite program with unsigned \(w\)-bit words, word-sized addresses and no advice, external oracle or free lookup table. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copies, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Computation involving multiple words pays for each constituent instruction. All initialization, input access, preprocessing, constructed tables, auxiliary computation and output writes are charged. Both correctness and the instruction bound hold on every input, without random choices or error.

The function \(h\) depends only on \(N\), not on the graph or its connectivity, and is only a bound rather than an oracle supplied to the program. The same algorithm has running time \(N^{1+o(1)}\): for every real \(\eta>0\), it runs in \(O(N^{1+\eta})\) for all sufficiently large \(N\), with the constant and threshold allowed to depend on \(\eta\). A different program for each fixed \(\eta\) is not the one-program assertion here. No separate space bound is imposed beyond the stated machine and charged time.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the stated algorithm, constants and bound, or a complete Lean-checked proof of their logical nonexistence in this model.

A positive answer must compute the exact value and an attaining vertex set on every allowed graph within the common worst-case time bound. A randomized algorithm, an approximation, a result for bounded connectivity or a conditional lower bound does not decide the full proposition. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this algorithm-existence target.
cards.why: Determine whether randomness is needed for almost-linear exact computation of a basic measure of network resilience. Finding the weakest vertex separation uniformly over sparse and dense graphs remains different from handling only small cuts.

cards.title: Polynomial-time computation of planar treewidth
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that computes the exact treewidth of every finite planar graph?

Precisely, do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that \(M\) halts on every binary input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and, for every finite simple planar graph \(G\) in the encoding below,
\[
M(\operatorname{enc}(G))=\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(\operatorname{tw}(G))?
\]
The output is the exact integer treewidth in the specified signed binary encoding. Graph size and treewidth are unrestricted; the polynomial is fixed independently of both. No planar embedding, tree decomposition or bound on treewidth is supplied with the graph.

This is the polynomial-time existence question stated in §4.6 of the 2016 seminar report. It asks for an exact algorithm, not an optimal numerical running-time exponent. A negative answer is the full negation of that existence assertion, not merely an NP-hardness theorem conditional on a separate complexity-class separation.
cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) for an integer \(n\ge0\), and \(E\) a set of two-element subsets of \(V\). Loops and parallel edges are absent; isolated vertices, disconnected graphs and the empty graph are allowed. Graphs are unweighted. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices joined by edges. A cycle is a closed sequence of at least three edges visiting no vertex twice except its starting and ending vertex. A nonempty finite tree is a finite simple connected graph with no cycle; it has a unique path between each pair of its vertices.

A graph is planar if its vertices can be mapped injectively to points of \(\mathbb R^2\), and each edge can be represented by a continuous injective curve \([0,1]\to\mathbb R^2\) whose endpoints are the points of its two vertices, such that no interior point of a curve is a vertex point and distinct edge curves intersect only at common endpoint vertices. The existence of such a drawing is a promise on the input graph; its curves and coordinates are not part of the input. The algorithm is not required to output a drawing.

A tree decomposition is a nonempty finite tree \(T\) with a bag \(B_t\subseteq V\) at each node \(t\in V(T)\), satisfying
\[
\bigcup_{t\in V(T)} B_t=V,
\qquad
\forall\{u,v\}\in E\ \exists t\in V(T):\{u,v\}\subseteq B_t,
\]
and the connectedness condition: for every \(v\in V\), the set \(\{t\in V(T):v\in B_t\}\) induces a connected subtree of \(T\). Equivalently, every node on the unique path between two bags containing \(v\) also has \(v\) in its bag. Empty bags are allowed. The width of this decomposition is \(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\), and
\[
\operatorname{tw}(G)=
\min_{(T,(B_t))\text{ a tree decomposition of }G}
\left(\max_{t\in V(T)}|B_t|-1\right).
\]
The one-node tree with bag \(V\) is a decomposition, so the minimum exists. For the empty graph this convention gives \(-1\); for any nonempty graph it is an integer between \(0\) and \(n-1\). The convention on the single empty graph does not affect polynomial-time solvability.

Encode \(G\) as the bitstring \(1^n0\) followed by exactly \(n(n-1)/2\) bits. These final bits list the indicators of \(\{i,j\}\in E\) in lexicographic order of pairs \((i,j)\) with \(0\le i<j<n\). Thus the encoding length is
\[
L(G)=n+1+\frac{n(n-1)}2.
\]
The empty graph is encoded by the single bit 0. The unary prefix includes every vertex, even if isolated. This explicit adjacency encoding and the ordinary explicit adjacency-list encoding are polynomially interconvertible, so the chosen representation does not alter the polynomial-time question.

The output encoding \(\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(z)\) for an integer \(z\) is one sign bit, 0 for a nonnegative integer and 1 for a negative integer, followed by the usual base-two representation of \(|z|\), with no leading zero except that zero has magnitude string 0. Negative zero is forbidden. For example, the output for the empty graph's treewidth is the sign bit 1 followed by the magnitude bit 1. Exact numerical equality is part of the algorithm's task; it is not an additional demand for an exact-value benchmark answer.

A deterministic multitape Turing machine has one finite program, a finite tape alphabet, a read-only binary input tape, finitely many work tapes initially blank, and a binary output tape. A transition inspects or changes only the scanned symbol on each tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including reading the graph, arithmetic, preprocessing and writing the answer. There is no oracle, random tape, advice depending on input length, unbounded-word unit-cost arithmetic or free preprocessing. The polynomial clock is worst case and applies to every bitstring, including malformed encodings and encodings of nonplanar graphs. On those inputs, correctness and the output format are unrestricted. Imposing this total clock does not change the promised polynomial-time question, because a candidate machine with fixed bounds can be stopped at its own polynomial clock.

An algorithm returning only the exact minimum width suffices; an optimal tree decomposition need not be printed. Conversely, any polynomial-time algorithm producing an optimal decomposition would also answer this question. Fixed-parameter algorithms whose dependence on treewidth is superpolynomial do not give the required single polynomial bound when treewidth is unrestricted.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the exact algorithm-existence proposition, or its full logical negation, using the definitions and encoding above.

A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic machine and fixed polynomial bound, prove the total clock, and prove that its output is the exact treewidth for every encoded planar graph. It must cover all sizes, components and treewidth values, without an embedding or decomposition in the input.

A negative answer must prove that for every finite deterministic machine \(M\) and every pair of integers \(C,k\ge1\), at least one of the following holds:
\[
\exists x\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad
M(x)\text{ does not halt within }C(|x|+1)^k\text{ transitions},
\]
or
\[
\exists G\text{ finite, simple and planar}:\quad
M(\operatorname{enc}(G))\text{ fails to halt with output }
\operatorname{bin}_{\pm}(\operatorname{tw}(G)).
\]
Failure includes a malformed output, an incorrect integer or nontermination. The graph or failing input may depend on the machine and its proposed bound. Refuting one particular algorithm is insufficient.

An NP-hardness proof together with a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would give a negative answer; NP-hardness alone is not the negation of polynomial-time solvability. Here \(\mathrm P\) is uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision, and \(\mathrm{NP}\) is uniform nondeterministic polynomial-time decision, with acceptance on at least one branch and polynomial clocks on all branches. A result for branchwidth, a proper subclass of planar graphs, an approximation guarantee, or a polynomial-time procedure per output object with potentially superpolynomially many output objects does not establish the positive assertion by itself. This is a yes/no running-time question. The numerical \(1/100\) benchmark tolerance does not change the exact integer function computed by its hypothetical algorithm.
cards.why: Treewidth is a central measure connecting graph structure with algorithms for otherwise difficult graph problems. An exact polynomial-time algorithm on planar graphs would make optimal width accessible on a large and important sparse graph class. A negative answer would locate a fundamental limitation of planarity despite efficient algorithms for the related branchwidth parameter. The issue is distinct from using a decomposition once one has already been supplied.

cards.context:
The 2016 seminar report explicitly asks whether the treewidth of a planar graph can be computed in polynomial time. It does not prescribe a fixed exponent, an approximation ratio, a bounded-width promise or a space restriction.

The 2025 potential-maximal-clique paper defines the standard tree decomposition and still describes exact planar treewidth as a long-standing question. Its graph convention is simple, undirected and unweighted; the present card spells out the finite encoding and computational model.

The related branchwidth parameter is polynomial-time computable for planar graphs. The cited sources emphasize that this does not by itself determine exact treewidth, though it supports approximation results.

The 2023 hardness result covers cubic graphs and certain three-dimensional grid subgraphs. Those input classes are not restricted to planar graphs, and its conclusion explicitly retains the planar question as open.

The 2025 algorithm has time polynomial in the graph size multiplied by the number of potential maximal cliques. Its polynomial delay guarantee controls the time between consecutive generated objects, and does not assert that every planar graph has only polynomially many such objects.

A September 2026 preprint improves a structural bound: a planar graph excluding a \(t\times t\) grid minor has treewidth at most \(4t+4\). This is a width-versus-grid theorem, not an exact polynomial-time computation theorem.

cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one finite constant C bounds \(\operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})/(\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n)\) for all n, all initial trees \(T_{0}\) and all finite access sequences X, or prove that this ratio is unbounded over those inputs. A counterexample to a particular proposed value of C alone does not refute the universal-constant claim.
cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.

cards.context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t_F^\star(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t_F^\star(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}\), a query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t_F^\star(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t_F^\star(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t_F^\star(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.
cards.why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.

cards.context:
A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further \(\Omega ((\log  n/\log  \log  n)^{2})\) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time static dictionaries
cards.formal: Is the following proposition true? For every fixed integer \(d\ge 1\) there are uniform deterministic construction and query programs \(A_{d},Q_{d}\) and a constant \(C_{d}\ge 1\) such that, for every \(n\ge 2\), every word length \(\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil \le w\le d\lceil \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\), and every n-record input with distinct w-bit integer keys and w-bit values, \(A_{d}\) builds a static dictionary in at most \(C_{d} n\) operations and \(C_{d} n\) words of total space, and \(Q_{d}\) answers every membership-and-value query in at most \(C_{d}\) operations.
cards.definitions: The universe is \(U_w=\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). An input is a list of n pairs \((x_{i},v_{i})\in U_{w}\times U_{w}\) with pairwise distinct \(x_{i}\) and arbitrary \(v_{i}\); the input order is unrestricted. On query \(q\in U_{w}\) the output is \((1,v_{i})\) if \(q=x_{i}\) and \((0,0)\) if q is absent. The stored set and values do not change after construction. The machine is a sequential word RAM with w-bit registers and cells. The primitive unit-cost instructions are memory reads and writes, copies, comparisons, conditional branches, addition and subtraction modulo \(2^w\), multiplication returning the full product in two words, integer quotient and remainder of two words with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least w returns zero; otherwise shifted-out bits are discarded. Addresses may occupy a fixed number of words, and all operations computing them are charged. Programs have finitely many instructions and constants, may receive n and w, and contain no input-size or word-size advice, random instruction, free table or special hashing primitive. Every table, parameter computation, memory initialization and output write performed by construction counts toward its time; input storage, the resulting dictionary and temporary storage count toward its space. Query reads the constructed representation and may use temporary workspace, with every operation charged; all retained information about the input is in the counted representation. The query must be correct on every q, including absent keys. Programs and constants may depend on d but not on n, w, the input or query. This spells out the saved \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) convention as a claim for every fixed polynomial-size universe; Pagh’s broader arbitrary-word-length formulation is not asserted equivalent here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition with deterministic algorithms meeting all three bounds for every fixed d, or disprove it for at least one fixed d. The negation says that no pair of admissible correct programs has simultaneously linear worst-case construction time, linear total space and constant worst-case query time for all inputs in that word-length range. Failure of a particular hash family, an average-input lower bound, or a lower bound in a comparison-only model is not that negation.
cards.why: Exact constant-time lookup is a basic component of many larger data structures. The unresolved cost is obtaining the representation deterministically in optimal time, so a resolution would settle whether randomness is essential to this combination of construction, storage and lookup guarantees.

cards.context:
A dictionary is an exact lookup table for a sparse set of keys. For example, records \((12,5), (47,9)\) and \((103,2)\) require the answers 9 on key 47 and absent on key 48. The values need not be unique. The problem is to prepare a representation in time proportional to the number of records and then answer every lookup in a bounded number of machine steps, regardless of whether the key is present.

Direct addressing uses the key itself as an array index. This achieves constant lookup time, but an array for a universe of \(n^{2}\) possible keys occupies \(n^{2}\) cells even if only n keys are present. Such space is outside the target. At the opposite extreme, keeping the keys in sorted order uses linear space but ordinary binary search needs logarithmically many comparisons. These examples show why construction, storage and query time must be required simultaneously.

Randomized perfect hashing already gives linear expected construction time, linear storage and constant worst-case lookup time. The randomness concerns finding a suitable representation during construction; once a valid dictionary has been built, lookup can be exact and have a worst-case bound. Thus the open issue is not whether every query can avoid probabilistic errors, but whether the construction time can be bounded linearly without any random choices.

Pagh obtained deterministic \(O(n \log  n)\) construction for logarithmic-size words. Ružić subsequently related construction cost to integer sorting with only a log log n overhead. The latter is a much smaller overhead, but it still grows with n. The source question asks for its complete removal while retaining the other two guarantees. A representation whose existence is known but whose parameters take longer to find does not meet the construction requirement.

The dependence on word length matters even when keys occupy one machine word. Here a fixed polynomial-size universe is intended: the constant relating w to log n is fixed before the inputs vary. Constants in the guarantees may depend on that fixed bound. This is the logarithmic-word version already selected for this card; it does not silently claim a solution for word lengths growing faster than log n.

Uniformity also matters. Earlier dictionary results sometimes supplied word-size-dependent constants at no construction cost. The present formulation charges for computing every table and parameter that is not part of a fixed program. A one-time computation on a particular physical machine cannot disappear from an asymptotic bound that covers arbitrarily large inputs.

The dependency remains visible in modern applications. The 2024 internal-pattern-matching paper uses constant-time deterministic dictionaries with a general \(O(m(\log  \log  m)^{2})\) construction bound for a dictionary of size m, and treats very small dictionaries separately. The surrounding text length can be much larger than m, so that application must not be read as fixing word length to \(\Theta (\log  m)\). Kosolobov’s 2026 compressed index likewise records a slowdown when dictionary randomness is removed.

These applications explain the scientific stakes: a basic lookup operation can determine whether a larger construction remains deterministic within its intended time bound. The 2026 index is evidence that the issue remains useful, rather than a theorem resolving this static linear-construction question.

cards.title: Polynomial lower bounds for adaptive dynamic data structures
cards.formal: Is there an explicit dynamic Boolean problem for which adaptive randomized polynomial-space cell-probe data structures require polynomial amortized cost? Precisely, seek one problem family for which, for every fixed space exponent s, there is \(\eta_s>0\) such that every structure using at most \(n^s\) cells incurs expected \(\Omega(n^{\eta_s})\) probes per operation on some polynomial-length operation sequence, for infinitely many n.
cards.definitions:
Editorial explicitness convention: a problem has a state of at most \(n^a\) bits, an initial all-zero state, updates, and Boolean queries, for one fixed constant a. Each operation type and argument has at most \(a\log_2(n+2)\) bits. State transitions and answers are specified by uniform deterministic algorithms running in polynomial time in n; they are independent of any data structure being lower-bounded. Queries do not change the abstract state.

A structure stores at most \(n^s\) addressable cells of \(w=\lceil c\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with fixed constants s,c; constants must permit addressing the memory. Within each operation arbitrary computation is free, and each cell read or write costs one probe. The next address may depend on earlier read contents, hence adaptivity is allowed. All information retained between operations, including registers, counts toward storage. Preprocessing may depend on n and the initial state but not future operations; its probes are not charged to the online sequence. Randomness is independent of the sequence. Each query must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every fixed legal sequence; a simultaneous all-queries success guarantee is not assumed.

The lower bound is on total expected probes divided by the number of operations in a fixed sequence chosen independently of the random coins. The sequence length is polynomial in n, with exponent permitted to depend on the structure and space exponent, and must include a query. This total-cost convention forces high amortized cost for at least one of updates and queries. The exponent eta may depend on the fixed space and word constants; it must be positive and independent of n. No external computational hardness assumption is part of the requested result.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit the explicit problem family and prove the stated lower bound in Lean against all adaptive bounded-error structures in this model. A bound only for nonadaptive probes, deterministic structures, restricted update/query tradeoffs, or superpolynomially long histories does not suffice. A negative resolution must prove that every problem in the specified explicit class admits structures excluding the asserted polynomial lower bound.
cards.why: A polynomial unconditional barrier would change the known limits of dynamic data structures beyond polylogarithmic lower bounds.

cards.title: Superlinear cell-probe lower bounds for succinct Boolean matrix-vector products
cards.formal:
For every family of deterministic exact static cell-probe data structures representing arbitrary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) in \(n^2+o(n^2)\) bits, with word length
\[w_n=\left\lceil\log_2(n^2+1)\right\rceil,\]
must its worst-case number \(T(n)\) of word probes for answering a Boolean matrix-vector query satisfy
\[T(n)=\omega(n)?\]
The representation may encode the whole matrix arbitrarily; it need not retain the original matrix as a separately readable array. Computation between probes and preprocessing time are uncharged, as specified below.
cards.definitions:
For \(M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) and a query \(v\in\{0,1\}^n\), the required answer is the entire vector \(y=Mv\in\{0,1\}^n\) over the Boolean semiring:
\[y_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^n(M_{ij}\wedge v_j),\qquad i\in[n].\]
Here \(\wedge\) and \(\vee\) are logical AND and OR. This is not multiplication over the two-element field, where addition would instead be parity. Every matrix and every query vector is allowed.

For each integer \(n\ge2\), choose an integer number of memory cells \(S_n\), with \(1\le S_n\le2^{w_n}\), and an encoding map
\[E_n:\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\longrightarrow(\{0,1\}^{w_n})^{S_n}.\]
The stored memory on input \(M\) is exactly \(E_n(M)\). All persistent matrix-dependent information must be in these cells. The space bound includes padding to complete words: define \(r_n=S_nw_n-n^2\), and require \(r_n\ge0\) and \(r_n/n^2\to0\). This is the meaning of succinct storage. No particular rate such as \(r_n=n^{7/4}\), and no smaller fixed redundancy budget, is imposed.

The query gets \(n\) and \(v\) for free, plus access to the stored cells at addresses \(0,\ldots,S_n-1\). One probe reads one entire \(w_n\)-bit word. The next address may depend on the query and all words previously read. Arbitrary finite computation and temporary workspace between probes cost nothing; reading the query vector and producing the output vector also cost nothing. Temporary state starts empty apart from the query and public size parameters, so there is no free matrix-dependent advice. The representation is static and read-only, and each query starts afresh; no state left by earlier queries is available.

Equivalently, for each \(n\) and query \(v\), the query rule is a finite decision tree whose internal nodes specify cell addresses, whose outgoing edges are indexed by possible word contents, and whose leaves specify an output vector. Its leaves must give the correct \(Mv\) on every stored encoding. The trees and their computations may depend on \(n\) and \(v\), but not on \(M\) except through the probed words. There is no restriction on their description size or on the encoding's preprocessing time. Thus the lower bound is in the usual permissive, nonuniform cell-probe model; restricting the query computation to an efficient word-RAM program would be a different target. The formulation fixes the deterministic exact version: no random coins or error probability are allowed in the data structures quantified over here.

For one such family \(\mathcal D\), let
\[T_{\mathcal D}(n)=\max_{M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n},\ v\in\{0,1\}^n}
\#\{\text{word probes on query }v\text{ after storing }M\}.\]
Repeated reads count repeatedly. The assertion means that for every eligible family \(\mathcal D\) and every real \(C>0\), some \(n_0\) satisfies \(T_{\mathcal D}(n)>Cn\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The threshold may depend on the family and \(C\). The fixed choice \(w_n=\Theta(\log n)\) makes words large enough for cell addresses without allowing one word to hold the whole matrix.

A systematic representation stores the unchanged matrix and separate redundant bits. That is a restriction on \(E_n\), not part of this general succinct target. The source page does not require that restriction; its example upper bound happens to have it. The distinction matters for applying later lower bounds.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal superlinear lower bound. An affirmative answer must cover every deterministic exact representation and adaptive query family with the stated \(n^2+o(n^2)\) total storage. A negative answer must exhibit an eligible family, a constant \(C>0\), and arbitrarily large \(n\) with \(T(n)\le Cn\); a bound holding at all sufficiently large sizes is sufficient but not necessary to negate the displayed limit. A lower bound only for systematic encodings, nonadaptive queries, smaller redundancy, individual matrix-entry probes, or charged word-RAM computation does not establish this statement without the needed conversion. This is exact asymptotic yes/no acceptance, not an approximation of a finite running time.
cards.why: A superlinear lower bound with almost no storage overhead would go beyond the standard static-data-structure barriers for this central problem. It would isolate an information-access obstruction independently of how much computation is performed between memory reads.

references.title: Tight Cell Probe Bounds for Succinct Boolean Matrix-Vector Multiplication
references.authors: Diptarka Chakraborty; Lior Kamma; Kasper Green Larsen
references.locator: STOC 2018, pp.1297–1306, DOI10.1145/3188745.3188830; full systematic/non-systematic distinction and Theorems 1.1–1.2 in §1.1. The lower bound counts individual entries read from the unchanged matrix while allowing access to all redundant bits.

cards.context:
The matrix contains n² independent bits, but one query asks only for n Boolean answers. Preprocessing can reorganize the information before any query arrives. The question asks whether nearly minimal storage still forces substantially more than n memory accesses on a worst-case query, even when all arithmetic and logical work is free.

The source contrasts this model with the online matrix-vector conjecture for ordinary computation. A time lower bound in a word-RAM model charges operations that the cell-probe model ignores. The online conjecture therefore cannot simply be substituted for an unconditional memory-access lower bound.

Larsen and Williams give a deterministic cell-probe structure using \(O(n^{7/4}/\sqrt w)\) probes per query and only \(O(n^{7/4}\sqrt w)\) bits beyond the stored matrix. With logarithmic words this is succinct and polynomially faster in probe count than scanning all matrix entries. It remains superlinear and hence does not refute the proposed lower bound.

The 2018 paper proves a much stronger tradeoff for systematic representations. Its Theorem 1.2 gives \(t_{\rm bit}r=\Omega(n^3)\) when \(n\le r\le n^2/4\), even for queries correct with probability at least \(1-1/n\), and permits reading all redundant bits. Here \(t_{\rm bit}\) counts original matrix entries, not words. A word-probe consequence loses a factor of \(w\), yielding \(\Omega(n^3/(rw))\) in that restricted representation model.

Two qualifications prevent that theorem from settling this card as stated. It retains the matrix in its original layout, whereas a general succinct representation may encode every bit differently. Moreover, even its word-probe consequence is superlinear only for suitably smaller redundancy; arbitrary o(n²) redundancy need not be o(n²/w). The title of a succinct-data-structure theorem alone does not establish the general claim.

The same paper improves the systematic upper bound to roughly n³ᐟ² probes and redundant bits, up to logarithmic factors at logarithmic word size, using randomized queries. This is useful progress on the tradeoff, while the exact deterministic lower-bound question here remains a separately specified target.

context_blocks.text: The matrix contains n² independent bits, but one query asks only for n Boolean answers. Preprocessing can reorganize the information before any query arrives. The question asks whether nearly minimal storage still forces substantially more than n memory accesses on a worst-case query, even when all arithmetic and logical work is free.

The source contrasts this model with the online matrix-vector conjecture for ordinary computation. A time lower bound in a word-RAM model charges operations that the cell-probe model ignores. The online conjecture therefore cannot simply be substituted for an unconditional memory-access lower bound.

Larsen and Williams give a deterministic cell-probe structure using \(O(n^{7/4}/\sqrt w)\) probes per query and only \(O(n^{7/4}\sqrt w)\) bits beyond the stored matrix. With logarithmic words this is succinct and polynomially faster in probe count than scanning all matrix entries. It remains superlinear and hence does not refute the proposed lower bound.

The 2018 paper proves a much stronger tradeoff for systematic representations. Its Theorem 1.2 gives \(t_{\rm bit}r=\Omega(n^3)\) when \(n\le r\le n^2/4\), even for queries correct with probability at least \(1-1/n\), and permits reading all redundant bits. Here \(t_{\rm bit}\) counts original matrix entries, not words. A word-probe consequence loses a factor of \(w\), yielding \(\Omega(n^3/(rw))\) in that restricted representation model.

Two qualifications prevent that theorem from settling this card as stated. It retains the matrix in its original layout, whereas a general succinct representation may encode every bit differently. Moreover, even its word-probe consequence is superlinear only for suitably smaller redundancy; arbitrary o(n²) redundancy need not be o(n²/w). The title of a succinct-data-structure theorem alone does not establish the general claim.

The same paper improves the systematic upper bound to roughly n³ᐟ² probes and redundant bits, up to logarithmic factors at logarithmic word size, using randomized queries. This is useful progress on the tradeoff, while the exact deterministic lower-bound question here remains a separately specified target.

cards.title: Strong SetDisjointness conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following statement true? For every admissible uniform static word-RAM data structure for SetDisjointness, with worst-case retained space \(S(N)\) words and worst-case query time \(T(N)\) steps, there exist constants \(c>0\), \(b\in\mathbb N\), and \(N_0\ge2\) such that \(S(N)T(N)^2\ge cN^2/(\log_2(N+2))^b\) for every integer \(N\ge N_0\). For every integer \(N\ge2\), the input is a list \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) of nonempty subsets of \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), with \(1\le m\le N\) and total size \(N=\sum_{i=1}^m|A_i|\). A query supplies indices \(i,j\in[m]\) and must return whether \(A_i\cap A_j=\varnothing\).
cards.definitions:
The input gives \(N\), \(m\), the lengths of the sets, and each set's elements explicitly as words, without repetitions within a set. Different listed sets may be equal. The indices of two stored sets are the whole query; there is no new query set. The case \(i=j\) is allowed. Each admissible data structure is a fixed pair of finite programs, one for preprocessing and one for queries, working for every input size. The word length is \(w=\lceil10\log_2(N+2)\rceil\). The sequential word RAM has word-sized registers and addressed memory cells; each read, write, comparison, branch, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero integer, Boolean bit operation, or logical shift costs one step. Arithmetic stored in a word is modulo \(2^w\), and a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Addresses fit in one word. Outputting the answer and all memory operations are charged.

Preprocessing must halt on every valid input and random execution, but its finite running time is unrestricted. Only the resulting stored representation is accessible to a query; the original input is not available for free. The representation includes all retained input-dependent tables, seeds, pointers and metadata. A query begins with its two indices, the input-size metadata and that representation, with no input-dependent private state inherited from earlier queries. It leaves the representation unchanged. Temporary query storage starts empty; accessing or filling it costs time. There is no advice, oracle, input-specific code, or uncharged precomputed table.

The two programs may generate independent uniformly random words in one step. For every fixed input and fixed valid query, the probability of the correct empty/nonempty answer, over preprocessing randomness and independent query randomness, is at least \(2/3\). The query bound holds for every random outcome, including erroneous ones. Let \(s(N)\) be the maximum retained word count over all valid inputs of total size exactly \(N\) and preprocessing outcomes, and let \(T(N)\ge1\) be the maximum query step count over those inputs, their produced representations, all valid queries and all query outcomes. These maxima are required to be finite. Use the saved card's space normalization \(S(N)=\max\{N,s(N)\}\), and restrict to structures with \(S(N)\le N^2\). Unused cells may be padded. All constants in the asserted bound may depend on the fixed programs, but not on \(N\), the input family, or the query. The displayed bound is the precise meaning of \(S(N)T(N)^2=\widetilde\Omega(N^2)\); it suppresses only fixed powers of a logarithm, not an arbitrary \(N^{o(1)}\) factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal lower bound or its logical negation in the specified model. A refutation must violate every admissible polylogarithmic lower-bound factor for one fixed admissible data structure; a fixed logarithmic improvement alone is not a refutation. The negation is an asymptotic assertion and need not have a finite counterexample. Results conditional on Strong SetDisjointness, or lower bounds only for preprocessing time, do not establish this lower bound.
cards.why: This conjecture underlies many space-query conditional lower bounds for text indexes, graph oracles and set systems.

cards.context:
Goldstein, Kopelowitz, Lewenstein and Porat formulate the Strong SetDisjointness conjecture as \(S=\widetilde\Omega(N^2/T^2)\). Their \(N\) is total set incidence count, not the number of sets. The source explicitly uses the tilde notation to suppress polylogarithmic factors.

A matching upper tradeoff has retained space \(O(N+N^2/t^2)\) words and query time \(O(t)\), in particular \(S T^2=O(N^2)\) in the relevant range \(1\le t\le\sqrt N\). This upper bound does not establish the conjectured universal lower bound.

The 2020 algorithms of Kopelowitz and Vassilevska Williams improve the tradeoff between preprocessing time and query time. Their analysis measures preprocessing time separately from retained storage, so its improved preprocessing bound does not refute this space-query conjecture.

Huang, Tao and Wang use the same space-query conjecture in their 2026 work on join sampling, in a word-RAM with logarithmic word length. Their Lemma 21 relates an expected-query-time formulation for exact answers to the formulation with deterministic query time. They assume the conjecture rather than prove its lower bound.

This review retains the card's explicitly chosen uniform, bounded-error word-RAM convention and normalized space range. The 2017 conjecture itself does not spell out these machine, uniformity and error details. Relabelling the elements of the union into \([N]\) preserves every intersection; empty sets and self-pair queries are trivial.

The Strong 3SUM-Indexing conjecture mentioned alongside SetDisjointness in the original paper was subsequently refuted. The 2019 bounded-universe paper explicitly distinguishes that development and continues to assume Strong SetDisjointness for its conditional results.
