cards.title: Logarithmic randomized online labeling
cards.formal: Is there one uniform randomized online list-labeling algorithm and a universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every capacity \(n\ge2\) and every obliviously fixed valid sequence of \(M\ge0\) insertions and deletions, its expected total movement cost is at most \[C\bigl(n+M\log_2(n+2)\bigr)?\] At most \(n\) items are live, and their order-preserving labels must lie in \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\). Cost, validity and the oblivious-adversary convention are defined below.
cards.definitions: Fix a capacity \(n\ge2\) and start with an empty ordered list. An insertion specifies the rank at which a new distinct item enters the list; a deletion names a live item. The list never contains more than \(n\) items. After each update the algorithm assigns distinct labels from \(\{1,\ldots,2n\}\) to the live items, in strictly increasing list order. Cost is one for the update plus the total number of relabelings of surviving items during it; assigning a label to the new item costs at most one additional unit. The input sequence is fixed independently of all random choices. Only relabelings are charged: local computation, rank search and auxiliary metadata are free, so this is a movement-cost model, not a word-RAM running-time target. The array has fixed constant slack; other label-universe regimes are outside this card. The algorithm is a fixed finite computable program taking the capacity as input, without advice or an oracle, and may use independent fair random bits. It receives updates sequentially, has no access to future updates, and must finish each operation almost surely with a valid ordered labeling. Its finite local computation and auxiliary storage are not charged by the movement objective. An oblivious sequence may depend on the algorithm and the capacity but not on the sampled random bits or observed random labels. The expectation is over the algorithm’s random choices for that fixed full sequence. A surviving item changed more than once during an update is counted for each relabeling; labels of live items must be valid at the end of the update.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one online algorithm meets the expected movement bound with one constant for all capacities and all obliviously fixed legal sequences, or refute the existence of such an algorithm under the same cost convention.
cards.why: The problem measures the unavoidable movement needed to maintain a sorted array with spare capacity, a primitive used throughout ordered storage and indexing.

references.authors: Michael A. Bender; Alex Conway; Martín Farach-Colton; Hanna Komlós; Michal Koucký; William Kuszmaul; Michael Saks
references.locator: Theorem 1: O(delta^{-1} log n (log log n)^3) for m=(1+delta)n and fixed delta in (0,1); introduction, movement cost and general randomized lower bound.

cards.context:
List labeling represents order by positions in an array with empty slots. An insertion supplies a new position in the logical order, but an empty array slot need not already be available between its neighbors. Other items may have to move. Deletions create space without prescribing where future insertions will occur.

The capacity is fixed and the array has twice that many slots. This gives a constant fraction of spare space even at maximum occupancy. A nearly full array or a polynomially larger label universe can have different bounds, so neither can silently replace this regime.

Movement and computation are separate resources here. A program can spend arbitrary finite effort deciding which labels to change; the objective counts the changes themselves. Similarly, expected amortized cost allows occasional expensive updates provided every fixed full sequence has the required expected total cost. It does not assert a worst-case time bound for each individual call.

The See-Saw theorem gives \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^3)\) amortized expected cost at any fixed positive constant slack. Its stated slack parameter may be fixed below one and its smaller array embedded in \([2n]\), giving the upper bound for this card. The paper records a general randomized lower bound of \(\Omega(\log n)\). Removing the remaining growing factor is the unresolved tight-bound issue.

Lower bounds for deterministic, history-independent, or other restricted labeling algorithms do not automatically apply to all randomized online algorithms. The adversary here commits to the whole sequence without observing random labels; adaptive choices based on those labels would change the game.

The selected target keeps constant slack, both insertions and deletions, and an oblivious adversary. It asks whether the known logarithmic lower-bound scale is achievable, without requesting the entire optimum if that endpoint fails.

cards.title: Deque conjecture
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every finite binary search tree \(T_0\) with \(n\ge0\) distinct ordered keys and every legal sequence \(\mathcal S\) of \(m\ge0\) deque operations, the specified bottom-up splay implementation satisfies
\[
W(T_0,\mathcal S)\le C(n+m)?
\]
The operations are insertion of a new minimum or maximum and deletion of the current minimum or maximum. Insertions make the new key the root; deletions splay the requested extremum to the root and remove it. The cost \(W\) counts operation overhead, search edges and rotations as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A binary search tree is a finite rooted tree with at most one left child and one right child per node. Each node carries a key; all keys in its left subtree are smaller, and all keys in its right subtree are larger. Keys are opaque elements of a totally ordered set and are used only through order comparisons. The initial tree may have any shape and is supplied as a tree, rather than built by charged insertions. The \(n\) term in the target is its allowed initial credit.

Insert-min supplies a key smaller than every currently present key. Allocate a new node with that key, no left child, and the former root as its right child; it becomes the root. Insert-max is symmetric. Both operations are allowed on an empty tree. Legality is promised, so no search to verify the new key’s extremal status is performed. A key that was deleted may be inserted again whenever the current extremal-order condition permits it.

Delete-min is allowed only on a nonempty tree. Follow left-child pointers from the root until reaching the leftmost node \(x\), splay \(x\) to the root, remove it and make its right child the root of the remaining tree. Delete-max follows right-child pointers, splays the rightmost node and retains its left subtree. Removing the only node leaves the tree empty. There are no searches for internal keys, other update operations, balance conditions or promises about the order of deletions.

A right rotation at a node \(p\) with left child \(x\) makes \(x\) replace \(p\), makes \(p\) the right child of \(x\), and makes the former right subtree of \(x\) the left subtree of \(p\), preserving all other attachments. A left rotation is the mirror image. Parent pointers and the root pointer are updated as needed. To splay \(x\), repeat until it is the root: if its parent \(p\) is the root, rotate \(x\) above \(p\) (zig); if \(x,p\) are both left children or both right children of their respective parents, first rotate \(p\) above its parent and then \(x\) above \(p\) (zig-zig); otherwise rotate \(x\) above \(p\) and then above its new parent (zig-zag). These are the standard bottom-up rules; the algorithm is fixed, not a choice among tree heuristics.

Let \(e\) be the total number of child edges traversed while finding extrema for deletions, and \(r\) the total number of single rotations performed by all splay steps. Define \(W=m+e+r\). A node has a constant number of child and parent pointers. Reading or changing one such pointer, comparing keys, allocating or deleting one node and executing a branch are constant-cost primitives. The standard direct implementation takes time within constant factors of \(W\), since each search edge, rotation and operation uses only a constant amount of additional work. Key bit lengths, memory-allocation system overhead and an alternative implementation’s avoidable extra work are not part of this combinatorial cost model.

The conjecture is a bound on the entire sequence, including sequences with insertions and deletions interleaved arbitrarily. It does not assert a constant worst-case cost for an individual deletion. The constant \(C\) must be independent of \(n,m\), all keys, the initial shape and the operation sequence. The empty sequence has cost zero.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal bound or its logical negation. A negative proof must show that for every proposed constant \(C\) there is a legal finite initial tree and sequence with \(W>C(n+m)\); equivalently, the cost ratio is unbounded over nonempty instances.

A constant-cost deque implemented by a different data structure does not answer this question. A slowly growing nonconstant amortized factor, a guarantee for only deletion sequences or special initial shapes, and a nonconstant competitive ratio against an optimal search tree do not establish the full linear bound. No additive approximation tolerance is allowed.
cards.why: I include this because it tests whether one general-purpose adaptive representation can recognize a workload whose optimal cost is linear. The remaining gap is tiny numerically but significant mathematically: a proof would explain why expensive local restructuring cannot accumulate across arbitrary alternations of the two ends.

cards.title: Log-log amortized decrease-key in standard pairing heaps
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that the standard two-pass pairing heap defined below satisfies \[W(\mathcal S)\le C\left(a(\mathcal S)+b(\mathcal S)\log_2(N+2)+c(\mathcal S)\log_2\log_2(N+4)\right)\] for every finite legal operation sequence \(\mathcal S\) starting from empty heaps and having at most \(N\ge1\) live items in total? Here \(a\) counts make-heap, insert, meld and find-min operations, \(b\) counts delete-min, and \(c\) counts decrease-key. The fixed algorithm and work measure \(W\) are defined below.
cards.definitions:
Each heap is empty or is a single rooted tree of items. Every item has an opaque key in a totally ordered set and a stable identity. Ties are resolved by a fixed total order on identities, so every comparison has a deterministic winner. A parent’s key, including this tie-breaking order, is no greater than a child’s. Children form a left-to-right list. A link of two disjoint trees compares their roots and makes the losing root the new leftmost child of the winner. A cut removes one parent-child edge and detaches the entire child subtree while preserving the order of remaining children.

Make-heap creates an empty heap. Find-min returns its root, or an empty marker. Insert creates a new singleton item, links it with the heap’s root if present and returns a stable item handle. Meld takes two distinct item-disjoint heaps, links their roots when both are nonempty and returns the resulting heap, invalidating the old heap handles. If either is empty, the other tree is returned. Item handles remain valid until their items are deleted, including through melds.

Decrease-key receives a heap handle, a handle to an item in it and a new key no larger than its old key. Replace the key. If the item is not the root, cut its entire subtree and link that subtree to the heap root, even if no heap-order violation would have occurred without the cut. If it is the root, no link or cut is needed. The operation’s inputs and membership promises are supplied, so searching for the item is not required.

Delete-min requires a nonempty heap. Remove its root and detach its children into their existing ordered root list. In the pairing pass, link the first and second roots, then the third and fourth, and so on from left to right, leaving a final unpaired root unchanged. The resulting trees retain their pair order. In the assembly pass, start with the rightmost resulting tree and repeatedly link it to the next tree to its left, moving right to left until one tree remains. This becomes the heap. If the deleted root had no children, the result is empty. Changing the order of either pass, omitting the assembly pass, adding rank-driven restructuring or using multiple retained trees defines a different heap.

A direct pointer implementation stores a constant number of fields per item, including the key and enough child, sibling and parent information for a cut given a handle in constant time. Comparisons of keys or identities, pointer reads and writes, branches and allocating or releasing a constant-size record are unit-cost primitives. There is no arithmetic on keys and no hidden balancing operation. Let \(\lambda\) be the number of links and \(\chi\) the number of edges cut, including child edges detached during delete-min. Define
\[
W(\mathcal S)=a(\mathcal S)+b(\mathcal S)+c(\mathcal S)+\lambda+\chi.
\]
This is within constant factors of the work of the specified direct implementation. Only this fixed sequential deterministic algorithm is being analyzed.

The integer \(N\ge1\) is a global upper bound on simultaneously live items throughout the sequence, not its total insertions, length, number of heap objects or final size. Sequences may create arbitrarily many heaps, interleave operations on them, merge them and leave items undeleted at the end. Every operation contributes to its count, even if it returns an empty result or changes no key value. The inequality must hold for every \(N\) and every sequence obeying that live-item bound, with no uncharged initial nonempty heaps or additive credit depending on the sequence.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed total-work bound for the specified standard two-pass pairing heap. A positive answer must use one universal constant with all three simultaneous operation charges. A negative answer must prove that for every proposed constant there are a live-item bound and a legal sequence violating the inequality; a finite example with a larger constant-factor cost is insufficient. The algorithm is fixed, so proving a bound for a modified heap does not answer the question.
cards.why: A tight analysis would resolve the central complexity uncertainty for one of the simplest and most widely studied self-adjusting priority queues.

cards.context:
The immediate decrease-key operation uses only a constant number of pointer changes. Its amortized charge measures the extra work these changes can cause during later delete-min operations.

Fredman proved an amortized \(\Omega(\log\log N)\) lower bound for decrease-key when the other operations have \(O(\log N)\) amortized charges, as stated in Iacono’s Introduction and Figure 1. This also rules out a smaller decrease-key charge under the stricter constant insert/meld convention here. The card asks for the matching \(O(\log\log N)\) upper charge for the fixed standard two-pass heap, simultaneously with its stated charges for every other operation. The lower-bound scope is checked through the later primary papers, not a new audit of Fredman’s full proof.

Iacono’s analysis gives constant insert and meld charges with logarithmic delete-min and decrease-key. Its comparison table explicitly warns against combining operation charges from unrelated amortized analyses.

Pettie’s sublogarithmic analysis also charges insert and meld a nonconstant amount. That result alone is not a simultaneous upper bound under this card’s constant-charge convention.

The July 2026 paper proves \(O(\log\log N\,\log\log\log N)\) for pure heaps and announces \(O((\log\log N)^2\log\log\log N)\) for standard heaps in forthcoming work. The announcement and the remaining tightness question are distinct; no companion proof was independently checked.

cards.title: Sorting-bound external-memory breadth-first search
cards.formal: Can exact single-source unweighted distances in every undirected graph be computed in O(S(n+m)) external-memory I/Os, even when M<n?
cards.definitions: Use the single-disk external-memory model with an internal store of M records and transfer blocks of B consecutive records, for all integers B≥1,M≥2B. One I/O reads or writes one block; all input reads, preprocessing transfers and output writes count. Records have a constant number of fields; vertex identifiers and pointers have O(log(n+m+2)) bits. Records and numeric fields are indivisible: no packing arbitrarily many labels or weights into one field, and no decoding such packed information by arithmetic. Internal comparison, copying, address calculation and permitted numeric arithmetic on resident fields are free, but internal storage remains M records. Use at most (n+m)^{O(1)} external records and a uniform deterministic algorithm knowing M,B. Let N=n+m and S(N)=max{1,N/B}·max{1,log_{M/B}(max{1,N/B})}; the max conventions include small inputs. The bound sought is O(S(N)) I/Os with an absolute constant for every permitted M,B, including M<n. Input is a contiguous vertex list and an arbitrarily ordered edge list for a simple undirected graph on [n], plus source s. Output is one record per vertex with its distance from s, using +∞ for unreachable vertices; no explicit list of every shortest path is required. Every edge has length one. Distances are integers in {0,…,n−1} or +∞, fitting one numeric field. Temporary numeric values and indices have O(log(n+m+2)) bits. The input may be disconnected and output records may be in any order provided every vertex is identified.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of all stated guarantees, or prove the precise target impossible. A lower bound assuming an additional complexity hypothesis settles the negative answer only if that hypothesis is also proved.
cards.why: This asks whether graph traversal can match the basic external-memory sorting bound.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
cards.definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
cards.why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.

cards.context:
Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

As checked on 15 September 2026, the official FOCS 2026 accepted-paper list includes Dynamic Connectivity, Minimum Spanning Tree, and 2-Edge Connectivity with Polylogarithmic Worst-Case Update Time, by Simon Meierhans, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg and Yu-Cheng Yeh. The inspected entry provides a title and authors, with no theorem or manuscript link. It does not specify whether the guarantee is deterministic. The current status is therefore recorded as uncertain; this announcement is neither treated as a verified matching solution nor ignored in favor of an older open-problem statement.

Probst Gutenberg’s publication page independently lists the same FOCS 2026 title and coauthors, again without a manuscript link in that entry. The conference is scheduled for November 2026; its acceptance announcement is distinct from an inspected proceedings paper. A complete statement is needed to decide whether the result meets this exact deterministic target.

cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon,a}\) and constants \(K,d,B\ge1\) with the following guarantees?

For every \(n\ge2\) and every valid oblivious sequence of \(T\le n^a\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty graph on \([n]\), the expected total initialization and update cost is at most
\[
K\left[n+T\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\right].
\]
With probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\), after every update the algorithm maintains an explicit matching \(M\) in the current graph \(G\) such that
\[
|M|\ge\frac{\nu(G)}{1+\varepsilon},
\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum matching cardinality. The same constants apply to every \(n,T\) and sequence for the fixed \(\varepsilon,a\).
cards.definitions:
At all times the graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, with the fixed vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Initially there are no edges. One update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge; only valid update sequences are required to be handled. The graph need not be bipartite or have bounded degree.

A matching is a subset of the current edges in which no vertex belongs to more than one edge. The integer \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum possible number of edges in a matching, and it is zero for an edgeless graph. The algorithm stores a mate array \(\operatorname{mate}[1..n]\): zero means unmatched, while a nonzero value \(\operatorname{mate}[v]=u\) must have \(u\ne v\), \(\operatorname{mate}[u]=v\) and \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Together with its stored cardinality, this explicitly represents \(M\). A size estimate or a fractional assignment to edges is not this representation.

After each completed update, reading the mate of any specified vertex or reading \(|M|\) takes at most a fixed constant number of word operations. Listing the full matching may scan the array in \(O(n)\) time, and need not be performed after every update. All work needed to modify the representation, including every changed array entry and the cardinality, counts toward update cost. External requests to read or list the maintained matching are charged their stated query costs separately; they do not excuse extra update work.

The update sequence is oblivious: for each guarantee it is any fixed sequence independent of the algorithm’s random bits. Updates are delivered one at a time, and the algorithm must finish processing one before seeing the next. It knows \(n\) and has the fixed parameters \(\varepsilon,a\), but the future sequence and its actual length are not supplied in advance. This is distinct from a computation receiving all updates at once, and it makes no guarantee against an adversary choosing updates from observed random-dependent outputs.

Use a word-RAM with word length \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with \(B\) a fixed positive integer for the algorithm. Memory cells have word addresses and initially contain zero; every access or write costs an operation, and untouched cells require no initialization work. The instruction set consists of word reads and writes, indirect addressing, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one operation. Stored random words and intermediate values use ordinary memory. Larger integers must use multiple words, with all operations charged; no arbitrary-precision operation, graph oracle or precomputed instance advice is available. No additional linear-space restriction is imposed.

Expectation is over the algorithm’s private randomness on each fixed sequence and includes the entire initialization and all \(T\) updates. The bound is amortized over that sequence, not a worst-case bound on each individual update. The required finite expectation includes termination with probability one. Separately, one event of probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\) must ensure the valid mate representation and approximation inequality after every update in the sequence simultaneously. A separate probability bound at each time without this joint guarantee is insufficient.

The parameters \(\varepsilon\) and \(a\) are fixed independently of \(n\). The machine and constants may depend on both; no polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) and no uniform compiler taking \(\varepsilon,a\) as inputs is required. Integer \(a\) covers every polynomial sequence-length regime. There is no demand for an infinite update sequence with one global success event. This is an exact existence proposition for the stated approximation scheme and resources, not a numerical question about \(\nu(G)\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply algorithms and a complete Lean-checked proof covering every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\), every fixed polynomial horizon, every \(n\), and every valid oblivious sequence, including the expected total cost, representation-access costs and simultaneous success event. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked refutation of these quantified guarantees; failure for one fixed accuracy and one fixed horizon exponent, for every admissible algorithm and constants, suffices.

An estimator without explicit matching edges, a fixed approximation factor bounded away from one, a partially dynamic algorithm, an algorithm receiving future updates, or an update bound larger than every fixed power of \(\log n\) does not prove the proposition. A lower bound requiring accuracy to shrink with \(n\), polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), or an adaptive adversary does not by itself refute this weaker stated target. Conditional lower bounds require their hypotheses and are not unconditional negative answers.
cards.why: A single insertion or deletion can change which edges should be used together in a large matching. The question asks whether a near-optimal explicit solution can be kept current at a cost that grows only polylogarithmically with graph size, combining approximation quality with efficient dynamic maintenance.

cards.context:
The maintained object must contain compatible graph edges. Reporting a good estimate of how many such edges could be chosen leaves a separate search and maintenance task, which the source explicitly distinguishes.

Azarmehr, Behnezhad and Roghani improve the approximation achievable in polylogarithmic update time for estimating matching size. Their result does not maintain the mate array required here.

Assadi, Khanna and Kiss obtain explicit near-optimal matching bounds governed by the density of ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Those graphs decompose into ordered matchings, each induced in the union of itself and the later matchings. The resulting structural dependence does not supply a universal polylogarithmic bound.

Pratt relates the density of those ordered graphs to the older unordered variant. The theorem resolves a comparison between two combinatorial quantities, rather than completing the dynamic matching algorithm target.

The fixed-accuracy convention matters: an algorithm may have very large dependence on the chosen accuracy. Lower bounds that require one polynomial dependence as accuracy shrinks with graph size cannot simply be transferred to this formulation.

A maximal matching cannot be extended by adding another edge, but it may be much smaller than a maximum matching. The 2026 deterministic maximal-matching result improves a different maintenance guarantee and does not yield approximation arbitrarily close to one.

cards.title: Dynamic APSP with edge-linear updates
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist integers \(a,d\ge1\) and \(B\ge c+3\), a real constant \(K\ge1\), and one uniform deterministic word-RAM data structure with the following guarantees for every \(n\ge2\) and supplied integer capacity \(n\le m\le n^2\)?

The data structure maintains a simple directed graph on the fixed vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with at most \(m\) live edges and edge weights in \(\{1,\ldots,n^c\}\), under online single-edge insertions, deletions and weight changes. It returns the exact current distance for every queried ordered vertex pair. Write \(\ell=\log_2(n+2)\). Preprocessing an arbitrary initial graph uses at most \(Kn^d\) instructions, and space is at most \(Kn^d\) words at every time. Every individual query uses at most \(K\ell^a\) instructions. After preprocessing, every finite valid sequence containing \(U\) updates and \(Q\) queries uses at most
\[
K\bigl(Um\ell^a+Q\ell^a\bigr)
\]
instructions in total. The constants and program may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n,m\), the initial graph or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions:
The initial graph is explicitly given as a list of ordered endpoint pairs and integer weights, together with \(n\) and \(m\). There are no self-loops, and each ordered pair has at most one edge. An insertion supplies an absent edge and its allowed weight, a deletion names a present edge, and a weight change supplies a new allowed weight for a present edge. Every resulting graph must have at most the fixed supplied capacity \(m\) edges. The algorithm must support all such valid sequences, however long. The value \(m\) is neither the number of updates nor the current number of edges.

A query supplies \(s,t\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and requests the minimum sum of edge weights along a directed path from \(s\) to \(t\), with distance zero when \(s=t\) and a distinguished symbol \(\infty\) when no path exists. Positive weights imply that every finite distance is at most \((n-1)n^c\). The output is this one distance, not a shortest path or a full matrix. Every answer must be correct. Operations arrive one at a time, and each must finish before the next is supplied; future operations are unavailable.

For a given \(n\), a machine word has exactly \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. Memory is indexed by unsigned words, and \(B\) must also be large enough to address the allowed \(Kn^d\) words. Unit-cost instructions are word reads and writes, unsigned comparisons and conditional branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), unsigned integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Finite distances and the infinity marker must have an unambiguous constant-word encoding. Arithmetic on larger integers must be implemented and charged through these operations. The program is finite and independent of \(n,m\); it receives no advice or uncharged precomputed tables.

Preprocessing includes reading and constructing all initial data. After it finishes, the displayed total bound applies to every finite prefix, including prefixes with no updates or no queries. There is no extra additive \(n^d\) allowance in that post-preprocessing bound. Individual updates may exceed their amortized charge, but each query also satisfies the stated worst-case bound, regardless of the preceding operations. All instruction counts include maintenance work and any rebuilding performed during the operation sequence. The space bound applies throughout preprocessing and all operations.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic data structure for every fixed \(c\), prove all exact query answers and the capacity-sensitive bounds for every allowed graph and operation prefix, and account for word size and polynomial space.

A negative answer must disprove the existence proposition in the stated model; a result conditional on an unproved complexity hypothesis remains a conditional obstruction and must identify that assumption. An update bound near \(n^2\) only has the requested dependence on \(m\) for sufficiently dense graphs. Approximate distances, offline sequences, planar graphs, insertion-only updates, or an amortized query bound alone do not establish the stated target. The fact that one edge change alters many pairwise distances is not by itself a lower bound on an implicit distance oracle.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
cards.formal:
For every fixed pair of integers \(a,b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized data structure that maintains the exact canonical minimum spanning forest of the graph below, with polynomial preprocessing and space and polylogarithmic worst-case time for each edge insertion or deletion? For every valid update sequence \(\sigma\) of length \(T\le n^a\) fixed independently of its randomness, require
\[\Pr_R\bigl[\widehat F_t=F(G_t)\text{ for every }0\le t\le T\bigr]\ge1-n^{-b}.\]
The event also requires every edge-change report to be valid as defined below. Here \(G_t\) is the graph after update \(t\), \(F(G_t)\) is its specified exact forest, and \(\widehat F_t\) is reconstructed from the reported edge changes. Each update must finish within its time bound on every execution, including executions on which the answer is wrong. The data structure receives no future updates in advance.
cards.definitions:
Graph and updates. Fix an integer \(n\ge2\), with labelled vertices \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The graph is simple and undirected: no loops or parallel edges. Initially \(G_0\) has no edges. An insertion supplies distinct endpoints \(u,v\) of an absent edge and an integer weight \(w\in\{1,\ldots,n^4\}\); a deletion supplies the endpoints of a present edge. A weight stays fixed until its edge is deleted. Reinsertion may assign a different weight. A valid sequence respects these rules at every prefix; disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and repeated insertions after deletions are allowed. Vertices are never inserted or deleted. The exponent four is the retained concrete choice of polynomial weight range.

Exact target and ties. A spanning forest has one spanning tree in each connected component, with an isolated vertex contributing no edges. Its cost is the sum of its edge weights, and a minimum spanning forest minimizes that sum. To specify one answer when several forests have the same cost, order edges by the triple \((w,\min(u,v),\max(u,v))\), in increasing lexicographic order. Define \(F(G)\) by starting with no edges, scanning the present edges in this order, and retaining an edge exactly when adding it does not create a cycle. This is the canonical minimum spanning forest; the scan defines the target and is not a required implementation. In particular \(F(G_0)=\varnothing\).

Required output. After each update, before receiving the next one, report a list \(D_t\) of forest edges removed and a list \(A_t\) of forest edges added, using unordered endpoint pairs represented with their smaller endpoint first. Starting from \(\widehat F_0=\varnothing\), the reported forest is \(\widehat F_t=(\widehat F_{t-1}\setminus D_t)\cup A_t\). On a correct execution these lists must be exactly \(F(G_{t-1})\setminus F(G_t)\) and \(F(G_t)\setminus F(G_{t-1})\), respectively. Each contains at most one edge for a single valid update. Printing all current tree edges is not required. Duplicate or invalid reports count as a correctness failure; they never excuse exceeding the time or space bound. No later query or background computation may postpone completing the report.

Machine and costs. Use a classical sequential word RAM, with word length \(w_n=\lambda\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for some fixed positive integer \(\lambda\) chosen with the data structure. Unit-cost operations are direct or indirect word reads and writes; word comparisons, branches and copies; addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w_n}\); integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor; bitwise Boolean operations; and shifts with zero fill and truncation to one word. A shift by at least the word length produces zero. One instruction may generate one independent uniformly random word. Larger integers require multiple words and their actual operations are charged. Endpoints and allowed weights occupy a constant number of words. Addressable memory cells contain words and have word-sized addresses. Input reading, output writing, random generation, memory access and all computation count. There is no rank oracle, free query to another graph algorithm, arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, parallel computation or uncharged lookup table.

Uniformity and resource bounds. For each fixed \(a,b\), choose one finite program, constants \(K\ge1\), integers \(C,D\ge1\), and \(\lambda\). These choices are independent of \(n\) and of the sequence. On input \(n\), initialization of the empty graph finishes within \(Kn^D\) steps and uses at most \(Kn^D\) words; all later memory use has the same bound. Initialized tables must be computed within this preprocessing budget. There is no advice or precomputed table varying with \(n\). For every valid sequence in the stated horizon and every realization of all random choices, update \(t\) finishes in at most
\[K\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^C\]
steps, including its report. Choose the word-length constant large enough to address the permitted memory. Randomness may be used in preprocessing and updates. The parameters \(a,b\) tune the allowable polynomial horizon and failure probability; the program and constants may depend on them. No uniform bound on that dependence is requested.

Probability convention. The entire input sequence is fixed before the data structure draws any random bits, so it is an oblivious sequence. The probability is over all random words \(R\), including initialization, and covers simultaneous correctness of every report throughout the sequence. Separate per-update probability bounds without a simultaneous bound are insufficient. The time and memory bounds themselves have no exceptional random outcomes. This is the retained Monte Carlo formulation: a small probability of a wrong answer is permitted, whereas an always-correct deterministic data structure would be a stronger positive answer.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, specify the programs for every fixed \(a,b\), their resource constants and randomization. Prove initialization, exact canonical forest maintenance, online reporting, worst-case time and space on every random execution, and the simultaneous probability bound for every valid oblivious sequence of length at most \(n^a\).

A negative answer must refute the stated quantified claim: for some fixed \(a,b\), no allowed uniform program and constants meet all requirements. It must cover randomized data structures with polynomial preprocessing and space in this word-RAM model. Failure of one technique or one logarithmic exponent, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an impossibility limited to a more restrictive access model does not suffice. A conditional lower bound must retain its assumptions and does not by itself refute this unconditional proposition.

Amortized polylogarithmic time, subpolynomial worst-case time, an expected-time bound alone, an approximate forest or a deferred expensive query does not meet the criterion. A result with probabilistic time bounds needs an explicit conversion satisfying the stated hard time cap and simultaneous correctness guarantee. A rank-query count or parallel span is not the sequential running time specified here.
cards.why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.

cards.context:
One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all \(n- 1\) tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic \(O(\log^4 n)\) amortized update bound. Amortization bounds the total cost across a sequence and permits individual updates to be much slower. The present target requires the current answer within the same polylogarithmic time budget after every single update, including a deletion chosen to expose a difficult replacement search.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain a Las Vegas algorithm: its answers are always correct, while each update has subpolynomial time in expectation and with high probability. These probability guarantees concern time. This card instead places a hard limit on time and allows a small probability of an incorrect forest. The two conventions must be distinguished even before comparing their asymptotic bounds.

Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case time for exact dynamic MSF. Subpolynomial remains weaker than polylogarithmic: \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\), for example, grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of \(n\) but faster than every fixed power of \(\log n\). Thus the deterministic theorem is a major improvement without meeting this card’s sharper running-time target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to \(\log (U)/\varepsilon\) for weights in \([1,U]\). The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

The dependence on \(\varepsilon\) prevents reading the approximate theorem as an exact polylogarithmic-time result. Integer forest costs differ by at least one, but a forest may have total weight as large as \((n-1)n^4\). Requiring multiplicative error small enough to certify exact cost in every instance introduces a polynomial, rather than polylogarithmic, overhead in the displayed guarantee. Exact cost would also still have to respect this card’s fixed choice among tied optima.

The ESA 2026 paper on dynamic matroids gives a deterministic algorithm maintaining a minimum-weight base with \(O(\log N)\) rank queries per update, where \(N\) is the matroid ground-set size. A rank query asks for the maximum size of an independent subset of an arbitrary supplied set. For a graph this requires determining the largest forest inside that edge set. The paper expressly distinguishes its oracle-query count from update time: it does not bound the cost of implementing these rank queries on a concrete matroid. Its proposition therefore does not settle the ordinary RAM problem here.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

source_formulation.text: The card preserves the previously selected randomized, oblivious-adversary, exact weighted-forest question, its importance score, the weight range \(\{1,\ldots,n^4\}\), canonical tie-breaking and polynomial sequence horizon. The original imported ICALP 2021 link concerned matching and was already identified as a citation mismatch; the MSF target is grounded instead in the sources listed here. The present review makes the standard RAM convention and probability/resource quantifiers explicit without adding deterministic or adaptive-adversary requirements.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. Inspected primary sources retain the gap between exact polylogarithmic amortized updates and exact subpolynomial worst-case updates. The SODA 2026 weighted extension is approximate, and ESA 2026 minimum-weight-base maintenance counts rank queries without bounding their implementation time. No matching exact polylogarithmic worst-case RAM resolution was found in the bounded source search; cited proofs were not independently formalized.

progress.text: Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup establish deterministic \(O(\log ^{4} n)\) amortized minimum-spanning-forest updates.
Holm–Rotenberg–Wulff-Nilsen improve amortized bounds; the \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) option uses randomized priority queues in the stated RAM model.
Nanongkai–Saranurak–Wulff-Nilsen give Las Vegas subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability.
Chuzhoy and coauthors obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case updates via deterministic expander decomposition.

Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s SODA paper gives expected polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity maintenance; its weighted extension is \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate with inverse-\(\varepsilon\) overhead.
De Vos–Grilnberger give logarithmically many rank queries per dynamic minimum-weight-base update, without a corresponding RAM update-time guarantee.

sentences: The data structure receives insertions and deletions of weighted edges in an initially empty simple graph.
After every update it must report the changes to the exact minimum spanning forest with fixed tie-breaking.
The target combines a hard polylogarithmic update-time cap with simultaneous high-probability correctness over every polynomial-length oblivious sequence.
A complete Lean proof must cover the charged word-RAM computation, polynomial initialization and space, and all program and probability quantifiers, or refute the full allowed class.
Amortized bounds, subpolynomial worst-case bounds, approximate forests and logarithmic rank-query counts do not settle this exact maintenance question.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized data structure maintaining the exact global minimum-cut value of a fully dynamic simple unweighted undirected graph with polylogarithmic expected amortized update time, polylogarithmic worst-case query time and polynomial space? Precisely, is there one algorithm \(A\) and fixed integers \(b\ge1,c\ge0\) such that, for every fixed integer confidence parameter \(a\ge1\), there is a constant \(C_a\ge1\) for which the following holds? For every \(n\ge2\), initialize on the empty graph on \([n]\). For every legal operation sequence \(\sigma\) fixed independently of the random bits, with \(U\) updates and \(Q\) queries and \(U+Q\le n^a\), require all of:
\[\text{space on every execution}\le C_a n^b\text{ words},\qquad \mathbb E[T_{\rm init}+T_{\rm updates}]\le C_a\bigl(n^b+U L^c\bigr),\]
\[\text{each query takes at most }C_aL^c\text{ steps on every execution},\qquad \Pr[\text{all }Q\text{ answers equal the current }\lambda(G)]\ge1-n^{-3},\]
where \(L=\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) and the machine model and costs are defined below. The exponents \(b,c\) and program are independent of \(a,n,\sigma\) and all cut values; constants may depend on \(a\).
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), fixed throughout the sequence. Each edge is an unordered pair \(\{u,v\}\) of distinct vertices and occurs at most once. A legal update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge. There are no loops, weights, parallel edges or vertex changes. For \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq[n]\), put \(\delta_G(S)=\{\{u,v\}\in E(G):|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\) and
\[\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq[n]}|\delta_G(S)|.\]
Thus \(0\le\lambda(G)\le n-1\), and \(\lambda(G)=0\) precisely for disconnected graphs, including the initial empty graph. A query returns just this integer, not a minimizing vertex set, edge list or prescribed-terminal cut. Isolated vertices are not discarded. There is no upper bound on connectivity other than \(n-1\).

The algorithm receives \(n\) and \(a\) at initialization. It then receives one operation at a time, represented by a query tag or an insertion/deletion tag with the two vertex indices. It is not given future operations. The external sequence is fixed in advance independently of the algorithm’s randomness, including any answers or internal state; its prefixes are legal. Correctness is simultaneous over all queries in each fixed sequence, not simultaneous over all possible sequences for one random seed. No correctness obligation is imposed on invalid update sequences. Initialization and updates must finish almost surely before the next operation is provided; the finite expectation bound applies to every legal sequence and hence to each prefix. Queries have the stated worst-case bound for every choice of random bits. Expected cost includes unsuccessful executions, not only those with correct answers.

Use a uniform word-RAM. For each fixed \(a\), the word length is \(w=B(a)L\) bits, where \(B(a)\ge1\) is an integer determined by a fixed computable function chosen with the algorithm, independently of \(n\) and the operations. Words represent unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). One step may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, compare two words, branch, apply a bitwise Boolean operation, shift, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or perform unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. A random instruction returns one fresh independent uniformly distributed \(w\)-bit word in one step. Arithmetic requiring more than one word is charged for its word operations; there are no real-number, unbounded-integer or oracle primitives. The finite program and computable word-length rule are common to all inputs, with no nonuniform advice or free precomputed tables.

Space counts all stored words, including tables and temporary work. Initialization work, random choices, rebuilding and all other computation belong to the operation during which they occur; there is no uncharged background work. The expectation bound includes initialization once and all update work. Query work is separately bounded, so expected total time is also at most \(C_a(n^b+(U+Q)L^c)\). The additive initialization allowance is polynomial, not an allowance repeated at each update. Amortization concerns the total over the supplied sequence, with no average over random input graphs. A query answer that differs from the exact integer is an error. The fixed failure bound \(n^{-3}\) applies to the entire sequence of length at most \(n^a\); \(a\) is supplied to set the horizon and confidence, not to reveal the actual sequence.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of a data structure satisfying every displayed requirement, or an unconditional proof of the negation in the same model. A positive answer must define one program and its computable word-length rule, establish fixed exponents, and prove the space, expected total update/initialization cost, worst-case query cost and joint correctness probability for every allowed parameter and oblivious sequence. A negative answer must rule out every such choice of program and exponents; a theorem conditional on a conjecture alone does not do so. An insertion-only algorithm, an approximation, a bounded-connectivity guarantee, superpolylogarithmic update time, or polylogarithmic updates accompanied by slower queries is insufficient. Lower bounds for weighted graphs or terminal cuts require a proved transfer preserving this exact model. The output is exact because the question asks for an exact-maintenance algorithm; there is no additive 1/100 approximation option.
cards.why: A central exact dynamic graph problem asking whether a global measure of edge connectivity can be updated as efficiently as basic connectivity, across the full range of cut values.

cards.context:
The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes \(\lambda =0\) from \(\lambda \ge 1\); the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to \(n- 1\).

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. Stability of the value alone does not specify whether an update changes it. The all-input guarantee includes long sequences in which different vertex partitions attain the minimum.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention \(\lambda =0\) for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup give a deterministic algorithm with polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. Its permitted updates only insert edges. The present target permits both insertions and deletions, including repeated removal and reinsertion of the same edge.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors give a randomized exact algorithm with \(\widetilde O(n)\) worst-case update time and a deterministic algorithm with \(\widetilde O(m^{29/31}n^{1/31})\) amortized time. Their March 2024 revision corrects an expander-decomposition running time. These bounds are substantial improvements over recomputing from scratch, but do not give the requested polylogarithmic guarantee. Here \(m\) denotes the current edge count and \(\widetilde O\) hides logarithmic factors.

The final June 2026 Algorithmica article by de Vos and Christiansen gives the deterministic exact amortized bound \(\widetilde O(\min\{m^{11/12},m^{11/13}n^{1/13},n^{3/2}\})\) for simple unweighted graphs. This is Theorem 6 in the journal version; the article distinguishes it from an erroneous earlier cited exponent. Returning a full cut has a separate output-sensitive bound. The theorem does not establish polylogarithmic maintenance for all graph densities.

The inherited SODA 2026 theorem of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li gives deterministic exact \(n^{o(1)}\) amortized update time within a cut-size range bounded by \(2^{\Theta((\log n)^{3/4-\eta})}\), for fixed \(0<\eta<3/4\) in its parameter regime. It extends the earlier small-connectivity range. Both restrictions matter: the theorem does not cover every value up to \(n-1\), and a subpolynomial time bound need not be a fixed power of \(\log n\).

The word “subpolynomial” permits bounds that are larger than every polylogarithm; for example, \(2^{\sqrt{\log_2 n}}=n^{o(1)}\) eventually exceeds \((\log_2 n)^c\) for every fixed \(c\). Thus replacing “polylogarithmic” by “subpolynomial” would change the target even if exactness and the cut-size range were otherwise identical.

El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm instead maintains a \((1+o(1))\)-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. A multiplicative estimate with relative error \(\epsilon\) can have additive error \(\epsilon\lambda\). Integrality does not turn such a guarantee into exactness uniformly over large \(\lambda\); the approximation accuracy and its effect on running time remain essential.

Kenneth-Mordoch’s February 2026 preprint reports a canonical exact minimum-cut algorithm with polylogarithmic worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n)\) queries. Its query procedure constructs a sparse contracted graph and computes a cut on that graph before reporting the result. Consequently, its stated query bound is not just the cost of printing the cut’s vertices, and the theorem does not provide the polylogarithmic value query required here.

The SOSA 2026 paper by Kenneth-Mordoch and Krauthgamer gives another tradeoff: its publisher abstract states \(\widetilde O(n/\lambda)\) worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n^2/\lambda^2)\) worst-case queries for positive connectivity. This becomes efficient in the high-connectivity range, but it is not a polylogarithmic bound uniform over all positive values of \(\lambda\). Disconnected graphs are also part of the present target.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

The SOSA 2026 paper by Kenneth-Mordoch and Krauthgamer gives another tradeoff: its publisher abstract states \(\widetilde O(n/\lambda)\) worst-case updates and \(\widetilde O(n^2/\lambda^2)\) worst-case queries for positive connectivity. This becomes efficient in the high-connectivity range, but it is not a polylogarithmic bound uniform over all positive values of \(\lambda\). Disconnected graphs are also part of the present target.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

cards.title: Near-linear incremental topological ordering
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform Las Vegas randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) that maintains a topological order of an initially empty directed graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), under edge insertions promised to preserve acyclicity, with all the following guarantees? Order-comparison queries take \(O(1)\) worst-case time, space is \(O((n+m)(\log_2(n+2))^C)\) words for one fixed \(C\ge0\), and for every real \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(K_\eta>0\) such that
\[
\mathbb E[\text{initialization and update instructions through any prefix}]
\le K_\eta(n+m)^{1+\eta}.
\]
Here \(m\) is the number of insertions in that prefix, and \(n\ge2\). The same algorithm must meet all exponents; \(q\) comparison queries add at most \(K_Qq\) instructions for one absolute constant \(K_Q\).
cards.definitions:
The input begins with \(n\). An insertion supplies an ordered pair \((u,v)\) with \(u\ne v\) whose directed edge is not already present. There are no loops, repeated insertions or deletions. Every prefix graph is promised to have no directed cycle. No requirement is imposed on operations violating this promise. The algorithm is online: it is not given future edges or the final edge count. Any finite insertion/query sequence must be handled; that sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices.

After initialization and each insertion the algorithm must represent some strict total order \(\prec\) of all \(n\) vertices such that \(u\prec v\) for every present edge \((u,v)\). A query on vertices \(u,v\) returns the bit indicating \(u\prec v\), including zero when \(u=v\). Every query between two successive insertions refers to the same maintained order. The algorithm may choose a new valid total order at an insertion. It need not enumerate the entire order after each change, and a comparison is not a reachability query. Every returned answer and maintained order must be correct; initialization and insertions terminate almost surely. Queries terminate within their fixed worst-case instruction bound on every random tape.

The RAM has one finite program, word registers and word-addressed memory. For some fixed integer constant \(a\ge3\) chosen with the algorithm, a word has \(w=a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. One instruction may copy, read or write an addressed word, compare, branch, perform Boolean bit operations or logical shifts, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or compute integer quotient or remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts of at least \(w\) bits return zero. Addresses must fit a word; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. An instruction may generate one independent uniform random word. There is no advice, free table or input-dependent oracle. All initialization, allocation, preprocessing, retained graph data, temporary workspace and random seeds count toward time or space as appropriate.

The memory bound applies on every execution, including temporary workspace during an operation, with \(m\) counting edges submitted through that operation. One fixed constant bounds space uniformly over all inputs and prefixes. The expected-time bound includes initialization and every insertion in the selected prefix; it averages the algorithm's private randomness on the fixed operation sequence. Each \(K_\eta\) is independent of \(n,m,q\) and the sequence. It may depend on \(\eta\) and the one chosen algorithm. There is no amortized cost charged against a future insertion not yet present in the prefix, and no extra additive bound depending on the final sequence length. Query instructions are charged separately by the displayed linear bound. Thus the target is total update time \((n+m)^{1+o(1)}\), not necessarily \(O((n+m)\operatorname{polylog} n)\).

No prediction of the update sequence, special graph class, computational conjecture or additional source of randomness is supplied. The full stated RAM instruction set is allowed; an undefined restriction to combinatorial algorithms is not part of this question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this existence claim or its logical negation. A positive answer must use one algorithm for every \(\eta>0\), preserve the promised order and constant worst-case comparisons, and prove the stated prefix expectation and memory bounds. A family choosing a different algorithm for each fixed exponent, near-linear cycle detection without an order, or a prediction-dependent speedup does not establish this target. A negative answer must refute the full allowed randomized RAM claim; failure of one method or a conjecture-based lower bound alone is insufficient.
cards.why: Maintaining an actual vertex order remains a central gap between static graph processing and incremental graph maintenance, even as cycle detection itself has become almost linear.

cards.title: Polynomial-time query outside DynFO
cards.formal: Editorial uniform-initialization variant: is there an isomorphism-invariant polynomial-time Boolean query on some fixed finite relational vocabulary that is not maintainable by any first-order dynamic program with built-in order, addition and multiplication and first-order initialization from the empty input?
cards.definitions:
For each n≥1 the domain is {0,…,n−1}. The fixed input vocabulary contains finitely many relation symbols of fixed arities; initially each input relation is empty. One update inserts or deletes a single tuple in one relation. Redundant insertion and deletion are allowed. A Boolean query assigns a truth value to every finite nonempty input structure and is unchanged by renaming domain elements. Polynomial time means a uniform deterministic Turing algorithm on explicit relation-table encodings.

A dynamic program has a finite auxiliary relational vocabulary, with any fixed finite arities and a designated zero-ary answer relation. The built-ins are order < and ternary Add and Mult, where Add(a,b,c) means a+b=c<n and Mult(a,b,c) means ab=c<n, using ordinary nonmodular arithmetic. For every input relation and update kind, one first-order formula for each auxiliary symbol defines its new tuples from the old state and the changed tuple. Evaluation is simultaneous; quantifiers range over the unchanged finite domain. There are no auxiliary functions.

Initial auxiliary relations are defined by fixed first-order formulas using only equality and the built-ins. The formulas are uniform in n and histories. The answer must be correct initially and after every update prefix. The question asks for one query outside this class, not a family requiring progressively larger arity. This precisely selects FO initialization; it does not ask for separation against arbitrary noncomputable advice in the initial state.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a concrete polynomial-time query with a complete Lean-checked proof that no program in this model maintains it, or prove every polynomial-time query has such a program. A lower bound only against bounded auxiliary arity or quantifier-free updates is insufficient.
cards.why: An unconditional separation would establish a basic expressive limit of dynamic descriptive complexity.

cards.title: Worst-case polylogarithmic fully dynamic planarity testing
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic fully dynamic planarity structure with polylogarithmic worst-case edge-update time and constant-time planarity queries?
cards.definitions: Use a deterministic uniform word RAM with word width \(w=\Theta(\log(n+2))\) large enough to address the stated space and with no nonuniform advice. Use the [integer word instructions](definitions.html#ram) at width \(w\). The vertex set [n] is fixed, graphs are simple and undirected, and updates insert an absent edge or delete a present edge. The graph starts empty and all outputs must be correct for every legal update sequence. Intermediate graphs may be nonplanar. A graph is planar when its vertices and edges can be drawn in the plane so that edges meet only at common endpoints. After every update a query must return the exact Boolean planarity value; neither an embedding nor an obstruction is requested. Require initialization O(n log^c(n+2)), space O((n+m)log^c(n+2)) words for current edge count m, O(log^c(n+2)) time for every individual update, and O(1) time for every query, for one absolute c. Rejected insertions or a promise that the graph stays planar are not allowed. The structure must reclaim unused edge storage within the stated space bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of the specified correctness and resource guarantees, or prove that this precise target is impossible. A lower bound under an additional complexity hypothesis settles the negative answer only together with a proof of that hypothesis.
cards.why: This asks whether dynamic topological feasibility can avoid all occasional expensive updates.
