The audit preserves the uniform ordinary-monoid target and score 96, fixes complete word notation and encodings, and adds full Lean acceptance and later-result scope checks.

sentences: An ordinary one-relation monoid identifies words using one fixed reversible literal replacement rule in arbitrary surrounding contexts.
The question asks whether a single algorithm can decide equality of any two words when the alphabet and defining relation are also supplied.
Empty words and length-changing relations are allowed, and the algorithm must halt on unequal pairs as well as equal ones.
Recent undecidability results for inverse monoids, submonoid membership and equations with unknowns concern different or broader problems.
A resolution would locate a central decidability boundary for equality under minimal finite algebraic presentations.

cards.title: Sum-of-square-roots problem
cards.formal:
Does the sum-of-square-roots decision problem belong to deterministic polynomial time? An instance explicitly gives an integer \(n\ge1\), signed integers \(c_1,\ldots,c_n\), and positive integers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), all in binary. The required answer is whether
\[
E(c,a)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_i\sqrt{a_i}\ \ge0,
\]
where each square root is the nonnegative real square root. There is no promise that \(E\ne0\), that the radicands are distinct or square-free, or that their magnitudes are polynomial in \(n\). The target is one uniform deterministic algorithm with a polynomial bound in the total input bit length. This selects the standard algorithmic question explicitly stated in the newer sources; the original TOPP entry principally asks for tight separation bounds, a related quantitative question distinguished below.
cards.definitions:
For \(a>0\), \(\sqrt a\) denotes the unique real \(r\ge0\) with \(r^2=a\). Coefficients may be positive, negative or zero, and repeated terms are permitted. The comparison is exact: when \(E=0\) the answer is yes, however close a nonzero \(E\) is to zero. No approximate value of \(E\), promise of a numerical gap or factorization of the radicands is supplied.

Fix the following binary encoding. For an integer \(r\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(r+1\); its code is \(\ell\) one-bits, one zero-bit and the \(\ell\)-bit binary expansion of \(r+1\). A signed integer \(c\) is encoded by the code of \(2c\) if \(c\ge0\), and of \(-2c-1\) otherwise. A valid instance is the code for \(n\ge1\), followed by the signed code for \(c_i\) and the code for \(a_i\ge1\), for each \(i=1,\ldots,n\) in order, with no trailing bits. Write \(L\) for the full encoded length. Define the language \(Q\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) to consist exactly of valid encodings for which \(E(c,a)\ge0\); every malformed string is outside \(Q\).

Computation uses a deterministic multitape Turing machine with finite control, one read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes. Its fixed alphabet is \(\{0,1,\#,\square\}\), with \(\square\) blank. Tapes have nonnegative integer cell indices, all heads start at zero, and the input tape holds the input bits followed by blanks. One transition reads all scanned symbols, updates the state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; a left move at zero stays at zero. Two halting states output zero and one. Each transition costs one, including all parsing and arithmetic work. The program and number of tapes are independent of the instance. There is no advice, randomness, oracle, exact-real register or unit-cost square-root instruction.

The statement \(Q\in\mathrm{P}\) means
\[
\exists M\ \exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists d\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\
\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*}:
\]
the single machine \(M\) halts within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) transitions and outputs one exactly when \(x\in Q\). Thus the clock holds on every binary input, and all binary magnitudes contribute to the measured length. No running-time dependence exponential in \(n\), in the largest radicand or in its bit length is hidden in the polynomial constants.
cards.answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(Q\in\mathrm{P}\), or that \(Q\notin\mathrm{P}\), for the stated encoding and machine model. A positive answer must provide the one finite machine and polynomial constants and prove termination, the uniform time bound and both correctness directions on all inputs. A negative answer must show that for every such machine \(M\) and every \(C\ge1,d\ge0\), some binary input either is not answered within \(C(|x|+1)^d\) transitions or is answered incorrectly.

A proof for equality testing alone, unary inputs, a fixed number of terms, inputs separated from zero by a promised gap, or a unit-cost real-arithmetic model does not meet the criterion. Nor does a lower bound against a particular numerical procedure prove the negative answer. This is an unconditional yes/no complexity question: a conditional separation of complexity classes or a merely conditional algorithm does not decide it.
cards.why: This is a basic barrier between exact geometric algorithms and computation on finite binary inputs. A general polynomial-time comparison procedure would remove a recurring obstacle to placing geometric decision and verification tasks in familiar discrete complexity classes. The problem also connects algebraic-number representation, exact numerical computation and the complexity of arithmetic circuits.

references.title: PosSLP and Sum of Squares
references.authors: Markus Bläser; Julian Dörfler; Gorav Jindal
references.locator: FSTTCS 2024 article 13, published 5 December 2024. Problem 1.7 and its surrounding discussion on p. 13:3 define the sign-list square-root problem and state its relation to PosSLP. This is distinct from the later sum-of-squares problems for succinct integers studied in that paper.

cards.context:
Euclidean distances between points with integer coordinates are square roots of integers. Comparing the lengths of two routes therefore leads to sums of these quantities. Binary input represents the integers compactly, while the comparison may depend on a very small difference between real numbers. Exact equality is part of the problem, rather than an excluded case.

TOPP Problem 33 primarily asks for tight upper and lower bounds on the minimum nonzero gap between two \(k\)-term square-root sums whose radicands are bounded by an integer \(B\). Its motivation asks whether the number of bits needed to separate the sums is polynomial in \(k\) and \(\log B\). This card explicitly chooses the standard polynomial-time decision question from the newer primary literature instead of presenting that separation problem as equivalent to it.

A sufficiently strong uniform separation bound would imply an efficient exact comparison algorithm. The converse is not asserted: TOPP explicitly allows that a polynomial-time comparison algorithm could exist even if its proposed precision bound fails. The algorithmic target places no requirement on how an algorithm represents its intermediate computation.

The signed-integer coefficient convention is the one used by Eisenbrand, Haeberle and Singer. The sign-list formulation in other references has the same polynomial-time decision status under polynomially related binary encodings. The card does not restrict to geometric instances, unary magnitudes or square-free radicands.

The 2024 separation theorem has a positive factor depending on the full tuple of radicands, without an explicit uniform bound on that dependence. Its improved dependence on the coefficients does not itself give a polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary binary instances. The unary result of Balaji and Datta instead supplies polynomial-size circuits, or polynomial-length advice depending on the input length; this is a different guarantee from one uniform algorithm.

Testing whether the sum is exactly zero is known to be polynomial-time decidable. Distinguishing a positive sum from a negative one remains the extra requirement. Recent work on succinct arithmetic-program encodings and on efficient practical exact comparison addresses other models or guarantees.

Individual source reading and a bounded later-work check through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution. progress.text: The last listed TOPP revision records the separation problem and explicitly distinguishes a polynomial precision bound from the possibility of a polynomial-time sign algorithm.

Gaillard and Jindal distinguish the already polynomial-time equality problem for explicitly represented integers from generalized versions with arithmetic-program inputs. Their results for power series and succinct equality do not decide general sign comparison.

Balaji and Datta prove that the unary variant has polynomial-size circuit families, written \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\), in Theorem 1. Both the restricted magnitude regime and the allowed nonuniform advice differ from this card.

Eisenbrand, Haeberle and Singer explicitly state polynomial-time exact comparison as open. Theorem 6 improves separation as the integer coefficients vary while the radicands are fixed, with a non-explicit constant depending on those radicands.

Bläser, Dörfler and Jindal restate the signed-root decision problem and its relation to positivity of straight-line-program outputs. Their sum-of-squares results concern arithmetic-program problems and do not settle this decision problem.

The question is whether one deterministic algorithm can decide exactly whether its value is nonnegative in polynomial time.
All input magnitudes count toward the bit length, and zero or extremely small values are included.
The original separation-bound question, equality testing, unary inputs and nonuniform circuit results provide related context without settling this target.
A complete Lean proof must establish the uniform algorithm and its bound or prove that no such algorithm exists.

cards.title: Polynomial-time finite-group isomorphism in the Cayley-table model
cards.formal:
Is isomorphism of finite groups given by their complete multiplication tables decidable in deterministic polynomial time?

Precisely, do there exist one uniform deterministic machine \(A\) and integers \(C,c\ge1\) such that, on every binary input of length \(N\), \(A\) halts within \(C(N+1)^c\) steps and outputs YES exactly when the input encodes two finite groups \(G,H\) and there is a bijection \(\varphi:G\to H\) satisfying
\[
\forall x,y\in G,\qquad
\varphi(x\cdot_G y)=\varphi(x)\cdot_H\varphi(y)?
\]
The constants and program are independent of the orders and structure of both groups.
cards.definitions:
A table of order \(n\ge1\) is a function \(T:[n]\times[n]\to[n]\), given by listing every one of its \(n^2\) entries. It defines a group precisely when the following three conditions hold:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall x,y,z\in[n],\quad T(T(x,y),z)=T(x,T(y,z));\\
&\exists e\in[n]\ \forall x\in[n],\quad T(e,x)=x=T(x,e);\\
&\forall x\in[n]\ \exists y\in[n],\quad T(x,y)=e=T(y,x).
\end{aligned}
\]
The identity \(e\) in the inverse condition is the same identity supplied by the second condition. All entries already belong to \([n]\), so closure is part of the table definition. Commutativity is not required. A group of order one is allowed; an empty group is not.

The input contains tables \(T_G\) and \(T_H\) of orders \(n\) and \(m\), respectively. If \(n\ne m\), they cannot be isomorphic. When \(n=m\), an isomorphism uses one bijection on elements in all three positions of the multiplication equation. Independent permutations of table rows, columns and entries are not the definition of the predicate. The labels \(1,\ldots,n\) have no mathematical significance, and the identity need not have label one.

Encode a table by \(1^n0\), followed by its \(n^2\) entries in row-major order, each in exactly \(\ell_n=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits, using ordinary most-significant-bit-first binary. Each entry must be in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Concatenate exactly two such encodings, with no trailing bits. The input bit length is
\[
N=n+m+2+n^2\ell_n+m^2\ell_m.
\]
Malformed encodings, entries outside the indicated range and tables failing any group axiom are NO instances. Group axioms can be checked in polynomial time, so this total-language convention does not add a new algorithmic obstacle to the promised-group version.

The output is only the decision bit. An explicit isomorphism, a canonical table and generators of an automorphism group are not required. There is no restriction to abelian, solvable, nilpotent or prime-power-order groups, and no distinguished subgroups, generators or decompositions are supplied.

The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite tape alphabets. Its input tape is read-only; work tapes begin blank. Each transition accesses only the cells under the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. Parsing, checking the group axioms, accessing table entries, computing auxiliary data and returning the answer all count. There is no randomness, advice, oracle or free preprocessing.

Polynomial time is measured in the full explicit bit length \(N\). For equal-order groups this is polynomially equivalent to polynomial time in \(n\), since the table already has \(n^2\) entries. It is not polynomial time in \(\log n\), the length needed merely to name the group order. An input consisting only of generators, a presentation, matrices, permutations or oracle access to multiplication would define a different representation model.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked construction of \(A,C,c\), proving exact correctness and the polynomial worst-case bound on all encoded pairs and invalid strings; or supply a complete Lean-checked proof that no such deterministic polynomial-time decider exists. A lower bound for bounded-depth circuits or a restricted algorithmic method is not a lower bound for this entire machine class. An algorithm for only a proper family of groups, an average-case guarantee, a quasipolynomial bound or an unverified claimed general algorithm does not settle the target.
cards.why: Group isomorphism asks whether two complete finite algebraic structures differ only in their element names. Even with every multiplication available explicitly, a polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary groups has resisted decades of work. Resolving it would clarify both the complexity of finite algebra and a central algebraic special case of graph isomorphism.

cards.context:
The inherited source studies dynamic membership and isomorphism for abelian groups, but its introduction separately states the unrestricted static P-membership question. The card keeps that general question.

Before the November 2026 manuscript, the standard general bound was quasipolynomial in the group order. The August 2026 paper studies circuit depth and proves a lower bound for restricted depth.

The March 2026 preprint gives polynomial-time tests for several families of extensions of abelian groups, including abelian-by-cyclic groups. An abelian-by-cyclic group has an abelian normal subgroup whose quotient group is cyclic. This is a proper structural promise, absent from the target.

The corrected September 2026 result requires solvable groups with abelian Sylow subgroups. The solvability restriction is explicit in version 2; the broader wording of the first version is not the current theorem. The restricted family does not contain all finite groups.

A March 2026 preprint also claims a polynomial-time algorithm via quasigroup isomorphism. The November result has a separate group-theoretic proof.

For malformed input, first check the table dimensions, entries, associativity, identity and inverses. Testing associativity on all triples takes polynomial time in the explicit input size. On valid inputs of equal order the isomorphism coset is nonempty exactly for a YES instance.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
cards.formal: Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), some Boolean circuit with at most \(Cn\) gates computes the exact product of every pair of unsigned \(n\)-bit integers, outputting all \(2n\) product bits? The gates are binary AND and OR and unary NOT; fan-out and depth are unrestricted, and the circuit family need not be uniform.
cards.definitions:
The \(2n\) inputs are bits \(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1},b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1}\), representing
\[
a=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_i2^i,\qquad b=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_i2^i.
\]
The ordered output bits \(c_0,\ldots,c_{2n-1}\) must satisfy
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1}c_j2^j=ab
\]
on every input, including inputs with leading zeros. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose internal gates apply the stated Boolean operations. Constant sources 0 and 1 are available. Size counts operation gates, excluding input nodes, constant sources and output wires. Wires may copy a bit to arbitrarily many gates or outputs without an additional charge. There is no randomness, approximation or restriction on depth.

Let \(\operatorname{Mult}_n:\{0,1\}^{2n}\to\{0,1\}^{2n}\) be the multiplication function just defined. Its minimum gate count is \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(\operatorname{Mult}_n)\), using the shared [DM convention](definitions.html#boolean-circuits). The proposition is \(\operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(\operatorname{Mult}_n)=O(n)\). The same \(C\) bounds all sufficiently large widths, but each width may use a different circuit, with no requirement to compute the family’s descriptions. A machine instruction multiplying entire words is not one Boolean gate. Any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes this linear-size question only by constant factors.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed proposition or its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one constant \(C\), a threshold \(n_0\), and the existence of correct circuits at every \(n\ge n_0\). It need not give a uniform algorithm constructing their descriptions.

A negative proof must establish
\[
\forall C>0\;\forall n_0\ge1\;\exists n\ge n_0:\ \operatorname{CC}_{\mathrm{DM}}(\operatorname{Mult}_n)>Cn.
\]
It may give a stronger asymptotic lower bound, but such a stronger bound at every sufficiently large length is not required. A fixed linear lower bound, a bound only for restricted depth or wiring, or the failure of one multiplication construction does not settle the target. A conditional lower bound proves only its conditional statement.
cards.why: Determine whether multiplication has the same order of Boolean hardware complexity as addition, or provide an explicit superlinear lower bound in the unrestricted circuit model.

Binary addition has linear gate complexity. Whether multiplication enjoys the same bound is an explicit candidate for separating two elementary arithmetic tasks in an unrestricted circuit model.

The full product is required. Computing only a residue or selected output bits, or counting whole-word multiplication instructions, measures a different task.

The 2019 paper reports an \(O(n\log n)\) multiplication construction and proves a matching lower bound under the undirected network-coding conjecture, in its bounded-degree circuit model. The hypothesis is essential to that lower bound.

Viola’s current manuscript still asks whether linear-size multiplication is possible and establishes equivalence with linear-size squaring. The manuscript’s revision year is not the date when this longstanding question originated.

The target allows a different circuit at each input width. It therefore differs from TCS-7174, which asks about uniform running time on a multitape Turing machine.

cards.title: Tensor decomposition at Kruskal’s uniqueness threshold
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized algorithm that, for every real third-order tensor having a decomposition satisfying Kruskal’s condition, recovers its rank decomposition in polynomial time in the exact algebraic model specified below? More precisely, are there constants \(C,c>0\) and one finite program whose cost is at most \(C(N+1)^c\) on every run and whose probability of outputting a correct decomposition is at least \(2/3\) on every promised input, where \(N=n_1n_2n_3\) is the number of input entries? The number of components and all Kruskal ranks may grow with the dimensions and are not supplied to the program.
cards.definitions:
An input consists of positive integers \(n_1,n_2,n_3\) in binary and the explicitly listed real entries of an array \(T\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_2\times n_3}\), held in exact real registers. It is promised that, for some integer \(R\ge2\), there exist nonzero vectors \(a_j\in\mathbb R^{n_1}\), \(b_j\in\mathbb R^{n_2}\), \(c_j\in\mathbb R^{n_3}\), \(1\le j\le R\), such that \(T_{uvw}=\sum_{j=1}^{R}(a_j)_u(b_j)_v(c_j)_w\). Write \(A=[a_1|\cdots|a_R]\), and likewise \(B,C\). The Kruskal rank \(k_A\) is the largest integer \(k\in\{0,\ldots,R\}\) for which every choice of \(k\) distinct columns of \(A\) is linearly independent over \(\mathbb R\); the empty choice is independent. The promise is \(k_A+k_B+k_C\ge2R+2\). No hidden vectors, rank values, decomposition certificate, conditioning bound or generic-position assumption beyond this promise are provided.

Tensor rank is the minimum number of nonzero rank-one terms in any such sum over \(\mathbb R\). Kruskal’s theorem states that the promised \(R\) is the tensor rank and that its decomposition is unique up to reordering and componentwise nonzero rescaling. A valid output is \(R\) and three explicitly listed real factor matrices giving exactly \(T\). Permuting their columns together, or multiplying the three columns of component \(j\) by nonzero scalars whose product is \(1\), gives an equivalent output. Exact equality of all tensor entries is required; an approximation or a decomposition with more terms is not the specified output.

The computational model is an exact algebraic random-access machine with real registers and finite binary control. Copying, reading or writing a real register, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and comparison of two reals each cost one operation. The only built-in real constants are \(0\) and \(1\). Integer arithmetic and control use ordinary binary bit operations, which also count. The model additionally has a real-root operation: given an explicitly listed coefficient vector \((u_0,\ldots,u_m)\) of a nonzero univariate polynomial, it returns all distinct real roots in increasing order, at cost \(m+1\); the coefficient-list construction and output storage count separately. This degree-cost convention is equivalent for polynomial-time existence to charging any fixed polynomial in the degree. An identically zero polynomial, or a division by zero, must be detected and handled without an undefined operation.

Each random instruction draws one independent real uniformly from \([0,1]\), at unit cost. Probability is taken over the product of these draws; the total running-time bound must hold on every run, including exceptional draws, on which the program may return failure. The finite program is independent of dimensions and input entries and has no advice, arbitrary input-dependent constants, multivariate-system oracle, floor operation or transcendental primitive. All reads, output writes, root calls and integer work are charged. The guarantee is a worst-case input bound with bounded failure probability, not an average over input tensors. This is an algebraic operation bound: it does not assert a bit-complexity or numerical-conditioning guarantee for approximations to the real entries.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical benchmark asks for a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm with the stated polynomial cost and success guarantee for every promised tensor, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists in this precise model. A bound whose exponent depends on \(R\) or on a Kruskal rank does not establish a uniform polynomial bound. This record is archived after checking an affirmative algebraic-model result; the editorial verification does not itself supply a Lean formalization.
cards.why: Kruskal’s condition guarantees that latent factors are mathematically determined by their tensor, but uniqueness alone does not provide an efficient recovery algorithm. Polynomial-time recovery throughout that regime connects identifiability with computation in models used for learning and signal analysis.

The source asks about algorithms throughout Kruskal’s uniqueness regime and separately discusses robustness to noisy entries. This card selects the exact polynomial-time recovery question. The explicit real algebraic model, including univariate root finding, follows the model of the 2026 resolution and states the output convention that the original short question leaves implicit. In ICALP 2026, Bhargava, Schulman and Sivan proved a randomized \((n_1+n_2+n_3)^{O(k)}\) upper bound, where \(k=2R+2-\max\{k_A+k_B,k_A+k_C,k_B+k_C\}\). Sivan’s September 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time recovery under the more general Lovitz–Petrov condition. Its Theorem 2.1 applies, in particular, to every Kruskal-promised tensor. cards.title: Exact Kronecker-polytope membership in polynomial time
cards.formal:
Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-bit-time algorithm which, given three partitions \(\lambda,\mu,\nu\) of the same positive integer \(k\), each as a list of \(n\) nonnegative binary integers, decides whether
\[
\left(\frac{\lambda}{k},\frac{\mu}{k},\frac{\nu}{k}\right)\in\Delta_n,
\]
where \(\Delta_n\) is the Kronecker polytope defined below? The dimension \(n\) is part of the input, and membership is exact, including points on the boundary.
cards.definitions:
A partition in this representation is a list \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0\) of integers with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=k\). Trailing zeros are allowed. The lists \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) obey the same conditions and have the same sum. Division by \(k\) is coordinatewise. All entries and list lengths use binary encoding with fixed length delimiters; the complete lists are given explicitly. Let \(N\) be the total input bit length. In particular the number of parts grows with the input, while \(k\) may be exponentially large relative to its bit length.

Here is a self-contained spectral definition of \(\Delta_n\). For an array \(z=(z_{abc})_{a,b,c=1}^n\in\mathbb C^{n\times n\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{a,b,c}|z_{abc}|^2=1\), form three \(n\times n\) matrices
\[
R^{(1)}_{aa'}=\sum_{b,c}z_{abc}\overline{z_{a'bc}},\quad
R^{(2)}_{bb'}=\sum_{a,c}z_{abc}\overline{z_{ab'c}},\quad
R^{(3)}_{cc'}=\sum_{a,b}z_{abc}\overline{z_{abc'}}.
\]
The bar denotes complex conjugation. These matrices are Hermitian positive semidefinite and have trace 1. Write \(\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R)\) for the length-\(n\) list of real eigenvalues, with multiplicity, in nonincreasing order. Define
\[
\Delta_n=\left\{
\bigl(\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(1)}),
\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(2)}),
\operatorname{spec}_{\downarrow}(R^{(3)})\bigr):
z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n\times n},\ \sum_{a,b,c}|z_{abc}|^2=1
\right\}.
\]
This is the usual rational convex Kronecker polytope. The spectral definition is equivalent to the representation-theoretic definition in the source and specifies the question without requiring a representation-theory oracle. The tensor \(z\) is existentially quantified in the definition; it is not part of the input, need not have rational coordinates and need not be output by the algorithm.

The target algorithm is one deterministic multi-tape Turing machine \(A\) with constants \(K>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\), which halts on every valid input within \(K(N+1)^d\) steps and returns the exact membership bit. There is no advice, randomness, supplied list of facets, or oracle. All integer and rational arithmetic has its actual bit cost. No positive distance from the boundary is promised and no additive tolerance is allowed. A different precomputed algorithm for each fixed \(n\) is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that this exact membership language is in deterministic polynomial time, or a proof that it is not. A positive answer must establish the full variable-dimension bit bound and exact correctness on boundary points. An approximate tensor-scaling result polynomial in inverse error, a nondeterministic certificate bound, or a fixed-dimension polytope computation does not suffice.
cards.why: Kronecker polytopes connect representation-theoretic multiplicities with possible spectra of quantum subsystems. Exact efficient membership would go beyond known certificate bounds and numerical scaling methods while avoiding the harder task of evaluating individual multiplicities.

The original question varies the number of parts. Fixing the dimension would permit precomputation of a single polytope and would miss the requested uniform complexity.

The certificate theorem gives polynomially verifiable evidence for both membership and nonmembership. It does not supply a deterministic polynomial-time search for those certificates.

Membership corresponds to positivity after some common positive integer stretching of the three partitions. Positivity of the single unstretched Kronecker coefficient is a different problem.

The spectral model identifies the polytope with triples of reduced-state eigenvalue lists of a pure tripartite state. This gives an exact analytic formulation of the same input question.

The 2025 treatment records tensor-scaling time polynomial in inverse tolerance and a separation bound involving the partition denominator and dimension-dependent facet sizes. Combining them does not yield a polynomial bound in the binary input length.

cards.title: Polynomial-time computation of addition-chain length
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(K>0\), \(a\in\mathbb N\) and one deterministic multitape Turing machine that, on every positive integer \(n\) supplied in binary, outputs the exact shortest addition-chain length \(\ell(n)\) in binary within \(K(b+1)^a\) steps, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1\) is the input length?
cards.definitions:
An addition chain for \(n\ge1\) is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
\[
1=a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_r=n
\]
such that for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) there exist indices \(j,k\in\{0,\ldots,i-1\}\) with \(a_i=a_j+a_k\). The two indices may coincide, and an earlier entry may be reused any number of times. The length is the number \(r\) of additions, not the number \(r+1\) of entries. Define \(\ell(n)\) as the minimum such length; in particular, \(\ell(1)=0\). The only initially available number is \(1\). Subtraction, division, multiplication of chain entries and additional initial constants are not chain operations. The sum need not use the immediately preceding entry.

The machine receives just the ordinary binary expansion of \(n\), with no leading zeros. Its output is the ordinary binary expansion of the integer \(\ell(n)\), with \(0\) written as a single zero bit. The same finite program and constants must work for all valid inputs. The program has the usual unrestricted finite alphabet and binary work tapes of a multitape Turing machine, but all work, input reads and output writing count in its worst-case step bound. It has no advice, oracle, random bits or uncharged preprocessing. Invalid input strings must be rejected within the same bound with \(b\) interpreted as their string length. No addition chain or auxiliary number-theoretic data are supplied.

The requested machine may use any deterministic computation to find the length; the restrictions on chain operations define the quantity being optimized, rather than restricting the machine's internal calculations. The output is only the optimal length, not a chain attaining it. The input is a single binary target, not a list of targets and not a unary string of length \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of an algorithm and fixed polynomial bound satisfying the exact-output task for every \(n\ge1\), or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. Exact integer output is part of this computational existence question, not an extra accuracy restriction on a numerical-value benchmark. A fast approximation, a heuristic, polynomial time in \(n\) instead of its bit length, or a result for special targets does not meet the stated guarantee. Hardness for a single target under an additional hypothesis settles the negative answer only with a proof of that hypothesis. Hardness for several prescribed targets addresses a different input problem.
cards.why: Addition chains express reuse in multiplication-only exponentiation. Their optimal length is small enough to have short certificates, yet finding that length for an arbitrary binary exponent has resisted a general complexity classification.

cards.title: VP versus VNP
cards.formal:
Over the complex field \(\mathbb C\), do there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some arithmetic circuit with at most \(B(n+1)^k\) operation gates computes the permanent polynomial
\[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}\ \in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]?\]
Circuits are division-free, have binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates, allow arbitrary complex constants and unrestricted reuse, and compute exact formal polynomials. No uniform construction of the circuits is required. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\), with the classes defined below? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
cards.definitions:
Polynomial and parameter. For \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(S_n\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) consists of \(n^2\) independent commuting indeterminates. The displayed sum has one product for each permutation; each product chooses one variable in each row and column. Its total degree is \(n\). The growing parameter in the size bound is the matrix dimension \(n\), not the number of monomials or the magnitude of a numerical input. The number of input variables is \(N=n^2\).

Circuit model. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a distinguished output node. Each input node carries either one of the indeterminates or one exact constant from \(\mathbb C\). Each other node has two ordered incoming wires and a label \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\); the same preceding node may feed both incoming wires. A node is evaluated in the commutative polynomial ring by applying its operation to the polynomials at its two predecessors. An input node itself may be the output. The circuit's size \(s(D)\) is the number of operation nodes; input nodes are not counted. A computed value may feed arbitrarily many subsequent nodes at no additional gate cost. Cancellations are allowed. Neither depth nor the degrees of intermediate polynomials are restricted. All constants are freely selected as part of the finite circuit and may depend on \(n\); their numerical bit lengths, descriptions or computability are not charged. Each arithmetic operation costs one gate. This is an arithmetic circuit measure, not a Turing-machine bit-time model. Input constants supply no operation other than their fixed field value: there are no bit-extraction, comparison, branching, oracle or division gates. Approximation and limits of circuits are also outside this model.

Exact computation and families. A circuit computes \(f\) when its output equals \(f\) as an element of the polynomial ring, meaning that every monomial has the same coefficient. Agreement at a selected finite set of matrices is not the correctness definition. Let \(c_{\mathbb C}(f)\) be the minimum size of such a circuit for \(f\). Every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum is a nonnegative integer. In the main question the quantifier order is
\[\exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists D_n:\quad s(D_n)\le B(n+1)^k,\quad D_n\text{ computes }\operatorname{perm}_n.\]
The constants \(B,k\) are shared across all matrix dimensions. The circuits themselves may be unrelated from one dimension to the next: no machine, advice-generation procedure or polynomial-time algorithm for producing them is part of the assertion. Restricting constants to integers or rationals, or asking for a uniform family, would change this selected model.

Complexity classes. A sequence \(a(n)\) of nonnegative integers is polynomially bounded if some integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfy \(a(n)\le B(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). A polynomial family is a sequence \((m(n),f_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(m(n)\ge0\) and \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\); both \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_n\) must be polynomially bounded. Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; for this boundedness condition give the zero polynomial degree zero. The family lies in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) if \(c_{\mathbb C}(f_n)\) is polynomially bounded as well, using the circuit model above. These are bounds on the resulting polynomials, not extra syntactic degree bounds at circuit gates.

Such a family lies in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if there are a polynomially bounded witness length \(w(n)\in\mathbb N\) and a family
\[g_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)},y_1,\ldots,y_{w(n)}]\]
in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\), with combined variable counts and total degrees polynomially bounded in \(n\), such that
\[f_n(x)=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^{w(n)}}g_n(x,a).\]
Each Boolean witness is embedded into \(\mathbb C^{w(n)}\) using the field elements zero and one; the sum is a finite algebraic sum over exactly those witnesses, not an existential quantifier and not a sum over all complex tuples. If \(w(n)=0\), there is one empty witness, so \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\). No uniformity is imposed on these families or their circuit constants. Class equality means equality of these collections of polynomial families.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish common integers \(B,k\ge1\) and an appropriate finite circuit for every \(n\), with exact polynomial identity and the size bound in this model. A uniform construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative answer must prove
\[\forall B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad c_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)>B(n+1)^k.\]
Equivalently, the violating dimension can be required to exceed any specified lower threshold, since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed into the coefficient \(B\). The lower bound must cover every finite circuit with arbitrary complex constants, cancellations and reuse. A result proved via the class-equality formulation must include the equivalence to this concrete permanent target. A fixed polynomial lower bound, even superlinear in \(n^2\), is insufficient to prove the negation. Lower bounds confined to formulas, monotone circuits, fixed depth, or superpolynomial determinantal complexity do not by themselves establish the required general-circuit separation. A numerical approximation scheme, a border-limit construction, or a result only over another field does not supply the exact circuits quantified here.
cards.why: This is the central equality question for general arithmetic computation. It asks whether a polynomial-size algebraic computation can always absorb a sum over exponentially many Boolean witnesses, with the permanent serving as a complete concrete target. A separation would establish a general limitation despite arbitrary constants, cancellations and reuse; equality would give polynomial-size circuits for every polynomial family in VNP.

cards.context:
The permanent of a matrix sums the weights of its perfect matchings when rows and columns form the two sides of a bipartite graph. For a zero-one matrix it counts perfect matchings. Already in dimension two, \(\operatorname{perm}_2(X)=x_{11}x_{22}+x_{12}x_{21}\), while the determinant subtracts the second product. This card concerns the symbolic polynomial for all complex inputs.

The determinant contains the same permutation products with signs, yet has polynomial-size division-free circuits. Thus factorially many displayed terms do not force factorial circuit size. Reusing expressions and canceling terms are central powers of the model. Counting perfect matchings on binary inputs is a related Boolean counting problem, but that bit-complexity problem is not the same as allowing arbitrary complex constants at unit arithmetic cost.

Valiant’s completeness theorem makes the permanent universal for \(\mathrm{VNP}\) over fields of characteristic different from two. Each VNP family can be obtained from a polynomially larger permanent by substituting variables and field constants. This establishes the equivalence in the question over \(\mathbb C\). The field choice matters: in characteristic two the permanent and determinant coincide.

Ryser’s identity gives an exponential-size upper bound, including formulas using \(O(n^2 2^n)\) arithmetic operations. In contrast, a positive answer here requires one fixed polynomial bound for all dimensions. A formula is a circuit whose intermediate results cannot be shared; forbidding reuse can substantially increase the needed size.

Limaye, Srinivasan and Tavenas proved superpolynomial lower bounds for every constant circuit depth over characteristic-zero fields. Their hard polynomial is an iterated matrix product entry, which itself has polynomial-size unrestricted circuits. The low-depth theorem therefore illustrates the power of removing a depth restriction rather than proving VP different from VNP. The result first appeared in 2021 and was published in the Journal of the ACM in 2025.

The 1 August 2026 OpenAI manuscript reports a lower bound \(\Omega(n^2\log\log n)\) for unrestricted division-free circuits computing the permanent, and \(\Omega(n^4/\log n)\) for formulas, including formulas with valid divisions. The circuit model in Chapter 5 matches this card, but the bound is still polynomial in matrix dimension and hence does not separate VP and VNP. The release supplies Lean certificates; this review checked the mathematical statements and repository description without replaying or independently auditing those certificates.

Narayanan’s work, published on ECCC on 9 August 2026 after a July submission, reports improved superlinear lower bounds for certain sublogarithmic depths and explicit elusive curves of exponential degree. The manuscript explicitly explains that its current parameters do not establish VP different from VNP. These are results with stated depth and degree qualifications, not a general superpolynomial permanent lower bound.

A determinantal representation expresses a polynomial as \(\det A(x)\), where every matrix entry is an affine linear form in its variables. Its minimum matrix dimension measures a more restricted representation than an arbitrary arithmetic circuit. A superpolynomial bound on that dimension alone does not settle this card; polynomial-size general circuits can be simulated by determinantal representations of quasipolynomial size. Exact representation must also be distinguished from taking limits of such representations.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint gives deterministic polynomial bit-time approximation of the permanent of nonnegative rational matrices within a factor \(\exp(O(n(\log\log n)^2/\log n))\). This is a recent algorithmic advance for numerical approximate counting. Its input restriction and multiplicative-error guarantee do not give exact formal-polynomial circuits over \(\mathbb C\).

cards.title: Superpolynomial arithmetic formula lower bounds
cards.formal:
Is the permanent family outside polynomial-size arithmetic formulas over \(\mathbb C\)? Precisely, is the following assertion true?
\[
\forall K,C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\forall F,\qquad
\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n
\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{size}(F)>K n^C,
\]
where \(F\) ranges over the arithmetic formulas defined below and
\[
\operatorname{Perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}
\in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:i,j\in[n]]?
\]
This card fixes the standard complex-field \(\mathrm{VNP}\)-versus-formula interpretation of the source’s broadly phrased explicit lower-bound challenge. By the permanent’s completeness under polynomially bounded projections, this asks whether some family in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) lacks polynomial-size formulas; it does not impose a separate uniform construction condition on the family of small formulas being ruled out. The source’s Open Problem 8 does not itself name a field or a particular hard family, so this precise choice is an explicit editorial specification.

Superpolynomial means that no single polynomial bound works for all dimensions. It does not demand one particular exponential rate or an eventually pointwise lower bound exceeding every polynomial. There are \(n^2\) input variables; \(n\) in the displayed size bound is the matrix dimension.
cards.definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge1\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \([n]\), and let \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) be a matrix of distinct commuting indeterminates. The permanent is the displayed sum with coefficient one on every permutation monomial. Equality of outputs is equality of formal polynomials, including all coefficients; there is no numerical input distribution, approximation error or promise on matrix entries.

An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted ordered binary tree. Each leaf is labelled by one variable \(x_{ij}\) or one constant in \(\mathbb C\); each internal vertex is labelled \(+\) or \(\times\). Its output \(\llbracket F\rrbracket\) is defined recursively by the corresponding operations in the polynomial ring. Every vertex other than the root has exactly one parent. Reusing an expression requires another copy of its subtree. A sum or product with more than two operands must be expanded into binary operations and its full tree is counted.

The size is the total number of vertices, including every occurrence of each constant and variable. Thus a leaf has size one and a binary node with subformulas \(A,B\) has size \(1+\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(B)\). This is one plus the edge count used by the original survey, an equivalent convention for polynomial boundedness. Arbitrary negative and nonreal constants are allowed; subtraction can be expressed using a constant \(-1\) and the permitted operations. There is no division gate, exponentiation gate, Boolean operation, test, conditional branch or determinant gate.

Constants have unit size regardless of their magnitude, algebraic degree, computability or description length. The finite tree and its constants may depend arbitrarily on \(n\); no algorithm for generating them and no finite binary encoding of arbitrary complex constants is required. A formula is a finite mathematical object with complex labels, not a bit-cost algorithm for evaluating a numerical matrix. There is no restriction on depth, cancellation, intermediate degree, repeated variables, monotonicity or homogeneity of intermediate polynomials. The output permanent is multilinear, but its subformulas need not be multilinear.

Define
\[
L_{\mathrm{perm}}(n)=\min\{\operatorname{size}(F):\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n\}.
\]
A finite formula exists by expanding the defining sum, so this integer minimum is well defined. The assertion is \(\forall K,C\ge1\ \exists n\ge1:\ L_{\mathrm{perm}}(n)>K n^C\). All finite initial exceptions to a prospective polynomial upper bound can be absorbed by increasing \(K\). Replacing \(n\) by the variable count \(n^2\) in the phrase polynomial size gives the same class of bounds.

For clarity, the class interpretation uses the following nonuniform algebraic definitions. A polynomial family \((f_t)_{t\ge1}\), with \(f_t\in\mathbb C[z_1,\ldots,z_{v(t)}]\), is in \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\) if its variable counts, degrees and formula sizes are bounded by fixed polynomials in \(t\). It is in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if its variable count is polynomially bounded and there is a polynomially bounded witness count \(w(t)\) and a family \(g_t(z,y)\) of polynomial degree and polynomial-size arithmetic circuits such that
\[
f_t(z)=\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{w(t)}}g_t(z,b).
\]
Here a circuit uses the same inputs and binary operations as a formula, but may share intermediate results in a finite directed acyclic graph. All bounds in these class definitions use constants independent of \(t\), while circuits and constants may depend on \(t\). The zero polynomial may be assigned degree zero for these bounds. A polynomially bounded projection substitutes variables or field constants into a member of another family whose index is polynomially bounded in \(t\). The direct permanent assertion is the acceptance target; these definitions explain its class-theoretic scope without adding an algorithmic requirement.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed assertion or its full negation for the specified formula model.

A positive answer must prove failure of every polynomial upper bound, with the quantifier order \(\forall K,C\ \exists n\ \forall F\) in the statement. A proof for another family suffices only if its implications for this exact target are also proved. One fixed polynomial lower bound, even with a larger exponent than all currently cited bounds, does not establish the assertion.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\exists K,C\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\
\exists F:\quad
\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Perm}_n
\ \land\ \operatorname{size}(F)\le K n^C.
\]
The same constants work for every dimension; individual formulas and complex constants may vary with the dimension. A uniform construction is sufficient if it meets the size guarantee, but is not an additional obligation.

A lower bound only for fixed depth, monotone formulas, multilinear subformulas, bounded coefficients, or noncommuting variables does not by itself cover the formulas in this card. A polynomial-size circuit permitting shared intermediate results does not by itself provide the required formula upper bound. The numerical \(1/100\) tolerance does not change this asymptotic class-separation question.
cards.why: Separating polynomial-size formulas from VNP would establish a basic limit of unrestricted algebraic expression trees for an explicit central polynomial. Formulas already allow arbitrary constants and cancellations, so their limitations are considerably harder to prove than those of many restricted algebraic models. This is a foundational lower-bound target within the hierarchy of algebraic complexity and is weaker than separating unrestricted circuits from VNP.

cards.title: Permanent versus determinant
cards.formal: Over \(\mathbb C\), is the determinantal complexity of the permanent not bounded above by any polynomial? Precisely, writing \(d_n=\operatorname{dc}_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)\) as defined below, is it true that for every triple of integers \(B,k,N\ge1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(d_n>B(n+1)^k\)? The matrices in the definition are unrestricted exact affine-linear representations over \(\mathbb C\).
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) consist of \(n^2\) algebraically independent commuting variables over \(\mathbb C\). Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}\). For any \(m\times m\) matrix \(M\) over a commutative ring, \(\det(M)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{a=1}^m M_{a,\pi(a)}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{|\{(a,b):a<b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}|}\). Define \(d_n\) to be the least integer \(m\ge1\) for which there exist constant matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}\), one \(A_{ij}\) for each input variable, such that \[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}A_{ij}\right)\] as an identity in \(\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]\). Thus every entry is a constant plus an arbitrary complex linear combination of all input variables. Equality means equality of every coefficient, equivalently equality for every complex assignment, not just Boolean assignments. Finite representations exist, so the minimum is defined; for example the known bound \(d_n\le2^n-1\) suffices. The resource is the matrix dimension \(m\), not its number of entries, coefficient bit lengths or time to find the matrices. Constants can be arbitrary complex numbers, independently for each \(n\), with no computability or uniform construction requirement. Variables may be reused in any number of entries. No symmetry, sparsity, rank condition on \(A_0\), sign restriction, read-once property or restriction on cancellation is imposed. A limit of determinants is not an exact representation unless some permitted matrix already has determinant equal to the permanent. Since every \(d_n\) is finite, the formal assertion is equivalent to nonexistence of integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfying \(d_n\le B(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\ge1\): finitely many exceptions to an upper bound can be absorbed into \(B\). The stated lower-bound quantifiers require arbitrarily large violating indices for every proposed polynomial, not eventual domination of that polynomial at every sufficiently large index.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified lower-bound proposition, or of its logical negation: there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) there exist an integer \(1\le m\le B(n+1)^k\) and complex matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity above. A negative answer may prove existence of this nonuniform family without an algorithm to generate its constants. A positive answer must exclude all allowed affine-linear matrices for the relevant \(n,m\), including those that break the permanent’s symmetries. A fixed-degree polynomial lower bound, a bound restricted to real coefficients or a restricted matrix class, or a lower bound for a different polynomial does not prove the proposition. A polynomial-size limiting representation alone does not refute this exact target.
cards.why: The permanent and determinant have almost identical permutation formulas, but the determinant is a basic efficiently computable polynomial whereas the permanent encodes algebraic counting. This conjecture asks whether enlarging the matrix and changing all its entries to affine forms can bridge that difference at polynomial cost. A superpolynomial lower bound would exclude an entire central model of algebraic computation, including polynomial-size algebraic branching programs and formulas.

cards.context:
The determinant attaches a permutation sign to each product that the permanent sums without signs. Simply changing signs on the original \(n\times n\) matrix is a very special representation; this card permits arbitrarily larger matrices and arbitrary affine entries. Its size parameter is \(n\), while the number of independent input variables is \(n^2\). Polynomial boundedness in either parameter is equivalent, but the distinction matters when describing a quadratic lower bound.

An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source and sink, whose edges carry affine-linear forms; it computes the sum, over source-to-sink paths, of the products of their edge labels. Polynomial-size branching programs and polynomial-size determinantal representations simulate each other with polynomial overhead. General arithmetic circuits are directed acyclic computations using addition and multiplication and may reuse earlier results more freely. The algebraic class \(\mathrm{VP}\) permits polynomial-size circuits for families with polynomially bounded degree and number of variables; \(\mathrm{VNP}\) additionally permits summation over polynomially many Boolean variables. The permanent is complete for \(\mathrm{VNP}\). A polynomial-size determinant family for it would imply \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VNP}\), but the requested superpolynomial determinant lower bound by itself is not a separation from every unrestricted arithmetic circuit.

Mignon and Ressayre’s characteristic-zero theorem gives \(d_n\ge n^2/2\), while Grenet’s construction gives \(d_n\le2^n-1\). The quadratic lower bound is only linear in the permanent’s \(n^2\) variables and falls short of excluding every polynomial. The 2026 Bogart–Valero introduction still presents a quadratic-versus-exponential gap for the ordinary permanent; its new bounds concern generalized permanent families. Historical or recent bounds for another polynomial are not automatically permanent bounds.

Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8 proves the \(2^n-1\) lower bound for \(n\ge3\) when a representation respects the action of left multiplication by permutation and invertible diagonal matrices, and Grenet’s construction meets it. This theorem restricts how symmetries of the input polynomial lift to the representation. It imposes more than the exact identity defining \(d_n\). No symmetry requirement of this kind is part of the question.

Orzel and coauthors define a Boolean sum by first identifying all selected variable positions with one new variable \(y\), then adding the results for \(y=0\) and \(y=1\). This is a two-term sum, even when two positions are selected. Their Theorem 6 proves that for at most two selected positions the permanent can absorb this operation through a simple projection with dimension increased by at most three, while no fixed additive dimension increase works uniformly for the determinant. A simple projection substitutes constants or individual variables and uses each surviving variable at most once, allowing a nonzero overall scalar. This restricted, constant-additive-cost distinction leaves the unrestricted polynomial-size affine representations in this card open.

Border determinantal complexity also admits coefficientwise limits of fixed-dimension determinant representations; their matrix coefficients may vary and become unbounded along the limit. It is at most exact determinantal complexity. Thus a border lower bound implies the same exact lower bound, while an exact lower bound does not automatically exclude limiting representations. Changing the coefficient field also changes the model: allowing \(\mathbb C\) can reduce complexity compared with \(\mathbb R\), and in characteristic two the permanent equals the determinant. These variants cannot silently replace the fixed complex-field target.

Sheshadri’s June 2026 preprint claims a quadratic border lower bound for the diagonal power sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^n\). That polynomial has \(n\) variables and is not the \(n\times n\) permanent. The inspected theorem therefore does not close this card’s gap, regardless of its stronger dependence on the number of variables. The preprint proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\)? More explicitly, let \((m_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) be any family with integers \(m_n\ge0\) and commutative polynomials \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m_n}]\). Suppose that some positive integer \(a\) satisfies \[m_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad \deg f_n\le(n+2)^a,\qquad c(f_n)\le(n+2)^a\quad\text{for all }n\ge1,\] where \(c\) is minimum arithmetic-circuit size in the model below. Must there exist a positive integer \(b\), depending on the whole family, such that \[\operatorname{abp}(f_n)\le(n+2)^b\quad\text{for all }n\ge1?\] Computation is exact and nonuniform over the complex field, and the competing branching programs are unrestricted.
cards.definitions:
A polynomial is a finite complex linear combination of commutative monomials in the listed variables. Its total degree is the maximum sum of exponents among nonzero monomials, with degree zero assigned to the zero polynomial. An arithmetic circuit is a finite acyclic graph with one designated output. Input gates are labelled by one listed variable or one arbitrary complex constant. Every other gate has two ordered input ports and is labelled by addition or multiplication in the polynomial ring; both ports may refer to the same predecessor, and any predecessor may be reused. There are no division gates. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires, counting each input port’s wire separately; constant and variable input gates each have unit cost. Intermediate degrees are not separately bounded: the degree hypothesis is on the output polynomial after cancellations. The minimum of this size among circuits computing \(f\) is \(c(f)\).

An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic multigraph with distinct designated vertices \(s,t\), no edges entering \(s\), and no edges leaving \(t\). Each edge \(e\) is labelled by an affine form \(\lambda_e=\alpha_{e,0}+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\alpha_{e,j}x_j\), with arbitrary complex coefficients. It computes \(\sum_{\pi:s\leadsto t}\prod_{e\in\pi}\lambda_e\), where distinct paths include their edge choices and an empty sum is zero. Its size is \[|V|+|E|+\sum_{e\in E}\left(\mathbf1_{\alpha_{e,0}\ne0}+2\bigl|\{j\in[m]:\alpha_{e,j}\ne0\}\bigr|\right).\] Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), including the empty set if \(m=0\), and \(\mathbf1_P\) is one when \(P\) holds and zero otherwise. Thus every nonzero scalar coefficient and its variable occurrence are charged; labels are not arbitrary polynomial oracles. There is no width, layering, variable-order, read-once, syntactic multilinearity, symmetry, homogeneity or monotonicity requirement. The minimum size computing \(f\) is \(\operatorname{abp}(f)\).

Both minima concern formal polynomial identities, not agreement on finitely many inputs or convergence of coefficients. Sizes count algebraic objects and field elements, not bits encoding complex numbers; coefficients need not have bounded or computable bit descriptions. No algorithm generating a family’s circuits, programs or constants is required. Every polynomial has finite representations in both models. Positive integer exponents in \((n+2)^a\) absorb multiplicative constants and finitely many initial values of any polynomial bound. The families meeting the circuit hypotheses define \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\); polynomially many variables and a polynomial ABP bound define \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\). ABP size already bounds output degree, and ABPs have polynomial-size circuit simulations, so only the displayed converse inclusion is at issue.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed inclusion or its negation, with the specified field, polynomial identities, resource accounting and quantifiers. A positive proof establishes a polynomial ABP bound for every family satisfying the circuit and degree hypotheses; it need not produce an efficient uniform converter. A negative proof establishes one family \((m_n,f_n)\) and one fixed positive integer \(a\) satisfying all three circuit-side bounds, but such that \[\forall b\ge1\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N,\quad \operatorname{abp}(f_n)>(n+2)^b.\] The lower bound must cover every permitted ABP over \(\mathbb C\), including arbitrary constants, reuse of variables and cancellations. There is no required effective generator for a separating family. A lower bound in a restricted ABP model, a family of exponential output degree, or a border-complexity separation does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: The question compares unrestricted arithmetic circuits with path-sum computation inside the class of efficiently representable polynomials. Equality would make polynomial-size determinants of affine matrices sufficient to express every polynomial-degree circuit family. Inequality would establish a fundamental separation within efficient algebraic computation, isolating power supplied by general multiplication together with reuse of intermediate results.

cards.context:
Circuits combine previously computed polynomials by both addition and multiplication, with unrestricted reuse. An ABP records sums of products along paths with affine labels. ABPs are polynomially equivalent to skew circuits, where each multiplication gate has at least one operand that is an input variable or constant. The conjectural gap concerns the size of exact representations under these two forms of computation, rather than which individual polynomials can be represented at all.

The polynomial-degree condition is essential. Small general circuits can have output degree exponential in their size, whereas an ABP with affine labels has degree at most its longest source-to-sink path. Such degree alone cannot separate the classes in this card because it is explicitly required to stay polynomial. The stated bounds concern the final polynomial; intermediate cancellations and degrees in a competing circuit are allowed.

Determinants give an equivalent structural description of \(\mathrm{VBP}\): a family belongs to this class exactly when it has representations \(f_n=\det(A_{n,0}+\sum_j x_j A_{n,j})\) with polynomially bounded matrix dimension and complex constant matrices. The determinant itself admits polynomial-size ABPs. Thus \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VBP}\) would make determinants universal for the circuit families in the statement. This is distinct from permanent versus determinant: the permanent is not known to have the polynomial-size general circuits required on the easy side of a separation here.

The classical Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction yields quasipolynomial simulations among formulas, ABPs and circuits for polynomial-degree families. The ITCS 2024 paper recalls that their quasipolynomial versions coincide, where a quasipolynomial bound means \(n^{(\log n)^{O(1)}}\). A polynomial bound \(n^{O(1)}\) is stronger. Approximation in coefficient space also defines separate border-complexity classes and does not supply an exact ABP identity.

Sinhababu and Thierauf prove factor closure over fields of characteristic zero: every factor of a nonzero polynomial with ABP size \(s\) has ABP size polynomial in \(s\). The result appeared at CCC 2020 and in Computational Complexity in October 2021. This gives ABPs a closure property already known for general circuits, without equating the models. The revised factoring survey of June 2026 still records that no inclusion in \(\mathrm{VF}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}\) is known to be strict.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt separate symmetric analogues of these three classes in their STOC 2026 work. Three differences matter: their polynomials obey a prescribed matrix-variable symmetry, their circuits are measured by the largest orbit of gates rather than total size, and their symmetric classes have no polynomial degree bound. The symmetry action must extend from input variables to the computation. These classes therefore cannot simply be substituted for the unrestricted classes in this card. The skew class is named symVBP in the January preprint and symVS in the conference abstract. Their additional completeness results for homomorphism polynomials are separate from an unconditional ordinary VP–VBP separation.

The January 2026 report by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff studies syntactically multilinear ABPs: on each source-to-sink path, a variable appears in at most one affine edge label. It characterizes aspects of a restricted lower-bound measure and recovers a separation of multilinear formulas from multilinear ABPs. Its own introduction still leaves superpolynomial lower bounds for general multilinear ABPs open. In this card even an output that happens to be multilinear may be computed using nonmultilinear intermediate expressions and cancellations. Lower bounds excluding those representations do not establish the unrestricted target.

The size conventions here make the algebraic model explicit. Counting all affine-label occurrences and using binary circuit gates changes customary vertex-only or edge-only presentations by polynomial overhead in the representation size and number of variables. It does not impose bit complexity or uniform constructibility on field constants. A complete answer must preserve these distinctions; a theorem about a min-plus semiring or a fixed-width program would concern different allowed operations or representations.

cards.title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
cards.formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(K,C\) such that for every integer \(n\ge1\) there is an arithmetic formula \(F_n\) over \(\mathbb C\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{size}(F_n)\le K n^C,\qquad \llbracket F_n\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n(X),\]
where \(\llbracket F_n\rrbracket\) is its output as a formal commutative polynomial and
\[\operatorname{Det}_n(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\pi(i)}?\]
The formula is a binary expression tree with arbitrary complex constants and addition, subtraction and multiplication. Computations may use cancellations, but intermediate expressions cannot be shared. The same constants \(K,C\) must work for all dimensions.
cards.definitions:
Polynomial and parameters. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) has \(n^2\) distinct commuting indeterminates as its entries. The positive integer \(n\) is the matrix dimension, not the number of variables. The set \(S_n\) consists of all permutations of \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Define \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}\), where \(\operatorname{inv}(\pi)\) counts pairs \(i<j\) with \(\pi(i)>\pi(j)\). All calculations take place in the polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[x_{11},\ldots,x_{nn}]\). In particular \(\operatorname{Det}_1=x_{11}\); no invertibility or numerical-entry promise is imposed.

Formula syntax and evaluation. A formula is a finite rooted binary tree with ordered children. A leaf is labelled by one input variable or one constant in \(\mathbb C\). Each internal node is labelled \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\) and computes the corresponding operation on the two child polynomials; subtraction uses left child minus right child. The root’s polynomial is denoted \(\llbracket F\rrbracket\). Every node other than the root has exactly one parent. Repeated uses of an expression therefore require separate copies of its entire subtree. No powers, determinants, summations or other compound expressions are primitive gates: any such shorthand in a proposed family must expand to allowed binary nodes.

Size. Every node counts once, including each occurrence of a variable or constant. Equivalently, a leaf has size one and a node with children \(A,B\) has size \(1+\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(B)\). Distinct leaves carrying the same value count separately. Define
\[L_{\det}(n)=\min\{\operatorname{size}(F):\llbracket F\rrbracket=\operatorname{Det}_n\}.\]
The set is nonempty by the finite permutation expansion, so this positive-integer minimum exists. The question is whether \(L_{\det}(n)\) is bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). Allowing real constants in a size bound rather than positive integer \(K,C\) would give the same polynomial-boundedness claim.

Constants and nonuniformity. Each constant leaf has unit size regardless of its magnitude, algebraic degree or description length. Constants and the tree may depend arbitrarily on \(n\), and complex constants need not be computable or rational. They cannot depend on the values later substituted for input variables. There is no algorithmic or efficiency requirement for generating the family, and no bit-cost bound on its representation: the resource is algebraic tree size. The field \(\mathbb C\) is fixed throughout; the target is not a simultaneous assertion for all fields.

Exact unrestricted computation. The equality at the root is an exact polynomial identity, coefficient by coefficient. Approximation of coefficients, a limit of formulas or correct evaluation only on a restricted input set does not meet it. Division, inverses, comparisons, branching, input-dependent constants and additional input variables are not allowed. There is no restriction on depth, homogeneity, signs or coefficient magnitudes. Intermediate polynomials may have powers or monomials absent from the determinant, provided they cancel in the final identity. A polynomial is multilinear if every variable has exponent at most one in every monomial. The output determinant is multilinear, but the formula is not required to be multilinear at intermediate nodes.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, prove the existence of allowed formula trees for every dimension, their exact determinant identity, and one common polynomial size bound. A uniform construction is welcome but is not required by this nonuniform target. Count all copied subtrees and constant occurrences.

A negative answer must prove
\[\forall K,C\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\ge1:\ L_{\det}(n)>K n^C.\]
It must cover arbitrary complex constants and all unrestricted intermediate computations permitted above. Equivalently, for every \(K,C,N\ge1\), there must be some \(n\ge N\) violating that polynomial bound; finitely many exceptional dimensions can always be absorbed into its constant. It is not necessary to prove that every sufficiently large dimension violates every given polynomial, a stronger eventual-growth claim.

A fixed-power lower bound, such as \(\Omega(n^3)\), leaves larger polynomial bounds possible. Lower bounds only for multilinear, homogeneous, symmetric, monotone, bounded-depth, bounded-coefficient or noncommutative computations do not refute the stated unrestricted commutative claim. An exact identity using a small circuit with shared intermediate results is not yet a small formula, and a large size for one particular determinant expansion is not a lower bound for all formulas. A proof conditional on an unresolved separation must keep that assumption explicit and does not settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: The canonical test of whether reusing intermediate expressions gives a superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic expression trees, even for an efficiently computable polynomial.
