references.title: A primer on the closure of algebraic complexity classes under factoring
references.authors: C. S. Bhargav; Prateek Dwivedi; Nitin Saxena
references.locator: TR25-083 revision 1, 12 June 2026; full §7.1, Definition 7.2, Remark 7.3 and pp.53–54 checked; includes 2025 formula-factoring progress while expressly leaving small symbolic determinant formulas unknown

cards.context:
The determinant is computationally easy when an algorithm may save intermediate work and reuse it. A formula imposes a stricter discipline: each computed quantity has only one consumer. To use the same expression twice, the expression must be copied. This can turn a compact computation graph into a much larger tree. The problem asks whether the determinant has an alternative expression that avoids this potential blow-up.

The permutation expansion has \(n!\) summands, but this does not prove that every formula is large. A product of short sums may represent many expanded monomials. For example, the \(2\times2\) determinant is \(x_{11}x_{22}-x_{12}x_{21}\), represented by seven nodes in the stated model. The challenge is one size bound for all dimensions, not finding finite expressions for individual matrices. Numerical Gaussian elimination also does not directly answer the symbolic tree-size question: its usual implementation reuses intermediate entries, divides and chooses pivots.

Berkowitz’s division-free construction gives polynomial-size arithmetic circuits of depth \(O(\log ^{2} n)\). Unfolding a bounded-fan-in circuit of that depth into a tree gives a formula of size \(2^{O(\log ^{2} n)}=n^{O(\log  n)}\). This is quasipolynomial, already far below the permutation expansion, but still larger than a fixed power of n. A polynomial-size formula would close this remaining gap.

The determinant is complete for polynomial-size algebraic branching programs. Such a program is a directed acyclic graph with a source and sink; affine-linear edge labels are multiplied along paths and the path products are summed. The class \(\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\) consists of polynomial families with polynomially many variables, polynomial degree and polynomial-size branching programs, while \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\) uses formula trees. Every formula has a polynomial-size branching program, and every such branching program has a polynomial-size determinant representation. Thus the existence claim here is equivalent to \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\).

The larger class \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) permits polynomial-size arithmetic circuits, where gates may have several consumers, while retaining polynomially many variables and polynomial degree. The June 2026 factoring primer records \(\mathrm{VF}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VBP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) without a known strict containment. It includes recent closure results for factoring formulas and still expressly leaves small determinant formulas unresolved. A positive answer here would identify the first two classes; it would not alone identify either with \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\).

An unrestricted lower bound is known, but it is only a fixed power. Kalorkoti proves \(\Omega (n^{3})\) formula size for the n by n determinant, even in a model allowing division. Here n is the matrix dimension; there are \(n^{2}\) independent variables. Thus the bound is cubic in dimension and only a power \(3/2\) in the number of variables. It must not be described as a cubic lower bound in the input-variable count.

Raz proves a much stronger \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) lower bound when every intermediate polynomial is multilinear. This restriction is substantive even though the final determinant is multilinear. For a simple illustration, \((x+y)^{2}- x^{2}- y^{2}\) equals 2xy, a multilinear output obtained through nonmultilinear intermediate terms. The example does not establish a size advantage, but it shows why output multilinearity alone cannot justify applying a theorem that assumes multilinearity throughout a computation.

Recent progress tests which determinant features are needed for that restricted lower bound. Boyapati, Chillara and Vempati prove the existence of sparse n by n symbolic matrices with only \(\Theta (n \log ^{6} n)\) nonzero entries whose determinants still require \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\) multilinear formulas. This shows that the dense \(n^{2}\)-variable presentation is not essential to Raz’s obstruction. It leaves the permission to use nonmultilinear intermediate computations untouched.

The question also organizes complexity outside generic matrices. Chaugule and coauthors connect small formulas for Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to small formulas for the general determinant. Such reductions make the determinant a useful benchmark for whether apparently special algebraic expressions really admit efficient tree computations. A separation would reveal a basic cost of forbidding reuse, already within problems that possess efficient arithmetic circuits.

cards.title: Shub–Smale \(\tau\)-conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist an integer \(C\geq1\), independent of the polynomial, such that every nonzero \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) satisfies \[z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq(1+\tau(f))^C,\] where \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\) is the number of distinct integer roots and \(\tau(f)\) is the minimum number of additions, subtractions and multiplications needed to construct \(f\) from only \(1\) and \(x\)?
cards.definitions:
The ring \(\mathbb Z[x]\) consists of formal univariate polynomials with integer coefficients. A straight-line program of length \(s\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) starts with registers \(g_0=1\) and \(g_1=x\). For each \(i=2,\ldots,s+1\), it chooses \(j_i,k_i<i\) and one operation from \(\{+,-,\times\}\), and sets \(g_i=g_{j_i}\mathbin{\circ_i}g_{k_i}\). Operands may coincide, and an earlier register may be used arbitrarily many times. One register is designated as output. The program computes \(f\) if this output equals \(f\) as a formal polynomial. Define \(\tau(f)\) to be the least possible \(s\) among such programs. Every integer polynomial can be constructed in finitely many operations, so this minimum exists. When \(s=0\), only \(1\) or \(x\) can be output.

Every new arithmetic register costs one operation, including operations used to build integer constants. In particular \(2\), \(0\) and \(-1\) are not additional free inputs. There is no division, primitive exponentiation, comparison, conditional branch or access to a supplied coefficient list. The finite program may be chosen separately for each polynomial; there is no uniformity requirement on these choices. Intermediate degrees, coefficient sizes and integer magnitudes are unrestricted. Cost measures arithmetic operations, not the number of bits in coefficients, a formula without shared registers or the bit length of the program encoding.

For \(f\ne0\), define \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)=|\{a\in\mathbb Z:f(a)=0\}|\), counting negative roots, zero and positive roots once each, regardless of multiplicity. This cardinality is finite because a nonzero univariate polynomial has at most its degree many roots; a nonzero constant has no roots. The zero polynomial is excluded. The exponent \(C\) must be one constant for all \(f\), without dependence on degree, coefficients, root sizes or the choice of an optimal program. The question asks only for a bound, not for an efficient root-counting or root-finding algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the universal bound or its logical negation, \(\forall C\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}\ \exists f\in\mathbb Z[x]\setminus\{0\}:z_{\mathbb Z}(f)>(1+\tau(f))^C\). A positive answer may use any one absolute exponent; a negative answer must exclude all such exponents. No computable rule for choosing the counterexample polynomials is required. A counterexample to just one proposed exponent, bounds for a restricted program class, multiplicity counts, or results only about real or complex roots do not settle this full target. Conditional consequences of the conjecture are not proofs of it.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether a polynomial compressed into a short arithmetic computation can nevertheless have very many distinct integer zeros. Its elementary statement links arithmetic structure to fundamental lower bounds in algebraic computation. A proof would imply separation of polynomial-time nondeterministic and deterministic computation over the complex numbers, as well as important constant-free circuit separations; neither consequence is presently supplied by the conjecture itself.

cards.context:
After \(s\) squarings, the program for \(x^{2^s}\) has only \(s\) operations but exponential degree. In general \(\deg f\leq2^{\tau(f)}\), giving only \(z_{\mathbb Z}(f)\leq2^{\tau(f)}\). The example has just one distinct integer root, although that root has multiplicity \(2^s\). This is why both the arithmetic compression and the word “distinct” matter.

The corresponding unrestricted real-root assertion is false. Let \(q_0(x)=x\) and \(q_{j+1}(x)=q_j(x)^2-2\). Building 2 once and using two operations per iteration gives \(\tau(q_j)\leq2j+1\). The identity \(q_j(2\cos\theta)=2\cos(2^j\theta)\) shows that \(q_j\) has \(2^j\) distinct real roots. Integer roots impose a substantially different constraint.

Smale’s Problem 4 records the root-count question, and Rojas gives exactly the \((1+\tau)^C\) convention used here. Allowing the fixed constants \(-1,0,1\) for free changes operation counts by at most two relative to the present convention; it does not change whether some polynomial root bound exists. Exact small-length records do depend on the convention. Arbitrary free integer constants constitute a different cost model.

Shub and Smale’s work connects short integer computations with feasibility of polynomial systems over \(\mathbb C\). Smale’s later Problem 4 explicitly states that the root conjecture implies \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb C}\ne\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb C}\) in the Blum–Shub–Smale model. This model has exact complex arithmetic and equality tests at unit cost. The implication is about that algebraic model; it does not itself assert Boolean \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

Rojas’s Theorem 1 proves that a polynomial bound just for integer roots congruent to 1 modulo one fixed prime already implies the full conjecture. His Theorem 3 gives a bound \(\exp(O(s\log(s+1)))\) on rational roots in terms of additive complexity \(s\), a measure charging additions while allowing powers and multiplicative expressions more freely. This does not give a polynomial bound in the full operation count \(\tau\).

Alekseev, Grigoriev, Hirsch and Tzameret record the implication \(\mathrm{VP}^0\ne\mathrm{VNP}^0\) for constant-free algebraic complexity, and obtain conditional lower bounds in the Ideal Proof System for a binary-value variant over rational functions. Their separate hypothesis about nonzero multiples of factorials yields a different lower bound over the rationals. These hypotheses and coefficient domains are distinct, and the results do not directly give Frege lower bounds for Boolean formulas.

Santibañez-Leal’s Zenodo preprint, version 0.03 dated 20 August 2026, reports an exhaustive census through eight operations using free constants \(-1,0,1\). The computation has not been independently reproduced for this card. A finite census, even if correct, does not establish or refute a bound with one exponent for every program length.

cards.title: Explicit three-dimensional tensors of superlinear rank
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A\), a real constant \(K>0\) and an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), on input \(1^n\) it outputs all entries of a rational tensor \(T_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) within \(K(n+1)^a\) bit operations, and \[\forall B\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)\ge Bn?\] Here rank is ordinary tensor rank over the complex numbers. Thus the required ratio \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb C}(T_n)/n\) tends to infinity, with no prescribed rate.
cards.definitions:
A tensor \(T\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n\times n}\) is the array \((T_{ijk})_{1\le i,j,k\le n}\), regarded as an element of \(\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\) through the usual inclusion of the rationals into the complex numbers. Its ordinary rank is the smallest integer \(r\ge0\) for which there are vectors \(u^{(s)},v^{(s)},w^{(s)}\in\mathbb C^n\), for \(1\le s\le r\), satisfying
\[
T_{ijk}=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u^{(s)}_i\,v^{(s)}_j\,w^{(s)}_k
\quad\text{for every }1\le i,j,k\le n.
\]
An empty sum is the zero tensor. The factors in a rank decomposition may be arbitrary complex vectors, although the constructed tensor entries are rational. No symmetry is required. The target is not matrix rank of an array rearrangement, slice rank, border rank, or an asymptotic tensor-power rank.

The machine outputs the \(n^3\) entries in lexicographic order of \((i,j,k)\). Each entry is an explicitly written signed binary integer numerator and positive binary integer denominator, with delimiters. All bits are charged, so their total length and each individual entry's bit length are polynomially bounded in \(n\). A symbolic power, root-of-unity description, unevaluated arithmetic expression or arbitrary real constant is not a rational-entry output under this convention. All input reading, integer arithmetic, preprocessing and output writing count. The finite program and \(K,a\) are independent of \(n\); there is no advice, oracle, randomness or uncharged preprocessing.

The algorithm is required on every positive integer dimension, and the rank guarantee holds for all sufficiently large dimensions for each \(B\). The integer threshold \(N\) may depend on \(B\) and the fixed family; it is not required to be computed. No rank decomposition, rank value or lower-bound certificate is an output requirement for \(A\); the rank-growth guarantee must instead be established by the submitted proof. Explicitness here means polynomial time in the dimension to write the whole tensor, not a separate polylogarithmic-time entry-query requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of such a finite construction algorithm, its uniform polynomial bit-cost bound and the entire eventual superlinear rank guarantee, or a complete Lean proof that no such algorithm exists. An existence proof without the construction cost, a fixed constant multiple of the dimension, growth only along an unspecified subsequence, or a conditional lower bound alone does not meet this target. Any growth rate tending to infinity in the displayed normalized rank suffices; a fixed positive power improvement is not required.
cards.why: Tensor rank measures the number of independent bilinear products needed to express a computation. Explicit superlinear-rank families would turn generic hardness into concrete examples and yield lower bounds for the corresponding constant-degree arithmetic computations.

cards.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
cards.formal:
Work over the complex field \(\mathbb C\). Is the following general cubic formulation of the asymptotic rank conjecture true?
\[\forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall T\in\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^n:\quad \bigl(\operatorname{rank}F_1(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_2(T)=\operatorname{rank}F_3(T)=n\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \widetilde R(T)=n,\]
where \(F_i(T)\) are the three matrix flattenings and
\[\widetilde R(T)=\lim_{k\to\infty}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}=\inf_{k\ge1}R(T^{\boxtimes k})^{1/k}?\]
Here \(R\) is exact tensor rank, and \(\boxtimes\) groups corresponding factors of tensor products. The tensor \(T\) and its dimension \(n\) are fixed while \(k\) tends to infinity. The quantifier covers all complex tensors satisfying the flattening condition; no additional symmetry, support or computational promise is imposed.
cards.definitions:
Tensors and flattenings. For a positive integer \(d\), let \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb C^d\). A tensor \(T\) in three factors of dimensions \(a,b,c\) is the coefficient array \((t_{ij\ell})_{(i,j,\ell)\in[a]\times[b]\times[c]}\), interpreted as \(\sum_{i,j,\ell}t_{ij\ell}e_i\otimes e_j\otimes e_\ell\). For the cubic format \(a=b=c=n\), define three \(n\)-by-\(n^2\) matrices by
\[(F_1(T))_{i,(j,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_2(T))_{j,(i,\ell)}=t_{ij\ell},\qquad(F_3(T))_{\ell,(i,j)}=t_{ij\ell}.\]
Pairs are ordered lexicographically; the ordering does not affect matrix rank. Matrix rank is the dimension of the column span over \(\mathbb C\). A tensor is concise in this format when all three matrix ranks are \(n\). This excludes zero tensors and tensors that effectively use a smaller subspace in some factor. For \(n=1\), it just means a nonzero scalar.

Exact rank. For any positive dimensions \(a,b,c\), define
\[R(S)=\min\left\{r\in\mathbb N:\ S=\sum_{s=1}^{r}u_s\otimes v_s\otimes w_s,\quad u_s\in\mathbb C^a,\ v_s\in\mathbb C^b,\ w_s\in\mathbb C^c\right\}.\]
The empty sum is zero. A pure tensor has coefficients \((u_i v_j w_\ell)\); equality in a decomposition is exact coefficientwise equality. Finite decompositions always exist, so the minimum is well-defined. The three vectors in a summand are independent choices: there is no symmetric-rank restriction. Their complex entries are unrestricted, including noncomputable numbers; the question does not ask for a finite input encoding or an algorithm to find the decomposition.

Grouped powers. For \(k\ge1\), the tensor \(T^{\boxtimes k}\) has exactly three factors, each with coordinates indexed by \([n]^k\), and hence each of dimension \(n^k\). Its entries are
\[(T^{\boxtimes k})_{(i_1,\ldots,i_k),(j_1,\ldots,j_k),(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k)}=\prod_{h=1}^{k}t_{i_h j_h\ell_h}.\]
Its rank is taken after this grouping. A vector in a rank decomposition may be any element of \(\mathbb C^{n^k}\); it need not itself split into \(k\) vectors of dimension \(n\). Thus ranks of grouped powers need not equal \(R(T)^k\).

Asymptotic value. Tensoring decompositions gives
\[R(T^{\boxtimes(k+\ell)})\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})R(T^{\boxtimes\ell}).\]
For a concise tensor the elementary flattening lower bound and a slice decomposition give
\[n^k\le R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le n^{2k}.\]
Subadditivity of the logarithms therefore proves existence of the positive real limit in the question and its equality with the displayed infimum. In particular \(n\le\widetilde R(T)\le n^2\). The proposed equality is equivalently
\[\forall n\ \forall T\text{ concise}\ \forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists K\ge1\ \forall k\ge K:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\le(n+\varepsilon)^k.\]
Here \(K\) may depend on \(n,T,\varepsilon\), with no uniform or effective rate required. The actual decompositions may depend on \(k\) as well. Neither attainment of the infimum at a finite power nor rank \(n^k\) for any finite power is asserted.

Related ranks. Border rank of \(S\) is the least integer \(r\) such that \(S\) is a Euclidean limit of tensors of exact rank at most \(r\) in its fixed complex coefficient space. The defining ranks in this card are exact ranks. A finite-power border-rank result or a finite-power exact-rank lower bound must be connected to the quantified asymptotic statement before it can settle this question.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its logical negation, including the stated limit convention. An affirmative proof must cover every positive dimension and every concise complex tensor, with arbitrarily small positive \(\varepsilon\) in the equivalent power bound. A negative proof must establish the existence of a positive integer \(n\), a concise \(T\) in the specified cubic format, and a real \(\eta>0\) such that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad R(T^{\boxtimes k})\ge(n+\eta)^k.\]
This is equivalent to a counterexample with \(\widetilde R(T)>n\); no explicitness or computability condition is added to the counterexample. A large rank at one power is insufficient. A result only for a restricted class of tensors, only over another field, or conditional on an unproved complexity assumption does not settle the universal complex-field target. This is an exact yes/no conjecture, so a fixed additive tolerance such as \(1/100\) does not replace the equality.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether every bilinear operation attains, in the exponential growth rate of jointly processed copies, the elementary lower bound already visible from matrices. A positive answer would force matrix multiplication exponent two and impose a simple common asymptotic law on all concise tensors. A negative answer would exhibit an obstruction that survives arbitrarily many grouped copies, beyond the familiar difficulty of decomposing a single tensor.

cards.context:
A rank decomposition expresses a three-factor tensor as a sum of elementary products. Allowing many copies to be processed jointly can save products because vectors in each grouped factor can correlate different copies. The conjecture says that these savings eventually leave no exponential overhead above the flattening lower bound. For the diagonal tensor \(\Delta_n=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\otimes e_i\otimes e_i\), the elementary decomposition and flattening bound already match at every power.

The matrix multiplication tensor \(M_m=\sum_{i,j,\ell=1}^{m}e_{ij}\otimes e_{j\ell}\otimes e_{\ell i}\) is concise in three factors of dimension \(m^2\). In particular \(\widetilde R(M_2)=2^\omega\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum of exponents for arithmetic matrix multiplication over \(\mathbb C\). The proposed equality for this tensor would give \(\omega=2\). The implication in the reverse direction is not known from this example; the card quantifies over far more than matrix multiplication tensors.

The literature uses both general and restricted formulations. The retained target is the general cubic concise formulation discussed in the primary source and in the April 2026 spectrum paper. Lee’s January 2026 Conjecture 1 additionally assumes tightness: after suitable basis choices, injective integer weights on each factor sum to zero on every nonzero coefficient. That extra support condition is absent here. The numerical census supplies data for upper bounds, not a proof of this universal equality.

The June 2026 revision of the primary paper proves that each asymptotic-rank sublevel set is defined by vanishing of finitely many polynomials, and that a nonincreasing sequence of attainable asymptotic ranks eventually stabilizes. Its threshold-decision theorem applies over computable fields and is nonuniform in the threshold. These structural results do not identify all values with the flattening bound or supply an effective solution for arbitrary complex coefficients.

Alman, Li and Pratt’s April 2026 paper characterizes one part of the asymptotic tensor spectrum and gives algorithms for its edge support functionals. The spectrum is a collection of normalized, additive, multiplicative and restriction-monotone tensor parameters; its full maximum describes asymptotic rank. Characterizing selected members does not prove that they exhaust the spectrum. The paper explicitly separates its edge results from the full rank conjecture.

Two September 2026 papers give new lower bounds for individual tensors. Yang treats exact rank of rectangular matrix multiplication; Mańdziuk determines border ranks for specified direct sums and products. Neither inspected theorem supplies a single concise cubic tensor with a positive asymptotic gap above its dimension. Such finite-tensor lower bounds are compatible with the conjecture.

Holtrup and Zuiddam’s 15 September 2026 preprint settles a different extremal question: it bounds and classifies the largest stabilizer dimension of concise cubic tensors. A stabilizer consists of invertible changes of basis that preserve the tensor. Maximizing that group dimension does not determine the rank growth of all tensor powers, so this new result is not a resolution of the card.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\)
cards.formal:
Is
\[\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}=\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\]
in the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered real field, with arbitrary real inputs and arbitrary finitely many fixed real machine constants? Equivalently, does every set of finite real tuples with polynomial-length real witnesses checkable in polynomial BSS time have a deterministic polynomial-time BSS decider? The decider and its finite constants may depend on the set, but must be fixed for all input lengths.
cards.definitions:
The input domain is the disjoint union \(\mathbb R^{*}=\bigsqcup_{n\ge0}\mathbb R^{n}\). An input is a tuple \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\); its size is its dimension \(n\), independent of the magnitudes, precision or computability of its coordinates. Length is supplied as part of the input convention. Distinct tuple lengths remain distinct even when trailing coordinates are zero.

A deterministic BSS machine has a finite control graph and real registers, initially containing the input and zeros elsewhere, with a fixed finite set of real constants including 0 and 1. Constants may be transcendental or uncomputable; there is no requirement for finite binary descriptions of their values. The same program and constants serve all inputs and all dimensions. Each arithmetic instruction adds, subtracts, multiplies or divides two stored reals, or loads a fixed machine constant; a division is allowed only with nonzero denominator. A branch tests equality to zero or order relative to zero, exactly. Copies, control steps and register shifts each have unit cost, as do arithmetic operations and tests. Accepting and rejecting states output the bits 1 and 0.

For a concrete standard register convention, use a doubly infinite sequence of real registers with finite support at every finite time. Ordinary arithmetic, copy and test instructions refer to finitely many fixed register offsets in the program. A shift moves the sequence one position left or right, giving access to arbitrary input coordinates over time. Initially register 0 holds \(n\), registers 1 through \(n\) hold the input, and the others hold zero. The verifier input similarly records the two lengths and the two tuples in adjacent registers. This is the ordinary shift-register presentation of BSS computation, polynomially equivalent to the source's restricted copy-address presentation. Division by zero is treated as rejection, so a proposed decider must still meet correctness and totality on every input. There is no primitive floor, digit extraction, transcendental-function evaluation, square root, oracle or random instruction. An arithmetic step costs one even when its value would need arbitrarily many bits in a discrete representation.

For \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^{*}\), membership in \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}\) means that there exist one such deterministic machine \(M\) and constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N\), with \(C\ge1\), such that, for every \(n\ge0\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), it halts within \(C(n+1)^d\) steps and accepts exactly when \(x\in L\).

Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\) means that there are one deterministic BSS verifier \(V\) and fixed polynomial bounds \(p,q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(V(x,y)\) halts within \(q(n)\) steps for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and every real tuple \(y\) of length at most \(p(n)\), and
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists m\le p(n)\;\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ V(x,y)=1.\]
The time bound depends on \(n\), not on the coordinate values; polynomial bounds may be written as \(C(n+1)^d\). A padded fixed witness length gives the same class. No-instance inputs must be rejected for every permitted witness. The witness contains arbitrary exact reals, not just rationals or finite strings. The verifier's constants and polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but not on \(x\), \(n\) or the witness. Equality of classes quantifies over every such \(L\), with no promise on input coordinates.

The notation \(\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}^{0}\) restricts the machine constants to 0 and 1. The Boolean part of a class restricts its input tuples to coordinates in \(\{0,1\}\); write it as \(\mathrm{BP}(\cdot)\). These are different restrictions from the full target. In particular, \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}^{0})\) concerns finitely encoded problems, while this card retains all real tuples and arbitrary fixed real constants. Neither finite-precision computation nor bit-cost arithmetic is the model being compared.

For the cited discrete comparison, PosSLP asks whether a finite arithmetic straight-line program, starting from 0 and 1 and using addition, subtraction and multiplication, outputs a positive integer. Such a program is an explicitly listed acyclic sequence of operations on earlier values. \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\) is ordinary polynomial-time Turing computation with a unit-cost yes/no oracle for this language; \(/\mathrm{poly}\) permits an additional polynomial-length advice string depending only on input length. The counting hierarchy is the union of the levels \(\mathrm C_0\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{P}\) and \(\mathrm C_{k+1}\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{PP}^{\mathrm C_k\mathrm{P}}\), where PP uses a strict majority of the computation paths of a polynomial-time nondeterministic binary machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete proof checked in Lean of the stated class equality or its negation in this precise full BSS model. A positive answer must establish a uniform polynomial-time BSS decider for every language having the defined verifier, allowing a different fixed program and finite constants for each language. A negative answer must establish some \(L\in\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\setminus\mathrm{P}_{\mathbb R}\), ruling out every polynomial-time deterministic BSS decider even with arbitrary finite real constants. A result only for constant-free machines, only for Boolean inputs, with extra oracle operations, or under an unproved complexity assumption does not alone prove the full unconditional target. All decisions are exact; numerical approximation tolerance does not apply.
cards.why: This is the central determinism-versus-verification question for exact algebraic computation. It would classify the cost of real polynomial feasibility in a model that isolates arithmetic complexity from finite-precision representation, linking complexity theory to real algebraic geometry.

cards.title: Superpolynomial noncommutative circuit lower bounds
cards.formal:
Does there exist a family
\[
f_n\in\mathbb Q\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\rangle\qquad(n\ge2)
\]
of polynomial degree with uniformly polynomial-time computable word coefficients, such that
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:
\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}(f_n)>n^k?
\]
Here \(k,N,n\) are integers and \(\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}\) is minimum size among unrestricted noncommutative arithmetic circuits with arbitrary complex constants. The family can be chosen freely subject to the explicitness and degree requirements below; it is not required to be a particular permanent or determinant family.
cards.definitions:
The free associative algebra \(\mathbb C\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\rangle\) consists of finite complex linear combinations of words in the symbols \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). Addition adds the coefficients of equal words. Multiplication concatenates words and distributes over sums; it is associative. Scalars commute with every word, but variable symbols do not commute. The empty word has value 1. Thus \(x_1x_2\) and \(x_2x_1\) are different monomials, and polynomial equality is exact equality of every word coefficient. This is not a problem about functions on scalar inputs or on matrices of one fixed dimension.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output. Input gates are variable symbols or arbitrary complex constants. An internal gate adds or multiplies two predecessor values. Each multiplication gate specifies a left and a right input; the same predecessor may occur in both positions. The size is the total number of gates, including inputs. There are no division gates, tests, approximation operations or limits. Fan-out, reuse of intermediate values and depth are unrestricted. Each scalar costs one input gate without a description-length restriction. Intermediate polynomials can have arbitrarily large degree and need not be homogeneous. \(\operatorname{NC}_{\mathbb C}(f)\) is the minimum size of any such circuit whose formal output is \(f\), with rational coefficients embedded in \(\mathbb C\).

Polynomial degree and uniform explicitness mean that there are fixed integers \(a,b\ge1\), a fixed real \(K>0\), and one deterministic multi-tape Turing machine \(M\) with the following properties. Every nonzero \(f_n\) has degree at most \(n^a\), where degree is the largest length of a word with nonzero coefficient; the zero polynomial is allowed. Given \(1^n\) and any explicitly listed word \(w\) of length \(\ell\) over \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(M\) outputs the exact coefficient \([w]f_n\) in at most
\[
K\bigl(n+(\ell+1)\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\bigr)^b
\]
Turing steps. Word symbols are written as fixed-width binary indices. The output is a reduced fraction \(p/q\) with binary integers \(p\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\); zero is \(0/1\). Words of length greater than \(n^a\) have coefficient zero. The empty word is included. The bound includes writing the output and thus also limits coefficient bit lengths. No advice depending on \(n\) is supplied to \(M\).

The explicitness requirement prevents choosing arbitrary hard coefficient tables by counting. It concerns an algorithm to compute any one coefficient, not an algorithm to list all coefficients or a small arithmetic circuit for the full polynomial. Conversely, the circuits being ruled out are nonuniform and may use complex constants even though the target family has efficiently computable rational coefficients. The lower-bound quantifiers mean absence of every polynomial family-size upper bound, witnessed at arbitrarily large indices; they do not require an eventual lower bound at every index.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this existence statement or its logical negation. A positive answer must define the family and its coefficient algorithm, prove the degree and uniform running-time bounds, and exclude every polynomial circuit-size upper bound in the stated unrestricted model. A negative answer must prove that every family meeting these requirements has a polynomial-size noncommutative circuit family over \(\mathbb C\). An exponential formula or branching-program lower bound does not suffice. Nor does a circuit lower bound for bounded depth, homogeneity, restricted syntactic degree, or a fixed polynomial exponent.
cards.why: Noncommutative computation retains the order of products and already supports strong formula lower bounds. Proving a superpolynomial bound that survives unrestricted reuse would establish a major circuit lower-bound milestone for an explicitly specified family.

cards.context:
The order of symbols gives a coefficient matrix method that proves exponential formula and branching-program lower bounds. A circuit can reuse an intermediate computation, so such a formula lower bound need not imply a comparably large circuit.

Uniform coefficient computation is a precise way to require an explicit family. Allowing only polynomial degree also prevents repeated squaring of a huge-degree monomial from masquerading as a meaningful circuit lower bound.

The January 2026 low-syntactic-degree result improves polynomial lower bounds under an intermediate-degree restriction. Later work must be considered before treating its stated unrestricted frontier as current.

The May 2026 preprint states a tight \(\Omega(nd)\) bound for the palindrome polynomial on two groups of \(n\) variables and degree \(2d\), with no syntactic-degree restriction. At \(d=n\), this is quadratic in the number of variables. Its matching \(O(nd)\) recursive circuit makes that particular family insufficient for the superpolynomial target.

The July revision of the concurrent Raz paper states \(\Omega(d\sqrt n)\) non-scalar multiplication lower bounds and discusses the stronger total-size palindrome result. These 2026 advances change the polynomial frontier without proving the superpolynomial statement.

cards.status_note: Solution assessment on November 23, 2026. The answer is yes by a consequence of Theorem 1.1. In n variables take the row-ordered permanent on an m by m array, where m is the integer part of the square root of n. A word has coefficient one precisely when it selects one variable per row in order and uses each column once. This is a uniform polynomial-time test and the degree is m. Making the variables commute maps every noncommutative circuit to a circuit for the ordinary permanent. At n = m², any polynomial bound would contradict the theorem.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

references.authors: Levent Alpöge; Manjul Bhargava; Wei Ho; Ari Shnidman
references.locator: Published online 1 December 2025; Inventiones mathematicae 243, 1129–1139 (March 2026). Publisher introduction, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 checked: all rings of integers, not their fraction fields.

cards.context:
Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively; rational solvability remains a different decision problem.

The Alpöge–Bhargava–Ho–Shnidman article appears online, proving a negative answer over the ring of integers of every number field; its print issue is March 2026.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

cards.context:
Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.

cards.title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo the prime \(p\). Its multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\) is \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) with multiplication modulo \(p\). The promise that \(g\) is a generator means that \(g^0,g^1,\ldots,g^{p-2}\), reduced modulo \(p\), list these \(p-1\) residues without repetition; hence the requested exponent exists and is unique. Each input integer is represented by its ordinary base-two expansion \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\), without leading zeros and with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Writing \(\ell(a)=|\operatorname{bin}(a)|\), set \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^{\ell(a)}0\operatorname{bin}(a)\). The complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(p)\operatorname{code}(g)\operatorname{code}(h)\), with \(p\) prime and \(1\le g,h<p\). Its length \(L=2(\ell(p)+\ell(g)+\ell(h))+3\) is \(\Theta(\log_2 p)\) on promised inputs. A successful output is exactly \(\operatorname{bin}(x)\); any different output or a designated failure symbol is unsuccessful. For \(p=2\), the sole promised pair is \(g=h=1\) and the answer is \(x=0\). The machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes and an output tape; each transition costs one step, and any random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. The time bound includes input processing, bit arithmetic, random-bit generation, output and all preprocessing. The same \(A,C,c\) work for every input, with no advice, oracle, precomputed table or supplied factorization of \(p-1\). Arbitrary classical computations on the concrete binary residues are permitted, not just generic group operations. Malformed encodings may be rejected as failure; on well-formed triples outside the mathematical promise, only the global time bound is required. The success guarantee is separately for each promised triple, over the machine’s coins, not over a distribution of primes or targets. The question concerns the multiplicative group of a prime field; additive groups, extension fields and elliptic-curve groups are different models.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,c\) with both the all-input, all-random-sequence time bound and the per-promised-input success guarantee, or a Lean-checked proof that no such triple exists. Equivalently, a negative answer must prove that every machine obeying some global polynomial clock has a promised input on which its probability of outputting the required exponent is less than \(2/3\). Failure of a particular algorithm, an average-case conjecture for a selected prime distribution, or a lower bound restricted to generic group operations does not establish this negation. A quantum algorithm, success only for selected prime families, or a bound polynomial in \(p\) rather than its bit length does not meet the positive target.
cards.why: Discrete logarithms expose a basic gap between efficient modular exponentiation and our ability to invert it. A uniform classical polynomial-time solver would defeat the corresponding finite-field discrete-logarithm assumptions and solve computational Diffie–Hellman in this setting. An unrestricted impossibility proof would establish a fundamental classical lower bound for a concrete arithmetic problem already solvable in quantum polynomial time.

cards.context:
For a supplied \(g\) and exponent \(x\), modular exponentiation takes time polynomial in their bit lengths. Inverting this operation would reveal the shared value \(g^{ab}\) from \(g,g^a,g^b\) in the corresponding Diffie–Hellman setting. This implication does not identify discrete-logarithm hardness with every Diffie–Hellman or encryption-security assumption. The card asks a worst-case algorithmic question; a negative answer alone does not prove average-case hardness for a cryptographic parameter distribution.

Candidate answers are efficiently verifiable by checking \(0\le x\le p-2\) and \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\). Thus, as an elementary consequence of verification, existence of the stated bounded-error algorithm is equivalent to existence of a Las Vegas solver that is never wrong and has a uniform polynomial expected running-time bound on every promised input. Independent verified repetition has bounded expected cost in one direction; truncation at three times an expected-time bound gives success at least \(2/3\) by Markov’s inequality in the other. This does not require every run of a Las Vegas solver to terminate, only probability-one termination and finite expected cost.

Schirokauer’s survey gives a conjectured expected-time NFS bound of the form \(\exp(O((\ln p)^{1/3}(\ln\ln p)^{2/3}))\) in the prime-field regime. This is a heuristic complexity analysis, not an unconditional polynomial-time theorem or an unrestricted lower bound. The displayed scale grows faster than every fixed power of \(\log p\). The 2024 Discrete Logarithm Factory paper separately studies costs shared across fields and targets; any such preprocessing must still fit this card’s complete single-input budget.

Shoup’s lower bound concerns randomly encoded group elements. If \(q\) is the largest prime divisor of a cyclic group’s order, constant success requires \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) generic group operations in that model. His parameter \(q\) is not the field characteristic \(p\); for this card the group order is \(p-1\). The theorem averages over the random encoding, exponent and algorithm coins. It does not exclude algorithms that use the actual integer residues and their arithmetic structure.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s Theorem 1.1 gives expected time \((p d)^{2\log_2 d+O(1)}\) for the multiplicative group of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\). For fixed \(p\) and growing extension degree \(d\), this is quasipolynomial in the input size. Substituting \(d=1\) supplies at most a polynomial-in-\(p\) guarantee, not the requested polynomial in \(\log p\). The occurrence of the product \(p d\) in their bound must not be confused with the field order \(p^d\).

Lido’s paper, published in March 2026, also proves a quasipolynomial expected-time theorem in small characteristic. In the inspected version its hypothesis is explicitly \(d>p\) for a field of size \(p^d\), excluding the growing prime-field family with \(d=1\). The source’s field-regime restriction remains part of the theorem even though all these problems share the name discrete logarithm.

Shor’s polynomial-time algorithm uses quantum computation. Wu and coauthors’ August 2026 preprint uses the same prime-field generator-input problem as an explicit classical-hardness assumption for a claim about estimating outputs of adaptive shallow quantum circuits. That assumption is not a proved classical lower bound; the reduction and its quantum resource claims were not independently verified in this review.

This would invert a basic arithmetic operation used in finite-field cryptography and match a known quantum capability.
A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm or rule out all algorithms in this model; generic lower bounds, quantum algorithms and small-characteristic extension-field results do not suffice.

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal:
Do there exist a real constant \(C>0\), a real constant \(K>0\), an integer \(k\geq1\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every pair of integers \(d\geq n\geq1\) and every explicitly encoded \(B\in\mathbb Q^{d\times n}\) with linearly independent columns, every run halts in at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit operations and returns a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), with
\[\Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\leq n^C\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\geq\frac23?\]
The input length \(N\) includes all matrix entries. The lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\), and \(\lambda_1\) is its shortest nonzero Euclidean length. Randomness consists of independent fair bits on that fixed input. The program and all constants are chosen once, before any input.
cards.definitions:
The input contains \(d,n\) and all \(dn\) rational entries in row-major order. To fix a binary encoding, let \(b(t)\) be the ordinary binary expansion of a nonnegative integer \(t\), using the one-bit string \(0\) for zero, and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\). Dimensions use \(E(d),E(n)\). A rational number is encoded by a sign bit followed by \(E(|a|)E(q)\), where it equals \(a/q\), \(q>0\), and \(\gcd(|a|,q)=1\); zero has positive sign and denominator one. There are exactly \(dn\) entries and no trailing bits. Valid inputs satisfy \(d\geq n\geq1\) and column independence over \(\mathbb Q\). The total number of encoded bits is \(N\). The polynomial clock applies on every binary input; behavior and output on malformed or dependent-basis inputs are otherwise unrestricted.

The Euclidean norm of \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The lattice consists of all integer combinations of the columns, with its usual embedding in \(\mathbb R^d\). Independence makes \(z\mapsto Bz\) injective and makes \(L(B)\) discrete in its real span. Thus
\[\lambda_1(L(B))=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}}\|Bz\|_2>0\]
is attained. No uniqueness of the shortest vector up to sign is assumed. The algorithm returns the coefficient vector: its \(n\) signed integer coordinates use a sign bit and \(E\) of the absolute value, with positive sign for zero. It must return a valid nonzero vector on every run on a valid input. An unsuccessful run may exceed the norm bound, but may not output zero, fail to halt or omit the vector. The squared norm can equivalently be used in the displayed guarantee with squared factor \(n^{2C}\).

Use one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a finite description independent of all input parameters. Its tapes have a fixed finite alphabet encoding bits. Each transition can read and write only a fixed number of cells and move each head by at most one cell. An additional instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit at unit cost. This describes ordinary uniform classical bit computation, with no advice, oracle, quantum operations, uncharged preprocessing or unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers. All reading, writing, arithmetic, memory manipulation and random-bit generation count toward the bound. The output uses the integer encoding specified above, and every bit written is charged.

For a given valid input, randomness is the product measure of independent uniform bits on an infinite random tape; the polynomial clock ensures that only finitely many are read. The success event is the displayed norm inequality, separately for every input. All runs, including those outside that event, must return a valid nonzero integer vector within the same clock. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as the special case that uses no random bits. Expected polynomial time alone is not the stated requirement.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,k,A\;\forall d,n,B\), with both the probability guarantee and the all-run clock imposed after choosing the input. In particular, \(C\) may be large but must be fixed. The factor is \(n^C\), determined by lattice rank; it is not a polynomial in the ambient dimension, the coefficient magnitude or the input bit length. In rank one it is exactly one. There is no input-distribution, shortest-vector uniqueness, ideal-lattice, conditioning, modular or basis-quality promise. The problem concerns arbitrary finite rational bases, including ones with very large coefficients.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and constants meeting every requirement, or of the logical negation of that existence statement. A negative answer must rule out every fixed exponent \(C>0\) and every permitted randomized polynomial-time algorithm, rather than only a deterministic algorithm or a selected small approximation factor. A positive answer must establish the actual nonzero-vector output, success on each basis and all-run bit clock, including coefficient and output lengths. A conditional complexity lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its assumption is proved. A gap-decision certificate, a factor depending without a rank bound on the input basis, a uniqueness-promised result, an oracle-call bound excluding subroutine time, or a quantum algorithm alone does not settle this classical search target. No additional numerical tolerance weakens this exact existence proposition.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient classical computation can find short vectors in every Euclidean lattice with a loss bounded by one fixed power of rank. The gap between known general algorithms and this regime is a basic obstacle in lattice complexity. Resolving it would clarify the relation between lattice geometry, efficient approximation and worst-case hardness assumptions used in cryptography; its consequences for particular schemes still depend on the exact problem and parameters.

cards.context:
For integer \(M\geq1\), the basis columns \((M,1)\) and \((M+1,1)\) are both long but their lattice contains \((1,0)\). Thus input column lengths alone do not determine the shortest lattice length. More generally, the same lattice has many bases, and the guarantee must be relative to its intrinsic minimum on every supplied basis.

With its standard parameter, LLL gives a nonzero vector of length at most \(2^{(n-1)/2}\lambda_1\) in polynomial bit time. The original paper separately controls the number of arithmetic operations and the binary lengths of their operands. Its approximation factor is exponential in rank even though the running time is polynomial; a runtime statement alone does not specify the quality of the vector.

Bennett’s 2023 survey summarizes improved general polynomial-time guarantees with factor \(2^{O(n\log\log n/\log n)}\). This established upper guarantee is still much larger than any fixed polynomial in rank. It does not prove that every algorithm must lose that much: whether the guarantee can be improved to some \(n^C\) is the existence question on this card.

Haviv and Regev prove hardness at factors \(2^{(\log n)^{1-\varepsilon}}\), for fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), unless NP has one-sided-error randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Under the stronger randomized subexponential-time assumption they obtain \(n^{c/\log\log n}\) for some fixed \(c>0\). Both factors are subpolynomial: for every fixed \(C>0\), they eventually lie below \(n^C\). Their theorem therefore does not rule out the looser approximation asked for here. The randomness assumptions are part of the result.

For \(\gamma\geq1\), GapSVP asks whether \(\lambda_1\leq r\) or \(\lambda_1>\gamma r\), promised one of those alternatives and given \(r>0\). Aharonov and Regev place this decision problem, for some factor \(\gamma=c\sqrt n\), in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\): each promised answer has a polynomial-length certificate verifiable in polynomial time. This is not a polynomial-time method of finding the requested vector. Their full Corollary 1.2 specifies a constant \(c\); it does not assert the result for every smaller factor hidden in big-O notation.

Bennett’s separate search-to-decision question underscores that approximate search SVP, gap decision, unique-SVP and shortest-independent-vectors problems must be distinguished. Cryptographic worst-case-to-average-case reductions concern specified variants at specified approximation and noise parameters. An algorithm here would change the search-SVP landscape; a security reduction alone does not make every cryptographic problem equivalent to it.

Shenoy’s 2024 article advertises an approximation expressed through \(1/(1-\delta)\). In the checked accepted manuscript, Theorem IV.2 defines \(\delta\) from the actual basis, and Corollary IV.3 retains that dependence in a squared-length bound. Merely knowing \(0\leq\delta<1\) supplies no fixed rank-polynomial upper bound on the factor. The manuscript is not counted as a solution of this card; its general convergence claim was not independently verified.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 theorem bounds the number of calls to PotENUM by a quantity polynomial in rank and input coefficient bit length for a fixed reduction parameter. The full Theorem 2 and Remark 2 separately retain an exponential-in-blocksize enumeration factor and the cost of processing each enumeration node. A polynomial number of calls is therefore not a polynomial total bit-time guarantee with arbitrary blocksize.

Hair and Sahai’s April 2026 revision gives a deterministic subexponential-time reduction from satisfiability to Euclidean GapSVP with a subpolynomial approximation gap. Its deterministic hardness conclusion assumes that NP is not contained in the intersection of deterministic time classes \(\operatorname{DTIME}(\exp(m^\eta))\) over all fixed \(\eta>0\), where \(m\) is the source input length. A deterministic reduction does not remove the stated complexity assumption, nor automatically exclude bounded-error randomized algorithms under that same deterministic assumption.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s paper, published at RANDOM on September 9, 2026, obtains deterministic constant-factor Euclidean hardness under an explicit lower-bound assumption against nondeterministic circuits. Its parameterized results use another resource measure. Wan’s September 8 revision separately claims unconditional deterministic reductions for every fixed constant factor, but explicitly removes its first version’s dimension-dependent claims after identifying a false tensor-product premise. Neither statement gives unconditional impossibility for all randomized algorithms and all polynomial factors. The new proofs were not independently verified.

The September Wan revision is the version used here: its Theorem 1.2 concerns fixed constant factors, and its introduction expressly withdraws the earlier dimension-dependent consequences. An older abstract or first-version summary must not be used to restore those withdrawn consequences.

Joglekar, Shinde and Agarkar’s September 9 revision concerns a generic metric supplied through a black-box distance oracle, for small constant approximation factors. Its adversary is permitted to perturb the metric. That is distinct from the explicit rational basis and fixed Euclidean norm on this card, and is not an unconditional lower bound for this target.

A classical algorithm satisfying this card also qualifies for the quantum approximation target TCS-7234. The converse is not automatic. Exact quantum search is separately retained as TCS-7169. The present target permits any fixed approximation exponent, rather than asking to optimize that exponent or requiring exact shortest-vector recovery.

cards.title: Vinogradov’s least quadratic nonresidue conjecture
cards.formal:
For an odd prime \(p\), let \(n(p)\) be the least positive quadratic nonresidue modulo \(p\), defined below. Is it true, unconditionally, that
\[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb R_{>0}\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_\varepsilon\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)\le p^{\varepsilon}?\]
Equivalently, is \(n(p)=p^{o(1)}\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through the odd primes? The threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the prime. No unproved analytic hypothesis is assumed.
cards.definitions:
For integers \(a,b\) and a positive integer \(p\), the congruence \(a\equiv b\pmod p\) means that \(p\) divides \(a-b\). An integer \(a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\) if there exists \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with \(x^2\equiv a\pmod p\); otherwise it is a quadratic nonresidue. Define
\[n(p)=\min\{a\in\{1,\ldots,p-1\}:\forall x\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\},\ x^2\not\equiv a\pmod p\}.\]
For an odd prime, exactly half of its nonzero residue classes are squares, so the set is nonempty. Representatives are ordered as ordinary positive integers; this is not the least absolute value among positive and negative representatives. Multiples of \(p\) are not counted as nonresidues.

The domain is all odd primes, not composite moduli, almost all primes, or one prescribed congruence class. The prime \(2\) is omitted because every nonzero residue modulo \(2\) is a square. Real powers have the convention \(p^\varepsilon=\exp(\varepsilon\log p)\), where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm.

The statement can equivalently be expressed using only integer powers:
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists P_k\in\mathbb N\ \forall p\ge P_k\text{ odd prime},\qquad n(p)^k\le p.\]
Likewise, the subpolynomial notation means \(\lim_{p\to\infty,\ p\ \mathrm{prime}}\log n(p)/\log p=0\). The source writes \(n(p)=O_\varepsilon(p^\varepsilon)\); since its claim quantifies over every positive exponent, the implicit constant can be absorbed by using a smaller exponent and increasing the threshold. The unit-leading-constant formulation above is therefore equivalent. The conjecture asks for existence of the thresholds, without an extra requirement to compute them effectively.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must establish a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) and arbitrarily large odd primes \(p\) with \(n(p)>p^{\varepsilon_0}\). A finite numerical exception cannot refute an eventual bound. A result for almost all primes, a bound with one fixed positive exponent, or a theorem assuming GRH or Elliott–Halberstam is insufficient without also proving the necessary hypothesis.
cards.why: A small quadratic nonresidue is a basic witness used in finite-field arithmetic, and its size measures how long the initial integers can all behave like squares modulo a prime. The conjecture asks for uniform cancellation strong enough to beat every fixed power of the modulus. It would cross a long-standing barrier in character sums and bound the range of deterministic searches for such witnesses; subpolynomial size in the modulus is not the same claim as polynomial size in its bit length.

cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in BQP
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform quantum algorithm and a polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? Given an integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times d}\) with \(m\ge d\ge1\) and linearly independent columns, the algorithm outputs a nonzero \(z\in\mathbb Z^d\) satisfying \[\|Bz\|_2=\min_{y\in\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}}\|By\|_2\] with probability at least \(2/3\). Every execution must take at most \(p(N)\) elementary steps, where \(N\) is the full binary length of the dimensions and all matrix entries.
cards.definitions:
The lattice is \(\Lambda(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^d\}\). Its rank is \(d\), its ambient dimension is \(m\), and its first minimum \(\lambda_1(\Lambda(B))\) is the Euclidean norm of a shortest nonzero vector. Full column rank guarantees a positive, attained minimum. The output gives the coefficient vector \(z\) in signed binary. Every vector attaining the minimum qualifies, including when there is a tie.

Use the [uniform quantum circuit model](definitions.html#quantum). On \(1^N\) a classical polynomial-time machine generates a circuit with an \(N\)-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillas, gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\) and computational-basis measurement. Classical decoding, circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing all have polynomial bounds in \(N\). The success guarantee applies separately to each valid basis. Malformed inputs and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. For rational bases, clearing denominators scales all lengths by the same factor and increases the encoding length only polynomially.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.
cards.why: A central test of quantum algorithms against worst-case lattice hardness.

cards.context:
The vectors \((100,1)\) and \((101,1)\) are both long, but their difference is \((1,0)\). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) is not known to be false.

The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about \(2^{0.6039d}\) and quantum time about \(2^{0.5411d}\), up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.
