cards.title: Efficient explicit constant-rate tree codes
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed finite output alphabet \(\Sigma\), constants \(0<\delta<1\) and \(0<\alpha<\delta/2\), and uniform deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for binary tree codes of every height \(N\ge1\), with relative tree distance at least \(\delta\) and decoding from suffix error fraction at most \(\alpha\)? Both \(|\Sigma|\) and the two positive distance parameters must be independent of \(N\). The binary information rate \(1/\log_2|\Sigma|\) is therefore a positive constant. The precise causal and decoding requirements are specified below.
cards.definitions:
Fix an integer \(q=|\Sigma|\ge2\) and identify \(\Sigma\) with \(\{0,\ldots,q-1\}\), represented by fixed-length binary symbols. For each height \(N\), an encoder defines maps \(C_N:\{0,1\}^{\le N}	o\Sigma^{\le N}\) with \(|C_N(x)|=|x|\), \(C_N(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\), and prefix consistency: if \(u\) is a prefix of \(x\), then \(C_N(u)\) is the prefix of \(C_N(x)\) of length \(|u|\). Thus an output symbol cannot depend on future input bits. For every \(N\ge1\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and distinct \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^{\ell}\), let \(j\) be the first input position where \(x_j
e y_j\). The tree-distance requirement is \[ igl|\{t\in\{j,\ldots,\ell\}:C_N(x)_t
e C_N(y)_t\} igr|\ \ge\ \delta(\ell-j+1).\] Divergence is defined using the input histories, even if some output labels coincide. For equal-length \(u,v\in\Sigma^\ell\), \(\ell\ge1\), define suffix distance \[d_{\mathrm{sfx}}(u,v)=\max_{1\le j\le\ell} rac{|\{t\in\{j,\ldots,\ell\}:u_t
e v_t\}|}{\ell-j+1}.\] A decoder receives \(1^N\) and any \(w\in\Sigma^\ell\), \(1\le\ell\le N\), and returns a binary string of length \(\ell\), or a failure symbol. For every \(x\in\{0,1\}^\ell\), if \(d_{\mathrm{sfx}}(w,C_N(x))\le\alpha\), the output must be exactly \(x\). No correctness requirement is imposed outside this promise, but the decoder must still halt within its time bound. The promise bounds errors in every suffix of the received prefix. It is not a bound on total Hamming error alone, which would not separate paths that diverge close to their end. The encoder and decoder are two fixed finite deterministic Turing-machine programs, with constants \(K,k\), each using at most \(K(N+1)^k\) bit steps per invocation on valid inputs. Encoding receives \(1^N\) and the currently available input prefix \(x\), and outputs \(C_N(x)\). The known horizon \(N\) is allowed; the code families for distinct horizons need not agree. All preprocessing, symbol calculations and output writes count toward the time bound, and there is no separately supplied table, advice, random seed, oracle or graph of the exponentially large tree. Constants and programs are independent of \(N\), \(\ell\), \(x\) and \(w\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction of the fixed alphabet, positive constants, uniform encoder and decoder, and proofs of prefix consistency, the distance inequality, the promised decoding guarantee and polynomial bit complexity; or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such collection exists. An existence proof for labels without efficient encoding and decoding does not fulfill the target. A growing alphabet, vanishing distance or decoding guarantee for selected input histories alone is insufficient. A limitation of an additional property not required above does not refute the stated existence claim.
cards.why: Tree codes protect communication whose later symbols depend on earlier interaction. A constant alphabet and positive tree distance would keep redundancy bounded while maintaining distinguishability after every possible divergence. Efficient deterministic encoding and decoding would supply a central explicit object in the theory of reliable interactive communication.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 15.34 explicitly requests efficient encoding and decoding, constant rate and constant relative distance. The card keeps all four requirements and uses the standard finite-height binary-input formulation.

The 2018 interactive-coding paper defines efficient tree-code decoding through suffix distance: a received prefix is decoded when every suffix has sufficiently few errors. This supplies a concrete promise for the otherwise unspecified decoding clause in the source question.

The checked May 2026 version of Cohen, Schulman and Srivastava records that constant-rate positive-distance tree codes exist nonconstructively, while the explicit constructions discussed there achieve rate \(\Omega(1/\log\log N)\) at constant distance. That rate tends to zero as the horizon grows.

cards.title: Positive-rate binary codes against adversarial deletions
cards.formal:
Determine the real zero-rate threshold
\[
p^*=\sup\{p\in[0,1]:\operatorname{Ach}(p)\},
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{Ach}(p)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\exists r\in(0,1]\ \forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[n\ge N\ \land\ |C|\ge 2^{rn}\ \land\
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right].
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\) means that every codeword in \(C\) can be recovered uniquely, with zero error, after any choice of at most \(t\) deleted positions. Deleted positions are not revealed, and the adversary may know the entire code and transmitted word. The positive rate \(r\) may depend on \(p\), but must remain fixed along the unbounded sequence of block lengths. This is a question about arbitrary code families, with no efficiency, linearity or uniform construction requirement. Benchmark acceptance is absolute error at most \(1/100\) in \(p^*\).
cards.definitions:
A binary word of length \(n\) is a sequence \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\), with each symbol represented by one bit. A code \(C\) is a nonempty subset of these words. It may be represented by its duplicate-free lexicographically ordered list of words; no bound on the size of this representation is imposed. A message can be identified with an integer in \(\{1,\ldots,|C|\}\), encoded as the corresponding word in this list. The information rate, in bits per transmitted bit, is
\[
R(C)=\frac{\log_2|C|}{n}.
\]
Only positive block lengths \(n\ge1\) are used.

A word \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) is a subsequence of \(x\) if there are indices \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_m\le n\) with \(y_j=x_{i_j}\) for every \(j\). The empty word is a subsequence. No surviving bit is changed or reordered. For \(0\le t\le n\), define the possible received words
\[
\mathcal D_t(x)=
\{y:\ y\text{ is a subsequence of }x,\quad n-t\le |y|\le n\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\operatorname{Correct}(C,t)\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\forall x,x'\in C,\quad x\ne x'\Longrightarrow
\mathcal D_t(x)\cap\mathcal D_t(x')=\varnothing.
\]
Equivalently, a deterministic decoder from the binary words of lengths \(0,\ldots,n\) to \(C\cup\{\bot\}\) can satisfy \(D(y)=x\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(y\in\mathcal D_t(x)\), where \(\bot\) denotes failure on other inputs. The decoder may know \(C,n,t\), but receives no deletion locations. Its computation time and storage are unrestricted. Success is required for every transmitted word and every allowed deletion pattern, rather than with a small average or probabilistic error.

For two words \(x,x'\), their longest-common-subsequence length \(\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')\) is the largest integer \(m\ge0\) for which some length-\(m\) word is a subsequence of both. The correction condition is equivalent to
\[
\forall x\ne x'\in C,\qquad
\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')<n-t.
\]
For \(t=\lfloor pn\rfloor\), this is also equivalent to \(\operatorname{LCS}(x,x')<(1-p)n\), since the LCS length is an integer and \(n-\lfloor pn\rfloor=\lceil(1-p)n\rceil\). This fixes the source's suppressed rounding conventions exactly.

The predicate \(\operatorname{Ach}(p)\) uses infinitely many, equivalently arbitrarily large, block lengths. It does not require a code at every sufficiently large length. The quantified codes may be arbitrary nonlinear subsets and need not be generated by a single algorithm. The model has no shared secret, public key, feedback, random channel, stochastic encoder or list output. It is the information-theoretic unique-decoding model.

The supremum exists as a real number: the achievable set is contained in \([0,1]\) and contains \(0\), witnessed by the full binary codes. Correcting a larger deletion budget implies correcting every smaller one, so achievability is downward closed. The definition does not assert that \(p^*\) itself is achievable, or that one fixed positive rate works for fractions approaching it.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a specified real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical expression defining it, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[
|a-p^*|\le\frac{1}{100}
\]
for the exact model and quantifiers above. The answer need not be an integer or an exactly attained deletion fraction. Merely repeating the supremum that defines \(p^*\) does not determine it.

One sufficient form is a certified interval: supply reals \(0\le l\le u\le1\), prove \(l\le p^*\le u\) and \(u-l\le1/50\), and take \(a=(l+u)/2\). The two bounds can be made fully explicit as follows:
\[
\forall p\in[0,l)\ \exists r\in(0,1]\
\forall N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\exists n\ge N\ \exists\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[|C|\ge2^{rn}\land
\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)\right],
\]
and
\[
\forall p\in(u,1]\ \forall r>0\
\exists N\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\ge N\ \forall\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\
\left[\operatorname{Correct}(C,\lfloor pn\rfloor)
\Longrightarrow |C|<2^{rn}\right].
\]
All block-length variables in these statements are integers. The lower statement allows rates and families to depend on \(p\), and the upper statement ranges over every code. Neither requires attainment at an endpoint. The Lean development must establish the stated correction property and its asymptotic quantifiers, not merely verify codes at finitely many lengths.

Exact determination is welcome but is not required. A one-sided estimate, a result for efficient or linear codes alone, a different alphabet, list decoding, or probabilistic deletion errors does not by itself meet this criterion.
cards.why: This threshold is a basic information-theoretic limit for synchronization errors over the smallest nontrivial alphabet. It links the geometry of large code families to unavoidable common subsequences in binary words and separates worst-case synchronization loss from substitution and erasure models. Determining it would settle the maximum deletion fraction compatible with nonvanishing binary communication rate, independently of implementation constraints. The numerical question remains significant after the qualitative discovery that the threshold is strictly below one half.

cards.title: Do nonlinear binary codes have a strictly better asymptotic rate?
cards.formal:
Does there exist a fixed real \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) such that
\[
R_2(\delta)>R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta),
\]
where these are the optimal asymptotic rates of arbitrary binary codes and binary linear codes, respectively, at relative minimum Hamming distance \(\delta\), as defined below? Any fixed strictly positive gap qualifies.
cards.definitions:
For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), let
\[
A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,
\ \forall x\ne y\in C,\ \Delta(x,y)\ge d\},
\]
where \(\Delta(x,y)=|\{j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_j\ne y_j\}|\). Let \(A_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d)\) be the same maximum restricted to vector subspaces \(C\le\mathbb F_2^n\), where addition is coordinatewise modulo two. The one-word code is allowed, and its pairwise distance condition is vacuous. Both finite maxima are well defined.

For a fixed real \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), define
\[
R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lfloor\delta n\rfloor)}{n},\qquad
R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(n,\lfloor\delta n\rfloor)}{n}.
\]
These bounded-sequence limit superiors are real numbers in \([0,1]\), measured in message bits per transmitted bit. The limsup of \((a_n)\) means \(\inf_{N\ge1}\sup_{n\ge N}a_n\). No assumption that the ordinary limits exist is made. The distance fraction is fixed before taking either limit superior.

All finite codes are eligible regardless of encoding, decoding, description or construction complexity. The arbitrary-code side includes linear codes. The linear side permits every binary subspace and every dimension. Affine translates do not change attainable cardinality and distance, so permitting affine codes on that side gives the same maximum.

A positive answer establishes \(R_2(\delta)\ge R_2^{\mathrm{lin}}(\delta)+\eta\) for some fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and \(\eta>0\). Neither constant has a prescribed magnitude. A negative answer proves equality of the two rates for every \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), since the reverse inequality always follows from inclusion. An isolated finite-block advantage, a subexponential size advantage, or a comparison with one particular linear construction is not sufficient. This is a binary existence question, not a request to approximate the two entire rate curves.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of a fixed relative distance with a strictly positive asymptotic rate gap. A positive result must compare with all binary linear codes, and a negative result must establish equality throughout (0,1/2). No minimum improvement such as 1/100 is imposed.
cards.why: Linearity makes coding algebraically tractable, but it is unknown in this regime whether it sacrifices a positive fraction of information per transmitted bit. Resolving the comparison would distinguish a fundamental cost of linearity from limitations of known constructions and bounds.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph with no loops or multiple edges. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A valid input list \(\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_r)\), \(r\ge0\), is encoded by the orders and full Boolean adjacency matrices of its members on \([|V(F_i)|]\); the matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal. Integer orders and list lengths are binary encoded with delimiters. Repeated graphs and the graph of order zero are allowed. For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\) consist of all graphs on \([n]\) with no induced copy of any \(F_i\). An induced copy of \(F_i\) is an injection \(\phi:V(F_i)\to[n]\) such that for every distinct \(u,v\), \(\{u,v\}\in E(F_i)\) if and only if \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(G)\). For a graph \(G\) on \([n]\), define \[d_{\mathcal F}(G)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|\] when the set is nonempty, and \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)=+\infty\) otherwise. Symmetric difference counts each added or deleted undirected edge once. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. For an integer \(s\ge1\), the canonical sampling test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of size \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries all \(\binom{|S|}{2}\) adjacency bits within it, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of \(\mathcal F\). Local sampling and finite pattern checking are not charged as adjacency queries. The polynomial sampling property means that there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph \(G\), this test with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). Probability is solely over the uniform subset. For every member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\), the test accepts with probability one. There is no extra promise on the host graph. The empty forbidden list defines all graphs; if the list contains the order-zero graph, every test rejects since the empty induced copy exists in every sample. These conventions also specify empty property classes at individual orders. The classifier takes only \(\mathcal F\), not \(n,\varepsilon,C\) or \(a\), and need not output the constants. It is one finite program with no advice or oracle, required to output YES exactly for lists with the sampling property and NO for all other valid lists. It may reject malformed encodings; it must halt on every input string.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total classifier exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such classifier exists. The affirmative answer must establish termination and both directions of correctness on every finite forbidden list. The negative answer must rule out every deterministic Turing program as a total correct classifier. An equivalent condition that still quantifies over unbounded host graphs and all accuracy parameters is not by itself a decision algorithm. Proving polynomial testability for one family or a finite collection of families does not meet the universal classification target.
cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

cards.context:
Each finite forbidden list defines an elementary graph-membership test: search the input graph for the listed induced patterns. The classification problem has a different input and quantifier structure. Given the list alone, it asks whether every sufficiently distant host graph has a small random sample witnessing a violation, with a single polynomial bound across all host orders and accuracy parameters.

The inherited card added an effectiveness requirement to the source’s structural characterization programme. This review preserves that choice and makes its machine model explicit. The source does not itself assert the decidability statement or its negation, so the current scientific status of this effective target is recorded as uncertain.

Hereditary properties are closed under taking induced subgraphs, and every forbidden-induced-pattern property here is hereditary. General hereditary testing gives some size-independent sample bound. It does not guarantee polynomial dependence on reciprocal distance, which is the distinction the classifier must recognize.

The finite list remains fixed during each sampling problem. Reading every pair in a sample squares the sample size, so polynomial vertex sampling and the resulting polynomial adjacency-query bound agree at this level of precision. The classifier itself is allowed arbitrary finite time; it is not a polynomial-time recognition question.

For nonempty finite families in the usual nontrivial setting, the checked sufficient condition is that the family contain a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph. Bipartite means a partition into two independent sets; co-bipartite means a partition into two cliques, with arbitrary edges between them; split means a partition into a clique and an independent set. One graph may fill several roles. A necessary condition requires bipartite and co-bipartite members.

The necessary and sufficient conditions do not coincide. The paper provides families meeting the former that are hard to test, and the split-graph property supplies a positive case outside the latter. For split graphs the forbidden list consists of the four-cycle, its complement and the five-cycle; none is itself split. These examples prevent turning either condition into a complete classification.

Even among single forbidden patterns, the induced four-cycle and its complement are the outstanding polynomial-testability cases identified by the survey. The four-vertex path case, whose free graphs are cographs, has a polynomial tester.

The checked induced-four-cycle theorem gives single-exponential reciprocal-distance dependence. It is relevant progress on a member of the class being classified, but does not establish the polynomial sampling property for that member.

The August 2026 container characterization supplies explicit quantitative translations between tester bounds and combinatorial container parameters. Its premises still range over all large host graphs and accuracy parameters. The inspected statements do not give a procedure that halts on each finite forbidden list and decides whether polynomial parameters exist.

An effective positive classification would turn a finite pattern description into a reliable recognition method for the polynomial testing regime. An undecidability result would instead limit such systematic recognition, even though checking any particular finite host graph against the list is straightforward.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

cards.context:
A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

The existing card explicitly selected the polynomial implication from the stronger quantitative question in the source. Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this card, but a proof of this card would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions. The present review preserves this previously recorded target.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.

cards.title: Sharp graph-removal bounds for fixed patterns
cards.formal: Determine the asymptotic order of the extremal copy-count function \(M_H(\varepsilon,n)\) defined below, for every fixed connected finite simple graph \(H\) with at least two edges. Both the proximity parameter \(\varepsilon\) and the graph order \(n\) vary. The requested precision is matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants depending only on \(H\), uniformly over all feasible pairs \((\varepsilon,n)\). Thus the answer must specify bounds \(B_H(\varepsilon,n)>0\) and prove that, for each such \(H\), there are constants \(0<c_H\le C_H<\infty\) such that \[c_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\le M_H(\varepsilon,n)\le C_H B_H(\varepsilon,n)\] for every feasible pair. The copies are ordinary subgraphs, with extra edges allowed.
cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(t=|V(H)|\). All graphs are undirected and have neither loops nor multiple edges. A graph is \(H\)-free if there is no injective map \(\phi:V(H)\to V(G)\) taking every edge of \(H\) to an edge of \(G\); nonedges of \(H\) impose no restriction. Let \(r_H(G)\) be the least number of edges that must be deleted from \(G\) to make it \(H\)-free. Allowing edge additions as well cannot decrease this minimum. Use the source's adjacency-matrix distance \(d_H(G)=2r_H(G)/n^{2}\): each changed undirected edge changes two matrix entries. Say that \(G\) is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\), with a strict inequality. Define \(N_H(G)\) to be the number of \(t\)-element subsets \(S\subseteq[n]\) for which \(G[S]\) contains an ordinary copy of \(H\), counting each such subset once even if it supports several embeddings. This fixes the copy convention suggested by the source's random-subset test; counting injective labelled embeddings instead changes the count by factors between one and \(t!\). A feasible pair is a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and an integer \(n\ge t\) for which at least one graph on \([n]\) has \(d_H(G)>\varepsilon\). On precisely this domain, set \[M_H(\varepsilon,n)=\min\{N_H(G):V(G)=[n],\ d_H(G)>\varepsilon\}.\] The minimum is over a nonempty finite set, so it is a positive integer. No value is requested for an infeasible pair. The constants in the matching bounds may depend on the whole fixed pattern \(H\), but not on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\); in particular, \(\varepsilon\) may decrease with \(n\). The target is the growth of this extremal function, not the running time of enumerating graphs. No extra minimum-degree, regularity, randomness or sparsity promise is imposed on \(G\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the matching asymptotic bounds in the formal statement and a complete Lean-checked proof of both inequalities for every permitted pattern and feasible parameter pair. The lower inequality must hold for every graph at the stated distance, and the upper inequality must establish existence of graphs with the claimed copy count. Merely restating the defining minimization, tabulating finitely many values, giving one-sided bounds, or establishing only that some positive removal bound exists does not meet this growth target. The precision here is a multiplicative constant factor depending only on the pattern, not additive \(1/100\) accuracy on a normalized copy density.
cards.why: Removal bounds quantify how visible a forbidden configuration must become once a graph is globally far from avoiding it. Their dependence on the distance parameter controls the sampling cost of detecting violations and connects dense-graph testing to extremal and additive combinatorics. Distinguishing polynomial from superpolynomial dependence identifies a broad boundary, but does not determine the rate on either side of it.

cards.context:
For a fixed pattern on \(t\) vertices, a random \(t\)-vertex subset detects a violation with probability exactly \(N_H(G)/\binom{n}{t}\). The extremal function asks how small that probability can be while repairing the whole graph still requires changing a positive fraction of its adjacency matrix. This connects a global repair requirement to the frequency of small observable witnesses.

Ordinary and induced removal are different questions. An ordinary copy only requires the pattern's edges to be present; an induced copy also requires its nonedges to remain absent. For example, three mutually adjacent vertices contain a three-vertex path as an ordinary subgraph, but not as an induced path. This card retains ordinary copies from Definition 8.16 and the connected-pattern scope of Open Problem 8.17.

The classical removal lemma ensures a positive copy density for every fixed positive distance, uniformly over graph order. Its quantitative content can nevertheless be extremely weak: the known general lower guarantee involves an inverse tower of exponentials, while nonbipartite examples exclude every fixed polynomial dependence on distance. A positive constant for each fixed distance therefore says much less than a sharp answer as the distance tends to zero.

The source asks for relatively tight bounds on a function of both distance and graph order. This card makes that precision explicit as constant-factor matching bounds with pattern-dependent constants, retaining both parameters and specifying the feasible domain. It does not silently replace the question by the triangle-only case, by a large-graph limit, or by the already known polynomial/nonpolynomial classification. The matrix normalization differs by a factor of two from the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention in several later papers.

The dependence on the host graph matters. A sufficiently large minimum degree can give linear removal bounds for cliques, whereas unrestricted hosts admit much smaller copy densities. Such a theorem clarifies a special regime and cannot supply a bound for every graph in the domain of this card.

cards.title: Polynomial-query submodularity testing
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized one-sided-error tester for submodularity of arbitrary real-valued set functions using a number of value queries polynomial in the dimension and reciprocal distance? Precisely, do there exist one tester \(A\) in the model below and integers \(C,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), and every function \(f:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\), the algorithm \(A^{f}(n,\varepsilon)\) halts and makes at most \(C((n+1)/\varepsilon)^{k}\) value queries on every execution, accepts with probability one if \(f\) is submodular, and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)\ge\varepsilon\)? The constants and program must work simultaneously for all parameters and functions.
cards.definitions: Here \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) is its set of all subsets, represented by their \(n\)-bit indicator vectors. The class \(\mathcal S_n\) consists of all functions \(g:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[g(S)+g(T)\ge g(S\cap T)+g(S\cup T)\qquad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\] The distance is normalized Hamming distance on the full domain: \[d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)=\min_{g\in\mathcal S_n}2^{-n}\bigl|\{S\subseteq[n]:f(S)\ne g(S)\}\bigr|.\] This minimum exists because attainable disagreement counts form a nonempty subset of the finite set \(\{0,\ldots,2^n\}\). It measures how many table entries change, regardless of the magnitudes of the changes. There is no promise of monotonicity, nonnegativity, bounded range, integrality or normalization at the empty set. The input supplies \(n\) in binary and \(\varepsilon\) as a ratio of positive binary integers; the full value table is accessible only through queries. One value query chooses a subset \(S\) and returns the exact real number \(f(S)\), at cost one. Queries may depend on earlier answers and random bits. To specify computation on these exact values, use a finite program with integer and bit-string work storage, real registers initialized by rational constants, exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values, and exact order/equality comparisons. Division by zero is forbidden. The program can request independent fair random bits and can copy queried real values into registers. There is no real-valued advice, noncomputable primitive or other oracle. Only value queries are charged; intervening computation and storage have no quantitative bound, but every execution must terminate after finitely many steps. Acceptance probabilities are over the independent random bits, for each fixed input function. Behavior is unrestricted when \(0<d_0(f,\mathcal S_n)<\varepsilon\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of a tester with every guarantee in the formal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover arbitrary real-valued functions and all dimensions and proximity parameters with one finite program and fixed polynomial constants. A negative answer must exclude every such program and every fixed choice of polynomial constants, not only a particular local tester. A result for average value error, a restricted value range, a monotonicity promise, or a constant-dimensional grid does not settle this target.
cards.why: Submodularity formalizes diminishing returns and underlies many optimization and valuation models. Its value table has exponentially many entries, while algorithms using a submodular value oracle typically see only a small part of it. Polynomial-query testing would determine whether global consistency with that structural assumption can be checked from comparably limited information, with rejection guaranteed for functions requiring widespread changes.

cards.context:
A set function assigns a value to each possible subset of a ground set. Submodularity says that adding an element cannot become more valuable merely because the receiving set has grown. Equivalently, it satisfies the union/intersection inequality in the definitions. With \(n\) elements there are \(2^{n}\) values, so inspecting a polynomial number of them is a small fraction of the complete object.

Testing allows an unresolved band of nearby nonsubmodular inputs. The tester must accept genuinely submodular functions and reject functions that disagree with every submodular function on at least an \(\varepsilon\)-fraction of subsets. It is not required to reconstruct the closest submodular function or to decide exact membership for every oracle.

Hamming distance treats any changed entry as one disagreement. In contrast, an \(\ell_p\) distance for finite \(p\) averages the magnitudes of changes. Many tiny discrepancies can therefore contribute little to that norm while affecting a large fraction of the table. The published constant-query result for bounded functions in an \(\ell_p\) metric does not imply polynomial-query testing in the Hamming metric used here.

The saved problem asks both for optimal query complexity and, specifically, whether polynomially many queries suffice. This card selects that explicitly posed polynomial threshold as its single yes/no target. The one-sided-error convention is taken from Definition 1.2 of the cited foundational paper. The finite-program exact-real convention makes the value-oracle interpretation explicit; it is not a claim about bit complexity or noisy measurements.

The existing upper and lower bounds leave a substantial gap: known general testing uses a subexponential number of queries for fixed distance, while a nearly quadratic lower bound rules out much smaller sample budgets. Neither result decides whether some fixed polynomial suffices. Bounds on the frequency of a particular kind of local violation also have a narrower scope than a lower bound against every adaptive tester.

Its constant-query theorem concerns bounded functions in \(\ell_p\) distance; its Hamming-distance results test separate component properties with subexponential bounds. These results do not supply the polynomial Hamming tester asked for here.

cards.title: Planar graphs from local neighborhoods
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a positive integer \(D=D(\varepsilon)\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every pair of finite simple planar graphs \(G,H\) on \(n\) vertices, equality of their multisets of rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhoods implies \[\min_{\phi:V(G)\cong V(H)}\left|\phi(E(G))\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)\right|\le\varepsilon n?\] The minimum is over all vertex bijections, and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference of edge sets. There is no maximum-degree bound; the radius may depend only on \(\varepsilon\).
cards.definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is a finite vertex set \(V\) and a set \(E\) of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Thus loops and multiple edges are excluded. A planar graph admits a drawing in the plane with distinct points for vertices and curves for edges whose interiors neither intersect one another nor meet a vertex. A drawing is not part of the data, and it is not used to compare neighborhoods. Graphs need not be connected. Their order is \(n=|V|\), and the two graphs in the question have the same order.

The graph distance \(\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path from \(u\) to \(v\), with distance infinity when no path exists. The rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhood \(B_G(v,D)\) is the subgraph induced by \(\{u\in V(G):\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\le D\}\), together with the distinguished root \(v\). An induced subgraph retains every edge whose two endpoints belong to that set. Rooted graphs are isomorphic when a bijection of their vertices preserves edges and sends one root to the other. Vertex labels, the planar drawing, any ordering of neighbors, and edges leaving the neighborhood are not part of its rooted isomorphism type.

The multiset of radius-\(D\) neighborhoods records each rooted isomorphism type with its multiplicity among the \(n\) possible roots. Equality means that, for every finite rooted graph \(F\), the number of vertices \(v\) for which \(B_G(v,D)\) is isomorphic to \(F\) equals the corresponding number in \(H\). Thus multiplicities matter. Although corresponding roots can be paired, their individual neighborhood isomorphisms need not agree on overlapping vertices. In particular, such a pairing is not already a global graph isomorphism. Even a radius-one neighborhood may contain arbitrarily many vertices, because degrees are unrestricted.

For a vertex bijection \(\phi:V(G)\to V(H)\), define \(\phi(E(G))=\{\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\). The symmetric difference consists of edges in exactly one of its two arguments. Its cardinality counts edge deletions plus edge additions, each at unit cost, after a free relabeling of vertices. Taking the minimum over bijections gives the edit distance to isomorphism. There are no vertex edits or isolated-vertex padding in this equal-order question. Intermediate graphs during edge editing are not required to be planar. The permitted number of edits is at most \(\varepsilon n\), normalized by vertex count rather than by the number of possible edges or by a degree bound. For \(n=1\) the conclusion is automatic. No algorithm for finding the bijection, a computable bound on \(D\), or property-testing oracle is requested; this is a structural existence statement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that for every positive integer \(D\), there are some \(n\ge1\) and simple planar \(n\)-vertex graphs \(G,H\) with identical radius-\(D\) neighborhood multisets but edit distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon_0 n\). The counterexample graphs and their orders may depend on \(D\); the same positive \(\varepsilon_0\) must work throughout. A proof restricted to bounded maximum degree or to outerplanar graphs does not establish the assertion for all planar graphs. Equality of the set of neighborhood types without multiplicities is a different hypothesis. A radius growing with \(n\) or maximum degree is insufficient. This is an exact yes/no implication, not a numerical approximation problem.
cards.why: This asks whether local structure determines approximate global structure throughout the planar family, even around vertices of very high degree. It isolates a structural obstruction behind extending sparse-graph testing beyond bounded-degree and outerplanar settings.

cards.context:
The broad imported question asked for a classification of graph properties testable with sublinear query complexity. This card now adopts the separate, concrete planar local-neighborhood question from the same source. The change of scope was explicitly selected on 16 September 2026; it does not claim to complete the original general classification programme.

The structural issue is whether sufficiently large local views determine a sparse planar graph up to a small linear number of edge edits. The neighborhoods carry no consistent global labels. Matching their multiplicities therefore supplies statistical local information, not a ready-made global correspondence.

For planar graphs with a fixed maximum degree, earlier local-to-global results provide a radius depending on both the error tolerance and that degree bound. The selected question asks whether the degree dependence can be removed completely. Planarity bounds average degree, but permits individual degrees growing with the graph order.

Babu, Khoury and Newman prove the required local-view implication for outerplanar graphs, with no maximum-degree bound. Outerplanar means that the graph has a plane drawing with every vertex incident to the exterior face. Their Theorem 4.4 states the same qualitative radius-versus-edge-distance conclusion for that subclass.

The source extends its methods to graphs with a fixed number of edge-removal outer layers. It distinguishes this from removing exterior vertices layer by layer, and explicitly retains the ordinary 2-outerplanar case as open at publication. Those positive results therefore must not be read as covering every planar graph.

The paper also obtains polylogarithmic-query property testers for its unbounded-degree subclasses, using ordered-neighbor and degree access. These algorithmic results explain the motivation for the structural question, but the selected target itself asks only for the stated finite-graph implication.

Basu, Kumar and Seshadhri sharpen the dependence on proximity for testing properties of bounded-degree planar graphs and show matching exponential behavior for isomorphism testing. Their results retain a maximum-degree bound and therefore do not settle the unbounded-degree local-view question.

Babu, Khoury and Newman prove the required local-view implication for outerplanar graphs, with no maximum-degree bound. Outerplanar means that the graph has a plane drawing with every vertex incident to the exterior face. Their Theorem 4.4 states the same qualitative radius-versus-edge-distance conclusion for that subclass.

The source extends its methods to graphs with a fixed number of edge-removal outer layers. It distinguishes this from removing exterior vertices layer by layer, and explicitly retains the ordinary 2-outerplanar case as open at publication. Those positive results therefore must not be read as covering every planar graph.

The paper also obtains polylogarithmic-query property testers for its unbounded-degree subclasses, using ordered-neighbor and degree access. These algorithmic results explain the motivation for the structural question, but the selected target itself asks only for the stated finite-graph implication.

Basu, Kumar and Seshadhri sharpen the dependence on proximity for testing properties of bounded-degree planar graphs and show matching exponential behavior for isomorphism testing. Their results retain a maximum-degree bound and therefore do not settle the unbounded-degree local-view question.

cards.title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
cards.formal:
Can isomorphism between two arbitrary bounded-degree graphs be tested with a sublinear number of adjacency-list queries? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized tester \(A\), with explicit inputs \(n\ge1\), a degree bound \(d\ge1\), and an integer \(q\ge2\), satisfying the following guarantees for every pair of allowed \(n\)-vertex input graphs \(G_1,G_2\)?
\[G_1\cong G_2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)\ge1/q\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ rejects}]\ge2/3.\]
For each fixed \(d,q\), its worst-case query bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) must satisfy
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{Q(n,d,q)}n=0.\]
Both graphs are given only through oracles. The graph model, distance and query accounting are specified below.
cards.definitions:
The graphs \(G_i=([n],E_i)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), are undirected and simple, with maximum degree at most \(d\). Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. There is no expansion, hyperfiniteness, component-size or randomness promise on their structure.

Graph \(G_i\) is represented by an incidence oracle \(g_i:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\cup\{\bot\}\). Its first \(\deg_{G_i}(v)\) entries at vertex \(v\) list the distinct neighbors of \(v\) in an arbitrary fixed order, and the remaining entries are \(\bot\). The oracles are promised consistent with undirected simple graphs. One adjacency query chooses \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \(v\in[n]\), and \(j\in[d]\), and receives \(g_i(v,j)\). Queries may depend on earlier answers. Correctness must hold for every permitted neighbor ordering.

For a permutation \(\sigma\) of \([n]\), put \(\sigma(E_2)=\{\{\sigma(u),\sigma(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E_2\}\). Define
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)=\frac1{dn}\min_{\sigma\in S_n}|E_1\mathbin{\triangle}\sigma(E_2)|,\]
where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference. Each deleted or added undirected edge counts once. Thus distance zero means graph isomorphism, and the rejection promise means at least \(dn/q\) edge edits are needed after the best vertex relabelling. Neighbor-list positions do not affect this distance. For nonisomorphic pairs at distance strictly below \(1/q\), either output is allowed.

The tester is a probabilistic oracle Turing algorithm given binary \(n,d,q\), access to both incidence oracles, independent fair random bits and a primitive returning an independent uniformly sampled vertex label in \([n]\). Count every incidence-oracle call and every such vertex-sampling call as one query. All other finite local computation is unrestricted, and the tester must halt. The bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) holds on every allowed pair, every representation and every sequence of random outcomes. Success probabilities include all internal randomness and vertex samples. No graph-dependent advice or full description of either graph is provided; any preprocessing uses only \(n,d,q\).

The degree and reciprocal proximity are fixed when taking the sublinear limit. There is no requirement for one bound uniform in growing \(d\) or \(q\), and no polynomial runtime requirement beyond the query guarantee. Using reciprocal integer accuracies covers all fixed positive proximities by choosing a smaller reciprocal threshold. The edge-edit normalization follows the saved card; the source also uses a convention with a factor of two in the edge threshold. That constant rescaling does not change the all-fixed-proximities existence question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a tester with the stated correctness, access and sublinear-query guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation of that existence statement. A positive answer must cover every pair of bounded-degree input graphs and every fixed proximity, with two-sided error at most \(1/3\). A near-linear bound that is not \(o(n)\), a guarantee for almost all graphs, a known-target tester, or a result only for small connected components is insufficient. A lower bound of order \(n^{2/3}\) up to logarithmic factors alone does not rule out sublinear testing.
cards.why: The problem asks whether two large sparse structures can be compared without reading a linear fraction of their neighborhoods. It isolates the information needed to recognize structural similarity when both objects are unknown. A resolution would locate a basic boundary of sublinear access and explain whether large connected components create an obstruction beyond the known distribution-like examples.

cards.title: Polynomial-query adaptive tolerant monotonicity testing
cards.formal: For every pair of fixed rational constants \(0<a<b\le1/2\), do there exist constants \(C_{a,b}>0\) and \(q_{a,b}\in\mathbb N_0\) such that \[Q(n;a,b)\le C_{a,b}(n+1)^{q_{a,b}}\qquad\text{for every }n\ge1?\] Here \(Q(n;a,b)\) is the randomized adaptive value-query complexity, defined below, of accepting Boolean functions at uniform distance at most \(a\) from monotonicity and rejecting those at distance at least \(b\), with success probability at least \(2/3\). Computation between queries is unrestricted.
cards.definitions:
The domain \(\{0,1\}^n\) has the coordinatewise partial order: \(x\le y\) if \(x_i\le y_i\) for all \(i\). A function \(g:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) is monotone if \(g(x)\le g(y)\) whenever \(x\le y\). For arbitrary \(f\), define \[\operatorname{dist}(f,\mathrm{MON}_n)=\min_{g\in\mathrm{MON}_n}2^{-n}|\{x:f(x)\ne g(x)\}|.\] The input function is unknown and is accessed by exact value queries at chosen vertices. Query locations may depend on all previous answers and internal randomness. Arbitrary computation between queries is free.

A tester must accept every function of distance at most \(a\) with probability at least \(2/3\), and reject every function of distance at least \(b\) with probability at least \(2/3\). No guarantee is imposed for distances strictly between the thresholds. Both types of errors are allowed. \(Q(n;a,b)\) is the smallest worst-case number of queries of any randomized decision tree satisfying these guarantees for all input functions. Probability is only over that tree's internal randomness. Repeated queries count as queries, and there is no free labelled sampling oracle; uniformly chosen test points can of course be queried. An entire truth-table query budget of \(2^n\) always makes the quantity finite.

The requested asymptotics take \(n\to\infty\) with \(a,b\) fixed; upper and lower multiplicative constants may depend on these thresholds. Since either the constant-zero or constant-one function differs from \(f\) on at most half the domain, every distance is at most \(1/2\). Therefore \(Q(n;a,b)=0\) when \(b>1/2\); those formal parameter pairs are trivial. The substantive regime has \(b\le1/2\).

A nonadaptive tester chooses all queried points before receiving any answers. A lower bound restricted to such testers does not automatically apply to the adaptive trees defining this card. Ordinary monotonicity testing is the separate case where the acceptance threshold is zero; tolerance here requires accepting all functions within positive distance \(a\).
cards.answer_criterion: For each fixed tolerance pair \(a,b\), prove in Lean a polynomial adaptive query bound for the two promised classes at success probability \(2/3\), or exhibit one fixed pair for which every polynomial query bound fails.
cards.why: Tolerance changes monotonicity testing from detecting defects to estimating distance, exposing a large unexplained query gap.

cards.title: Efficient black-box testing of high-dimensional convexity
cards.formal: For each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), is there a randomized adaptive membership-query tester that, for every dimension \(n\) and every Borel set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), distinguishes convexity from Gaussian distance at least \(\varepsilon\) to every convex set using at most \(C_\varepsilon n^{c_\varepsilon}\) queries and with error probability at most \(1/3\) on each promised input? This is ordinary two-sided testing, not tolerant testing.
cards.definitions:
The standard Gaussian measure \(\gamma_n\) has density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\). A set \(K\) is convex if \((1-t)x+ty\in K\) for every \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). Its distance from \(S\) is the Gaussian measure of the symmetric difference, \(\gamma_n(S\triangle K)\). Define distance to convexity as the infimum of this quantity over Borel convex sets \(K\), including the empty set and all of \(\mathbb R^n\).

An oracle returns the exact bit \(1_S(x)\) for a requested point \(x\). Queries can be chosen adaptively. The query model is an information model over exact real points: a randomized decision tree may choose points by measurable functions of its internal randomness and previous answer bits, with arbitrary measurable computation free. Independent Gaussian random points can be generated internally, but obtaining their membership labels costs queries. There is no oracle supplying samples conditioned on membership in \(S\), a boundary, a separation hyperplane or a finite description of the set.

The tester must accept every convex input with probability at least \(2/3\), and reject every input whose distance to convexity is at least \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either output is allowed in the gap. Success probability is over its internal randomness on each fixed oracle, and the query bound is worst-case over oracles and random choices. Both false acceptance and false rejection are permitted. Constants and the polynomial degree may depend on the fixed accuracy but not on dimension or the set. This is an oracle-query claim, not a polynomial bound on finite-precision arithmetic or point representation.

Restricting to Borel inputs makes all measures and probabilities defined; the source's arbitrary measurable-set formulation is interpreted with this regularity convention. A tolerant tester would also have to accept nonconvex sets close to convexity. That additional promise is not required here.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked affirmative proof of a family of testers with the stated polynomial query bounds for every fixed accuracy, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must exclude adaptive two-sided testers, not only one-sided or nonadaptive procedures. A sample-only lower bound or a tolerant-testing lower bound is insufficient. A theorem about query count alone need not prove a comparable bound on all arithmetic operations.
cards.why: This asks whether a basic high-dimensional geometric property is accessible through a small black-box interface.

cards.title: Linear-query lower bound for sparse binary matrix rank estimation
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge2\), a fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\ge1\), such that \[Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\ge cn\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge n_0?\] Here \(Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\) is the minimum randomized adaptive row/column-query cost, defined below, for estimating the rank over \(\mathbb F_2\) of every \(n\)-by-\(n\) matrix having at most \(d\) ones per row and column, to additive error \(\varepsilon n\) with success probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) uses arithmetic modulo two. Rank is the dimension of the span of the columns over that field, and belongs to \(\{0,\ldots,n\}\). Both row and column degree bounds are promises; there are no symmetry or graph-incidence promises. The all-zero matrix and zero rows or columns are allowed.

A row query gives a label \(i\in[n]\) and receives the complete list of indices j for which \(A_{ij}=1\), in increasing order. A column query analogously returns every i with \(A_{ij}=1\). Each list query costs one, and contains at most d indices. Query choices may depend on all previous answers and random coins. There is no free access to matrix-vector products or uniformly random nonzero entries. Random row or column labels can be chosen internally, but their lists still cost queries.

Define \(Q_d(n,\varepsilon)\) as the minimum worst-case number of queries of a randomized decision tree returning a real estimate r with \(\Pr[|r-\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}(A)|\le\varepsilon n]\ge2/3\) on each eligible matrix. Arbitrary computation on the transcript is free. Query complexity is at most n by reading every row. The asymptotic limit is n tending to infinity with d and accuracy fixed; matching constants may depend on both. This is not an algorithm whose total time must be sublinear.

The original problem list includes rectangular matrices over finite fields; the imported card selected square matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\). For binary matrices, the neighbor lists determine all nonzero values, so the interface is complete. Its conjectured general linear lower bound should mean a fixed nontrivial degree and accuracy regime, not a claim for every d: the d=1 class, for example, has much simpler rank structure.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean a linear row/column-query lower bound at every sufficiently large dimension for one fixed degree bound and precision. A refutation must negate this order of quantifiers using the same adaptive access and per-input success requirements.
cards.why: Rank estimation tests whether a global algebraic invariant can be recovered from local sparse access.

cards.title: Efficient characterization of instance-optimal identity testing
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(\Phi\) and a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite rational probability vector \(q\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1\),
\[C^{-1}n_*(q,\varepsilon)\le\Phi(q,\varepsilon)\le Cn_*(q,\varepsilon)?\]
The integer \(n_*(q,\varepsilon)\) is the smallest fixed number of independent samples needed to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon\), with each error probability at most \(1/3\), when the reference \(q\) is known and the unknown distribution \(p\) is otherwise arbitrary. Computation of the statistical test is unrestricted. Polynomial time is required of the evaluator of the characterization, in the binary input length of \((q,\varepsilon)\), and the multiplicative constant must hold at the same input \(\varepsilon\).

This is the finite, explicitly encoded version of the efficient-computability branch of the source's Open Question 1. The source also allows countably infinite domains and leaves “succinct” open to a closed-form interpretation; this card makes its computational interpretation and finite rational input scope explicit rather than treating those broader interpretations as equivalent.
cards.definitions:
For an integer \(d\ge1\), write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and \(\Delta_d=\{p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{d}:\sum_i p_i=1\}\). The input lists every entry of \(q\in\Delta_d\cap\mathbb Q^d\), including zeros, and the rational number \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\). Rationals are represented by binary nonnegative numerators and positive denominators in lowest terms, with delimiters; let \(B\) be the total bit length, including the length encoding of the list. No oracle or compressed description replaces this list. The alternative \(p\) ranges over all of \(\Delta_d\), including irrational probabilities and mass on coordinates where \(q_i=0\). Total variation is
\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{d}|p_i-q_i|.\]

For a nonnegative integer \(s\), a possibly randomized statistical test is specified by a function \(\tau:[d]^s\to[0,1]\); \(\tau(x)\) is its conditional probability of rejecting the null on sample sequence \(x\). There is no time, space or representation constraint on this finite table of real probabilities. The product law \(p^{\otimes s}\) means that all \(s\) observations are independent and have law \(p\). A valid test satisfies
\[\mathbb E_{q^{\otimes s}}\tau\le1/3,\qquad
\forall p\in\Delta_d\text{ with }d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_{p^{\otimes s}}\tau\ge2/3.\]
The same test must work for every alternative at that fixed \((q,\varepsilon)\); it cannot be chosen after learning \(p\). The minimum such \(s\) defines \(n_*\). It is finite on every permitted input. The sample count is fixed in advance, not an expected stopping time, and the two errors are bounded separately. Cases with \(0<d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\le\varepsilon\) impose no condition.

The zero-sample case is included: \([d]^0\) is a singleton. The alternative is empty exactly when \(\varepsilon\ge1-\min_iq_i\), since the largest possible distance from \(q\) in this simplex is \(1-\min_iq_i\). In that case \(n_*=0\); otherwise \(n_*\ge1\). Thus the claimed multiplicative guarantee requires the evaluator to return exactly zero in empty-alternative cases, including \(d=1\). The strict inequality in the alternative is intentional.

The evaluator is a single finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machine. It outputs a nonnegative integer in binary and halts within \(K(B+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(K,a\), independent of \(d,q,\varepsilon\); input reading, bit arithmetic and output writing all count. It has no advice or oracles, and must halt within the same bound on malformed encodings, whose outputs are irrelevant. The quantifier order is existence of the evaluator and constants, followed by all valid inputs. There is no permission for polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) in place of polynomial dependence on its encoded length. The statistical tester whose existence defines \(n_*\) is a separate object and need not be produced by this evaluator.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence claim. A positive answer must specify the evaluator and prove its uniform polynomial running time and both bounds with one universal finite factor \(C\). A negative answer must refute the existence of every such evaluator and constant; failure of one proposed expression is insufficient. Neither defining \(\Phi\) by the minimum over all statistical tests without proving efficient evaluation, nor comparing upper and lower bounds at different multiples of \(\varepsilon\), satisfies this target. A conditional computational obstruction alone does not prove the unconditional negative claim. Countably infinite or implicitly described references are outside this explicitly selected variant.
cards.why: Two reference distributions on the same domain can require very different numbers of samples to test. A computable characterization at the exact requested distance would identify the information needed for each reference profile, including distributions for which existing bounds disagree by unbounded factors. It would also separate the statistical cost of testing from the cost of evaluating that cost.

cards.title: Linear-in-state-count symmetric Markov-chain identity testing
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized tester and a universal constant \(C>0\) that, for every integer \(n\ge2\), rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1/4\), and explicitly supplied symmetric reference transition matrix \(Q\), tests an unknown symmetric chain \(P\) using at most \(\lceil Cn/\varepsilon\rceil\) observed transitions of one trajectory? For every starting state it must accept with probability at least \(2/3\) when \(P=Q\) and reject with probability at least \(2/3\) when \[\Delta(P,Q)=1-\rho\!\left((\sqrt{P_{ij}Q_{ij}})_{i,j}\right)>\varepsilon.\] Here \(\rho\) is spectral radius. The access model below permits neither resets nor a chosen starting state; reducible chains are included.
cards.definitions: A chain on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) has a transition matrix \(P\in[0,1]^{n\times n}\) with \(\sum_jP_{ij}=1\) for each \(i\). Symmetry means \(P_{ij}=P_{ji}\). Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers, and zeros, holding probabilities and disconnected state spaces are allowed. For two such matrices set \[R(P,Q)_{ij}=\sqrt{P_{ij}Q_{ij}},\qquad \Delta(P,Q)=1-\rho(R(P,Q)),\] where \(\rho\) is the spectral radius, the maximum absolute value of an eigenvalue. The square root is entrywise; it is not a matrix square root. The resulting discrepancy lies in \([0,1]\), but it need not be a metric. The tester receives \(n\), rational \(\varepsilon\), the complete reference matrix \(Q\), and observations from one trajectory of an unknown symmetric matrix \(P\). For every initial state \(x\in[n]\), \(X_0=x\) and \[\Pr[X_{t+1}=j\mid X_0,\ldots,X_t]=P_{X_t,j}.\] The tester sees \(X_0\) without a transition cost; each subsequent observed transition costs one. It cannot choose the initial state, reset the chain, request a transition from an arbitrary state, or inspect entries of \(P\). It may stop early, but it must stop within the claimed worst-case number of transitions. It accepts with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(P=Q\), and rejects with probability at least \(2/3\) if \(\Delta(P,Q)>\varepsilon\), for every starting state. No guarantee is imposed for other unequal pairs. Probabilities include both the Markov trajectory and independent internal fair random bits. Correctness for every fixed starting state also covers every starting distribution. The tester is one finite uniform program across all \(n,\varepsilon,Q\), with integer and bit-string work storage and exact real registers holding the supplied entries of \(Q\). It has rational constants, exact arithmetic \(+,-,\times,\div\) with division by zero forbidden, nonnegative square root, and exact order/equality comparisons; it has no advice or other oracle. The integer and rational parameters use binary encodings. These conventions specify exact numerical access; no bit-time guarantee for arbitrary real input is being requested. Local computation, memory and access to the explicitly supplied \(Q\) are uncharged, but every execution terminates. For each \(n,\varepsilon\), let \(M(n,\varepsilon)\) be the least integer \(m\) attained as a worst-case transition bound by a uniform tester correct for every permitted parameter value, reference and unknown chain. The worst case includes every \(Q,P\), starting state and execution. Set \(M=+\infty\) if no finite bound exists. This is a worst-reference minimax quantity, rather than a reference-dependent hitting-time or mixing-time complexity. The full symmetric class in the original boxed problem is retained; irreducibility, aperiodicity and stationary initialization are not extra promises.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that one tester with one universal \(C\) achieves both guarantees with at most \(\lceil Cn/\varepsilon\rceil\) transitions from every initial state, or refute that claim in the same single-trajectory model.
cards.why: This asks how much dependent data is needed to validate an entire stochastic transition rule when the experiment cannot be restarted or directed toward unvisited states. Sharp bounds would separate the intrinsic information cost of testing dynamics from the cost of fully exploring the reference chain, extending the foundations of distribution testing beyond independent samples.

cards.context:
Independent distribution samples can be collected from scratch. Here the next observation is constrained by the current state, so revisiting an uninformative region may consume many observations. The reference matrix is fully known; only the transition rule that generated the trajectory is unknown.

A worst-case start makes some unequal chains indistinguishable: they may share a closed component with identical transitions, and the trajectory may never leave it. The source chooses a spectral discrepancy that vanishes in such cases. Replacing it with a maximum row distance would impose rejection obligations that a single trajectory might never be able to meet.

The square-root overlap matrix compares both transition rules on the same labeled state space. Its leading spectral behavior measures how quickly the distributions of long trajectories can separate. Testing equality of stationary distributions alone would not test this object; in particular, symmetric chains all admit the uniform stationary distribution.

The original sample cost counts observed states; this card counts transitions after the initial state, a difference of one. The selected binary target is the source’s conjectured linear-in-state-count, inverse-proximity upper bound, with its strict farness convention.

The original upper bound includes a reference hitting-time term, and its lower bound is \(\Omega(n/\varepsilon)\). The hitting time is the largest expected time to reach a specified state from another state; it may be very large or infinite. Section 6 conjectures that a matching order-\(n/\varepsilon\) bound should avoid that dependence.

The 2019 paper removes hitting-time dependence in its stated irreducible symmetric setting, with bound \(\widetilde O(n/\varepsilon^4)\). Its Section 5 still asks whether the reciprocal-distance gap can be closed. This review records the irreducibility assumption from Section 2.1 rather than silently treating that theorem as an unrestricted statement about every reducible input.

Later work extends this line to reversible chains with additional stationary-distribution conditions, and develops a geometric reduction. Those extensions address broader types of transition matrix under promises; the checked results do not establish matching joint bounds for the full original symmetric problem.

Bounds in a matrix norm, experiments with a controlled restart interface, or results stated after assuming stationary initialization solve distinct testing problems. The source also asks other questions about its discrepancy and more general chains; those directions are not additional targets of this card.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
cards.why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.
