cards.context:
A promise CSP uses a stronger and a weaker version of each local requirement. For fixed integers \(2\leq k\leq c\), the templates \(A=K_k\) and \(B=K_c\), with the inequality edge relation, distinguish graphs that admit a proper \(k\)-colouring from graphs that admit no proper \(c\)-colouring. A proper colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. Instances between these two cases impose no answer requirement. This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Bulatov and Zhuk independently established the finite-template CSP dichotomy in 2017: every such exact satisfaction problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. Classifying the two endpoint CSPs separately does not classify the promise problem, because the weaker required answer can make it easier than either endpoint.

One concrete polynomial-time example has Boolean domains, the stronger ternary relation \(\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}\), and the weaker relation \(\{0,1\}^3\setminus\{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)\}\). Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This describes operations that combine stronger solutions into a weaker solution. Unlike operations on a single domain, these maps do not generally allow unrestricted self-composition. This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. Symmetry remains a substantive restriction; this does not classify arbitrary Boolean relations or arbitrary finite domains.

The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.

The question asks whether every fixed finite template pair has a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm or is NP-hard under promise-preserving many-one reductions.

cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
cards.formal: Do there exist an absolute integer \(C\geq3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, outputs a proper colouring using at most \(C\) colours with probability at least \(2/3\)? The same palette bound and finite program must work for all graph sizes. This card retains the explicitly adopted randomized version of the constant-palette problem.
cards.definitions:
The input is an explicit finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\geq1\), a unary size header and an adjacency matrix. There are no loops or parallel edges; isolated vertices count toward \(n\). The binary input length \(N\) is of order \(n^2+1\). The promise asserts the existence of a proper colouring with at most three colours, but supplies no colouring or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). A successful output explicitly lists one binary colour index in \([C]\) for each vertex, in vertex order. The algorithm may instead output a failure symbol. A candidate can be checked against the palette bound and all edges in polynomial time; invalid candidates can be converted to failure. Successful runs must colour every vertex and leave no monochromatic edge.

Use one randomized multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(K,d\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(N+1)^d\) bit operations on every graph and every random-bit sequence. All arithmetic precision, output and random-bit generation are included. The random bits are independent and fair, there are polynomially many of them in each run, and the machine has no advice or oracle. Deterministic algorithms are included. No correctness or success-probability requirement is imposed outside the three-colourability promise, but the time bound still applies.

For every promised graph, the probability of a valid \(C\)-colouring must be at least \(2/3\), over the internal bits alone. This is a guarantee for each individual input, not an average over random graphs. The existentially chosen \(C,K,d,A\) are fixed before the graph: \(C\) cannot depend on \(n\), degree, density or the particular input. The exponent and constants may depend on the selected palette bound because only one constant palette is required. Independent repetition can amplify the success probability after checking outputs; exact recognition of the three-colourability promise is not required.

There is no planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition assumption. A palette of six, one hundred or any other fixed integer could establish a positive answer. A number of colours growing with \(n\), however slowly, does not satisfy the constant-palette requirement.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of at least one such constant \(C\) and algorithm, or a proof in Lean that no such pair exists. A positive answer must verify all-input worst-case polynomial bit complexity and, for every promised graph, success probability at least \(2/3\) with a proper colouring of the full graph using that one palette.

A negative answer must exclude every absolute \(C\geq3\) and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm with the stated guarantee. Unconditional NP-hardness of each three-versus-\(C\) decision promise would give a complexity-theoretic obstruction, but deducing nonexistence of these randomized algorithms from it additionally requires \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\). An unproved separation or Label Cover hypothesis cannot be treated as established in an answer to this unconditional question. Hardness for five colours alone, fixed-point-logic inexpressibility, an algorithm with a growing palette, partial colouring, or a restricted input family does not settle the full target.
cards.why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.

cards.context:
The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

The algebraic PCSP theorem gives unconditional NP-hardness of the three-versus-five decision gap. A randomized five-colouring search algorithm with the guarantee in this card would yield an RP algorithm for SAT after applying the reduction and checking its output, so excluding such a randomized algorithm requires \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{RP}\). Here RP means polynomial time with no accepting computation on a NO-instance and acceptance probability at least one half on every YES-instance. The result addresses only small fixed palettes, leaving six, one hundred and every other larger constant unexcluded by that theorem alone.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Fixed-point logic with counting augments first-order descriptions by iterative fixed points and counting operators. On unordered graphs it does not express every polynomial-time algorithm available on an explicit binary encoding. Thus the March 2026 theorem is an unconditional limitation of a powerful logic, but a different machine using the encoding’s order is not covered.

The14September2026 Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game theorem and, in Corollary1.7, NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k colouring gap. Its complete proof has not been independently audited here. If established, this removes the extra Label Cover conjecture from that hardness claim, but excluding the randomized search algorithms in this card would still require NP different from RP. The distinction follows because candidate colourings are efficiently checkable, giving one-sided error after a gap reduction.

cards.title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
cards.formal:
For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous relational structure \(A\) over a finite signature, and every first-order reduct \(B\) of \(A\) with a finite relational signature, is
\[\operatorname{CSP}(B)\in\mathrm{P}\quad\lor\quad\operatorname{CSP}(B)\text{ is NP-complete}\ ?\]
NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The templates are fixed before the finite input is supplied. This is the unconditional complexity dichotomy, without requiring an algebraic criterion identifying the two sides.
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) interprets an \(r\)-ary symbol as a subset \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) of tuples over its domain. Countable means finite or countably infinite. Empty domains, if admitted, have trivial CSPs and do not affect the question. Nullary relations can likewise be processed separately.

The induced substructure on a subset \(S\) of a domain restricts every relation to tuples from \(S\). An embedding is an injective map \(e:D\to E\) with \(\bar d\in R^D\) if and only if \(e(\bar d)\in R^E\) for every relation and tuple; it preserves both presence and absence of relation tuples. An isomorphism is a bijective embedding, and an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself. The structure \(A\) is homogeneous when every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of \(A\).

The structure \(A\) is finitely bounded when there is a finite list \(\mathcal N\) of finite structures in its signature such that, for every finite structure \(D\) in that signature,
\[D\text{ embeds into }A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no }N\in\mathcal N\text{ embeds into }D.\]
Thus the finite patterns occurring inside \(A\) are precisely those avoiding finitely many forbidden induced patterns. Homogeneity is an additional condition, not part of finite boundedness alone.

A first-order reduct \(B\) has the same domain as \(A\). Each of its finitely many relations is defined by a fixed first-order formula over the relations of \(A\) and logical equality, using Boolean connectives and quantifiers over elements of \(A\), without naming parameters. It may forget original relations and introduce newly definable ones. Both signatures, \(A,B\), the defining formulas and a finite bound list witnessing the hypothesis are fixed; none is an input to the individual CSP.

An input \(I\) has finite domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicit list of tuples for each relation in the signature of \(B\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to B\) is any map such that \((i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in R^I\) implies \((h(i_1),\ldots,h(i_r))\in R^B\). It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples. The decision problem accepts exactly when such a map exists. Repeated coordinates and isolated input elements are allowed; duplicate listed tuples are harmless. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

Encode \(n\) in unary and each relation by a unary list length followed by binary tuple coordinates, in fixed signature order, with delimiters. Let \(L\) be total bit length. Invalid encodings are rejected. Polynomial time means a deterministic multitape Turing machine halts correctly on every input within \(C(L+1)^k\) bit steps for constants \(C,k\) depending on \(B\). No randomness, infinite-domain oracle, advice, supplied homomorphism, common polynomial exponent or algorithm choosing the correct side from template descriptions is required.

Use the shared definition of [NP](definitions.html#p-np). A problem \(Q\) is NP-hard under the stated reductions when, for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), a total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) satisfies \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f(x)\in Q\). NP-complete means NP-hard and in NP. Every CSP in the displayed scope is already known to be in NP. The two alternatives are not required to be disjoint without a separation assumption: if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), every such problem satisfies the first alternative.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition, or of its logical negation, retaining every permitted structure and reduct. A negative answer must establish one permitted \(A,B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated many-one reductions; membership in NP already follows from the hypotheses. No separation assumption is added to the proposition. A classification for one reduct family, the first-order/logarithmic-space-hard boundary, or a procedure deciding an algebraic meta-problem does not prove the full dichotomy. The stronger algebraic tractability conjecture would suffice if proved, but is not substituted for the existing bare complexity target.
cards.why: The main tractability-classification conjecture for well-behaved infinite-domain CSPs. It links algorithm design, universal algebra and model theory, and would extend the finite-domain dichotomy to substantially richer constraint languages.

cards.context:
The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain. Homogeneity over a finite relational signature also gives quantifier elimination, so each fixed first-order reduct relation can be tested on that finite pattern by a fixed quantifier-free formula.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q} ;<)\) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification. A model-complete core is a homomorphically equivalent template in which every endomorphism agrees, on each finite subset, with some automorphism; an endomorphism is a homomorphism from the template to itself.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open. Here first-order definability means that one fixed first-order sentence on finite inputs decides the CSP, and L denotes deterministic logarithmic work space.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded homogeneous Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card. The Ramsey condition says that for every pair of finite patterns P,Q and every finite number of colours, a larger finite pattern exists in which every colouring of embeddings of P has a copy of Q whose internal P-embeddings all receive one colour.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

cards.title: Algorithmic threshold for random k-SAT
cards.formal: Does the randomized polynomial-time satisfying-assignment threshold for random \(k\)-SAT satisfy \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)}{2^{k}\ln(k)/k}=1?\] For each fixed \(k\), \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) is the supremum of constant clause densities at which some polynomial-time algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with probability tending to one as the number \(n\) of variables tends to infinity. The distribution and quantifiers are specified below.
cards.definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\geq3\) and a real constant density \(\alpha\geq0\). On Boolean variables \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\), generate \(m=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) ordered clauses. Each clause has \(k\) literal positions, each independently uniform among \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\neg x_{1},\ldots,\neg x_{n}\). The formula is the AND of these OR clauses. Sampling is with replacement: repeated literals, tautological clauses and repeated clauses are allowed.

The algorithm receives the entire explicit formula, with variable indices in binary, together with \(n\). It must output one full assignment in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) satisfying every clause. It may report failure otherwise. The input is sampled without conditioning on satisfiability and without planting or revealing any assignment.

A density \(\alpha\) is algorithmically attainable at width \(k\) if there is a classical randomized algorithm \(A\), with no advice depending on \(n\), such that its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the explicit input length and \(n\) on every input and random tape, and
\[\Pr_{\Phi,A}[A(\Phi)\text{ outputs a satisfying assignment of }\Phi]\longrightarrow1
\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]
The probability includes both the random formula and the algorithm's internal randomness. One fixed algorithm must work for all \(n\) at the chosen \(k,\alpha\). Its code, polynomial degree and constants may depend on those fixed parameters. They are not allowed to depend separately on each input length.

Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) be the supremum of all such densities. Attainment at the supremum is not required. First take \(n\to\infty\) at fixed \(k,\alpha\); only then consider the asymptotic behavior as \(k\to\infty\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This is a leading-order asymptotic question, not a request for an exact critical density at a particular small \(k\).

The target ranges over all randomized polynomial-time assignment-finding algorithms. It imposes no locality, stability, low-degree representation or restriction to a named heuristic. Deciding satisfiability without producing an assignment, satisfying only most clauses, or proving a barrier for a restricted algorithm family is a different guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed asymptotic equality, or refute it. The known algorithm gives the lower bound \(1-o_{k}(1)\) on the ratio, so the missing positive direction is the matching upper bound for all polynomial-time algorithms. A refutation must change the limiting leading-order behavior along arbitrarily large widths; an improvement confined to one fixed small width or a lower-order term does not suffice.
cards.why: Pinpoints a possible computational barrier inside a regime where satisfying assignments typically exist. A resolution would clarify whether the geometry of random constraint problems predicts the power of arbitrary efficient algorithms, beyond individual heuristics and restricted computational models.

cards.context:
For sufficiently large fixed \(k\), the satisfiability threshold is known and is asymptotic to \(2^{k}\ln 2\). This is about existence of an assignment; it does not provide an efficient way to find one throughout that range.

Coja-Oghlan’s Fix algorithm finds a satisfying assignment with high probability below \((1-\varepsilon_{k})2^{k}\ln(k)/k\), where \(\varepsilon_{k}\to0\). Thus the conjecture asks whether its leading asymptotic scale is optimal among all polynomial-time algorithms.

Bresler and Huang prove a low-degree obstruction above a constant multiple of this scale; their main stated constant is about \(4.911\), and their appendix discusses improvements. Theorem 2.6 concerns a specified normalized polynomial representation and requires a quantitatively small failure probability, stronger than an arbitrary \(o(1)\) failure rate. Their local-algorithm theorem rules out much smaller success probabilities within a narrower class. Neither theorem covers all polynomial-time algorithms.

The 2025 source explicitly retains the algorithmic conjecture. Its sharp geometric results for random SAT use growing clause width in the relevant exact-solution regime. They do not establish the fixed-width, all-algorithm upper bound asked here.

For random 3-SAT, a 2026 theorem gives an algorithm to approximate the density at which satisfying assignments cease to exist. The present question asks at which densities an efficient algorithm can actually find an assignment as the clause width grows.

cards.title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
cards.formal: For every fixed pair \((A,B)\) of finite nonempty relational structures over the same finite signature with \(A\to B\), does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept every finite \(X\) with \(X\to A\) and reject every \(X\) with \(X\not\to B\). Search receives \(X\) with the promise \(X\to A\) and must output an explicit homomorphism \(X\to B\). Both algorithms are deterministic and have polynomial worst-case running time on all inputs; the programs and polynomial bounds may depend on \(A,B\).
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature is a finite ordered list of relation symbols, each assigned a positive integer arity. A structure \(D\) consists of a domain and, for each symbol \(R\) of arity \(r\), a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\). A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function satisfying
\[(d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\ \Longrightarrow\ (h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\]
for every relation and tuple. It need not be injective. The notation \(D\to E\) asserts existence of such a map. Templates \(A,B\), including their finite relation tables and a numbering of their domains, are fixed constants, not part of the input. No stronger assignment is supplied with an input.

The input structure \(X\) has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Repeated coordinates and empty relations are allowed. Encode \(n\) in unary, followed by the tuple lists in signature order with unary list lengths; each coordinate has \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Let \(N\) be the total bit length, which counts isolated variables. Duplicate listed tuples have no effect. A search output is the list of images of all \(n\) elements in the fixed domain of \(B\), or a failure symbol. The empty input has the empty homomorphism.

A decision algorithm returns one bit. If \(X\not\to A\) but \(X\to B\), either bit is permitted; this is the intermediate region of the promise. Since \(A\to B\), no input simultaneously requires both answers. On search inputs outside the promise \(X\to A\), any output is permitted, including failure. Both machines halt on every binary input within \(C(N+1)^k\) steps for positive integers \(C,k\); malformed strings may be rejected. Cost is measured on a deterministic multitape Turing machine, without advice, oracle or randomness.

The quantifier order is \(\forall(A,B)\,[\exists D\text{ with the decision guarantee}\Rightarrow\exists S\text{ with the search guarantee}]\). Constants and exponents can depend on the fixed template. There is no required effective procedure that recognizes tractable templates or constructs \(S\) from arbitrary \(A,B,D\), no common exponent over templates, and no requirement that \(S\) use \(D\) as a black-box subroutine. The target is the tractability implication between the two fixed-template problems.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish a search machine with the stated promised output and all-input polynomial bound whenever a qualifying decision machine exists. A negative proof must exhibit a fixed finite \(A\to B\), prove its decision promise solvable in deterministic polynomial time, and prove that no deterministic polynomial-time promised search algorithm exists. Hardness of rounding all inputs accepted by a particular relaxation, undecidability when the template varies, or failure of a particular black-box reduction does not refute this statement. A conditional separation is partial progress and must retain its unproved hypothesis; the target itself is unconditional.
cards.why: Many applications need an assignment rather than recognition that an assignment must exist. A universal implication would connect tractability classifications of promise decision problems to actual construction across finite local constraint languages. A separation would identify a fixed finite promise problem whose decision gap is efficiently recognizable while its promised solutions resist every deterministic polynomial-time search algorithm.

cards.context:
The strong template A describes the constraints guaranteed to be simultaneously satisfiable; B describes the weaker constraints an answer must satisfy. The map from A to B proves that a weak answer exists whenever a strong one exists, but the input supplies only that existence promise. A decision algorithm recognizes the promised gap, whereas search must actually construct the weaker assignment.

For graph colouring, one may take A and B to be complete graphs on three and six vertices. Search then asks for a six-colouring of a graph promised to admit a three-colouring. Decision only separates three-colourable graphs from graphs admitting no six-colouring; it has no required behaviour on graphs with chromatic number four, five or six. This example illustrates the promise and does not assert tractability for that particular pair.

A polynomial-time search algorithm implies decision by returning a proposed weak assignment that can be checked. The reverse implication is known for ordinary fixed finite CSPs, where A=B. With two templates, fixing a variable to a weak-domain value can destroy the stronger promise, so ordinary decision self-reducibility does not automatically apply.

Known constructive cases include templates admitting a fixed finite intermediate structure C with A→C→B and tractable CSP(C). The survey also discusses tractable promise problems whose explanation requires more than such a finite intermediate problem, under the usual separation assumptions. Thus the ordinary CSP case does not supply the general statement.

Larrauri studies rounding for three standard decision relaxations: the basic linear program using consistent local distributions, an affine integer program, and their combination. Finding a weak assignment on every input accepted by one of these relaxations can encode arbitrary total NP search problems. A total NP search problem has a polynomially checkable, polynomially bounded witness for every input. Relaxation acceptance is a weaker promise than the existence of a homomorphism to A.

The May 2026 revision explicitly retains the general implication here as open. Its undecidability theorems instead concern recognizing classes of templates when A and B vary as input. A nonuniform choice of one finite program for each fixed template, as allowed here, is compatible with undecidability of that recognition problem.

The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives constructive guarantees for special preservation structures, including Boolean templates preserved by all odd-arity majority operations. Here preservation means that applying coordinatewise majority to strong satisfying tuples produces a weak satisfying tuple. These results handle almost satisfiable instances with quantitative error guarantees, but require an additional structural hypothesis absent from the general implication.

A total NP search problem has a polynomially checkable, polynomially bounded witness for every input. Relaxation acceptance is a weaker promise than the existence of a homomorphism to A.

The May 2026 revision explicitly retains the general implication here as open. Its undecidability theorems instead concern recognizing classes of templates when A and B vary as input. A nonuniform choice of one finite program for each fixed template, as allowed here, is compatible with undecidability of that recognition problem.

The February 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives constructive guarantees for special preservation structures, including Boolean templates preserved by all odd-arity majority operations. Here preservation means that applying coordinatewise majority to strong satisfying tuples produces a weak satisfying tuple. These results handle almost satisfiable instances with quantitative error guarantees, but require an additional structural hypothesis absent from the general implication.

cards.title: Dichotomy for finite-domain restricted CSPs
cards.formal:
Assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\). For every finite relational signature \(\tau\), every finite \(\tau\)-structure \(A\), and every possibly infinite \(\tau\)-structure \(B\) for which \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is decidable, must \(\operatorname{RCSP}(A,B)\) be either polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard in the source’s completion sense? Explicitly, let
\[\mathcal S_{A,B}=\{S\subseteq\{0,1\}^*:S\text{ is decidable and }S\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)=\operatorname{CSP}(A)\cap\operatorname{CSP}(B)\}.\]
Is it always true that
\[\bigl(\exists S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\in\mathrm{P}\bigr)\quad\lor\quad\bigl(\forall S\in\mathcal S_{A,B}:S\text{ is NP-hard}\bigr)?\]
The input is a finite structure \(X\) promised to map homomorphically to \(B\); on that promise the decision is whether \(X\) maps to \(A\).
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols of positive integer arities. A \(\tau\)-structure \(D\) has a domain and a relation \(R^D\subseteq D^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. The target \(A\) is finite; the restriction \(B\) may have an arbitrary infinite domain. A homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a function preserving every relation tuple: \((d_1,\ldots,d_r)\in R^D\) implies \((h(d_1),\ldots,h(d_r))\in R^E\). Write \(D\to E\) for existence of such a map. Maps need not be injective. Neither \(A\to B\) nor \(B\to A\) is assumed.

Input structures have domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed tuples for each relation. Encode \(n\) in unary, then the relation lists in signature order with unary list lengths and binary coordinate indices. Let \(N\) be the total bit length. Empty relations, repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; repeated listed tuples are harmless. Define \(\operatorname{CSP}(D)\) as the set of valid encodings of finite \(X\) with \(X\to D\). Invalid encodings do not belong to this set. Empty template domains may be included; their trivial boundary cases do not alter the question.

For each problem \(A,B,\tau\) are fixed, and only \(X\) is supplied. An input in \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) must be accepted exactly when it lies in \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\); outside the promise either answer is allowed. A completion \(S\) is a total decidable language with precisely this behaviour on the promise. Since \(A\) is finite, \(\operatorname{CSP}(A)\) is a decidable completion, so \(\mathcal S_{A,B}\) is never empty. Decidability of \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\) is a hypothesis recovered from the source, not a polynomial-time promise-recognition assumption. No description, relation-table algorithm, homomorphism into \(B\), or oracle for \(B\) is supplied. Infinite restrictions are not limited to finitely presented or categorically specified structures.

A completion is in \(\mathrm{P}\) if a deterministic multitape Turing machine accepts exactly it and halts on every string of length \(N\) within \(C(N+1)^k\) bit steps for fixed positive integers \(C,k\). The machine and constants may depend on \(A,B\). Decidable means a deterministic machine halts and decides membership, without any time bound. No uniform procedure for constructing these machines from templates, common polynomial exponent, advice or randomness is requested.

A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has polynomially bounded certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time. A language \(S\) is NP-hard here under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions: for every \(K\in\mathrm{NP}\), there is a total polynomial-time function \(f_K\) with \(x\in K\) if and only if \(f_K(x)\in S\). Equivalently, it suffices to reduce Boolean three-clause satisfiability, where each clause has at most three literals. This is hardness of the total language \(S\), not a claim that \(S\) itself lies in NP.

The promise-hardness quantifiers are \(\forall\text{ decidable completions }S\ \exists\text{ suitable reductions to }S\). Reductions may depend on \(S\); no single reduction whose images always satisfy \(X\to B\) is required by this definition. A uniform reduction landing inside the promise would suffice, but is not silently substituted for the source’s definition. Under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) the two displayed alternatives are disjoint. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), the first alternative already holds for every finite \(A\), since its ordinary CSP is in NP.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean, under the stated \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis, that the displayed dichotomy holds for every permitted \(A,B\), or that it fails. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite \(A\) and a permitted possibly infinite \(B\) such that no completion is in P and at least one decidable completion is not NP-hard under the stated reductions. A positive answer must cover every infinite restriction with decidable CSP, retaining the completion quantifiers. Proving only the already known finite-restriction case, treating an arbitrary input class that is not \(\operatorname{CSP}(B)\), or disproving a stronger uniform hardness requirement does not settle this question. No additional unproved hypothesis may replace the explicitly stated separation assumption.
cards.why: This asks whether the finite-domain CSP dichotomy survives every decidable restriction described by homomorphisms into a fixed, possibly infinite structure. A positive answer would sharply constrain the complexity introduced by such promises. A counterexample would demonstrate intermediate promise behaviour even though all satisfying assignments still use a fixed finite domain.

cards.context:
Restricted CSPs impose a promise on which input structures must be handled. For example, RCSP(K₃,K₄) asks whether a graph promised to be four-colourable is three-colourable; Kᵣ is the complete loopless graph on r vertices. Unlike a promise CSP, the promise here restricts the input class on both yes and no sides rather than relaxing which assignments count as solutions.

The source proves that a finite restriction B permits a reduction to an ordinary CSP on the exponential structure A^B. Its elements are functions from B to A, with relations defined by preservation along relation tuples of B. If A and B are both finite, this is again a finite structure, so the ordinary finite-domain decision dichotomy applies. Theorem 18 records the resulting restricted dichotomy.

An infinite B can impose familiar global input conditions. For directed graphs, the structure on rational numbers with the strict-order relation admits a homomorphism from exactly the finite acyclic digraphs. Such a restriction remains decidable even though its representing structure is infinite. This illustrates why finite assignment domains do not make the promise finite.

The general question preserves arbitrary decidable homomorphism restrictions. It is separate from the source’s neighbouring conjecture asking for a particular algebraic criterion for tractability. The finite exponential construction does not remain a finite template when B is infinite, so the known finite-restriction reduction alone does not prove the target.

The completion definition is essential: an algorithm must be correct only on the promised class, yet it must halt on every input. Hardness quantifies over every decidable total extension of that promised behaviour. Saying merely that the intersection of two CSP languages is NP-hard would describe one particular extension and would not prove the required universal hardness.

cards.title: Boolean decision-Holant dichotomy
cards.formal:
Classify the polynomial-time solvable Boolean decision-Holant problems for all fixed finite families of Boolean relations. More precisely, under \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\), determine the entire characteristic function
\[\chi_{\mathrm H}(\mathcal F)=\begin{cases}1,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\in\mathrm{P},\\0,&\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\notin\mathrm{P},\end{cases}\]
with absolute error at most \(1/100\) at every finite family \(\mathcal F\). The answer must give a substantive structural criterion on the allowed relations, with algorithms and complementary lower bounds, rather than merely restating the definition of polynomial-time solvability. The model is the source’s Boolean edge-CSP interpretation of decision Holant, specified below.
cards.definitions:
A Boolean relation of arity \(r\geq1\) is a subset \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), equivalently its zero-one indicator function \(f_R\). A signature family \(\mathcal F\) is a finite ordered list of such relations given by their full finite truth tables; empty relations and the empty family are allowed. For each decision problem the family and all arities are fixed before inputs are supplied. Arbitrarily large fixed arities are covered across the classification.

A signature grid is a finite undirected loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\), together with a label \(R_v\in\mathcal F\) at each vertex and an ordering \((e_{v,1},\ldots,e_{v,r_v})\) of its incident edges, where \(r_v\) equals the arity of \(R_v\). Parallel edges are permitted and are separate variables. The graph need not be planar or bipartite. Each edge has two distinct endpoints and appears exactly once at each endpoint. The incidence order is part of the input, since relations need not be symmetric. This is the explicit convention of Definitions 1–3 in the cited edge-CSP paper: a variable is in exactly two distinct constraint scopes, without a repeated coordinate within one scope.

A Boolean assignment is a map \(\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}\). It is satisfying when \((\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v}))\in R_v\) for every vertex. Define
\[H_{\mathcal F}(G)=\sum_{\sigma:E\to\{0,1\}}\prod_{v\in V} f_{R_v}(\sigma(e_{v,1}),\ldots,\sigma(e_{v,r_v})).\]
The task \(\operatorname{DecHolant}(\mathcal F)\) accepts exactly the grids with \(H_{\mathcal F}(G)>0\). It asks for one yes/no answer, not the number or a list of satisfying assignments. The empty graph has value one, by the empty-product convention. A grid containing an empty relation is unsatisfiable. Nullary indicators, if included, can be processed separately: zero rejects the instance and one is deleted, so restricting the signature tables to positive arities loses no tractability class.

Encode the numbers of vertices and edges in unary; list binary endpoint indices for each numbered edge, the fixed-family index at each vertex, and its ordered list of edge indices. Let \(N\) be total bit length. Validity of the encoding is checked in polynomial time; malformed strings are rejected. A polynomial-time algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts with the correct answer on every input in at most \(C(N+1)^k\) bit steps, for positive constants \(C,k\) depending on \(\mathcal F\). There is no randomness, oracle or advice. Programs may depend on the fixed family, and no common running-time exponent across all families is requested.

No unary relation, pinning constant, equality relation, edge weight or graph restriction is freely added to \(\mathcal F\). The at-most-two-occurrences decision model used in the survey has the same complexity under this scope convention: remove unused variables, take two copies of the instance, and identify corresponding variables that occurred only once. This gives exactly two occurrences and preserves satisfiability without new relations. The target does not impose a uniform input-template algorithm or require a polynomial-time procedure for recognizing the tractable families from their truth tables.

Use the shared definitions of [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np). Every fixed-family problem above is in NP, with the edge assignment as certificate. NP-hardness, when used in the classification, means deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions from every language in NP; NP-complete means both NP-hard and in NP. This is an explicit reduction convention. The separation assumption makes a tractability classification nontrivial; if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), the function is identically one. A rational answer within \(1/100\) of a zero-one value determines that value, but the requested result is the structural description of the whole function, not numerical experiments on selected families.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of an exhaustive structural characterization of \(\chi_{\mathrm H}\) with the stated absolute \(1/100\) accuracy, under the explicit \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) hypothesis. Prove correct polynomial-time decision algorithms for every family assigned one and a matching exclusion of polynomial time for every family assigned zero; NP-hardness under the stated reductions is a sufficient exclusion. The result must cover all finite Boolean signature families, including arbitrary delta-matroid relations, with the graph and occurrence conventions above. A characterization cannot simply rename the existence of a polynomial-time machine. Classifying only symmetric signatures, only even delta-matroids, planar inputs, weighted counting, or a language enlarged by freely available unary signatures does not answer the full question. If additional complexity cases arise instead of the expected polynomial-time/NP-complete dichotomy, identify and justify them rather than asserting that every nontractable case is NP-complete without proof.
cards.why: A full classification would explain exactly which local Boolean constraints remain tractable when each variable has two incidences. The unresolved region contains broad generalizations of matching rather than only the standard Boolean CSP algorithms. Resolving it would connect delta-matroid structure with the boundary between polynomial-time graph algorithms and NP-hardness.

cards.context:
In ordinary CSP a variable may constrain many locations. In a Holant grid each variable is an edge linking two local constraints. This restriction creates new algorithms: an ExactOne relation accepts precisely tuples with one coordinate equal to one, and using it at every vertex asks for a perfect matching. Thus tractability is not exhausted by the familiar Boolean CSP cases.

For a nonempty relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^r\), the delta-matroid exchange property says: if \(x,y\in R\) differ at coordinate \(i\), then either flipping \(i\) in \(x\) stays in \(R\), or there is a different coordinate \(j\) at which \(x,y\) differ such that flipping both \(i,j\) stays in \(R\). An even delta-matroid additionally has the same parity of Hamming weight for all its tuples; that parity may be odd. Empty relations are handled separately by immediate rejection when used.

The source’s Theorem 8 records Feder’s boundary: if a family contains a relation failing the delta-matroid exchange property, its decision-Holant complexity agrees with that of ordinary CSP on the family. Schaefer’s Boolean CSP dichotomy then supplies a polynomial-time algorithm or NP-completeness. The remaining general region consists of families whose relations all satisfy the exchange property.

For symmetric relations, membership depends only on the number of one coordinates. The delta-matroid condition then says that between consecutive permitted weights there is at most one forbidden integer. Such families are tractable as general factor problems. This permits relations with both parities; it is a different sufficient condition from the even delta-matroid algorithm.

Kazda, Kolmogorov and Rolínek generalize the matching blossom algorithm to arbitrary even delta-matroid relations given by tuple lists, and extend it to a further class they call efficiently coverable. Their planar Boolean CSP classification is a consequence. It does not classify arbitrary delta-matroid constraints in general edge-CSP grids.

The 2023 general-factor paper explicitly retains the general Boolean edge-CSP classification as open, while proving a strongly polynomial algorithm for particular weighted symmetric constraints. It records the conjecture that every delta-matroid family is tractable. The card retains the full classification question, so it does not assume this conjectured answer in its target.

A counting dichotomy concerns computing the entire sum H, which can be harder than deciding whether H is positive. Counting Holant results for real or complex signatures therefore cannot by themselves classify this zero-one decision task. Availability of all unary signatures and restrictions to planar grids also define different problems.

cards.title: Universal representation of NP by \(\omega\)-categorical CSPs
cards.formal:
For every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\), does there exist a countable \(\omega\)-categorical relational structure \(\Gamma\) in a finite relational signature such that
\[L\equiv_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\ ?\]
The relation \(\equiv_T^p\) means deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions in both directions. This reduction convention follows the source’s accompanying non-dichotomy results and the explicit definition in the later monograph; Question 2 itself abbreviates it as polynomial-time equivalence.
cards.definitions:
A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a fixed positive integer arity. A structure \(\Gamma\) has a nonempty finite or countably infinite domain and an interpretation \(R^\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^r\) for each \(r\)-ary symbol. A homomorphism \(h:I\to\Gamma\) maps elements of \(I\) to domain values and preserves every positive relation tuple. It need not be injective and need not preserve absence of tuples.

An automorphism of \(\Gamma\) is a bijection of its domain preserving both membership and nonmembership in every relation. It acts on an ordered tuple by applying the same bijection to all coordinates. Two tuples are in the same orbit if some automorphism maps one to the other. The structure is \(\omega\)-categorical here if for every positive integer \(k\), there are only finitely many orbits of ordered \(k\)-tuples. For countably infinite structures in a finite signature, this is equivalent to their complete first-order theory having a unique countably infinite model up to isomorphism. Finite structures are admitted by the same orbit convention. The bound on the number of orbits can depend on \(k\); no fixed global bound, algorithm for orbits, homogeneity or finite list of forbidden patterns is assumed.

A CSP instance is a finite \(\tau\)-structure \(I\) with domain \([n]\), \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. It is accepted exactly when \(I\to\Gamma\). Repeated coordinates and isolated elements are allowed; duplicate tuples are harmless. The empty structure has the empty homomorphism. Encode \(n\) in unary, then in signature order each relation’s unary list length and its tuples of binary indices, with delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. This defines a total language \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) of finite bit strings. The signature and structure are fixed for this language; no infinite table, presentation algorithm or value from \(\Gamma\) is supplied with an instance.

A language lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is witnessed by a certificate of length polynomial in the input bit length and checked by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. A reduction \(K\leq_T^p Q\) is a deterministic oracle Turing machine deciding membership in \(K\) using exact yes/no membership queries to \(Q\). On every input \(x\), all its computation, query writing and answer processing take at most \(C(|x|+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed positive constants \(C,d\). Thus query lengths and their number are polynomially bounded. The oracle supplies each membership bit at unit query cost; its own computation is not part of the reduction. Queries may depend on earlier answers, and answers may be negated. No randomness or advice is available.

Polynomial-time Turing equivalence means \(L\leq_T^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\leq_T^p L\). The two programs and their constants may depend on \(L,\Gamma\), but each works on every finite input. The quantifiers are \(\forall L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists\tau,\Gamma,M_1,M_2,C_1,C_2,d_1,d_2\). No uniform algorithm turning an NP verifier into a template or into these reductions is requested. The source explicitly permits defining a fixed CSP without fixing an effective representation of its infinite template.

This is equivalence of computational problems, not equality of their input classes or their logical definitions. Turing equivalence is also weaker than requiring many-one reductions, which produce one target instance with the same membership answer. No additional hypothesis \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{NP}\) is inserted: Turing equivalence to an NP language alone implies membership in \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{NP}}\), the class decided by polynomial-time machines with an NP oracle, rather than closure inside NP. The original question does not separately impose that extra condition. Trivial languages are included and cause no difficulty under Turing reductions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every language in NP and produce existence of a finite-signature omega-categorical template with both deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. A negative answer must establish a language in NP for which no permitted template has the required equivalence. Giving an arbitrary infinite template, only one reduction direction, a weaker oracle-complexity upper bound, or a representation for only NP-complete languages does not settle the question. No unproved complexity separation is assumed; conditional constructions or obstructions settle only their conditional statements.
cards.why: The question tests whether the symmetry framework that supports infinite-domain algebraic CSP methods is computationally universal for NP under the source’s equivalence convention. A positive answer would place every NP degree into that framework; a negative answer would exhibit a complexity limitation imposed by omega-categoricity itself.

references.title: Three Fundamental Questions in Modern Infinite-Domain Constraint Satisfaction
references.authors: Michael Pinsker; Jakub Rydval; Moritz Schöbi; Christoph Spiess; Paul Winkler
references.locator: Version 4, 6 May 2026; §1.2 distinguishes omega-categoricity from finite bounded homogeneous reducts and explains that omega-categoricity alone does not force low computational complexity.

cards.context:
Infinite templates vastly enlarge the class of possible CSPs, but omega-categoricity retains finitely many symmetry types at each tuple length. It is the structural hypothesis behind many preservation theorems used in algebraic CSP theory. The question asks whether imposing this symmetry still permits representation of every NP computational problem up to the stated reductions.

Bodirsky and Grohe prove that every decision language has a polynomial-time Turing equivalent CSP with an unrestricted infinite template. Their construction is not omega-categorical. Thus arbitrary-template universality is an established starting point, and the symmetry condition is the entire additional issue.

For omega-categorical templates their Theorem 2 instead gives, for any decision language \(L\), a template with \(L\leq_m^p\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\) and \(\operatorname{CSP}(\Gamma)\in\mathrm{coNP}^{L}\). Here the first relation is a polynomial-time many-one reduction and \(\mathrm{coNP}^{L}\) means complements of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time machines with exact oracle \(L\). This upper bound does not supply the required deterministic polynomial-time oracle reduction back to \(L\).

The same work constructs omega-categorical templates with coNP-complete CSPs and, conditionally, coNP-intermediate CSPs. These results demonstrate broad complexity within the symmetry class, but they do not establish equivalence to each prescribed NP language. The later book separately retains the question of NP-intermediate omega-categorical CSPs; that question explicitly requires NP membership, unlike bare Turing equivalence.

The stronger restrictions in the Bodirsky–Pinsker dichotomy concern reducts of finitely bounded homogeneous structures. They ensure finite-pattern certificates and hence NP membership. The present target quantifies over all omega-categorical templates and imposes neither restriction; proving that narrower dichotomy would not settle this representation question.

Logical representation is also a different issue. Two templates may define different finite-instance CSPs yet have polynomial-time equivalent decision problems. The source’s neighbouring question about whether a particular SNP-definable CSP has an omega-categorical template asks for the same accepted input class, which is stronger than computational equivalence and has separate counterexamples.

cards.title: Characterizing CSP languages with linear non-redundancy
cards.formal: Characterize all finite constraint languages \(\Gamma\) over arbitrary finite nonempty domains for which every \(n\)-variable formula has a subformula with at most \(C_\Gamma n\) constraints and exactly the same set of satisfying assignments, for some constant \(C_\Gamma\) independent of the formula and \(n\). Equivalently, determine the class-membership function \(\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}\) on all such finite languages, taking value \(1\) when this property holds and \(0\) otherwise. The target is the full classification from Question 8; it is not restricted to Boolean domains or to a proposed sufficient condition.
cards.definitions:
A language \(\Gamma\) consists of a finite nonempty domain \(D=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and a finite list of named relations \(R\subseteq D^{r}\), each with a positive integer arity \(r\). Empty and full relations, and the empty list of relations, are permitted. The domain, arities and relation tables give the entire description. A formula \(F\) on variables \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(n\geq1\), is a finite conjunction of constraints \(R(x_1,\ldots,x_{r})\) from this language. Variable repetitions and repeated constraints are permitted. An assignment \(a:V\to D\) satisfies the constraint when \((a(x_1),\ldots,a(x_{r}))\in R\), and satisfies \(F\) when it satisfies every constraint. Write \(\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)\subseteq D^{V}\) for this set; it may be empty.

A subformula \(F'\subseteq F\) is obtained only by deleting constraint occurrences, keeping the same variables and domain. It may have isolated variables and no constraints. The preservation requirement is \(\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F')=\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)\), as sets of assignments on the original \(V\). It is stronger than merely preserving whether a satisfying assignment exists. No new constraints, new variables, weights or relaxation of relations are allowed.

Define
\[\operatorname{nr}_\Gamma(n)=\max_{F}\ \min_{\substack{F'\subseteq F\\\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F')=\operatorname{Sol}_{D}(F)}} |F'|,\]
where \(F\) ranges over all formulas on these \(n\) variables and \(|F'|\) counts constraint occurrences. This maximum is finite: duplicate occurrences do not change solutions, and there are at most \(\sum_{R\in\Gamma}n^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\) distinct constraints. An equivalent definition is the maximum size of a formula in which every constraint is non-redundant. A constraint \(C\) is non-redundant when there is an assignment satisfying all other constraints but violating \(C\). Unsatisfiable formulas are included; no satisfiability promise is made.

The numerical function being classified is
\[\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Gamma)=\begin{cases}1,&\exists C\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\ \forall n\geq1:\ \operatorname{nr}_\Gamma(n)\leq Cn,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
Its domain consists of every finite language just defined, with no global bound on domain size, arity or number of relations. The hidden constant may depend on the whole fixed language. Requiring the bound at all positive \(n\) is equivalent to asymptotic \(O(n)\), since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed in the constant. A bound of \(n\log n\) or \(n^{1+o(1)}\) does not meet it.

This is a mathematical classification of an extremal property. No polynomial-time procedure for finding \(F'\), recognizing languages, or deciding satisfiability is built into the target. A structural criterion or another substantive unambiguous mathematical description of the membership function can specify an answer without a predetermined syntactic form. Introducing the characteristic function records the same classification target, rather than replacing it with an optimal-growth problem for \(\operatorname{nr}_\Gamma\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a real-valued function \(g\) on the stated full domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|g(\Gamma)-\chi_{\mathrm{lin}}(\Gamma)|\leq1/100\) for every finite language \(\Gamma\). An exact necessary-and-sufficient characterization of class membership also qualifies. The supplied description must determine membership substantively; merely renaming the defining optimization or repeating that a language is linear exactly when it has linear non-redundancy is not an answer. No efficient recognition algorithm is required. Prove both membership and nonmembership sides of the characterization, including all domains and arities. A sufficient algebraic condition, a finite table of small languages, a near-linear bound or a decision-preserving kernel alone does not settle the full target.
cards.why: A full classification would explain which systems of local relations always have a linear-sized exact description using their own constraints. It would organize connections among logical redundancy, sparsification, preprocessing and algebra across all finite domains. The distinction between existence of a small subformula and efficiently finding it is essential to interpreting the result.

cards.context:
A constraint can be logically unnecessary even when its relation occurs many times. For example, equality constraints connecting a set of variables can often be deleted while preserving the same equality requirements on all assignments. Non-redundancy asks how large a collection can remain when every member has its own witness to being essential.

This is a question about the amount of information in a system, not the difficulty of finding a satisfying assignment. Some NP-hard fixed predicates have linear non-redundancy. Conversely, the binary positive-OR relation has quadratic non-redundancy despite the simplicity of deciding its satisfiability. These contrasting examples separate this classification from the usual tractability dichotomy.

The 2020 Boolean work supplies linear sparsification through representations by degree-one equations over integer rings. The December 2025 manuscript identifies the Boolean languages admitting the more general Mal’tsev embedding condition with the corresponding balanced class, while exhibiting genuinely noncommutative behavior on larger domains. This clarifies known sufficient conditions without proving that they capture all languages with linear non-redundancy.

The 2025 manuscript realizes every rational non-redundancy exponent at least one over suitable finite domains. The resulting range is much richer than a choice between linear growth and the trivial maximal-arity bound. It does not supply a complete description of the languages at the linear endpoint.

The 2026 shrinking paper develops further superlinear lower bounds while retaining the general linear or near-linear classification as an open question.

The CP 2026 paper almost classifies Boolean arity four, leaving one predicate unresolved and exhibiting non-polynomial asymptotics. This is a restricted family within the all-language target.

cards.title: Polynomial-time tractability testing for core crisp CSP languages
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite crisp constraint language \(\Gamma\) over an explicitly given finite domain D and promised that \(\Gamma\) is a core, decides whether \(\Gamma\) admits an idempotent Siggers polymorphism? Equivalently on the core promise, decide whether \(\Gamma\) is solvable in the algebraic sense of the finite-domain CSP dichotomy. The polynomial must be uniform in the entire input, including |D|, the number of relations, their arities and their listed tuples; neither a polymorphism nor a tractability certificate is supplied.
cards.definitions: A crisp language is a finite set \(\Gamma\) of relations \(R\subseteq D^r\) of possibly different finite arities on a finite nonempty explicitly listed domain D. Each relation is given by its arity and a list of its allowed tuples; unlisted tuples are forbidden. This is equivalent to a cost function with value 0 on allowed tuples and +∞ elsewhere. The input size N includes D, relation delimiters, arities and the binary encodings of all listed entries. There is no fixed bound on |D| or arity imposed outside the input. An m-ary operation \(g:D^{m}\to D\) preserves an r-ary relation R if, for every m tuples \(a^{1},\ldots ,a^{m}\in R\), the coordinatewise tuple \((g(a^{1}_{1},\ldots ,a^{m}_{1}),\ldots ,g(a^{1}_{r},\ldots ,a^{m}_{r}))\) lies in R. A polymorphism of \(\Gamma\) preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\). The language is a core if every unary polymorphism \(u:D\to D\) is bijective; for a finite relational structure such a map is an automorphism. Core status is promised rather than something the requested algorithm must verify. An idempotent Siggers polymorphism is a four-ary operation \(s:D^{4}\to D\) that preserves every relation and satisfies \(s(x,x,x,x)=x\) for all \(x\in D\) and \(s(r,a,r,e)=s(a,r,e,a)\) for every \(r,a,e\in D\). On a core, existence of a Siggers operation without the idempotence identity is equivalent to existence of an idempotent one. An ordinary \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma )\) instance has variables and constraints requiring selected variable tuples to belong to relations of \(\Gamma\); it asks for a satisfying assignment from D. In the source’s terminology, solvable means satisfying the dichotomy’s polymorphism criterion. Such languages have polynomial-time CSP algorithms when \(\Gamma\) is fixed; failure of the criterion gives NP-hardness. The present target tests that algebraic criterion and does not assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in order to define its yes/no answers. The requested machine must halt in \(N^{O(1)}\) time on all inputs and be correct on every input satisfying the core promise. Its behavior on non-core inputs is unrestricted. The task only asks to decide existence, not to output the operation table, although a four-ary table has \(|D|^{4}\) entries and gives a polynomial-size, polynomially checkable existence certificate.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with one polynomial running-time bound in N that accepts exactly the promised core languages having such a polymorphism, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness statement requires the core promise to be respected. Testing whether the input is a core, classifying languages without that promise, or solving CSP instances for one fixed tractable template does not settle this meta-decision problem.
cards.why: Would make the finite-domain CSP tractability criterion efficiently recognizable when the core is already given, connecting the structural dichotomy to algorithms whose template also varies as input.

Theorem 16 gives a polynomial algorithm for the relevant binary symmetric fractional polymorphism of a core finite-valued language. Crisp relations use forbidden assignments with infinite cost, so that finite-valued theorem does not provide this Siggers test.

cards.title: Conjunctive-query containment under bag semantics
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine that halts on every pair \((q_1,q_2)\) of finite conjunctive queries with the same output arity and correctly decides whether
\[
 \forall\text{ finite bag databases }D\quad
 \forall a\in U_D^r:\qquad q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a),
\]
with the unrestricted syntax and natural-number sum-product semantics defined below? Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
cards.definitions:
A relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a specified nonnegative integer arity. It is part of the query input, with no fixed bound on the number of symbols or their arities. Both queries use a common signature; unused relation symbols have no effect. They also use a finite set \(C\) of named constants. A finite bag database \(D\) consists of a finite domain \(U_D\), an injective interpretation \(\iota_D:C\to U_D\) of the constant names, and a function
\[
 D_R:U_D^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\to\mathbb N
 \quad\text{for every }R\in\tau,
\]
where \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). The value is the tuple's multiplicity; zero means absence. All natural multiplicities and all finite domain sizes are allowed, without a bound determined in advance. No key, dependency or other integrity constraint is imposed. The domain may be empty when there are no constants. A nullary relation has one possible tuple, the empty tuple.

A conjunctive query has syntax
\[
 q(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\;:\!-\;A_1,\ldots,A_m,
\]
where each \(A_j\) is a positive relational atom \(R_j(t_{j,1},\ldots,t_{j,a_j})\), \(a_j\) is the arity of \(R_j\), and each term is a variable or a named constant. Every variable occurs in at least one body atom. The head \((x_1,\ldots,x_r)\) is a list of variables from the body; variables may repeat in the head. Body variables not in the head are existentially quantified. Distinct variable names may be assigned the same domain element, and a variable may be assigned the value of a constant. Different named constants denote distinct elements. The body is a list of atom occurrences: relation names, variables and entire atoms may repeat. There is no disjunction, negation, inequality, built-in comparison, aggregation syntax, recursion or duplicate-elimination operation. Identifying variables can enforce equality, but no additional predicate is interpreted specially.

Write \(\operatorname{Var}(q)\) for the finite set of variables in \(q\). For an assignment \(h:\operatorname{Var}(q)\to U_D\), extend \(h\) to constants by \(h(c)=\iota_D(c)\), and write \(D(A_j[h])\) for \(D_{R_j}\) evaluated at the instantiated tuple. For every output tuple \(a\in U_D^r\), define
\[
 q(D)(a)=
 \sum_{\substack{h:\operatorname{Var}(q)\to U_D\\
                  (h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_r))=a}}
       \prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h]).
\]
The arithmetic is ordinary exact addition and multiplication of nonnegative integers. The sum is finite; an empty sum is zero and an empty product is one. Each repeated occurrence contributes its own factor. For example, the bodies \(R(x)\) and \(R(x),R(x)\) give multiplicities \(D_R(a)\) and \(D_R(a)^2\), respectively. Output tuples that violate equalities forced by repeated head variables receive zero.

A Boolean query has \(r=0\) and returns a natural multiplicity at the unique empty tuple; it does not merely report whether a witness exists. An empty body is permitted only with no variables, hence has empty head and returns one. These conventions also define evaluation on empty domains.

Input queries, signatures, variable names and constant names have finite, effectively parseable binary encodings, for example length-prefixed symbol lists and atom lists. The machine receives only these two queries and their signature, not a database or a database-size bound. It must accept exactly when the displayed inequality holds for every database and every output tuple and reject otherwise. It can reject ill-formed encodings immediately. There is no required bound on its running time beyond halting on every input, and there is no noncomputable advice or external oracle. The inequality is exact and one-sided, with no input scale factor or additive slack.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total decision algorithm exists, with an implementation and proofs of termination and correctness on every input, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists.

Enumerating finite counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment and does not establish decidability. A decision procedure for equivalence, set semantics, or a proper query subclass is insufficient on its own. A theorem about bag-set inputs may be used only together with a proved effective reduction covering the bag-valued input model here. Undecidability after adding unions, inequalities, integrity constraints or a numerical transformation of the query count must likewise be reduced to this exact plain-CQ problem. No approximation tolerance or complexity-class upper bound is requested.
cards.why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.

With duplicates, a join multiplies tuple multiplicities and projection adds contributions of different assignments. Queries returning the same set of answers can therefore produce different numbers of copies.

Every proposed counterexample is a finite database with exactly computable counts. Exhaustively searching databases will eventually discover a counterexample when one exists, but gives no stopping rule for true containment.

The join-on-free theorem allows existential variables but forbids joins between body atoms through those variables in the contained query. Its decidability result therefore covers more than projection-free queries, while keeping a restriction absent from this target.

The literature relates bag-bag and bag-set containment by transformations of the query input. This does not justify silently treating the same original relations as sets; repeated atoms can affect the original bag comparison.

Nearby undecidability results add unions, comparisons or a transformation of the count. The June 2025 CQ-versus-UCQ paper still leaves the ordinary two-CQ inequality open.

The August 2026 discussion continues to identify general CQ bag containment as unresolved.

The September 2026 finite-witness result addresses equivalence in a mixed set/bag framework. Equality of two query functions and a one-sided inequality are distinct decision predicates; that abstract does not provide a general containment decision algorithm.
