cards.title: Constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Does there exist a total deterministic algorithm which, given any finite conjunctive query \(q\), decides whether all distinct answers to \(q\) can be enumerated on every finite database \(D\) with \(O_q(N)\) preprocessing time and \(O_q(1)\) worst-case delay?

Self-joins and projection are allowed. Here \(N\) is the database size defined below; the enumeration model is the specified deterministic word-RAM. The classifier has no prescribed running-time bound.
cards.definitions:
A conjunctive query is finite syntax
\[
q(\bar x)=\exists\bar y\;\bigwedge_{i=1}^{s}R_i(\bar z_i).
\]
The head \(\bar x\) is an ordered list of distinct variables, and \(\bar y\) lists the other variables. Each variable occurs in an atom. Each relation symbol has one fixed positive integer arity within the query, and the length of each argument list agrees with it. A symbol may occur in several atoms (a self-join); a variable may repeat within an atom. There are no constants, negation, disequalities, aggregation, or additional constraints on the database. All relation arities and the complete formula are part of the classifier input, not fixed globally. An empty conjunction has no variables and is the constantly true Boolean query.

A database for the query has domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), for any integer \(n\ge0\), and explicitly lists each relation \(R^D\subseteq[n]^{\operatorname{arity}(R)}\). Each tuple occurs at most once in its relation list; list order is arbitrary. Domain elements outside all relations are permitted. Define the word size of the data by
\[
N=1+n+\sum_R\operatorname{arity}(R)\,|R^D|.
\]
All tuple entries and \(n\) are provided as binary integers. In particular, the domain-size contribution to the resource parameter is \(n\), not merely its binary encoding length. No succinct relation representation or data-access oracle is provided.

An assignment maps query variables to domain elements. It satisfies an atom exactly when the resulting tuple belongs to that relation. The answer set \(q(D)\) consists of head tuples having at least one satisfying extension to \(\bar y\). Different witnesses for the same head tuple give just one answer. An empty head gives either no answer or the one empty tuple, according to whether the query is false or true.

For a fixed query, an enumerator is a finite deterministic word-RAM program, with constants \(B,C\ge1\) independent of the database; \(B\) is an integer. Its word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) bits. The address universe contains \(2^w\) initially zero cells. Each read, write, indirect access, comparison, conditional branch, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient or remainder by a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operation, or shift costs one operation. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return results modulo \(2^w\); a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger values occupy multiple words with all operations charged. No random instruction, arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, database-specific advice or oracle is available.

Every accessed cell and every output operation is charged. Unused addresses require no initialization. There is no further requirement that memory used in preprocessing be linear, or that enumeration use only constant additional memory. The fixed exponent implicit in the address universe may depend on the query and algorithm. Writing an answer writes its head coordinates, or one marker for the empty tuple; the output is append-only.

The program first finishes a preprocessing phase of at most \(CN\) operations, then enumerates exactly \(q(D)\) in any order without repetition and halts. After preprocessing, the time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to halting is at most \(C\). If there are no answers, it must halt within \(C\) operations after preprocessing. The same constants and program must work on every database for that query.

The classifier is a deterministic Turing machine on a full finite encoding of query syntax, with relation names, variable names and arities encoded by finite binary strings. It halts on every valid query and says yes exactly when an enumerator and constants as above exist; malformed encodings may be rejected. Its input is \(q\), not a database. It need not produce an enumerator or the constants, and its running time has no required bound. The property being classified is actual, unconditional existence of an enumerator. A classification under an unproved complexity hypothesis is not silently substituted for that property. This effective existence proposition is the previously selected precise version of the source’s broader classification request.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a total classifier and a complete Lean-checked proof of its correctness for every query in the stated syntax and enumeration model, or give a complete Lean-checked proof that no such total classifier exists. A positive answer need not effectively construct the enumerators whose existence it classifies.

An algorithm for only a restricted query family, or sufficient and necessary conditions leaving other queries unclassified, is not complete. Exhibiting a query without efficient enumeration does not refute the existence of a classifier: a correct classifier may reject that query. Conditional exclusions must retain their hypotheses and do not by themselves establish an unconditional answer.
cards.why: Database queries can have far more answers than input tuples. Constant delay after linear preprocessing gives both output-sensitive total time and a bounded wait for each answer. A complete effective classification would identify exactly which query patterns allow this guarantee, including repeated uses of the same relation.

cards.context:
For example, \(q(x,z)=\exists y\,R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\) asks for endpoint pairs linked through some intermediate element. Many choices of the intermediate element can witness the same answer, which still has to be printed just once.

The query is fixed while the database varies. Query-dependent constants are therefore allowed, even though the separate classifier receives the query as its input. Its task is to decide an algorithm-existence property, rather than to enumerate answers itself.

A query hypergraph has variables as vertices and the variable set of each atom as a hyperedge. It is acyclic if the hyperedges have a join tree in which those containing each variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex acyclicity additionally requires this after adding the head-variable set as an edge. The source recalls the classical linear-preprocessing, constant-delay algorithm for this condition.

The corresponding hardness statements for self-join-free queries use hypotheses about Boolean matrix multiplication or hyperclique detection. They should not be read as unconditional proofs that all other queries are intractable.

Self-joins permit further tractable structures: §7.1 gives cyclic mirror queries with constant-delay enumeration. Their memory during enumeration may grow with output size. Imposing constant additional workspace would therefore change the class under consideration.

The preliminary 2025 report studies acyclic queries with unary or binary atoms, including projections. It develops partial conditions and explicitly leaves queries outside the classified cases. That atom-arity restriction does not cover the arbitrary-arity input of this card.

The author’s 2026 announcement of joint work on self-joins and projections still reports unclassified examples. Its unavailable manuscript is not treated as a verified complete classification.

cards.title: Dichotomy for consistent query answering under primary keys
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite relational schema with one designated nonempty primary key for each relation, and every fixed Boolean conjunctive query \(q\) over that schema, is the language \(\operatorname{CERTAINTY}(q)\) either in deterministic polynomial time or coNP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?

The input to this language is an explicitly represented finite database \(D\), possibly violating its keys. It is accepted exactly when \(q\) is true in every inclusion-maximal subdatabase of \(D\) that satisfies the keys. Repeated occurrences of a relation in \(q\), called self-joins, are allowed.
cards.definitions:
A schema lists relation names and their positive integer arities. Each relation has a fixed nonempty subset of its positions as its primary key. A database is a finite set of tuples for each relation, with values encoded as finite binary strings. A key is satisfied if any two tuples agreeing in all key positions also agree in every position. A subdatabase deletes tuples without inserting or changing values. A repair is such a subdatabase that satisfies all keys and cannot be enlarged by putting back any deleted tuple while still satisfying them. Thus, for each nonempty group of conflicting tuples with one key value, a repair chooses exactly one tuple; this is inclusion maximality, not an optimization over all possible edits.

A Boolean conjunctive query is a finite nonempty conjunction of relational atoms with all its variables existentially quantified; variables may repeat within and across atoms, and fixed constants are allowed. It contains no negation, disjunction, inequality, function symbol or aggregation. Truth means that some assignment of its variables makes every atom a stored tuple. Query and schema, including keys, are fixed separately for each language; only the database varies. Time is measured in the total bit length of its explicit encoding, with constants and polynomial degree allowed to depend on the fixed query/schema.

Use [P and coNP](definitions.html#p-np) and polynomial-time [many-one reductions](definitions.html#reductions) for coNP-completeness. The two-case classification is for each fixed query. It requires neither an effective classifier taking the query as input nor a separation of P from coNP.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated proposition. Results for a restricted query family do not settle its universal scope. A conditional negative result must retain its unproved assumptions and is not an unconditional refutation.
cards.why: Conflicting primary-key records are routine in integrated data. This question asks whether every fixed database query is either efficiently answerable with certainty across all repairs or computationally complete for a standard hard class.

cards.title: Dichotomy for deletion resilience of relational queries
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite relational schema and every fixed Boolean union of conjunctive queries \(q\), is \(\operatorname{RES}(q)\) either in deterministic polynomial time or NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?

An input consists of a finite bag database \(D\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\). It belongs to \(\operatorname{RES}(q)\) if at most \(k\) individual tuple occurrences can be deleted so that \(q\) becomes false. All occurrences may be deleted, and all relation arities and self-joins are allowed.
cards.definitions:
A schema is a finite list of relation names of positive integer arity. A bag database gives an explicit list of tuple occurrences for each relation; duplicates are allowed and count as separate deletions. Domain values are finite binary strings. Multiplicities are represented by repeated occurrences, not exponentially compressed binary counts. The budget k is written in binary. Input length is the bit length of these lists and the budget.

The fixed query is a finite disjunction of Boolean conjunctive queries. Each disjunct is an existentially quantified, nonempty finite conjunction of relational atoms using variables, with no constants, equality, inequality, negation or function symbols. Every variable occurs in an atom. A disjunct is true when a variable assignment maps every atom to a tuple whose remaining multiplicity is positive. Repeated uses of one relation and disconnected conjunctions are permitted. Query truth uses the support of the remaining database, while deletion cost counts occurrences. The empty database therefore makes the query false. The minimum deletion cost is called its resilience; it is zero if the query is already false.

Only D and k vary in RES(q); the schema and query are fixed, so running-time constants and polynomial degree may depend on them. Use the shared definitions of [P and NP](definitions.html#p-np). NP-completeness means membership in NP and polynomial-time many-one hardness for every NP language. The proposition asks whether an intermediate complexity can occur anywhere in this family. It does not demand an effective syntactic classifier or the stronger algebraic characterization from the source, and it does not assume P differs from NP.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated proposition. Results for a restricted query family do not settle its universal scope. A conditional negative result must retain its unproved assumptions and is not an unconditional refutation.

cards.title: Decidability of conjunctive-query entailment in SROIQ
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Is Boolean conjunctive-query entailment for classical SROIQ decidable under semantics allowing both finite and infinite models? Precisely, does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(D\) such that for every finite legal SROIQ knowledge base \(K\) and every Boolean conjunctive query \(q\), in the syntax and semantics below, \(D(K,q)\) halts with a bit satisfying
\[D(K,q)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\models q?\]
Both \(K\) and \(q\) are input. Query atoms may use non-simple roles, including roles made transitive or affected by legal role chains. There is no bound on the size of models and no finite-model, named-witness, Horn or simple-query-role restriction. No running-time bound is requested beyond termination on every legal pair.
cards.definitions:
Names and role expressions. Use disjoint countable sets of ordinary concept names \(A\), nominal concept names \(o\), individual names \(a\), ordinary role names \(r\), and query variables \(x\), each effectively indexed by natural numbers. There is also a distinguished universal role \(U\). A role expression is \(r\), \(r^{-}\), or \(U\). The operation \(\operatorname{Inv}\) swaps \(r\) and \(r^{-}\) and fixes \(U\). Only finitely many names occur in an input. Nominal concepts and individual names are different syntactic sorts; a nominal will denote a singleton, while an individual denotes an element. They can be linked by an assertion \(o(a)\). There are no datatypes, datatype predicates or additional rule language.

Role hierarchies and regularity. The knowledge base includes a finite role hierarchy \(\mathcal H\) of inclusions \(R_1\cdots R_\ell\sqsubseteq r\), with \(\ell\ge1\), every \(R_i\ne U\), and \(r\) an ordinary role name. We use the normalized syntax of classical SROIQ: an inverse on the right can be removed by inverting both sides and reversing the left-hand string. Trivial self-inclusions are omitted; aliases connected by cycles of ordinary role equivalences can first be identified consistently throughout the knowledge base and query. The formal input domain here consists of the normalized inclusions satisfying the following finite regularity test.

There must exist an irreflexive transitive relation \(\prec\) on the occurring non-universal role expressions and their inverses such that \(S\prec R\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Inv}(S)\prec R\). Every inclusion \(w\sqsubseteq r\) must have one of the forms
\[w=rr,\qquad w=r^{-},\qquad w=S_1\cdots S_t,\qquad w=rS_1\cdots S_t,\qquad w=S_1\cdots S_t r,\]
where, in the last three cases, \(t\ge1\) and \(S_i\prec r\) for every \(i\). The same order must work for the whole hierarchy. It need not be supplied with the input. This excludes arbitrary mutually recursive role-chain rules. Transitivity and symmetry of a role name can be written as \(rr\sqsubseteq r\) and \(r^{-}\sqsubseteq r\), respectively.

Simple roles and role assertions. Declare a role non-simple if it belongs to the least set \(\mathcal N\) satisfying these closure rules: the right-hand role of every inclusion whose left side has length at least two lies in \(\mathcal N\); \(R\in\mathcal N\) implies \(\operatorname{Inv}(R)\in\mathcal N\); and an ordinary single-role inclusion \(R\sqsubseteq S\) propagates membership from \(R\) to \(S\). For the last rule also include the inverse inclusion \(\operatorname{Inv}(R)\sqsubseteq\operatorname{Inv}(S)\) for each single-role inclusion. Every other role is simple. In the selected 2006 syntax, \(U\) is absent from role hierarchies and is simple; number restrictions on \(U\) are allowed and count all elements of the qualified concept. This makes the original universal-role convention explicit, rather than substituting the separate OWL2 syntax restrictions.

Besides \(\mathcal H\), the role box may contain \(\operatorname{Ref}(R)\), \(\operatorname{Irr}(S)\), \(\operatorname{Asy}(S)\), and \(\operatorname{Dis}(S,T)\). Here \(R,S,T\ne U\), and \(S,T\) must be simple, while the reflexive role \(R\) need not be simple. Asymmetry is strict: an edge forbids its reverse, even on the diagonal.

Concepts and the rest of the knowledge base. Concepts are the finite expressions generated by
\[C::=A\mid o\mid\top\mid\bot\mid\neg C\mid(C\sqcap C)\mid(C\sqcup C)\mid\exists R.C\mid\forall R.C\mid(\ge h\,S.C)\mid(\le h\,S.C)\mid\exists S.\mathsf{Self}.\]
The role \(R\) is arbitrary, \(S\) must be simple, and \(h\) is any nonnegative integer written in binary. A finite knowledge base \(K\) consists of the legal role box, a finite TBox of inclusions \(C\sqsubseteq E\), and a finite ABox of assertions \(C(a)\), \(R(a,b)\), \(\neg R(a,b)\), or \(a\ne b\). Positive and negative role assertions may use non-simple roles. In particular, number restrictions, self restrictions and role-property assertions have the simplicity restrictions just stated, but ordinary ABox role assertions do not acquire an extra simplicity restriction.

Interpretations. An interpretation \(\mathcal I\) has a nonempty set \(\Delta^{\mathcal I}\), finite or infinite. Each ordinary concept denotes a subset, each nominal denotes a singleton subset, each individual name denotes an element, and each ordinary role denotes a binary relation on this domain. Different names need not denote different elements or sets. Set \(U^{\mathcal I}=\Delta^{\mathcal I}\times\Delta^{\mathcal I}\) and \((r^{-})^{\mathcal I}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in r^{\mathcal I}\}\). The relation for a string \(R_1\cdots R_\ell\) contains \((d_0,d_\ell)\) exactly when there exist intermediate elements \(d_1,\ldots,d_{\ell-1}\) with \((d_{i-1},d_i)\in R_i^{\mathcal I}\) for all \(i\).

Interpret \(\top\) as the whole domain, \(\bot\) as the empty set, negation as complement in the domain, and \(\sqcap,\sqcup\) as intersection and union. An element belongs to \((\exists R.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if it has an \(R\)-successor in \(C^{\mathcal I}\), and to \((\forall R.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if all its \(R\)-successors are in \(C^{\mathcal I}\). It belongs to \((\ge h\,S.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if at least \(h\) distinct \(S\)-successors lie in \(C^{\mathcal I}\), and to \((\le h\,S.C)^{\mathcal I}\) if there are no \(h+1\) distinct such successors. These definitions also apply to infinite successor sets. Finally \((\exists S.\mathsf{Self})^{\mathcal I}=\{d:(d,d)\in S^{\mathcal I}\}\).

A hierarchy inclusion requires inclusion of the corresponding binary relations. Reflexivity means that every \((d,d)\) belongs to the role relation; irreflexivity means that no such pair belongs; asymmetry means that \((d,e)\) in the relation excludes \((e,d)\); disjointness means the two role relations have empty intersection. A TBox inclusion requires \(C^{\mathcal I}\subseteq E^{\mathcal I}\). An ABox concept assertion requires membership of \(a^{\mathcal I}\), a positive or negative role assertion requires membership or nonmembership of \((a^{\mathcal I},b^{\mathcal I})\), and inequality requires \(a^{\mathcal I}\ne b^{\mathcal I}\). A model of \(K\) satisfies every one of its axioms and assertions.

Queries and entailment. A Boolean conjunctive query is a finite formula
\[q=\exists x_1\cdots\exists x_t\ \bigwedge_{j=1}^{b}\alpha_j,\qquad t,b\ge0,\]
whose terms are the displayed variables or individual names. Each atom is \(A(v)\), \(o(v)\), or \(r(v,w)\), allowing also the role name \(U\). All variables occurring in atoms are bound. Ordinary query role names may be simple or non-simple. Query symbols need not occur in \(K\); their interpretation still obeys the name conventions above. No query negation, inequality, equality atom, disjunction, counting, self operator or regular-path operator is included. Repeated terms are allowed, so \(r(x,x)\) is allowed without being the concept constructor \(\exists r.\mathsf{Self}\). Query assignments map variables to arbitrary domain elements, may identify different variables and may use unnamed elements. The same assignment must make every atom true; individual terms keep their interpretations. The empty conjunction is true. Write \(\mathcal I\models q\) when such an assignment exists, and \(K\models q\) when every model of \(K\) satisfies it. If \(K\) has no models, it entails every query.

Effective decision problem. Encode the finite sets of axioms and query as fully parenthesized prefix expressions, with fixed distinct tags for the constructors and name sorts, binary indices for names, and binary counts for number restrictions, separated by delimiters. Lists of expressions are delimited as finite lists. This is a finite-string representation with effective parsing; replacing it by another computably equivalent explicit encoding does not change decidability. The finite syntax, simplicity and regularity conditions are part of legal input, and can be checked effectively. The requested machine has one finite program, no oracle or nonuniform advice, and must halt with the correct bit on every legal pair. No bound on its time, space or intermediate objects is prescribed; behavior on malformed pairs is irrelevant.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that one such total decision procedure exists, or a proof of its logical negation. For a positive answer, establish soundness, completeness and termination on every finite legal pair in the full language, including arbitrary non-simple query predicates and knowledge bases whose only models are infinite. For a negative answer, establish that every deterministic Turing machine fails on some legal pair by not halting with a bit or by returning the wrong entailment answer. Undecidability only for finite-model semantics or for a stronger query or axiom language does not settle this target. Likewise, a terminating method only for Horn knowledge bases, simple-role queries, satisfiable instances with a finite model bound, or other proper restrictions is insufficient. Empirical termination of a reasoner is not a universal termination proof.
cards.why: A basic decidability boundary for querying expressive ontologies: the logic has decidable consistency, but unrestricted conjunctive-query entailment still lacks a general resolution.

references.title: Revisiting Conjunctive Query Entailment for S
references.authors: Yazmín Ibáñez-García; Jean Christoph Jung; Vincent Michielini; Filip Murlak
references.locator: AAAI2026,40(23),19152–19159, DOI10.1609/aaai.v40i23.38989. Full version2,8 May2026: introduction and Theorem1, 2ExpTime-completeness for S and Boolean-CQ hardness with two transitive roles; v1 submitted11 November2025.

cards.context:
A knowledge base describes incomplete information about a world. Its assertions name some objects, while its general axioms can require additional unnamed objects in every possible world. A Boolean query asks whether a finite relational pattern must exist. The problem is to decide whether the pattern follows from the whole specification, rather than whether it can be found among explicitly stored facts.

For example, let the knowledge base assert \(\mathsf{Person}(a)\) and \(\mathsf{Person}\sqsubseteq\exists\mathsf{knows}.\mathsf{Person}\). Every model then satisfies \(\exists x\exists y\,(\mathsf{Person}(x)\land\mathsf{knows}(x,y)\land\mathsf{Person}(y))\). No named witness for \(y\) is required. The same domain element may serve as both variables if the model permits it. A query that reuses variables across several atoms requires one common assignment satisfying all those atoms.

SROIQ combines concept negation, existential and universal restrictions, singleton concepts, inverse roles, counting and regular role chains. This expressive combination underlies the logical core of OWL 2 DL. The role restrictions in the definitions are substantive: removing regularity or allowing arbitrary counting over composite roles produces different logics. The original SROIQ paper supplies a decision procedure for consistency, but that alone does not answer arbitrary conjunctive queries.

The conjunction of K with \(\neg q\) is inconsistent exactly when K entails q, but the negation of an arbitrary joined relational pattern need not be expressible as a SROIQ knowledge base. Likewise, a finite graph built by a consistency tableau is usually a compact representation of models, not an ordinary database on which evaluating q automatically gives the right answer. Unfolding repeated nodes can change whether a query cycle exists.

Rudolph and Glimm resolved a major part of the surrounding question in 2010. They handle nominals, inverse roles and counting together, and obtain decidability for SROIQ when all binary query predicates are simple roles. Thus the mere presence of those three constructors is not the remaining obstacle. The full question on this card also allows the query to inspect roles affected by transitivity and more general role compositions.

A different positive frontier comes from Horn restrictions. Ortiz, Rudolph and Šimkus show decidability even for a stronger path-query language over Horn-SROIQ, with doubly exponential combined complexity. Horn knowledge bases exclude forms of disjunctive choice that full SROIQ permits. Their result is therefore highly relevant progress, while leaving the unrestricted combination of knowledge-base features and query joins unresolved.

The distinction between all models and finite models is particularly consequential. Rudolph proves undecidability of finite conjunctive-query entailment already in a fragment of SROIQ. This is not an undecidability proof for the semantics chosen here: the sets of countermodels differ, and the distinction can affect the answer even on a small example.

The finite-model distinction already appears with one simple role \(r\). Require \(\top\sqsubseteq(\ge1\,r.\top)\sqcap(\le1\,r.\top)\), \(\top\sqsubseteq(\le1\,r^{-}.\top)\), and \((\le0\,r^{-}.\top)(a)\). These axioms describe an injective total successor function with a named element outside its image. They have the natural-number successor chain as a model but have no finite model, since an injective function on a finite set is surjective. A fresh ordinary concept \(A\) can be empty on that infinite model, so \(\exists x\,A(x)\) is not entailed under the chosen semantics. It is vacuously entailed if only finite models are considered.

Steigmiller and Glimm’s 2019 absorption method addresses practical entailment checking in very expressive logics and is implemented in Konclude. Its termination argument depends on a bounded supply of newly generated nominals in the difficult feature combination. Useful empirical behavior and termination on substantial fragments do not establish a total procedure for every SROIQ input. This conditional termination is exactly why the inherited source continues to present full decidability as open.

There is relevant progress as recently as 2026, but on a different slice of the language. Ibáñez-García, Jung, Michielini and Murlak show that conjunctive-query entailment for S, which adds transitive roles to ALC, is 2ExpTime-complete; hardness already uses two transitive roles and a Boolean conjunctive query. Their May 2026 full version also treats restrictions giving smaller upper bounds. This settles a complexity question for S, not the decidability of full SROIQ.

A positive solution would establish that general finite query patterns can always be answered against this expressive ontology language in principle. A negative solution would identify a sharp gap between consistency checking and pattern entailment inside a standard logical framework. Either outcome would clarify which expressive features can be combined while retaining an algorithmic foundation for querying incomplete knowledge.

cards.title: Computability of entropic query-size bounds
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Is the logarithmic entropic query-size bound uniformly computable? More precisely, does a single deterministic Turing machine, given any finite set of degree constraints \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) on \([n]\) with nonnegative rational logarithmic budgets, and any \(m\in\mathbb N\), halt and output either \(+\infty\) when \(E(\mathcal D)=+\infty\), or a rational \(q\) satisfying \(|q-E(\mathcal D)|\leq 2^{-m}\) when
\[E(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\overline{\Gamma_n^*},\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\ (1\leq i\leq k)\}<+\infty?\]
Here \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) is the closure of the discrete entropy region defined below; \(n\) is part of the input.
cards.definitions:
Let \(n\geq1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) be its set of subsets. Given jointly distributed discrete random variables \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\), each with a finite alphabet, their entropy vector is the real set function
\[h(S)=H(Z_S)=-\sum_z\Pr[Z_S=z]\log_2\Pr[Z_S=z],\qquad h(\varnothing)=0,\]
where \(Z_S\) is the tuple with indices in \(S\), and \(0\log_2 0=0\). Alphabets and real joint probabilities are unrestricted. The set of all such vectors is \(\Gamma_n^*\). Its closure \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space of subset coordinates consists of all limits of sequences of entropy vectors and is the almost-entropic cone. Neither alphabet sizes nor convergence rates are input bounds. Continuous differential entropy is not used.

A degree constraint is a triple \((X,Y,b)\), where \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\). It bounds the conditional entropy \(h(Y)-h(X)\). The case \(X=\varnothing\) gives a cardinality-type constraint, and \(b=0\) gives a functional dependency. Equal sets, repeated triples and an empty list are permitted. The all-zero entropy vector is always feasible, so the supremum is in \([0,+\infty]\). The optimization is over the closed almost-entropic cone, not just the nonclosed set of entropy vectors satisfying the constraints exactly; this distinction matters on faces defined by zero budgets.

For a database interpretation, a full conjunctive query returns the natural join of finite relations: an output tuple assigns all variables and its projection onto each relation's columns is present in that relation. There are no duplicate output tuples and no existentially projected variables. A bound of \(N\) on the number of extensions from columns \(X\) to columns \(Y\) gives the entropy budget \(b=\log_2 N\). Drawing a join tuple uniformly makes its full entropy the logarithm of the join size. The quantity \(2^{E(\mathcal D)}\) is the information-theoretic upper bound; the question asks to compute its logarithm, rather than to enumerate joins or compute the exact maximum size of a finite database instance.

The finite encoding used here writes \(n\) and the list length in unary, every subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and each rational budget as a nonnegative binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, with delimiters. The precision \(m\) is given in unary. This is an explicit rational logarithmic-budget version of the source's numerical problem, with no real-number oracle. At the level of computability it also covers positive integer degree bounds supplied as \(N\): cone homogeneity handles rational budgets by scaling them to integer logarithms, while positive values \(\log_2 N\) can be bracketed multiplicatively by rational numbers, keeping zero budgets exactly zero. This equivalence concerns computability, not polynomial-time equivalence of the two encodings.

Unbounded inputs are included. They can be recognized by starting with \(S=\varnothing\) and repeatedly adjoining \(Y_i\) whenever \(X_i\subseteq S\). The optimum is finite exactly when the resulting closure is \([n]\). In that case conditional-entropy inequalities and subadditivity supply an explicit finite upper bound. If some variables remain outside, let them all share an arbitrarily high-entropy random variable and make the other variables constant; every constraint is satisfied while the objective is unbounded. Thus recognizing infinity is not the unknown part of the problem.

The machine must halt on every valid input, with a finite binary rational output in the bounded case; malformed strings may be rejected. There is no time or space bound, no advice, oracle, fixed dimension or randomness. Accuracy is absolute in base-two entropy units. In particular the machine must achieve error at most \(1/100\), by taking \(m=7\), and also every finer requested accuracy. A one-sided sequence of estimates without a computable error guarantee does not suffice.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the displayed uniform machine exists, or that it does not. An affirmative proof must provide an effective procedure and prove termination and the requested two-sided absolute error for every finite dimension, rational degree-constraint list and precision, including zero budgets and the stated infinity convention. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this particular functional, not merely undecidability of a different entropy-region membership or information-inequality problem. An exact symbolic formula is unnecessary, while a computable value for each separately fixed input without one uniform procedure is insufficient. There are no unproved complexity assumptions in the target.
cards.why: The strongest information-theoretic query estimates are useful algorithmically only if their numerical values can be obtained effectively. A computability theorem would make this extremal use of arbitrary discrete distributions accessible to uniform algorithms; a noncomputability theorem would identify a fundamental limit on exact information-theoretic database estimation, even with unlimited running time.

cards.context:
The seminar groups several algorithmic questions about information-theoretic database bounds. Question 7.1 asks for computability of the entropic bound; Question 7.2 separately asks about the complexity of its polymatroid relaxation. The first issue is whether any terminating numerical algorithm exists, before asking whether one is efficient.

Entropy inequalities constrain correlations among columns in a join. Using every valid inequality gives a potentially sharper bound than the familiar Shannon inequalities alone. Suciu formulates the entropic upper bound by such inequalities and identifies its value with optimization over the closed almost-entropic cone. This closure specifies which limiting entropy vectors belong to the target.

Replacing the almost-entropic cone by normalized monotone submodular set functions gives a finite linear program, with exponentially many subset coordinates. This yields a computable upper relaxation, but a gap between that relaxation and the entropic optimum prevents it from settling the question. Restricting alphabet sizes also changes the feasible region unless a sufficient effective approximation theorem is proved.

For simple degree constraints, where every conditioning set has size at most one, the entropic and polymatroid bounds coincide and a polynomial-size linear program is available. This tractable subclass does not cover arbitrary conditioning sets or all zero-budget functional dependencies.

Mengel and Romashchenko still describe general computability as unresolved in August 2026. Their new work examines acyclic dependencies and shows that allowing projected variables can create gaps between entropy and polymatroid bounds. That result concerns the comparison of bounds in a richer query setting, not an algorithm or impossibility proof for the full general numerical target here.

cards.title: BDD/FC conjecture
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is every finite set \(R\) of existential tuple-generating dependencies with bounded derivation depth finitely controllable? Use the precise query-rewriting definition of bounded derivation depth below. The required conclusion is that for every finite database \(I\) and every Boolean conjunctive query \(q\), \[(I,R)\models q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(I,R)\models_{\mathrm{fin}}q.\] The left side quantifies over all models extending \(I\) and satisfying \(R\); the right side quantifies only over finite such models. The conjecture quantifies over every finite relational signature of arbitrary finite arities, and permits conjunctions of several atoms in rule heads.
cards.definitions: A relational signature is a finite collection of relation symbols, each with a fixed nonnegative integer arity. An atom has the form \(P(t_1,\ldots,t_a)\), with repeated arguments allowed. In rules and queries the arguments are variables; there are no function symbols, built-in equality or inequality, negation, or interpreted order. A rule is the sentence \(\forall\bar x\,\forall\bar y\,(B(\bar x,\bar y)\to\exists\bar z\,H(\bar y,\bar z))\), where \(B,H\) are finite nonempty conjunctions of atoms, each universal variable occurs in \(B\), and the only universal variables in \(H\) come from \(\bar y\). The tuples of universal and existential variables are disjoint. The existential tuple may be empty, so ordinary positive Datalog rules are included. A rule set is finite, and rule heads may contain several atoms. A database \(I\) is a finite set of relational facts on finitely many named distinct elements; its active domain is the set of elements appearing in these facts. Empty active domains and nullary facts are allowed. A model extending \(I\) has a nonempty domain containing its named elements and includes every fact of \(I\); it may add elements and facts, including new facts on old elements. It satisfies \(R\) with ordinary first-order semantics, and must preserve the identities of the named database elements. “Finite model” means a finite domain, with no prescribed cardinality bound. A conjunctive query \(q(\bar u)=\exists\bar v\,A(\bar u,\bar v)\) uses a finite nonempty conjunction of relational atoms, with every displayed free variable occurring in an atom. A Boolean query has no free variables. A union of conjunctive queries is a finite disjunction of such queries with the same free variables; the empty disjunction denotes false. Query evaluation on a database means a variable assignment into its active domain satisfying all required facts, and for a union means satisfaction of at least one disjunct. For an answer tuple \(\bar a\) from the active domain, \((I,R)\models q(\bar a)\) means that every model extending \(I\) and satisfying \(R\) satisfies this instantiated query. Define \(R\) to have bounded derivation depth if for every conjunctive query \(q(\bar u)\) there is a finite union of conjunctive queries \(Q(\bar u)\) over the same signature such that, for every finite database \(I\) and every compatible answer tuple \(\bar a\), \((I,R)\models q(\bar a)\) if and only if \(I\models Q(\bar a)\). The rewriting \(Q\) may depend on \(R,q\) but not on the database or answer tuple. This is the source’s equivalent positive query-rewriting formulation of bounded derivation depth; it does not require one depth bound for all queries. Finite controllability is the displayed unrestricted-versus-finite equivalence for every \(I,q\). There is no syntactic guardedness, stickiness, binary-arity or single-head restriction on \(R\), and no time bound for constructing a rewriting or countermodel.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication for every finite signature and rule set, or refute it. A positive answer must show that whenever a Boolean conjunctive query fails in some possibly infinite model of \(I,R\), it also fails in some finite model of the same database and rules, assuming only the stated bounded derivation depth property. A negative answer must provide one finite signature and rule set \(R\), prove its rewriting property for every conjunctive query, and provide a finite database \(I\) and Boolean conjunctive query \(q\) such that every finite model of \(I,R\) satisfies \(q\) but some infinite model does not. Showing bounded behavior for a single query does not establish the premise on \(R\). A counterexample whose rules lack bounded derivation depth, or a theorem for binary single-head rules alone, does not settle this target.
cards.why: Bounded derivation depth permits queries under existential rules to be answered through finite positive rewritings on the original database. Finite controllability asks whether considering only finite possible worlds changes those answers. Connecting the two would clarify when this useful query-processing property also supports finite-model semantics, across arbitrary relational arities.

cards.title: Linear-round convergence over stable semirings
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
Does there exist a universal real constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(p\ge0\), integer \(n\ge1\), commutative \(p\)-stable semiring \(S\), and polynomial map \(F:S^n\to S^n\) with coefficients in \(S\), the synchronous sequence
\[
x^{(0)}=(0,\ldots,0),\qquad x^{(t+1)}=F(x^{(t)})
\]
satisfies \(x^{(t+1)}=x^{(t)}\) for some integer \(0\le t\le C(p+1)n\)? The constant must be independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials and polynomial degrees. Only the number of rounds is measured.
cards.definitions:
A commutative semiring is a set \(S\) with binary operations \(\oplus,\otimes\) and elements \(0,1\) such that \((S,\oplus,0)\) and \((S,\otimes,1)\) are commutative monoids, multiplication distributes over addition, and \(0\otimes a=a\otimes0=0\). No additive inverses, additive idempotence, order, finiteness or effective encoding is assumed. The trivial semiring is allowed. All equalities are equalities of semiring elements.

For \(a\in S\), set \(a^0=1\) and \(a^{j+1}=a^j\otimes a\). The semiring is \(p\)-stable when
\[
\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p}a^j=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{p+1}a^j\qquad\text{for every }a\in S.
\]
The same integer \(p\) must work for every element, not merely for the coefficients appearing in one system. It need not be the smallest possible stability index. The case \(p=0\) means \(1\oplus a=1\) for all \(a\).

Each coordinate of \(F\) is given by a finite polynomial expression, equivalently
\[
F_i(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\bigoplus_{j\in J_i}\left(a_{ij}\otimes\bigotimes_{r=1}^{n}x_r^{e_{ijr}}\right),
\]
where \(J_i\) is a finite index set, \(a_{ij}\in S\) and \(e_{ijr}\in\mathbb N\). An empty sum is 0 and an empty product is 1. Repeated monomials, arbitrary finite exponents and constant terms are allowed. There is no bound on the degrees or the number of terms, and no requirement of linearity. The coefficients remain fixed during iteration.

One round evaluates every \(F_i\) from the entire previous vector \(x^{(t)}\). Partially updated coordinates cannot be reused within that round. The rule is precisely \(F\), not a replacement such as \(x\mapsto x\oplus F(x)\), unless their iteration behavior is proved to agree for the system under consideration. The initial vector is always zero. Once two successive vectors are equal, all later vectors equal them because the map is fixed.

The dimension \(n\) counts all coordinates, including those that stay zero. In a grounded Datalog system they represent potential derived facts, each carrying a semiring annotation. The statement counts applications of the polynomial map, irrespective of the arithmetic work, representation size or equality-testing cost within a round. It therefore asks for an algebraic convergence theorem, not a fast implementation of one database operation.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal bound or its logical negation. A positive proof must use one constant valid simultaneously for every \(p,n,S,F\) in the definitions, including \(p=0\) and nonlinear systems of unbounded finite degree.

A negative proof must establish that, for every proposed constant \(C\), some allowed system has no fixed-point equality at any integer \(t\le C(p+1)n\). Equivalently, the first fixed-point times divided by \((p+1)n\) are unbounded, treating nonconvergence as infinite time. One example requiring more than \(n\) rounds does not refute an unspecified universal constant. A bound with an additional growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients or dimension, or a faster method using a different update rule, does not prove this exact synchronous-round target. A title announcing optimal convergence is not a substitute for a theorem with the required hypotheses and quantifiers.
cards.why: The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. A universal linear bound would explain why a broad class of annotated recursive computations needs only an output-scale number of rounds, while a separation would expose a fundamental cost of nonlinear interactions.

cards.title: Uniform reliability of homomorphism-closed queries
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is the following dichotomy true? For every finite relational signature \(\sigma\) of arbitrary fixed finite arities and every homomorphism-closed Boolean query \(Q\) on finite \(\sigma\)-instances, at least one of the following holds: (i) \(Q\) is equivalent on all finite instances to a finite union of conjunctive queries \(U\) for which exact tuple-independent probabilistic query evaluation \(\mathrm{PQE}(U)\) is computable in deterministic polynomial time; (ii) the function \(\mathrm{UR}_Q(I)=|\{J\subseteq I:Q(J)=1\}|\) is \(\#\mathrm{P}\)-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. This is the semantic formulation below of the source's proposed safe-UCQ versus hardness dichotomy; it retains arbitrary homomorphism-closed \(Q\), not only queries expressed by a UCQ.
cards.definitions: A signature is a finite set of relation symbols, each with a nonnegative integer arity; no function symbols, distinguished constants or built-in relations are supplied. An instance \(I\) is a finite set of facts \(R(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\), with \(r\) the arity of \(R\) and elements \(a_i\) drawn from \(\mathbb N\). Facts have set semantics, with no multiplicities. The active domain \(\operatorname{dom}(I)\) consists of elements occurring in its facts; for arity zero a fact has an empty tuple. Empty instances are allowed. A homomorphism \(h:I\to K\) is a function \(\operatorname{dom}(I)\to\operatorname{dom}(K)\) mapping every fact of \(I\) to a fact of \(K\) with the same relation symbol. The function \(Q\) is homomorphism-closed if \(Q(I)=1\) and \(h:I\to K\) imply \(Q(K)=1\). No finite syntactic representation, decidability or polynomial-time evaluation of \(Q\) is assumed. A subinstance \(J\subseteq I\) is an arbitrary subset of facts, with its own active domain; it is not an induced substructure. A finite Boolean UCQ can be specified by finitely many finite pattern instances \(A_1,\ldots,A_t\): it holds on \(I\) exactly when some \(A_i\) has a homomorphism to \(I\). The empty list expresses false, and an empty pattern expresses true. Repeated relation symbols are allowed. Equivalence means agreement on every finite instance. For a fixed query \(U\), \(\mathrm{PQE}(U)\) takes an instance \(I\) and a rational probability \(p_F\in[0,1]\) for each fact \(F\in I\), and returns the exact rational number \[\sum_{J\subseteq I,\ U(J)=1}\ \prod_{F\in J}p_F\prod_{F\in I\setminus J}(1-p_F).\] Facts are sampled independently. Probabilities are input as binary integer numerators and positive denominators; the output is a reduced binary numerator/denominator pair. For \(\mathrm{UR}_Q\), only \(I\) is input and the output is the exact count in binary. It equals \(2^{|I|}\) times the probability when every fact has probability exactly \(1/2\); there are no mandatory facts. Encode an instance by its list of distinct facts, with binary element names and fixed relation identifiers. Polynomial time refers to the total bit length on a deterministic Turing machine, including rational encodings for \(\mathrm{PQE}\); the fixed query, signature, algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on one another. No uniform procedure taking \(Q\) as an additional input is required. The class \(\#\mathrm{P}\) consists of functions counting accepting paths of polynomial-time nondeterministic Turing machines. Turing hardness means that every such function can be computed by a deterministic polynomial-time oracle machine with access to exact values of \(\mathrm{UR}_Q\) on encoded instances; polynomially many adaptive oracle calls are permitted. No membership of \(\mathrm{UR}_Q\) in \(\#\mathrm{P}\) is asserted for arbitrary \(Q\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated universal dichotomy, or a Lean-checked refutation: a finite signature \(\sigma\) and homomorphism-closed Boolean query \(Q\) for which there is no equivalent finite UCQ with polynomial-time exact \(\mathrm{PQE}\), and \(\mathrm{UR}_Q\) is not \(\#\mathrm{P}\)-hard under the specified reductions. The target covers every fixed finite arity and permits queries of unrestricted evaluation complexity. A result only for maximum arity two, only for UCQs, or only for approximation does not settle the full statement. The alternatives are not required to be disjoint, and no assumption separating \(\mathrm{FP}\) from \(\#\mathrm{P}\) is imposed.
cards.why: A complete dichotomy would identify exactly when independently retaining each database fact with probability one half permits tractable exact query evaluation. It would connect finite logical descriptions and recursive query behavior to the complexity of counting possible databases, extending the established weighted-query theory to a basic unweighted model.

cards.context:
The original question asks which fixed homomorphism-closed queries allow polynomial-time counting of satisfying subdatabases, and whether the remaining cases are hard. Its linked paper states the proposed boundary explicitly: queries equivalent to a safe finite UCQ are tractable, and all others should be #P-hard. The present card uses the equivalent semantic formulation through tractability of weighted PQE on finite UCQs; it does not require an algorithm deciding a query's side from a query description.

Dalvi and Suciu establish the dichotomy for arbitrary rational fact probabilities on finite UCQs. This supplies the known tractable boundary used in the semantic formulation. Restricting every fact to probability one half prevents simply importing all weighted hardness results.

For conjunctive queries without repeated relation symbols, uniform reliability is in polynomial time when every two variables occur in nested or disjoint sets of atoms, and is #P-complete otherwise. The full question also allows repeated symbols, finite unions and queries beyond finite UCQs.

The 2023 theorem proves hardness for every homomorphism-closed query on a signature of maximum arity two that is not equivalent to any finite UCQ. Its conclusion explicitly leaves arbitrary-arity unbounded queries and the general finite-UCQ case as the remaining parts of the conjecture. It allows even undecidable queries, which is why the full target asserts hardness rather than completeness in #P.

The 2024 Shapley-value paper distinguishes ordinary model counting from generalized counting, where some facts must be present. Its cited full graph-query dichotomy concerns that generalized model.

The 2025 work on probabilistic graphs studies approximation guarantees and does not provide an exact-counting resolution of the statement here.

cards.title: Fractional-edge-cover load for general-message parallel joins
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite natural-join schema \(Q\), is there a randomized MPC algorithm computing its full join in a constant number of communication rounds with load
\[
\widetilde O_Q\!\left(\frac{m}{p^{1/\rho(Q)}}\right)
\]
on every database instance of total input size \(m\), using \(p\) machines with \(2\le p\) and \(p^3\le m\)?

Precisely, for every \(Q\) and every fixed word-size multiplier \(a\ge1\), must there exist one algorithm \(A_{Q,a}\), constants \(C_{Q,a}>0\), and integers \(R_{Q,a},d_{Q,a}\ge1\), such that it halts within \(R_{Q,a}\) rounds on every execution and, for each valid instance and initial distribution, with probability at least \(1-p^{-2}\) both outputs exactly the join and has load at most
\[
C_{Q,a}\frac{m}{p^{1/\rho(Q)}}
       \bigl(\log_2(m+2)\bigr)^{d_{Q,a}}?
\]
Messages may encode arbitrary information; they are not restricted to complete input tuples. This broader model is the explicit user choice.
cards.definitions:
A schema is a finite nonempty attribute set \(V\) and a finite indexed list of nonempty subsets \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\subseteq V\) with union \(V\). Attribute names, arities, relation names and \(r\) are fixed independently of \(m,p\). Schemas may have repeated subsets. An instance supplies a finite set \(R_i\) of tuples on \(e_i\) for each \(i\). A tuple on \(e_i\) assigns one domain value to each attribute in \(e_i\). Relations have set semantics; duplicate copies within a relation do not contribute multiplicity. The total input size is \(m=\sum_i|R_i|\). The output is the full relation
\[
J_Q(R_1,\ldots,R_r)
=\{t:V\to\mathrm{dom}:\ \forall i,\ t|_{e_i}\in R_i\}.
\]
Every attribute is output; there is no projection, aggregation or bag multiplicity.

The fractional edge-cover number depends only on the schema:
\[
\rho(Q)=\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r x_i:
x_i\ge0,\quad
\forall v\in V,\ \sum_{i:v\in e_i}x_i\ge1\right\}.
\]
It is finite and at least one. The variables \(x_i\) are real weights on relation schemas, not data values or relation sizes.

For a precise finite encoding, fix an integer \(a\ge1\) and let a machine word contain \(w=a\lceil\log_2(m+2)\rceil\) bits. Domain values are arbitrary \(w\)-bit strings, with equality of strings deciding attribute matches. A tuple occupies a constant number of words depending only on \(Q\), including its relation tag. Quantification over every fixed \(a\) gives the usual polynomial-size-domain word convention. A message word can contain any \(w\)-bit string computed by its sender; its interpretation is not restricted to a tuple, identifier, count or comparison result.

There are \(p\) machines with distinct indices \(1,\ldots,p\), each able to communicate directly with every other machine. The total input is initially partitioned without replication, with each machine holding at most \(2\lceil m/p\rceil\) tagged tuples. The algorithm must work for every such partition. All machines know \(Q,a,m,p\), the encoding and their own index, but receive no other instance-specific advice, preprocessing or statistics for free.

Each synchronous round consists of arbitrary finite local computation followed by message transmission. All messages in the transmission phase must have been prepared before receiving any message from that phase. A machine may send different messages to different recipients, and later rounds may depend on earlier messages. The load is
\[
\max_{\text{round }j,\ \text{machine }u}
\{\text{number of words received by }u\text{ in round }j\}.
\]
Headers and transmitted metadata count; a word sent to several recipients is received separately by each. Local computation, local storage, outgoing traffic as a separate metric, and local output are uncharged. There is no additional memory cap or running-time requirement, but each local phase must terminate.

Output uses a local emission operation on an explicitly written full tuple. Every output tuple must appear on at least one machine, no non-result tuple may appear on any machine, and repeated emissions of a valid tuple are allowed. A factorized representation, tuple count or emptiness bit is not the required output. A machine may derive and emit a tuple from arbitrary received information; it need not have received all its witness input tuples as intact records.

The algorithm is a single finite effective program for each fixed \(Q,a\), with independent private random bits and no advice depending on \(m,p\) or the data. Its joint correctness/load event has probability at least \(1-p^{-2}\) on every instance. All constants in the displayed bound may depend on \(Q,a\), but not on relation contents, input size, machine count or initial partition. The one-machine case is trivial and does not affect the target. The source's polynomial slack condition \(p^3\le m\) is retained rather than enlarged to all machine counts.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified existence assertion. A positive answer must cover every fixed schema, arbitrary data skew and every valid initial distribution, with the required full output and simultaneous round/load guarantee. A negative answer must show that the target fails for at least one fixed schema in the general-message model. An impossibility restricted to transmitting whole tuples or to a single round is insufficient. This is a binary resource-existence question; no numerical \(1/100\) approximation convention relaxes its bound or exact join output on successful runs.
cards.why: Parallel join processing must distribute related information so that machines can produce all compatible output tuples. The fractional edge-cover number captures a fundamental structural feature of the query. Whether it still suffices for communication with unrestricted messages separates a general information limit from limitations of algorithms that move database rows intact.

cards.context:
The source focuses on data complexity: a schema is fixed, while its input relations grow. It measures communication received by the busiest machine, and treats local processing and emission of output tuples as free. Its binary-relation result uses three rounds and the edge-cover load scale up to polylogarithmic factors.

The source distinguishes one-round bounds from constant-round algorithms. Its one-round structural parameter can exceed the fractional edge-cover number, so a one-round lower bound does not answer the multiround question.

The later JACM result gives a cyclic boat schema with \(\rho=2\) for which tuple-based algorithms need load \(\Omega(m/p^{1/3})\) in the relevant machine regime. This exceeds the proposed scale \(\widetilde O(m/p^{1/2})\). The restriction to tuple-based algorithms is explicit in both its model and theorem.

In that restricted model, input rows are atoms, and reporting an output tuple requires receiving all of its input witnesses. This card allows arbitrary encodings and inferences instead. Consequently the published restricted lower bound is not presented as a refutation of the selected target.

The same JACM article obtains the edge-cover scale for acyclic joins and distinguishes their behavior from cyclic queries in the tuple-based setting. Thus the failure of the universal tuple-based claim does not negate the established special cases.

The March 2026 κ-Join preprint gives a schema-dependent load bound based on a reduced quasi vertex-cover parameter. It conjectures matching lower bounds for tuple-based algorithms and explicitly says that general tightness remains unresolved. It does not establish the claimed edge-cover bound for arbitrary coded messages.

cards.title: Sunflower conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(r\ge3\), does there exist a real constant \(C_r\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite set \(X\), and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{S\subseteq X:|S|=k\}\),
\[
|\mathcal F|>C_r^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\text{ distinct }S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal F\ \exists K\subseteq X\ \forall i\ne j:\ S_i\cap S_j=K?
\]
The constant may depend on \(r\) but not on the set size \(k\), the ground set or the family. The conclusion is the existence of an ordinary \(r\)-sunflower.
cards.definitions:
A family here is a finite set of subsets, so identical members are not repeated. It is \(k\)-uniform when every member has exactly \(k\) elements. There is no bound on the finite ground-set size \(|X|\). An \(r\)-sunflower consists of \(r\) pairwise distinct members whose pairwise intersections are all the same set \(K\), called the core. For \(r\ge3\), this core also equals the intersection of all selected members. Removing \(K\) leaves pairwise disjoint petals. The core may be empty, in which case the selected sets are pairwise disjoint. For distinct equal-sized members their petals are nonempty.

The quantifier order is \(\forall r\,\exists C_r\,\forall k,X,\mathcal F\). No single base independent of \(r\) is requested. One may equivalently require an integer \(C_r\ge2\), since a larger integer base preserves the upper bound. An eventual bound for all sufficiently large \(k\), with the threshold depending on \(r\), also yields the displayed all-\(k\) formulation by enlarging \(C_r\) to cover finitely many small sizes.

The classical sunflower lemma bounds the size of any sunflower-free \(k\)-uniform family by \(k!(r-1)^k\), independently of its ground set. Consequently the largest such size \(S_r(k)\) exists as a finite integer, even though the ground set is unrestricted. The conjecture is equivalently \(S_r(k)\le C_r^k\) for all \(k\). It does not ask for the exact value, a numerical estimate or constant-factor asymptotics of \(S_r(k)\).

The source also states the conjecture for sets of size at most \(k\). Padding every smaller set to size \(k\) with fresh elements unique to that member preserves pairwise intersections and reduces that variant to the displayed one. This observation is not a claim about robust sunflowers: their probabilistic coverage requirement is stronger, and lower bounds for that stronger structure do not refute the ordinary conjecture.

There is no computational requirement on finding the sunflower or computing the constants. This is a quantified extremal-combinatorial proposition, so the numerical absolute-error convention does not replace it.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed conjecture or its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite base for every fixed \(r\ge3\). A negative proof must supply one fixed \(r\ge3\) for which every candidate base \(C\ge1\) admits a \(k\)-uniform family of more than \(C^k\) members with no \(r\)-sunflower. Improving known superconstant bases, proving only the case of one petal count, or disproving a robust-sunflower variant does not decide the full statement.
cards.why: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.

cards.title: \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every partial order \(P=([n],\le _{P})\) that is not a total order, do there exist incomparable elements \(x,y\in [n]\) such that \(e(P)/3\le e_{P}(x,y)\le 2e(P)/3\)?
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge2\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A partial order \(\le_P\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive binary relation on \([n]\). Distinct elements \(x,y\) are incomparable if neither \(x\le_P y\) nor \(y\le_P x\); a total order has no incomparable pair. A linear extension is a bijection \(L:[n]\to[n]\) such that \(L(a)<L(b)\) whenever \(a\le_P b\) and \(a\ne b\). Let \(E(P)\) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, \(e(P)=|E(P)|\), and \(e_P(x,y)=|\{L\in E(P):L(x)<L(y)\}|\). Probabilities use the uniform distribution on the entire set \(E(P)\), so \(\Pr[L(x)<L(y)]=e_P(x,y)/e(P)\). The endpoints \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are included. The pair may depend on the full finite order; there is no algorithmic or representation restriction. In the context, width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements, height the largest size of a totally ordered subset, and the cover graph joins \(x,y\) if one is strictly below the other with no element strictly between them. The balance constant is \(\beta(P)=\max_{x\ne y}\min\{e_P(x,y),e_P(y,x)\}/e(P)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite non-total partial order has an incomparable pair with \(e(P)/3\le e_P(x,y)\le2e(P)/3\), or a complete Lean-checked refutation: a finite non-total order for which every incomparable pair violates that closed interval. All extension counts and probabilities must use the full set of linear extensions defined here.
cards.why: Asks for the sharp universal quality of a comparison when sorting with partial information. It connects uncertainty among compatible rankings to an extremal property of every finite partial order.

cards.context:
A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (P)\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (P)\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

cards.title: Exponential growth base of the diagonal Ramsey numbers
cards.formal:
For \(n\ge2\), let \(R(n,n)\) be the least \(N\) such that every red–blue coloring of the edges of \(K_N\) contains a monochromatic \(K_n\). Determine whether the exponential base
\[b=\lim_{n\to\infty} R(n,n)^{1/n}\]
exists. If it exists, determine \(b\) to absolute error at most \(1/100\). If it fails to exist, prove divergence.
cards.definitions:
The complete graph \(K_N\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and one edge for each unordered pair of distinct vertices. The coloring assigns either color to each edge. A monochromatic \(K_n\) is a set of \(n\) vertices whose pairwise edges all have the same color. Finite Ramsey’s theorem makes \(R(n,n)\) a positive finite integer. Set \(b_n=R(n,n)^{1/n}\), taking the positive real root. The elementary bound \(R(n,n)\le\binom{2n-2}{n-1}\) bounds this sequence.

If the limit exists, \(R(n,n)=(b+o(1))^n\). The numerical tolerance applies to the base \(b\) itself. Convergence means that for each real \(\eta>0\) there is a threshold beyond which \(|b_n-b|<\eta\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of one of two outcomes. For convergence, prove that \(b_n\) has a limit, supply an independently specified real \(a\), and prove \(|a-b|\le1/100\). After proving convergence, [certified bounds](definitions.html#numerical-answers) on \(b\) of width at most \(1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. For divergence, prove that \(\liminf b_n<\limsup b_n\), or an equivalent failure of convergence. Narrow bounds on the two limiting extrema alone leave the existence question open.
cards.why: This is the classical quantitative question for two-color graph Ramsey theory. It asks how many vertices force a clique of a given size even in the coloring that avoids it for as long as possible.

cards.title: Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite set \(U\) and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^U\) containing a nonempty member and closed under union, is there an element \(u\in U\) belonging to at least \(|\mathcal F|/2\) members of \(\mathcal F\)?
cards.definitions: The power set \(2^U\) consists of all subsets of U. A family is a set of distinct subsets, with no multiplicities. Closure under union means that A and B in the family imply that their union is also in it. The frequency of u is the integer \(|\{A\in\mathcal F:u\in A\}|\). Empty members are permitted, but the family consisting only of the empty set is excluded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that some element belongs to at least half the members of each permitted union-closed family. To refute the assertion, give one such finite family and prove that every element belongs to strictly fewer than half its members.
cards.why: A basic closure principle for set systems, connected to information inequalities through entropy methods.

cards.formal: For every positive integer \(n\), does there exist a \(4n\)-by-\(4n\) matrix \(H\) whose entries belong to \(\{-1,1\}\) and satisfy \(HH^{\mathsf T}=4nI_{4n}\)?

cards.title: Rota's basis conjecture for matroids
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge1\), every finite matroid of rank n, and every n bases \(B_1,\ldots,B_n\), can the elements in each \(B_i\) be ordered as \(b_{i,1},\ldots,b_{i,n}\) so that, for every j, the set \(\{b_{1,j},\ldots,b_{n,j}\}\) is also a basis?
cards.definitions: A matroid consists of a finite set E and a collection I of independent subsets. The empty set belongs to I; subsets of independent sets are independent; and if A,B are independent with |A|<|B|, some element of B outside A can be added to A while retaining independence. A basis is a maximal independent subset, and the rank is its size, the same for all bases. Input bases may overlap: occurrences in different rows are separately positioned, but a column must contain n distinct independent elements of E. The target concerns arbitrary finite matroids, not only independence of vectors over a field.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that every permitted list of \(n\) bases can be ordered so that all columns are bases. A counterexample must specify a finite matroid and a list of bases for which every choice of row orders has a dependent column.
cards.why: A universal exchange principle for independence systems underlying greedy algorithms and matroid optimization.

cards.title: Asymptotic exponent of the largest cap set
cards.formal:
Determine, to additive accuracy \(0.01\), the exponent
\[\gamma=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_3 M(n)}{n},\]
where \(M(n)\) is the largest size of a subset \(A\subseteq\mathbb F_3^n\) such that \(x+y+z=0\) for \(x,y,z\in A\) implies \(x=y=z\).
cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_3\) has elements 0, 1 and 2 with arithmetic modulo 3; vector addition is coordinatewise. A set satisfying the stated condition is a cap set: it contains no nonconstant three-term arithmetic progression. The logarithm has base 3. Cartesian products of cap sets are cap sets, so \(M(n+m)\ge M(n)M(m)\). Together with \(1\le M(n)\le3^n\), this ensures that the limit exists and equals the supremum of the displayed ratios. For ambient size \(N=3^n\), the maximum is \(N^{\gamma+o(1)}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Output a rational number \(q\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|q-\gamma|\le0.01\). Equivalently, give rational endpoints \(L,U\) and prove \(L\le\gamma\le U\) and \(U-L\le1/50\). Return the rational midpoint \((L+U)/2\).
cards.why: This asks for the quantitative limit of the polynomial method in additive combinatorics, a source of techniques for algorithms and lower bounds.

cards.title: Feige's small-deviation conjecture
cards.formal:
For every positive integer n and independent nonnegative real random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) with \(\mathbb E X_i\le1\), is
\[\mathbb P\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n X_i<\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E X_i+1\right]\ge e^{-1}?\]
cards.definitions: Variables are defined on an arbitrary probability space and may have discrete, continuous or mixed distributions. Nonnegative means almost surely at least zero. Their expectations are finite by the hypotheses; independence is joint independence. The symbol e denotes the base of the natural logarithm. The inequality inside the probability is strict. No bound on the values or variances is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated probability bound in Lean for every permitted independent family. A counterexample must specify the laws, verify independence and the mean bounds, and give probability strictly below \(e^{-1}\) for the displayed strict event.
cards.why: A sharp probability bound for sums with minimal hypotheses, arising in randomized algorithms and probabilistic combinatorics.

cards.title: Nivat's conjecture on rectangular pattern complexity
cards.formal: Let \(A\) be a finite nonempty alphabet and \(c:\mathbb Z^2\to A\) a configuration. If for some positive integers m,n the number \(P_c(m,n)\) of distinct m-by-n rectangular patterns occurring in c is at most mn, must c have a nonzero global period?
cards.definitions: Put \(R_{m,n}=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\). A pattern occurring at translation t is the function on this rectangle that sends z to c(z+t). The number of distinct such functions as \(t\in\mathbb Z^2\) varies is \(P_c(m,n)\). A nonzero global period is a vector \(h\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\) such that c(z+h)=c(z) for every z. Only one period is required, not two linearly independent periods.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that every configuration satisfying the rectangular pattern bound has a nonzero period. A counterexample must exhibit a configuration and a rectangle meeting the bound, and prove that every nonzero translation changes the configuration somewhere.
cards.why: This connects the information in local pictures to global regularity, extending a central theorem about words to two-dimensional symbolic systems.

cards.title: Lonely runner conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(k\ge1\) and all distinct positive integers \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\), does there exist a real number \(t\ge0\) such that
\[\min_{1\le i\le k}\|tv_i\|_{\mathbb R/\mathbb Z}\ge\frac1{k+1}?\]
cards.definitions: Here \(\|x\|_{\mathbb R/\mathbb Z}=\min_{m\in\mathbb Z}|x-m|\) is distance to the nearest integer. Think of k runners of speeds \(v_i\) starting with a stationary observer on a circle of circumference one. The formula asks for a time when every moving runner is at least 1/(k+1) away from that observer around the circle. The number of runners and speeds are unrestricted; no time bound is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that a suitable time exists for every permitted set of speeds. To refute the assertion, give a finite set of distinct positive integer speeds for which at each time some runner is strictly closer than \(1/(k+1)\) to an integer.
cards.why: A simultaneous separation question linking number theory, discrete geometry and graph coloring.

cards.title: Erdős's distinct subset sums conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute real constant \(c>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every increasing sequence of positive integers \(a_1<\cdots<a_n\) with all \(2^n\) subset sums distinct, one has \(a_n\ge c\,2^n\)?
cards.definitions: For \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), its subset sum is \(\sum_{i\in S}a_i\), with the empty sum equal to zero. Distinct subsets must have different sums. The same \(c\) must work for every \(n\) and every admissible sequence. A refutation must make \(a_n/2^n\) arbitrarily small.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated proposition, with all its quantifiers and hypotheses. Verification of finitely many parameter values does not establish the universal assertion.
cards.why: How economically can binary choices be encoded by adding integer weights? This is an extremal counterpart of subset-sum encoding.

benchmark_eligibility.reason: Epoch AI and Thomas Bloom selected this question as open in August 2026. The dated September announcement reports the disproof.
